0.title: The Acts of the Apostles
0.overview:
Acts is not primarily a history of the early church — it is the history of the risen Christ continuing his work through the Spirit he promised and poured out. Luke begins with a deliberate hinge: the “first book” (his Gospel) recorded all that Jesus “began to do and teach.” The operative word is began. What follows in Acts is what Jesus continued — not in the flesh now, but in the power of the Spirit, through the mouths and feet and wounds of his witnesses.

Luke wrote for Theophilus, likely a Roman official being catechised in the faith. But the scope of the narrative exceeds any single reader. Luke traces the gospel’s movement along the spine of the Roman Empire — Jerusalem to Rome, Jewish synagogue to Gentile household, from a frightened upper room to Caesar’s capital. This is not accident; it is Providence. The same God who told Abraham “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” is the God who compels a tentmaker from Tarsus to stand in the Areopagus and announce that the Unknown God has a name.

The Holy Spirit is the true protagonist of Acts. He falls at Pentecost like a sovereign flame. He speaks through Philip on a desert road. He stops Paul from entering Asia. He binds Paul to go to Jerusalem though chains await. He is not a vague presence but a Person with a will — the third Person of the Trinity, sent by the risen Son at the command of the Father, to accomplish the Father’s eternal purpose: a people for his name drawn from every tongue and tribe and nation.

Reformed readers will find in Acts not an argument for the faith but something far more bracing: the sovereignty of God in mission. The gates of hell do not hold. Persecution only scatters the seed further. Imprisonment opens courts to preach. Shipwreck lands an apostle on the right island. Nothing is accidental; everything is appointed. The book ends with Paul in Rome, under house arrest, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” The final words are without hindrance. The empire could chain the man but not the Word.

Who wrote Acts, and when? The same author as Luke’s Gospel: both are addressed to Theophilus, and Acts begins by referring back to the first book (1:1). In several passages the story shifts to “we” (16:10–17; 20:5–28:16), so the writer travelled with Paul, and the early church agreed that he was Luke, the beloved physician (Col 4:14; cf. Philem 24; 2 Tim 4:11). Some date Acts in the 80s. The more likely date is the early 60s: the book ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome after two years (28:30), and says nothing of his death, Nero’s persecution or the fall of Jerusalem, events Luke could hardly have left out had they already happened.

Should churches copy everything in Acts? Acts is history, the record of what God did as the church was founded. What it describes is not automatically a command. A pattern binds us when the rest of the New Testament teaches it, or when Luke shows it as God’s settled way: preaching Christ, baptizing believers, appointing elders, devotion to the apostles’ teaching and prayer. But the casting of lots (1:26), the sharing of all property (4:32), and the signs that marked the apostles (2:43; 5:12) belonged to that unrepeatable time.

Read Acts with your eyes open to the God who is always working — in the upper room, in the council chambers, in the storm, in the jail at midnight. He is the same God today.

1.title: The Promise and the Wait
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, <sup>2</sup>until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. <sup>3</sup>He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. <sup>4</sup>And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me; <sup>5</sup>for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” <sup>6</sup>So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” <sup>7</sup>He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. <sup>8</sup>But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” <sup>9</sup>And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. <sup>10</sup>And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes, <sup>11</sup>and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” <sup>12</sup>Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. <sup>13</sup>And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James. <sup>14</sup>All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. <sup>15</sup>In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said, <sup>16</sup>“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. <sup>17</sup>For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.” <sup>18</sup>(Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. <sup>19</sup>And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.) <sup>20</sup>“For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it’; and ‘Let another take his office.’ <sup>21</sup>So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, <sup>22</sup>beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us—one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.” <sup>23</sup>And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. <sup>24</sup>And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen <sup>25</sup>to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.” <sup>26</sup>And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
1.overview:
Acts is the second volume of Luke’s work, written for the same Theophilus as his Gospel. The Gospel told what Jesus began to do and teach; Acts tells what the risen Jesus goes on doing by his Spirit through his church, as the gospel spreads from Jerusalem to Rome in about thirty years. Chapter 1 is the hinge between the two volumes. The risen Jesus shows himself alive for forty days, tells the apostles to wait for the Holy Spirit, sends them as his witnesses to the end of the earth, and is taken up into heaven, with the promise that he will return in the same way.

The second half shows the church waiting: about a hundred and twenty believers praying together in an upper room. Peter explains from the Psalms that Judas’s place must be filled, so that the Twelve, standing for the renewed Israel, are complete before the Spirit comes, and Matthias is chosen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Risen Lord Sends His Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Luke’s preface, the forty days of proofs and teaching, the command to wait for the Spirit, the apostles’ question about the kingdom and Jesus’ answer, which sets out the mission of the whole book, and the ascension, with the angels’ promise of his return.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascension and the Reign of Christ

The ascension is not the absence of Jesus but his exaltation. The church acts under the authority of its enthroned King. The cloud that received him is the glory cloud of the Old Testament, and Daniel had described the scene from the other side (Daniel 7:13-14). The ascension belongs to the gospel itself: through it Christ sends the Spirit (John 16:7), intercedes for his people (Hebrews 7:25), and carries our nature into the presence of God, where it now permanently is.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Eleven men were given a promise with no date, a mission far beyond their means, and an order to stay put until God moved. They obeyed the hardest part first, which was the waiting.

Now: The church lives in the same interval, between the cloud that took him and the cloud that brings him back. The temptations are unchanged: timetables the Father reserved to himself, or rushing at the work in a strength that was never promised. The command is the same as it was on the hillside: receive, and then witness.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts is the second volume of Luke’s two-part work. The Gospel told what Jesus began to do and teach; Acts tells what he continued to do and teach, from heaven, by the Holy Spirit, through his apostles. It covers about thirty years, from the ascension (around AD 30) to Paul under house arrest in Rome (around AD 62). It tells how the gospel went from Jerusalem to Rome, and how God kept his promise to bless all nations through Abraham’s offspring. Its hero is not Peter or Paul but the risen Lord, working by his Spirit.

In the first book, O Theophilus. The first book is Luke’s Gospel, also written for Theophilus (Luke 1:1–4). His name means friend of God. In the Gospel he is most excellent Theophilus (Luke 1:3), a courtesy Luke gives elsewhere only to the governors Felix and Festus (23:26; 26:25), so he was probably a real man of rank; here the honorific has quietly gone, like a friendship that has moved indoors. The man writing is Luke the doctor, Paul’s travelling companion (Colossians 4:14), who seems to slip into the story himself in chapter 16 with a quiet change from “they” to “we”.

All that Jesus began to do and teach. This sentence gives the whole book its shape: the story did not finish at the tomb, or at the cloud. Volume one was the beginning of the works and words of Jesus; volume two is their continuation, and it is still Jesus doing them. It is the Lord who adds to the church (2:47), pours out the Spirit (2:33), asks why do you persecute me (9:4–5), and opens Lydia’s heart (16:14). The apostles are the instruments. The agent has not changed.

A book with no last page. Paul is in a rented house in Rome, preaching to whoever comes, and Luke simply stops: no verdict, no farewell. Of the theories offered for the abruptness, the simplest is that a book about what Jesus continues to do has no natural last page, because the work has not stopped. If you want to know what the risen Christ is occupied with this morning, the title of this book is the answer.

Until the day when he was taken up. The ascension is where the two books meet. Luke’s Gospel ends with it (Luke 24:50–51) and Acts begins with it: once as the close of the earthly ministry and once as the launch of the heavenly one. (A few early manuscripts lack the words and was carried up into heaven at Luke 24:51; most include them, and the ESV prints them with a note.) What looks like an ending from the ground is, from the throne, a beginning.

Commands through the Holy Spirit. The risen Son, with all authority already granted him, still speaks and acts by the Spirit, as his whole ministry had been carried out in that power (Luke 4:18). So the Spirit about to fall at Pentecost is not a replacement brought in to cover an absence. He is the Spirit by whom Jesus was conceived and anointed, and the church is given the Spirit of Christ, and therefore Christ. When the Spirit lives in a believer, Jesus himself is present with him, not a deputy standing in while he is away. Paul can say in one breath that a Christian has the Spirit of Christ and that Christ is in him (Romans 8:9–10).

To the apostles whom he had chosen. They did not apply. He chose them, after a night of prayer on a mountain (Luke 6:12–13), and their authority in the rest of this book is never their own. Everything they will say with such boldness rests on the fact that they were picked and sent.

Did Luke contradict himself about the ascension? There is a difficulty here worth meeting head-on before it ambushes anyone. Luke’s Gospel appears to run from the empty tomb to the ascension in one unbroken stretch, so that a reader closes Luke 24 with the impression that Jesus went up on Easter evening, while Acts 1 says forty days. But it is the same man writing, with his own first volume at his elbow, quoting its opening line in his second sentence. He is not correcting himself; he is filling in. Luke 24 names events in order without dating them, which is what compressed endings do in every language: the close of a scroll contracts and the opening of the sequel expands. If the two accounts genuinely cancelled each other, the author would have to have forgotten his own ending within a paragraph of citing it.

So how is Jesus still working today? He works chiefly where he promised to: through the gospel preached and believed, through his Spirit giving new birth, through the Scriptures read and obeyed, through prayer, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and through ordinary believers caring for one another. That sounds less dramatic than Acts, but it is the same Lord doing the same work. When a hardened man is converted, when a believer endures grief without letting go of God, when a small church keeps preaching Christ for decades, Jesus is acting from heaven. He does not need you to detect a sensation before you may believe he is at work. His promise is enough: I am with you always (Matthew 28:20).
verseByVerse.note: “The first book” is Luke’s Gospel, also written for Theophilus. “Began” implies that Acts records what Jesus continued to do through his Spirit and his church.

verseByVerse.quote: He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, "you heard from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By many proofs. Many proofs renders tekmēria, a law-court and medical term for evidence that settles a matter, found nowhere else in the New Testament. The careful investigator of Luke 1:3 reaches for the strongest word available, and says what it consisted of: not one apparition in a dim room, but appearances spread across forty days, to individuals and to crowds, on roads and beside a lake and behind locked doors, with conversation, and with food. Jesus let them touch him and showed them his wounds (Luke 24:39; John 20:27), and Paul could list more than five hundred witnesses, most of them still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:5–8).

Ghosts do not get hungry. Staying with them in verse 4 may equally be rendered eating with them, and Luke has already shown us the risen Jesus eating broiled fish while they watched (Luke 24:41–43). Visions do not chew. Whatever happened on the third day happened to a body, and the men who are about to be flogged for saying so had eaten breakfast with the evidence.

Forty days. Forty is a number Scripture uses for seasons of preparation before a new stage: Moses forty days on the mountain before the law was given (Exodus 24:18), Elijah forty days on the road to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), Jesus forty days in the wilderness before his ministry began (Luke 4:2). Now forty days of the risen Lord, before the church is sent.

Speaking about the kingdom of God. Forty days of teaching, and Luke reproduces not one sentence of it, because the rest of the volume is the exposition. What the apostles preach from Pentecost on, that the crucified Nazarene is Lord and Christ and the door stands open to Gentiles, is not something they pieced together afterwards in committee; it is what he told them (28:31). Acts is the transcript: men living on it, and dying on it.

Evidence and surrender. Evidence and surrender are not the same thing. In this very book men will hear the apostolic testimony, find nothing in it they can refute, and stroll away amused (17:32). Others will hear it and tremble and still do nothing but postpone (24:25). Good evidence removes an excuse; it does not manufacture a will. So the honest thing to say to a friend who insists he would believe if only the case were stronger is that the case is already stronger than he thinks, and that for many of us the deepest obstacle lies in the will as much as in the case.

Wait for the promise of the Father. A man with a message that is going to remake the world tells eleven men to go nowhere: to wait. It costs a willing person more than any other command, because it looks like doing nothing. But the promise had to arrive before the mission did. The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, promised through the prophets (Joel 2:28) and by Jesus himself (Luke 24:49; John 14:16–17). They must not begin their mission in their own strength.

Why Jerusalem. He made them wait in the city where they had failed, where Peter had sworn he had never met the man. He kept them still until what they needed was inside them, and then sent them out from the very place of their shame, so that the first sermon of the church would be preached in the same city where its preacher had collapsed.

If the resurrection is so well proved, why do I still have doubts? Because doubt is not only a matter of evidence. Fear, grief, tiredness, temperament and the pressure of a world that assumes the dead stay dead all press on a believer’s mind. Even some who saw the risen Jesus doubted at first (Matthew 28:17; Luke 24:41), and he did not throw them out; he showed them his hands and ate in front of them. So when doubt comes, do not pretend it is not there, and do not treat it as proof that you have no faith. Go back to the evidence the Spirit has preserved for you, the Gospels and 1 Corinthians 15, and pray with the father in Mark 9:24: I believe; help my unbelief. Faith that has looked at its doubts honestly and is still holding on is not weak faith.

Does this mean I should wait for a feeling before I serve God? No. The waiting in this verse was unique. The Spirit had not yet been poured out, and the apostles were told to stay put until a once-for-all event in history arrived. That event has happened. Every believer now has the Spirit (Romans 8:9), and nobody needs to wait for an experience before obeying a clear command, such as loving a neighbour, confessing sin or telling a friend about Christ. What does carry over is the posture: dependence before activity. Pray before you plan. Ask God for help before you start the thing you think you can manage on your own, because the work of God is never done in human strength.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days recalls other periods of preparation in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For John baptized with water. John the Baptist had drawn this contrast himself: I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, and he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16). John’s baptism was outward, a sign of repentance. Water was the picture; the Spirit is the thing pictured. Water goes over a man. The Spirit goes into him.

Baptized with the Holy Spirit. The word baptizō means to immerse, to plunge, to drench. They are about to be plunged into the life of God himself, overwhelmed by the Spirit as a man is overwhelmed by water.

Not many days from now. It turns out to mean about ten; they knew only that it was near. This is very often the shape of Christian waiting: a promise that is certain, a nearness that is real, and a date that is withheld. Ten days is long enough for a man to wonder whether he misheard.

The one who holds the Spirit. John could pour a river over a man; he could not pour God into him. Only God gives God. In the Old Testament it is always the LORD who promises his own Spirit: I will pour out my Spirit (Joel 2:28); I will put my Spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:27). Here the risen Jesus speaks of that outpouring as his own appointment, and Peter will say that he has poured him out (2:33). Jesus speaks of God’s own Spirit as his to send, something no prophet, priest or angel ever dared to say.

Why the phrase is contested. A large and sincere part of the church teaches that baptism with the Holy Spirit is a second work of grace after conversion, usually with tongues as the sign. The case is built almost entirely from this book, and not out of nothing: in Acts the Spirit does sometimes come visibly and later.

The four doors. The difficulty is that Acts is narrative, and narrative tells you what happened, not always what must happen. When the letters take up the phrase directly, they define it the other way: in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). All, not the advanced; and the effect is membership, not promotion. And the four occasions in Acts where the Spirit comes with visible drama are the four boundary-crossings of the mission: Jews (chapter 2), Samaritans (chapter 8), Gentiles (chapter 10), and men still inside John’s baptism (chapter 19). Each is a first, with apostles present as witnesses. Luke is not laying down a pattern for private experience; he is recording how the door was opened, one hinge at a time, and how heaven certified it in public so that nobody could later say the wrong people had been let in.

Where Christians differ: Spirit baptism. Pentecostal and charismatic teaching holds that Spirit baptism is a second blessing after conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues, and that every believer should seek it. This commentary’s view: Pentecost was a unique, unrepeatable event in the history of salvation: the Spirit poured out on the church once for all, as the cross and resurrection happened once for all. For believers since, Spirit baptism happens at conversion: all believers have been baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). We are to be filled with the Spirit continually (Ephesians 5:18), but there is no second-class Christian waiting for a second baptism. Brothers and sisters who hold the other view love Christ and often shame the rest of us by their prayerfulness and zeal, and the difference should be argued from Scripture with warmth, not contempt.

Not second-class, and not content. If the Spirit is what makes a man belong to Christ at all (Romans 8:9), then a believer who has never had an experience he could point to, but trusts Christ, hates his sin and loves the brethren, has the Spirit, whatever his emotional weather has been. There is no unbaptised remainder in the body of Christ. But this same book describes men already filled at Pentecost being filled again in a shaken room (4:31), so fresh and powerful visitations of God are a biblical category, not an embarrassment. To want more of God is right. The label may be wrong; the hunger is not.

Then what does being filled with the Spirit mean? Being baptised with the Spirit is the once-for-all beginning: God joins you to Christ and comes to live in you. Being filled is the ongoing condition of a believer whose life is increasingly yielded to the Spirit’s control, and it can grow and be renewed. Paul’s command is in the present tense, keep on being filled (Ephesians 5:18), and he describes what it looks like: singing to the Lord, giving thanks always, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ (5:19–21). The parallel passage puts the word of Christ dwelling richly in you in the same place (Colossians 3:16). So in practice you seek the Spirit’s fullness by staying close to Scripture, confessing sin quickly, praying, and obeying what you already know. And you may ask: the heavenly Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had come together, they asked him, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" He said to them, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? This is the last question Luke records the apostles putting to Jesus on earth, and it is about politics. After some three years of teaching, a crucifixion, a resurrection and six weeks of instruction on the kingdom of God, what they want to know is whether the occupation is about to end. Many expected the Messiah to restore Israel’s political independence, driving out the Romans and re-establishing David’s kingdom; the two on the Emmaus road had hoped he was the one to redeem Israel (Luke 24:21). And think what they were living in: a foreign garrison in the temple city, a governor who had already executed their master to keep the peace, taxes flowing to a Caesar hailed as the son of a god. Their Scriptures had promised a son of David on a real throne. They were not inventing the expectation. They were asking when the book would come true.

He does not call the question foolish. And Jesus does not tell them the hope is wrong. He has just spent forty days on the kingdom, and he corrects two things only: the timing, and their assumed right to know it.

Times or seasons. Times (chronous) are durations; seasons (kairous) are appointed moments. Both are fixed by the Father by his own authority, and they are not theirs to know. Jesus had said the same of the day of his return: concerning that day or that hour, no one knows (Mark 13:32). Date-setting for the end is forbidden ground.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom and Israel. Dispensationalists (who see God’s purposes for Israel and for the church as two distinct tracks) read this to mean that a political kingdom will be restored to national Israel in a future millennium, and that Jesus only postponed it. This commentary’s view: Jesus redirects their question from a political kingdom to a worldwide mission: his next sentence begins with but (v. 8). The kingdom is restored to Israel as the Messiah reigns from heaven (2:30–36) and gathers a renewed Israel of Jewish and Gentile believers (15:16–17; Galatians 6:16). The Old Testament promises are fulfilled in Christ and his church, and will be completed in the new creation. This is the amillennial view. On the most natural reading of Romans 11:25–26, held here with humility, Paul still hopes for a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ. It does not follow that God is finished with the Jewish people, and the New Testament will not let that conclusion stand (Romans 11:1). A reader can hold the mission of verse 8 with both hands and still expect God to keep every promise he ever made, without needing a chart to show him how.

A throne higher than the one they asked for. The answer arrived within a fortnight and was larger than the question. At Pentecost Peter will tell this city that God has seated David’s son on his throne: Jesus, raised from the dead and exalted to God’s right hand, is the one David called Lord (2:30–36). The kingdom was not postponed on the Mount of Olives. They asked whether the King would take back the land. He was about to take the world.

What does amillennial mean? The word comes from Revelation 20, where Christ reigns for a thousand years. Amillennialists understand that thousand years not as a future golden age on earth after Christ returns, but as the present reign of Christ from heaven, between his first and second comings, while the gospel goes to the nations and the saints who have died reign with him. On this view there is one return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, the world is judged and the new creation begins. The kingdom is already here, because the King is on his throne; and it is not yet complete, because his enemies are still being made his footstool (Psalm 110:1; 1 Corinthians 15:25). Premillennial brothers, many of them faithful and learned, see a further earthly reign after his return; the difference is real, but it is not a difference about whether Jesus is coming. Dispensational believers, many of whom expect Christ to take his church away before a time of great tribulation and later to reign from Jerusalem, are brothers and sisters too, often with a deep love for Scripture and for the Jewish people. The reason for holding the amillennial view is that the apostles themselves read the promise of David’s throne as fulfilled in Jesus’ enthronement in heaven (2:30–36), and that the New Testament speaks of one return, with resurrection and judgement together (John 5:28–29).

The cost of the calendar. The practical edge of the rebuke has cut every generation since. Hardly a decade has passed without someone announcing the date; farms have been sold and careers abandoned, and the morning after has always come, with the faithful poorer and the watching world confirmed in its suspicion. When a teacher tells you he has worked out what the Father reserved to his own authority, you have all the information you need about him, and you need not examine his arithmetic.

A secret, not an evasion. Jesus did not say there is no date. He said the date is not yours. It is a certainty withheld to keep them free. A man who knew the date would spend his life either presuming on the time remaining or paralysed by its shortness. Not knowing, he is left to do the only sane thing, which is to be found faithful whenever it comes. And wanting the date is very often wanting control: managing the future instead of trusting the one who holds it.

Is it wrong to think about the end times at all? No. The New Testament talks about the last things constantly, and always for the same reasons: to give hope to the suffering, to warn the careless, and to keep believers awake and faithful (1 Thessalonians 4:18; 2 Peter 3:11–14). What Jesus forbids is not interest in his return but the attempt to fix its date and to read the calendar out of the newspapers. So study what Scripture plainly teaches: Christ will come personally and visibly, the dead will be raised, all will be judged, and God will make all things new. Hold the details loosely where good Christians differ. And if a book or a preacher leaves you more fascinated by charts than eager to love Christ and your neighbour, put it down.

For worship. The Son himself lived by the Father’s calendar. In John’s Gospel his hour has not yet come, again and again (John 7:30), and then, on the night of the supper, it has (John 13:1); he walked into it without flinching, because the hour of his death was a season the Father had fixed. The same hand that appointed the day of the cross and the morning of the empty tomb holds the day that is still to come. The Father kept every appointment he made with his Son, and he will keep the last one.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected the Messiah to restore Israel’s political independence.

verseByVerse.quote: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will receive power. He answers a question about the calendar with a sentence about a map, and the first word is not an instruction but a gift: you will receive power. Not summon it: receive it. The word is dynamis: ability, strength, the capacity to do what you could not otherwise do. It is not political power, and it is not given for private experience. It is given for witness.

What the power turned out to be. Within three chapters these men are in custody; within seven, Stephen is dead under a pile of stones. The power promised here did not make them untouchable; it made them unstoppable, which is a different and better thing. What Luke actually records after Pentecost is boldness where there had been hiding, clarity where there had been confusion, and joy in places where joy has no business being: a flogging that ends in rejoicing (5:41), a midnight hymn from a prison floor (16:25). A Christian waiting for power to feel like invincibility may miss it when it comes as the ability to speak where speaking costs him something.

My witnesses. Not preachers or strategists, but witnesses. A witness tells what he has seen and heard: we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard (4:20). The word is martyres, and English took it over as martyr, not because the word means dying, but because of what kept happening to the people it described. Luke watches the shift begin (22:20). But keep the courtroom sense first, because it is the one that sets a nervous believer free. A witness is not the barrister. He is not asked to win the case; he is asked one thing: say what you saw. He may be cross-examined by people cleverer than he is, and it does not touch his qualification, because he was there and they were not. Anyone who has been dealt with by Jesus Christ has standing in that witness box, and nobody can take his testimony away from him.

Is this command to every believer, or a promise to the apostles? In the first place it was spoken to the apostles, who would be witnesses of the resurrection in a unique sense, as eyewitnesses (v. 22). But Acts goes on to show ordinary believers telling the good news wherever they went (8:1–4), and Peter tells every Christian to be ready to give a reason for his hope (1 Peter 3:15). The apostles’ eyewitness testimony is now written down; the witness to it belongs to all.

To the end of the earth. The geography doubles as the table of contents. Jerusalem fills chapters 1 to 7; Judea and Samaria, chapters 8 to 12; the end of the earth, chapters 13 to 28, ending in Rome, the centre of the known world. Samaria, the people a Judean might cross the Jordan to avoid, sits not last but second, so that no one could reach the ends of the earth while stepping over the neighbours he despised. And the end of the earth comes from Isaiah’s servant, appointed as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6), which Paul will one day pick up and apply to his own mission (13:47).

The Servant’s light in his witnesses’ hands. In Isaiah the light for the nations is the Servant of the LORD, and Simeon has already named him: a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32). So the end of the earth is not a target the church has set itself. It is the Servant’s own commission, the reach God promised to his Son, and Jesus hands it to his witnesses because the light they carry is himself. The Servant is still shining, through the mouths of those he sends.

What it does not mean. This verse is regularly turned into a method, reach your Jerusalem first, then your Judea, then the world, as though local outreach must be completed before anyone may go abroad. That is not what the sentence is. It is Luke’s map of one historical expansion, not a sequence of permissions, and the book itself refuses the reading: the gospel reaches Samaria because a persecution scattered people who had no strategy at all (8:1–4), and Antioch is evangelised by men whose names Luke does not even record (11:20). God has never waited for a city to be finished before starting on another one.

Does power mean I should expect miracles? The Spirit’s power is promised to every believer, but its main form in this verse is witness: courage, clarity and endurance in speaking of Christ. The signs and wonders in Acts cluster around the apostles and those closely linked to them, and the New Testament calls them the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12), given to confirm the message when it was first delivered (Hebrews 2:3–4). With the foundation laid and the Scriptures complete, we hold that those revelatory and sign gifts have ceased, though many fine Christians disagree. This view, called cessationism, rests on the link the New Testament makes between such signs and the apostles’ foundational witness (Ephesians 2:20); continuationist brothers and sisters, Reformed believers among them, read 1 Corinthians 12–14 as describing gifts for the whole church age, and their case deserves a respectful hearing. But God has not stopped acting. He answers prayer, he heals when he pleases, and he does the greatest miracle of all every time a dead heart is made alive. Expect that power, and pray for it.

So what do I actually do? Start with the people already in your life, and with what Christ has done for you. You do not need a speech, only honesty when someone asks why you go to church or how you got through the year. Pray by name for a few people who do not know Christ, ask for one opportunity this week, and when it comes, say one true thing about Jesus and leave the results with him.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly whether there is a Samaria in your life, a person or a kind of person you would quietly prefer the gospel to skip. The map Jesus drew went straight through the people his disciples least wanted to meet, and he has not redrawn it for you. None of us witnesses as faithfully as we should; the Servant obeyed the Father perfectly in our place, so failure here does not undo your standing, and his Spirit sends you out again.

For worship. He spoke of the end of the earth to eleven provincials with no money and no standing, as already settled. That is the confidence of a King who has bought what he is about to claim. The nations were his inheritance before a single witness set out (Psalm 2:8), and the Spirit he promised has carried his name into languages Luke never heard of and as far as the reader of this page.
verseByVerse.note: This verse outlines the book: Jerusalem (chs 1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–12), and the end of the earth (13–28).

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were looking on. Luke’s care as a reporter shows: they did not infer it from an empty hillside; they watched it happen. It was not a fading or a dissolving. He was lifted, a cloud came between, and the hillside was one man emptier. The ascension was a real, bodily event, and it marks his exaltation to the right hand of the Father, where he reigns over all things (2:33; Ephesians 1:20–22) and intercedes for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

A cloud took him. The cloud is the detail everything turns on, and it is not weather. All through Israel’s Scriptures the cloud is where God is pleased to be visible without being looked at. It leads Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21), wraps Sinai (Exodus 19:16), fills the tabernacle and the temple so that no one can stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11), and overshadows the mount of transfiguration (Luke 9:34–35). When a cloud takes a man out of sight in this literature, he has not gone behind a weather front. He has gone inside the glory. That presence was never safe for sinners to approach (Exodus 19:12). Jesus is received into it as into his own home, and he enters as our representative, carrying our nature where no sinner could stand.

The underside of a coronation. The scene has to be read from both ends. From the hillside it is a departure, and it looks like loss. From the other side of the cloud it is an arrival, and Daniel had described it centuries before: one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, presented before the Ancient of Days, and given dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). In Daniel he is not coming down to earth; he is coming up to the throne. The disciples are watching the underside of a coronation. And the psalm the apostles quote more than any other says what happens when he gets there: sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool (Psalm 110:1). Peter will preach it within a fortnight (2:34–35).

Two men stood by them in white robes. Angels, as at the tomb (Luke 24:4): the same kind of messengers explain the empty grave and the empty sky.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that heaven is a distance measurable in miles above Jerusalem, as if Jesus flew upward through space. That mistakes a sign for a map. He went up because a body must leave visibly if witnesses are to testify that it left, and because upward is what exaltation looks like to creatures who walk about on the ground. The direction was for their eyes. The destination was the throne.

He took his body with him. There is at this moment, in the presence of God, a human being, with hands, with a voice, with a memory of Nazareth and of nails, and he is not visiting. The nature he assumed in the womb of a Galilean girl he has never laid down and never will. The Reformed churches have insisted on care here: a real body is somewhere, and being somewhere means not being everywhere, so when Christ promises to be with his people always he is with them by his Spirit and in his deity, not by his flesh being spread thin across the world. Lutheran Christians take a different line on that point, but the disagreement is not about whether Christ is truly present with his church. The pastoral weight of it belongs to everyone. Our nature is not a costume he wore for thirty years; it has been carried into the immediate presence of God and seated there.

Why did Jesus have to leave? Wouldn’t it be better if he were still here? Jesus himself said no: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you (John 16:7). While he walked in Galilee, he could be in only one village at a time. Now, by his Spirit, he is present with every believer in every place at once. And his going was not retirement but enthronement: from the Father’s right hand he rules history for the good of his church, sends the Spirit, and prays for his people. You are not worse off than the disciples who could see him. In one way you are better placed, because the Spirit they had to wait ten days for has been given to you.

What is Jesus doing now? He is reigning, with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), working all things toward the day his enemies are put under his feet. He is interceding: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), so that at this moment a man who knows your name is praying for you in the presence of God. He is preparing a place for his people (John 14:2–3). He is building his church through the gospel. And he is waiting, with perfect patience, for the day the Father has fixed, when he will come back.

On a Tuesday. When you pray, remember who is on the other end: a man in our nature at the Father’s right hand, who knows tiredness, hunger and grief from the inside. Bring him the small things as well as the large.
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s glorious presence.

parallels.desc: two men in dazzling apparel

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? Angels have a way of asking questions that are really instructions. The men are not doing anything wrong; they are doing something finished. He has gone. The sky has nothing further to show them, and the next thing God has for them is at the bottom of the hill. And they are addressed as men of Galilee, which is not a compliment in Jerusalem. It is the label that will be thrown at Peter beside a fire and at the whole company at Pentecost (2:7). Provincials with an accent. Heaven uses the word without a flicker of apology, and then tells these particular provincials that the next act of world history runs through them.

This Jesus. The same Jesus, personally: not a successor or a spirit distinct from the man. The one they had walked the roads with is the one who will return.

In the same way. The anchor of Christian hope: the return will match the ascension. He left personally, and a person will come back: not an influence, not a movement, not an era of improved conditions. He left bodily, and a body will return: the same body, the same man, the same face. He left visibly, and the world will not be informed of the return; it will see it, every eye (Revelation 1:7). And he left in a cloud, which is where Daniel had said the Son of Man belonged, and where Jesus said he would be seen coming with power and great glory (Matthew 24:30).

What the phrase rules out. That phrase rules out the teaching that Christ already returned invisibly, whether in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 or at some private date since. Something did happen in AD 70, as Jesus said it would; but the angels say: like that. It equally rules out the reduction of the second coming to a figure of speech for death, or for the gradual improvement of the human race. The Christian expectation is not that things will get better. It is that a particular man will arrive.

Where Christians differ: a secret rapture? Some teach that Christ will return secretly to remove believers before a tribulation (a time of great distress before the end), then visibly later. This commentary’s view: the angels promise one return, in the same way he went: visible and bodily. The New Testament knows one second coming, at which believers are gathered, the dead raised, and the world judged (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). No secret rapture.

But doesn’t 1 Thessalonians 4 speak of being caught up? It does, and it is anything but secret: a cry of command, the voice of an archangel, the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). It is hard to imagine a noisier passage in the Bible. Paul says believers will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, and the word for meet was used of citizens going out of a city to greet an arriving king and escort him back in. The picture is not of the church being taken away while the world carries on, but of his people going out to welcome him as he comes. The same chapter flows straight into the day of the Lord (5:1–3). One coming, seen by all, with his people gathered to him. Many faithful Christians were taught to expect a rapture before a great tribulation, and they often long for his appearing more eagerly than the rest of us; the disagreement is over how to read these texts, not over whether he is coming.

A docket that has been kept. This is the sentence a great many Christians have died holding. Measure it against what is actually wrong with the world. Someone who was harmed as a child has watched the man who did it live comfortably into old age and die unaccused. Injustices are not merely unpunished; whole categories of them are now unrecoverable, the witnesses dead, the record lost. To all of it this sentence says: there is a date, and on that date the one who was in the room the whole time will come back in the open, and nothing will be left buried. That is not a poetic way of saying things will feel better eventually; it is a man on a cloud, and a docket that has been kept.

It has been two thousand years. Is he really coming? Yes, and the delay is not forgetfulness. Peter met this very objection in his own lifetime, from scoffers who said that everything goes on as it always has. His answer was that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and that the Lord is not slow as some count slowness, but patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:3–9). Every year the world has had since Olivet is a year of mercy, in which more people have been brought to repentance. The waiting is long by our clocks. It is not long by his, and it is not empty.

How do I live ready without being anxious? Readiness in the New Testament is not nervous watching of the sky; it is faithful work and trust in Christ. The servants in Jesus’ parables are ready because they are doing what their master told them, not because they have guessed the hour (Luke 12:42–43). If you belong to Christ, his coming is not a threat hanging over you but the arrival of your Saviour, and there is no condemnation waiting for you (Romans 8:1). So keep short accounts with God, love the people around you, do your ordinary work well, and say each night, as the church has said from the beginning, come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20).

For worship. The Lord who went up from Olivet will come again in glory, not as a rumour or a mood but as himself, with the same scarred hands that blessed his disciples as he left. He went in a cloud, attended by angels, with no one but eleven men to watch; he will come with the clouds, and the whole world will watch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Waiting Church and the Reconstituted Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church waits and prays in an upper room: the eleven, the women, Mary and Jesus’ brothers, about a hundred and twenty in all. Peter explains from the Psalms what has become of Judas and why his office must be filled, and after prayer the lot falls on Matthias, who is added to the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Twelve and Their Significance

Filling the Twelve before Pentecost is deliberate. The Twelve answer to the twelve tribes and stand for the restored people of God (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30). The qualifications Peter states (v. 22) make the apostles a closed group anchored in history, the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and foundations are laid once. Judas stands as the sober warning at the door of the book: he was numbered among them and trusted with the money, and nearness to Jesus did not save him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A hundred and twenty people with no standing prayed together for ten days, settled a painful question from Scripture, and appointed a man who is never mentioned again.

Now: The church still prepares for what God intends to do in the same way: gathered, praying, working from the text, willing to be led, and made up very largely of people whose names will appear nowhere.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They returned to Jerusalem. It is an act of obedience with a cost: Jerusalem was the last place on earth a follower of the executed Nazarene had any business being. Jesus had told them to stay there (v. 4), and so they went back into it. Luke’s Gospel adds that they went back with great joy (Luke 24:52).

From the mount called Olivet. The Mount of Olives rises east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley; Luke 24:50 places the ascension near Bethany, on its eastern slope. Zechariah had foretold the day when the LORD’s feet would stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4), and the King left the world from that same hill.

A Sabbath day’s journey away. A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance the rabbis permitted on the day of rest, about two thousand cubits, roughly a kilometre (compare Exodus 16:29), probably kept because it is how the people who were there described the distance.

The eleven by name. Luke writes out every name, matching the list in his Gospel (Luke 6:14–16), minus Judas Iscariot. A movement staking everything on the claim that certain men saw a dead man alive has to be able to say who they were, and Luke names them, in a city where they could be found and questioned. John has moved up beside Peter, because those two are about to work as a pair through the opening chapters (3:1; 4:13; 8:14).

Judas the son of James. Judas the son of James is not Iscariot, and Luke says so by naming the father; he is probably Thaddaeus in the other lists. A church inventing its own records would hardly saddle itself with a second Judas.

Simon the Zealot and Matthew. Simon bore a name that points to zeal for the law, and possibly to the movement that believed the answer to Rome was a knife. Sitting in the same small room is Matthew, who had made his living collecting Rome’s money from his own people. If Simon’s zeal was of that fiercer kind, those two were natural enemies: the collaborator and the man who thought collaborators traitors to God. Now they are praying together. What held them was not a compromise between their causes but a Lord who had died for them both, and who had shown each of them that the thing he was trying to save the nation from was smaller than the thing he himself had been saved from.

The upper room. Probably a borrowed space up the stairs of a Jerusalem house, perhaps the room of the Passover, or the house of Mary the mother of John Mark (12:12). What matters is the scale. The risen Lord of heaven and earth has been enthroned at the right hand of God, and his visible operation in Jerusalem is a borrowed room upstairs with about a hundred and twenty people in it, most of whom have no money and one of whom is still living down the worst night of his life. Everything in this book grows from that room.

What if my church contains people whose politics I find hard to bear? Then you are in the church Jesus built. He deliberately chose a tax collector and a zealot and put them in the same company, not by asking them to stop caring about the world but by giving them a Lord who mattered more than their causes. You may still hold your convictions, and some political questions are moral questions on which Scripture speaks. But the person across the aisle who votes differently is, if he trusts Christ, your brother for eternity, and the election will be forgotten long before he is. Pray with him. Eat with him. Let the gospel be louder in your conversation than the news, and you will find, as Matthew and Simon did, that you have more in common than you had in conflict.
verseByVerse.note: A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance the traditions allowed on the Sabbath, a little over half a mile. The list of eleven matches the Gospels’ lists; Judas the son of James is probably Thaddaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
With one accord. Luke’s signature adverb for the early church: homothymadon, of one mind and one impulse together (2:46; 4:24; 5:12). And the verb (proskarterountes) is continuous: they were devoting themselves to prayer, the way a man keeps at something he cannot do without. They had been given a promise with no date attached, and the only work available to them was asking.

Together with the women. These are probably the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee, supported him from their own means and witnessed the cross and the empty tomb (Luke 8:2–3; 23:49; 24:10). Women, whose word carried little weight in a court, had been the last at the cross, the first at the tomb, and are now in the founding prayer meeting of the Christian church. Someone constructing a respectable origin story in the first century would hardly have arranged it that way.

And Mary the mother of Jesus. Mary is there too, and this is the last time she is named in the New Testament. Scripture leaves her not on a platform, and not being asked for anything, but praying in a crowded room with a hundred and nineteen other people, waiting for the Holy Spirit like everyone else. She is blessed among women, and the church should not be so nervous of the abuse that it forgets the text; but she is honoured as one of the redeemed, not as a channel of redemption. Her son had said as much when a woman in a crowd blessed the womb that bore him and he answered, blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11:27–28). Here she is doing exactly that, which is an honourable place to leave her.

Should Christians pray to Mary? No. Scripture never shows a believer praying to Mary or to any departed saint, and it gives a reason why we need not: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Mary herself called God her Saviour (Luke 1:47), which means she needed saving like the rest of us. The right way to honour her is the way the Bible does: to call her blessed, to imitate her faith and humility, let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38), and to do what she told the servants at Cana, do whatever he tells you (John 2:5). Her last recorded words in the Gospels turn every eye to her Son, and so should ours.

And his brothers. These are the men who had come to collect him because they thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), who did not believe in him (John 7:5). And now they are in the prayer meeting. One of them, James, will be leading the Jerusalem church within a few years, giving the decisive judgement at the council that settles the Gentile question (15:13–19). His letter calls his own elder brother Lord and himself his servant, as Jude’s does. Whatever else happened in the forty days, this happened: then he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7).

Who were these brothers? The natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus (Matthew 13:55–56); once unbelieving (John 7:5), they are now among the praying disciples. (See Luke 8:19 for the fuller answer.)

For the one praying for an unbelieving relative. No formula here, but this: it took years. Mary lived in a house where her other sons thought her firstborn was mad, with no assurance given; what she was given, eventually, was a room with all of them in it. The case is never closed while a man is alive; the risen Christ went looking for one of them personally. That is not a promise that every son and every brother will come. It is a plain fact that the hardest cases in the New Testament include the ones who had shared a childhood with him, and they came.

About a hundred and twenty. A strikingly modest number set against the end of the earth: ten times twelve, perhaps a quiet hint of a renewed Israel. Within a chapter it will be three thousand more.

Why pray, if God has already promised? Because the promise is the reason to pray, not a reason to stop. The disciples knew the Spirit was coming; Jesus had said so. And they spent the ten days asking for exactly that. Daniel did the same when he read in Jeremiah that the exile would last seventy years: he did not sit back, he turned to God in prayer (Daniel 9:2–3). God has chosen to bring about his purposes through the prayers of his people, so that when the answer comes they know it came from him. Pray most confidently for what God has promised: the spread of the gospel, the holiness of his church, the coming of his kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Most prayer meetings are small, unglamorous and easy to skip. Go to yours; the promised Spirit came on a church that was praying.

For worship. The boy Jesus was once submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51); now the order of that house has been turned the right way up. The mother is a disciple on her knees, the brothers are servants waiting on his word, and the son who once did as he was told in a carpenter’s home is the Lord of heaven about to pour out what he promised. The grace that reached into that household does not stop at the door of ours.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ brothers, who had not believed during his ministry, are now among the believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Scripture had to be fulfilled. The last time Luke showed us Peter speaking about Jesus in Jerusalem, he was swearing at a fire that he had never met the man. Now he is opening the Scriptures on the hardest subject the young church has, the treachery of one of their own. This is what restoration looks like a few weeks later (John 21:15–19): not a man excused, but a man working. Had to (edei) is the language of divine necessity, the same word Jesus used of his own suffering (Luke 24:26). Even the betrayal had been foretold. God was not surprised.

In the flow. Peter’s speech (vv. 16–22) is the only scene Luke places between the ascension and Pentecost, and it answers one question: what is to be done about the hole Judas left? Before the Spirit comes and the witness begins in Jerusalem (v. 8), the Twelve must be twelve again, because they stand for the renewed Israel the Messiah is gathering (Luke 22:30). The speech moves from Scripture fulfilled (v. 16) to Scripture obeyed (vv. 20–22).

By the mouth of David. The double authorship is stated without any awkwardness: the Spirit spoke, and he spoke by the mouth of David. Not through David as a hollow pipe: David’s grief at a friend who turned on him, and the Holy Spirit speaking in all of it. Scripture has a divine author and a human author (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21), and that is how these men understood the book they were reading. It is why Peter can treat a thousand-year-old lament as an instruction for a decision this week.

A guide. The man who knew the garden because he had prayed in it with Jesus led the soldiers there with torches.

If God planned it, was Judas to blame? Had to be raises the question that has troubled thoughtful readers ever since, and it should be met plainly: if Scripture had to be fulfilled, was Judas ever free to do otherwise, and is God then the author of the worst act in human history? Luke does not dodge this, and he will state both halves of the answer twice more in the next few chapters, very starkly. At Pentecost Peter says Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath says you crucified and killed him (2:23). In a prayer meeting a few weeks later the church says that Herod and Pilate and the nations gathered to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (4:27–28). The Bible never treats these as two positions to be chosen between. It puts them in one sentence.

God did not put the greed there. What Scripture never says is that God implanted the sin. Judas was not overpowered. He was a thief with his hand in the common purse long before he went to the priests (John 12:6), and what he did in the end was exactly what he had been doing in small amounts for years, which is to convert Jesus into money. He was not a man forced into a role; he was a man who found a buyer. God did not implant the appetite, and he did not compel the transaction. He wove a free and filthy act into a purpose that the man committing it knew nothing about. That is not tyranny. It is something more frightening and more reassuring: there is no evil so deliberate that it can get outside the plan of God, and no evil so useful to that plan that the man doing it is thereby excused. The Westminster Confession says it with care: God ordains whatever comes to pass, yet so that he is not the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creature (Westminster 3.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1 says the same).

Mercy held out to the last. And no one may say he was never given a chance. He had some three years of it. His feet were washed by the man he had already agreed to sell. He was warned in a way that let him withdraw without public exposure, and was called friend in the garden with the kiss still wet on the face. Whatever mystery sits behind the word predestined, it does not sit between Judas and a door he wanted to go through.

Numbered among us. Judas was not an outsider who got in. He was on the list. He was sent out to preach with the rest and trusted with the money. When Jesus said at the table that one of them would betray him, the eleven did not turn on Judas; each asked, is it I (Mark 14:19). Three years closer to Jesus than almost anyone has ever been, and it did not save him. He was a real apostle outwardly, and yet he was never truly Christ’s (John 6:70; 17:12). Office and outward service are not proof of salvation: on that day many will say, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and he will say, I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). Proximity is not possession.

Judas is not your mirror. That sentence has frightened tender consciences, so one thing must be added. Judas is not a mirror for the believer who is afraid he loves Christ too little. Judas was never afraid of that for a moment. He did not want Christ and fear he was failing him; he wanted what Christ could be turned into, and when the exchange rate disappointed him he cashed out. A man who is anxious because he longs to love Jesus more than he does has already given the evidence that Judas never gave in all those years of standing closer than anyone.

How do I examine myself without falling into despair? Scripture tells us to examine ourselves (2 Corinthians 13:5), but it never tells us to look only at ourselves. Ask simple questions. Am I trusting Christ, not my record, for my acceptance with God? Do I hate my sin and want to be rid of it, even when I fail? Do I love God’s word and God’s people, however weakly? Those are the marks of the Spirit’s work. Then look away from yourself to Christ, because assurance grows by looking at him, not by staring at your own pulse. If you find no faith at all, the answer is not to despair but to come to him now: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: (Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man acquired a field. These two verses are most likely Luke talking, not Peter. Peter’s hearers would not have said in their own language; Luke has stepped out of the speech, and many English Bibles rightly put it in brackets.

Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood. A story invented at a distance would hardly preserve the local Aramaic name of a piece of ground still in use, which any reader in Jerusalem could have gone and looked at. Legends do not usually leave a forwarding address. It was called Field of Blood because it was bought with blood money, and because of the bloody death that took place there. Tradition places it in the Hinnom valley south of Jerusalem, the valley whose name became Gehenna, the word Jesus used for hell.

Who bought the field? Two apparent collisions with Matthew’s account have to be faced, and they come apart more easily than their reputation suggests, though what follows is a likely harmonisation rather than a proof. The first is the purchase. Matthew says the chief priests took the returned silver and bought the field, because it was blood money and could not go into the treasury (Matthew 27:3–8); Luke says Judas acquired it with the reward of his wickedness. But that is natural speech about a dead man’s money. The silver was legally his; the priests would not touch it for sacred use and could not simply return it to a corpse, so it was spent on his account, and the ground went down under his name. Luke is not picturing a man house-hunting between the betrayal and the rope. He is telling you whose money paid for it, which is precisely why the city attached his crime to the deed and called the place what it called it.

Falling headlong. The second is the death itself. Matthew says he hanged himself; Luke says he fell headlong and burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. Read as two claims about the same instant they are irreconcilable, and read as two moments in one afternoon they are not. A body left hanging does not stay hanging indefinitely, and the ravine country south of Jerusalem is rock. The rope gives, or the branch does, or the corpse comes down of its own weight in the heat, and what is found at the bottom is what Luke describes, with a doctor’s plainness. Matthew tells you what Judas did. Luke tells you what was found, and why the field got the name it kept. On this reading neither writer contradicts the other; they are standing at different ends of the same terrible day. Not every detail can be recovered now, and believers hold both accounts true while admitting that some questions remain open.

The blood the field was named for. Matthew records that Judas came back to the priests saying he had betrayed innocent blood, and that they counted the silver as the price of blood (Matthew 27:4–6). The blood in Akeldama is first of all the blood of Jesus, priced and sold. The blood that could buy a traitor only a field of shame is the blood with which God obtained the church (20:28). The one innocent man in the whole transaction was led outside the city walls and paid in full the wages Judas earned, for everyone who will come to him. The field of blood is a grave; the blood of Christ is a purchase.

What it does not mean. This passage is read by people carrying something heavy. Judas is not in Scripture as a case study in suicide, and he must not be used as one. What is said about him is said about a man who sold the Son of God for money and never once repented of the wanting, only of the outcome. The manner of his death is reported; it is not what he is condemned for. A reader who has buried someone who took their own life, a son, a wife, a friend who was in agony and could not see a morning, is not looking at that person’s portrait in these verses, and anyone who hands it to them as one has misread the passage badly. Despair and treachery are not the same sin, and the God who reads hearts has never confused them.

Can a Christian who takes his own life be saved? Suicide is a grave sin, the taking of a life God gave, and no one should ever think of it as a way out. But Scripture nowhere calls it the unforgivable sin, and salvation does not depend on the state of a person’s mind in his last moment. It depends on Christ, who saves to the uttermost those who come to God through him, and from whose hand no one can snatch his sheep (John 10:28). A true believer overwhelmed by illness or despair is still covered by the blood that covered all his sins. If you are grieving such a loss, bring your grief and your questions to God and to your pastor. If you are thinking of ending your life yourself, please tell someone today, a pastor, a doctor, a friend, and let them help you carry what you cannot carry alone.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you are tempted to trade Christ for: a promotion, a relationship, a reputation, a comfortable silence when you should speak. You were bought with blood worth more than all of them.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought the field; the two accounts are often harmonised as a hanging followed by a fall. Akeldama is Aramaic.

verseByVerse.quote: "For it is written in the Book of Psalms, 'May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it'; and 'Let another take his office.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Written in the Book of Psalms. Peter’s warrant is two lines of Hebrew poetry, and how he uses them shows how the first Christians read their Bible. Psalm 69 is David hunted and hated, drowning in trouble, with the scorn of those who reproach God falling on him. It is among the psalms most often applied to Jesus (John 2:17; 15:25; Romans 15:3). Psalm 109 is David betrayed by a man he had loved, who repaid friendship with accusation. Neither psalm names Judas; both are the cry of the Lord’s anointed under treachery. If David’s sufferings were the shadow, then the greater Son of David betrayed by a table companion is the substance, and if the righteous sufferer is Christ, his chief enemy is the man who sold him.

May his camp become desolate. He alters one thing, openly. The psalm has their camp and their tents, plural, a whole party of enemies (Psalm 69:25); Peter makes it singular, his camp. He is not misquoting but narrowing a corporate judgement onto the representative case. The word (epaulis) means a homestead. The field of blood is the camp, and no one would ever live there.

Let another take his office. The second citation, Psalm 109:8, is the operative one. The word behind office (episkopē) means oversight, the position of responsibility, and it is the word that would later give the church its term for an overseer, or bishop. Peter reads it as a mandate, not a comment. The seat is not abolished by the man who disgraced it; it is vacated, and it is to be filled.

The office outlived the man. This steadies people who have watched a leader fall. Treachery at the top did not destroy the apostolate. When someone trusted is found to be a fraud, the temptation is to conclude that the whole thing was a fraud, or that the position should quietly be left empty. Peter’s answer is to open the Scriptures and appoint a successor. The work is bigger than the worst man who ever did it.

Does this mean every psalm is about Jesus? Not in the sense that every line is a coded prediction. Read each psalm first as what it is: a real prayer of a real believer, often David, in a real situation. Then ask how it fits into the larger story. Some psalms speak directly of the coming King (Psalms 2 and 110). Many are the prayers of the anointed king, and Christ is the King who prays them most truly. Others are the prayers of God’s people, and we pray them in Christ, with him as our representative. Some lines, such as David’s confessions of sin in Psalm 51, Jesus could not pray of himself, though he bore those sins for us. Following the apostles, you will find the Psalms lead you to Christ again and again.

The prayers that ask God to ruin somebody. These are the imprecatory psalms, prayers that call down God’s judgement on an enemy. Anyone who turns up Psalm 109 to check the reference will find that the line immediately after the one Peter quotes asks that the man’s children be fatherless and his wife a widow. How is a Christian, who has been told to pray for those who persecute him, supposed to hold a book that contains prayers like that?

Three things that make it bearable. First, an imprecation is the opposite of vengeance, not an instance of it. A man who prays that God will judge his enemy has handed the matter to a court and taken his own hands off it. Paul makes the same move: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:19). The alternative to the imprecatory psalm is not gentleness; it is the knife. Second, the enemies in view are not personal irritants but the settled adversaries of God’s anointed and God’s purpose, which is why Peter can apply the psalm to a man who sold the Son of God, not to a neighbour who is difficult about the boundary hedge. And third, these prayers are ultimately in the mouth of Christ himself, the righteous sufferer the psalms were describing all along, and he is the one who has the right to ask for judgement and the one who on a cross asked for the opposite.

A caution and a permission. There is a caution here, and a permission. The caution is that no Christian may use these psalms as ammunition for a grudge; the moment a man prays desolation on someone who has merely wounded his pride, he has stopped praying and started cursing. The permission is for the other reader, the one who has been genuinely and terribly wronged, who has discovered that he wants justice with an intensity that frightens him, and who has concluded that wanting it makes him a bad Christian. It does not. Scripture has given him words for that, and the words are prayers, which means the right destination for the fiercest thing in him was never the offender, and never the polite suppression of it either, but God.

For worship. One office in this story will never fall vacant. Judas left his post, and another had to take it; but the Righteous Sufferer of the Psalms holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues for ever (Hebrews 7:24). No one will ever have to stand up in a room and propose his successor.

parallels.desc: may their camp be a desolation
may another take his office

verseByVerse.quote: So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us — one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the men who have accompanied us. Peter’s job description is remarkably narrow: the man must have been with them from John’s baptism to the ascension, and must have seen the risen Lord. Nothing about gifting or eloquence. The apostolic office is not a set of abilities. It is a position in history.

The ones who stayed. Peter assumes there is more than one such man, and two are produced: for some three years there had been people following Jesus from the Jordan to Olivet, through the crowds and the opposition and the night of the arrest, whose names appear nowhere in any Gospel. They were there when almost everyone walked away (John 6:66). And the qualification for the highest office the church would ever have turned out to be precisely the thing they had been doing unnoticed the entire time, which was staying.

A witness to his resurrection. The office in one phrase: not a visionary or the holder of a private revelation, but a man under oath about an event. Paul argues his own apostleship the same way: have I not seen Jesus our Lord? (1 Corinthians 9:1). Everything the church has to say begins with a factual claim about a particular Sunday, and the Twelve exist to say they were there.

Are there apostles today? In the wider sense of a sent one, a pioneering missionary, the New Testament allows the word (14:14; 2 Corinthians 8:23), and that ministry is badly needed; in the sense of the office Peter is filling here, no. (See 1 Corinthians 9:1 for the fuller answer.)

A foundation is laid once. The office Peter is filling is closed by the very terms he has just read out. Nobody alive has accompanied Jesus from John’s baptism to the ascension, or seen the risen Christ in the way this qualification demands. A builder who keeps returning to lay more foundation has stopped building.
