Where Christians differ: apostolic succession. Roman Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican teaching hold that bishops today are successors of the apostles, with their authority passed down. This commentary’s view: by these qualifications, no one after the first generation could be an apostle in this sense. Paul was the exception, as one who saw the risen Lord, as to one untimely born (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles laid the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Their authority continues today not in successors but in their writings, the New Testament. When James was killed (12:2), no replacement was chosen.

A test any believer can apply. This gives an ordinary Christian a workable test: not what a man calls himself; it is what he claims his title entitles him to. If a leader means that he plants churches, no harm is done. If he means that his word carries the weight the apostles’ words carried, that he may add to Scripture, or bind a conscience where Scripture has not, or require obedience that is not accountable to the text, then he is claiming something Peter’s own criteria exclude him from, and the humblest believer in the room has the right to say so with a Bible open at this page.

So do pastors and elders have any authority today? Yes, but it is a derived and limited authority, not an apostolic one. Elders are given by Christ to shepherd and oversee his flock (20:28; 1 Peter 5:1–3), and believers are told to obey their leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over souls (Hebrews 13:17). But their authority is the authority of the word they teach. They may not invent doctrine, bind consciences beyond Scripture, or lord it over the flock. Christians differ on the best form of church government, with elders, bishops or congregations holding different roles, and each tradition makes its case from Scripture. All agree that every leader is under the word, accountable for how he handles it, and answerable to the Chief Shepherd.

The comfort of a closed door. Peter measures the office from the baptism of John to the day the Lord Jesus was taken up. The apostles are defined entirely by his life. Their office closed because his work had closed: he died once for sins, was raised never to die again (Romans 6:9), and ascended once to the right hand of God. There is nothing more to see, and so no more need of eyewitnesses. Nobody is going to arrive with a revelation that changes the terms, because nobody is going to arrive with a further work of Christ to report.

On a Tuesday. When you open the New Testament, you are hearing the apostles. Before you take up a confident new teaching, ask whether it agrees with what the eyewitnesses wrote.

verseByVerse.quote: And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They put forward two. The church does its part, choosing qualified candidates. Joseph carries three names, Hebrew, family and Latin: the ordinary signature of a Jew who moved easily in the wider world of the empire. Both men clear the bar Peter has just set. Of Matthias nothing more is known from Scripture, and later traditions about where he preached are unreliable.

Then one of them is not chosen. Barsabbas was not passed over for a defect, or a sin. He was found fit, publicly, and then he lost, in front of a hundred and twenty people, and had to walk home through Jerusalem knowing that the man beside him was now one of the Twelve and he was not.

The taste of being passed over. It is not the same as failure, which at least gives you something to work on. This is being genuinely good enough, being told so, and watching it go elsewhere: the post you had trained for and he had not; the ministry you would plainly have done well, handed to someone whose only advantage was that God chose him. It is a lonely grief, because there is nobody to blame and therefore nothing to do with it.

No cheap comfort. Scripture does not say God had something better in mind for Barsabbas, or that everything worked out. It says he was not chosen, and then it never mentions him again. Sometimes faithfulness has to be carried on without an explanation, and pretending otherwise only adds a lie to a disappointment.

He stayed. There is no schism and no faction of the aggrieved. The natural reading is that he was still among the believers all together in one place when the Spirit fell a few days later (2:1). Whatever it cost him, nothing suggests he walked away.

What the lot could not take. What qualified him was years with Jesus and the risen Lord seen with his own eyes. The lot decided an office; it could not touch that. Jesus had once told disciples returning elated from a mission not to rejoice that the spirits were subject to them, but that their names were written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Barsabbas walked home without the apostleship. He did not walk home without Christ.

Is it wrong to want a position of service, or to put myself forward? No. Paul says that if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task (1 Timothy 3:1), and both these men allowed their names to go forward. Wanting to serve Christ in a particular way is not pride, provided the desire is held open-handed. Test it: would you be glad to see someone else chosen, and keep serving gladly in the background? Are you willing for the church to say no? Let others weigh your gifts and character, pray, and accept the outcome as from the Lord. The aim is not the title but the glory of Christ, and he can be glorified as much by the one who was not chosen as by the one who was.

For worship. Our Lord knows the taste of this from the inside. A few weeks earlier, in the same city, a crowd had been offered a choice between two men, and it asked for Barabbas and shouted that Jesus should be crucified (Luke 23:18–21). He was despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3). So there is no believer who has watched the honour go elsewhere whom he cannot understand, and none whom he will ever pass over. The one man the world refused to choose is the one who chose us, and his choosing never falls on anyone by accident.

parallels.desc: Judas called Barsabbas

verseByVerse.quote: And they prayed and said, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They prayed. The prayer is short, with no preamble: they tell God what they cannot do, ask him to do it, and stop.

Who know the hearts of all. Kardiognōstēs, heart-knower, appears only here and at 15:8, and both times the church is trying to decide who truly belongs: two candidates identical from the outside, and a house full of Gentiles nobody expected God to accept. Both times the church has run out of evidence it can see, and reaches for the one who reads what no one else can. Knowing the heart is a divine attribute: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10).

Praying to Jesus. They say Lord, and the most natural reading takes that to be the one who chose the original apostles (v. 2): Jesus, who knew what was in man (John 2:24–25). Some take the Lord here to be the Father, and the prayer would still be remarkable; but Luke has just reminded us that Jesus did the first choosing, and later in this book a dying believer calls on him by name, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (7:59). So within a few weeks of the ascension, before a single council, creed or doctrinal controversy, a room full of Jewish monotheists is praying to a man they had eaten breakfast with, addressing him by a title that in their Scriptures belongs to God, and attributing to him the knowledge of every human heart. On that reading, the first recorded prayer of the church is addressed to the risen Jesus. Nobody argues for it; they simply do it. Even if this prayer is to the Father, Stephen’s cry shows that the deity of Christ was not voted in at a later council; it was already the posture of the church.

A searching mercy. He is not taken in by anyone’s best behaviour. Your church’s estimate of you is assembled from what you have let it see; his is not. That cuts in the direction most people fear first: he has read the thing you would resign over if it were known. It also cuts the other way, and this is the side worth resting on. He has read the part of you that nobody has ever believed: the repentance that was real even though nothing changed for months, the love for him that survives in someone whose life makes it look implausible, the reason you did the thing that everyone misread. There is one person in the universe who has never once misunderstood you, and he is the one who went to a cross knowing all of it in advance.

Show which one you have chosen. Not help us choose, but show us whom you have already chosen. And they did the work first: they established the qualifications from Scripture, applied them honestly, narrowed the field to two men who genuinely met them, and only then said: show us. Guidance in the Bible often arrives on the far side of homework.

His own place. The word for the place he leaves (topos) is used again of where he goes, the darkest clause in the chapter, and the church neither enlarges on it nor softens it. It says only that he arrived somewhere that fitted him, a destination matched to a direction he had been travelling for years. Where Scripture draws a line and stops, it is safest to stop there too, and it is telling that the men who had most cause to be bitter about Judas said less about his end than almost any preacher since.

Does his own place mean Judas is lost? That is the most natural reading, and the rest of Scripture supports it. Jesus said of his betrayer that it would have been better for that man if he had not been born (Mark 14:21), and called him the son of destruction (John 17:12). Those words could not be said of anyone who would finally be saved. Scripture teaches that those who die without Christ face conscious, eternal punishment, and Judas, who stood closest to the light and turned from it, is its most solemn example. But mark the church’s restraint, and copy it. We are not told to speculate about the eternal state of people we have known; we are told to warn the living and to flee to Christ ourselves.

On a Tuesday. Pray with honesty to the Lord who knows your heart: you cannot impress him and you need not perform.

parallels.desc: God, who knows the heart

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cast lots. Luke does not say how the lot was cast; perhaps two marked stones were shaken until one fell out. A modern reader is right to find it startling, but it was not superstition. Casting lots was a means God had himself appointed in Israel. It divided the land, chose the goat for the Day of Atonement and arranged the priests’ duties (Joshua 18:6; Leviticus 16:8; Luke 1:9). The proverb that governs the practice says exactly what the eleven were counting on: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Proverbs 16:33). They were using an instrument of the old order on one of the last mornings before the Spirit came.

The lot fell on Matthias. Then the lot disappears from the New Testament, because within days the Spirit came. The Twelve stand complete, and the church, a renewed Israel gathered round its Messiah, is ready for what is about to happen to it.

The King keeps his number. Behind the lot stands a promise of Jesus. At the last supper he told the Twelve that they would eat and drink at his table in his kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Luke 22:30), and that same night one of them led the arresting party to him. Judas’s treachery tore a hole in that promise, and the risen Lord fills it. The number Jesus set at the beginning stands whole on the morning of Pentecost. He keeps his promises down to the arithmetic.

Did they get it wrong? One more question hangs over this passage and is asked more often than any other about it. A good many teachers have said the eleven acted in the flesh, using lots before the Spirit had come, jumping ahead of God, and that the real twelfth apostle was Paul, whom the Lord would choose himself a few chapters later. It is usually pressed by noting that Matthias is never mentioned again.

The evidence does not support it. Luke records the episode without a breath of disapproval, and he is not a man who hides the church’s failures: he will tell us about Ananias lying to the Spirit, about the Greek-speaking widows being neglected, about Paul and Barnabas quarrelling so sharply that they parted company. Here there is no such note. On the contrary, when the Spirit falls in the next chapter Peter stands up with the eleven (2:14), which makes twelve, and Luke says nothing to suggest the number is wrong. Nor were they improvising: Peter is following a text, and the text says let another take his office (Psalm 109:8). They prayed before they drew, and they used the means God himself had appointed for exactly this purpose (Proverbs 16:33).

Why not Paul. The silence about Matthias afterwards proves nothing either, because Acts is silent about nearly all of them. Ten of the Twelve are never heard from again in this book as actors in the story; only Peter and John, with a brief mention of James’s death, get a narrative. By that test the whole apostolate was a mistake. And Paul cannot have been the man in view here, because he fails the stated qualification in the plainest way: the replacement had to have accompanied Jesus from John’s baptism to the ascension, and Paul had done nothing of the kind. He is not the twelfth apostle to Israel; he is the apostle to the Gentiles, which is a different thing and no smaller. The Twelve had to be twelve because they answer to the twelve tribes, and the gap had to be closed before Pentecost.

Where Christians differ: should we cast lots today? Some say the apostles were wrong to do this, and should have waited for Paul. Others use lots or similar methods for guidance today. This commentary’s view: Luke records no disapproval, and the choice was valid. But after Pentecost, the church never cast lots again. With the Spirit given and the Scriptures complete, God guides his people through his word, prayer, wise counsel and the judgment of the church (15:28; Romans 12:2). We don’t need dice.

So how does God guide you today, if not by lots? Not by dice, omens, opening the Bible at random or putting out a fleece, but by the settled means he has since given in fuller measure: his completed word, a lamp to my feet and a light to my path (Psalm 119:105), the indwelling Spirit, prayer, sanctified wisdom, and the counsel of godly friends. The lot belonged to the brief gap before Pentecost and before the New Testament was written; we stand on the far side of both, and are the richer for it.

How do I make a big decision, then, practically? First, settle what Scripture commands or forbids; God will never lead you against his word. Second, if more than one path is right, pray, and ask God for wisdom, which he promises to give generously (James 1:5). Third, gather the facts honestly and think, because a renewed mind is meant to be used (Romans 12:2). Fourth, ask mature Christians who know you, and listen especially if they all say the same thing. Fifth, weigh your gifts, your responsibilities to family and church, and the opportunities actually in front of you. Then decide, and do not torment yourself afterwards about whether you missed a hidden signal. Within the bounds of his word, God is glad for his children to choose, and he rules over the outcome either way.
verseByVerse.note: Casting lots left the choice to God; it is not mentioned again after the Spirit is given.

parallels.desc: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD

1.theology: The Ascension and the Reign of Christ. The ascension is easily overlooked, yet it is not simply that Jesus left; he was enthroned. Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament texts the New Testament quotes most often, because it explains so much: Christ reigns now, at the Father’s right hand, over all things, for his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). His kingdom is already here, hidden but real, advancing through the witness of the Spirit-filled church, and every soul converted is the work of the reigning Christ.
1.examples:
Then: The disciples, staring at the sky and confused about timing and the kingdom, learned that faithfulness between the ascension and the return looks like prayer and witness.

Now: We live in the same interval, between the first coming and the second. The temptation is still to stand looking into heaven, absorbed in the date of the return, while the mission sits unfinished at our feet. He is coming; in the meantime, there is work.

2.title: The Spirit Poured Out

you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. <sup>24</sup>God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. <sup>25</sup>For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; <sup>26</sup>therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope. <sup>27</sup>For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. <sup>28</sup>You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.’ <sup>29</sup>“Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. <sup>30</sup>Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne, <sup>31</sup>he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. <sup>32</sup>This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses. <sup>33</sup>Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. <sup>34</sup>For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, <sup>35</sup>until I make your enemies your footstool.’ <sup>36</sup>Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.” <sup>37</sup>Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” <sup>38</sup>And Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. <sup>39</sup>For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.” <sup>40</sup>And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” <sup>41</sup>So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls. <sup>42</sup>And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. <sup>43</sup>And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. <sup>44</sup>And all who believed were together and had all things in common. <sup>45</sup>And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need. <sup>46</sup>And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, <sup>47</sup>praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
2.overview:
Pentecost (Greek for “fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when Israel offered the first loaves of the wheat harvest (Leviticus 23:15–21); some Jews also linked it with the giving of the law at Sinai. On that day, with Jerusalem full of pilgrims, the Spirit came as Jesus had promised, and the disciples declared God’s mighty works in the native languages of the crowd. At Babel God scattered the nations by confusing their speech; here he begins to gather them by speaking in every tongue.

Peter’s sermon explains the morning from Joel, then proclaims Jesus: handed over by God’s plan and killed by lawless hands, raised as David foresaw, exalted to God’s right hand as the giver of the Spirit, and made both Lord and Christ. Cut to the heart, about three thousand repent and are baptised, and the chapter ends with the life of the new community, which the Lord himself grows day by day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Coming of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit comes with a sound like wind and tongues as of fire, and pilgrims from Parthia to Rome hear God’s mighty works in their own tongues. Some are amazed and ask what it means; others mock.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Age He Opens

The Old Testament promised a day when God would put his Spirit not on a few officeholders but on all his people (Joel 2; Ezekiel 36–37; Jeremiah 31), as Moses had once wished aloud (Numbers 11:29). Pentecost is that day. The Spirit's coming is not a reward for people who prayed hard enough but a once-for-all act in the history of salvation, like the cross and the empty tomb. What is repeated afterwards is the filling, a word Luke uses again of Peter and the church (4:8, 4:31) and of Paul (13:9), so what happened to them is not sealed inside one morning in the first century.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The first names on Luke's list are exile addresses, and the descendants of the deported stood in a Jerusalem street hearing God's mighty works in the language of their exile. Now: The same thing happens whenever the Bible is put into a language that has never had it. The God who gave the church its first sermon in many languages at once does not make anyone learn a holy one first.

verseByVerse.quote: When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 2 is the birthday of the church as the Spirit-filled people of the new covenant. Pentecost is a once-for-all event in the history of salvation, like the cross and the resurrection: the risen and exalted Christ pours out the Holy Spirit, as promised, to dwell in God’s people for ever.

When the day of Pentecost arrived. Pentecost means fiftieth: it was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12). Seven full weeks had been counted off from Passover week by observant Jews wherever they lived; and on the morning the count reached its end, the thing the counting had been counting toward walked into the room. Jews from across the world were in Jerusalem for it.

The feast of firstfruits. At Passover a farmer brought the first sheaf of barley and waved it before the LORD. Fifty days later, at Weeks, he brought two loaves of ordinary bread baked from the new wheat, and, unusually among Israel’s offerings, baked with leaven (Leviticus 23:17). The whole feast was firstfruits: a handful brought in early as the guarantee that the fields were coming. Before the day is out, three thousand people will be brought in as the firstfruits of a harvest that is still coming. Later Jewish tradition also linked the feast with the giving of the law at Sinai, and if that link was already known, the fit is exact: on the day Israel remembered the law written on stone, the Spirit came to write it on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3).

Counted from an empty tomb. The fifty days ran from the waving of that first sheaf in Passover week (Leviticus 23:10–16), and that year Passover week was the week of the cross and the empty tomb. Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the harvest feast that falls fifty days later is the day his harvest begins to come in. John had already said that the Spirit could not be given until Jesus was glorified (John 7:39), and Peter will say before the morning is out that it is the exalted Jesus who has poured him out (2:33). Pentecost is counted from Easter, because it is the risen Lord’s gift.

In the flow. This is where the book has been heading since its first paragraph: the disciples were to stay in the city until they were clothed with power from on high (Luke 24:49) and the Spirit would make them witnesses to the end of the earth (1:4–8). Everything that follows in Acts is the work of the Spirit who arrives on this morning.

All together. Probably the hundred and twenty (1:15), perhaps in the upper room, perhaps somewhere in the temple courts, where a crowd could gather quickly. Luke does not say, and the point is not the building but the company: all of them, together, where obedience had put them.

A sound like wind. Luke marks the comparison carefully: not a wind, but a sound like one; what filled the house was the noise of a gale. In both Hebrew (ruach) and Greek (pneuma) the same word can mean wind, breath and spirit, and Jesus had compared the Spirit to the wind that blows where it wishes (John 3:8). The word Luke chooses here, pnoē, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7 for the breath God breathed into a figure of dust until it became a living man. Ezekiel had watched the breath come into a valley of bones until they stood up, an exceedingly great army (Ezekiel 37:9–14). The same breath is in this room, and what is about to stand up is the church.

The whole house. It filled the house, and then, in the next verse, the people. The glory cloud had once filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) and the temple (1 Kings 8:10–11); now God’s presence fills his new temple, which is his people.

They were sitting. When it happened, the hundred and twenty were sitting. They had been told to stay in the city and wait (1:4), and they had done that and nothing else: no campaign, no technique, no working up of atmosphere. Pentecost is not something anybody in that room produced. Hold onto that if you have been told the Spirit’s work can be triggered by sufficient intensity, have tried it, and concluded that the failure must be yours. It cannot be triggered. It can only be received, in the place obedience has put you.

Should my church pray for another Pentecost? Not for a repeat of this day. Pentecost was the once-for-all arrival of the Spirit to dwell in the church, as the cross was the once-for-all sacrifice, and it no more needs repeating than Calvary does. The Spirit came and has never left. But you may and should pray for what Acts itself goes on to show: that the Spirit already given would fill his people afresh, make them bold, and bring many to Christ (4:29–31). Church history is full of seasons when God did exactly that, in revivals and awakenings, through the ordinary preaching of the gospel. Pray for those. Pray expectantly. Just do not imagine the Spirit is absent until something dramatic happens.

For worship. The first Adam received the breath of God into his dust, and lost the life it gave him. The last Adam went down into death for those who had lost it, and rose to become a life-giving spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45). On this morning the breath comes from his throne, and a room of frightened disciples stands up alive.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost (“fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, celebrating the wheat harvest. Wind and breath picture the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Weeks

verseByVerse.quote: And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tongues as of fire. Fire in Scripture is where God is and where God may not be touched: the bush that burned and was not consumed (Exodus 3:2), the mountain wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire (Exodus 19:18), the fire that fell on Carmel, the coal from the altar at Isaiah’s mouth. Nearly every one is a fire kept at a distance. Here it comes down and settles on people’s heads, and nobody dies. John the Baptist had promised that the coming one would baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16). The whole gospel is in that picture: the fire that could not be approached has come to rest on the very thing it should have consumed, and it is shaped like tongues: tongues for speaking.

On each one. The first detail is divided. Fire can be shared without being lessened; light a hundred candles from a single flame and the flame you started with is no smaller. The Spirit is not being rationed out in portions, a larger share for the apostles and a thinner one for everybody else. The second is each one of them. In the old covenant the Spirit came on particular leaders and craftsmen for particular tasks; now the flame settles on a fisherman, on Mary, on brothers who had once thought Jesus out of his mind, on many whose names Luke does not record. Moses had said out loud that he wished it were so: would that all the LORD’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:29). Every believer receives the Spirit (v. 38).

Filled with the Holy Spirit. Filled means controlled and empowered, and Luke uses the word again and again for being empowered to speak (4:8, 31; 13:9). It is not a quantity poured into a container but a Person taking hold of a person for the work in front of him, very often the work of speaking about Christ. That is why the same man can be filled again; Peter is filled here, and filled afresh when he stands before the council (4:8).

Other tongues. The Greek word for tongues (glōssai) is the same word Luke has just used for the tongues of fire; the sign was shaped like the gift it announced. And the gift itself is unambiguous in this chapter: other tongues (heterais glōssais) means other languages, real, existing, human languages, because the crowd outside identifies them three times (vv. 6, 8, 11). And here is the reversal of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9). There God confused the languages and scattered people in judgment; here he gives languages to gather the nations in grace.

The fire he longed to cast. Luke had heard Jesus speak of this fire, and of what it would cost him. I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! (Luke 12:49–50). The baptism he meant was his death. Seven weeks after the cross the fire falls, and it falls from him (2:33); the price of those flames was paid on a hill outside the city.

Is this the gift Paul discusses at Corinth? That is the question every reader of this chapter eventually asks, and the two are not obviously identical. What happens here is understood instantly by native speakers; what happens at Corinth needs an interpreter and is unintelligible to the hearer without one (1 Corinthians 14:2). Some conclude they are two gifts sharing a name. Others, more probably, take them as one gift in two settings: a genuine language is a sign to the man who owns it and undecipherable noise to everyone else, and the Corinthian assembly, it seems, had no native speakers of the languages being used. The text does not settle it, and a reader is allowed to leave it unsettled.

Where Christians differ: tongues today. Pentecostals and charismatics teach that tongues continue today, often as a prayer language, and some that it is the sign of Spirit baptism. This commentary’s view: the tongues of Pentecost were known languages, a sign that the gospel was for every nation. Tongues and other sign gifts served to confirm the apostolic message in the founding era (Hebrews 2:3–4; 1 Corinthians 14:22), and the church’s historic testimony is that they ceased. This is the cessationist position (that these sign gifts ceased with the apostles), held charitably: we gladly acknowledge that many charismatic believers love Christ deeply. Continuationists answer that no text ends the gifts before Christ returns, reading 1 Corinthians 13:8–12 that way; this is a difference among faithful believers about the Spirit’s gifts, never about his gospel. The Spirit himself, and his saving and sanctifying work, continue in full.

Is this the baptism in the Spirit that Pentecostal Christians teach? Pentecostal teaching describes a second experience after conversion, marked by tongues. But Pentecost was the once-for-all outpouring of the Spirit on the church, promised by Jesus (1:5). From now on, every believer receives the Spirit when he believes: in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Those who were added later this same day received the gift of the Spirit on repentance and faith (v. 38), and Luke records no tongues among the three thousand. Many Pentecostal believers who hold this love Christ deeply, and their longing for more of the Spirit is right; the difference is over how Scripture describes his coming, not over whether we need him.

A test Scripture will not carry. What should not be left unsettled is the pastoral use this verse is put to: it is regularly held over believers as the test of whether the Spirit is truly in them. Paul asks a church that prized the gift above everything, in a run of questions expecting the answer no: do all speak with tongues? (1 Corinthians 12:30). A Christian who has never spoken a syllable of another language lacks nothing of the Spirit. And the traffic runs both ways: the same chapter forbids the contempt that says I have no need of you. Beneath the demand for a sign there is often an old ache of the heart: wanting something we can feel and point to, so that we need not simply trust what God has said. But the Spirit’s witness that we are God’s children comes as we cry Abba, Father (Romans 8:15–16), and its ground is Christ’s finished work, not the intensity of any experience.

What do I say to a Christian friend who speaks in tongues? Begin by remembering that he is your brother, and that the things you share, Christ crucified and risen, the authority of Scripture, salvation by grace, are vastly greater than this difference. You can tell him honestly why you believe the sign gifts served the founding of the church and have ceased, and point him to what Acts 2 shows: known languages, declaring God’s mighty works, understood by hearers. But do not mock or question his faith. Ask him what the experience means to him, and listen. Agree together that every gift must build up others and point to Christ (1 Corinthians 14:12), and that love is greater than any gift (1 Corinthians 13). Then pray together. That kind of conversation honours the Spirit far more than winning the argument.

What the fire was for. It is not an experience. The first recorded act of the Spirit in the church is to make ordinary people talk about God to strangers, out loud, in words the strangers can understand. The Spirit who filled the mouths of fishermen is in you: ask him to fill yours with the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Fire often signals God’s presence.

parallels.desc: the LORD descended on it in fire

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dwelling in Jerusalem. The word Luke uses, dwelling, does not mean visiting; he has a separate word for visitors and uses it five verses later of the Romans. These are residents: Jews born in Parthia or Egypt or Cappadocia who had come back and settled. The Dispersion may have numbered several million across the Roman and Parthian empires, and some had probably come home to die in the land. On this morning such men heard, in the language they had learned as children, that a man had been raised from the dead.

Devout men. Devout (eulabeis) is Luke’s word for a certain kind of serious Israelite: God-fearing, careful, pious. He uses it of old Simeon waiting in the temple for the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25), and later of the men brave enough to bury Stephen (8:2). These are not sightseers at a festival. They are the people who had been waiting.

Bewildered. The Greek verb is the one the Greek Old Testament uses at Babel, where the LORD confused the language of all the earth (Genesis 11:9). At Babel men were thrown into confusion because they suddenly could not understand one another. Here they are thrown into confusion because they suddenly can.

His own language. They are staggered not by volume but by intelligibility: each man is hearing his own language, his dialektos, his native dialect. Verse 4 has already settled that the miracle was in the mouths, not the ears: God did not adjust fifteen nationalities of hearing. He gave a hundred and twenty Galileans fifteen nationalities of speech.

God crosses the room. He could have done this in Hebrew, the language of the covenant, and required every nation to come and learn it. He did the opposite. The first sermon of the Christian era was delivered in the languages people count money in, swear in when they drop something, and sing over their children at night. He had already done it once, at far greater cost: the eternal Word took flesh, learned to talk at his mother’s knee, and spoke the Aramaic of Galilean villages. Pentecost carries the logic of the incarnation into every tongue. From the first morning of the church, God has been the one who crosses the room.

Why does God care which language people hear him in? Because he wants to be understood, not merely obeyed. A message in a borrowed language can be followed with the mind; a message in your mother tongue reaches the heart. God’s purpose is not only to save individuals but to gather worshippers from every nation, tribe, people and language (Revelation 7:9), and he does not ask them to become culturally Jewish, or English, or anything else first. That is why the church has always translated the Scriptures rather than requiring people to learn a sacred language, and why missionaries still spend decades learning languages with a few thousand speakers. Every translation is a small Pentecost.
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews born abroad settled in Jerusalem, and huge numbers came as pilgrims for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were amazed and astonished, saying, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? The crowd’s objection is an accent, and everyone in that street knew what a Galilean sounded like. The northern pronunciation was easy to mock; later rabbinic stories laugh at Galileans for swallowing their gutturals so badly that a hearer could not tell which word was meant. It was the accent of the provinces: fishing villages, small farms, no great rabbinic schools within a day’s walk.

The accent that once betrayed him. Some fifty days before this, in a high priest’s courtyard, a bystander looked at Peter and said that his accent betrayed him (Matthew 26:73), and he swore he had never met the man. The accent that exposed him as a coward is the accent now filling a public square with the resurrection. God did not give Peter a new voice; he gave him a new message and sent him back into the same city with the voice that had denied it.

The first Galilean. The accent was not only Peter’s. Jesus grew up in Nazareth, and the Pharisees were sure that no prophet arises from Galilee (John 7:52). Yet Isaiah had said the LORD would make glorious Galilee of the nations, and the people who walked in darkness would see a great light (Isaiah 9:1–2). The scorn the crowd aimed at the disciples had first been aimed at him.

The disqualifications we hold against ourselves. The disqualification this crowd cannot get past is a regional accent, and the ones most believers privately hold against themselves are of precisely that order: not enough education, the wrong background, a stammer, a criminal record, a voice that goes thin exactly when it matters. The council will lodge the same complaint a few weeks later, that these are uneducated, common men, and will stumble on the answer without meaning to: they recognised that they had been with Jesus (4:13).

How is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language? Literally, the language in which we were born. Most of these men would have understood Greek or Aramaic well enough to trade in it, but they hear the gospel in their mother tongue, the language of the heart. God speaks to people in their own language, and this is the root of the long Christian work of Bible translation, from the Greek Old Testament to the Latin, Gothic and Syriac Bibles to the translators still at work today.

Amazed and astonished. Luke stacks two verbs on the crowd. The first is the word he uses of Jairus and his wife when their dead daughter sat up (Luke 8:56). By verse 8 several thousand sober, widely travelled men have no category left to put the thing in, exactly the right condition in which to hear a sermon.

Should I support Bible translation, and why does it matter if most people speak a trade language? Yes, and it matters for the reason this verse shows. People can do business in a second language and still hear God as a foreigner. Hundreds of millions of people still have no complete Bible in the language they think and pray in. Supporting translation, by prayer, giving, or going, is joining the work God began on this morning. And at home it means taking care to explain the gospel in everyday speech, not church jargon, to people who do not share your background.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Parthians and Medes. Luke’s list reads as a map, running roughly from east to west. It opens outside the empire altogether, in Parthia beyond the Euphrates, the one great power Rome never conquered. Then Media and Elam and Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers that had been Babylon, and those names are exile addresses. When Assyria carried the northern tribes away it settled them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6), and Babylon later took Judah. On this morning God gathers a scattering that history never repaired.

Judea. Judea is strange in a roll-call of foreign parts; most likely Luke is tracing the arc of the Fertile Crescent and Judea lies on it, or he means that even the locals heard their own speech.

Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia. The list sweeps north and west through Asia Minor, very nearly the route Paul will spend the second half of this book walking. Years later Peter writes a letter to the exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1). Some of the people he addressed may first have heard the gospel in this street.

Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene. Then south to Egypt, whose Jewish community at Alexandria was large enough to have produced its own Greek translation of the Scriptures, and along the coast of North Africa to Cyrene, whose Jews turn up again in this book both as opponents (6:9) and as the men who first preached to Greeks at Antioch (11:20). One of them had carried a cross up a hill outside this city only weeks earlier: Simon of Cyrene (Luke 23:26).

And visitors from Rome. And the list ends at Rome, which is where Luke’s own second volume ends (28:16). He names his destination on page two. These visitors may well have been among the beginnings of the church in Rome, to which Paul later wrote.

A promise kept in the wrong order. Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8). On the first morning, the end of the earth has come to Jerusalem. Before a single missionary has packed a bag, the gospel is heard by men who will carry it home to Parthia and Egypt and Rome.

Gathered to the root of Jesse. Behind the exile addresses stands a promise about the Messiah. Isaiah said that the root of Jesse would stand as a signal for the peoples, and that the Lord would recover the remnant of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Elam and from Shinar, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:10–12). John tells us why Jesus died: to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad (John 11:52). This morning the scattered stand in one street, gathered to a crucified and risen son of David, who is himself the signal raised for the nations.

Why does a list of places matter to me? Because it is a map of God’s faithfulness and a preview of his plan. Every name on it was a place where God’s people had been scattered by judgment, exile or trade, and every one of them is being gathered back to hear of Christ. If you are a Gentile believer, your own people are somewhere on the long extension of this list, and it reached you because God meant it to. The list also reminds us that the gospel is not owned by any one culture. It belonged to Parthians and Libyans before it belonged to Europeans, and it belongs today to the churches of Africa, Asia and Latin America as much as to anyone.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the nations today, by name. Choose one of the places in this list, find out what the church there is facing now, and pray for it. Many of these lands, once full of churches, now have very few believers. The God who gathered them once can do it again.
verseByVerse.note: The list runs roughly from east (Parthia, beyond the Euphrates) to west (Rome): the whole Jewish world scattered among the nations.

parallels.desc: the table of nations
Babel, where languages were confused

verseByVerse.quote: both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians — we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both Jews and proselytes. The list ends with two words that widen it past nationality altogether. Proselytes were Gentiles who had gone the whole distance into Judaism: renouncing their family gods, circumcised as adults, probably immersed, bringing an offering, and having paid all of it they remained, in many eyes, a second-tier member of the covenant. Such men are in this crowd, hearing the wonders of God in their own language, and within twenty years the church will meet in this same city to decide whether Gentiles need any of that machinery at all (15:1–11). The door they crawled through is about to be taken off its hinges.

Cretans and Arabians. Then Cretans and Arabians, island and desert, west and east, the far margins added as if to say the list could go on. Paul would later leave Titus in Crete (Titus 1:5) and spend time himself in Arabia (Galatians 1:17).

The mighty works of God. The mighty works (ta megaleia) are the great things God has done. The phrase belongs to the Old Testament’s language for the great things God did in bringing Israel out of Egypt: his mighty hand, the signs, the sea (Deuteronomy 11:2–4). The first Christian speech was not moral instruction or a report of religious feelings but a recital of things God had done, in the same register Israel used for the exodus, now attached to a tomb outside a city wall.

The exodus he accomplished at Jerusalem. Luke has prepared us for this. On the mountain of transfiguration, he tells us, Moses and Elijah appeared with Jesus and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The word for departure is exodos. Moses had led Israel out through the sea; Jesus led his people out through death itself, out of the bondage of sin and the grip of the grave, and came up on the other side alive.

News before advice. Christianity is first news and only afterwards advice. Suppose nothing happened in Jerusalem that spring, and what is left is a philosophy of life. A believer’s own story matters; Paul’s conversion is told three times in this book. But on the first morning the street was filled not with a hundred and twenty people describing what had happened to them, but with what God had done.

What are the mighty works of God I should be telling? Start with the ones the apostles told. God created the world and made us for himself. We turned away and came under his judgment. God sent his Son, who lived the life we should have lived, died on the cross in the place of sinners, bearing their punishment, and rose bodily from the dead. He has ascended and reigns, and he has poured out his Spirit. He will come again to judge the living and the dead. Everyone who turns from sin and trusts him is forgiven and made new. Your own story fits inside that one: tell what God has done for you, but make sure the cross and the empty tomb are in it.
verseByVerse.note: Proselytes were Gentiles who had converted to Judaism.

parallels.desc: Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch

verseByVerse.quote: And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, "What does this mean?" But others mocking said, "They are filled with new wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, What does this mean? Every crowd that has ever heard the gospel is inside these two sentences. The first is a real question. These men have no explanation and they say so, and by saying so they hold a door open. It is the right question, and the whole of the rest of the book is an answer to it; Peter begins answering it in the next verse. It is also, in miniature, the difference between the two halves of this crowd: one group has run out of explanations and admits it, the other has run out of explanations and invents one.

New wine. The second sentence is not an argument, and it is a poor explanation. The word is gleukos, sweet new wine, an odd charge in late spring with the grape harvest still months away, whatever sweet wine had been kept. And nine in the morning on a feast day is no hour for drinking, which is precisely the point Peter makes in his first breath. Perhaps those who heard only languages they did not understand thought it was drunken babble; Paul later warns that uninterpreted tongues make outsiders think believers are out of their minds (1 Corinthians 14:23). But the mockers were not weighing evidence; they grabbed the nearest insult.

What the sneer concedes. Drunkenness was the closest thing they could find to what they were watching: people who had stopped guarding themselves. Paul plays the comparison back the other way: do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18).

Called a drunkard before them. The sneer had been used on their Master. Jesus had said what his generation made of him: the Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard (Luke 7:34). The world that dismissed the Lord with a joke about wine dismisses his Spirit-filled people with the same joke, which is exactly what he told them to expect: a servant is not greater than his master (John 15:20). There is an honour hidden in it: the life in the church is unmistakably his.

Nobody beyond the next twenty minutes. Peter preaches to both halves of this crowd without distinguishing between them, and by evening three thousand have been baptised. Some of the men shouting about new wine at nine in the morning may well have been in the water before dark. The gospel has a long history of being sneered at by people who go on to preach it.

What should I do when someone mocks my faith? Do not answer mockery with mockery, and do not take it as the last word. Peter’s response was calm: he corrected the misunderstanding in a sentence and then told them about Jesus. You can do the same. A light, honest reply, a question back, or a simple statement of what you believe and why, often does more than a long argument. Be gentle and respectful (1 Peter 3:15–16). Remember that the mocker may be closer to faith than he looks, and keep praying for him personally. And if the mockery hurts, remember that your Lord was mocked first, and bore it for you.

For worship. On the cross, with the mocking going on around him, Jesus prayed, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). That prayer did not end at Golgotha. Seven weeks later his Spirit is poured out, the world calls it drunkenness, and the answer from heaven is not fire but a sermon, an offer of pardon to everyone standing there, scoffers included. The mercy that prayed on the cross preaches in the street.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–36 — Peter's Sermon: The Risen Christ Proclaimed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter answers the mockers: this is what Joel foretold for the last days, the Spirit poured out on all kinds of people and salvation for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord. Then he proclaims Jesus of Nazareth, crucified by God’s plan and lawless hands, raised as David foresaw, and exalted as Lord and Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
How Peter Reads the Psalms

Peter's use of Psalm 16 is a method, and he shows his working. David wrote you will not let your Holy One see corruption; David died and was buried, and his tomb was a short walk away. So the words say more than David's own life could bear, and the man they fit is the one whose tomb is empty. Psalm 110 is read the same way: David did not ascend into the heavens, so the psalm in which he hears the LORD speak to my Lord is about someone greater. The risen Christ had taught them to read like this (Luke 24:27, 44). It is not squeezing Christ out of texts but recognising that the Spirit who wrote the Scriptures knew where the story was going and left its shape in the words.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who were personally implicated, this Jesus whom you crucified, and said it to their faces seven weeks after they had done it. He did not soften the charge to get a hearing, and three thousand were baptised before dark. Now: A gospel that never implicates the hearer has nothing to forgive him for. This crowd asked what shall we do because Peter had left them with something that needed doing; preaching about sin in general, committed by people in general, will not produce that question.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: "Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter, standing with the eleven. Eleven beside him makes twelve, the number restored at the end of chapter 1 (1:26): the apostolic band stands complete on its first working day, one voice for the twelve. What follows is testimony, not personality.

Lifted up his voice. Lifted up his voice is Old Testament language for a solemn public declaration (Judges 9:7). And addressed (apephthenxato) is the same word as utterance in verse 4: Peter speaks out boldly, as one moved by the Spirit.

Men of Judea. He addresses the settled residents of verse 5, the Diaspora that had come home, alongside the people of the city. These people had spent their lives waiting, and he opens by telling them the waiting is over.

Only the third hour. The defence is almost dry. The third hour was about nine in the morning, and, as later Jewish sources describe the custom, devout Jews ate and drank nothing on a feast day until the morning prayer was over. He disposes of the charge in a sentence and never returns to it; it is only the door the mockers accidentally held open for him.

In the flow. The first Christian sermon moves in three steps: Scripture explains what the crowd has seen (vv. 16–21); Jesus, crucified, risen and exalted, explains Scripture (vv. 22–36); and then comes the call to repent and be baptised (vv. 38–40). Nearly every later sermon in Acts comes to the same point: the risen Jesus and what a hearer must do about him.

The same voice. This is the same voice that, not two months ago in this city, under pressure from a servant girl, said I do not know the man, three times, with oaths and curses. It is now telling a great crowd, in the city whose authorities arranged the execution, that the man they killed is alive and is Lord. Between those two mornings Peter attended no course. Nor did he simply resolve to do better; he had already promised he would die first, and had folded inside a few hours. What came between was the risen Christ, and then Pentecost.

Not more determination. The standard advice to a frightened Christian is to try harder, and Peter’s history refutes it. He had determination in quantity, and at the point of testing it was worth nothing. What he lacked was the Spirit; and when the Spirit came, the courage came with him, not as a technique to be mastered but as a Person to be received. That is an enormous relief to anybody who has already found out what his own resolve is worth.

I am timid by nature. Can the Spirit really make me bold? Yes, though boldness may not look like Peter shouting to thousands. In Acts it usually means speaking plainly about Jesus when it would be easier to stay silent, and the Spirit gives it to quiet people as well as loud ones. Ask for it directly; the church prayed exactly this, grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness (4:29), and God answered. Then take one small step in the direction of courage, a sentence, an invitation, an honest answer, and expect his help in the step rather than before it. Remember too that Peter’s past did not disqualify him. Yours does not disqualify you.

For worship. On the night of the denials the Lord turned and looked at Peter across the courtyard (Luke 22:61). That look did not end the friendship; it began the restoration. He did not replace the apostle who denied him. He kept him, and filled him, and made him the first preacher of the resurrection. Our Lord does not need strong men. He makes weak men strong, and the glory of it is his.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour was about 9 a.m. — far too early for drunkenness.

parallels.desc: do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Uttered through Joel. This is that. Peter’s first move is not to explain the phenomenon, or defend it, but to open the Bible and say that this was on the schedule. Nothing new has happened; something promised has happened. And that is the first principle of all true spiritual experience: the Spirit’s work is always in line with Scripture, because he is its author.

A book about locusts. Joel is not the obvious place to go on a morning of glory. Joel is about locusts: a real swarm had stripped a real country, wave after wave, until the grain offering was cut off from the house of the LORD and the cattle groaned for want of pasture. Out of that ruin God makes the promise everybody knows: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten (Joel 2:25). And immediately after it comes the promise of the Spirit.

The years the locust has eaten. The outpouring this crowd is watching is the sequel to a promise made to people who had lost everything, and it is the sign that God means to put the years back. Anyone who has lost years, to an illness, to a marriage that came apart, to a decade of his own stupidity, is reading a promise addressed to exactly that condition. The Spirit is not given first to the flourishing. He is promised to a field that has been eaten bare, as the down payment on a harvest that is coming back.

A fisherman reading the prophets. A fisherman stands up in front of scholars and tells them what their own Scriptures are about, and he is not guessing. Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, the risen Jesus had interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). So this is that is ultimately a sentence about Christ: Joel’s promise has landed because the one it was waiting for has died, risen and been exalted, and the Spirit filling the street is the Spirit he has poured out (2:33).

How do I test a spiritual experience by Scripture? Ask what Peter asked: does this match what God has said? First, does it exalt Jesus Christ as he is presented in Scripture, crucified, risen and Lord (1 John 4:2–3; John 16:14)? Second, does it agree with the plain teaching of the Bible, or does it add to it or contradict it? Third, does it lead to holiness, love and humility, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), or to pride and division? An experience can be intense and still be mistaken; feelings are not the test. And if something is not taught in Scripture, you are not bound to seek it, however many people around you claim it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the last days. Joel 2:28 has afterward; Peter, by the Spirit, interprets it as the last days, and declares them to have arrived at Pentecost. So in the Bible’s reckoning the last days are not only a short future window before the end; they are the whole gospel age, from Christ’s first coming to his return. In these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:2); it is the last hour (1 John 2:18). Scripture does speak of the days growing harder as the end nears (2 Timothy 3:1), but the era as a whole is already underway. The effect is urgency, not date-setting: we live in the final act of God’s story, awaiting only the King’s return.

Where Christians differ: when are the last days? Dispensational teaching usually places the last days chiefly in a future period connected with a restored national Israel, a seven-year tribulation and an earthly millennium, with the church age as a parenthesis. This commentary’s view: Peter says the last days began at Pentecost, and the New Testament consistently treats the whole time between Christ’s first and second comings as the last days. This is the amillennial reading (the view that the thousand years of Revelation 20 picture Christ’s present reign from heaven, not a future earthly kingdom): Christ reigns now from heaven, the Spirit has been poured out, the gospel goes to the nations, and the next great event on God’s calendar is the return of Christ, the resurrection and the judgment. Faithful brothers, including some in the Reformed tradition who expect an earthly reign of Christ after his return, read the prophetic timetable differently, and the difference should be held with patience.

The roll of the Spirit-bearers. Who had the Spirit of God under the old covenant? A very short roll, nearly every name on it holding an office: Moses and the seventy elders, Bezalel, Gideon and Samson, Saul and David, the prophets. The Spirit came upon them for the work and could depart again, which is precisely what David is terrified of when he begs God not to take his Holy Spirit from him (Psalm 51:11).

The last name on the roll. The roll ends with one more name, and it changes all the rest. At the Jordan the Spirit came down on Jesus (Luke 3:22) and remained on him (John 1:32); in Nazareth he read, the Spirit of the Lord is upon me (Luke 4:18). David feared losing the Spirit. The Son never could. And Pentecost is what happens when the anointed one is exalted: the Spirit who was given to him without measure (John 3:34) flows from him, the head, to all his people.

On all flesh. Now read Joel’s list against that. All flesh does not mean every individual without exception, but all kinds of people without distinction. Sons and daughters, young men and old men, and then male servants and female servants: the word means slaves. The lowest person in the household, with no property and no standing, is written into a promise about the Spirit of God. No social barrier keeps anyone from the Spirit (Galatians 3:28). And before long the promise will reach the Gentiles too (10:45).

What Peter adds. Two more of Peter’s changes run the same way as the last days. He inserts God declares, so that the sentence is signed. And where Joel’s line about the male and female servants ends, Peter adds and they shall prophesy: an apostle saying what the text turned out to mean, and refusing to let the slaves be dropped from the promise on the way past.

Prophecy, visions and dreams. In the Old Testament prophecy was rare. Now the Spirit-given knowledge of God and the ability to speak his truth is spread among all his people. Prophecy here, in the setting of this chapter, means speaking God’s word, declaring his mighty works (v. 11). The visions and dreams are poetic parallelism: all will know God directly, from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:34).

The daughters of Philip. What does it mean that the daughters prophesy? Luke shows us four of them, the unmarried daughters of Philip the evangelist, prophesying at Caesarea (21:9). Whatever prophecy is in Acts, it plainly includes women. What this verse establishes past argument is that the gift of the Spirit is distributed with no regard to sex, age or social rank.

Where Christians differ: prophecy today. Charismatic Christians see ongoing prophecy as new words from God. This commentary’s view: Joel’s promise is fulfilled in the Spirit given to all believers, who all know God and declare his word. In the apostolic era this included revelatory prophecy, which laid the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20; 3:5). With the canon complete, the prophetic word continues in the Spirit-empowered proclamation of Scripture. Women as well as men proclaim God’s mighty works, while the office of elder and preaching in the gathered church belongs to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). Continuationist brothers, who believe prophecy continues and must always be weighed by Scripture, are fellow believers, and the difference is held in love.

Do women, and men, still prophesy today? Joel’s promise was fulfilled at Pentecost: the Spirit is now poured out on all God’s people, men and women, young and old. Continuationists believe the gift of prophecy continues as a gift to be weighed by the church (1 Corinthians 14:29). The more likely reading is that prophecy as new revelation belonged to the founding of the church, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and has ceased with the completed Scriptures. What continues is the Spirit empowering every believer to speak of Christ (1:8): the mother teaching her children, the old man telling his grandson what God has done, the young woman explaining the gospel to a friend at work.

So what may a woman do with this gift? A great deal. She is filled with the same Spirit as any apostle. She may pray and speak God’s truth, tell the gospel to anyone, teach children and other women (Titus 2:3–5), explain the way of God more accurately, as Priscilla did with her husband to Apollos (18:26), counsel, encourage, serve and lead in many ministries. The New Testament restricts one thing: the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church belong to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). That restriction is about order in God’s household, not about worth or gifting, and it is never a licence for men to belittle or silence women. Paul grounds it in creation, not in the customs of his day (1 Timothy 2:13), and Christians who read these passages differently remain brothers and sisters to be heard with respect. The Spirit came on the daughters as fully as on the sons.

On a Tuesday. If you are old and think your usefulness is over, or young and inexperienced, or in a humble job, read the list again: old men, young men, servants. The Spirit poured out on them has been poured out on you; speak of God’s mighty works to someone today.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh
would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!
Philip’s four daughters prophesied

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wonders and signs. Peter has just said this is that, yet none of the blood, fire and darkened sun had happened in Jerusalem that morning. Peter adds three words to Joel, above, below and signs, linking the passage to the signs Jesus did (v. 22). Three things go a long way toward resolving the difficulty.

The language of a world ending. The first is that this is how the prophets speak of the fall of a power. When Isaiah announces the end of Babylon the sun will be dark at its rising (Isaiah 13:10); when Ezekiel announces the end of Egypt, God covers the sun with a cloud (Ezekiel 32:7). Babylon fell. Egypt was humbled. The sun came up through the whole of it. This is not failed prediction; it is the settled idiom of Scripture for saying that a world is ending. Jesus used the same kind of language when he spoke of the fall of Jerusalem and of his own coming (Luke 21:20–28), and the fall of Jerusalem arrived inside the lifetime of some of the men standing in that street.

They had stood under a darkened sun. The second is that a piece of it had happened. Only weeks earlier, in this city, at midday, the sun’s light failed for three hours while a man died on a hill outside the wall (Luke 23:44–45). Peter is quoting a prophecy about a darkened sun to people who had stood under one and never been given an account of it.

The great and magnificent day. The third is the shape of the whole promise. The day of the Lord, the day of God’s judgment and salvation, has begun with Christ’s first coming and will be complete at his return. The whole age of the church lies between, and Peter is opening an era, not closing one. The signs belong to it, and so does the sentence he is driving toward: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.

Should I be worried when I hear about blood moons or world events as signs of the end? No. Wars, earthquakes, eclipses and disasters have filled every century, and Jesus said such things must take place but the end is not yet (Matthew 24:6). They remind us that this world is passing and that judgment is real. But they are not a code, and no one can read the date from them. The right response to any sign is the one Peter draws: call on the Lord, live faithfully, and tell others. A believer who knows Christ does not need to fear the day of the Lord, because the judge is his Saviour.

For worship. Amos warned an Israel that longed for the day of the LORD what was in it: it is darkness, and not light (Amos 5:18). And at midday on a Friday the darkness of that day came down on one man. The Son of God stood under the judgement the great day will bring, and took its night into himself, so that for everyone who calls on him the day will dawn as light. The judge on the throne of that day will be the one who was judged in their place.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: darkness at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The climax. This is the line the whole citation has been climbing toward, the point of the sermon, and Peter stops the quotation here; the end of Joel’s verse, about those whom the LORD calls, he will pick up when he closes (v. 39).

Everyone. No qualifier of nation, class, sex, age or record, and spoken over a crowd in the city that had killed the Son of God.

Calls upon the name of the Lord. The single condition, and it is not a work, an achievement or a standard of behaviour; it is the noise a man makes when he has run out. To call on the Lord’s name is to appeal to him, trusting him for rescue. It is faith expressed in prayer.

Shall be saved. Not may be, not stands a better chance. Peter is quoting a promise, not proposing a scheme.

The name of the LORD, applied to Jesus. In Joel it is the LORD in small capitals, the ESV’s sign for the covenant name of God, Yahweh, the name Israel would not say aloud. Fifteen verses later Peter tells the same crowd who the Lord is: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (v. 36). To call on Jesus is to call on Yahweh.

Not a slip. Nor is it a slip in the excitement of a first sermon. Peter will say there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (4:12); those who call on your name is soon the ordinary description of a Christian (9:14); Paul quotes this very line of Joel and applies it to Jesus without pausing to justify himself (Romans 10:9–13). And Stephen dies praying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit: a Jewish monotheist praying to Jesus with his last breath (7:59).

How the deity of Christ entered the church. There was no committee, no vote, no slow inflation of a human teacher into a god across three centuries, which is a story often told. Jewish monotheists, men who would sooner have died than pray to a creature, began praying to Jesus within weeks of the resurrection, and reached for the Old Testament’s texts about the LORD to explain why. Someone may answer that Luke wrote these speeches down decades later. But Paul’s letters, written within about twenty-five years of the cross, show the same worship, including an Aramaic prayer that must go back to the earliest Jewish believers: Maranatha, Our Lord, come (1 Corinthians 16:22).

What does calling on the name actually look like? It is where a reader most needs help, because the phrase sounds like something one would have to know how to do. It is not a formula and it is not a technique. It is what the tax collector did at the back of the temple when he would not even lift up his eyes, and beat his breast, and said, God, be merciful to me, a sinner. No preparation, no cleaning himself up first, no promise of improvement, and he went home justified (Luke 18:13–14). Justified means declared right with God by the Judge himself: not made perfect on the spot, but acquitted and accepted, on the ground not of his record but of God’s mercy, a mercy the cross shows to rest on Christ (Romans 3:24–26). A man who believes he must repair himself before he is entitled to call has the order exactly backwards; calling is what the unrepaired do. If you have never called on Christ, you can do it now, in your own words: Lord Jesus, I have sinned; you died and rose again; save me.

But if salvation is for everyone who calls, how does that fit with God’s choosing? Both are true, and Peter holds them together in this very sermon: the promise is for everyone, and it is for everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself (v. 39). The invitation is genuinely universal, and no one who calls on Christ will ever be turned away. At the same time, no one calls on him unless God first opens his heart (16:14). The two do not compete. God’s choosing is the reason anyone calls at all, and it never makes the offer insincere. You do not need to know whether you are chosen before you call. Call, and your calling will be the evidence that he chose you.
verseByVerse.note: In Joel “the Lord” is the LORD; Peter applies the name to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men of Israel, hear these words. Now the sermon turns from explaining the morning to announcing the man.

Attested by God. Jesus was a real man, from a real town, and God showed his approval of him publicly. Attested means accredited, as a man’s credentials are produced in court.

As you yourselves know. He is not introducing a stranger. Jesus had worked in public, in their own country, within the last few years, and even his enemies did not deny the miracles; they put them down to Beelzebul (Luke 11:15). Peter appeals to the memory of a hostile crowd, within weeks of the events and in the city where they happened, which is a dangerous way to preach unless it is true.

The definite plan. Two claims about one event are welded together, with no attempt to soften either. Definite plan (hōrismenē boulē) is a fixed purpose; the participle is built on the verb for marking out a boundary, the root of our word horizon. The cross was not an accident or a tragedy that took God by surprise; it lay inside a line drawn before the world was made (4:27–28; 1 Peter 1:20; Revelation 13:8). And foreknowledge (prognōsis) here is not God peering ahead to see what people would decide; his foreknowing carries his settled purpose.

By the hands of lawless men. The second claim is every bit as sharp: not circumstances, but you; and the men without the law are the Romans, so Peter distributes the guilt without diluting it. The Jerusalem crowd wanted it done; the empire’s soldiers did it; nobody in the transaction is a mere instrument and nobody’s hands are clean. They did it freely and wickedly; God planned it for good. As Joseph said to his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20).

Hold the two together. Take away the plan and the cross becomes a tragedy God salvaged, which is comfort of a very thin sort. Take away the guilt and the cross becomes theatre in which nobody is responsible, and there is nothing left for it to forgive. Scripture has kept them in one sentence since Isaiah, who watched God send Assyria as the rod of his anger, though the Assyrian did not so intend, and then punish the king of Assyria for the arrogance of his heart (Isaiah 10:5–12).

What it does not mean. This verse does not make God the author of sin, or say that he forced anyone to sin: Peter charges his hearers with murder in the same breath in which he says it was planned, and no preacher could do that if the real agent of the crime were God. Nor does it mean that the Jews are uniquely guilty. All of us, by our sins, put Christ there, and Gentiles and Jews together crucified him (4:27). The long and wicked history of Christians blaming the Jewish people for the death of Christ has no ground here; Peter is speaking as a Jew to his own people, and offering them pardon within the hour. And this is not a sentence to be handed to a suffering person as a tidy explanation of what has happened to him, because Peter is not explaining a tragedy at all.
