He is announcing that the worst thing the human race has ever done is the thing God used to save it.

If God planned the cross, why did Jesus have to die at all? Because there was no other way to save sinners justly. God’s plan was not arbitrary. Our sin deserved God’s judgment, and God could not simply overlook it without ceasing to be just. So in love he planned that his own Son would bear our sin and its punishment in our place, that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The plan was the plan of a God who loved sinners enough to give his Son, and who is holy enough that only such a sacrifice would do. That is why the cross is both the greatest crime and the greatest gift.

There has never been a plan B. If the murder of the Son of God did not fall outside the plan, nothing does. Whatever a reader has done that he believes has put him permanently beyond reach, and whatever has been done to him that looks like the end of every good purpose, is smaller than this and stands inside the same sovereignty. There has never been a plan B.
verseByVerse.note: Lawless men are the Romans, who did not have God’s law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raised him up. The heart of the apostolic preaching: you killed him; God raised him, and reversed their verdict.

Loosing the pangs of death. The word for pangs (ōdinas) is the word for labour pains, which the Greek Old Testament uses where David is caught in the cords of death and of Sheol (Psalm 18:4–5): death is in labour, and it cannot keep what it is carrying. Paul calls the risen Christ the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18), and fittingly so, because on one particular Sunday a tomb behaved like a womb.

Not possible. Not unlikely. Not difficult. Not possible. The New Testament gives several reasons why not.

Because of who he is. One is who he is. Peter himself will say a chapter later that Jerusalem killed the Author of life (3:15), and life does not stay dead any more than fire stays cold.

Because of what he had not done. Death in Scripture is not a natural process; it is a wage, paid to those who have earned it (Romans 6:23). Jesus had earned nothing; the ruler of this world had no claim on him (John 14:30). He had gone in voluntarily, carrying other men’s debts; once those were discharged there was no ground in law on which he could be detained another hour. The stone was not rolled back to let him out. It was rolled back to let the world in to look.

Because God had sworn it. The third is that God had promised it, in Psalm 16, which Peter goes straight on to quote: God’s Holy One would not see corruption.

What it does not mean. Not possible for him to be held is not not possible to die. He really died. The blood ran out, the body went cold, friends made the arrangements, and women prepared spices for a job that genuinely needed doing (Luke 23:56). Anything less than a real death would leave the human race precisely where it was.

What does Christ’s resurrection mean for my own death? It means that death is not the end for anyone who belongs to him. Because he was raised, those united to him will be raised too, bodily, at his return (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and his body rests until the resurrection. There is no soul sleep and no purgatory in between; to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). So you may grieve at a Christian’s graveside, but not as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

On a Tuesday. Most of us carry one grave we cannot think about calmly: our own, or that of someone we love. This verse does not ask you to stop grieving. It tells you that death has already met a man it could not hold, and that if you belong to him it will not be able to hold you either.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David says concerning him, 'I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For David says concerning him. Peter settles a question about a man who died seven weeks ago by quoting a poem written a thousand years earlier, Psalm 16:8–11, by the method the whole New Testament uses.

The words fit the writer, and then overflow him. Psalm 16 is a psalm of trust, and it is genuinely David’s: he meant every word of it about himself. That is the ordinary way prophecy works in the Psalms. David could say my flesh also will dwell in hope and mean that God would bring him through the present trouble alive. What he could not do was make the sentence come true in the full sense the words will bear, and Peter is about to point at his grave to prove it.

Always before me. The psalm reads I have set the LORD always before me: a deliberate act of keeping God in view, not a feeling that he is near. It describes perfect trust in God, never broken, true of David in part, but fully true only of Christ. Even on the cross, when he bore the judgement our sins deserved and felt himself forsaken, he did not let go: his cry was still My God (Mark 15:34).

At my right hand. It is often pointed out that a soldier’s shield hung on his left arm, so his right side was the exposed one, and what a man in a battle line wanted above everything was somebody he trusted standing at his right, covering the side he could not cover himself. That is where the psalm puts God.

Heart, tongue and flesh. The gladness works outward until even the flesh is included, the part of a man that knows perfectly well it is going to die. This is not stoicism, which teaches a man to expect nothing and so not be disappointed. It is a man expecting his own body to have a future, even as it is laid in the grave.

What held the Son of God steady. These are words Peter puts into the mouth of Christ, so we are being told what held the Son of God steady on the road to the cross: not the absence of dread, for in Gethsemane he was greatly distressed and troubled (Mark 14:33–34), but the Father in view. That is also what is asked of anyone walking into something he cannot get out of: a diagnosis, a court date, a conversation he has been dreading for a month.

How do I set the Lord always before me when I cannot feel him near? By deliberate attention, not by feeling. Start the day by reading a few verses and turning them into prayer, so that the first voice you hear is his. Through the day, bring your thoughts back to him: before a hard conversation, in the car, at the hospital bed. Remind yourself of what is true whether you feel it or not, that he is at your right hand, that he is for you, that he has promised never to leave you (Hebrews 13:5). Feelings of his nearness come and go, even for mature believers. Setting him before you is something you do, and he honours it.

parallels.desc: I have set the LORD always before me

verseByVerse.quote: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not abandoned to Hades. Hades here is not hell. It is the realm of the dead; the psalm Peter is quoting says Sheol (Psalm 16:10), the place where the dead simply are. God would not leave him there.

See corruption. To see corruption (diaphthora) is to undergo decay; what is denied is not death but decay. Peter’s hearers knew what the sentence described: the dead were laid on a shelf in a rock tomb for a year until the bones could be gathered into a box. Martha warned Jesus that by the fourth day there would be an odour (John 11:39), and the women went out on the Sunday morning carrying spices (Luke 24:1); they were not expecting a resurrection. And when the tomb was opened, nothing had begun. Jesus was raised on the third day, before decay could set in.

He descended into hell. This verse lies behind the line in the Apostles’ Creed that has made congregations uneasy: he descended into hell. Nobody in the mainstream of the church has taught that Jesus went somewhere to be punished further after the cross; the punishment was finished there, and he said so: it is finished. Some read the phrase as meaning simply that he was truly dead and went where the dead go. Others, in the Reformed tradition especially, take it to describe the God-forsakenness of the cross itself, when he bore the wrath of God in our place. Others again have held that he went to announce his victory among the dead, drawing on 1 Peter 3:19, a passage read in several ways. And the psalm claims something more modest than what people fear: not that he would not go there, but that he would not be abandoned there.

Where did Jesus go between his death and resurrection? His body lay in the tomb. His human soul went, as he promised the thief, to paradise: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and he committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46). He did not go to a place of further suffering, and he did not go to give the dead a second chance; Scripture gives no such chance after death (Hebrews 9:27). His death was real and complete, body and soul truly separated, as ours will be. And because he has walked that road and come back, a believer facing death walks a road with his Lord’s footprints on it.

The paths of life. The word is plural, paths: roads, a whole country to walk in and not a bare survival. The path through death to life is fulfilled in Christ’s resurrection and ascension.

With your presence. In the Greek, the phrase is literally with your face. Suppose the resurrection delivered everything except that one thing: a body that never failed again, a world with no funerals in it, and God himself somewhere else, benevolent and absent. It would not be enough. The psalm describes the joy of the risen Christ not as a location or a condition but as a presence. Whatever else the life to come is, it is the end of God being somewhere else.
verseByVerse.note: Hades (Sheol) is the realm of the dead.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His tomb is with us. Peter now does the boldest thing in the sermon: he appeals to a landmark. David’s tomb was a real building on the southern ridge of the city, known to everybody in that street (Nehemiah 3:16); Peter could have raised his arm and pointed at it while he was speaking.

Two graves in one city. He has staked the argument on a grave anyone could visit that afternoon. David’s tomb is occupied: go and see. His argument needs the tomb of Jesus to be empty, and the earliest counter-story we know of, that the disciples stole the body, quietly admits that it was (Matthew 28:11–15). Legends usually need distance and time to grow. This claim was made in the town where the events happened, within weeks, in front of the people best placed to demolish it.

Being therefore a prophet. David is not merely a poet who happened to write past himself without noticing. He was a prophet, speaking by the Spirit (1:16); the Spirit of the LORD speaks by me, he said at the end of his life (2 Samuel 23:2). He knew, at least in part, what he was doing.

Sworn with an oath. He knew because he had been given a promise on oath: that God would set one of his own offspring on his throne, and that the throne would have no end (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 132:11). David wrote Psalm 16 as a man who had been told his family would produce a king whose reign would never stop, which is a promise that cannot be kept unless somebody in that family stops dying.

The hidden child. Look at what God had to steer in order to keep that oath. The royal line ran through adultery and murder in its first generation, through kings who burned their own children as offerings, through exile, when the throne stood empty for centuries and the family ended up as village carpenters. At one point the whole line came down to a single infant, hidden in the house of the LORD for six years while the queen who had killed every royal child she could reach ruled the country (2 Kings 11:1–3). The oath God swore to David hung on whether a hidden child would cry at the wrong moment.

Where Christians differ: is Christ on David’s throne now? Dispensational and other premillennial teaching holds that the promise of David’s throne will be fulfilled chiefly in a future earthly reign of Christ from Jerusalem during a millennium after his return. This commentary’s view: Peter says the oath to set David’s descendant on his throne was what David foresaw when he spoke of the resurrection (vv. 30–31), and that Jesus, raised and exalted to God’s right hand, now reigns (vv. 33–36). The throne of David is fulfilled in Christ’s present heavenly reign, which the New Testament calls the kingdom already come (Luke 1:32–33; Colossians 1:13; Hebrews 1:8–13). This is the amillennial reading, which takes the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a picture of Christ’s present reign. Christ reigns now, until his enemies are made his footstool, and his reign will be seen by all at his return, in the new creation. Brothers who expect a future millennium love the same King and await the same return, and the difference is held in charity.

Waiting on a promise that looks past saving. Anybody waiting on a promise of God that looks beyond rescue may take heart. The promise did not fail in exile, or while the throne stood empty, or while the last heir was a toddler hidden in the temple; it is kept, in the end, by a man from Nazareth whom this crowd had watched die.

What promises of God can I rely on in my own waiting? Rely on what God has actually promised in Scripture, not on what you wish he had promised. He has promised to forgive all who confess their sins (1 John 1:9), never to leave or forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5), to work all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), to give wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5), to complete the work he began in you (Philippians 1:6), and to raise you on the last day (John 6:40). He has not promised every specific outcome you pray for, such as a particular healing or a particular marriage. But every promise he has made is yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and the story of David’s line shows how far he will go to keep them.

For worship. David’s tomb is still sealed on the ridge, and his greater Son’s is open. But the story does not leave David there. The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of Man and come out (John 5:28–29), and on that day the son will call the father out of his grave. Among those who rise at his word will be the shepherd king who wrote of him, glad at last in the presence he sang about.
verseByVerse.note: David’s tomb was a known landmark in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: the LORD swore to David a sure oath

verseByVerse.quote: "he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He foresaw and spoke. The psalm is not an accident that happens to fit. David looked ahead and wrote of the Messiah’s resurrection, which means the resurrection was not the salvage of a wrecked plan. It was announced in Israel’s hymn book centuries before there was a tomb for it to empty. Jesus had taught the apostles to read the Old Testament this way: that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead (Luke 24:44–47).

In no one else. Fulfilled in Jesus, and in no one else. Every other son of David lies on the ridge.

We all are witnesses. Then Peter puts the psalm down and argues from the eleven men standing beside him. We all: not I, and not a report that reached him. The qualification for the vacancy in chapter 1 was exactly this: a man who had been with them the whole time and had seen the risen Lord (1:21–22). These are named men, in their own city, within weeks of the event, open to cross-examination from a crowd that may well have included friends of the men who arranged the execution. Scripture foretold it; eyewitnesses confirm it.

Men in a position to know. People say that nobody dies for a lie. In fact people die for lies constantly; the world is full of sincere martyrs for things that are not true. The real point is narrower and much harder to get round: these particular men were in a position to know whether it was a lie. A man may die for a doctrine he was taught and cannot check. He does not ordinarily die for a body he moved himself. And floggings, prisons, and for many of them, by early tradition, execution, are not the record of men who had the option of quietly correcting themselves.

An inheritance and a limit. The inheritance: Christian faith is not a philosophy that would survive the disproof of its own history. It rests on something that either happened outside a wall in Jerusalem or did not, and Peter is content for it to be tested. The limit: nobody today is a witness in the sense Peter means. What the church holds is the testimony of the men who were, written down while people who could have contradicted them were still alive. That is enough to build a life on; but its honest name is testimony received rather than experience possessed, and no believer should feel awkward saying so.

If I did not see it, how can my faith be certain? Because God has given you something better than a private sighting: the public testimony of chosen eyewitnesses, preserved by the Spirit in Scripture, and the Spirit himself bearing witness in your heart that it is true. Jesus said to Thomas, blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (John 20:29), and John wrote his Gospel so that you may believe (John 20:31). Your faith rests on the same event the apostles saw, through their words. That is not second-hand faith; it is the faith God intended for every generation after the first.

verseByVerse.quote: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exalted at the right hand. The right hand of God is the place of highest honour and power. But nobody in that street could see the exaltation. How can a crowd know it?

Seeing and hearing. Peter points at the noise. You cannot see a throne in heaven; you can hear a hundred and twenty Galileans speaking Parthian. The crowd came out looking for an explanation of a noise, and Peter tells them it is the sound of a coronation that has already taken place somewhere they cannot look. And only God pours out God’s Spirit: in Joel it was I, the LORD, who would pour it out (Joel 2:28), and here it is Jesus.

Received from the Father. Three persons are named in this single sentence, doing three different things: Jesus is exalted at the right hand of God, receives the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, and pours out the Spirit. The doctrine of the Trinity means that there is one God, existing eternally as three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God, distinct but never divided: not three gods, and not one person taking turns in three roles. It is not a later theory laid over the gospel. It is the shape of the gospel’s first sermon.

The coronation gift. An accession in the ancient world was marked by largesse: gifts scattered, debts remitted, prisoners released. Psalm 68, which Paul applies to the ascension, pictures the conqueror going up on high and receiving gifts among men (Psalm 68:18; Ephesians 4:8). The first recorded act of Jesus after his enthronement is to give, and what he gives is not a benefit but a Person: the coronation gift of a King who had nothing left to prove and gave anyway.

A receipt from the throne. Every time a believer understands a verse that was closed to him a year ago, or finds he wants to pray when he does not feel like praying, or discovers that a sin which used to own him has quietly loosened its grip, he is holding a piece of evidence about where Jesus is. That is Peter’s argument, and it did not stop working when the languages did. The Spirit’s presence in an ordinary life is a receipt, and the transaction it records took place at the right hand of God.

David did not ascend. Peter introduces his second psalm with the logic he used on the first. David’s body is on the ridge. David did not go up. So whatever the psalm is about, it is not about him; it is about the one he calls his Lord.

The Lord said to my Lord. This is Psalm 110:1, often said to be the Old Testament text most quoted in the New, and Jesus used it himself (Luke 20:41–44). The ESV prints the first in small capitals, the LORD says to my Lord: the first is the covenant name of God, the second a title for a master. So David, the king, with nobody above him in Israel, overhears God addressing somebody David himself has to call his master. Jesus had put that puzzle to the scholars in this city only weeks earlier: if the Christ is David’s son, how does David call him Lord? The son of David turns out to be the master of David.

How do I know the Spirit is in me? Look for the evidence Peter points to: the things only the Spirit produces. Do you confess that Jesus is Lord and mean it (1 Corinthians 12:3)? Do you, however weakly, love God and want to obey him? Do you call God Father with trust (Romans 8:15–16)? Is there some growth, however slow, in love, joy, patience and self-control? Do you love other Christians? These are not achievements that earn the Spirit; they are the fruit of his presence. Nobody has them perfectly, and they do not grow where the Spirit has not been at work. If they are there, even in seed form, the King has given you his gift. And if you are asking the question anxiously, the anxiety is itself a good sign: a heart dead to God does not worry whether it is alive to him.

On a Tuesday. When you feel far from God, remember that the Spirit was given as a gift from a King, not earned as a wage. He has not been withdrawn because you had a bad week.

parallels.desc: “Sit at my right hand”

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.' Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your footstool. The picture is concrete and it is not gentle. Ancient kings put their feet on the necks of defeated enemies (Joshua 10:24), and footstools were carved with bound captives. That is the image: not a negotiated settlement with the powers that oppose God, but their subjugation, placed under the feet of a man who is sitting still. Christ reigns now, until every enemy is subdued, the last being death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

The King who sits. And the sitting matters. The priests in the temple across the city never sat down at their work, because it was never finished; every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, but Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and sat down (Hebrews 10:11–12). Nor does until mean that the reign expires when the job is done; it means the reign is what does the job. He is not waiting for reinforcements. He is waiting for the last of it to be brought in.

Know for certain. The conclusion of the sermon. For certain (asphalōs) means beyond doubt, securely. It is the root Luke used when he told Theophilus he was writing so that he might have certainty (Luke 1:4). Peter is announcing a fact.

Both Lord and Christ. Lord was the title used in the Greek Old Testament for God, translating the divine name. Christ is the Messiah, the anointed king. Read carelessly the sentence sounds as though a good man was handed a divine job at Easter, and it is quoted today by those who say the church made Jesus God. It will not carry the weight, and three things show why.

The verb. The first is the verb. Made, in a sentence of this kind, is appointment language, and Greek uses it that way constantly. The Greek Old Testament says the LORD made Moses and Aaron (1 Samuel 12:6), which English Bibles render appointed. The Gospels say Jesus made twelve, meaning he appointed them (Mark 3:14). To be made Lord in this sense is to be installed in an office, not brought into existence.

The man writing it down. The second is the man writing it down. Luke has already told us, in the first volume of this same work, what an angel said over a newborn at Bethlehem: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord (Luke 2:11). Whatever Luke meant here, he cannot have meant that Jesus acquired those two titles that spring, because he had already used both of them of a baby in a manger.

Declared, not created. The third is what the resurrection is actually said to have done. Paul puts it precisely: Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4), with a verb built on the same root as the definite plan in verse 23. What is new at Easter is not the nature but the office, publicly entered. The eternal Son, who humbled himself, is exalted in his human nature to the highest place, and given the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). A king’s son is royal from birth and may be crowned years later; nobody at the coronation supposes the crown created the man.

This Jesus whom you crucified. This is not a statement about promotion but the closing move of a prosecution. A court in this city examined a man, found against him, and had him put to death. Heaven has reviewed the case. The verdict is overturned, and the prisoner has been seated on the bench. The judge under the new arrangement is the defendant from the old one.

What does it mean for me that Jesus is Lord? It means he has the right to rule every part of your life, and that he is able to. Lord is not a title you confer on him when you are ready; it is the office God has given him, and the only question is whether you will bow now, gladly, or later, unwillingly (Philippians 2:10–11). In practice, it means bringing your money, your sexuality, your time, your work, your plans and your fears under his word. But it also means that the one who rules you is the one who died for you. His lordship is not a tyrant’s; it is the rule of the Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep. To call him Lord is to be safe.

On a Tuesday. Is there an area of your life where Jesus is Saviour but not yet Lord? Name it, and bow to him there today. The hand that claims it was pierced for you, and the Spirit he poured out is in you to make the yielding real.

For worship. He has been given the name above every name, yet the first exercise of that power is not a reckoning. The crowd that hears what it has done is told that it may repent, be forgiven, and receive the very Spirit it had been jeering at an hour before. The first thing he does as Lord is offer his murderers himself.
verseByVerse.note: “Lord” was the title used in the Greek Old Testament for God’s name; “Christ” means the Messiah.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what to do. Peter calls them to repent and be baptised for the forgiveness of their sins, with the promise of the Spirit, and about three thousand receive the word. Luke then sketches the new community, devoted, generous and growing as the Lord adds to it day by day.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Four Marks of the Apostolic Church

Verse 42 names four practices, each with its definite article: the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. They are definite things a visitor could have been shown, and the church has rightly read them as the lasting shape of its life. The apostles' teaching, now the New Testament, governs everything else, so that no experience, however vivid, may correct it. The fellowship is a shared life the Spirit creates, and in this chapter it costs money within three verses. The breaking of bread is the Supper in which his death is proclaimed until he comes. The prayers are the church's dependence made audible. A congregation that quietly lets one of the four go will be the poorer for it, often without noticing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The immersion pools were standing ready on the morning three thousand needed baptising. Now: God does not wait for ideal conditions. He uses what is already to hand: a borrowed upper room, a set of ritual baths and a preacher with a provincial accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, "Brothers, what shall we do?" And Peter said to them, "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cut to the heart. The word (katenygēsan) means pierced, stabbed. It is the language of a blade, and the blade is the Spirit’s: when he comes, Jesus had said, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8). The crowd recognises its city’s guilt and its own share in it.

They looked on him whom they had pierced. Luke does not cite it, but the scene fits Zechariah closely. God promised to pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, so that when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child (Zechariah 12:10). John applies that verse to the spear at the cross (John 19:37). Here it comes true in order: the Spirit is poured out on Jerusalem, the city is shown the one it pierced, and the piercing turns back on the hearers’ own hearts. The pierced one is the one who has sent the Spirit to wound them in order to heal them.

Brothers, what shall we do? It is the right question, the best possible response to the gospel: the response of people who take it seriously enough to ask what it demands. They call the apostles brothers, as Peter had called them (v. 29). An hour earlier some in this crowd were calling these men drunk.

Repent. Repent (metanoēsate) means to change your mind, to turn around: a change of mind about Jesus, and about sin, leading to a change of life. Repentance is not penance, a payment made in tears. It is a turning of the whole self, from sin to God, from trusting yourself to trusting Christ.

Repentance for the religious. Look at who is being told to repent. Not pagans, but devout men, many of whom had crossed the world to keep this feast. Repentance is not only for people whose lives are obviously wrecked. It is possible to keep every festival and say every prayer and still have rejected God’s Christ, trusting your religion to do what only he can do. The moralist and the rebel stand in the same line here, and both are offered the same pardon.

Every one of you. Baptism publicly marks the turn and identifies the believer with Jesus: his death, his burial, his rising (Romans 6:3–4). In the name of Jesus Christ means by his authority, into union with him and under his ownership. Every one of you: each person who repents, individually. Nobody is baptised by proxy, and nobody comes in by belonging to a nation.

In the name of Jesus, and in the name of the Father, Son and Spirit. This is no contradiction of Matthew 28:19. In the name of Jesus Christ is not a different formula but a statement of whose disciple one becomes: to be baptised into Jesus is to be baptised into the God who raised him, the Spirit he poured out, and the Father who sent him. The earliest manual of church practice outside the New Testament prescribes the threefold name (Didache 7), and this chapter shows why: Jesus receives the Spirit from the Father and pours him out (v. 33), a scene that requires three persons.

For the forgiveness of your sins. Sins forgiven, all of them, even the sin of crucifying the Messiah, offered in full in the same breath in which Peter charges them.

The gift of the Holy Spirit. Not the gifts of the Spirit, but the gift who is the Spirit: the same Spirit poured out on the apostles that morning, given to every believer. The three thousand did not have to wait ten days; he was given to them as they repented and believed.

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some read this to mean that baptism itself brings forgiveness (baptismal regeneration), so that forgiveness depends on baptism. This commentary’s view: the preposition for (eis) can mean with a view to or in connection with. Throughout Acts forgiveness is received by faith (10:43; 13:38–39; 26:18), and Cornelius received the Spirit before baptism (10:44–48). Repentance and faith receive forgiveness; baptism is the God-given sign of it, closely linked, normally following at once. It is commanded, and no believer should neglect it, but it is not the cause of salvation.

Does the water wash sins away? No. Forgiveness is by grace through faith in the blood of Christ: everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name (10:43; Ephesians 1:7). That is why the dying thief was saved with no baptism at all (Luke 23:43). So we do not rest our hope in the water but in Christ, to whom the water points. To call baptism a sign, as the 1689 London Baptist Confession does (1689 29.1), means this: a sign points to something real beyond itself, as a wedding ring points to a marriage. It does not make the thing it marks; it is God’s kind way of assuring us that it is ours. Paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the infants of believers, also call it a seal, as the Westminster Confession does (Westminster 28.1), drawing on Romans 4:11, as a wax seal marks a letter as the king’s. Roman Catholic Christians, and some in the Churches of Christ, read the verse differently, holding that baptism actually conveys the new birth; the difference is real, and turns on whether the rite signifies grace or effects it. But Peter does not treat baptism as optional either. It is the first act of obedience of a new believer, the public flag of a changed allegiance.

I trusted Christ years ago but was never baptised as a believer. What should I do? Be baptised. You are not less saved for having waited, but the Lord commands it, and in the New Testament it is the normal first step of every believer (8:36–38; 16:33). Speak to your pastor or elders. If you were baptised as an infant and have since come to personal faith, you will want to weigh this carefully and humbly: we believe the New Testament pattern is baptism after repentance and faith, as here, and so we would encourage baptism as a believer. Paedobaptist brothers and sisters, out of real conviction, would not; respect them, and act on your own conscience before God, from Scripture.

On a Tuesday. No sin is too great to be forgiven. If there is something you have never believed God could forgive, bring it to him today, by name, and turn from it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You and your children. You: those present, people of the city that called for his death. Your children: the next generation, their descendants. The promise is the one Peter has just named, forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit.

All who are far off. All who are far off came to include the Gentiles, though it will take a vision and a centurion’s house to show Peter how far (10:28, 34). Paul takes the phrase from Isaiah 57:19 and tells us what closed the distance: you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13). The promise travels outward from Jerusalem because the one who made peace by his cross is doing the preaching, through every mouth that carries it.

Whom the Lord calls. The promise has its boundary, not ethnic or geographic but the call of God. That call is more than an invitation: through the preached word the Spirit opens the heart and makes a sinner willing to come, as the Lord opened Lydia’s heart (16:14). Peter commands all to repent (v. 38) and assures them that the promise rests on God’s call (see 2:21 on how the two fit). The gospel is universal in its offer; the Spirit is sovereign in its application.

Where Christians differ: baptism and children. Paedobaptists (Christians who baptise the infants of believers) read for you and your children as a covenant promise to believers’ infants, supporting infant baptism. This commentary’s view: the promise is to children as to everyone, whom the Lord calls: it is received by those who repent (v. 38), and those baptised were those who received the word (v. 41). Believer’s baptism is the New Testament pattern. Children of believers are in a place of great privilege, and the promise is for them as they come to faith. Paedobaptist brothers and sisters hold their view in good conscience, and we hold ours charitably.

The friendly disagreement. Presbyterians see an unbroken covenant pattern, the sign given to believers’ children then in circumcision (Genesis 17) and now in baptism; Baptists note the next clause, everyone whom the Lord our God calls, and baptise those who profess faith. The difference turns on how much the old covenant sign carries into the new. The point both sides shout together: the promise is sheer grace, and it is offered to you and yours.

What does this mean for my children? It means you may pray for them with great confidence, and raise them with great hope. They are not saved by being born to you, and they will need to repent and believe for themselves. But they live near the promise every day: they hear the gospel at your table, see it in your life, and sit under it in church. God very often calls the children of believers to himself, sometimes so early that they cannot remember not trusting Christ. So tell them plainly that the promise is for them, teach them the Scriptures (2 Timothy 3:15), pray with them and for them, and welcome every sign of real faith. When they profess it credibly, rejoice to see them baptised.

For worship. Jesus once said that he had other sheep, not of this fold, and that he must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice (John 10:16). The call in this verse is that voice. It went from the men who crucified him to peoples Peter had never seen, and it has never once failed to reach the sheep it was sent for.
verseByVerse.note: “All who are far off” came to include the Gentiles.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many other words. We have a digest, not the whole sermon: what survives takes about three minutes to read aloud. He kept going.

Save yourselves. Save yourselves from this crooked generation sounds in English like an instruction to perform a rescue. In Greek it is passive: be saved. Peter is telling them to let themselves be saved, to stop resisting a rescue that is being carried out on them. A man in a burning building is not told to put the fire out; he is told to stop arguing and be carried down the stairs. And the one doing the carrying is Jesus, made Lord and Christ (vv. 21, 36). That is the heart of the difference between grace and self-rescue, sitting inside a verse often quoted to prove the opposite.

From this crooked generation. Crooked (skolias) means twisted, perverse, and the phrase comes from the Song of Moses, where God calls his own covenant people a crooked and twisted generation (Deuteronomy 32:5). Peter lays Moses’ description of Israel on the devout Israel in front of him. A generation is not something a man can resign from. Nobody chooses his parents, his decade, or the assumptions he absorbed before he could examine them. He can only be taken out.

Received his word. Receiving the word, then baptism: faith first, the order Luke gives throughout Acts (on children, see v. 39).

Where do you baptise three thousand people in a city with no river? One practical question a reader may feel too foolish to ask. The answer is that Jerusalem was already built for it. The southern approach to the temple was honeycombed with stepped immersion pools cut into the bedrock so that pilgrims could purify themselves before going up; many have been excavated and can still be walked into today, and the great pools of Siloam and Bethesda lay within the city. The apostles did not have to improvise. The plumbing of the old covenant was standing ready on the morning the new one needed it.

About three thousand souls. When Moses came down from Sinai and found the nation dancing round a calf, about three thousand men fell that day (Exodus 32:28). The law came, and three thousand died. Here the Spirit comes, and three thousand live. Paul later reduced the principle to a sentence: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6).

What it does not mean. This verse has bruised many faithful people. Three thousand in a day is not the measure of a ministry. The same Spirit produced this and produced Jeremiah, who preached for forty years to a nation that would not turn, and was right the whole time. Numbers are God’s business and are not issued as a report card. What is asked of a preacher is what Peter did here: bear witness, keep exhorting, and leave the cutting of hearts to somebody better qualified.

How do I know whether I have truly received the word? Not by remembering a particular moment, though some do, but by what the word has done and is doing in you. Do you believe what it says about Jesus, that he died for sinners and rose again, and are you trusting him rather than yourself? Have you turned, however imperfectly, from the life you lived without him? Do you want to keep hearing his word and obeying it? Those who received the word that day went straight on to devote themselves to the apostles’ teaching (v. 42). The best evidence that the seed has taken root is that it keeps growing.

For worship. Pentecost was the feast of the wheat harvest, and Jesus had told his disciples what kind of harvest he meant to bring in: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). Seven weeks after the grain went into the ground, three thousand are gathered in a single day. Every one of them is fruit of his dying, and the harvest of that one death is still coming in.
verseByVerse.note: Three thousand died when Israel worshipped the golden calf at Sinai; now three thousand receive life.

parallels.desc: a crooked and twisted generation

verseByVerse.quote: And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they devoted themselves. Luke’s word (proskarterountes) means to stick at a thing, to hold on; it is used of the apostles refusing to be pulled off prayer and the word (6:4), and of Simon the magician attaching himself to Philip (8:13). It is not the vocabulary of attendance but of a man who has got hold of something and will not be prised off it, and the tense means they kept on doing it.

In the flow. The wind and the fire lasted a morning; what remained was a people. This is the first of several short summaries in Acts (4:32–35; 5:12–16) showing that the Spirit builds a community around the apostles’ word.

Four things you could be shown. Each has its definite article: the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. Not four qualities to aspire to, but four things you could have been taken to and shown.

To the apostles’ teaching. The apostles’ teaching comes first because everything else has to be measured against it. Three thousand brand-new believers had just witnessed wind, fire and a miracle of languages, and what they were put on was a syllabus: the correction of an overwhelming experience is not more experience but more truth. What they taught is preserved for us in the New Testament, so there is no way to be devoted to the apostles’ teaching and casual about Scripture.

And the fellowship. Fellowship (koinōnia) is a word worn thin by use. In this chapter it costs money within three verses. It means sharing, partnership, common life. It is not the conversation afterwards over coffee but a shared life in Christ, in which what belongs to one is genuinely available to another (v. 44).

To the breaking of bread. The breaking of bread almost certainly covers both ordinary meals and the Lord’s Supper, which in this period were not separated: the table where the bread was broken in remembrance was the table where supper was eaten (20:7; 1 Corinthians 11:20–26). Luke has used the phrase before: at Emmaus the risen Lord was known to them in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:30–35). Christ’s chosen memorial of himself is not a monument or a pilgrimage but the most ordinary act of a human day, and at that table he still makes himself known.

And the prayers. The prayers, plural and definite, very likely include the set hours of prayer at the temple, which the apostles were still keeping a chapter later (3:1), as well as their own gatherings. The first Christians did not invent a devotional life from nothing. They took the one they already had and prayed it to a Lord they could now name.

Not a stick. This is a description of what the Spirit produced in a healthy church, not a set of hoops to be cleared for approval. Nobody in this verse is doing these four things in order to be accepted. They had been forgiven that morning. This is simply what forgiven people turned out to want.

What if my church is weak in one of these? Most churches are stronger in some than others: rich teaching but thin fellowship, warm fellowship but little prayer, frequent meetings but shallow teaching. Do not leave at once, and do not grumble. Start by being devoted yourself in the area that is weak: come to the prayer meeting, open your home, take the Supper seriously, read the Scriptures with others. Speak graciously to your elders about what you long to see. And pray for your church. But if a church has abandoned the apostles’ teaching itself, denying the gospel or the authority of Scripture, then it has lost the first mark, and you should find a church that holds it.
verseByVerse.note: “The breaking of bread” likely included the Lord’s Supper within a shared meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And awe came upon every soul. The word can simply be rendered fear (phobos): reverence, a sense of God’s presence; the same reaction runs through the church again in chapter 5, on a far darker morning. This fear is not the dread of a prisoner before a hostile judge, for these people had just been forgiven. It is the trembling of people who have realised that the holy God is really among them, and that he has come near not to consume them but to save them.

Joy and fear together. The first church was joyful; Luke says so explicitly three verses later. It was also afraid. It did not experience the two as being in competition, and any picture of God that has to shed one in order to keep the other has quietly lost him.

Through the apostles. Were being done: a season rather than a single burst. And through the apostles specifically: the signs marked them as Christ’s authorised messengers (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4).

Jesus Christ heals you. The apostles knew whose power it was. A chapter later Peter tells the staring crowd not to look at him as though he had healed the lame man: the name of Jesus, by faith in that name, has made this man strong (3:12, 16); at Lydda he says, Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you (9:34). The wonders are the risen Lord’s own works, continued from heaven, and the awe that fell on every soul was awe at him.

Do such signs continue? Luke ties them to the apostles (5:12), and Paul calls them the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). Continuationist Christians believe they continue in the church. The more likely reading is that they confirmed the apostles’ message and ceased with the apostolic age, which is the cessationist position (that these sign gifts belonged to the apostles’ founding work), held charitably toward brothers who see it otherwise. God still heals in answer to prayer, as he wills, and we should pray for the sick with faith (James 5:14–15).

All things in common. In common (koina) means shared: they treated their possessions as available to one another. Three things need saying.

It was not compulsory. First, it was not compulsory. Peter says so outright a few chapters on, when Ananias sells a field and lies about the price: while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? (5:4). Luke is describing not a system imposed on a community but something a community did.

It did not abolish ownership. Second, it did not abolish ownership as such. They still had homes to break bread in two verses later, and Mary the mother of John Mark still has a house with a gate and a servant girl in chapter 12. This is selling as needs arose, not the founding of a commune.

None of that lets the reader off. Third, the text still says that these people held what they owned so loosely that men sold land in order to feed fellow believers they had met that month, and that in consequence there was not a needy person among them (4:34). A church can be perfectly orthodox about private property and completely unlike this.

Would anyone know? Which suggests a question, and it is narrower and less comfortable than the one usually asked. The question is not whether a Christian would give if he were asked. It is whether he would know. In a congregation of any size, is there anyone quietly going without whom nobody has noticed? The Jerusalem church knew, which means somebody had asked, and the asking is where the whole thing begins.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were selling. The tenses carry this verse: they were selling and distributing, continuous, repeated, as needs came up. A single dramatic renunciation has the great advantage of being over. What Luke describes is the far more expensive business of remaining permanently available.

As any had need. Not equally, not by formula: the measure is need, which means somebody had to know what the needs were, in a community close enough that a widow’s circumstances are not a private matter she has to raise herself.

The arrangement was not perfect. Within four chapters the distribution has broken down along language lines, the Greek-speaking widows overlooked, and the apostles had to restructure the leadership to put it right (6:1). Luke could have left that out. Radical love does not exempt an institution from needing structures, and the people who complained were right to complain.

Where Christians differ: was this communism? Some have seen here a model for Christian communism, or a rule that all Christians must give up private property. This commentary’s view: it was a spontaneous, voluntary expression of love, not a compulsory system imposed by any authority. It met real needs, perhaps of pilgrims who stayed on in Jerusalem. The abiding principle is generous, sacrificial sharing with fellow believers in need (2 Corinthians 8:13–15; 1 John 3:17), not a particular economic model.

Generosity as a symptom. This verse is often preached in a way that leaves Christians vaguely guilty about owning a house, which produces unease and no actual giving. These people did not resolve to become generous. They had, that spring, been forgiven an unpayable debt by the man their city had killed, and had been handed the Spirit of God as a free gift when what they had coming was judgement. Money went out of their hands because something enormous had come into them. Generosity here is a symptom, and symptoms are not produced by being scolded about symptoms.

How much should I give, then? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage for believers, but it sets the bar by grace, not by law. Give regularly, as the Lord has prospered you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give proportionately, more as you have more. Give cheerfully, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to the needs of your own church family and its ministry, and then more widely. Many Christians find a tenth a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. And keep some margin in your life so that you can respond when a real need appears, as the Jerusalem church did. Above all, look at the cross first: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).

On a Tuesday. Is anyone in your church in need? Not only money can meet it: a meal, a lift, an evening’s help, a spare room. Look at your diary and your bank statement this week, and ask the Spirit to make you more available. Your giving will never be perfect; only Christ’s was, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours, so ask this in gratitude, not as a test of your standing.
verseByVerse.note: Selling was voluntary and as needs arose, not the abolition of property.

parallels.desc: there will be no poor among you

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Attending the temple together. Two settings in one sentence, and the church has needed both ever since. In the temple, some thirty-five acres of stone, a man is one voice among thousands; they met in Solomon’s Portico (5:12). These are not people who have walked out of Israel’s worship but Jews who have found in the Messiah what the temple was for. The break comes later, and it is forced on them.

Where he had taught daily. That is where Jesus himself had taught every day in his last week (Luke 19:47), and Luke’s Gospel ends with the disciples continually in the temple blessing God (Luke 24:53). Now the church is back in those courts, because the Lord who taught there is still teaching, through them.

In their homes. A room where the loaf has to be passed from hand to hand and everybody present is known by name. Nothing the temple does can be done in the kitchen, and nothing the kitchen does can be done in the temple. Congregations tend to be strong in one and thin in the other, and to make a virtue of whichever they happen to have.

Day by day. The phrase appears twice, of their meeting and of the Lord’s adding. It describes what they did, not a rule for a modern week: nobody told them to meet daily; they wanted to.

Glad and generous hearts. Glad (agalliasis) is exultant joy, the leaping kind. Generous (aphelotēs), found nowhere else in the New Testament, means something like singleness, simplicity: the absence of a hidden agenda. It describes a table at which nobody is angling for anything, and anyone who has sat at the other kind of table will recognise that as rarer than it sounds.

Favor with all the people. It does not last. Within two chapters the apostles are under arrest; within five, Stephen is dead; within six, persecution has scattered the church. Luke is describing a season, not issuing a promise. It is a mistake to think a faithful church will always be liked, and an equal mistake to treat unpopularity as evidence of faithfulness: sometimes a church is disliked because it is faithful and sometimes because it is unpleasant. And for a church the wish to be liked is a quiet idol. The first church enjoyed the people’s favour without living for it, and when the favour turned to flogging, the apostles went out rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (5:41).

The Lord added. Not the apostles, not the preaching: the Lord added, and in this chapter the Lord is the one God has made both Lord and Christ (v. 36). Church growth is the risen Jesus’ own work, and being saved is in the present tense: day by day he kept on doing it. Peter had preached the sermon of his life, and when Luke summarises, the credit goes elsewhere.

If the Lord adds, what part do we play? The part he has given us, done faithfully. We preach the gospel, pray, welcome, love, and live in a way that commends Christ. The Lord uses all of it, and he usually saves people through the words and lives of ordinary believers. But we cannot make anyone a Christian; only he can open a heart. That frees us from two errors. One is laziness, as if God’s sovereignty meant we need do nothing; the Jerusalem church did a great deal. The other is anxiety and manipulation, as if growth depended on our technique. Plant and water faithfully, and pray for the Lord of the harvest to do what only he can do.

For worship. Everything in this chapter comes down from somewhere else: the wind, the fire, the languages, the cutting of three thousand hearts, and now the daily arrival of people who were being saved. The church did not launch itself and has never once grown itself. He was adding on the first morning of the church, and he has not missed a morning since.
verseByVerse.note: The believers still worshipped at the temple while meeting in homes.

2.theology: The Sovereignty of God at the Cross. Acts 2:23 holds two truths in one sentence. The cross happened “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”: God’s settled purpose, formed before the world began (1 Peter 1:20; Revelation 13:8), not God merely looking ahead to see what people would choose. Yet the guilt is wholly human: lawless hands did it, and Peter charges his hearers with it. God is not the author of sin, and sin does not escape his purpose. The worst thing people have ever done became the means of the greatest gift God has ever given.
2.examples:
Then: A harvest feast became the birthday of the church. Three thousand were gathered in.

Now: The same Spirit, the same word and the same call to repentance are at work every Lord’s Day, and the same Lord still adds to his church. The question for each congregation is whether it holds to the four things that first church did; the power behind them has not diminished.

3.title: The Lame Man and the Living Lord
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. <sup>2</sup>And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple. <sup>3</sup>Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms. <sup>4</sup>And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.” <sup>5</sup>And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them. <sup>6</sup>But Peter said, “I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!” <sup>7</sup>And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. <sup>8</sup>And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. <sup>9</sup>And all the people saw him walking and praising God, <sup>10</sup>and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. <sup>11</sup>While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s. <sup>12</sup>And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk? <sup>13</sup>The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. <sup>14</sup>But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, <sup>15</sup>and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses. <sup>16</sup>And his name—by faith in his name—has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all. <sup>17</sup>“And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. <sup>18</sup>But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. <sup>19</sup>Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, <sup>20</sup>that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, <sup>21</sup>whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago. <sup>22</sup>Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you. <sup>23</sup>And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people.’ <sup>24</sup>And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days. <sup>25</sup>You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ <sup>26</sup>God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.”
3.overview:
Luke now shows one of the “wonders and signs” of 2:43 in detail. At the hour of prayer Peter and John meet a man lame from birth, carried daily to beg at the temple gate called Beautiful. Peter has no money, but in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth the man is made strong, and he goes into the temple walking, leaping and praising God, as Isaiah had promised the lame would leap when God came to save.

A crowd gathers at Solomon’s Portico, and Peter preaches his second sermon. The power was not theirs but the name of Jesus, the Servant whom God has glorified and raised after the crowd disowned him. They must repent and turn back, that their sins may be blotted out. Jesus is the prophet like Moses and the offspring of Abraham, sent first to Israel to bless them by turning them from their wickedness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Healing at the Beautiful Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter gives a lame beggar not money but the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, and the man goes into the temple walking, leaping and praising God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Signs, and What They Are Signs Of

The healings in Acts are called signs, and a sign is not the destination but a board at the roadside with the destination's name on it. They are not the working of an impersonal force but the personal act of a risen King through men he has authorised, and they point to the repair of a world broken since Eden: a man's ankles made whole in Jerusalem are a down payment on a whole creation put right. They also confirmed the apostles' message, which is why Scripture ties them so closely to the apostles, and why the debate over whether such signs continue is about their purpose, never about whether God is able.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The man asked for alms and got his legs, and more: he went into the temple, through the gate that had been the limit of his days. He received his body back, and his place with it. Now: The church still meets people asking for the small thing because it is the only thing they know to ask for, and it still has no silver worth mentioning. What it has is a name.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The healing at the gate is a sign of what Jesus does for all who believe: those who could never walk into God’s presence are made whole and enter, praising God. And it sets off the first persecution (chapter 4).

The ninth hour. The ninth hour was about three in the afternoon, when the evening lamb was offered and the incense went up. It is also the hour at which Jesus died (Luke 23:44–46). Peter and John are going up to pray at the hour of the sacrifice, not long after the real Lamb died at that same hour. Luke makes nothing of it. He simply tells us the time.

Peter and John. Luke keeps putting these two together: partners in fishing (Luke 5:10), sent ahead to prepare the Passover (Luke 22:8), and later sent down together to Samaria (8:14). The loud one and, as far as we can tell, the quieter one: the church is not an arrangement in which everybody has to be the same shape.

A man lame from birth. Not an accident, not an illness he might have recovered from; he had never taken a step. The next chapter tells us he was over forty years old (4:22), which turns a phrase into a life. Somebody carried him to the gate every day (v. 2): years of lifting that nobody recorded.

The Beautiful Gate. The Beautiful Gate was most likely the great doorway of Corinthian bronze between the Court of the Gentiles and the Court of the Women; Josephus says it took twenty men to close it. So he sat at the most magnificent doorway in the Jewish world, and could not go through it. The law barred a lame priest from the altar (Leviticus 21:18), and an old saying kept the blind and the lame out of the house (2 Samuel 5:8). Whether or not any rule formally shut this man out, everyone knew where he belonged: outside, at the door, with his hand out.

To ask alms. People on their way to pray are at their most generous. So a man is carried daily to the threshold of the place where God had promised to meet his people, and set down where he can see in without going in: the most beautiful gate in the world, a man who cannot walk through it, and a system with nothing to offer him but the small change of the people who can.

What it does not mean. Nothing here suggests the man’s condition was a punishment, or that it revealed anything whatever about him personally, and Jesus had already refused that entire way of thinking: it was not that this man sinned, or his parents (John 9:3). What the exclusion at the gate exposes is not a defect in the man. It is a limit in the arrangement.

Outside the gate. The one who will open this gate was himself put outside one. Hebrews draws the line from the old sacrifices: the bodies of the animals were burned outside the camp, so Jesus also suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:11–12). The lame man sat at the edge of the holy place because the system had no room for him; the Son of God was led out to the edge of the city to make room for people like him. In his last week the blind and the lame came to him in the temple and he healed them (Matthew 21:14); this afternoon he does it again, from heaven.

Why were Peter and John still going to the temple? The first Jewish believers continued in the temple’s hours of prayer, both because it was their habit and because it was the place to reach their people. They had not left the faith of Israel; they had found its fulfilment. The break came gradually, through Stephen’s preaching, the persecution, and finally the destruction of the temple in AD 70. Hebrews later explains that the old system has become obsolete and is ready to vanish away (Hebrews 8:13), because Christ is the true temple, priest and sacrifice. Christians are not bound to Jewish worship practices, though there is wisdom in keeping regular times of prayer.

Who are the people at the gate today? Look for those who are near the church but cannot get in: the disabled person who cannot climb the steps or follow the service, the visitor who does not know the songs, the mentally ill man who makes people uncomfortable, the single mother who cannot manage the children alone in the pew, the elderly widow nobody visits. Many of them are carried to the door by someone else and left there. A church that loves Christ will notice them, make room for them, and above all bring them the gospel, which is the one thing that gets anyone through the gate.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the time of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer. The Beautiful Gate is not named elsewhere; it was probably a great bronze gate into the temple courts.

parallels.desc: the evening offering

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asked to receive alms. Giving alms was a religious duty, especially on the way to prayer (Matthew 6:2). He has asked ten thousand times, and the words will be out before he has properly looked at them.

Reasonable and enormously too small. He does not ask to be healed; it does not occur to him. Why would it? Nothing in forty years has suggested another possibility. He asks for what he expected: money. The request is entirely reasonable and enormously too small.

Our prayers are not the ceiling. This is not an argument that God is obliged to produce whatever larger things we ask, a doctrine with a great deal of wreckage behind it. The point is quieter. We do not know what to pray for as we ought (Romans 8:26), which is not a rebuke but a mercy, because it means our prayers are not the ceiling. God is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20). This man was still expecting coins when Peter took hold of his hand.

Why was he still lame? But a harder question sits in this verse, and it should not be walked past, because a suffering reader will find it whether or not anyone points at it. This man was carried to that gate day after day, quite possibly for years. Jesus of Nazareth went in and out of that temple repeatedly, feast after feast, for about three years. He may well have passed him. And the man was still lame on the afternoon Peter came by.

Healing is not delivered evenly. There is no way of making that comfortable. What can be said is that Scripture never presents God’s healing as a service delivered evenly. At a pool in this same city a multitude of sick people lay in five colonnades, and Jesus healed one man and left (John 5:2–9). Elisha cleansed a foreign general and left many lepers in Israel uncleansed, and Jesus said so in his first sermon, to a congregation that tried to throw him off a cliff for it (Luke 4:27).

Kept for an afternoon. Forty years of lameness looked, from inside, like forty years of nothing happening. It turns out to have been a life kept for an afternoon when his healing would be seen by the whole city, admitted as undeniable by the highest court in the nation, and followed by a sermon after which the men alone numbered about five thousand (4:4). He had not been overlooked. That is said about this man, and it is not a formula to lay over anyone else’s forty years: Luke tells us what God did here, not what he is doing in every case. But this delay had a shape, and from inside a delay there appears to be none.

Healed by a living Lord. Had this man been healed on one of the days Jesus taught in the temple, it would have been one more wonder in a ministry that ended on a cross. Done weeks after the crucifixion, by two men with nothing but a name, it could mean only one thing, and Peter draws it out at once: the Jesus they killed is alive, and his name has made this man strong (3:15–16). The beggar’s new legs became a witness to an empty tomb.

Should I keep praying for a healing that has not come? Yes, unless God has made it plain that the answer is no, as he did to Paul about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Jesus told a parable so that his people would always pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1), and James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14–15). Pray honestly, and keep praying. But pray as a child, not as a negotiator: ask for healing, and ask also for what God may be giving instead, endurance, his nearness, a deeper trust. And hold on to the certain promise behind all the uncertain ones. Every believer will be healed completely at the resurrection, when he will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).
verseByVerse.note: Beggars sat where worshippers passed, since giving alms was a religious duty.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, "Look at us." And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter directed his gaze. The verb (atenisas) is a fixed, deliberate stare, the word used of Stephen gazing into heaven (7:55). Most passers-by avoided looking at beggars. Peter looks him in the eye.

How the beggar’s pitch works. A beggar’s pitch is arranged so that nobody has to look at anybody: the hand goes out, the eyes go down, the coin drops from above. Both are protected by it, the giver from the person, and the beggar from the humiliation of being seen.

Look at us. Peter dismantles the arrangement before there is any healing on offer. Look at us is not a request to be admired. It turns the man’s hope toward the two men who are about to give him the name of Jesus.

Looked at by the Lord. Peter had learned this look somewhere. On the night of his denial, as the rooster crowed in the high priest’s courtyard, the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Luke 22:61), and Peter went out and wept bitterly. The man who now fixes his eyes on a beggar has himself been looked at by Jesus at his worst and not discarded. And the look serves a name: Peter draws the man’s eyes to himself only so that, a moment later, he can turn them past himself to Jesus of Nazareth.

Attention before help. This is not a method to be copied for results, but the order travels: attention comes before help. The church cannot do anything for people it will not look at, and every person at the gate is made in the image of God.

Expecting to receive something. Then the man’s side of it. He is wrong about what and entirely right about who. God has a long record of meeting people exactly there.

Should I give money to people who beg? Scripture commands generosity to the poor (Proverbs 19:17; Galatians 2:10), and it also calls for wisdom, because some gifts help and some harm. There is no single rule. Sometimes giving a little money is right; sometimes buying food, sharing a meal or pointing someone to a church mercy ministry or local shelter does more good; sometimes the most loving thing is to give through an organisation that knows the person’s situation. What is never right is contempt, or walking past as if the person were not there. Whatever you give or do not give, look the person in the eye, speak kindly, and if you can, ask his name.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!" And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have no silver and gold. The leading apostle of the church, in the days of its greatest power, is standing at the temple gate without money; what money was given went to the needy (2:45; 4:35). And he does not brush the man’s need aside either. He gives what he has, and it is far more than was asked for.

In the name of Jesus Christ. A name in that world stood for the person and his authority, as a king’s officer acted in the name of the king. Peter is not reciting an incantation; he has no power of his own, and he will say so (v. 12). He acts on his master’s authority, in public. Jesus is the healer, from heaven.

Of Nazareth. And see which name he uses. Of Nazareth: the address, the sneer, the thing written on the board over the cross not long before for the whole city to read on its way past (John 19:19). Peter uses the name that had been used to dismiss and execute him, and it puts a lame man on his feet. The despised man from the despised town is the Lord of all.

Raised him up. Then the touch. Peter does what he had watched Jesus do, when Jesus took Peter’s own mother-in-law and Jairus’s daughter by the hand (Mark 1:31; 5:41). And raised him up (ēgeiren) is the word this same chapter uses of the resurrection (3:15). The gesture is a small enactment of the thing being announced: a man who cannot get up is pulled upright by somebody who has met the one God raised.

Feet and ankles. Luke, whom Paul calls the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), gets specific, using a term for the ankle bones found nowhere else in the New Testament. The healing was instant and complete, of a condition from birth.

Silver and gold have I none. An old story tells of a medieval pope showing a visitor the treasures of Rome and remarking that the church could no longer say silver and gold have I none, and being answered, neither can she now say rise up and walk. Whether it happened or not, the point is worth keeping. Power in the church has never been carried in its purse.

What it does not mean. Set this beside the teaching that God’s favour shows itself in wealth. The man through whom this miracle came has nothing in his pockets. Not that poverty is holiness: this same church will handle money carefully. But what Peter had to give was not for sale.

The name is not a lever. Luke supplies the guard himself: men at Ephesus who heard about the name and tried to work it as a formula, adjuring evil spirits by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims, and it went badly for them (19:13–16). The name works here because Peter belongs to the one who owns it, and it has never once worked for anybody who wanted the effect without the allegiance.

Do healings like this still happen, and should churches have healing ministries? God still heals, in answer to prayer and by ordinary means such as medicine, as he wills. But this healing was a sign that confirmed the apostles’ message about the risen Christ. Many Christians believe such gifts continue in the church; the more likely reading is that healings of this apostolic kind, instant, complete, at a word, belonged to the foundational age, and that position, cessationism, is held charitably toward those who see it differently. The church today prays for the sick (James 5:14–15), and expects God to answer; but no one holds the apostles’ gift.
