What does it mean to pray in Jesus’ name? It is not a phrase to add at the end like a password. It means coming to God on the basis of who Jesus is and what he has done, not your own worthiness; asking as his representative, for things that fit his character and purposes; and trusting his authority, not your technique. That is why Jesus promised that whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son (John 14:13). A prayer that is truly in his name is a prayer he would sign, and you can pray it with great boldness.

For worship. A man asked two strangers for the price of a meal, and was answered from the throne of God. The power that raised Christ from the dead came down to a pair of ankle bones, at three in the afternoon, at the door of a building he had sat outside for years. That is how low the risen Lord’s reign stoops. What he gives the poor is not silver or gold but his own strength, put into their feet.
verseByVerse.note: “In the name of” means by his authority and power.

verseByVerse.quote: And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leaping up. Luke piles up seven verbs in one sentence, and the pile is the point: this is a man who had never walked a step.

A man who never learned to walk. A man lame from birth has never learned the balance and coordination that are learned in infancy over months of falling down. He does not fall down. He is given the legs and the use of them in the same instant, and his first instinct with a working body is to jump.

Then shall the lame man leap like a deer. Isaiah had used that very picture: then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isaiah 35:6). Isaiah 35 is a poem about a desert that blossoms and the ransomed of the LORD coming home to Zion with everlasting joy upon their heads. The leaping man is one line in a song about the end of exile.

The lame walk. And Jesus had already claimed that song as his own. When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether he was the one who was to come, Jesus answered with Isaiah’s list: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk (Luke 7:22). So when a lame man leaps in the temple courts weeks after the crucifixion, the sign adds one thing: the one who was to come has not stopped coming. What breaks out at the Beautiful Gate is a fragment of Isaiah’s homecoming arriving early, under the name of the King who leads it.

Entered the temple. Set down at that gate morning after morning and never once through it, he now walks in, on his own feet, making a scene. It is a picture of salvation: you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ, and through him we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:13, 18). A believer may come to God in prayer at any hour, as a child to his father, with no gate, priest or animal sacrifice in between, because Christ’s blood has opened the way (Hebrews 10:19–22).

Walking and leaping and praising God. He does not go home, or look for work; he goes into the house of God and praises, and Luke says it twice in two verses (vv. 8–9). Not praising Peter, but God.

Why don’t I feel like leaping any more? Because joy fades when memory fades, and familiarity dulls even the greatest gifts. The answer is not to manufacture excitement but to remember. Go back over what you were without Christ: guilty, far off, without hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12). Recall specific mercies, the answered prayer, the sin forgiven, the dark year he carried you through. Read the Gospels and watch what he did for you. Sing truths, not just feelings. And sit near those who have just come to faith; their wonder is contagious. Joy in God is not always loud, but it grows wherever grace is remembered.

parallels.desc: then shall the lame man leap like a deer

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people saw him walking and praising God, and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the people saw. These two verses are the hinge on which the next chapter turns: a public miracle, at the busiest hour, in the busiest place.

They recognised him. That word recognised carries the whole evidential weight of the chapter. He had been at that gate day after day; every worshipper going up to pray had stepped round him. There was no room for a substitution or mistaken identity.

We cannot deny it. The council runs into this the following morning. Hostile, with every motive to find a hole in the story, it examines the case and concludes that a notable sign has been done, that all Jerusalem knows it, and that we cannot deny it (4:16). It then forbids the apostles to speak, which is not what men do when they have exposed a fraud.

The same Jesus, still at work. Luke opened this book by calling his Gospel an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (1:1), and here is what he meant. The scene at the gate has happened before. When Jesus healed a man born blind, his neighbours said, Is this not the man who used to sit and beg? (John 9:8). The hands are different now, but the work is the same, because the worker is the same. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (Hebrews 13:8), and the risen Lord is still straightening legs from the right hand of God.

Wonder and amazement. The first word means a stunned wonder; the second (ekstasis) is being put out of one’s own mind. Neither is faith, and Luke never confuses the two: a crowd can be amazed at an act of God and still need telling what it means. Which is why the miracle takes ten verses and the sermon takes fifteen.

Why doesn’t God do public miracles today to convince sceptics? Partly because miracles do not by themselves produce faith: the council saw this one, admitted it, and still refused to believe. Jesus said that if people will not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). And partly because the great public signs have already been given and recorded. The healing at the gate, and above all the resurrection, were done in the open and written down so that you may believe (John 20:31). God now works chiefly through his word and Spirit, and his most persuasive evidence today is often a changed life: a man who was known for one thing and is now known for Christ.

On a Tuesday. A changed life opens doors for the gospel. The people who knew you before Christ are the ones best placed to notice what he has done, and they are also the ones you are most tempted to hide it from. Do not hide it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Solomon’s Portico Peter refuses the credit: the God of their fathers has glorified his servant Jesus, whom they disowned and killed and God raised. Peter calls them to repent and turn back, that their sins may be blotted out, until the Christ returns to restore all things.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus as the Fulfilment of the Covenant with Abraham

Peter closes on the promise to Abraham, in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed (v. 25; cf. Genesis 22:18; 28:14). The gospel is not God abandoning his promises to Israel but their arrival: the first plan reaching its appointed date. One covenant of grace runs from Genesis to Revelation and finds its full form in Christ, which is why Peter can preach this to Jews in the temple courts without once suggesting that they should change religion.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who bore the most direct responsibility there was, you denied the Holy and Righteous One, then called them brothers three verses later and told them the blessing was coming to them first. Now: A gospel that cannot name what a man has done has nothing to forgive him for; a gospel that names it and leaves him standing there is not the gospel at all. Peter does both in one sermon, and the second half is longer than the first.

verseByVerse.quote: While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon's. And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he clung to Peter and John. The first thing Luke tells us about the healed man is that he would not let go. A man dependent his whole life has just been made independent, and his instinct is to hang on to the two people who did it.

Solomon’s Portico. Solomon’s Portico was the long covered colonnade down the eastern side of the temple platform. It is where Jesus was walking at the Feast of Dedication when the crowd demanded that he tell them plainly whether he was the Christ, and picked up stones to kill him for the answer (John 10:23–31). Peter is preaching Christ on the very stones where Christ was nearly stoned for preaching himself.

In the flow. As at Pentecost, the sign draws the crowd and the word explains it. The sermon (vv. 12–26) moves from who did this (vv. 13–16), to what they had done and what God did with it (vv. 17–18), to what they must now do (vv. 19–26); and it lights the fuse of chapter 4 (4:1).

Why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us? Then the refusal, and it repays taking word by word. Peter refuses the attention.

As though by our own power or piety we have made him walk? Peter disclaims two things, and the second is the one people miss. He disclaims the power, which anybody would expect. He also disclaims the piety: the word means godliness, personal devotion, and that is the harder disclaimer, because it is the flattering one. A crowd watching a miracle will always conclude that the men involved must be unusually holy, and that is a conclusion which is extremely pleasant to leave uncorrected. Miracles were not rewards for holiness.

A matter of information. Remember who is speaking. This is the man who, a short walk from where he now stands, told a servant girl that he did not know Jesus (Luke 22:57). If any man in Jerusalem had reason to know that his own godliness was not the operative factor in anything, it was Peter. The deflection is not modesty. It is a matter of information.

Who are people looking at? But consider what kind of deflection it is, because there is a counterfeit that looks similar and achieves the opposite. Peter does not say it was nothing, and he does not perform the shuffling embarrassment that draws quite as much attention as accepting the credit would have done. He redirects. He names somebody else, immediately and at length, and the crowd’s attention goes where he sends it. False modesty keeps the light on the man by making him interesting; genuine deflection moves it. The test of true ministry is simple enough: when the sentence is finished, whom has it made much of?

Because he went to the Father. Peter can deflect so completely because he knows where the power came from. Jesus had said that whoever believes in him will do the works he does, and greater works than these, because I am going to the Father (John 14:12). The healing at the gate is that promise beginning to be kept: the work of a Lord who acts from the Father’s side through the men he left behind.

How do I accept thanks without stealing glory? Simply and honestly. When someone thanks you, you need not deny that you did anything; say thank you, and where it is true and natural, say who really did it: I am so glad God used it, or the Lord was kind to us. Do not fish for more praise, and do not perform humility. Then, privately, hand the compliment straight on to God in prayer. Keep a short memory of your successes and a long memory of his mercies. And watch your heart when you are not thanked: if that stings badly, it is a sign you were collecting the glory for yourself.
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s portico was a covered colonnade along the east side of the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of our fathers. Peter opens with the oldest name in Israel’s vocabulary. It is the name God gave himself at the burning bush (Exodus 3:6, 15). Peter is not announcing a new God or a new religion; he is telling a Jewish crowd in the Jewish temple that the God they have worshipped all their lives has just acted in Jesus.

Glorified his servant Jesus. The term (pais) sits very close to the opening line of the last of Isaiah’s Servant Songs in the Greek Old Testament: behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted (Isaiah 52:13). That sentence runs straight on into Isaiah 53: the wounds, the silence before the shearers, the Servant bearing the sin of many. For hearers who knew that chapter, one word put it into the air. Jesus is the Suffering Servant, now glorified by God in his resurrection and in the healing done in his name.

In the presence of Pilate. God glorified him; you denied him. And the comparison with Pilate is deliberate and brutal. A pagan governor with no covenant, no Scriptures and no particular appetite for justice had worked out that the prisoner ought to be let go (Luke 23:4, 14–16, 22). The covenant people insisted otherwise, and many listening remembered it.

Denied. One word in the charge changes the temperature of the whole sermon. Denied is the word Luke used of Peter himself in the high priest’s courtyard: but he denied it, saying, Woman, I do not know him (Luke 22:57). Peter is accusing a crowd of a sin whose exact name is written against him, and he has been forgiven for it by the man he is now preaching, which is why he can say this to their faces and call them brothers four verses later.

Is the God of the Old Testament the same as the Father of Jesus? Yes, and this verse says so as plainly as anything in Scripture. Some, from the ancient heretic Marcion to modern writers, have set an angry Old Testament God against a loving New Testament Jesus. Peter knows nothing of it. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is the God who glorified Jesus. The same God shows mercy and judgment in both testaments: the Old Testament is full of his steadfast love, and the New Testament speaks of his wrath as plainly as the Old. Jesus himself said the Scriptures bear witness about me (John 5:39). Read your whole Bible as one story, told by one God, about one Saviour.

On a Tuesday. If you have been avoiding the Old Testament, start this week with Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12, and read it with the cross in view.
verseByVerse.note: “His servant” echoes Isaiah’s Servant, who would be “lifted up” and glorified.

parallels.desc: my servant shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: "But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Holy and Righteous One. The Holy One (Psalm 16:10; Mark 1:24) and the Righteous One (Isaiah 53:11; 7:52; 22:14) were both used of the Messiah, and both are the opposite of what a court is supposed to condemn. The Holy One is the very name of Israel’s God in Isaiah (Isaiah 1:4), and that holiness was in the man they handed over: the only sinless man who ever lived. You denied him: the second time in two verses, because the denial was a choice, made out loud, in daylight.

A murderer granted to you. That is Barabbas (Luke 23:18–19, 25), and nobody needed reminding. A guilty man was released and an innocent man executed in his place, at the crowd’s request. Barabbas is the first man who could say, in the most literal sense, that Jesus died in his place. What the crowd arranged as a miscarriage of justice turned out to be a working picture of the atonement, Christ putting sinners right with God by taking their place, and they built it without the faintest idea what they were making.

The Author of life. The word (archēgos) is the founder, the pioneer and prince, the one who goes first and opens a way; Hebrews uses it of the founder of our salvation (Hebrews 2:10). Peter sets it directly against killed: life itself put to death. They spared the murderer and killed the life-giver.

To this we are witnesses. Then the reversal and the apostolic signature: we saw him alive.

What it does not mean. These verses have been used to do enormous harm. You denied, you killed: sentences of this kind have been read out from pulpits in Christian Europe and followed within days by violence against Jewish neighbours. Read the paragraph they sit in. The speaker is a Jew. The audience is Jewish. The setting is the Jewish temple at the hour of Jewish prayer. He calls them brothers; he says in the next breath that they acted in ignorance; he tells them God sent his servant to you first; and the entire sermon is a plea that they should be blessed. This is a prophet of Israel addressing Israel, as Isaiah called its rulers the rulers of Sodom (Isaiah 1:10), and nobody has ever thought Isaiah an enemy of the Jews. Peter is not indicting a people across the centuries. He is telling the men in front of him what they did, in order to tell them what may now be done about it.

Am I like Barabbas? In the way that matters most, yes. Every believer is a guilty person set free because an innocent one took his place. Scripture says Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18), and that God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). He bore the penalty our sins deserved, the wrath of God against sin, so that we would never have to bear it. Barabbas walked out of prison with nothing to do but go home. You walk out with everything to live for, and a Saviour to thank.

verseByVerse.quote: "And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith in his name. This is one of the most tangled sentences in Acts, and a reader who finds it hard to follow is not being slow: Peter doubles back on himself, getting the name in twice and the faith in twice in his hurry to make sure the credit lands in the right place. The name of Jesus, his person and power, made the man strong; faith in his name was the means. The power is Christ’s; faith is the hand that receives it.

Whose faith? Underneath the tangle is a question that has to be settled, and it is a pastoral question of the first order. It cannot straightforwardly be the man’s, at least not before the healing. Look back at verse 5. He was expecting to receive something from them: a coin. He had no expectation of healing, had not asked for it, did not know it was available, and had, as far as Luke tells us, no opinion whatever about Jesus of Nazareth. He was not healed because he believed hard enough. The faith in view is most probably the apostles’, and perhaps the man’s as he responded when Peter took his hand.

Through Jesus. Whatever faith is operating in this verse comes through Christ. Even the faith is his gift: by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). That does not mean God believes for us. It means he opens our eyes to see Christ as he is, so that we trust him, as the Lord opened Lydia’s heart (16:14).

What it does not mean. An entire style of teaching is built on the opposite reading, and it wounds people badly. It tells the sick that they are not healed because their faith was insufficient; it sends them home from a meeting worse off than they came, carrying the illness and an accusation on top of it. It should be said plainly that this verse cannot be used that way. Here is a man whose healing Peter credits in so many words to faith in the name of Jesus, and an hour earlier he had shown no interest in the name at all.

Perfect health. The word (holoklēria), found nowhere else in the New Testament, means wholeness: sound in every part. Not managed, not improved: whole, and in the presence of you all, public and checkable, since the man is standing there still holding on to him.

What part does faith play when I pray for healing? Pray in faith, trusting that God is able and good, as James tells us to (James 5:15). But faith is trust in God, not a force that guarantees a particular result. Paul had great faith and prayed three times, and his thorn was not removed; Timothy had a weak stomach and was told to take a little wine (1 Timothy 5:23); Trophimus was left ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). So never conclude that someone remains ill because they did not believe enough, and never say it to them. Ask boldly, submit humbly, and keep trusting God whatever the answer, because his love is proved at the cross, not by the outcome of a particular prayer.

For worship. The name of Jesus took a man who had never stood and made him sound in every part. That is how our Lord saves: not by patching, but by making new. What he did for one man’s ankles he will do for the whole body of every believer on the day of resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, brothers. Here the sermon turns, and it turns on one word. Two verses ago they were the people who denied the Holy One and killed the Author of life. Now they are family, fellow Jews, brothers. The facts have not changed; Peter has arrived at the reason he was reciting them.

You acted in ignorance. This is not an acquittal, and Peter does not present it as one; he has just spent three verses establishing precisely what they did. It means they did not know who Jesus truly was, and its force lies in how Israel’s law handled the distinction.

Two kinds of sin. For sin committed unintentionally, through ignorance, there was a sacrifice and atonement: the offender brought his offering and was forgiven. For sin committed with a high hand, in open defiance, the law made no provision; that man was to be cut off from among his people (Numbers 15:27–31). So when Peter says you acted in ignorance, he is telling a crowd who have just realised they killed the Messiah which side of that line they stand on, and handing them the only door the law of Moses ever left open.

Father, forgive them. Paul makes the same judgement: none of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). And Luke alone records the prayer from the cross that says it first and most simply: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). Some early copies lack the sentence, but it is very old and it is what the rest of the New Testament assumes. Peter is preaching his master’s own prayer back over the heads of the men it was prayed for.

Ignorance is not innocence. Two guards. First, ignorance is not innocence. Paul says of his own persecuting years that he received mercy because he had acted ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:13), which is a sentence about mercy, not about acquittal; he still called himself the foremost of sinners. Second, Scripture is perfectly capable of condemning sincere ignorance, saying elsewhere of Israel that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Romans 10:2). Ignorance opens a door. It does not walk anybody through it.

What God foretold. All the prophets point to a suffering Messiah (Luke 24:25–27; 1 Peter 1:10–11). God fulfilled his own word through their ignorant wickedness. Both are true at once, and Peter does not choose between them.

The man who fears he cannot be forgiven. A reader frightened that he has done the thing which cannot be forgiven should look hard at who is being addressed. These people had shared in the judicial murder of the Son of God and chosen a murderer over him. And they are being called brothers, and offered forgiveness weeks later, by one of his friends. Whatever the unforgivable sin may be, it is evidently not this.

What is the unforgivable sin, then? Jesus spoke of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28–30), when religious leaders, faced with his plain works of power, attributed them to Satan. It is not a single careless word or a terrible deed done in weakness. It is a settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s clear testimony to Christ, persisted in until the heart no longer wants forgiveness at all. That is why it cannot be forgiven: not because Christ’s blood is too weak, but because the person refuses the only remedy. If you are worried that you have committed it, your worry is itself strong evidence that you have not. Come to Christ: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

On a Tuesday. When someone wrongs you, consider whether they truly knew what they were doing, and pray for them as Jesus prayed for his executioners.

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repent therefore, and turn back. Two commands, not one said twice. Repent (metanoēsate) names what happens in the mind: a reversal of judgement. Turn back (epistrepsate) names what happens to the feet: the thing a man does in a street when he realises he has been walking the wrong way. The mind changes, and then the body goes somewhere different, away from sin and towards God in Christ. A repentance that never reaches the feet has stopped halfway; and a change of direction with no change of mind is only a new set of habits, and will not last the winter.

In the flow. Therefore ties the command to everything before it: because the Servant they killed is alive and his name has made this man strong, the door is open. It is the same call as at Pentecost (2:38).

What it does not mean. Neither word means feeling bad. Sorrow often comes with repentance and there is nothing wrong with it, but a man can be extremely sorry and turn round nothing at all, and Scripture has a name for that: worldly grief produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Nor is this penance: Peter is not asking them to pay for the crucifixion. He is telling them to change their minds about the man they crucified and to walk the other way.

Blotted out. The word (exaleiphthēnai) means wiped away, and the picture is exact. Ancient carbon ink sat on the surface of papyrus, and a wet sponge took it off and left the sheet clean. Not the debt reduced, not the file closed and put in a drawer it can be fetched out of: wiped off. David prayed for it: blot out my transgressions (Psalm 51:1, 9). God promised it: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isaiah 43:25). And at the cross he did it, cancelling the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14).

Wiped by the death they demanded. The record that is wiped away was nailed to a cross, and it was the cross their own city had shouted for in front of Pilate (Luke 23:21). The death they caused is the death that cleans their page. Their sin is not overlooked; Jesus himself, crucified at their demand, is the way it is removed. There is no forgiveness anywhere except through the man they rejected, and no rejection of him so complete that his blood cannot wipe it out.

The private file. Ask a man at eleven in the morning whether his sins are forgiven and he will say yes. Ask him what happens at three in the morning, when a particular memory arrives, the thing he said, the person he damaged, the year he does not talk about, and a different answer comes out. He agrees that God wiped the record, and goes on consulting a copy he keeps privately, and calls it humility. It is not humility. It is a quiet insistence that the sponge did not work. If the record can come off the page for a crowd whose city murdered the Son of God, the private file a believer keeps on himself proves nothing except that he has not yet fully believed the sentence. If that is you, the struggle does not mean you are unforgiven; it is a weak faith wrestling with a strong memory, and Christ does not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20).

How do I stop keeping my own copy? Start by naming the thing to God plainly, once more if you need to, and then thank him that it is gone: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). Where you can, put right what you damaged, because restitution is part of repentance. Then, when the memory comes at three in the morning, answer it with Scripture rather than argument: as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us (Psalm 103:12). Remember that your accuser is not God; the Lord’s verdict on you in Christ is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Regret may remain for a while; guilt has been wiped off the page. If the memory still crushes you, speak to a pastor or a mature friend. You were not meant to carry it alone.

Is it fair that men who called for the cross could be wiped clean so quickly? It would not be fair if the forgiveness were cheap, and it was not. The record was wiped because it was nailed to a cross, and the one nailed there was the man they had rejected (Colossians 2:14). God did not lower his standard to forgive them; he met it himself, in his Son. And the objection often hides another: that the person raising it needs the sponge less. Peter’s sermon will not allow that. The respectable worshipper on his way to the three o’clock prayers needed the same blotting out as the man who shouted at Pilate, for there is no distinction: all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:22–23). Grace is not unfair to the good. It is the only hope of anyone.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you have repented of in your mind but not yet with your feet: a habit, a relationship, a way of speaking? The record against you was nailed to Christ’s cross; turn today, leaning on the Spirit he has given rather than on fresh resolutions.

parallels.desc: I am he who blots out your transgressions

verseByVerse.quote: "that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Times of refreshing. Two promises come out of that turning. The first is times of refreshing. The word (anapsyxis) means a breathing space, relief from pressure; the Greek Old Testament uses it when the plague of frogs stopped and Pharaoh saw that there was a respite (Exodus 8:15). And the relief comes not from a change in circumstances but from the presence of the Lord, which is the difference between a man whose troubles have lifted and a man who has stopped being alone inside them. The blessings of salvation come now, in measure, and finally at Christ’s return.

The Christ appointed for you. This is the second coming: the one appointed beforehand as their Messiah will be sent from heaven again.

Whom heaven must receive. The second promise says how long Jesus stays in heaven. The must is the word of divine necessity, the same sort of must that stood over the cross: there is an appointed span and he is keeping it, which settles every claim that he has quietly returned already. Then comes the restoring of all things (apokatastasis): the renewal of all creation, which Jesus called the new world (Matthew 19:28) and John the making of all things new (Revelation 21:5).

Spoken by the prophets. Isaiah, among many: behold, I create new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). The restoration is not a new idea of the apostles. It is the old promise of the prophets, now attached to the return of Jesus.

Will everyone be saved in the end? That phrase, restoring all things, deserves a note, because it is the anchor text of those who teach that in the end everyone will be saved and hell will empty. The Greek behind it gave the doctrine its historic name, and it has been pressed into service from Origen’s day to our own. The hope is understandable; more than one Christian has privately wished it were so. But Peter defines his own term two verses later, and he leaves no room for it: every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people (v. 23). A man does not promise universal salvation and then, in the next breath, warn of being cut off. The restoration he means is the one the prophets promised: the renewal of a broken creation, the world put right. It is the healing of the world, not the reversal of the judgment; and this whole sermon is a plea to repent precisely because that judgment is real.

Where Christians differ: restoration of all things. Some (universalists) take restoring all things to mean that every person will eventually be saved. Others (dispensationalists) take it as an earthly millennial kingdom for Israel. This commentary’s view: the restoration is of all things about which God spoke by the prophets, the renewal of creation, which the prophets also say includes judgment on the wicked (Isaiah 66:24). And the next verses warn that those who refuse Christ will be destroyed (v. 23). It is the new creation at Christ’s single return, not the salvation of all, nor an interim kingdom. Dispensational believers share the same hope of Christ’s return, and the difference with them is held in charity.

Does Christ’s return depend on Israel’s repentance? Dispensational Christians read Peter as offering the kingdom to Israel, postponed when they refused. But Peter is calling his hearers to repent so that they may share in the times of refreshing when Christ comes. The day of his return is fixed by the Father (1:7), and it does not wait on any nation’s response. What depends on their repentance is whether they will be ready.

What will the restoration of all things look like? Scripture gives us real glimpses, not a full map. It will be a renewed creation, not an escape from creation: new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). God’s people will have resurrection bodies, like Christ’s (Philippians 3:21). There will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain (Revelation 21:4), no more curse (Revelation 22:3), and no more sin. The nations will bring their glory into it. And at its centre will be God himself: the dwelling place of God is with man (Revelation 21:3). It will be everything good in this world, healed, and far more besides.

The not-yet. The restoration is certain, it is dated, and it is not here. The refreshing is available now, and it is not the same thing: a breathing space in a world still broken. Anybody told that the Christian life ought to feel like the new creation already has been sold something Peter did not offer. What he offers is enough air to keep going, and the certainty that the one who fixed the date is coming back.

parallels.desc: new heavens and a new earth

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses said, 'The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses said. Peter reaches for the promise in the books of Moses that another prophet like Moses is coming (Deuteronomy 18:15–19). Israel waited for that prophet; crowds would later ask whether Jesus was the one (John 1:21; 6:14; 7:40). Peter says he is.

A voice they could live through. At the foot of the mountain the people had heard God speak out of the fire, and begged Moses: let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die. God said they were right, and made the promise Peter is quoting: I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth (Deuteronomy 18:16–18). What he finally sent was his Son, who could be listened to by fishermen on a hillside without anybody dying of it.

A prophet like me. The likeness is specific. Moses spoke with God face to face, mediated a covenant, did signs, brought a people out of slavery and gave them God’s word. Every one of those is true of Jesus and truer: Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6).

Listen to him. Not consider him, not weigh him against other authorities. Listen. The Father said the same at the transfiguration, with Moses himself standing there: this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him (Luke 9:35). The obligation to obey Jesus does not originate with Christians; it was laid on Israel by Moses, in the law they revere.

Does this verse point to Muhammad? One question a reader may well have met should be answered briefly, since it is pressed with some force. Many Muslim teachers claim this verse for Muhammad, on the ground that he came from among the brothers of Israel, that is, from Ishmael’s line. The text will not carry it. In Deuteronomy the phrase from among your brothers is used repeatedly of a fellow Israelite and is set directly against the foreigner: Israel’s king must be one from among your brothers; you may not put a foreigner over you (Deuteronomy 17:15). The prophet is promised from inside Israel, as the answer to Israel’s own request at Israel’s own mountain. And the New Testament shows the question being asked in precisely those terms in the first century, crowds asking whether Jesus is the Prophet (John 7:40), and priests sending men to ask John the Baptist the same thing (John 1:21). Peter is settling a question his hearers already had, not inventing one.

How do I listen to Jesus today? Chiefly by listening to Scripture, because the Prophet speaks there. The words of Jesus in the Gospels, the teaching of the apostles he sent, and the Old Testament he said testified about him are all his voice. So read the Bible as his word to you, and sit under faithful preaching of it. Listen to all of it, not only the parts you like: whatever he tells you. Do not look for him in inner impressions that go beyond or against what he has said in Scripture. And listening in the Bible always means obeying: be doers of the word, and not hearers only (James 1:22).

On a Tuesday. You will never obey him perfectly; he obeyed the Father perfectly in your place, and that obedience is counted as yours, so you can open his commands without dread. Is there one you have been politely ignoring because it is inconvenient? Read it again today, and ask his Spirit for strength to do it.

For worship. Moses once begged to be blotted out of God’s book for the sake of his sinning people, and God would not take him in their place (Exodus 32:32–33). The prophet like Moses gave himself for his people, and the Father accepted the offering. He is not only the voice they could bear to hear; he bore what they could never have borne, and rose to speak peace to them.

parallels.desc: a prophet like me from among you

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Destroyed from the people. Verse 23 is the hardest sentence in the chapter. In Deuteronomy God says of the man who will not listen, I myself will require it of him (Deuteronomy 18:19). Peter finishes the sentence with Leviticus in mind: shall be cut off from his people, the fate pronounced on anyone who refuses to afflict himself on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 23:29). To refuse the Prophet is like standing outside on the one day in the year when the nation’s sin was dealt with. And that sacrifice has now been offered once for all in Jesus (Hebrews 9:11–12), so to refuse him is to refuse the only atonement there is. From now on belonging to God’s people turns on one’s response to Jesus.

Why the warning is not cruel. A warning is cruel if it is false, or too late to act on, or if there is no way out. This one is true, it is early, and Peter has just described the way out. And a reader who fears he has not listened well enough is already listening: the warning is for those who will not hear, not for those anxious that they hear too faintly. The unkind thing would have been to leave the sentence out.

What about people who have never heard of Jesus? This verse speaks of those who hear the Prophet and refuse him, and they carry the greater guilt (Luke 12:47–48). But Scripture is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ: there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (4:12), and how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? (Romans 10:14). Those who never hear are not condemned for rejecting a gospel they never knew, but for their sin against the light God gave them in creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16), and God judges them justly. We hold, with many in the Reformed tradition, that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases, as the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession both say (1689 10.3; Westminster 10.3). Grieving parents may take real comfort here: Scripture shows a God tender toward little ones (2 Samuel 12:23; Mark 10:14), and many Reformed pastors have believed that all who die in infancy are among his elect. The answer to this question is not speculation but mission: it is why the church sends and goes.

From Samuel. With Samuel the line of the prophets properly begins after Moses, and Samuel anointed David, so the prophetic succession and the royal line start on the same page. The whole tradition, prophets and kings together, has been pointing toward these days.

These days. These days: an ordinary afternoon at the three o’clock prayers. A Christian in a life that feels entirely unremarkable is living inside the period the prophets strained forward to see. The prophets searched and inquired carefully about this grace, and the angels long to look into it (1 Peter 1:10–12).

On a Tuesday. If someone you love has heard the gospel and is still refusing it, do not stop warning them, and do not stop loving them. Warn with tears, not with triumph, and point to the way out in the same breath.

parallels.desc: Nathan’s prophecy in Samuel’s days

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, 'And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.' God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sons of the covenant. Peter ends by telling them who they are: not late arrivals to a religion, but heirs. Everything he has been quoting at them is family property.

In your offspring. Then the covenant text itself (Genesis 22:18; 12:3), the promise to Abraham of blessing for all nations through his offspring. Paul says the offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The gospel to the Gentiles is no departure from the Old Testament; it is its fulfilment.

On the mountain of the substitute. The promise is repeated on a mountain in Genesis 22, after the knife is stopped and the ram is found caught in a thicket by his horns. The promise that the whole world would be blessed through Abraham’s line is given at the exact moment God provides a substitute for a beloved son. Peter quotes it in a sermon about a beloved Son for whom no substitute was provided, and no ram was found, and the knife was not stopped. Abraham got his boy back down the mountain. God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32).

To you first. To you first: to Israel first, then to the nations (13:46; Romans 1:16). In the city that killed him, to the crowd that asked for a murderer instead, the offer arrives before it goes anywhere else in the world. That is the pattern of the whole book, and a window onto the character of God, who deals with the people who have wronged him worst by putting them at the front of the queue.

To bless you. The definition is not what we usually mean by the word: health, safety, a scan that came back clear. Peter defines the blessing promised to Abraham for the whole world, and it is being turned away from your own wickedness. The blessing of Abraham is not first prosperity but forgiveness and transformation. Jesus saves his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21), not in them.

Two lives. Suppose a man were given a long and easy life, well provided for, with everyone he loves kept safe, and arrived at the end exactly as he began, still governed by the temper, the appetite, the coldness or the dishonesty he had at twenty. Was he blessed? By this verse he was never touched. And suppose another man loses most of what he owned and half of what he hoped for, and is prised loose over thirty years from the thing that was quietly destroying him. Peter says God blessed the second one.

So is it wrong to pray for health and provision? No. Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread, and God delights to give good gifts to his children (Matthew 7:11). Health, work, safety and family are real blessings, and we should ask for them and thank him for them. But they are not the greatest blessing, and they are not the measure of God’s favour. Pray for them, and pray more for the blessing Peter names: that God would turn you, and those you love, from sin and toward himself. If he grants the lesser gifts, receive them gladly. If he withholds them, he has not withheld the greater one.

For worship. God raised up his Servant and sent him first to the people who had killed him, not with a bribe or an amnesty on the old terms, but to change them: to take hold of them one at a time and turn every one of them from their wickedness. The Son who was not spared comes carrying the blessing he bought with his blood. In Abraham’s offspring all the families of the earth are blessed, and the blessing has reached even us.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

3.theology: The Name of Jesus. Peter credits the healing to the name of Jesus and to faith in that name (v. 16), and he means a person, not a formula. Peter is not invoking magic; he acts in the delegated authority of the reigning Christ, and the healing is the risen Lord’s own act through his servant. Faith is the hand that receives what the name offers, and what it offers is the power of the one who conquered death, for a broken body and a guilty conscience alike.
3.examples:
Then: A man lame from birth sat daily at the gate of a temple he could not enter, with an empty hand held out. In the name of Jesus he walked in.

Now: The church still carries what the world cannot give. Programmes, therapy and public help have real worth, but they cannot raise the dead. The church’s temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by its true wealth and offer silver and gold instead. The world has plenty of silver and gold. It has only one name by which it can be saved.

4.title: Boldness Before the Council
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, <sup>2</sup>greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. <sup>3</sup>And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. <sup>4</sup>But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. <sup>5</sup>On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, <sup>6</sup>with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. <sup>7</sup>And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, “By what power or by what name did you do this?” <sup>8</sup>Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders, <sup>9</sup>if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, <sup>10</sup>let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man is standing before you well. <sup>11</sup>This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. <sup>12</sup>And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” <sup>13</sup>Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. <sup>14</sup>But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. <sup>15</sup>But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, <sup>16</sup>saying, “What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. <sup>17</sup>But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.” <sup>18</sup>So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. <sup>19</sup>But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, <sup>20</sup>for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” <sup>21</sup>And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God for what had happened. <sup>22</sup>For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old. <sup>23</sup>When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. <sup>24</sup>And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them, <sup>25</sup>who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? <sup>26</sup>The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’— <sup>27</sup>for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, <sup>28</sup>to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. <sup>29</sup>And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, <sup>30</sup>while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” <sup>31</sup>And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness. <sup>32</sup>Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. <sup>33</sup>And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. <sup>34</sup>There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold <sup>35</sup>and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need. <sup>36</sup>Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, <sup>37</sup>sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
4.overview:
The healing at the temple gate and Peter’s sermon bring the first persecution. The Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy who denied the resurrection, have Peter and John brought before the Sanhedrin, the council that had condemned Jesus. Peter answers that the man was healed by the name of the crucified and risen Jesus, and that there is salvation in no other name. Forbidden to speak in that name, the apostles say they must obey God.

Released, they go back to the church, which prays Psalm 2 and asks not for safety but for boldness. God shakes the room and fills them with the Spirit, and they go on speaking. The chapter ends with the church’s open hands, and with Barnabas, whose gift is the real thing that the next chapter’s counterfeit will copy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the council that condemned Jesus, Peter names Jesus, the rejected stone God has made the cornerstone, and declares that there is salvation in no one else. The council cannot deny the miracle, so it forbids the name.
verseByVerse.theology:
The exclusivity of Christ

Verse 12 is among the clearest statements in Scripture that salvation is found in Christ alone, and it is spoken in a courtroom, to men who could imprison Peter for it. The claim follows from the incarnation itself: if God became flesh in one particular person, then salvation is tied to that person and cannot be detached from him. And the same logic that makes the claim exclusive makes it universal. The name is given among men, held out to all; the door is single, and it is not shut.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Two laymen without rabbinic training stood in the middle of Israel’s supreme court, and their boldness astonished the men trying them. Now: The same Spirit is given to every believer. Boldness in the New Testament is not a temperament but a gift, asked for and granted, and it is perfectly compatible with being frightened.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 4 tells of the first persecution of the church, and shows the pattern of the whole book: opposition cannot stop the word of God; it only spreads it.

As they were speaking. They do not wait for the sermon to finish.

The captain of the temple. Three groups come down on them. The priests were the men on duty. The captain of the temple commanded the temple police, with the power of arrest. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple and cooperated with Rome; they gave the five books of Moses a unique authority and, as Luke says later, denied that there is any resurrection, or angel, or spirit (23:8). Their whole position rested on the temple continuing as it was.

Greatly annoyed. Luke tells us what put them out, in two parts. The first is that the apostles were teaching the people: two laymen with no standing, instructing a crowd on the priests’ own premises without anybody’s permission.

In Jesus the resurrection. The second is the content. This is the doctrine the Sadducees had built a career on denying, and the apostles are naming the man. In Jesus: his resurrection is the proof and the guarantee of the general resurrection, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). Only weeks earlier these officials had believed the matter closed: a stone and, as Matthew records, a seal and a guard (Matthew 27:62–66). Now the claim is back, in their own courtyard, with a healed man standing next to it.

He had answered them once already. The Sadducees had tried this argument on Jesus himself, in these same courts, with a riddle about a woman married to seven brothers in turn. He answered them from the books of Moses they accepted, where God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him (Luke 20:27–38). They had no reply. Now the argument has been settled in a way no riddle could answer: the man who told them that God is the God of the living is himself alive, and his name has just made a lame man walk.

The third irritant. There is a third irritant Luke does not need to state, because the previous chapter supplied it: the apostles were telling Jerusalem that its rulers had handed the Messiah to Pilate and killed him.

Should I expect opposition if I speak about Jesus? Some, yes, though not always and not usually in this form. Jesus said, if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20), and Paul that all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). In many places that means prison or death; in others it means mockery, exclusion, a lost promotion or a cold family. Do not go looking for it, and do not provoke it by being needlessly offensive. But do not be surprised by it, and do not take it as a sign that you have done something wrong. Often it is a sign that the gospel has touched something people would rather not have touched.
verseByVerse.note: The captain of the temple commanded the temple police and ranked next to the high priest. The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until the next day. By the rules later written down in the Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, capital cases were not to be tried at night, which makes the night hearing of Jesus all the more irregular. So the two men spend the night in custody: the first Christian imprisonment. By the end of this book it will be so routine that Luke barely stops to comment on it.

Along the master’s road. Jesus too was seized at night by the temple authorities and led before the council at daybreak (Luke 22:54, 66). He had told them they would be delivered up for his name’s sake, and that it would be their opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). But the roads part in the morning. His night ended at a cross; theirs ends in release and a sermon, and the master who walked the road first walks it now beside them.

But many believed. They can stop the speaker; they cannot retrieve what has already been said. They took the preachers into custody and left the sermon at large. Paul would write the same from his own chains: I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound! (2 Timothy 2:9).

About five thousand. The word (andrōn) is the one for adult males, perhaps heads of households. Add wives and households, and the community in Jerusalem may already be well past ten thousand: from a hundred and twenty, to three thousand, to this. No wonder the authorities were alarmed.

My church is small and getting smaller. Has God failed? No. God has promised to build his church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18), but he has not promised that every congregation will grow, or grow now. Churches rise and fall; whole regions once full of believers now have few, and others that had none now have millions. Ask honestly whether your church is faithful to the gospel, prayerful, loving and outward-looking, and repent of anything that is not. Then keep sowing, and leave the harvest to the Lord. Faithfulness, not size, is what he asks of you, and a small faithful church is precious to him.

On a Tuesday. Perhaps you once spoke to someone about Christ and saw nothing come of it. That conversation is in God’s hands now, and it may still be working in a heart you cannot see.
verseByVerse.note: Hearings were not normally held at night.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rulers and elders and scribes. The full apparatus assembles. Rulers, elders and scribes is Luke’s shorthand for the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council (by later Jewish tradition seventy-one men), with authority over religious law, over the temple, and, within the limits Rome allowed, over life and death. This is the body that had condemned Jesus a few months earlier. The room, the procedure, and most of the faces are the same. Only the defendants have changed.

With Annas the high priest and Caiaphas. Luke writes Annas the high priest, but Caiaphas held the office, from about AD 18 to 36, and this has been produced as evidence that Luke did not know the Jerusalem he was writing about.

The family firm. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15, until a Roman prefect removed him; but by the law of Moses the high priesthood was for life. Five of his sons held the office after him, and so did his son-in-law Caiaphas. Annas ran the family firm out of the chair and in charge, which is why the arrested Jesus was taken to Annas first (John 18:13, 24). Luke, who dates John the Baptist’s ministry to Annas and Caiaphas together (Luke 3:2), is not confused. He names both the office-holder and the power.

John and Alexander. They were probably members of the family; a Jonathan son of Annas later became high priest, and some manuscripts read Jonathan here. Names like these, which lead nowhere in the story, suggest Luke was drawing on people who remembered who was in the room.

The arithmetic of the morning. On one side: the high-priestly dynasty, controlling the temple, its treasury, its police and its courts, seated where they had sentenced a man to death. On the other: two fishermen who had spent the night in a cell, with no lawyer and no allies in the building. By the end of the session it will be the judges who cannot think what to do.

Seated at the right hand. The last time Jesus stood before this council, at daybreak, they asked whether he was the Christ, and he told them: from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God (Luke 22:69). Now the evidence for that sentence is about to be brought in, a man standing on his own feet by the name of the one they condemned. The prisoner of that morning has taken his seat, and this morning’s session is being held in his sight.

How should I think about powerful people who oppose the faith? Neither with fear nor with hatred. Not with fear, because they are men, and the Lord laughs at the rulers who take counsel against him (Psalm 2:4); their power is real but borrowed and temporary. Not with hatred, because Jesus told us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44), and because some of them will be converted: within a few chapters a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (6:7), and Saul of Tarsus had been trained by one of its members, Gamaliel (22:3). Pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), honour their office where you can, and keep speaking the truth.
verseByVerse.note: The rulers, elders and scribes made up the Sanhedrin. Annas had been high priest earlier and remained head of the family; Caiaphas was the serving high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, "By what power or by what name did you do this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the midst. The phrase describes the room. According to later Jewish tradition the Sanhedrin sat in a semicircle so that every member could see every other, with the accused placed in the open space at the centre. It is a room designed to make a man feel the weight of the institution before a word is spoken.

By what power or by what name did you do this? Then the question. It sounds neutral and it is not. They do not deny the miracle; they want to know its source. Asking a man to name the power and the name behind a wonder is the language of the world of magic and exorcism, where results were obtained by invoking a particular being and everything depended on which one you had used. The council is not enquiring into a healing; it is inviting Peter to identify his source, and there is a trap under the invitation. Israel’s law prescribed death for a man who worked a sign or a wonder and used it to draw the people after other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). Give the wrong answer here and the charge need not be disorderly preaching. It could be capital.

The old move. When Jesus cast out demons, the accusation was not that nothing had happened; it was that he did it by Beelzebul, the prince of demons (Luke 11:15). It is a durable tactic: it concedes the event and poisons the source.

The small contempt. Not by what power did you heal this man, but did you do this: an unnamed this, an incident. And the you is emphatic, probably scornful: people like you? Peter is about to make them say what it was.

The right question. Without meaning to, the council has asked the right question, and they have asked it before. In these same courts the chief priests, scribes and elders had put almost the same words to Jesus: tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority (Luke 20:2). Now they ask his servants, and this time they will get a straight answer. By what power and by what name: that is the question the whole book of Acts exists to answer, and its one answer is the name of the man they asked first.

How do I answer when someone asks why I believe? Be ready, as Peter tells every Christian to be, to make a defence to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). You do not need to be an expert. Start with the person of Jesus: who he is, what he did, and that God raised him from the dead. Then say honestly what he has done for you. If you do not know the answer to a hard question, say so, and offer to find out. Think through, before you are asked, three or four sentences that explain the gospel and why you trust it. The question by what name is still the right one, and Jesus is still the answer.

parallels.desc: by what authority?

verseByVerse.quote: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, "Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Filled with the Holy Spirit. This is the second time Luke has said it of Peter, and it will be said of the whole church before the chapter is out (2:4; 4:31). Pentecost has not worn off; Luke’s filling language describes a repeated equipping for particular moments. A man about to speak for his life is given what he needs at the hour he needs it and not before.

The promise kept. Which is exactly what had been promised. When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say (Luke 12:11–12; 21:12–15). Peter is standing in the sentence, finding out that it was not a figure of speech.

What it does not mean. The promise is not a general licence to go into the pulpit unprepared and call it faith; the setting Jesus specified is the dock, not the desk, and the same New Testament tells a teacher to do his best to present himself to God as a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15). What is promised is that when a believer is put on the spot for Christ, in a courtroom, a hostile family, an interview, he will not be left to improvise alone.

Rulers of the people and elders. Peter begins courteously: the proper address, no sneering. Boldness in this chapter never once shades into rudeness; being obnoxious is not being faithful.

A good deed. He takes the vague this of the council’s question and names it. Examined is courtroom language, and he reads the charge sheet aloud in words nobody would want in the minutes: we are on trial for making a cripple walk. He has not raised his voice, and he has already made the court’s position sound absurd, which is what it was.

Has been healed. One word in that sentence carries the whole speech, and English hides it. The verb Peter uses for healed (sesōstai) is the ordinary Greek word for saved. He uses it here of a man’s ankles. Three verses later he will use it of the whole world’s only hope (v. 12). The council asked him about a body, and he is going to answer about a soul with the same word.

What if I freeze when I am put on the spot? Most of us have, and Peter himself once did, beside a fire, in front of a servant girl. The promise is not that you will never feel fear but that you are not alone in it. Pray before hard conversations, even a sentence under your breath. Say less rather than more: one true, kind sentence about Jesus is better than a flustered argument. If you fail, do what Peter did after the courtyard: go back to the Lord, receive his forgiveness, and try again. The Spirit who filled Peter in the council is the same Spirit who lives in you, and he delights to help weak people speak.

For worship. The Lord Jesus promised his frightened friends that in the hour of trial the Spirit would teach them what to say, and in the high priest’s court the promise came true to the letter. He does not send his people into the dock and leave them there; he puts into weak mouths the calm and the courage he himself showed before the same judges.

parallels.desc: I will give you a mouth and wisdom

verseByVerse.quote: "let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let it be known. They asked for a name; they get the name, with the crucifixion and the resurrection attached, without a syllable of diplomacy.

Whom you crucified, whom God raised. Two verbs, two subjects, side by side: what you did, and what God did about it. It is the gospel in one sentence, said to the men who did the first one.

Standing before you well. Peter can point while he says it, because the healed man is in the chamber; verse 14 tells us so. The court’s exhibit walked in on his own feet. All his life he had been carried to the temple gate and no further; this morning he is inside the supreme court of Israel.

The stone that was rejected. Psalm 118:22 is the last of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover, and a crowd had shouted its lines about the one who comes in the name of the Lord at a man riding into this city on a donkey a few months before.

Finishing his master’s sentence. Jesus had quoted this identical verse to these same men, in the temple, at the end of the parable of the tenants who killed the owner’s son, and they perceived that he had told it against them and sought to lay hands on him at that very hour (Luke 20:17–19). Peter is finishing his master’s sentence in front of the same audience. He also adjusts the psalm deliberately, putting in by you, so that the builders have faces. The charge is not a technical error, but that they looked at him and judged him worthless.

The spoil heap and the corner. Judging which block goes where is the whole of a builder’s competence. These men examined this stone with the best professional judgement in the nation and threw it on the spoil heap. God took it off the heap and set it at the corner, where every line in the building is measured from. Jesus is the cornerstone of the new temple, the church, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:4–8).

Wrong about the most important thing. The most qualified people in the nation, in its highest court, with every appearance of due process, were wrong about the most important thing that has ever happened. It is a caution against being impressed by consensus, and a comfort to anybody who has been weighed by people with every right to weigh him and found to be of no value.

What does it mean to build my life on the cornerstone? It means taking your measurements from Jesus rather than from anyone else. Your worth is set by what he says about you, not by the verdict of employers, family or friends. Your choices are lined up with his word. Your hope for the future rests on his promises, not on your plans. And when other supports give way, health, money, reputation, relationships, you discover what the whole building was really resting on. Practically, that means returning to him daily in Scripture and prayer, and asking of each decision: does this fit the line of the cornerstone?

parallels.desc: the stone the builders rejected

verseByVerse.quote: "And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salvation in no one else. The sentence the chapter is famous for is an answer to a question about a pair of ankles. The word for saved that described the healing in verse 9 now runs into its largest meaning: you want to know how one man got his legs back; I will tell you how anybody gets anything back. Saved here means rescued from the guilt of sin, from the just anger of a holy God, and from death itself, and brought whole into his presence, of which the man’s new legs were a small picture.

No other name under heaven. Every clause tightens it. No other name: no other person, no other way. Under heaven: anywhere in the world, not merely nowhere in Israel. The name is given, by God, a gift handed down rather than a prize achieved. And the last phrase carries a quiet necessity: by which we must be saved. Peter includes himself in that we: he is not standing over the council as a man who found the way; he is standing beside them as a man who needed it. This is the exclusive claim of the gospel, spoken to the highest religious court of the only nation that knew the true God.

In the flow. The name has been the thread of the whole episode: the healing was done in the name (3:6), the council asked by what name (4:7), and it will soon forbid the name (4:17–18). At Pentecost Peter quoted Joel’s promise that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (2:21); now he says whose name that is. And if there is only one name, every nation must hear it (1:8).

How can Jesus be the only way? This is also one of the great apologetic verses, for the world calls it narrow and arrogant. Three things help. First, it is not a boast about Christians but a confession about Christ: if God himself became man and died and rose to save sinners, then salvation simply is found in him and nowhere else, not because we are better, but because there is only one Saviour who did this. Second, the one narrow door opens to all: narrow in the way, one Saviour, and infinitely wide in the welcome, for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). Third, sincerity cannot save. A man can be sincerely wrong, as one who sincerely drinks poison thinking it medicine; salvation rests on the truth of who Christ is, not the earnestness of the seeker.

Where Christians differ: are there other ways of salvation? Pluralists hold that all religions lead to God; inclusivists that people may be saved by Christ through other religions, without knowing him. This commentary’s view: no other name is unmistakable. Even Israel’s religion, without Christ, could not save. Salvation is found in Jesus alone, through faith in him (John 14:6; 1 Timothy 2:5). This is why the gospel must be preached to every nation (Romans 10:13–15). It is said not with arrogance, but with urgency and love.

Could people be saved through Christ without ever knowing him? Inclusivist Christians think so: they point to Old Testament believers saved before Christ came, to Cornelius before Peter arrived (10:1–4), and to Romans 2:14–16. But Old Testament saints trusted the promise God had given about the coming Saviour; Cornelius was told to send for Peter to hear a message by which he would be saved (11:14); and Romans 2 is about how all are judged, not how any are saved. The more likely reading is the plain one: there is salvation in no one else. As for those who never hear, Scripture’s answer is honest and sobering: all are accountable for the light they have (Romans 1:20), none seek God on their own (Romans 3:11), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases. And therefore we must go and tell (Romans 10:14), leaving the secret things to God (Deuteronomy 29:29).

Said by a prisoner. Peter says it not in a lecture hall but under arrest, before a court that could flog him and had recently arranged an execution, answering a question that could have trapped him into a capital charge. A man in that position has every incentive to find a broader formula: Jesus as one road among several, and the council not implicated. Peter tells them instead that the man they threw away is the only name there is, and that they too must be saved by it. The narrowness people object to was spoken by a prisoner who gained nothing by it, and it included an invitation to them.

How do I say this to friends of other faiths without arrogance? By remembering that you stand where the lame man at the Beautiful Gate stood, with nothing to boast of except what was done for you, not as a winner looking down on losers. Listen first, and understand what your friend actually believes; respect his sincerity and the good in his life. Speak of Jesus himself, not of your religion’s superiority. Admit your own sin and need. Be honest that you believe Jesus is the only Saviour, because he said so (John 14:6), and explain why that is good news, not bad: God has provided the way himself. Let your life show the love you speak of. And pray, because only God can open a heart.

For worship. There is one name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved, and God gave it. He did not leave the world to find its own way back to him; he came himself, in his Son, and wrote his name over the only door. The name Jesus means the LORD saves, and he has never failed to save anyone who called on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The boldness. The word Luke uses is parrēsia, boldness or frankness, and it carried weight in the Greek world. In classical Athens it named the citizen’s freedom to speak his mind in the assembly, which a slave or a foreigner did not have. Two prisoners, fetched up from a cell, are talking like free men.
