The theme word of Acts. The church prays for it in this chapter (v. 29) and receives it (v. 31), and the last line of Acts leaves Paul under house arrest, proclaiming the kingdom of God with all boldness (28:31). It is a fair candidate for the theme word of the book, and it is the Spirit’s gift.

Uneducated, common men. Uneducated does not mean illiterate; it means without formal training in the rabbinic schools: no letters after the name. And common men (idiōtai) means laymen, private persons, amateurs as opposed to professionals. They have not sat at the feet of a Gamaliel, as the young Saul of Tarsus had, and Galilean fishermen are arguing from Scripture with the scholars of Israel.

Do I need training before I can speak for Jesus? Not to be a witness. Peter and John spoke of what they had seen and heard (v. 20), and every believer can say what Christ has done and who he is. But notice that they were not untaught: they had spent about three years with the best teacher who ever lived, and Peter’s answer is full of Scripture. So learn all you can, read, ask, sit under good teaching; but do not wait until you feel qualified. The fear of not being impressive enough is usually a love of being approved, and the council’s sneer did not stop God from using these two men.

They had been with Jesus. Recognised is the word Luke used of the crowd recognising the beggar (3:10): not a guess but an identification. Something in the bearing of these two men made a hostile court think of a prisoner it had condemned. Jesus too had astonished them without formal training: how is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied? (John 7:15). Time spent with Jesus leaves a residue which outlasts any argument, and the people who dislike him are often the first to spot it.

Nothing to say in opposition. You cannot argue with a walking man. A man who had spent his life at the edge of the temple now stood in the highest court in the land, beside the accused, and his standing there ended the argument. Luke gives him not one line of dialogue. He stood where everybody could see him, which is very largely what the church has been asked to do ever since.

How do I spend time with Jesus, now that he is in heaven? The apostles had walked with him for some three years; we meet him now by his Spirit through his word. Read the Gospels slowly and often, watching how he speaks, treats people and prays. Pray to him, honestly and regularly, not only in emergencies. Meet him at the Lord’s Table with his people. Obey what he says, because he said that whoever keeps his commandments is the one who loves him, and he will manifest himself to him (John 14:21). And keep company with others who love him. The residue the council noticed was not produced in a weekend, and it will not be in you either; it grows by daily nearness.
verseByVerse.note: “Uneducated, common men” means they had no formal training in the law under a rabbi — not that they were illiterate.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying, "What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They conferred with one another. How does Luke know what was said in a closed session? This council was not sealed: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were members (John 3:1–2; Luke 23:50–51), within two chapters a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith (6:7), and Saul had worked closely with the council’s leaders (9:1–2). Men who had sat in that room, or near it, had changed sides.

What shall we do with these men? It is the question this council had asked about Jesus himself. John tells us that after the raising of Lazarus they gathered and said, What are we to do? For this man performs many signs (John 11:47). That meeting ended with Caiaphas advising that one man should die for the people, and John adds that he spoke better than he knew: Jesus would die for the nation, and to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:50–52). Their worst decision became the means of the world’s salvation. Now the same men meet over the same problem, and the problem is still Jesus. The fishermen are only the latest sign that he is alive.

We cannot deny it. This is a hostile court in closed session, with no audience to perform for and every motive to find a flaw. They examine the case intending to destroy it, and their finding is that denial is not available to them. And in the next breath they resolve to shut it down.

The obstacle was never the evidence. Put this passage in front of anyone who assumes that unbelief is fundamentally an information problem: that if only the case were laid out clearly enough, people would believe. Here is a case laid out with total clarity and conceded in private by qualified and hostile investigators, followed immediately by a decision to suppress it. Their problem was not proof, but unwillingness.

What it does not mean. That does not make evidence worthless. Peter’s speech is an appeal to evidence, the healed man is in the room because he is evidence, and Luke wrote so that his reader might have certainty (Luke 1:4). Facts are necessary and not sufficient: a man may be persuaded in his understanding and remain unwilling in his will, and the second is where the real business is transacted.

With these men. At Pentecost a crowd told they had crucified the Messiah cried out, Brothers, what shall we do? (2:37). Here a council told the same thing asks, What shall we do with these men? One is asking to be changed; the other is asking how to make the problem go away.

Why won’t my friend believe when the evidence seems so clear? Because, as this passage shows, unbelief is not only in the head. Pride, fear of what others will think, love of a way of life, or simple unwillingness to bow to God can all hold a person back when the arguments are answered. Jesus said that people loved the darkness rather than the light (John 3:19). So keep giving reasons, patiently and kindly, because God uses them. But do not imagine that the right argument will do what only God can do. Pray for your friend’s heart, not only his mind, that God who said let light shine out of darkness would shine in his heart (2 Corinthians 4:6). And keep loving him, whatever he decides.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself the council’s question, and Pentecost’s. When God’s word confronts you with something uncomfortable, are you asking what shall I do, or what shall I do with this? The first leads to life. The second leads to the closed door of verse 17.

For worship. The council could not deny the sign and would not bow to it, and their will held out against the plainest evidence in Jerusalem. Only God can change a will like that, and he does. The risen Lord who was condemned in that chamber went on to win men from its own circle, including a young Pharisee who would call himself the foremost of sinners. No heart is so closed that Christ cannot open it, and every believer is someone whose unwillingness he overcame.

verseByVerse.quote: "But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name." So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That it may spread no further. They had run out of arguments: no rival account, no enquiry into fraud, straight to damage control. It is an administrative answer to a theological problem, what institutions reach for when they have lost the argument and kept the power. And the measure taken to stop the name travelling is recorded in a book that carried the name to Rome.

In this name. Look at what they prohibit. Not healing, gathering, charity or prayer. They ban a name. Jesus had told them it would come to this: you will be hated by all for my name’s sake (Luke 21:17). The council had grasped the essential point better than some of the church’s friends have since: everything in this movement is carried in a person. And they say this name: in the private session they never once pronounce it.

Not to speak or teach at all. A direct order from the highest religious authority in Israel: the first ban on evangelism. Many have followed.

Soup without the sentence. Christian activity of most kinds is welcome nearly everywhere: the food bank, the night shelter, the hospice. It is the speech that draws the objection: the claim that this particular man is Lord. Institutions happy to fund the soup will often ask that the sentence not be said. That is the council’s exact position, and the church’s answer has been on the record since the next verse.

What it does not mean. It should be said plainly, by comfortable Western Christians most of all, that there is an enormous distance between being thought awkward at work and a night in a cell under the temple, and a further distance again between either of those and what believers in a good many countries will face this week. The apostles are flogged for this in the next chapter. A man who finds a conversation uncomfortable and calls it persecution has not read the passage he is quoting.

My employer has told me not to talk about my faith at work. What should I do? Think carefully about what is actually being asked. A reasonable rule about how you use working time, or a ban on pressuring colleagues or customers, is not the same as a command to deny Christ, and you can obey it gladly while being honest when someone asks you a direct question in a break or outside work. Be a diligent, kind and truthful worker; that itself speaks. But if you are told to lie, to affirm what Scripture calls sin, or never to admit that you are a Christian, then you have reached the line in the next verse, and you must obey God, respectfully, and accept the cost. Seek advice from your pastor and, where needed, from Christian legal organisations.

On a Tuesday. The world often says: believe what you like, but don’t speak in Jesus’ name. Notice whether you have already given in to it without anyone asking, by doing the good works and quietly leaving out the name. If you have, the name you left out belongs to the one who forgives; take it up again.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and John answered them, "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter and John answered them. What is usually missed is the form: Peter asks the court a question and leaves it with them.

You must judge. He puts the case to the men trying him, and they cannot deliver the verdict, because the only answer dismantles their own order. A body whose entire authority rests on claiming to represent God has just been asked, on the record, whether God ought to be obeyed.

We cannot but speak. Not we will not stop, but we are not able: a statement of incapacity rather than defiance: the position of a man who has seen something and cannot arrange to un-see it. Jeremiah knew it: there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in (Jeremiah 20:9). Paul knew it: necessity is laid upon me (1 Corinthians 9:16). A witness can be silenced and cannot be un-witnessed, and that is the whole of Peter’s case.

What we have seen and heard. The claim is also modest. The apostles are not claiming a temperament but an experience: that a man they watched die was afterwards alive in front of them, and that they had eaten with him. Everything the church has ever said rests on that being either true or false.

Where Christians differ: civil disobedience. Some say Christians must always obey the government; others that they may resist any unjust law. This commentary’s view: Christians are to submit to governing authorities and pray for them (1 Timothy 2:1–2), honouring even unjust rulers (1 Peter 2:13–17). But where the state commands sin or forbids obedience to God, as in forbidding the gospel, we must obey God, openly, peacefully, and accept the consequences, as the apostles did. This is not rebellion but faithfulness.

When may a Christian disobey the authorities? Christians are to submit to governing authorities (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). Human authority is real and must normally be obeyed. But where they command what God forbids, or forbid what God commands, as here, we must obey God rather than men (5:29). And the apostles disobeyed openly and accepted the punishment, without rebellion or violence. Not long afterwards these same two men, with the other apostles, gave the same answer to the same court, and were flogged for it (5:29, 40).

Does this mean I may break any law I think is unjust? No. The apostles did not refuse a law because it was inconvenient, unfair or badly made; they refused one specific command that required them to disobey God. Paul told Christians under Nero to pay taxes and give honour to whom honour is owed (Romans 13:7), and Peter told slaves to be subject even to unjust masters (1 Peter 2:18). Christians may work by lawful means to change bad laws, through voting, persuasion, petitions and the courts. But disobedience is reserved for the narrow case where obeying man means disobeying God, and even then it is open, peaceful and willing to bear the penalty.

The smaller room. Most Christians meet this verse in a much smaller room than a Sanhedrin. A conversation turns, and there is a sentence that would be honest and a silence that would be easier. The cost is a slight chill, a reputation for being that sort of person. But the mechanism Peter names is the same: a believer is asked not to pretend he has not seen what he has seen. And when he takes the easier silence, as every believer has, the way back is the one Peter took after the fire: to the Lord who never once kept back the true word before his judges, whose perfect faithfulness is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and whose Spirit gives the next sentence.

parallels.desc: we must obey God rather than men

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God for what had happened. For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They let them go. Threats, but no punishment. Yet.

Because of the people. Not because it was persuaded, and not because it had scruples. The restraint is a calculation about public opinion. Men whose position depends on popular acquiescence cannot afford to flog the heroes of the hour, as public opinion had protected Jesus for a time (Luke 20:19; 22:2).

A gauge that moves. A few months earlier a crowd in this city had asked a Roman governor for a murderer instead of Jesus. Public opinion killed the Master and is now shielding the servants, and it will swing again: by chapter 7 a crowd is stoning Stephen, and by chapter 8 persecution has scattered the church. A church that reads its safety off the public mood is watching a gauge that moves.

He did not entrust himself to them. Jesus had read this crowd long before. John tells us that at an earlier Passover many in Jerusalem believed in his name when they saw his signs, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people and knew what was in man (John 2:23–25). His apostles now learn the same freedom. Their safety this morning does not finally rest on the crowd’s mood, but on the Lord who knows every heart in that city and governs it, and who will still be governing it when the crowd turns.

Praising God. Not the apostles. Peter had spent the whole of the previous chapter pushing the attention off himself and onto a name, and here is Luke’s quiet note that it worked.

More than forty years old. Luke has held this back until it functions as evidence, the kind of fact a court enters in a record. Forty years puts the case beyond any question of a passing complaint or a good day: a lifetime of public disability, ended in an afternoon.

The result is on file. The supreme council of the nation has examined the case of two fishermen and a healed man and established exactly two things: that it happened, and that nothing can be done about it. It is the first recorded attempt by human authority to stop the gospel, and the result is on file.

Should Christians care about public opinion? Care about it, but do not live by it. Scripture wants believers to have a good reputation with outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7) and to live such honourable lives that slander falls flat (1 Peter 2:12). It is right to be grieved when the church is despised for its own failures, and right to be glad when God gives it favour, as here. But public opinion is not the measure of faithfulness. It can protect you one month and turn on you the next. Aim to please God, do good to all, and leave your reputation in his hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–37 — Prayer, Power, and the Community of Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church reads its own week in Psalm 2 and asks for boldness, and God fills them all with the Spirit. Luke then shows the same Spirit at work in open hands, and in Barnabas.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sovereignty of God and human responsibility

Verses 27 and 28 hold together real human guilt and a real divine purpose: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel acted freely and wickedly, and did whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. This prayer shows what holding the two together is for. If the murder of the Son of God fell inside the plan, then a threat delivered that morning falls inside it too.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luke’s there was not a needy person among them echoes Deuteronomy 15:4, a hope the law held out and Israel never reached. Now: The particular form belonged to a moment; the open hand does not. And Luke sets the giving beside the preaching in one paragraph, so that the church’s life and the apostles’ message are not two subjects but one.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, "Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To their friends. Literally, to their own: the church, with a formal charge still hanging over them. Nobody suggests that association with them has become dangerous, which by any sensible reckoning it now had.

They reported. They tell the church everything. There is no pretending the threat was smaller than it was, and no heroics. The church hears the facts and takes them straight to God.

Together. The word for together (homothymadon) is a favourite of Luke’s for the early church: with one accord, of one mind, all facing the same way. He uses it of the hundred and twenty waiting in the upper room (1:14) and of the daily meetings in the temple (2:46). Whether they spoke in unison or one man led, what Luke describes is a room in which nobody is a spectator.

In the flow. Verses 23–31 are the church’s answer to verses 1–22: the council has ordered silence, so the church goes to a higher court. The prayer moves from who God is (v. 24), to what Scripture foretold and has now happened (vv. 25–28), to what they ask (vv. 29–30); then God answers (v. 31).

Sovereign Lord. Then the address, and it is not the usual one. They call God Despota: an absolute master, the owner of a household with total authority over everyone in it, not the ordinary word for Lord. Simeon used it holding the infant Christ: Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace (Luke 2:29). They begin not with their problem, but with God’s sovereignty.

Who made the heaven and the earth. Before a single word about the council, four clauses about creation, a line out of the Ten Commandments and the Psalms (Exodus 20:11; Psalm 146:6). They have a real emergency, and they open the prayer with doctrine, not to avoid the subject but to get it into proportion. The Sanhedrin controls the temple, the treasury and the police. It did not make the sea.

Even winds and water. Peter and John were very probably in the boat when Jesus rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and the disciples asked who this could be, who commands even winds and water, and they obey him (Luke 8:22–25). This prayer stands on the answer: the Son who calmed that storm now sits at the Father’s right hand, and a council is a smaller thing than a storm. Prayer under pressure tends to begin at the pressure and stay there, and God invites us to bring exactly those things. But by the time this church raises the threat in verse 29, it has been set inside a universe that has a Maker in it, and come down to something like its actual size.

Why does it matter that they went back to the church? Because Christians were never meant to face pressure alone. In trouble, the instinct is often to withdraw, to protect others from our problems or ourselves from their questions. Peter and John did the opposite: they went to their own people, told them everything, and prayed together. That is what the church is for. If you are under pressure, at work, at home, from illness or from opposition, tell some trusted believers and ask them to pray with you. And if you are part of a church, be the kind of friend a frightened brother can come back to.

parallels.desc: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them

verseByVerse.quote: "who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, 'Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed' —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through the mouth of David. Before the quotation there is a sentence about how Scripture came to exist, dropped in without fuss. God is the speaker; the Holy Spirit is the speaker; David’s mouth is the instrument (as at 1:16). These believers held together without difficulty that David composed a poem out of his own heart and that God said it. (Psalm 2 has no title in the Hebrew Bible, but the church, like many Jews of the day, received it as David’s; and the KJV follows later manuscripts that leave out the Holy Spirit here, while the earliest include him, in Greek that is famously awkward.) One of the clearest statements about inspiration in Acts comes in the middle of a prayer, where nobody was trying to prove anything: what Scripture says, God says (2 Timothy 3:16), and it is enough for a frightened church to stand on.

Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? Then Psalm 2 itself (Psalm 2:1–2). It is a royal psalm, a coronation psalm, written for the day the LORD’s king was crowned in Zion, when the vassal states looked at a new and untested king and began calculating their odds. In vain means empty, hollow, to no purpose. The psalm is not describing feeble opposition. It is describing furious, well-resourced, entirely serious opposition, and calling it empty.

Against his Anointed. His Anointed is his Christ, his Messiah, and opposition to the Messiah is opposition to God. The church is not hunting for a verse that suits its mood; it is reading its own week and finding it already written down. The Sanhedrin met that very morning, and Psalm 2 has the minutes.

He who sits in the heavens laughs. They stop the quotation just before the line every person in the room had known since childhood: he who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision (Psalm 2:4). It lies underneath the prayer, and it accounts for the extraordinary confidence of what they are about to ask for.

Futile, not harmless. The point is not that opposition to God is comic and can be laughed off by his people. Two of the men praying this had been in custody overnight, and within a few years Herod would put one of the apostles to the sword (12:2). The point is that from the only vantage that finally matters, the raging is futile: not harmless, not painless, but futile. The kings of the earth have been setting themselves against the Lord’s Anointed for three thousand years, and that psalm has never once needed rewriting.

You are my Son. The psalm does not end with the laughter. The Lord goes on to speak of his King: I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill, and then, You are my Son; today I have begotten you (Psalm 2:6–7). Paul, preaching later in this book, reads that line as fulfilled when God raised Jesus from the dead (13:33). The Anointed against whom the rulers gathered has already been enthroned, not by a coronation in Jerusalem but by an empty tomb.

How can I pray Scripture like this? Take a passage, especially a psalm, and read it slowly, asking what it says about God and what situation it describes. Then bring your own situation into it, as this church did: name the people and pressures, and pray the psalm’s truths over them. Psalm 2 for opposition, Psalm 23 for fear, Psalm 51 for guilt, Psalm 46 for upheaval, Psalm 121 for travel, Psalm 139 for feeling unseen. You are not twisting the text; you are letting God’s words shape your requests. Over time you will find that Scripture gives you words when you have none, and that it changes what you ask for.

On a Tuesday. Read Psalm 2 today, the whole of it, aloud. Then think of the thing in the world that most frightens you about the future of the church, and read verse 4 again.

For worship. The kings of the earth set themselves against the Lord’s Anointed, and he let them do their worst, because their worst was the road to his throne. Every throne that has risen against him has fallen, and his throne stands, and those who take refuge in his Son are as safe as his throne.

parallels.desc: why do the nations rage?

verseByVerse.quote: "for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your holy servant Jesus. Now the church puts names into the psalm: the gathering against God’s Anointed happened here, in this very city. (Where the KJV has thy holy child Jesus, it translates the same word, pais, which can mean child or servant; here it recalls the Servant of the Lord in Isaiah.)

Herod and Pontius Pilate. Psalm 2 lists four parties, and the prayer supplies the roster: the kings, Herod Antipas; the rulers, Pontius Pilate; the nations, the Romans; the peoples, the peoples of Israel. The sum of them is one Friday morning in this city: Jew and Gentile together crucified him, and all humanity is implicated. Luke’s Gospel alone records the meeting of Herod and Pilate over Jesus, and that the two enemies became friends that day (Luke 23:6–12).

Your hand and your plan. Predestined (proōrisen) means decided beforehand; it is the word used of election in Romans 8:29–30 and Ephesians 1:5, 11. They did what they wanted, wickedly; and they did exactly what God had determined: God’s sovereignty over evil without his being its author (2:23).

A doctrine to stand on. Predestination is usually met as a controversy. Here it is in its native habitat, and the setting is the entire point. Frightened people the morning after a night in custody are putting their weight on it, and it holds.

The floor they stand on. If the worst single act in the history of the world, carried out freely, wickedly, by a coalition of everybody, was inside the hand and plan of God, then what happened in a council chamber that morning is inside it too. Verse 28 runs straight on into verse 29 without a breath. The sovereignty is not the conclusion they are working toward. It is the floor they are standing on in order to ask for something.

If God predestined the cross, how were Herod and Pilate guilty? Both are true. God ordained the event, and it happened through the free and wicked choices of men who acted from their own motives and were fully responsible. So it was with Joseph, whose brothers intended harm while God intended it for good (Genesis 50:20). God is never the author of sin; he governs even sin for good, and holds sinners accountable. The cross is the clearest proof that both truths stand together.

How does God’s sovereignty help me when I am suffering? It does not explain every detail; it rarely tells you why. But it tells you that what is happening to you is not random, not out of control, and not outside the care of a Father who did not spare his own Son. If God could take the worst thing ever done and make it the salvation of the world, he can work your trouble together for good, as he has promised to those who love him (Romans 8:28). That does not make the pain less real, and you may still weep and ask him to take it away. But you weep inside a plan, held by a hand that was pierced for you.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look upon their threats. Now, at last, the problem. They do not ask for the threats to be withdrawn, or for God to judge the council, or for protection, or even for wisdom about proceeding more discreetly. Every one of those would be a reasonable Christian prayer, and not one of them is here.

With all boldness. They ask to keep doing what they were forbidden to do. Not safety, but courage. At verse 24 they addressed God as Sovereign Lord, the absolute master of a household. Here they call themselves your servants (doulois), and the word is the ordinary one for slaves. It is not a negotiation. A slave does not ask his master to arrange easier work; he asks for what he needs to do the work he has been given.

Asking for what they already had. And the word they choose for boldness is the very word the council had noticed in them at verse 13. They already had it, and they come back for more the same day.

Stretch out your hand. This is more of the exact thing that started the trouble. The council forbade the name, and the church asks God to make the name more conspicuous, and God did (5:12).

Your hand, twice. Two sentences earlier the church confessed that Herod and Pilate did whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (v. 28). Now it asks the same hand to stretch out and heal through the name of your holy servant Jesus. The hand that ordained the Servant’s suffering is the hand that now heals in the Servant’s name, and the healing flows from the suffering.

Should we pray for signs and wonders today? This church prayed for boldness first, and for God to confirm the apostles’ word. Continuationist Christians see the prayer as a model for every church. The more likely reading is that the signs accompanying the apostles’ witness belonged to that founding period and are not promised as normal church life; that is the cessationist view, held charitably. What we may always pray for is what they asked first: boldness to speak God’s word, and God’s help for the sick and suffering, as he wills. The reason for the cessationist reading is that the New Testament ties such signs to the apostles in particular (5:12; 2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, and whole churches that love the gospel, read these chapters differently, and they deserve to be heard as brothers and sisters, not dismissed. And God still heals in answer to prayer (James 5:14–15).

What it does not mean. It would be a serious mistake to conclude that praying for safety is unspiritual. Paul asks the Romans to pray that he may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea (Romans 15:31); the church in chapter 12 prays earnestly for Peter in prison; Jesus taught his disciples to pray, deliver us from evil (Matthew 6:13). A parent praying for a sick child does not need to be told that his praying is insufficiently missionary.

What a prayer reveals. What the passage shows is what these people wanted most when they were badly frightened. A prayer reveals what is actually being protected, and the Master is glad to change what we want most when we ask him.

How should I pray for persecuted Christians? Very often as they ask to be prayed for, like this church: that they would stand firm, speak boldly and love their persecutors, as well as for their protection and release (Hebrews 13:3). (See Matthew 10:20 for the fuller answer.)

parallels.desc: pray that words may be given me to open my mouth boldly

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The place was shaken. God does not reply in words. He moves the building. In Scripture a shaking like this is what happens when God arrives: Sinai trembling (Exodus 19:18), the thresholds shaking when Isaiah saw the Lord (Isaiah 6:4). The council could threaten; God shakes the building. That should sober as well as cheer: the Father who answers his children is never to be prayed to as if he were small.

All filled with the Holy Spirit. All of them, not the apostles only. And filled once again: the same word used of these same people at Pentecost (2:4), and of Peter twenty-three verses ago. This is not a second Pentecost; the Spirit has never left. It is fresh supply for fresh demand, so the church is not living off a reserve laid down once and running down. Believers who already have the Spirit can be filled again and again for new tasks (Ephesians 5:18).

Poured out from the throne. Peter had already told Jerusalem where this filling comes from: Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God, had received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and poured him out (2:33). The council banned the name; the one who bears it answered by filling every person in the house. The church does not receive courage in the abstract. It receives the Spirit of Jesus, and the courage is his.

Continued to speak. The answer proper. Not felt bold. Spoke. Continued: they kept on doing it, which is the only form courage takes that can actually be measured.

Nerve, not a changed situation. The answer is exactly what was asked for and not one item more. The council was not struck down. The prohibition was not lifted. The danger did not decrease: by the next chapter these men are arrested again and flogged. God supplied nerve and left every circumstance standing. That is one of the ways God answers: not by removing the situation but by re-equipping the person who is inside it.

What it does not mean. A shaking like this comes only rarely in Acts (compare 16:25–26), and nobody in the New Testament goes looking for it or suggests that a prayer without a physical sign has gone unheard. Luke’s evidence that God had answered is not that the walls moved. It is that a roomful of intimidated people went straight back out and said the thing they had been forbidden to say.

Is being filled with the Spirit a feeling? Not essentially. It may come with deep feelings of joy, peace or courage, and sometimes it does. But Luke measures it by what it produces: here, bold speaking of God’s word; elsewhere, wisdom, faith, joy and love (6:3, 5; 13:52). Paul describes it in terms of worship, gratitude and humble submission to one another (Ephesians 5:18–21). So do not judge whether you are filled by the temperature of your emotions on a given day. Ask whether you are yielding to the Spirit’s word and leading, and whether the fruit of Christlikeness and courage for Christ is growing. Ask God to fill you, and then obey him; the filling is often recognised afterwards, in what you found you were able to do.

parallels.desc: the whole mountain trembled

verseByVerse.quote: Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One heart and soul. Luke’s Greek readers would have stopped here. A well-worn saying called a friend a single soul in two bodies, and an older proverb said friends hold all things in common: ideals thought out of reach except between two rare individuals. Luke uses both of a congregation of several thousand who had mostly met months before. This is unity, not uniformity: the answer to Jesus’ prayer that they may all be one (John 17:21).

In the flow. This is Luke’s second summary of the church’s life (the first is 2:42–47). The Spirit who filled the room in verse 31 shows himself in open hands as well as open mouths, and the summary prepares the next scene, where one man’s gift shows the real thing and another’s the counterfeit (4:36 to 5:11).

No one said. It does not say that nobody owned anything; Luke uses the language of possession. Ownership survived. The claim was dropped. They still owned things, but held them loosely, as belonging to God and available to others.

A change in what people assumed. Anybody can be talked into a scheme. What Luke reports is people who still held the deeds and had stopped speaking as though the deeds settled anything.

With great power. Dropped into the middle of all that, verse 33: the central message. Luke puts the preaching inside the paragraph about the money. The community that had stopped saying mine is the community in which the resurrection was announced with power,: people who know that Jesus is risen know that their future is secure, and people whose future is secure can afford to open their hands. The empty tomb had loosened their grip on their fields.

Great grace. The last clause can be read two ways and probably means both. Great grace was the favour of God resting on the whole company, and equally the goodwill of a watching city, which is how Luke used a related phrase two chapters earlier (2:47).

How can a large church be of one heart and soul? Not by everyone becoming the same, or agreeing on every opinion, but by sharing one Lord, one gospel and one love. The early church held together because the risen Christ mattered more to each of them than their differences or possessions. In practice, unity grows when believers keep the gospel at the centre, pray together, deal quickly and honestly with offences (Matthew 18:15), refuse gossip, bear with one another in love (Ephesians 4:2–3), and actually share life, in small groups, homes and service, so that the large church becomes a family of families. It is the Spirit’s work, and he loves to give it to those who ask.

verseByVerse.quote: There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not a needy person. Luke is echoing the law. Deuteronomy promises: there will be no poor among you, if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God; and seven verses later says flatly that there will never cease to be poor in the land (Deuteronomy 15:4–5, 11). In all the centuries of covenant history the Old Testament never records that sentence as fact. Luke uses it as a plain statement of fact: the new covenant community did, by the Spirit, what Israel was meant to do.

The year of release. The promise Luke echoes belonged to the year of release, when debts were cancelled and the poor given a fresh start (Deuteronomy 15:1–2). Jesus opened his ministry in the synagogue at Nazareth by reading from Isaiah that he had been anointed to proclaim good news to the poor, liberty to the captives and the year of the Lord’s favour, and then saying that this Scripture was fulfilled that day in their hearing (Luke 4:18–21). A church with no needy person in it is what his release looks like when it reaches people’s purses: debtors he has set free, setting others free.

Sold them. Nothing was collected and nobody was assessed: as needs arose, people who owned land or houses sold them, voluntarily (5:4).

At the apostles’ feet. Not handed to the apostles: laid at their feet. That placed the gifts under their authority to distribute; the apostles managed the fund until the seven took over the daily distribution (6:1–6). It is also the posture of anonymity: the widow eating that week need not know whose field paid for it. The arrangement works against patronage, which has dogged religious giving in every century since. Then it was distributed to each as any had need: need, not equality, was the principle.

Was this Christian communism? A word here, since this is sometimes called Christian communism and pressed into political service: it was nothing of the kind. It was wholly voluntary. Peter tells Ananias that the land remained his own while it was unsold, and the money was at his disposal after it was sold (5:4), so private property was kept and giving was free, never compelled. It was love-driven and Spirit-prompted, flowing from hearts made one, not enforced by any state. And it was needs-based generosity, as any had need, not mechanical equalising. This is the very opposite of coercive collectivism: it is the free, glad open-handedness of people whom the Spirit had loosed from the grip of money. The abiding call is that same generosity and care for the needy among us; the particular form was one Spirit-filled moment’s response.

Did this sharing make the Jerusalem church poor? Scripture never calls it a mistake, but neither does it repeat or command it; Ananias was free to keep his property (5:4). The Jerusalem church later needed help from the Gentile churches (Romans 15:26), probably because of the famine (11:28–30) and persecution. The lasting lesson is generosity, not a single economic system.

Would you be willing for the gift to be untraceable? Which suggests a test, and a sharper one than the usual question of whether a person would give if he were asked. Would you be willing for the gift to be untraceable? Not merely for your name to be left off a list, but for the person helped never to discover that it was you, never to be grateful to you, never to know that they owe you anything whatever. That is the arrangement Luke is describing. The money went on the floor at the apostles’ feet, and after that it was nobody’s.

Should all my giving be anonymous? Not necessarily, but most of it can be, and the motive should always be. Jesus said, when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret (Matthew 6:3–4). The danger he names is giving in order to be seen. Sometimes it is right for a gift to be known: Barnabas’s gift is recorded in the next verse, and Paul publicly praised the Macedonians’ generosity to stir others (2 Corinthians 8:1–5). But it is wise to give much of what you give through the church or quietly, so that the glory goes to God and the receiver is beholden to no one but him.

On a Tuesday. Somewhere in your church there is probably a need nobody has mentioned out loud: a bill, a broken boiler, a cupboard running low. Begin by asking the deacons whether there is a family they are quietly worried about.

For worship. The Lord of glory was rich and became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich, and in Jerusalem his riches showed up as fields sold and widows fed. Every time a believer’s need is met in secret by a brother’s gift, the generosity on show is not finally the brother’s. It is Christ’s, running down through his people to the poor.
verseByVerse.note: Laying gifts at someone’s feet placed them under his authority.

parallels.desc: there will be no poor among you

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Son of encouragement. Now Luke gives the pattern a face. The man’s name is Joseph, but the apostles’ nickname stuck so completely that the New Testament uses it more than twenty times. Son of, in Hebrew idiom, means characterised by. (Scholars debate which Aramaic words lie behind the name, but Luke tells us what it meant to the church.) The word behind encouragement (paraklēsis) is related to the Spirit’s own title, the Helper, the one called alongside (John 14:16): the apostles named this man after something the Holy Spirit does.

A Levite, a native of Cyprus. Cyprus had a big Jewish community, and he would later preach there (13:4). Some readers have assumed an irregularity in a Levite owning a field (Numbers 18:20). There is probably none: the restriction concerned tribal allotment, and the priest Jeremiah bought a field long before (Jeremiah 32:6–9).

A Levite with a better portion. There is a deeper fitness in a Levite letting go of land. The Levites were given no share of the land because the LORD was their inheritance (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 18:2), and that was always meant to be enough. Barnabas, a Levite who owned a field after all, sells it and lays it down, and lives out the old promise in its new form: whoever has Christ has an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4). At Antioch the whole content of his encouragement was Christ: he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose (11:23).

Sold a field. Before a single word he ever said, the first fact on file about Barnabas is that he sold a field, put the money down, and made no speech about it.

Three things to come. He is about to do three things on which much of Acts turns. When every Christian was too frightened to go near the converted Saul, Barnabas brought him to the apostles and vouched for him (9:26–27). When the gospel broke out among Greeks at Antioch, he rejoiced at the grace of God and fetched Saul from Tarsus into the work (11:22–26). And when Paul refused to take John Mark again, Barnabas took him anyway and lost his partnership with Paul over it (15:37–39). Years later Paul writes asking for Mark, for he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11).

The real thing and the imitation. The chapter break conceals it: the next sentence in Luke’s narrative begins: but a man named Ananias. Barnabas and Ananias are two halves of one paragraph, the real thing and the imitation, set side by side, both selling property and both laying money at the apostles’ feet, and one of them dead the day he brought it (5:1–11). Luke has put the genuine article first so that the reader knows exactly what the counterfeit was copying.

How can I be a Barnabas? Look for the people others are wary of, overlooking or giving up on: the new believer with a bad past, the young person who failed, the newcomer nobody has spoken to, the struggling servant who is about to quit. Go and stand beside them. Speak specific, honest words of encouragement about what God is doing in them; Barnabas saw the grace of God and was glad (11:23). Vouch for people when it costs you something. Give practically, as he did. And be patient with those who have let you down; Mark is in the New Testament partly because Barnabas would not write him off. You will rarely be thanked, but you may be helping to raise the next Paul.
verseByVerse.note: Cyprus was a large island in the eastern Mediterranean with a big Jewish community.

4.theology: The sovereignty of God and mission. The prayer of verses 24 to 30 addresses God as Sovereign Lord, the Maker of everything, and confesses that Herod, Pilate and the nations did whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. This is not fatalism but God’s providence applied to the darkest day in history, and it leads not to passivity but to boldness: if God ruled over the crucifixion, he rules over every threat to the gospel. The church does not need favourable conditions to advance. It needs the Spirit and the word, and God gives both.
4.examples:
Then: A church a few weeks old, with two of its leaders just out of custody and no legal protection or political allies, prayed for boldness and was given it.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces the same choice between silence and speech. The God who shook that room still gives boldness to those who ask.

5.title: The Fear of the Lord
5.text: <sup>1</sup>But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, <sup>2</sup>and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet. <sup>3</sup>But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? <sup>4</sup>While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God.” <sup>5</sup>When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. <sup>6</sup>The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him. <sup>7</sup>After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. <sup>8</sup>And Peter said to her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” And she said, “Yes, for so much.” <sup>9</sup>But Peter said to her, “How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” <sup>10</sup>Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband. <sup>11</sup>And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things. <sup>12</sup>Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico. <sup>13</sup>None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem. <sup>14</sup>And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women, <sup>15</sup>so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. <sup>16</sup>The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed. <sup>17</sup>But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy <sup>18</sup>they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. <sup>19</sup>But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, <sup>20</sup>“Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life.” <sup>21</sup>And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel and sent to the prison to have them brought. <sup>22</sup>But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, <sup>23</sup>“We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside.” <sup>24</sup>Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. <sup>25</sup>And someone came and told them, “Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.” <sup>26</sup>Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. <sup>27</sup>And when they had brought them, they set them before the council. And the high priest questioned them, <sup>28</sup>saying, “We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.” <sup>29</sup>But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. <sup>30</sup>The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. <sup>31</sup>God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. <sup>32</sup>And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.” <sup>33</sup>When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. <sup>34</sup>But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. <sup>35</sup>And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. <sup>36</sup>For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing. <sup>37</sup>After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. <sup>38</sup>So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; <sup>39</sup>but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!” So they took his advice, <sup>40</sup>and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. <sup>41</sup>Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. <sup>42</sup>And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
5.overview:
After Barnabas comes the counterfeit. Ananias and Sapphira give part of a price while pretending it is the whole, lie to the Holy Spirit, and die; great fear comes on the whole church, here first called the church. The signs go on, and multitudes of men and women believe.

Jealous, the high priest jails the apostles, but an angel opens the doors and sends them back to the temple. Before the council again they say they must obey God rather than men, and preach the risen Jesus as Leader and Saviour. Gamaliel, a revered Pharisee, talks the council out of killing them. They are flogged, leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name, and go on teaching every day that the Christ is Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Holiness and Power in the Young Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ananias and Sapphira copy Barnabas’s gift outwardly while secretly keeping back part of the price. Peter exposes the lie as a lie to the Holy Spirit, and God strikes both down. Great fear falls on the church, and the same holiness that keeps the half-hearted away draws many to the Lord, as the apostles’ signs reach the sick of the whole region.
verseByVerse.theology:
The holiness of God and the danger of hypocrisy

When God begins something holy, the first sin against it is often judged with startling swiftness: Nadab and Abihu, Achan, Uzzah, and here the first hypocrisy in the church. These are representative judgements, set down once, not the rule; God’s ordinary way is the patient kindness meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4). The gospel does not lower that holiness but satisfies it, so that those in Christ may come near with confidence.
verseByVerse.examples: Now: Two cautions belong with this passage. It is not a lever for extracting money: Peter says the field and the proceeds were theirs. And the fear here came from what God did, not from what the leaders did; a congregation frightened of its elders has reproduced what this chapter killed.

verseByVerse.quote: But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, and with his wife's knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 5 shows the church threatened from within and from without. From within, by deceit: Ananias and Sapphira lie to the Holy Spirit and die. From without, by persecution: the apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, flogged, and go away rejoicing. In both, God protects his church: by purifying it, and by preserving it. The chapter teaches the holiness of God, the reality of the Spirit’s presence among his people, and the strange joy of suffering for Christ. And it ends with the name the council would not say being spoken in every house in Jerusalem.

But a man named Ananias. Everything depends on the word Luke opens with. But. The paragraph before this one introduced Barnabas, who sold a field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet (4:36–37). Luke then sets beside him two people who did the identical thing and were not the same at all: the same field sold, the same money on the same floor. Even the names are a sad irony. Ananias means the Lord is gracious; Sapphira means beautiful.

He kept back. The word, nosphizomai, is rare: elsewhere in the New Testament it describes slaves pilfering from their masters (Titus 2:10), and in the Greek Old Testament it turns up at one unforgettable place: Joshua 7:1, where Achan takes for himself some of what had been devoted to God at Jericho, hides it in his tent, and stands in the assembly as though nothing had happened, while Israel is defeated at Ai. Luke has reached for Achan’s own word. The first sin inside Israel’s new life in the land was a private theft concealed in public, and the church’s new order meets the same sin in the same vocabulary.

What they were really buying. It was not money they were after. They could have kept the whole field and sinned in nothing, or sold it and given a tenth openly and been thanked. What they wanted was something the honest options could not supply: the reputation of total surrender, at a price negotiated down in private. They bought applause with counterfeit currency. Barnabas’s gift had just been noticed and named, and it is easy to want that kind of name cheaply.

Great grace was upon them all. Luke has set the whole scene of sharing around one sentence (4:33). That is where Barnabas’s gift came from. People who had been given everything in a risen Saviour found that land was easy to let go (2 Corinthians 8:9). His gift was an answer to grace. Ananias and Sapphira turned the same act into a purchase: they tried to buy with a field the one thing Christ gives for nothing, a name and a place among his people. Every believer in that room stood there because Jesus had paid in full, and no one needed to pay for his standing a second time.

With his wife’s knowledge. It was not a moment’s weakness. Two people sat down together, discussed a figure, agreed what they would say, and rehearsed a story well enough that she could still deliver it three hours after he was dead. Every private sin has a moment where it could have been stopped by one person saying no. This one had two people in the room and neither of them said it. The marriage that should have been the safest place for an honest word became the place where the lie was made airtight.

The ordinary version. Before anyone comforts himself that this is an extreme case, measure it against the everyday form. The testimony allowed to stand a little better than the facts warrant. The prayer that lengthens and warms when other people are listening. The reply “we’ve been praying about that” when the last time you prayed about it was in March. The struggle described in the past tense because the present tense would cost too much. None of that is what Ananias did on the scale he did it. But it is the same transaction: buying a reputation for a devotion you have not got. If you recognise yourself here, that recognition is a mercy, not a sentence: the way out is the honest word to God, who already knows and receives the honest gladly (Psalm 32:5).

What it does not mean. This chapter has been misused for money more often than almost any other. It is not a warning about giving too little. Peter will say in two verses that the field was theirs and the proceeds were theirs, and no one had any claim on either. The sin here was not withholding; it was pretending. And the pressure to perform generosity is nearer to what killed them than the withholding ever was.

Why would Luke put such an ugly story in the church’s golden age? Because he is an honest historian and a pastor. He has just painted the church at its most beautiful: one heart and soul, no needy person among them (4:32–35). He could have stopped there and left us a legend. Instead he shows that the first serious danger to the church came not from Rome or the Sanhedrin but from inside, from people who sat in the meetings and handled holy things. That is a mercy to us. It tells us not to be shocked when a church we love proves to have hypocrites in it, and not to imagine that any golden age was free of them. It also tells us where to look first when we look for the danger: in our own hearts.

parallels.desc: Achan keeps back what was devoted to God

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? Peter’s Spirit-given discernment exposes the sin at once, and he names it precisely. It was not keeping the money, which was entirely their right. It was the lie: presenting part as the whole, a generosity they were not practising. And Peter means it really and personally: Satan genuinely instigated the sin. The image of being filled is the dark mirror of being filled with the Spirit (2:4; 4:8, 31; Ephesians 5:18). To be filled with the Spirit is not a warm feeling; it is to be so wholly taken up and governed by God that his presence controls one’s words and courage. Here the same idea runs the other way. Satan floods and masters Ananias’s heart, so that his tongue and his deed are ruled toward a lie. The whole church had just been filled with the Spirit (4:31); one man in it had let another tenant in.

Beside Judas. This sets Ananias next to Judas, into whom Satan entered to betray Jesus for money (Luke 22:3; John 13:2, 27). Behind the deceit stood the personal adversary, striking the newborn church from within at the very hour the gospel advanced with power. Having failed from outside with threats (4:21), he tried from inside with a lie.

Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? Yet Satan’s hand is no excuse. In the same breath Peter asks why Ananias planned it. Both are true at once: Satan filled his heart, and Ananias schemed it in his own. Scripture holds these together everywhere (Luke 22:3 beside 22:22; Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23). The tempter does not override the will; he inflames a heart already willing. As James says, each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire (James 1:14). Ananias’s lie fed on his own covetousness and his craving for praise, and Satan fanned the flame. “The devil made me do it” is no excuse, and Peter offers none. The verb Peter uses means to set or lay down: the deed was put in place in the heart before it was done in the room. It was premeditated.

The world, the flesh and the devil. Is every sin, then, a special act of Satan like this? Lying bears his family likeness, for Jesus calls him the father of lies (John 8:44). But the ordinary spring of sin is the human heart itself (Mark 7:21–23), not a direct filling by Satan as here and with Judas. Paul gathers the three sources in one breath (Ephesians 2:2–3): the course of this world, human life organised against God; the prince of the power of the air; and the passions of our flesh, the fallen self we carry from Adam. So we neither blame every sin on demons nor pretend he has no hand in it.

The promise of the Holy Spirit. Whom did Ananias lie to? To the Spirit whom Peter, weeks before, had said the exalted Jesus poured out from the right hand of God (2:33). The Spirit in that room was the risen Christ’s own gift, the way he keeps his promise not to leave his people as orphans but to come to them (John 14:16–18). So the lie was told in the presence of the ascended Lord of the church, and the adversary who tried to spoil his body from inside is the one Jesus had already met and defeated: he refused Satan’s offers in the wilderness, and at the cross he disarmed the powers and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). Satan could fill one man’s heart; he could not take the church out of Christ’s hands.

While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Their sin was not keeping part of the money but pretending to give it all. They were free to keep the land, or to keep the money. Giving was voluntary, and private property was not abolished (2:45). The church in Jerusalem was not a commune with compulsory pooling; it was a family in which people sold things as needs arose and gave freely. Peter’s two questions protect every Christian’s freedom to own and to give as he decides before God (2 Corinthians 9:7). God loves a cheerful giver, and he has no use for a pretended one.

You have not lied to man but to God. In verse 3 Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit; here, to God. The Holy Spirit is God. This is one of the clearest statements of the Spirit’s deity and personhood in Scripture. You cannot lie to a force or an influence; you lie to a person. And the Spirit dwelling in the church is the living God himself, so to deceive his people in their worship is to lie to him (1 Corinthians 3:16). They paraded a lie of wholehearted devotion before the One who reads the heart, as though he could be fooled, and God is not mocked (Galatians 6:7).

Can a true Christian be filled by Satan like this? Scripture never speaks of a believer, in whom the Holy Spirit dwells, being owned or possessed by Satan; the Spirit does not share his house as a lodger (1 John 4:4). But believers can certainly be deceived, tempted and used by him for a moment. Peter himself heard the words, get behind me, Satan, soon after his great confession (Matthew 16:23), and Paul warns Christians not to give the devil a foothold through unresolved anger (Ephesians 4:26–27). Whether Ananias was a true believer Luke does not say, and we should not pretend to know. The practical point is plain: do not leave a door open. Unconfessed resentment, a secret love of praise, a hidden sin that is being managed rather than fought, these are footholds. Close them by bringing them into the light.
verseByVerse.note: Their sin was not keeping part of the money but pretending to give it all. Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He fell down and breathed his last. Luke does not linger over Ananias. The death is unannounced. Peter pronounces no sentence and calls down no curse; he only exposes the sin. It is God’s act, not Peter’s punishment. And its result is a church that suddenly grasps whom it is dealing with. The Spirit among them is no benevolent force that winks at religious play-acting. He is the holy God himself. Holy means more than good. It means utterly set apart: pure light with no darkness in it, so far above sin that the seraphim, who have never sinned, cover their faces before him and cry holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:2–3). Ananias had treated that God as someone who would not notice.

Why so severe? Nearly every liar walks away still breathing. Why this one? Because Scripture shows a pattern: when God inaugurates something holy, the first sin against it is judged with startling swiftness. Nadab and Abihu at the dawn of the priesthood offered unauthorised fire and died (Leviticus 10:1–2). Achan died at Israel’s entry into the land (Joshua 7). Uzzah was struck as the ark came home (2 Samuel 6:6–7). And here is the first hypocrisy at the birth of the church. These are representative judgments: one public sample of what all sin deserves, set down once to stamp God’s holiness on his people and to keep a young, tender church from being poisoned at its core. Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, God said over Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:3). Nearness to God raises the demand for reverence; it never lowers it.

Then why do the rest of us not fall dead at every lie? Because these are the exception, not the rule. God’s ordinary way is patient kindness, meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4; Psalm 130:3). One Ananias, recorded for ever, teaches the whole church age: the lightning flashes once to light up the whole landscape. And for the believer the deepest answer is the cross. The judgment our sin deserves has already fallen on Christ. So the fear Luke records is not the terror that drives us from God but the awe that keeps us from trifling with him: the reverence of a people who have seen, close up, that their God is holy.

Wrapped him up. Four verbs, no pause, and no funeral. A Jewish death set in motion days of formal mourning; none of that happens. He is in the ground within hours. Luke reports it without comment, which is itself a comment. The church buried him, quietly and fast, and the men who carried him out came back and, three hours later, had to do it a second time.

Where Christians differ: was Ananias saved? Some think this proves he was never a believer, a false professor exposed like Achan; they point out that Satan had filled his heart (v. 3) and that his sin was a deliberate attempt to deceive the Holy Spirit. Others think a true believer can be disciplined by death without losing salvation, as Paul says of some at Corinth who were sick or had died, judged by the Lord so that they would not be condemned with the world (1 Corinthians 11:30–32; 5:5). This commentary’s view: Scripture does not tell us, and we should not pretend to know. What is clear is that God takes sin in his church seriously, especially hypocrisy, and that he may discipline severely. It is not a pattern to expect in every case; it is a warning written at the church’s beginning.

Does God still strike people dead for sin today? He is free to, and Scripture shows he has done it more than once (Acts 12:23; 1 Corinthians 11:30). But the New Testament never teaches us to expect it, and we should never interpret a particular death, illness or accident as God’s verdict on someone’s hidden sin. Jesus explicitly forbade that kind of reasoning about the Galileans Pilate killed and the eighteen crushed by the tower in Siloam (Luke 13:1–5). His conclusion was not that they were worse sinners, but: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. That is the right use of Acts 5 too. It is not for diagnosing other people’s funerals. It is for searching your own heart while there is time.
verseByVerse.note: Burial usually took place the same day.

parallels.desc: Nadab and Abihu struck down

verseByVerse.quote: After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. And Peter said to her, "Tell me whether you sold the land for so much." And she said, "Yes, for so much."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About three hours. Three hours. Luke times it, and the interval is a mercy. Somewhere in the city she is going about her day, and her husband has been dead for three hours, and nobody has come to tell her. Then she walks in through the door into a room where every person present knows exactly what has happened, and what she is about to say.

Tell me. Peter does not accuse her or tell her that her husband is dead. He asks a question, as easy to answer truthfully as a question can be made: a door held open. God gave her the last three hours and then he gave her the question.

Peter knew what a question can do. The man asking Sapphira this question had once been asked one himself. Not long before, on a beach in Galilee, the risen Jesus had faced the disciple who denied him three times and asked him three times, do you love me? (John 21:15–17). No accusation, no recital of the charge: a question, held open until Peter could answer it truly, and on the other side of the answer, a commission. That is the way of Christ with sinners, and it is the way Peter now takes with Sapphira. Through his apostle, the Lord who had restored Peter with a question offered her the same road back. The difference between the two scenes is not in the Lord who asked but in the answer that was given.

Yes, for so much. She keeps to the lie. Two words in the Greek, the sound of a rehearsed line. And she was under no pressure: her husband was not beside her, and nobody was watching to see whether she would hold the line. She kept it anyway, alone and freely, which is precisely why Peter’s next words treat her as a principal and not as a wife who was dragged along.

A wife and her husband’s sin. This passage speaks to something on which women have been badly counselled. A wife is nowhere in Scripture required to follow her husband into sin, and a husband’s headship has never included the authority to make a liar of her. Headship in Scripture is self-giving love modelled on Christ’s love for the church (Ephesians 5:25), and Christ never asks his bride to sin. The principle is the same one the apostles will state to the highest court in the land later in this very chapter: we must obey God rather than men (v. 29). If that holds against a Sanhedrin, it holds against a husband, and it holds in a kitchen. Scripture gives the picture: Abigail went round her husband’s ruinous folly, acted without his knowledge to stop it, and is commended for it in the text and by David himself (1 Samuel 25). Sapphira had the same road open and did not take it. Her tragedy is not that she submitted; it is that she agreed.

What if refusing my husband would put me in danger? Then the issue is no longer submission at all but safety, and Scripture never asks a wife to stay in harm’s way. A husband who threatens, intimidates or harms his wife has abandoned the Christ-like headship Scripture describes; abuse is never to be tolerated or covered by a church. If you are afraid of what will happen if you say no, tell someone you trust today: a pastor or elder, a wise friend, and if you are in danger, the police. Getting safe is not rebellion. Abigail acted to save lives, and was praised for it. In ordinary disagreements, a godly wife can refuse to sin respectfully and gently, as Sapphira could have done, and leave the rest with God.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to her, "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out." Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Peter names what she has done as a partnership. You have agreed together. The verb is symphōneō, to sound together, the word behind our symphony. It is one of the good gifts of marriage that two people can come to one mind, and here it is, working perfectly, in the service of a lie. They had harmony, and they had used it to make the deception airtight. A spouse’s calling is to help the other toward God, never away from him.

Testing God. The word (peirazō) means to put God to the proof: to presume on him, to dare him, to find out whether he is really watching and will really act. Israel did it at Massah, asking, is the LORD among us or not? (Exodus 17:2, 7; Psalm 95:9). Ananias and Sapphira had, in effect, laid a wager that the Spirit would not notice, or would notice and not mind. They had watched the Spirit fall; they simply did not believe he was paying attention to them. He was.

You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. Set the two scenes side by side. On the pinnacle of the temple the devil invited Jesus to presume on his Father, and the Son refused: he would not stage a display to make God prove himself (Matthew 4:5–7). Ananias and Sapphira, with Satan filling their hearts, staged one before the church and dared the Spirit not to notice. Israel failed that test at Massah, and these two failed it in the church. One Man has passed it on our behalf, trusting his Father all the way to a cross where no angel caught him. The obedience they lacked is the obedience he offers to everyone who takes refuge in him.

The feet at the door. She learns in one sentence that she is a widow and about to follow him. Peter passes no sentence and claims no power to strike; he knows by the Spirit what is about to happen and says so. The judgment in this chapter is God’s, twice.

At his feet. Go back eight verses: on that spot her husband laid the money at the apostles’ feet (v. 2). That square of floor and the watching room were the whole object of the exercise, and it is the exact spot where she falls. The place they had wanted to be seen is the place she is carried from.

Beside her husband. The young men come back in and do again what they had done three hours earlier. Together in the planning, together in the rehearsing, together in the ground.

Terrible but not arbitrary. The passage is terrible, but not arbitrary. God was not defending his dignity against an insult; he was defending a very young church against the one thing that kills churches from the inside, which is people who have learned to perform a devotion they do not have and to be admired for it. Everything the early chapters describe, the one heart and soul, the goods held loosely, the apostles’ teaching received as the word of God, depends on the assumption that when a Christian says a thing, it is so. Two people set out to prove that assumption could be exploited. The Lord of the church answered in a way the church would never forget.

What does testing God look like today? Usually it is quiet. It is sinning on purpose because you are sure you will be forgiven afterwards. It is taking a risk God has warned against and daring him to protect you. It is living as though he does not see what happens on a phone at midnight, or in the accounts, or in a marriage behind closed doors. It is also, at the other end, demanding that God prove himself on your terms before you will trust him. The cure is the one Jesus used: answer the temptation with the word of God, and remember that the Lord who sees in secret is the same Lord who loves you.
