You do not need to test a Father you can trust.

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD your God to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great fear. Twice now Luke tells us the effect rather than the event (v. 5): this is what the episode was for. And it did not stay indoors. Jerusalem heard, outsiders as well as believers, and drew its own conclusions about what sort of company this was.

The first time the church is called the church. This is the first time in Acts that he calls the believers the church (ekklēsia): the assembly, the called-out people (some later manuscripts already have the word at 2:47). In the Greek Old Testament the word was used of Israel assembled before God at Sinai and in the temple; now it is the people of the Messiah. Luke does not use it at Pentecost, nor in the golden paragraph about having all things in common, but here, in the silence after two funerals, in a room that has just learned what it is living with. To be the church is, before anything else, to reckon with the holiness of the God who has moved in.

The soil of the church’s life. This fear is not the enemy of the church’s life; it is the soil of it. Watch what grows in the next three verses: signs and wonders, a people all together in Solomon’s Portico, and more than ever believers added to the Lord. The awe did not freeze the church. It purified it and then filled it. A church without the fear of God is not a happier church, but a weaker one.

The man at the hearth. This is not cringing terror but reverent awe that draws near in love and yet will not trifle: the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10; 2 Corinthians 7:1; Hebrews 12:28–29). Picture a man at his hearth on a winter night. He loves the fire, pulls his chair as close as he can bear, and would not dream of putting his hand into it, because he knows perfectly well what it is. He is nearer to it than anyone else in the house. That is the fear of the Lord, and Luke will later name it as the very mark of a healthy church: walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit (9:31). Both, in one sentence, without embarrassment.

Am I Ananias, if I know I am not what I appear to be? There is a particular person who reads Acts 5 and lies awake: who knows he is not what he appears to be in his church, who can name the exaggeration and the unconfessed thing, and who now half expects the floor to open. That fear deserves a straight answer rather than a soothing one. Ananias was not caught out by a God waiting to pounce. He engineered a lie in the presence of God in advance, with a partner, and was given a question at the end of it that he could have answered honestly. So was she. Neither of them wanted to be found out; both wanted to be admired more than they wanted to be true. A man who is trembling because he longs to be genuine and knows he is not yet is describing an entirely different condition, and the trembling itself is the evidence. The Spirit does not produce that ache in people he is about to strike down. He produces it in people he is not going to leave alone. And the door out of it is open and has always been open: say the true thing, to God first and then to whoever needs to hear it, and the whole weight of it goes. No one who confesses his sin and trusts Christ is in their position.

If God is this holy, how can I come near him at all? Only through Christ, and through Christ, with confidence. The fire at the hearth is not safer because you keep your distance; it is safe because someone has made a way to sit beside it. Jesus is the way. His blood has opened a new and living way into the very presence of God, so that we may draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith (Hebrews 10:19–22). The writer to the Hebrews puts the two together just as Luke does: let us offer acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:28–29), and let us with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (4:16). Reverence and confidence are not opposites. They are the two hands with which a forgiven sinner holds on to a holy God.

On a Tuesday. Before you next walk into a church service, pause at the door for ten seconds and remember whose house you are entering and who is present among his people. Then go in glad and careful. Let that same awareness follow you home on Monday: the God who is present in the assembly is present at your desk.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Acts uses the word “church.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon's Portico.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many signs and wonders. God answers the prayer of 4:30. A sign points beyond itself; a wonder astonishes. They were meant to authenticate the message and its messengers: God’s seal on the apostolic gospel. The Lord bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands (14:3). The wonder was the wrapping; the word was the gift. That is why Jesus rebuked those who craved signs for their own sake (Matthew 12:39).

By the hands of the apostles. Luke is careful about whose hands. The signs in these chapters are done by the apostles, and Paul could call them the marks of an apostle precisely because they marked out the men whom Christ had sent. The church prayed; the apostles’ hands were the instruments; the risen Christ was the healer (3:6, 16; 9:34).

Where Christians differ: have the sign gifts ceased? Many Christians, called continuationists, believe that the gifts of healing, tongues and prophecy continue in the church today. They point out that 1 Corinthians 12–14 was written to an ordinary church, that Paul urges believers to earnestly desire the spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 14:1), and that no verse says plainly that the gifts would cease before Christ returns. The historic Reformed church has held that these apostolic sign gifts have ceased, and its case is drawn from Scripture, not mere observation. The signs marked out the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12), and the apostles were a foundation laid once: the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid only once. Their office could not be handed on, for its men had to be eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, and Paul calls himself last of all (1 Corinthians 15:8). The revelation the signs authenticated is complete: the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). Once the foundation was laid and the message set down in Scripture, the credentials that attested the foundation-layers had served their purpose, like scaffolding taken down once the building stands. This commentary’s view: the cessationist reading is the more likely one: the apostolic sign gifts, as standing credentials of new revelation, belonged to the foundation age and have ceased. This is held charitably. Our continuationist brothers love the same Christ and the same Bible, and many of them are at least as zealous for Scripture’s sufficiency as we are.

Two honest qualifications. First, no verse says outright that miracles will cease when the apostles die. The certain ground is the purpose of the signs; the timing of their ceasing is a strong inference from that purpose, joined to the close of the apostolic age and the completed canon, not a single proof text. Paul does say that tongues and prophecy will pass away (1 Corinthians 13:8–10), though believers differ over when the perfect comes. Second, this does not mean God no longer works miracles. He remains free to heal and to act wonderfully in answer to prayer, and he often does. What ceased is the apostolic sign gift as a standing credential of new revelation, not God’s power or his nearness.

Does that mean I should not pray for healing? Not at all. Pray, and pray boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them, anointing with oil, and promises that the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick (James 5:14–15). God answers such prayers, sometimes with healing that doctors cannot explain, sometimes through medicine, sometimes by giving grace to bear what he does not remove (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). The cessationist conviction is not that God has stopped healing; it is that no one today holds an apostle’s gift to heal at will, and that no new revelation is being added to Scripture. Ask your Father freely, and trust his answer.

Solomon’s Portico. A roofed colonnade along the east side of the temple’s outer court, where Peter had preached after healing the lame man (3:11). The believers were not huddled in hiding but gathered openly in the most public religious space in Jerusalem.

The works bear witness. Solomon’s Portico had heard this before. It was there, in winter, that Jesus was pressed to say plainly whether he was the Christ, and answered that his works bore witness about him (John 10:24–25). Now the same colonnade sees the same kind of works, done by other hands in his name (3:6, 16) and pointing to the same Person. The rulers who rejected his works then are watching them go on, because he is not absent at all. He is reigning, and his hand is stretched out through theirs.
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s Portico was a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of the rest dared join them. Luke can hardly mean the believers, and open unbelievers had no wish to join at all. The word join (kollasthai) means to throw in one’s lot with someone. So the rest are most naturally the fringe: the curious and the would-be hangers-on who might have attached themselves to so admired a movement for the prestige or the perks. After Ananias and Sapphira, no one dared. The community’s fearful holiness (vv. 5, 11) had made plain that you do not attach yourself to this people for mixed motives.

Held them in high esteem. They respected them from a distance. The church’s public welcome runs hot and cold through Acts: esteemed here, arrested a few verses on (vv. 17–18), and soon Stephen stoned amid great persecution (chapters 7–8). Both favour and hostility come from God’s hand. He grants seasons of favour to open doors (2:47) and permits persecution to scatter the seed (8:1–4).

The road their Lord had walked. Luke’s Gospel had shown the same pattern around Jesus: the people hung on his words while the chief priests and scribes sought to destroy him (Luke 19:47–48). Jesus received the people’s favour without ever leaning on it, for he knew what was in man (John 2:24–25), and he did not lose his way when it vanished. The apostles are walking the road their Master walked, as he told them to expect (John 15:20). So the believer should be neither intoxicated by esteem nor crushed by opposition. Esteem is a gift to be spent for Christ; opposition is the long-run lot of faithful witness (2 Timothy 3:12). Both, in God’s hands, advance the same kingdom.

Is it wrong to want my church to be well thought of? No; it is right to want it, as long as you want it on the right terms. Paul wanted elders to be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7), and Peter wanted Christians to live such good lives among unbelievers that they would see their good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). What is wrong is buying respect by hiding what is distinctive: softening the gospel, dropping holiness, or becoming so much like the world that nobody could be offended. The esteem in this verse came to a church that was holy, honest and unashamed of Christ. That is the only kind of good reputation worth having, and it is one God may give or withhold as he pleases.

verseByVerse.quote: And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women,
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than ever. Two people have dropped dead in the meeting, nobody dares attach himself casually any more (v. 13), and the result is not decline but more believers than before. Holiness did not shrink the church; it grew it.

Against modern instinct. We assume a church grows by being easier to belong to, less demanding, more like the surrounding culture with a religious accent. Luke reports the opposite. When it became unmistakably clear that the God in that room was real, the pretenders stopped coming and everyone else started. Verses 13 and 14 are a single movement, the same holiness keeping the casual away and drawing the needy in. A church can be crowded and thin at the same time.

Not a licence for severity. This has been abused. The fear in Acts 5 came from something God did, not from something the leadership did. Peter did not strike anyone, threaten anyone, or run a campaign of discipline; he asked two honest questions and God did the rest. A church where people are frightened of the elders, watch their words in the foyer, and cannot admit a struggle without consequences has not reproduced this chapter. It has produced the very thing this chapter killed: a community where everyone performs. The fear of God makes people honest. The fear of men is what made Ananias lie.

Added to the Lord. They were added to the Lord: not to a movement or a register. In Acts the Lord is the risen Jesus, whom God has made both Lord and Christ (2:36). What happens when a person is converted is that he is joined to him, united to the living Christ by faith, and membership among the people follows because they belong to him too. What does union with Christ actually mean? That you are bound to him so closely that what is his becomes yours: his death counts as your death to sin, his righteousness is counted as yours, and his life flows into you as sap flows from the vine into the branch (Romans 6:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21; John 15:5). Anyone who wonders whether he is in because he signed something or attends something has the answer here: the attachment that counts was made to the Lord himself, and it will therefore outlast every congregation any of us ever belongs to. And it was God who did the adding: the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved (2:47). The church grows by his gathering, not by its marketing.

Multitudes of both men and women. Luke counts the women, in a world where a crowd was ordinarily numbered by its men, and he does it repeatedly (8:12; 16:13–15; 17:4, 12). Joel’s promise of the Spirit on sons and daughters alike (2:17–18) is showing in the arithmetic. The gospel was for both alike, and both alike were added to the Lord.

So will a strict church always grow? No, and this verse does not promise it. Churches have been holy and small for generations, and faithful churches have shrunk under persecution. Numbers are in God’s hands, not ours; Paul planted and Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). What this verse forbids is the opposite assumption: that holiness is a hindrance to growth and must be traded away for it. Our task is to be faithful, honest and unashamed of Christ, and to leave the arithmetic to the Lord who adds.

For worship. The Lord who added them is the Lord to whom they were added: he gathers, and he is the home of the gathered. Every man and every woman in that crowd was a sheep the Good Shepherd had laid down his life for and now called by name (John 10:11, 16). Not one of them came by accident, and not one would be lost (John 6:37–39). The Shepherd of multitudes counts his flock one by one.

verseByVerse.quote: so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At least his shadow. The healing ministry has reached a scale that draws the whole Jerusalem region. Ancient people often believed that a person’s shadow carried something of his power. Luke does not say the shadow healed anyone; he reports what people hoped. This is popular faith expressing itself in folk terms, and God was gracious to that imperfect faith, as with the woman who touched the fringe of Jesus’ garment (Luke 8:44) and the handkerchiefs carried from Paul (19:11–12). The power was God’s, not Peter’s shadow.

From the towns around Jerusalem. The word spreads beyond the city, as Jesus said it would (1:8).

Unclean spirits. Here we should say only what Scripture tells us. Unclean spirits are real, personal, evil spirit beings, what the Gospels equally call demons (Mark 5:2, 12–15; 7:25–26). They are not mere symbols, nor simply an ancient label for illness. The New Testament treats them as intelligent beings with will and speech, part of the kingdom of Satan (Matthew 12:24–26), commonly understood as fallen angels (Revelation 12:9). Unclean marks their nature: defiling, the opposite of God’s holiness. They can oppress and torment, and at times control a person, with effects both physical (Mark 5:3–4; 9:18) and inward (Mark 5:5). But Scripture does not blame every sickness on demons. It lists the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits as two distinct groups, here and in Mark 1:32–34. So we are neither to deny the demonic nor to see a demon behind every illness.

Their relation to Christ. What Scripture stresses above all is how they stand before Jesus. The unclean spirits recognise him and tremble (Mark 1:24; James 2:19). They are utterly subject to his authority and to his name on the lips of his servants (Luke 10:17; Acts 16:18). They flee before the advancing kingdom (Matthew 12:28). At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). On how exactly a spirit afflicts, or why some and not others, Scripture is reticent, and so are we. It gives us enough to take the reality seriously, never to fear it, and to look only to the Conqueror: he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

All healed. All, as in Jesus’ own ministry (Luke 4:40; 6:19). It was an extraordinary season: the kingdom had arrived, creation was being restored, and a preview of the new creation was visible in the streets of Jerusalem.

In the flow. Verses 12–16 are Luke’s third summary picture of the church (2:42–47; 4:32–35). The holiness that struck down two pretenders drew a whole region to the risen Christ, and this success is what fills the high priest with jealousy (v. 17).

Where Christians differ: relics and holy objects. Some have used verses like this to support venerating relics or objects linked with saints. This commentary’s view: Luke reports; he does not prescribe. The healing came from the risen Christ, who was confirming his apostles’ message. The New Testament never teaches believers to seek power through objects, shadows or relics, and the apostles would have been horrified to be venerated (14:14–15). Look to Christ, not to his servants or their belongings.

Should we expect healing through objects or special people today? No. Peter’s shadow is the description of a unique moment, not a method to copy. Prayer cloths sent in the post, anointed water, a celebrity healer whose touch is said to carry power: none of these has a promise behind it, and the danger of superstition, and of people being exploited when they are most desperate, is real. God still heals in answer to prayer, and the ordinary means he has given are prayer, the elders of the church, and medicine received with thanks (James 5:14–15; 1 Timothy 5:23). Bring your sick to Christ directly. You do not need anyone’s shadow.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? A true Christian is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and belongs to Christ, bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Scripture nowhere describes a believer being owned or controlled by a demon, and it assures us that the evil one does not touch the one born of God (1 John 5:18). But believers are attacked. They are tempted, accused, and oppressed in their minds, which is why we are told to put on the whole armour of God and to resist the devil, who will flee (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). If you are troubled by dark fears, do not go looking for a specialist in exorcism. Go to Christ in prayer, fill your mind with Scripture, tell your pastor, and see a doctor as well, because much that feels spiritual is also bodily, and God uses both kinds of help.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jealous of the apostles’ success, the high priest has them jailed, but an angel opens the doors and sends them back to the temple at dawn. Before the council they answer that they must obey God rather than men, and Peter preaches the crucified Jesus as exalted Leader and Saviour. The council wants them dead; Gamaliel persuades it to wait and see. They are flogged, leave rejoicing, and go on teaching daily in the temple and from house to house.
verseByVerse.theology:
Obeying God rather than men

Gamaliel’s advice tests movements by whether they last, not whether they are true, and avoids the one question in the room, whether God raised Jesus. God used it to restrain the council; it is not a theological authority. The apostles stand on something else: a hierarchy of obedience. The state’s authority is real and derived from God, and when it forbids what God commands it has run out of warrant at that point and no further. The same New Testament commands submission under Nero (Romans 13:1). And the apostles did not resist arrest, raise the crowd or flee. They took the flogging, which is what biblical civil disobedience looks like.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The man leading the apostles out of the council, rejoicing, was the one who months earlier had denied knowing Jesus to a servant girl beside a fire.

Now: Joy in suffering for the name is not a duty to be manufactured in advance; it was given to those men on the way out of the building. And the suffering in view is dishonour incurred for Christ, so this is not a text to hand a grieving or ill person, nor a slogan for defying laws one merely dislikes.

verseByVerse.quote: But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The party of the Sadducees. The second attack, from outside. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy of Jerusalem: the wealthy families who controlled the temple, with the high priest at their head. They profited from the status quo and cooperated closely with Rome to keep their power. Theologically they held to the written law of Moses, rejected the oral traditions the Pharisees prized, and, crucially here, denied the resurrection of the dead, along with angels and spirits (23:8).

Why the heat. The apostles were proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead (4:2), the very doctrine the Sadducees denied, and drawing the people’s allegiance away from the temple establishment. The gospel struck at both their theology and their power.

Filled with jealousy. The word (zēlos) is not petty envy but hot zeal: the burning of men who believe something precious is being taken from them, which is exactly what a religious establishment feels when the people begin listening to somebody else. It is the same motive that handed Jesus over: Pilate perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up (Mark 15:10). Again and again in Acts, the attempts to close the church down are prompted by the gospel’s advance.

The public prison. All the apostles this time, and the common lock-up: it was meant to be seen, and to be degrading: the men Jerusalem had begun to admire, walked through the streets and put in with the ordinary criminals.

They never investigate the claim. The men now running the case against the resurrection are the party that has staked its theology on there being no such thing. In encounter after encounter, from the guards’ report at the tomb (Matthew 28:11–15) to this morning’s empty cell, not one of the men pressing the case is recorded as asking the only question that matters: is it true? They investigate the preachers. They never investigate the claim. It is possible to hold the highest office in the religion of the living God and to have no interest whatever in whether he has done something.

How do I fight envy when God blesses someone else? Name it first, because envy almost never calls itself by its name; it calls itself concern, or discernment, or a sense that something is not quite right about that ministry. Then bring it to God as sin, not as an assessment. Pray, by name, for the person or church whose blessing stings, and ask God to bless them more, until your heart catches up with your prayer. Remember that everything anyone has is a gift (1 Corinthians 4:7), and that the Master of the vineyard is free to be generous to whom he will (Matthew 20:15). And rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15), even if at first it is an act of obedience rather than a feeling.

verseByVerse.quote: But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, "Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel of the Lord. Luke spends one clause on the miracle; the escape is not the story. And the humour is not lost: the Sadducees, who denied angels (23:8), are thwarted by one. Angels are ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and here one of them serves with a key.

Go and stand in the temple. What the angel says next is the story. Not go home, not leave Jerusalem. They are told to go straight back to the building owned and policed by the men who had just locked them up and do precisely the thing they were arrested for doing. The rescue was a transfer to the front.

All the words of this Life. Not eternal life in the abstract. This Life: the thing standing in front of everybody, the life that came out of a sealed tomb and is now visibly loose in Jerusalem, healing people in the street and putting courage into fishermen. Speak all of it, the angel says, not the parts the council will tolerate.

Why does God open this door and not others? A prison that opens raises a question that has to be met honestly, because it is the question a suffering reader will bring, and Acts itself refuses to duck it. Turn forward seven chapters and Luke tells of another night, another angel, another set of chains falling off Peter; and in the same paragraph, James the brother of John is put to death with the sword, and no angel came (12:1–11). One apostle walks out past the guards; the other is buried. Luke sets them side by side without a word of explanation, and he did not have to. He could have left the beheading out. Later in the same book Paul sits in custody for two full years while a governor waits for a bribe (24:26–27), and no angel comes for him either, and the gospel goes on regardless, to a governor and a king (24:24–25; 26:1–29).

No promise for the faithful. So this passage must never be turned into a promise that the door opens for the faithful. The doors that stayed shut in this very book were shut on better men than most of us, and it was never a question of whether they had believed hard enough. What Acts teaches is narrower and steadier: God opens what he needs opened for the gospel to go where he intends, and he owes no one an explanation of his choices. James’s death stopped nothing, and if a door in your own life has stayed shut, it is not because you believed too little.

What have you been let out for? That gives an ordinary Christian a better question than why my door has not opened. Look at what the angel did with these men once they were out. Every deliverance in Acts is for the mission, never for the comfort of the delivered, and this one lasted only a few hours before the same men were arrested again and flogged the same day. Anyone who has been brought out of something, a diagnosis or a debt or a marriage that nearly ended, has a plainer thing to ask than why it happened to him and not to someone else. He can ask what he has been let out for. In this chapter the answer came with the door.

Do angels still rescue people today? God still sends his angels to serve his people; Hebrews speaks of them in the present tense, and some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2). But Scripture never tells us to seek angelic visits, to pray to angels, or to expect to see them, and it warns against the worship of angels (Colossians 2:18). Most of their work is unseen, and most of God’s deliverances come through ordinary means: a doctor, a friend, a changed decision. Thank God for his unseen care, and keep your eyes on the Lord of the angels, not on them.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At daybreak. They heard, they went, they taught: let out in the night, they went straight there and waited for the doors. There is no interval in the sentence for asking whether it might be wiser to let a day pass. A great deal of what passes for seeking God’s will is in fact the search for a delay he has not granted. These men had every reason to want one, and they did not take it.

Early in the morning in the temple. In the last week of his life, Jesus taught daily in the temple, and early in the morning all the people came to him there to hear him (Luke 21:37–38). And on the morning of his trial, when day came, the assembly of the elders gathered and had him led to their council (Luke 22:66). Now both halves happen again at the same hour. The difference is the empty tomb. Then the council had the Teacher in its hands; now it cannot even find his messengers. The Lord they condemned at dawn is the Lord who sends his servants out at dawn.

All the senate. The council is the Sanhedrin, the supreme court of the Jewish nation, presided over by the high priest; under Rome a death sentence needed the governor’s ratification (John 18:31). The senate (gerousia) is the council of elders. Luke piles term upon term to stress that they convened the entire body in its most solemn session.

Sent to the prison. Here the comedy begins. The grandest court in Israel grinds into motion to fetch prisoners God has already set free, who are at that very hour teaching in the temple.

But shouldn’t I pray before I act? Yes, about the things God has not already told you. Prayer for guidance is right when Scripture leaves a real choice open: which job, which city, whom to marry among believers. But when God has already spoken, praying about it can become a pious way of not doing it. The apostles did not need to pray about whether to preach; they had been told. You do not need to pray about whether to forgive, to tell the truth, or to be kind to the colleague who wronged you. Those are settled. Pray for strength to obey, and then obey, today.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, "We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one inside. Luke lets the officers’ report stand without comment. Every element of the system worked perfectly and the men are gone, and nobody in the room can account for it.

The signature of the miracle. Nothing was broken and nobody was hurt. This is not power straining against resistance; it is power to which locked doors are not an obstacle worth damaging.

The same shape as the tomb. Look at the shape of what these men are asked to explain. A sealed place. Guards posted. An occupant who was certainly there last night. And in the morning, everything secure and the place empty, with nothing but an account nobody can produce. Jerusalem had heard that story once already, about a tomb with guards and a seal (Matthew 27:62–66; 28:11–15), and this council had done its best to keep the lid on it. Now the same shape has turned up in their own jail, before Sadducees who say there is no resurrection, nor angel (23:8).

Could someone inside simply have let them out? It is the sceptic’s obvious question, and the officers’ report goes a long way toward answering it. A friendly jailer who freed twelve prisoners would hardly lock the doors again behind them and leave the guards standing at their posts, guards who, as Acts later shows, could pay with their lives for an escape (12:19). Nor would men who had slipped out by a bribe walk straight into the temple at dawn, the one place the authorities were certain to look. Luke, who tells us he investigated everything carefully (Luke 1:3), says plainly that an angel of the Lord opened the doors. The council itself never offered a natural explanation. It simply ordered the men to stop talking.

How should I speak to someone whose mind is already closed? Patiently, honestly, and with prayer, because the problem is not finally in the evidence but in the heart, and only God can open a heart (16:14). Give the reasons for your hope when you are asked (1 Peter 3:15), but do not imagine that a cleverer argument will do what only the Spirit can do. Ask gentle questions that help a person notice what he has ruled out in advance: what would you accept as evidence? Live in a way that makes your faith hard to dismiss. And keep praying for him. Saul of Tarsus had his mind closed tighter than anyone in this council, and the risen Christ opened it on a road.

For worship. Locked doors have never been an obstacle to this Lord. On the evening of his rising, with the doors shut for fear, Jesus came and stood among his disciples and said, Peace be with you (John 20:19). The same quiet power that walked his apostles out of a bolted prison walks into rooms bolted by fear, and into hearts bolted against him, and opens them without breaking anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, "Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greatly perplexed. The word (diēporoun) means at a complete loss, out of explanations. They are not asking what has happened but where it ends. It is a more honest reaction than anything they will say for the rest of the day: they have lost control, and they know it.

The captain of the temple and the chief priests. The captain of the temple was second in rank only to the high priest: a senior priest who commanded the Levitical temple guard, kept order in the precincts and held the power of arrest. It was his office that helped seize Jesus (Luke 22:4, 52) and the apostles (4:1). With the chief priests, here is the temple’s entire ruling establishment, its head of security and its senior clergy, standing helpless before an empty cell.

Standing in the temple. Then the anticlimax: Look! Not fled or hiding. Standing in the establishment’s own building, doing the very thing at which they were interrupted, while the establishment holds an emergency session about where they might have gone.

Why does Luke make the authorities look so foolish? Not to mock them for sport, but to show us the truth about every power that sets itself against Christ. Psalm 2 had already described it: the kings of the earth set themselves and the rulers take counsel together against the LORD and against his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens laughs. The church had prayed that very psalm not long before (4:25–28). Luke lets us see the answer to their prayer in the form of a farce. When Christians feel small before powerful opponents, this is the scene to remember. The opponents are not in control, and the comedy is God’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But not by force. The head of temple security, in his own precinct, arresting men he has the legal right to arrest, does it carefully, almost politely, because he is frightened of the crowd. The men who hold every instrument of power in Jerusalem cannot use any of it.

Two kinds of fear. Luke has built this chapter around one word. Great fear came upon all who heard (v. 5). Great fear came upon the whole church (v. 11). And now fear again, in the other party, with a different object. The church is afraid of God. The council is afraid of the public. Nobody in the Sanhedrin appears to be afraid of God at all, and that is exactly why they are afraid of everybody else.

The rope round the neck. A man who genuinely fears God has one thing to be afraid of and is therefore free of nearly everything; a man who does not ends up managing a long and growing list. The council cannot act on its convictions or follow its own legal judgment, because it has to keep watching the temple courts to see how it is playing. That is the price of replacing conscience with reputation, and anyone who has softened a conviction because of what a room would think has felt the same rope round the same neck. The fear of man lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25).

Before the council. The apostles, standing in a temple full of people who admire them, could slip away or let the crowd do what the officers fear. They do none of it. They walk back with the officers and stand before the council. They submit to arrest, and then refuse to submit on the question of preaching. The one group in Jerusalem with real reason to be afraid is the one group behaving as though there were nothing to fear.

Put your sword into its sheath. Peter had been at an arrest before. In Gethsemane, when the temple officers came for Jesus with lanterns and weapons, it was Peter who drew a sword, and Jesus who told him to put it away: shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? (John 18:3–11). Jesus went out to meet the men who came for him, and gave himself up to them. Now Peter has learned what his Lord was doing that night. He does not reach for the crowd as he once reached for the sword. He walks back with the officers as quietly as Jesus did, because he serves a King who conquered by being handed over.

How do I get free of the fear of what people think? Not by trying to care less about people, but by fearing God more. The fear of man shrinks when God grows large in your sight. Jesus put it with startling directness: do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell (Matthew 10:28), and then in the next breath, you are of more value than many sparrows. Fear God, and know that God loves you. Practically, begin small: say the true thing in the next meeting where you would usually stay quiet, and notice that you survive it. Ask what you would do if only God were watching, and do that. He is the only one who is always watching.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest questioned them, saying, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not to teach in this name. The high priest again avoids saying the name of Jesus: this man, he will say in a moment. It is one more failed attempt to suppress him by silence.

You have filled Jerusalem. An unintended compliment. The council is complaining, in open session, that the gospel is unstoppable. The prosecution has just entered the defence’s best evidence into the record.

The third filling. Filled Jerusalem is the third filling in twenty-eight verses. Satan filled Ananias’s heart to lie (v. 3). The high priest and his party were filled with jealousy (v. 17). And now the city itself is filled with the message they were forbidden to speak. Everything in the chapter that sets itself against the Spirit is also full of something, and none of it can hold its ground. A heart full of the adversary lasted a morning. A council full of envy could reach no further than a whip. The teaching filled a capital city and has not stopped.

This man’s blood. The phrase is an old biblical idiom for bloodguilt: to hold someone responsible for a death, to lay the guilt of it at his door (Joshua 2:19; 2 Samuel 1:16). The council fears the apostles are publicly fastening on them the charge of having murdered Jesus, and they are right to fear it, for that is exactly what the apostles have been doing (2:23, 36; 3:15; 5:30). The irony is bitter. At Jesus’ trial the crowd stirred up by this same leadership had cried, his blood be on us and on our children! (Matthew 27:25). They once called the bloodguilt down on themselves; now they are terrified of being held to it.

The accusation and the cure. They want to silence the accusation rather than be cleansed of the blood. There was a way to be rid of this man’s blood, and it was not to muzzle the preachers but to be washed in the very blood they had shed. The blood that lay upon them as guilt was being held out to them as atonement: repent and be baptised for the forgiveness of your sins (2:36–38). Christ bore the penalty in the sinner’s place (Isaiah 53:5–6). The blood of Jesus speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood cried for vengeance; his cries for pardon. The accusation and the cure were one and the same blood.

Were the Jewish people as a whole guilty of Christ’s death? No, not in the way that has so often been claimed. The apostles charge the particular leaders and crowds of Jerusalem who handed Jesus over, and they do it in order to call them to repentance and forgiveness, not to curse a nation. The church itself in Acts prayed that Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against Jesus to do what God’s hand had predestined (4:27–28). Jew and Gentile together crucified him, and the deeper truth is that our sins put him there. The centuries in which Christians used Matthew 27:25 to persecute Jewish people were a grievous sin against Christ, who was himself a Jew, and against the apostles, who were all Jews. The right response to this verse is not to point at anyone, but to plead the blood for ourselves.

For worship. The risen Lord had told his apostles that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47): beginning, that is, in the city that shed it, with the men who called for it. The first offer of pardon went to the very men who had handed him over. There is no guilt so close to the cross that the cross cannot reach it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must obey God rather than men. No preamble and no apology. The verb (dei) means it is necessary, binding: Peter is not claiming a right but describing an obligation he has no power to set aside. It has been the motto of martyrs through the centuries.

Conscience asks first. The first time they said it to this court, it was a question for the council to answer (4:19); now it is a statement. Christian conscience it does not usually start by shouting. It asks first, and only hardens when the asking has been refused.

Putting the frame back. Without its frame this sentence becomes a slogan for whatever a believer wants to defy. The New Testament’s ordinary teaching about government is not resistance but submission, stated in the strongest terms by men living under an empire that, by early Christian tradition, would shortly execute both of them. Let every person be subject to the governing authorities, Paul writes, for there is no authority except from God (Romans 13:1), and he wrote it to Christians in Nero’s capital. Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, writes Peter; honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:13–17), and he is the man speaking these very words. Both regarded it as obedience to God.

Real and derived. So how do the two fit? A government’s authority is real and derived: genuine, and held on delegation. A magistrate has his warrant from God, which is why a Christian obeys him in the ordinary run of things without needing to agree with him. But a delegated authority that commands what the one who delegated it forbids has, at that precise point, run out of warrant, and only at that point. Scripture supplies the pattern before Acts ever does: midwives who would not kill the boys (Exodus 1:17), three men who would not bow to a statue and said so without knowing whether they would be spared (Daniel 3:16–18), an old official who kept his windows open toward Jerusalem when praying had been made a capital offence (Daniel 6:10). God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster Confession 20.2).

The test. The test an ordinary Christian can apply is narrower than most people who quote this verse would like. The question is not whether a law is unwise, unfair, expensive or offensive to me. The question is whether I am being commanded to do what God forbids, or forbidden to do what God commands. The apostles are in the second case: God had told them, that very night and through an angel, to go and speak (v. 20). A tax I resent, a policy I judge foolish, a regulation that inconveniences my church: none of these is Acts 5, and dressing them in this verse cheapens it for the day it is genuinely needed.

The half that is always dropped. These men do not resist arrest, summon the crowd, or flee the city. They walk in, state their position, take a flogging for it, and go back to work. Biblical civil disobedience is characteristically joined to a willingness to bear the penalty, not to a search for an escape clause. Anyone appealing to this verse who is unwilling to pay the fine, take the sentence or lose the position is appealing to something other than what Peter is doing here.

The God of our fathers raised Jesus. Having refused the court’s authority, Peter preaches to it on the spot. The God of our fathers claims continuity: this is not a foreign God or a new religion appearing beside Israel’s, but the God of Abraham keeping his word, and it is the council, not the apostles, who have broken step. Whom you killed is said to their faces, in their own chamber, by a man with no legal standing whatsoever.

Hanging him on a tree. Peter could have said crucified. Instead he reaches for the language of Deuteronomy, where a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God, a body to be taken down before nightfall so that the land is not defiled (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). The leaders very probably meant the cross to show that Jesus was cursed by God. Peter picks the description most offensive to every man listening, because it is the truth. The curse was real. It fell. It simply was not his. He was hanged on that tree under a curse he had not earned, in the place of people who had earned it and could not carry it: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). To redeem is to buy out of slavery, and the price was the Son himself. And the God of their fathers raised him to show the account was settled. There is no gospel that does not go through that sentence, and Peter puts it in front of his judges within a minute of being told to be silent.

What if I am not sure whether a command crosses the line? Then go slowly, and go with others. Ask the test plainly: am I being made to sin, or kept from a clear duty? Search the Scriptures, not your preferences. Seek the counsel of your elders and of mature Christians who will tell you the truth, because one person’s conscience can be either too tender or too hard. Where the matter is genuinely unclear, lean toward submission and courtesy, for Scripture’s default is honour for those in authority. Where it is clear, be respectful in manner and firm in substance, and be ready to bear the cost without bitterness. Daniel served a pagan king faithfully for decades, and still knew exactly where the line was when it came.

On a Tuesday. At work and at home this week, be the most willing, cheerful and law-abiding person in the room, so that if the day ever comes when you must say no for Christ’s sake, it is plain that you are not saying it from a rebellious spirit. And if that day has come, say it calmly, take what follows, and keep speaking of him.

For worship. Before Peter ever said it, one Man lived it. Jesus obeyed his Father rather than men at every step, when crowds wanted to make him king and when rulers wanted him silent, and he became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). That obedience is the whole of our righteousness: by the one Man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19). And the perfect obedience of that faithful Son covers the faltering obedience of all his people.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leader and Savior. The crucified one is now the Leader who blazed the trail through death to resurrection, and the Saviour who offers repentance and forgiveness. Leader renders archēgos (3:15): the pioneer who cuts the track others will walk. Jesus did not arrange a rescue from a safe distance; he went through death first, and the road exists because he made it. Nobody who follows him into that country will be going anywhere he has not already been. And Saviour (sōtēr), rescuer, is a title the Old Testament gives to God himself: I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior (Isaiah 43:11). Peter gives it to Jesus without hesitation, before the very court that condemned him for blasphemy. The seat at a king’s right hand belonged to the one who shared his honour and wielded his power: Jesus is not resting in heaven; he is ruling, with authority over every power and as head over all things for the church (Ephesians 1:20–22).

To give repentance. Then the phrase that ought to stop anybody who has tried and failed to repent: repentance itself is here a thing handed over, not achieved (11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). Repentance means a change of mind that becomes a change of direction: seeing sin as God sees it, hating it, and turning from it to him (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Forgiveness means God cancels the debt (Colossians 2:13–14). That cuts against the way most people instinctively hear the command, as though God stands at a distance requiring a change of heart that we must manufacture before he will look at us. Anyone who has wanted to be sorry for something and found that he could only regret the consequences knows the difference between working up remorse and being given a new mind about a thing. The second is a gift, from the one exalted to give it. And yet we are commanded to repent (3:19). Both are true: God commands what he gives, and gives what he commands.

And so is the Holy Spirit. Two witnesses, as the law required (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Jesus had promised exactly this pairing: the Spirit of truth will bear witness about me, and you also will bear witness (John 15:26–27). The apostles are human eyewitnesses of the resurrection. The Spirit testifies by his very outpouring, which only the exalted Christ could send (2:33), by speaking through the witnesses (4:8, 31), and inwardly by convicting the world (John 16:8–11). So the council faces not merely the word of a few fishermen but the testimony of God himself, a witness they can imprison no more than they could keep the prison shut.

In the flow. Peter’s reply is a whole sermon in four sentences: the principle (v. 29), the cross (v. 30), the exaltation and the offer (v. 31), and the witnesses (v. 32), now pressed on the very court that condemned Jesus, with repentance offered even to the men who killed him.

Whom God has given to those who obey him. Read carelessly, this clause turns the Spirit into a wage. But the obedience Peter has in mind is not a record of performance. It is the same word he used of himself three verses earlier, when he said we must obey God rather than men, and what he meant there was believing God’s word about his Son and acting on it. That is what the New Testament calls obeying the gospel, or the obedience of faith (6:7; Romans 1:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:8). The Spirit is not the prize for a life already put right. He is the one who puts it right, and he comes to people whose response to the message about Jesus has been surrender rather than management.

If repentance is a gift, do I just wait for it? No. You ask for it, and you act on the light you have. The gifts of God come through the means he has appointed: hearing his word, praying, and turning toward him even when the turning feels weak. Ask Christ plainly: give me a true sorrow for this sin, and a hatred of it, and the strength to leave it. Then take the next step you can see, and confess it, put it right, remove the occasion. If you find any desire at all to repent, that desire is already the gift beginning. The man who says he would like to repent but cannot feel it is not far from the kingdom; he is being drawn.

How can I know I have the Holy Spirit? Not mainly by dramatic experiences, but by what the Spirit always does. He makes Jesus precious to you, so that you confess him as Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3). He bears witness with your spirit that you are a child of God, so that you call God Father (Romans 8:15–16). He makes you hate your sin and fight it (Galatians 5:17). And he grows his fruit in you, slowly, over years: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). If you trust Christ, the Spirit has been given to you (Ephesians 1:13). You do not have to earn a second blessing (a later, separate experience some teach every believer must seek); you have to walk in the one you have been given.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enraged. Rage, not refutation. The verb (dieprionto) is used literally of sawing: they were cut to the quick. Set that beside the day of Pentecost, when the people who heard the same message were cut to the heart and said, brothers, what shall we do? (2:37). Here the same message produces a decision to kill. Stephen will meet the same word from the same body two chapters later, and it will finish the way it wanted to finish here (7:54).

The gospel is never neutral. The gospel either breaks a man open or hardens him, and the wound feels much the same from the inside at first. Three thousand went one way in chapter 2; this council went the other. We are the aroma of Christ, Paul says, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life (2 Corinthians 2:15–16). Often what decides it is what a man is holding on to. These men had the temple, the people’s deference and the last word in Jerusalem, and a risen Christ threatened all three. Rage is what control sounds like when it is slipping.

Appointed for the fall and rising of many. The dividing line runs through a Person. Simeon told the infant Jesus’ mother that the child was appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, a sign that would be opposed, so that the thoughts of many hearts would be revealed (Luke 2:34–35). At Pentecost many rose; in this council many fall. No one meets him and stays the same, because he is not an idea to be weighed but the Lord, and every heart is laid bare before him.

A Pharisee named Gamaliel. With murder openly proposed, God sends not an angel this time but a Pharisee. A respected old teacher stands up and asks for the room to be cleared, and the apostles live. Providence sometimes arrives as the one person present whose opinion the others cannot afford to dismiss. The Pharisees were a minority in the council but popular with the people.

Who was Gamaliel? Beyond the New Testament, Jewish sources tell us a fair amount about him, though it is best weighed as tradition rather than certified biography. He is remembered as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, one of the most honoured sages of his age and, by Jewish tradition, a descendant (commonly said to be the grandson) of the famous Hillel and a leader of Hillel’s school. He is traditionally reckoned the first to bear the exalted title Rabban, our master, a rank above Rabbi. The Mishnah, the early collection of rabbinic law, pays him a striking tribute: when Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the law ceased, and purity and abstinence died (Sotah 9:15). Tradition credits him with several rulings for the public good, including protections for women in the law of divorce. And, as Luke notes elsewhere, the young Saul of Tarsus was educated at the feet of Gamaliel (22:3). A much later Christian legend claimed that Gamaliel secretly became a believer; it has no historical foundation and should be set aside.

Outside for a little while. Luke, of course, knows what was said; perhaps Saul himself, Gamaliel’s pupil, later told it.

Why does the same message soften some and harden others? Because the difference is not finally in the message or the messenger but in the work of God in the hearer. Faith is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8), and it is the Lord who opens hearts to pay attention to what is said (16:14). Luke says it plainly later: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (13:48). Scripture’s word for this is election: God chose a people for himself in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything he foresaw in them, and in his time he opens each of their hearts (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11). Many Christians understand election instead as God choosing those he foresaw would believe; Reformed Christians read it as the cause of faith rather than its reward, because Paul says the choice was made before either child had done anything good or bad. That does not make the hardened man a puppet; he chooses his rage freely and is responsible for it. But it should humble every Christian. If you were cut to the heart rather than sawn through, it was grace, not your superior openness. And it should free every preacher and every ordinary witness: our task is to speak Christ faithfully; the opening of hearts belongs to God.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, and Paul’s teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care. To a court that has just proposed killing the apostles without a trial, he says be careful. He is the only man in the chamber who says anything of the kind.

Claiming to be somebody. Judea in living memory had produced a run of men who gathered a following, claimed to be somebody, and came to nothing when they were killed. Josephus says the land was full of them. His reasoning is simple: movements of that kind collapse when their leader dies, so let time do the work and keep the council’s hands clean.

Came to nothing. As practical advice, Gamaliel’s case is shrewd, and God used it. As a way of settling what is true, it is worthless, and the same reasoning is offered constantly today. Durability is not a test of truth. Plenty of false things last for centuries; Gamaliel was making his case inside a temple that had stood a long time and would be rubble within forty years. Plenty of true things are crushed early and stay crushed for a generation. Applied consistently, his rule would have condemned nearly every prophet Israel ever had.

A decision not to look. The deeper problem is that Gamaliel’s rule avoids the only question in the room. The apostles had made a factual claim: God raised Jesus from the dead, and we saw him. That claim has witnesses, a date, and a tomb nobody in that chamber claimed was still occupied. Gamaliel proposes instead that they wait and see, which is a decision not to look.

Waiting is itself an answer. That posture is common, and presented as open-mindedness. It sounds humble, and it is the one position that cannot be held. A man deciding whether Jesus rose from the dead is not an observer of the case; he is a party to it. Waiting to see how it turns out is itself an answer.

I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. Gamaliel’s pattern, a leader killed and his followers dispersed, had already happened once more. On the night of his arrest Jesus quoted Zechariah to his disciples: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Mark 14:27; Zechariah 13:7). Within hours the Shepherd was struck and his followers ran. By Gamaliel’s rule that should have been the end. But in the same breath Jesus had added, after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (Mark 14:28). The flock in Solomon’s Portico is a scattered flock gathered again by a living Shepherd.
verseByVerse.note: Theudas is otherwise unknown from this period; Josephus mentions a later rebel of the same name.

verseByVerse.quote: "After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas the Galilean. He led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6, under Quirinius, and Josephus confirms it. He taught that paying taxes to Rome was slavery and that God alone was king, and his movement is often thought to have fed the later Zealots.

Did Luke get his history wrong? These two names carry a well-known objection, and since Luke’s standing as a historian matters to this whole book, it should be met. Josephus describes a Theudas who led a revolt under the procurator Fadus, about AD 44 to 46, a decade or more after Gamaliel is speaking. And Gamaliel places Judas the Galilean, whose rising came at the census of AD 6, after Theudas. On the face of it Luke has the order backwards and the date impossible, and this is regularly produced as proof that he invented the speech. Two things need saying. First, Theudas need not have been the only man of that name in a country full of failed insurgents. Josephus himself says that after Herod the Great died in 4 BC there were countless disturbances in Judea, and he names several leaders who gathered a following and were cut down. Gamaliel’s Theudas had about four hundred men; the one Josephus dates to the forties drew a great crowd to the Jordan. There is no difficulty in supposing two men of the same name, decades apart, in a generation that produced rebels by the dozen. No harmonisation here can be proved, and it is honest to say so; but it is a reasonable answer, not a desperate one.

The benefit of the doubt. Second, the objection assumes that where Luke and Josephus differ, Josephus is the standard; but Josephus is careless in places. Luke was long said to have blundered over the titles of local officials: the city authorities of Thessalonica, the proconsul of Cyprus, the chief man of Malta. Inscriptions have since shown him right, in details that were easy to get wrong. That does not prove every sentence he wrote, but a writer with that record has earned the benefit of the doubt about a rebel’s name.

Was Jesus a political rebel like these men? No, and the comparison shows the difference. Judas the Galilean said that paying taxes to Caesar was treason against God; Jesus said, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s (Mark 12:17). Theudas and Judas raised armed followings; Jesus told Peter to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52) and said to Pilate, my kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). The would-be messiahs wanted a throne in Jerusalem; Jesus took a cross outside it. His kingdom does come, and it overturns every power in the end, but it comes by the word and the Spirit, not the sword. Christians who try to advance it by force or by political domination have misunderstood their King.

For worship. Luke tells of another census, a decree from Caesar Augustus that sent a carpenter and his betrothed wife to Bethlehem, where the true King was born and laid in a manger (Luke 2:1–7). God did not fight the empire to bring his Son into the world; he used its paperwork to fulfil his promise about the city of David. The King came without a sword, and his kingdom cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28).
verseByVerse.note: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" So they took his advice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If it is of God. Gamaliel’s last sentence is the sharpest thing said in the chamber all day, and he almost certainly did not know how sharp it was.

You might even be found opposing God! The word (theomachoi, God-fighters) appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It belongs above all to the world of Greek tragedy, where the man who sets himself against heaven is destroyed by the attempt, usually while believing he is defending something. Gamaliel raises it as a remote hazard, a possibility worth insuring against. It is the actual position of every man he is speaking to. The wisest man in the room got nearer to the truth than anyone else present and still treated it as a remote contingency. It is possible to be right about God in the conditional and wrong about him in the indicative: to say if this is of God, and never to admit that it is.

His most famous student. A further irony: two chapters from here a young man stands at a stoning, holding the coats, approving; and he tells us himself that he was brought up in this city at the feet of this same Gamaliel (22:3). Saul of Tarsus had this exact warning from his own teacher, and went out and did the very thing it warned against, until a voice on the Damascus road said to him, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads (26:14). Gamaliel’s word turned out to be a prophecy about his most famous student.

Where Christians differ: is Gamaliel’s test reliable? Some treat it as a sure rule: if something succeeds, it is from God. This commentary’s view: it is wise caution, and true in the long run, but not a full test. False religions have lasted centuries, and God’s work can look as if it is failing for a time. The true test is Scripture and Christ (1 John 4:1–3). Gamaliel’s advice was sensible, but it was neutrality, not faith. Neutrality towards Christ is not enough.

Delivered by an argument they did not make. The sentence to carry away from this scene is not about Gamaliel at all. Twelve men who could not defend themselves, in the hands of a court that wanted them dead, were delivered by an argument they did not make, from a man who was not on their side, for reasons that were not the right ones. The church’s survival did not depend on its enemies being reasonable. It never has. What Gamaliel offered as a warning against a possibility, the apostles could have offered as a statement of fact: nothing that is of God will be overthrown.

In the flow. Gamaliel’s conditional sentence is the thesis of the whole book, spoken by a man who did not believe it. The Sanhedrin, Herod, mobs and a shipwreck all try to overthrow the work, and the word of God increased and multiplied (12:24). The book ends with Paul under guard in Rome, proclaiming the kingdom with all boldness and without hindrance (28:31). Luke lets an unbeliever ask the question in chapter 5 and spends the rest of the book answering it.

So how do I test a movement or a teacher? By Scripture first, and by Christ at the centre. Does it confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, truly God and truly man, crucified and risen (1 John 4:1–3)? Does it agree with what the apostles taught, as the Bereans checked even Paul against the Scriptures (17:11)? Does it make much of Christ, or of a leader, a method or an experience? And what fruit grows in the lives of its leaders and followers over time: humility, holiness, love, or pride, money and control (Matthew 7:15–20)? Size and success are not on the list. Neither is how moving the meetings are. A small, faithful church preaching Christ crucified passes the test that a famous movement may fail.

For worship. No one has ever fought against God and won. Pharaoh tried, and the sea closed over his chariots. But the fiercest battle ever fought against God was fought at a cross, and there the One under attack prayed for his attackers: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). That is how this God wins. While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10).

verseByVerse.quote: and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They beat them. The council cannot kill the apostles, but it can punish them. It was probably the synagogue flogging, forty strokes less one: the law permitted forty, and the practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could not break it (Deuteronomy 25:1–3). The strokes were laid on with a leather strap across the bared chest and back, and men were carried away from it. Paul, who received the same punishment five separate times, thought it worth listing among the things that nearly killed him (2 Corinthians 11:24). Jesus had warned them: they will flog you in their synagogues (Matthew 10:17).

The incoherence of it. Minutes earlier the council was warned by its most honoured member that it might be found fighting against God, and it accepted the advice. Then it had the men beaten and told them again to stop speaking. They kept the verdict and lowered the sentence, which is what men do when they have decided the question already and are only negotiating the cost.

What does it mean to speak in the name of Jesus? In the Bible a name stands for the whole person: his identity, his character and above all his authority. To do or say something in someone’s name is to act on his behalf, as his representative, by his authority, the way an ambassador speaks not his own mind but his king’s, or a constable says stop in the name of the law. So when the apostles spoke in the name of Jesus, they were not merely mentioning him. They were publicly proclaiming who he is, the crucified and risen Lord, and calling people to trust and obey him, as his authorised messengers, backed by his authority and not their own (3:6; 4:12). That is exactly what the council wanted to stop: not idle talk, but the announcement that Jesus is Lord. To forbid the name was to forbid Christ himself.

And what does it mean to pray in Jesus’ name? The same thing, turned toward heaven. Praying in Jesus’ name is not adding a formula to the end of a prayer. It is coming to the Father on the ground of who Jesus is and what he has done, not on the ground of our own worthiness, and asking for what he would want, as people who belong to him (John 14:13–14; 16:23–24). It means we come with confidence, because his name opens the door; and it means we come with humility, because we are asking for his glory and not merely our wishes. When you end a prayer with in Jesus’ name, you are saying, I have no standing of my own here; I come in his.
verseByVerse.note: The beating was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes.

parallels.desc: forty stripes

verseByVerse.quote: Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoicing. The apostles walk out with their backs opened, and Luke says they were rejoicing: not resigned, not bearing it well. Not because pain is good, but because suffering for Christ is an honour (Matthew 5:11–12; 1 Peter 4:13–16; Philippians 1:29).

Counted worthy to suffer dishonour. The phrase should not be able to exist. To be counted worthy is to be honoured, singled out, judged fit for something valuable; dishonour is public shame, the thing every man in that culture organised his life to avoid. Luke welds them. Not long before, this same group had been arguing on a road about which of them was the greatest (Mark 9:33–34). The prize turned out to be a flogging. Honour was the currency of their world, as approval is of ours, and these men had found an approval that outweighed the whole city’s contempt: his.

For the name. Luke does not say whose name. In Jewish speech the Name was how you referred to the God of Israel when you would not pronounce the divine name itself. Luke uses it absolutely of a carpenter executed outside the city wall, and among these people there was no confusion. In time John could write simply of believers who had gone out for the sake of the name (3 John 7). The council in this very chapter refused to say the name at all, calling him this man (v. 28). The apostles have stopped needing to say it, for the opposite reason.

What it does not mean. This verse has been laid on suffering people as a demand, and it is not one. Three things keep it honest. First, they are not rejoicing in the pain; they are rejoicing in what the pain meant, that the Lord they had abandoned in a garden had now counted them fit to be shamed on his account. Nobody is asked to enjoy a scourge. Second, this is a specific kind of suffering: dishonour incurred for Christ, in the course of obeying him. A diagnosis is not dishonour for the name. Neither is a bereavement, a betrayal, or a depression that will not lift. Those are real, and Scripture speaks to them elsewhere and at length; this verse is not the text to beat a grieving person with. Third, this joy is a thing given, not manufactured. It arrived in them on the way out of that building. It is not a mood that a Christian owes in advance and is failing to produce.

I could never do that. To anyone who quietly concludes he could never do it, that if it cost him his job, his family’s standing or a beating, he would fold: look at who is walking out of that chamber. The man in front is Peter. Only a short while ago, with nothing at stake but a servant girl’s opinion beside a fire, he said he did not know Jesus, and then went out and wept. What changed was not his temperament. Something was given to him that had not been there in the courtyard, and it is given when it is needed and not before. The measure of what you could bear today is not the measure of what you would be carried through tomorrow.

Is it right to want to suffer for Christ? Not to seek it. The apostles did not court the flogging; they obeyed and accepted what came. Jesus told his disciples to flee from one town to the next when persecuted (Matthew 10:23), and Paul used his Roman citizenship to escape unjust punishment (22:25). Some in the early church rushed to martyrdom, and wise pastors rebuked them. What is right is to be willing: to love Christ more than comfort or reputation, so that when faithfulness costs something, you pay it gladly. Do not go looking for the cross. Do not run from it when it is laid on you for his sake.

In the temple and from house to house. Every day, from that day. In the temple, the most dangerous place in the city; and house to house, at kitchen tables, where the church has always done most of its real work. Public and private together: the pattern Paul would later describe to the Ephesian elders: teaching you in public and from house to house (20:20).

That the Christ is Jesus. Preaching (euangelizomenoi) is announcing good news, and the heart of it is one sentence: the Messiah is Jesus. All the hopes of Israel have a name and a face, the man the council would not name. Arrest, imprisonment, trial, flogging and injunction had been brought to bear on twelve provincials, and the only measurable result was that the message was being preached in more houses than before. He is worth this, was the verdict of the men with the wounds.

Must I go house to house? Not necessarily door to door with leaflets, though some are called to that. But every Christian has a house, and the house is where the gospel has always travelled furthest. Open your home: a meal with a neighbour, a Bible read with your children, a conversation over coffee with a friend who is struggling. Speak of Christ where you already are, naturally and honestly, and support the public preaching of your church with your presence and prayers. The temple and the house belong together. Your pastor preaches in the one; you are sent into the other.

In the flow. With verse 42 the first great movement of Acts comes to rest. The chapter began with a threat from inside and ends with a threat from outside, and both have failed: nothing can stop his name being spoken.

For worship. The Name the apostles carried out of that council chamber is the name above every name. It belongs to the Christ who endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2), and his joy is the joy that filled them on the road home. He counted it worth it to be shamed for them; they counted it worth it to be shamed for him.

5.theology: The holiness of God in the new covenant community. As Nadab and Abihu died at the founding of the tabernacle worship (Leviticus 10), so at the birth of the church God makes his holiness unmistakable. It is not that God is more severe in the new covenant than in the old. It is that the church lives closer to the Holy Spirit than any generation before it, and nearness to holiness calls for honesty and purity.
5.examples:
Then: A church a few weeks old learned that the Spirit who fills it also searches it, and that the God of grace is the God of holiness. The fear did not empty the church: within a few verses believers were added to the Lord in multitudes.

Now: We speak, rightly, of grace, love and welcome. But grace is not tame, and Ananias and Sapphira remind every generation that the Spirit cannot be fooled and that our God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29).

6.title: The Choosing of the Seven
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily
