distribution. <sup>2</sup>And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. <sup>4</sup>But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” <sup>5</sup>And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. <sup>6</sup>These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <sup>7</sup>And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. <sup>8</sup>And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. <sup>9</sup>Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen. <sup>10</sup>But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. <sup>11</sup>Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” <sup>12</sup>And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council, <sup>13</sup>and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, <sup>14</sup>for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.” <sup>15</sup>And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
6.overview:
The growing church meets a problem from within. Greek-speaking believers, the Hellenists, complain that their widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The church chooses seven men full of the Spirit and of wisdom to oversee the care, and the apostles keep to prayer and the word. The seven, all with Greek names, appear to come from the very group that complained, and the word spreads, even to many priests.

Then Luke turns to one of the seven, Stephen, full of grace and power. Unable to answer his wisdom, his opponents bring false witnesses who say he speaks against the temple and the law, and before the council his face is seen to be like the face of an angel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Appointment of the Seven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Growth exposes a failure: the Hellenist widows are being missed in the daily distribution. The church chooses seven Spirit-filled men to oversee the care, so that the apostles can keep to prayer and the word. The apostles pray and lay hands on them, and the word of God goes on spreading in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and service in the church

The apostles’ refusal to give up preaching the word of God to serve tables (v. 2) is about calling, not dignity: the men appointed to the tables must be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, which is not a lower bar. Waiting on widows and preaching are two forms of one service. What the passage protects is the church’s food supply in both senses: a congregation whose teachers are buried in administration will in time be starved of the word, and a congregation whose widows are overlooked is contradicting what it preaches.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The overlooked widows had no land and no clan to fall back on. Now: The question every congregation has to keep asking is not whether it would refuse anyone, but who is currently being looked past.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 6 shows a third threat to the church: division. The neglect of some widows threatens to split Greek-speaking and Aramaic-speaking believers. The apostles solve it by appointing seven men to oversee the care, so that they can keep to prayer and the word. The word spreads further, and even priests believe. Then one of the seven, Stephen, becomes the first great witness to suffer death, and his story leads the gospel out of Jerusalem. The chapter that begins with bread for widows ends with a face shining like Moses’ before the highest court in Israel.

When the disciples were increasing. Luke ties the trouble to the growth: there was more of the church than the existing arrangements could see. Growth brings new problems, and a church that is never troubled by them is usually not growing.

Hellenists and Hebrews. Both groups in this quarrel are Jews and both are Christians. The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews, mostly born in the Jewish communities scattered across the empire, now settled in Jerusalem. The Hebrews were Aramaic-speaking Jews native to the land. The line between them is language and culture, not theology.

The word for complaint. Luke’s word (gongysmos) is grumbling, the word the Greek Old Testament uses again and again for Israel muttering in the wilderness. But Luke does not rebuke the complainers, and neither do the apostles. The grievance was true, and it was acted on. Not every complaint in a church is a spiritual failure in the person making it. Sometimes the murmuring is right.

The daily distribution. Widows in that world had no pension and no state support; the church fed them daily. Some Jews of the dispersion had come to Jerusalem in old age to be buried near the temple, and their widows were left in a city where they owned no land, had no clan to fall back on, and could not always follow what was said around them. They were the most exposed people in the congregation, and they were the ones who got missed.

Overlooked, not rejected. Nobody had decided that these women should go without. In the press of a distribution serving thousands, run by men who spoke a different language at home, the ones without a voice were simply not seen. It was oversight, not malice, and that is how this kind of injustice nearly always happens.

He looked up and saw a poor widow. The church that missed these women belonged to a Lord who never missed one. Luke’s Gospel is full of widows seen by Jesus when everyone else looked past them. At the gate of Nain he saw a widow following her only son’s bier, had compassion on her, and gave the boy back to his mother (Luke 7:11–15). In the temple, among the rich with their large gifts, he looked up and saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins, and said she had given more than all of them (Luke 21:1–4). The daily distribution was the church learning its Master’s eyes. To overlook a widow was to forget whose table they were serving at.

The full number of the disciples. The Twelve could have adjusted the rota and said nothing. Instead the failure is put in public, in front of the very people who had been neglected.

To serve tables. It is not a clergyman declining a menial job. The men who are to do that job must be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, which is not a lower standard, and two of these men go on to preach in synagogues and evangelise Samaria. Serving tables is not beneath the apostles; their calling is the word, and if they did everything, the word would suffer. A congregation whose teachers disappear into administration will be starved within a generation, and the widows will still not be fed.

If this church was full of the Spirit, how could it fail its widows? Because being filled with the Spirit does not make a church sinless or all-seeing. The Spirit had come, the apostles were preaching, thousands had believed, and still some hungry women were missed. Luke does not hide it, and that honesty is part of why his account can be trusted: he is not selling a perfect church. The test of a Spirit-filled church is not that it never fails, but what it does when its failure is pointed out. This one listened, owned it, and put it right within a single meeting.

What should I do if I feel overlooked in my church? Say so, gently and to the right people. The Hellenists raised their complaint, and it was heard; that is the pattern. Go to an elder or deacon, describe what has happened rather than accusing anyone of motives, and assume, as is usually true, that it was oversight rather than contempt. Then give the leaders time to act. Avoid the wilderness kind of grumbling, which talks to everyone except the people who can help and nurses a grievance instead of solving it. And if you have been overlooked, you will know better than most how to notice others who are. Become the person who sees them.

Who is being looked past? That leaves a question a reader can put to his own church, and it is sharper than the one usually asked. Not, would we turn anybody away? Almost nobody would. But who is currently being looked past: who is in the building and not in anybody’s line of sight, because they were never in the middle of the room, and because asking would require somebody to find out? The widow who comes alone, the international student, the family whose English is halting, the man with a disability who leaves before the coffee.

For worship. The God of this church is father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Psalm 68:5), who watches over the sojourner and upholds the widow and the fatherless (Psalm 146:9). And when his Son hung dying, carrying the sin of the world, he still looked down and saw his mother standing by the cross, and gave her into the keeping of the disciple he loved (John 19:26–27). His eyes find the one at the edge of the crowd, even from a cross.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jewish believers, many born outside the land; the Hebrews spoke Aramaic. Widows without family depended on the community’s daily food distribution.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven men of good repute. For men who are to hand out food, the apostles ask three qualifications, and not one of them is administrative: good reputation, filled with the Spirit, wise. Handling money and caring for vulnerable people requires character before it requires skill, and Paul’s later qualifications for deacons are similar (1 Timothy 3:8–13).

The congregation chooses. The apostles set the standard and the congregation chooses; no slate is presented. The apostles then appoint. And the word for duty in the phrase whom we will appoint to this duty (chreia) is need: the office exists because of a need, not a need because of an office.

Prayer and the ministry of the word. The verb for devote is the one Luke used of the whole church at 2:42: to stick at a thing and refuse to be prised off it. And prayer is named first. It is the one thing nobody would have noticed them dropping. These are the priorities of pastoral ministry, and both are labour (1 Timothy 4:13; 2 Timothy 4:2). A minister who neglects them for administration fails his flock, however busy he looks.

Service of tables, service of the word. The word for ministry (diakonia) is service, and the verb for serving tables is from the same root. That is the whole argument. Waiting on widows and preaching to thousands are not two categories, a menial one and a spiritual one. They are two forms of the one thing, and the only question is which one a particular man is called to.

I am among you as the one who serves. These twelve men had learned that word at a table. At the Last Supper, while they argued about which of them was the greatest, Jesus asked who is greater, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves, and answered: I am among you as the one who serves (Luke 22:24–27). Their Lord had waited on them. So when the apostles hand the tables to the seven, they are not stepping up out of service into something grander; they are keeping to the service he gave them, and giving his other service to men fit to do it.

Where Christians differ: were the seven the first deacons? They are not called deacons here, though the verb serve (diakonein) and the noun (diakonia) are used. Luke never calls these men deacons anywhere; later he simply calls Philip one of the seven (21:8). This commentary’s view: many rightly see here the pattern for the office of deacon, which appears formally later (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8–13): men set apart to oversee practical care so that elders can give themselves to the word and prayer. The two offices, elders and deacons, are the New Testament pattern for church leadership.

Not an administrative committee. But do not reduce these seven to a committee. Stephen is arguing in synagogues within a paragraph and is dead within a chapter. Philip takes the gospel to Samaria, baptises an Ethiopian official on a desert road, and is still called an evangelist twenty years later. Neither of them stayed at the tables. Whatever the church later made of the office, it began with men so full of the Spirit that the job could not hold them.

Does this mean only men may serve as deacons? Luke uses the word for men, and the seven were chosen for a public trust in the church. Christians differ on whether women may hold the office of deacon. Paul calls Phoebe a servant of the church at Cenchreae, using the same word (Romans 16:1), and 1 Timothy 3:11 may speak of women deacons or of deacons’ wives. Many complementarian churches appoint women as deacons, since the office is one of service, not of teaching and ruling, which belong to the elders; others reserve it for men. What is plain is that women served the early church in many ways, and that every church needs their gifts.

How can I help my pastors keep to prayer and the word? By taking up the tasks that do not need them. Every church has a hundred necessary jobs that someone other than the minister can do: the rota, the accounts, the building, the visits, the meals for the new mother, the lifts for the elderly. When you do one of them well and without being asked twice, you are not doing something lesser than preaching; you are serving the word by clearing room for it. And pray for each of your pastors, that their study would be fruitful and their prayers persevering. Then guard their time kindly: not every question needs the pastor.

parallels.desc: Jethro advises Moses to share the load

verseByVerse.quote: And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It pleased the whole gathering. Unity restored: a church with money, a grievance and an ethnic fault line running through it settles the matter in one meeting, by giving the power away.

They chose Stephen. Stephen will be the first martyr (chapter 7). But how could anyone tell that a man was full of the Spirit? The apostles told the church to pick out such men (v. 3), so the fullness was no hidden claim but something the congregation could recognise. It shows itself in character, the fruit the Spirit grows (Galatians 5:22–23), steady enough to earn good repute; in wisdom, and Stephen’s opponents could not withstand his (v. 10); and in faith, a settled trust and boldness. They saw the Spirit in how he lived, spoke and served (Matthew 7:16). And these Spirit-filled men were chosen to wait tables: fullness of the Spirit is proved first in humble, everyday service.

Full of the Holy Spirit. Luke has used that description before, and the first time it was of Jesus, returning from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit to face the devil in the wilderness (Luke 4:1). He chooses it now for Stephen with care, because Stephen’s story is about to follow his Lord’s step by step: false witnesses, a charge about the temple, a hearing before the council, a death outside the city with a prayer committing his spirit and a prayer for his killers (6:11–14; 7:59–60). The Spirit who filled Jesus for his ministry is the Spirit the exalted Jesus has poured out on his people, and he forms them in their Master’s likeness. Stephen will shine because Christ is shining through him.

Philip. Later Philip the evangelist (21:8), who takes the gospel to Samaria and to the Ethiopian official (chapter 8).

Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon and Parmenas. Otherwise unknown. Four men, named once in Scripture and never again, trusted with widows’ bread and forgotten by history. They are remembered by God.

Nicolaus, a proselyte. A Gentile convert to Judaism, and then to Christ, now helping run the welfare of the Jerusalem church. Antioch will become the great centre of the Gentile mission (11:19–26).

Was this Nicolaus the founder of the Nicolaitans? Revelation condemns a group called the Nicolaitans (Revelation 2:6, 15), and some early writers, from Irenaeus on, linked them with this man. Scripture does not. Luke presents him as a man of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, chosen by the whole church, and the link is uncertain at best. The name was not rare. It is wise not to blacken a man whom the Bible honours on the strength of a later guess.

All seven have Greek names. Greek names were not unknown among Aramaic-speaking Jews (Andrew and Philip bore them), so this is not proof, but it strongly suggests that the seven came from the Hellenists. A minority group had complained that its widows were overlooked. The majority could have appointed four Hebrews and three Hellenists, which would have been fair and would have left the Hebrews in control of the money. Instead, it seems, they handed the whole operation to the people who had raised the complaint.

They laid their hands on them. The Bible uses this gesture for blessing (Mark 10:16), for identifying with a sacrifice (Leviticus 1:4), and, closest here, for commissioning to an office. The pattern is Moses and Joshua. God told Moses to take Joshua, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay his hand on him and commission him (Numbers 27:18–23), and afterwards Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him (Deuteronomy 34:9). So the seven are publicly set apart, with prayer that God would equip them. The New Testament keeps the practice for appointing to ministry (13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6).

Not magic. It is never magic: it is always joined to prayer, and it is the prayer that asks God to act, not the hands that transfer power. And it is a public act of recognition. Scripture warns against doing it lightly: do not be hasty in the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 5:22).

How do we heal division in a church? The way this church did. Take the complaint seriously instead of explaining it away. Bring it into the open with the whole church rather than handling it in corners. Look for godly people from the group that feels unheard and give them real responsibility, not a token seat. Pray over the solution together. And keep the gospel at the centre, because the deepest unity in a church is not a compromise between groups but a shared belonging to Christ, in whom there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28). Division usually grows where people feel unseen. It shrinks when they are seen and trusted.
verseByVerse.note: All seven have Greek names, suggesting they came from the Hellenist side. Laying on hands marked commissioning for a task.

parallels.desc: Moses lays hands on Joshua

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word increased. Luke uses a formula of this shape several times (9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20) to close a section. Here it closes the church’s Jerusalem years; what follows is Stephen, persecution, Samaria, then the world.

The word grows. The subject of the clause is odd: not the church increased, but the word of God increased. Luke treats the message as the living thing and the congregation its visible result. God’s word does not return to him empty; it accomplishes what he purposes (Isaiah 55:10–11).

A great many of the priests. This is not the high-priestly families, who appear in this book only as opponents. The ordinary priesthood was an enormous body, Josephus reckons some twenty thousand, divided into courses that served at the temple for a week or two each year and spent the rest at home in the villages of Judea (Luke 1:8–9). Zechariah, John the Baptist’s father, was one of them: the temple’s rank and file, often poor.

The cost of their faith. A priest who confessed Jesus was saying that the sacrifice he assisted at, the altar his family existed to serve and that gave his household its livelihood, had done its work: the shadow had given way to the substance. A shadow is real, but it is only the outline thrown ahead of someone coming; the morning lamb was that kind of outline, and Christ is the one who cast it (Hebrews 10:1). Some of them may well have been serving in the temple at the Passover when Jesus died outside the wall, and John’s Gospel sets his death on the day the Passover lambs were killed (John 19:14). The letter to the Hebrews would later explain at length what they had grasped: Christ has offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:12).

Obedient to the faith. Not persuaded of it: they became obedient to it. The faith is something a man obeys, which is exactly how Paul frames the whole business at both ends of his letter to Rome (Romans 1:5; 16:26). In the New Testament, believing is a thing you do with your feet as well as your mind.

The quiet argument of the chapter. Luke reports a row about widows and bread, and in the next sentence tells us the word spread and the priests started coming. He does not say the one caused the other, and it would be crude to pretend that sorting out administration produces revival. But he has put the two side by side. A church whose Greek-speaking widows go hungry while it preaches that the risen Christ has made one people out of many is making an argument against itself. Remove the contradiction and the message can be heard for what it is.

Can people still come to Christ from the heart of another religion? Yes, and this verse is one of the great encouragements to pray for them. These priests had more invested in the old system than anyone: training, income, family identity and the respect of their village. God brought them to Christ anyway. The same God still calls imams, monks, rabbis, priests of other faiths and convinced atheists, often at great personal cost. Do not write anyone off as too religious, too devoted or too committed elsewhere to be reached. The word of God increases in the most unlikely soil, and the Spirit who opened the hearts of temple priests can open any heart.

For worship. These priests, serving in courses a week or two a year, found a High Priest whose course never ends. He holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues for ever, and he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:24–25). No lot has to fall to him, and he has never once been off duty for his people.
verseByVerse.note: There were many thousands of ordinary priests, serving in rotation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Stephen: The Man Who Couldn't Be Stopped
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stephen, full of grace and power, works wonders and debates with Greek-speaking Jews from the synagogue of the Freedmen. Unable to withstand his wisdom, they plant false witnesses, turn the crowd against him and bring him before the council, charged with speaking against the temple and the law. The court looks at him and sees a face like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cost of witness

Stephen’s arrest follows the shape of his Master’s: planted witnesses, a charge about the temple and the law, a council, a verdict of blasphemy. The servant is handed his Master’s charge sheet (Mark 14:58). Where the gospel threatens entrenched religious power it often meets resistance of the same kind, because the objection is finally not to the argument, which was lost at verse 10, but to what conceding it would cost. And Stephen’s case adds that winning the argument and losing one’s life are entirely compatible, and Luke did not consider the second a reversal of the first.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen’s opponents could not withstand his wisdom, and rather than yield to it they found men who would swear to blasphemy. Now: A believer put on the spot for Christ is promised a mouth, not a result: he will not be left with nothing to say. Whether he is believed, and what it costs him, are in God’s hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Full of grace and power. Three verses ago this man was chosen to see that the widows got their bread; now he is working great wonders. Luke praises him more warmly than most of the Twelve, and tells us nothing else about him: no home town, no trade, no family. He has two chapters, one sermon and a shining face.

A man filled with God. Stephen is described as full four times: of the Spirit and of wisdom (v. 3, the standard he was chosen to meet), of faith and of the Holy Spirit (v. 5), of grace and power (here), and of the Holy Spirit as he dies (7:55). Grace carries two notes: the favour of God resting on him, nothing of it earned, and the winsome graciousness such favour produces. Power is the Spirit’s enabling might, which Jesus promised (1:8). (The KJV, following later manuscripts, reads full of faith and power here; the earliest manuscripts have grace.)

Grace first, then power. Luke names grace first, and the power flows out of a life already full of grace. Power without grace is a dangerous thing, and the church has seen enough gifted men without grace to know it. Luke has shown us that order once before. Of the boy Jesus he wrote that the favour, the grace, of God was upon him (Luke 2:40); of the grown man, that he returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee (Luke 4:14). Peter would later sum up that whole life in a sentence: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed (10:38). Stephen’s grace and power are his Master’s, shared with a servant.

Great wonders and signs. Stephen is the first non-apostle in Acts to do signs, and it comes after the apostles laid their hands on him (v. 6). In these chapters signs go with the apostles and with men closely linked to them, such as Philip (8:6).

Stephen was not an apostle, so how does this fit the view that signs belonged to the apostles? Stephen and Philip were among the seven on whom the apostles had laid their hands, and their signs belong to the same foundational ministry. The signs were not given to every believer, but to those closely tied to the apostles as the gospel first spread, and on the cessationist reading, the more likely one, held charitably, they did not continue as standing gifts beyond that generation, because they attested the apostolic foundation. Christians who believe such gifts continue today read these chapters as a pattern for every age; they love the same Lord, and the question deserves patient study rather than scorn. What did continue, and continues today, is what Stephen had first: grace, faith, wisdom and the Spirit. Those are not for a few. They are for every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The synagogue. The first mention of a synagogue in Acts: the local Jewish assembly and meeting house for reading Scripture, prayer and teaching, found in every town where Jews lived. Jerusalem held many, often grouped by homeland or language.

Who were the Freedmen? Freed slaves and their descendants. The likeliest background is that these were Jews, or the children of Jews, taken captive when the Roman general Pompey conquered Jerusalem in 63 BC, carried to Rome as slaves, later set free, and forming a distinct community; some settled again in Jerusalem with their own synagogue. An inscription found in Jerusalem records a synagogue built by one Theodotus, with lodging for those coming from abroad, which gives a vivid picture of exactly this kind of community. Whether Luke means one synagogue or several is grammatically uncertain; the number is not the point.

Cyrenians and Alexandrians. Greek-speaking Jews from North Africa (Cyrene), Egypt (Alexandria), and Asia Minor (Cilicia and Asia). These were all Hellenists, the group Stephen himself very probably belonged to (v. 1). So this first great clash is Hellenist against Hellenist: Stephen seems to have gone to those he knew best.

Cilicia. Cilicia’s capital was Tarsus, the home city of Saul (21:39), who appears at the end of the next chapter, standing by and approving Stephen’s death (7:58; 8:1). Scripture does not say Saul was among these disputants, but the synagogue debate may well be the place where the future apostle Paul first set himself against the name of Jesus.

As was his custom, in the synagogue. Luke has told this story before. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read from Isaiah, announced that the Scripture was fulfilled that day in their hearing, and spoke with such gracious words that all marvelled; then, when his words cut too close, they rose up, drove him out of the town, and tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:16–30). Stephen’s story runs along the same line: a synagogue, gracious and unanswerable words, men rising up, and in the end a man driven out of the city to die (7:58). The servant is walking where the Master walked, and the hostility he meets is hostility to the One he speaks of.

How do I start speaking about Christ to people I know? Begin where Stephen did: with your own circle, the people who share your language, background and world. You understand their questions better than an outsider would, and they know you well enough to see whether your faith is real. You do not need to win debates. Ask good questions about what they believe and why, listen properly, and say honestly what Christ means to you and why you believe he rose from the dead. Pray before and after. Be ready for some to argue and some to listen. And remember that the man arguing hardest may, like Saul, be closer to the kingdom than anyone would guess.
verseByVerse.note: The Freedmen were descendants of Jews once enslaved and later freed, perhaps taken captive to Rome. Cilicia, in south-east Asia Minor, was Paul’s home province.

parallels.desc: Tarsus in Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They could not withstand. A promise is being kept word for word. Not long before, in the temple, Jesus had told his disciples what would happen when they were dragged before synagogues and rulers: I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict (Luke 21:15). Luke records its fulfilment with the same verb and the same word for wisdom: the promise and then the receipt.

Whom they failed to withstand. Stephen has no training that Luke mentions and a job seeing that widows are fed. The men across the room were literate, argumentative, at home in Greek, men who had spent their lives in exactly this kind of dispute. They lost.

What it does not mean. This verse does not say Stephen’s opponents were persuaded. He won the argument comprehensively and was dead within a chapter. What is promised is both better than a debating record and more limited than one. When a Christian is put on the spot for Christ, he will not be left with nothing to say. Not that he will be believed. Not that he will be safe. That he will not be silenced.

The fear of standing there empty. Think of the family lunch where the subject suddenly arrives. Most people’s fear then is not of being argued into a corner but of standing there empty, and this verse speaks to that fear exactly. The mouth is promised; the outcome is not.

Does this mean I need not prepare to explain my faith? No. The promise is not an excuse for laziness. Peter tells every Christian to be prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks for the reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Stephen’s wisdom came from the Spirit, but the Spirit had a man soaked in Scripture to work with, as the next chapter shows. So read your Bible, learn the reasons for the resurrection, think through the questions your friends actually ask. Then, when the moment comes and your preparation feels thin, trust the promise. The Spirit brings to mind what you have learned (John 14:26).

parallels.desc: a mouth and wisdom none can withstand

verseByVerse.quote: Then they secretly instigated men who said, "We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God." And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Secretly instigated. The word Luke uses for what they did (hypoballō) occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It means to suborn: to put a man up to something underhand, to plant him. They did not find witnesses. They installed them, as false witnesses had been found against Jesus (Mark 14:55–59). Somebody had to find men willing to swear a false oath in a capital case and brief them. This is not a crowd losing its temper. It is a considered operation, undertaken by religious men against someone they had failed to answer in open debate.

Against Moses and God. The charge carried the death penalty (Leviticus 24:16). To blaspheme is to speak of God in a way that insults him, the gravest crime of speech in Israel. And Moses comes first. In an accusation drafted to secure a conviction, the name placed first is probably the one expected to do the work, and here it is not God’s. What they had actually heard Stephen discuss concerned the law and the temple, and they knew perfectly well which half of that would move a room.

They stirred up the people. This is the turning point of the narrative, easily read past. When Peter and John were arrested, the council could find no way to punish them because of the people (4:21). When the apostles were seized the second time, the captain brought them in without force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people (5:26). Twice now the crowd has been the church’s protection and the authorities’ constraint. Here, for the first time, the crowd is turned against the church, and the moment it turns, the church has its first martyr. Peter walked out of that chamber alive. Stephen will not.

When a man cannot be answered, he is re-described. It is the oldest mechanism there is: change what he is accused of, so the argument never has to be had again. It works because a crowd cannot check, and because a summary always travels faster than the thing it summarises.

Two warnings for Christians. First, this describes what was done to a man who was genuinely innocent, and it is not a licence to file every criticism under persecution. Some criticism of Christians is accurate, and reaching for Acts 6 is a very efficient way of never having to look at it. Second, and harder, the church has over the centuries run this exact operation on others: the misquoted opponent, the summarised heretic, the man whose actual words nobody troubled to read. Luke is describing a human technique, and the people using it here were the religious ones.

Why would devout men lie to defend God? Because their religion had become their own possession. The law and the temple were not only how they served God; they were how they stood before him and before everyone else, the proof that they were in the right. A message that the shadows had done their work threatened more than an opinion. It threatened the self they had built. When a man’s standing rests on his religious record, he will defend the record even at the cost of the truth. Yet grace reached this very circle: one of the men nearest the scene was Saul, who later wrote that he had acted ignorantly in unbelief and received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13).

What should I do if I am falsely accused? First, take it to God before you take it to anyone else, as Jesus did, who when he was reviled did not revile in return, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Second, ask honestly whether there is any truth in it, and own whatever there is. Third, where a false accusation does real harm, it is right to correct it calmly and through proper channels; Paul defended himself repeatedly in Acts, and appealed to Caesar. But do not retaliate, do not slander back, and do not let it make you bitter. God sees, and he will vindicate his servants, sometimes in this life and always on the last day.

For worship. Every charge against Stephen was false, and so was every charge against his Lord, who stood silent like a lamb before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7). Against us the charges are true. Yet the innocent One, condemned on false testimony, carried our true guilt, and so the question rings out: who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; Christ Jesus is the one who died, who was raised, and who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34).
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

parallels.desc: false witnesses against Naboth

verseByVerse.quote: and they set up false witnesses who said, "This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against this holy place and the law. Luke gives the verdict before the evidence: false witnesses. Yet much of what they said was true.

Will destroy this place. Jesus had spoken about this temple being thrown down, not one stone left on another (Luke 21:6). He had also said something about destroying a temple and raising it in three days, which his hearers misunderstood at the time and which John tells us was about his body (John 2:19–21; Mark 14:58). Stephen probably taught that Jesus is the true temple, and that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as he will say in the next chapter (7:48). The false witnesses twist the truth into a lie.

Will change the customs. The customs delivered by Moses were indeed going to change, as Hebrews argues at length. Stephen probably taught that the law is fulfilled in Christ (Matthew 5:17), and that its ceremonies were a shadow of the good things to come (Hebrews 10:1). Not against the law, but beyond its shadows to its substance.

They kept the topic and removed the reason. The subject matter is genuinely Stephen’s. What the witnesses did was subtler than invention. Destroy in place of fulfil. Change in place of complete. Nothing about a new covenant; nothing about a temple that had finished the work it was built for; nothing about the one in whom God had come to live among his people. It is the technique of describing a surgeon as a man who cuts people open with a knife. Every word is true. The account is a lie.

Two finishing touches. Never ceases suggests an obsessive. And this holy place, said inside the building to the men who ran it, makes the offence personal.

In the flow. These two charges set the agenda for the longest speech in Acts. Stephen answers by retelling Israel’s story: God met his people far from this holy place, and it was Israel, not Stephen, who refused Moses and did not keep the law (7:35–39, 53). If God is not tied to one building, the gospel can go to Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8), and two chapters later it does.

Something worth distorting. Christians who are misrepresented reach for this passage naturally. First ask a hard question: is the thing being distorted actually something I said? Stephen was not misquoted about his views. He was misrepresented about his reasons. If a man is going to be misrepresented, let it be because he said something worth distorting.

Did Christianity abolish the law of Moses? It fulfilled it. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still shows God’s holy will and guides the Christian life, though it no longer condemns those who are in Christ (Romans 8:1; 13:8–10). The ceremonial law, the sacrifices, priesthood, food laws and temple rituals, pointed forward to Christ and has been fulfilled in him, so we no longer keep it (Colossians 2:16–17). The civil laws of Israel as a nation have expired with that nation, though their general principles of justice remain wise (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.3–5; the Westminster Confession 19.3–5). This threefold division is the classic Reformed way of reading the law; some Christians draw the lines differently, but nearly all agree that Christ fulfils it. So Stephen did not speak against Moses. He spoke of the one Moses wrote about (John 5:46).

verseByVerse.quote: And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the face of an angel. Luke closes the chapter on a sentence he never explains. The verb (atenizō) is a fixed gaze, and it is the whole court of Israel looking at the same face.

The face of Moses. This is very probably more precise than a remark about serenity. Stephen is on trial for speaking blasphemous words against Moses. There is exactly one man in the Old Testament whose face is described as having been altered by nearness to God, and it is Moses. The skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God (Exodus 34:29–35). The court assembled to try a man for defaming Moses looks up and sees the one face in Jerusalem that looks like Moses’ did. They have the charge sheet in front of them and the answer to it in front of them at the same moment, and they proceed with the trial.

The appearance of his face was altered. Luke’s reader has seen a shining face before, with Moses there too. On the mountain, as Jesus prayed, the appearance of his face was altered and his clothing became dazzling white, and Moses and Elijah appeared in glory and spoke with him about the departure he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:29–31). Moses’ face shone because he had been with God, and the shining faded (2 Corinthians 3:7). Jesus’ face shone with a glory that was his own, and Moses stood beside him to see it. Now a servant of Jesus stands before the court of Moses with that same light on him.

They knew what they were looking at. Two chapters ago the same council recognised that two uneducated men had been with Jesus (4:13). Calm, radiant and unafraid, Stephen is visibly vindicated by God before he speaks a word.

What it does not mean. This verse turns into a burden quickly. It does not establish that a faithful Christian will look radiant under pressure. A great many faithful people have gone to prison, to a diagnosis or to their deaths looking precisely as frightened as they were, and Scripture nowhere treats that as a failure of faith. The Lord himself was greatly distressed in a garden and asked for the cup to be taken away (Mark 14:33–36). This is not a standard anyone is being asked to meet. It is a gift, given once, to one man, and Luke is careful to report it as something the observers saw rather than something Stephen felt.

What kind of God does this? He does not deliver Stephen. There is no earthquake, no angel opening a prison door as there had been for Peter, no crowd too dangerous to defy. Before long this man will be dragged outside the wall and killed with stones by people who have just heard him preach. What God gives him instead is a face. He is not spared, and he is not left alone. The same glory that met Moses on the mountain comes to rest on a man about to be executed for allegedly slandering him, in the last hour of his life, where every one of his judges can see it. Whatever else this is, it is not the conduct of a God who has lost control of the proceedings. Then Luke lets the sentence hang, and the next thing that happens is that the high priest turns to the shining man and asks him whether these things are so.

Will God give me peace when I face my worst moment? He promises to be with you, and he promises a peace that surpasses understanding to those who bring their requests to him (Philippians 4:6–7). He does not promise that you will feel calm or look radiant. Sometimes his peace is felt as a deep stillness; sometimes it is simply the strength to keep going, one step at a time, while afraid. Both are his gift. Paul says that we all, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). That transformation is going on in every believer now, mostly unseen. One day it will be seen in full.

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

6.theology: Word and deed, order and Spirit. The body has different members with different callings; no one person can or should do everything; the qualification for all ministry, however practical, is character shaped by the Spirit; and when ministry is rightly ordered, it is the word, not the institution or its ministers, that grows.
6.examples:
Then: A fast-growing church learned that love without structure lets real women go hungry, and that structure without love is dead religion. The seven brought both.

Now: Every growing church faces the same tension: how to care well for people without its leaders becoming so busy with management that the word is starved. The answer is to raise up people of Spirit and wisdom to share the load.

7.title: The Speech of Stephen
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the high priest said, “Are these things so?” <sup>2</sup>And Stephen said: “Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, <sup>3</sup>and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.’ <sup>4</sup>Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. <sup>5</sup>Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. <sup>6</sup>And God spoke to this effect—that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. <sup>7</sup>But I will judge the nation that they serve, said God, and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’ <sup>8</sup>And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. <sup>9</sup>“And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him <sup>10</sup>and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. <sup>11</sup>Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. <sup>12</sup>But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit. <sup>13</sup>And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. <sup>14</sup>And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all. <sup>15</sup>And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, <sup>16</sup>and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem. <sup>17</sup>“But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt <sup>18</sup>until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. <sup>19</sup>He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. <sup>20</sup>At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house, <sup>21</sup>and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. <sup>22</sup>And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds. <sup>23</sup>“When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. <sup>24</sup>And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. <sup>25</sup>He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. <sup>26</sup>And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’ <sup>27</sup>But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? <sup>28</sup>Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ <sup>29</sup>At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. <sup>30</sup>“Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. <sup>31</sup>When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. <sup>33</sup>Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. <sup>34</sup>I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’ <sup>35</sup>“This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. <sup>36</sup>This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. <sup>37</sup>This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ <sup>38</sup>This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us. <sup>39</sup>Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, <sup>40</sup>saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’ <sup>41</sup>And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. <sup>42</sup>But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? <sup>43</sup>You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’ <sup>44</sup>“Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. <sup>45</sup>Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David, <sup>46</sup>who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. <sup>47</sup>But it was Solomon who built a house for him. <sup>48</sup>Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, <sup>49</sup>‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? <sup>50</sup>Did not my hand make all these things?’ <sup>51</sup>“You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you. <sup>52</sup>Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, <sup>53</sup>you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.” <sup>54</sup>Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. <sup>55</sup>But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. <sup>56</sup>And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” <sup>57</sup>But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. <sup>58</sup>Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. <sup>59</sup>And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” <sup>60</sup>And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
7.overview:
Stephen’s speech is the longest in Acts. Accused of speaking against the temple and the law, he answers by retelling Israel’s history, and two threads run through it. First, God has never been confined to one land or one building: he met Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, called a patch of desert holy ground, and chose to live among his people in a tent. Second, Israel has always rejected the deliverers God sent, from Joseph and Moses to the prophets. The pattern ends where Stephen’s hearers stand: they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One.

The council rushes at him, and Stephen, full of the Spirit, sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He dies as his Lord did, committing his spirit to Jesus and praying for his killers, while a young man named Saul looks after the coats.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–50 — Stephen's Defense: Israel's History and God's Patience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asked whether the charges are true, Stephen answers with Israel’s history from Abraham to Solomon. God keeps meeting his people outside the land and outside any building: in Mesopotamia, in Egypt, at a burning bush in the desert, in a tent carried through the wilderness. And Israel keeps refusing the deliverer God sends: the brothers sell Joseph, and the people thrust Moses aside and turn to a golden calf. The section ends with Isaiah’s question: what house could anyone build for the God who made heaven and earth?
verseByVerse.theology:
The temple and the greatness of God

Stephen’s climax, the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (v. 48), is not an outsider’s attack on the temple. Solomon said it on the day he dedicated the building (1 Kings 8:27), and Isaiah said it within sight of it. The problem was never the temple but the shrinking of God to a location: the belief that having the building meant having God in a form that could be managed and defended. Stephen is not against the sign: God designed the tent and filled the temple. Now he dwells in Christ and, through him, in his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abraham had the covenant and no land; the patriarchs had the promise and a grave; Moses had holy ground in a foreign desert; Israel had a sanctuary that could be packed up in a day. Now: The question the speech puts to a congregation is not whether it values its building, its tradition or its structures; Stephen valued the tabernacle and said God designed it. It is whether it could lose them and still know where to find God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest said, "Are these things so?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 7 is Stephen’s defence, the longest speech in Acts, and his martyrdom. Charged with speaking against the temple and the law (6:13–14), he retells Israel’s history. He makes two points. First, God was never confined to the land or the temple: he appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, spoke to Moses in Midian, and walked with his people in a tent. Second, Israel always rejected the deliverers God sent: Joseph, Moses, the prophets, and now Jesus. Then Stephen sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand, and dies forgiving his killers. A young man named Saul watches.

Are these things so? Four words, and they hand Stephen the longest speech in the book. The high priest, probably Caiaphas, is following procedure: the charges have been read, and the accused is invited to answer them. It is the formal opening of a trial.

Not a history lesson but a brief. A man asked a direct question answers with fifty verses of history and not one word of denial. Hold the two charges in mind, speaking against this holy place and saying that Jesus would change the customs Moses delivered, and the history lesson becomes a brief.

The temple charge answered by geography. God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia. God was with Joseph in Egypt. God called a patch of desert holy ground. God designed his own sanctuary as a tent with carrying poles. God told David he had never asked for a building. Isaiah asked what kind of house anyone imagined they could put him in. Stephen does not argue that the temple is bad. He lets his accusers see from their own Scriptures that God has spent the entire story refusing to be located.

The Moses charge answered by turning it round. Stephen honours Moses extravagantly, and in the middle of the tribute he points out that Israel rejected him twice, and made a golden calf while he was on the mountain receiving the law. By verse 53 the man accused of despising the law is telling the court that they received it from angels and did not keep it.

He never asks to be let off. He produces no character witnesses and does not show that the testimony was perjured, which it was. Given the last opportunity of his life to save it, he uses it on the people who are going to take it.

Why does Stephen hardly mention Jesus until the end? Because he is letting the story do the work. He never names Jesus in the speech itself; he calls him the Righteous One only in verse 52, and names him only in his dying prayer. But Jesus is everywhere in it. Joseph, rejected by his brothers and raised up to save them; Moses, thrust aside and sent back as ruler and redeemer; the prophet like Moses; the true dwelling of God that no hands built. Stephen lays out the pattern so clearly that when he finally says, you have now betrayed and murdered the Righteous One, every man in the room already knows whom he means. It is a lesson in reading the Old Testament: it is Christ’s story from the beginning (Luke 24:27).

For worship. The court meant the charges, but the question reaches further: has God really been working one plan through famines and slavery, deserts and rebellions? The answer does not rest on Stephen’s eloquence. Before the hour is out heaven itself opens and gives it, with the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. He vindicates his Son, and every rejection of his messengers he has already woven into the rescue of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen said: "Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers and fathers, hear me. He calls the court that is going to kill him his family, with the respect a younger man owes his elders; there will be no defiance until verse 51. Paul uses the same opening years later before a mob in this city (22:1): this is an argument inside the house, not an attack from outside it.

The God of glory. The first clause is the whole thesis. The God of glory is the psalmist’s title (Psalm 29:3), and glory is the temple word: it filled the tabernacle when it was finished and the house when Solomon dedicated it, until the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). If anything belongs to their building, these men believe, it is the glory. (The Hebrew word carries the idea of weight: the shining out of who God is.) Stephen attaches the title to an event before Israel existed, in what is now southern Iraq, roughly six hundred miles from the room they are sitting in.

Ur or Haran? He is careful about the timing: before he lived in Haran. Genesis 12:1 records the call in Haran; Stephen follows the earlier summons in Ur, which Scripture itself records: I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 15:7; Nehemiah 9:7). Either God called him twice, or the call that began in Ur was renewed in Haran. So the very first appearance of God to the founder of the covenant people happened in a pagan city, in a family that served other gods (Joshua 24:2), to a man with nothing to go on but the voice that spoke to him.

Go out from your land. In that world land and kindred were not sentiment but survival (Genesis 12:1): your kindred fed you in a bad harvest and avenged you if you were wronged. To leave both was to make yourself a man with no protection. And he is not told where he is going. God gives him the leaving in full detail and the arriving not at all.

The ordinary shape of obedience. There is much here for anyone asked to obey without being shown the destination: the move, the resignation, the relationship ended, the thing put down that cannot be picked up again. That is the ordinary shape of obedience, and Scripture holds up the man who managed it as the father of all who believe (Romans 4:11; Hebrews 11:8).

From the God of glory to the glory of God. The speech opens with the God of glory appearing to Abraham, and the chapter closes with Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, gazing into heaven and seeing the glory of God, and Jesus standing at his right hand (7:55). The glory that met an idolater in Mesopotamia now has a face: the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Jesus said that Abraham rejoiced that he would see his day (John 8:56). The man who left everything for a land he had not been shown was walking toward the Son in whom that glory would dwell among us (John 1:14).

Does God still speak to people as he spoke to Abraham? God spoke to Abraham directly because there was as yet no written word. Now he has spoken to us finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and that word is recorded for us, complete and sufficient, in Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16–17). So you should not wait for a voice before you obey. The commands you need are already written, and the promises are already given. God still guides his people, through his word, through the wisdom he gives in prayer, through the counsel of mature believers, and through his providence opening and shutting doors. Christians differ here: many sincere believers, especially in charismatic churches, expect God still to give personal words, while this commentary holds that such direct revelation ended with the apostles, because Scripture is now complete; all agree that any impression must be tested by the written word. But the voice that called Abraham is now heard whenever the Bible is opened, and it calls us, as it called him, to trust and go.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen retells Israel’s story to show that God was never confined to one land or building, and that Israel repeatedly rejected his messengers.

parallels.desc: go to the land that I will show you

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haran. Haran, in northern Mesopotamia, was a stopping place on the road west. Stephen sets two facts side by side, the land given to live in and no inheritance in it, and he wants the collision.

Did Terah die before Abraham left? There is a difficulty buried in the clause, and a reader with Genesis open will find it. Genesis appears to say Terah was seventy when he fathered Abram (Genesis 11:26), died at two hundred and five (11:32), and Abram left Haran at seventy-five (12:4). That would leave Terah alive for another sixty years. But look at how Genesis writes these lines. When Terah had lived seventy years, he fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran does not mean all three arrived that year; it means that is when he began having sons. Genesis uses the identical formula of Noah, five hundred years old when he fathered Shem, Ham and Japheth, and nobody imagines triplets there. In both places the sons are listed by prominence rather than birth order, which is why Abram heads a list he may well have come last in. Put Abram’s birth in Terah’s hundred and thirtieth year and every number falls into line: Terah dies at two hundred and five, Abram is seventy-five, and he leaves exactly as Stephen says. Ancient readers noticed the question too: the Samaritan copies of the law give Terah’s age at death as a hundred and forty-five, and Philo agrees with Stephen. Some also suggest Stephen means that Terah, an idolater (Joshua 24:2), was spiritually dead. It does not affect his point. This is a harmonisation rather than a proof, but a strong one, and believers can hold Stephen’s words true while admitting that Genesis leaves the question to careful reading.

Not even a foot’s length. The man to whom the entire country was promised died holding title to one thing in it: a cave with his wife buried in it, bought from a Hittite (Genesis 23). He lived in tents, a stranger in a land that was his by promise and other men’s by law (Hebrews 11:9). Stephen says this to men whose case rests on a plot of land and a building on it. God’s promises were never exhausted by the land.

Though he had no child. Abraham had no land and no child, only God’s word, and he believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6).

The heir who owned nothing. The offspring of the promise is singular, Paul insists: Christ (Galatians 3:16). So the strange shape of Abraham’s life is repeated in the true Offspring. The Son whom God appointed heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2) had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), and died owning the clothes the soldiers divided. Then God raised him and gave him the nations for his inheritance (Psalm 2:8). Those who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29).

Is the land of Israel still promised to the Jewish people? Christians answer differently, and this commentary presents the views fairly. Some believe God’s promise of the land to Abraham’s physical descendants still stands and will have a future fulfilment, and they point to the unconditional language of the promise and to Romans 11. Others believe the land promise is fulfilled and enlarged in Christ: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs themselves were looking for a better country, a heavenly one (Hebrews 11:13–16). All agree on what Stephen shows here: that Abraham’s true hope was never a piece of real estate but God himself and the city he has prepared, and that every Christian shares that hope with him.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. 'But I will judge the nation that they serve,' said God, 'and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four hundred years. The promise as God gave it (Genesis 15:13–14) contained four centuries of slavery, announced in advance: not a failure of the plan but part of it.

The gap between word and fulfilment. God fills the gap between word and fulfilment with things nobody would have chosen. Anyone who concludes from four months of silence that God has changed his mind should look at the arithmetic Abraham was handed, and still believed.

Four hundred or four hundred and thirty? Stephen is quoting God’s word to Abraham, which says four hundred. Exodus gives the sojourn as four hundred and thirty years (Exodus 12:40), and Paul uses that longer figure too (Galatians 3:17). The two are easily reconciled. Four hundred is the round number for the affliction, spoken to Abraham in the shape a promise takes rather than a ledger; four hundred and thirty is the precise span, counted from a different starting point. Scripture is quite capable of giving a figure to the year in one place and rounding it in another, exactly as we do.

I will judge the nation. The plagues on Egypt were foretold centuries before Pharaoh was born. The oppressor is not out of God’s reach, even when he is out of the oppressed people’s sight.

Worship me in this place. Stephen blends Genesis 15:14 with Exodus 3:12, where this place means the mountain in the desert. The first national worship God promised his rescued people was at Sinai, hundreds of miles from the building these men are prosecuting Stephen to protect. Worship, not land, was the goal of the exodus.

Something greater than the temple. The place of worship was first a mountain, then a tent, then a house in Jerusalem, and Stephen’s accusers thought the line ended at the house. Jesus said it ends in him: something greater than the temple is here (Matthew 12:6), and he spoke of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21). On the mountain Moses and Elijah spoke with him about the exodus he would accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). That greater exodus brings a people out of a worse slavery than Egypt’s, and the place where they come to worship God is Christ himself.

How do I keep trusting when God’s promise seems delayed? Remember that delay is not denial. God told Abraham about the four hundred years in advance precisely so that later generations would not mistake the waiting for abandonment. Fill the waiting with what you know: his character, his past faithfulness, his written promises. Keep obeying in the meantime, as Israel kept having children in Egypt. Bring your impatience honestly to him, as the psalmists did: how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1). And remember that the greatest delay in history, the long wait for the Messiah, ended exactly on time, when the fullness of time had come (Galatians 4:4). He is not late with you either.

parallels.desc: your offspring will be sojourners, afflicted four hundred years
you shall serve God on this mountain

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. The sign is given when Abraham has no land and not yet the son of the promise (Genesis 17:9–14), long before the temple. And Stephen honours it.

A sign that travels. The mark of belonging to God is put on the flesh, not on a plot of ground, and so it travels. It went into Egypt and out again, and through seventy years in Babylon with no temple to go to.

Why call it the covenant of circumcision? The phrase names the covenant by its sign. The covenant itself was God’s promise to Abraham: a people, a land, and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12; 15; 17). When God formalised it, he gave circumcision as its token: this is my covenant, every male among you shall be circumcised, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you (Genesis 17:10–11). Sign and covenant became so bound together that the whole could be called by the sign. And two things are worth holding. The sign sealed a promise already received by faith: Abraham was counted righteous before he was ever circumcised (Genesis 15:6; 17), so circumcision was a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith (Romans 4:11). The mark never earned the promise; it pointed to it.

The twelve patriarchs. Three generations in a single sentence, and a nation exists by the end of it. No one in that room can dispute the point: that everything essential to being the people of God was in place and working generations before there was a land to live in or a house to worship in.

The son circumcised on the eighth day. The sign Abraham gave Isaac on the eighth day was given to another son of Abraham (Luke 2:21). The Son of God took the covenant mark in his own flesh, born under the law to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). The sign was borne by the one it pointed to, keeping the covenant his people had broken, so that the blessing promised through Abraham could at last flow out to the nations.

Where Christians differ: does baptism replace circumcision? Our paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers) in the Presbyterian and Reformed churches see baptism as the new covenant sign that takes the place of circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12), and so give it to the infant children of believers, as circumcision was given to Isaac on the eighth day. They do so out of a sincere conviction about God’s covenant faithfulness to families, and we honour them for it. Credobaptists (those who baptise only on profession of faith) answer that the new covenant is different in its membership: all its members know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), and its true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:29). In Colossians 2 the circumcision that answers to baptism is the one made without hands, the new birth, and in Acts baptism follows repentance and faith (2:38, 41; 8:12). This commentary’s view: baptism is for those who profess faith in Christ (1689 London Baptist Confession 29.2). Circumcision marked out a physical family through whom Christ would come; baptism marks out those who have been united to Christ by faith. Both sides agree on what matters most here: the sign never saves, and the promise is received by faith alone.

For worship. The covenant God gave Abraham was always too large for one family. It reached toward the blessing of all the nations (Galatians 3:8). Men and women who never bore the old mark, from places Abraham never heard of, have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13), and given the circumcision that was always the point, of the heart, by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jealous of Joseph. Consider whom Stephen is saying that to. On the high priest’s breastpiece were engraved the twelve names (Exodus 28:21), worn over the heart of the man presiding at this trial. Stephen describes them, without softening, as men who sold their brother into slavery because they could not stand him. The fathers of Israel rejected the one God had chosen to save them, out of jealousy, the same motive as the leaders who handed Jesus over (Mark 15:10; Acts 5:17).

The pattern appears. The pattern of the whole speech is now visible: the man his brothers got rid of turns out to be the man they cannot live without. Joseph goes down into Egypt in a slave train and comes up as the only source of food in the world, and the brothers who sold him arrive at his door to beg.

But God was with him. Where was God with him? Not in the promised land, but in a slave caravan, in an Egyptian official’s household, and in a prison cell on a false accusation, for some thirteen years between the pit and the palace. Joseph had no priest and no place of worship, and God was with him.

Out of all his afflictions. God’s presence did not keep him out of prison. God rescued him out of all his afflictions, which means he was in them first, one after another. The rescue ran through the trouble rather than round it. Then God exalted the rejected one, and he became the saviour of his brothers: God sent me before you to preserve life; you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 45:5–8; 50:20).

What it does not promise. There is a version of this story preached as a guarantee: hold on, because your Egypt is preparing you for a throne. Scripture does not promise that. Joseph received a visible reward within his lifetime; a great many faithful people do not, and the letter to the Hebrews says plainly of a long list of them that they died still waiting. What this passage does establish is the thing Stephen needs, and it is enough to build a life on: there is no place a believer can be taken, sold, imprisoned, deported, forgotten or simply stuck, where God is not already there ahead of him, and no institution whose absence can put him out of reach.

Is it right to see Joseph as a picture of Jesus? Yes, because Stephen does, and because the shape is unmistakable. The beloved son of his father, hated by his brothers, sold for silver, falsely accused, brought down into the depths, then raised to the right hand of the throne, and from there giving bread to the very people who betrayed him. The Old Testament is full of such patterns, which the New Testament calls types: real events and people that God shaped to point forward to Christ (Romans 5:14; Hebrews 10:1). We should not invent fanciful links, but where Scripture itself draws the line, as here, we should follow it with joy.

For worship. God was with Joseph in the pit, the caravan and the cell. The greater Joseph went further down, to the one place where even that comfort was withdrawn, and cried out that God had forsaken him (Matthew 27:46). He was abandoned so that his brothers never will be, and now he is Immanuel, God with us, in every Egypt they are carried to. Raised to the right hand of the Majesty on high, he feeds the people who sold him, and forgives with tears, and calls to come near.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph, rejected by his brothers but raised up by God, is the first of Stephen’s rejected deliverers.
