verseByVerse.quote: "Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A famine. In the ancient world a household in famine ate its stores, then its animals, then its seed corn, and then it moved, or it died (Genesis 41:54–57).

No food. The chosen family, in the land of promise, could find no food; the grain was in the pagan empire down the road. His accusers hold that God’s favour and God’s land belong together. Stephen observes that the covenant family’s first great crisis was solved by leaving.

Grain in Egypt. A rumour reaches an old man in Hebron that there is wheat for sale in the south, and he sends his sons to buy some. There is no vision, no angel and no word from God. A man acts sensibly on a piece of market news, and sets in motion the descent into Egypt, the four hundred years, the exodus, Sinai and the whole national existence of Israel. And on that first visit they did not recognise Joseph (Genesis 42:8).

How providence usually works. Very little of what God does in a life arrives labelled. It arrives as the price of wheat, a conversation that ran long, a job that fell through, a piece of news somebody happened to mention. Jacob was being practical, not spiritual, and without the faintest suspicion of it he was delivering his household into the hands of the son he had spent twenty years mourning.

Not fatalism. That God governs the ordinary does not mean ordinary decisions are unimportant. Jacob still had to weigh the risk and send the boys, and if he had not, they would have starved. What it means is that a man doing the sensible next thing in front of him, with no sense of destiny about it whatever, may be doing something that is still being discussed thousands of years later.

Bread only in the hands of the rejected. The brothers have no bread, and the only bread in the world is in the hands of the brother they sold, though they do not know it. Stephen’s hearers stand in the same place. The Jesus they handed over is now the one through whom alone God gives life, and there is salvation in no one else (4:12). Jesus called himself the bread of life, and promised that whoever comes to him shall not hunger (John 6:35). Every sinner who comes to Christ comes the way Jacob’s sons came to Egypt: hungry, empty-handed and unaware, to find that the one they wronged has been ready for them all along.

Does God send famines and disasters? Scripture teaches that God governs all things, including famines, storms and pandemics, and that nothing happens outside his wise and holy providence (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.1 and the Westminster Confession 5.1; Amos 3:6). Genesis says plainly that God sent the famine as part of his plan to save many lives (Genesis 45:5–7). But God is never the author of sin, and his purposes in a disaster are usually hidden from us. Jesus forbade us to read a disaster as proof that its victims were worse sinners (Luke 13:1–5). The right response is not to explain other people’s suffering, but to humble ourselves, help the hungry, and trust that the God who governed Joseph’s famine is governing ours for the good of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second visit. Everything turns on the second visit (Genesis 45:1–4). Genesis gives it four chapters; Stephen gives it a clause, because he needs the shape. The brothers had assumed for twenty years that they had got away with it, and the man they had wronged had meanwhile been put in charge of the only food in the world, and could have done anything he liked with them.

Recognised the second time. Many see a hint Stephen means his hearers to catch: later Moses too is not understood when he first comes to his brothers (7:25), and returns as ruler and redeemer. Israel did not recognise Jesus when he came, and acted in ignorance, as Peter told them (3:17). Now, risen and exalted, he is making himself known through the preaching of men like Stephen. The scene in Genesis, with Joseph weeping and telling the men who sold him that he is their brother, is the gospel in miniature: the wronged one reveals himself in order to save.

Known to Pharaoh. A household of shepherds was presented at court, and the king assigned them the best of the land in Goshen. Israel came to Egypt by royal invitation, under the protection of the second man in the kingdom. That is why the new king of verse 18 is such a catastrophe: everything had rested on one man’s standing at court, and courts forget.

Seventy or seventy-five? Genesis puts the number at seventy (Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1:5). Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which Greek-speaking Jews used everywhere in his day, and which reads seventy-five, counting several more of Joseph’s descendants born in Egypt. A difference in counting between two textual traditions, not an error; a Hebrew copy of Exodus found among the Dead Sea Scrolls also reads seventy-five. Either way Stephen’s point holds.

Will Israel recognise Jesus at a second visit? Christians hold different views about Israel’s future, and this commentary presents them fairly. Many believe Romans 11 foretells a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, when all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–26). Others read all Israel as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, gathered in through the gospel age. All agree that God has not cast away his people, that Jewish men and women are coming to Christ now as they did in Acts, and that the church should pray and long for Jewish people to see in Jesus the brother they did not recognise.

For worship. The brothers dreaded for twenty years the face of the man they had wronged, and when they saw it, it was wet with tears and turned toward them in welcome. Christ has a face like that. The one with every right to condemn us is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and he gives his people more than Goshen: an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading (1 Peter 1:4).
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which gives seventy-five; the Hebrew text counts seventy.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He died, he and our fathers. A single clause for the death of a generation, but Stephen stops for the burial. These men died outside the land, and their bodies were carried back across the desert so that they could lie in ground they had never owned. Joseph made his brothers swear to it on his deathbed, and four hundred years later a nation walking out of Egypt in a hurry took his coffin with them (Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19).

A tomb as evidence. The only real estate any of the patriarchs held in the promised land was a grave and a field. They arranged their own funerals around the promise. Stephen’s accusers hold the land, the city and the temple, and are about to kill a man over a building. The founding fathers held a tomb, and held on to God.

Two purchases in one clause. Genesis records two separate transactions: Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23), and Jacob bought the plot at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19). Jacob himself was buried at Machpelah (Genesis 50:13); Joseph’s bones were laid at Shechem, in Jacob’s plot (Joshua 24:32). Stephen has folded two purchases and two burial grounds into a single clause.

If Stephen compressed the history, can I trust the Bible? Yes. The natural explanation is compression. Stephen is racing through more than a thousand years in one speech, on trial for his life, and he telescopes the patriarchal burials into a summary phrase, as speakers often did; he is not filing a title deed. His hearers knew the law better than we do, and as far as Luke records they do not challenge his history. They rage at his conclusion, not his facts. A few have suggested Abraham made a further, unrecorded purchase at Shechem, where he built his first altar in the land (Genesis 12:6–7): possible, but speculative. And consider what Scripture is doing. Luke’s task is to report the sermon faithfully, and he has. Inspiration guarantees a true record of what Stephen said, as it guarantees a true record of what Job’s friends said. Nothing hangs on this detail, and believers can hold Scripture true while admitting that no explanation here is certain. What Stephen came to say, that God was never confined to this land or that building, stands untouched.

Why did the patriarchs care so much where they were buried? Because their burial was an act of faith in God’s promise and, at its deepest, in the resurrection. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus and gave directions concerning his bones (Hebrews 11:22). He wanted to be where God’s promise would be kept, because he expected to share in it. Christians bury their dead with the same hope, not because the place saves, but because the body matters to God and will be raised. A Christian funeral is a statement of faith about the future, made beside a grave.

Joseph’s field and Jacob’s well. The patriarchs lie at Shechem, in despised Samaria. There Jesus sat by Jacob’s well at Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph (John 4:5–6). Beside the burial ground of the patriarch who died waiting, the one he waited for told a Samaritan woman that he was the Messiah (John 4:26). And in the next chapter Philip preaches Christ in Samaria (8:5–12). The fathers were buried in Samaritan ground in hope, and their hope came and sat down beside them.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen compresses two purchases: Abraham bought a tomb at Hebron, and Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, where Joseph was buried.

verseByVerse.quote: "But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. With verse 17 Stephen moves to Moses, the very man the charge sheet named (6:11). The two threads run on: God at work outside the land, and Israel refusing the deliverer God sends.

The time of the promise. The four hundred years named in verse 6 are nearly up, and what happens as they run out is not a softening of Israel’s circumstances but a hardening of them.

Another king. Blessing and persecution arrive in the same sentence (Exodus 1:7–8), and the second follows from the first: a rapidly growing foreign population in the delta is precisely what alarms a new regime.

Did not know Joseph. A man had saved the country from starvation, and within a few generations the palace has no idea who he was. Nations forget their benefactors fast.

The whip and the promise. Israel in Egypt before this king was doing well: land in Goshen, growing numbers, standing because of Joseph, and no recorded sign of wanting to leave. The promise required them to go, and what finally made them willing was the whip. It does not follow that every hardship is God prising somebody loose from a comfort, and it is never a thing to say to a person in the middle of one; a friend who explains your suffering to you has stopped being a friend. What can be said is only what the text says: this affliction fell inside a promise made four hundred years before, and the people groaning under it could not see that, and found out afterwards.

Settled where we were never meant to settle. A member of the covenant people can prosper quietly in a place he was never meant to settle, for a very long time, with no intention whatever of moving. Christians are sojourners and exiles (1 Peter 2:11), and the danger of comfort is that we forget it.

When the fullness of time had come. Stephen’s phrase, the time of the promise drew near, is the language of the whole Bible’s waiting. The first deliverance came when God’s appointed years ran out in Egypt. The greater one came the same way: when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son (Galatians 4:4), into a land ruled by a foreign emperor whose census decided where he was born (Luke 2:1–7). Every promise that drew near in Egypt was drawing near to him.

How do I wait for God’s timing without becoming passive? Waiting on God in Scripture is never idleness. Israel waited in Egypt by having children, working, and keeping the memory of the promise alive; Joseph had made them promise to carry his bones out, so every generation knew they were not home. Wait like that. Do your work well, raise your children in the faith, pray for what God has promised, and hold your present comforts loosely, ready to move when he moves you. Waiting is active trust: doing today’s duty while looking for tomorrow’s fulfilment.

verseByVerse.quote: "He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God's sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father's house,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He dealt shrewdly. The persecution was policy, escalated by stages (Exodus 1:10, 22): forced labour, then the midwives, then the decree that every son be thrown into the Nile. It is the coldest thing in the chapter, because it was calculated.

Our fathers. Stephen puts the horror exactly where it belongs: Pharaoh forced our fathers to expose their infants. To expose was to abandon a baby to die, a common practice in the ancient world, and early Christians became known for taking in such abandoned babies.

Beautiful in God’s sight. God’s answer to the machinery of a superpower is very small: a baby, born to slaves, in the middle of the programme designed to kill precisely him. The phrase means exceptionally fine, pleasing to God (Exodus 2:2).

Three months. Hidden where one cry would have finished the whole family. Hebrews picks up the detail: by faith Moses was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict (Hebrews 11:23). The first act of faith in Israel’s deliverance was performed by a mother and a father with a basket.

The other babies. Rescues are not universal. The other babies died, and for their households the deliverer born down the street was, at the time, no help at all. Scripture neither explains them nor pretends they were not there. Any reading of this passage that suggests God protects the children of the faithful as a general rule must be kept well away from anyone who has buried one. What the passage does say is that a state which had decided to end a people could not kill one particular child, and ended up paying for his upbringing. That is not an explanation of the others. It is a statement about who was in charge of the outcome, made to a court that thought it was.

Another child under a king’s decree. Matthew tells the birth of Jesus to recall this one. A king hears of a child who threatens his throne and orders the boys of a whole district killed; the child is carried to safety; and then the angel tells Joseph to return, for those who sought the child’s life are dead (Matthew 2:16, 20), almost the words God spoke to Moses in Midian (Exodus 4:19). The deliverer born under a death sentence was a preview of a greater one. And the greater one did more than escape the decree as a baby. At the end he walked into the death sentence on purpose, so that it would fall on him and not on his people.

What does this say about the value of unborn and newborn children? That every child is precious to God, including the ones the powerful find inconvenient. Each is made in his image and known by him before birth (Genesis 1:27; Psalm 139:13–16). Pharaoh’s policy was condemned by God, and so is every modern equivalent, including abortion and the abandonment of the unwanted. Christians should speak for the voiceless (Proverbs 31:8), and should do it as the early church did, by caring practically for mothers and children. And to anyone carrying the grief or guilt of an ended pregnancy: there is full forgiveness in Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). The church is meant to be a place of refuge for you, not judgment. And Scripture gives grieving parents real hope: we believe that God in his mercy saves the elect infants who die in infancy (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3 and the Westminster Confession 10.3; 2 Samuel 12:23). If you have lost a little one, you may rest that child in the hands of a Father who is kinder than we are, and who knew and loved your baby before you did.

verseByVerse.quote: "and when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s daughter. The rescue is arranged by the daughter of the man who signed the death warrant (Exodus 2:5–10). Stephen does not need to comment on the irony.

All the wisdom of the Egyptians. Egypt was the great seat of learning in the ancient world; even of Solomon it is said that his wisdom surpassed all the wisdom of Egypt (1 Kings 4:30). Exodus does not say Moses received a prince’s education; it is the natural inference, preserved in Jewish tradition. God prepared him in a pagan court.

Mighty in his words. Moses would later say he was not eloquent (Exodus 4:10), but his words carried power. Stephen’s point is aimed at the temple charge again: God’s man is formed in a pagan palace, at the expense of the pagan state.

A prophet mighty in deed and word. On the Emmaus road two disciples on the Emmaus road described Jesus of Nazareth as a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people (Luke 24:19), and the risen Jesus then showed them from Moses and all the Prophets the things concerning himself (24:27). The difference is as telling as the likeness. Moses was a son adopted into a palace that was not his; Jesus is the Son who came from the Father into a world he had made. Moses learned all the wisdom of Egypt; in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).

Equipped, but not the deliverer. For all his Egyptian learning and natural greatness, Moses’ first attempt to deliver Israel in his own strength failed (vv. 23–29), and he had to wait forty years in the desert for God’s call. The world’s finest wisdom equipped him, but it did not make him the deliverer. God did.

Should Christians pursue a secular education? Yes, with open eyes. Moses learned the wisdom of Egypt, Daniel the literature of Babylon (Daniel 1:4, 17), and Paul quoted pagan poets (17:28). All truth is God’s truth, and learning is a gift to be used for his glory and our neighbour’s good. But neither Moses nor Daniel let the school decide who they were. Daniel resolved not to defile himself; Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter (Hebrews 11:24). So study hard, and study well, and take your faith into the classroom with you. Learn everything you can, and let God’s word judge it all.

For worship. The Lord used Pharaoh’s own daughter to raise the man who would bring Pharaoh down, and Egypt’s treasury to pay for the schooling of Israel’s deliverer. He makes the wrath of man to praise him (Psalm 76:10). He did it again, on a scale that dwarfs Egypt, at the cross: the rulers who gathered against his Son did only what his hand and his plan had predestined to take place (4:28), and their worst became the rescue of the world.
verseByVerse.note: Tradition held that Moses received a full Egyptian education.

verseByVerse.quote: "When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It came into his heart. Something rose in him, and it was a decision about who he was: a man raised as an Egyptian must eventually settle which of the two peoples inside him will win.

A renunciation. The letter to the Hebrews describes the moment as a refusal: he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin (Hebrews 11:24–26). He chose to identify with his oppressed people, and it cost him a kingdom.

The reproach of Christ. In the same breath Hebrews adds a startling phrase: Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt (Hebrews 11:26). His choice had the shape of Christ’s before Christ came, and the contrast tells as much as the likeness. Moses left a palace and took a life; the Son left glory and gave his. He too saw his brothers wronged, by sin and death and the devil, and came down to defend them, but he struck down no one. He let himself be struck, and by his wounds we are healed (1 Peter 2:24).

He defended the oppressed man. And then he kills a man (Exodus 2:11–12). Exodus settles the moral question: Moses looked this way and that, and seeing no one, struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Those are the movements of a man who knows exactly what he has done.

Right about the cause, wrong about the method. The loyalty was right and the hands were his own. God had not sent him; there is no word from God anywhere in these verses. The deliverer who eventually stands before Pharaoh will do it with a staff and a message and no violence of his own. The method cost him forty years. The pattern is common and does not look like sin from the inside: a man is right about the injustice, then forces the issue in his own strength. The wrongness is not in the caring but in the assumption that being right about the cause authorises whatever gets it done.

Forgiven, but not spared. And then the mercy: God did not discard him. The man who buried an Egyptian at forty was standing before a burning bush at eighty, and the intervening decades turned out to be preparation rather than punishment. But they were real decades. He lost forty years, Israel’s slavery went on, and being forgiven was never the same thing as being spared the consequences.

When should a Christian step in to defend someone being wronged? Often, and gladly, by right means. Scripture commands us to open our mouths for the mute and defend the rights of the poor and needy (Proverbs 31:8–9), and Moses’ instinct to stand with the oppressed was right. But we act within the law and through proper channels: we report abuse to the authorities, speak up at work, give evidence, support the vulnerable, and in an emergency we protect life. What we do not do is take private vengeance; vengeance belongs to God and to the authorities he has appointed (Romans 12:19; 13:4). Care deeply, act wisely, and do not let zeal for justice become an excuse for sin.

For worship. Moses looked this way and that before he struck. The Son of God did his saving work in full view, lifted up outside the city, with nothing to hide and no blood on his hands but his own. One blow cost Moses forty years in the desert; one offering of Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). This deliverer was never too early, never too late, and never wrong in his method.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows a tradition that divided Moses’ 120 years into three forties.

verseByVerse.quote: "He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He supposed. Verse 25 is not in Exodus: Stephen interprets, and the interpretation unlocks the speech. God was giving Israel salvation (sōtēria) by Moses’ hand; Moses supposed they would grasp it. They did not. The people he had come to rescue saw a palace-raised Egyptian who had killed a man.

The failure is in the seeing. The failure is not in the sending but in the seeing, and they did not understand hangs over everything that follows. God giving salvation by the hand of a deliverer his people did not recognise is the story of Jesus before it is the story of Moses. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11); the rulers acted in ignorance (3:17); and yet God was giving salvation by his hand all the same. The cross they did not understand was the salvation itself.

The following day. Yesterday he stepped between an Egyptian and a Hebrew, an obvious oppressor and victim. Today he steps between two Hebrews, where both men have a grievance and neither wants him there. Anyone who has tried to make peace inside a family or a congregation knows which day is harder, and what tends to happen next: two parties who agree about nothing else unite instantly against the man who came to help.

Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other? A plea for unity: true, and precisely what neither of them wished to hear.

How should I try to make peace between two people? Carefully, prayerfully and humbly. Begin by praying for both. Go to each privately before bringing them together, and listen far more than you speak. Remind them, as Moses did, of what they share: if they are believers, they are brothers and sisters for whom Christ died. Do not take sides before you understand, and do not carry tales between them. Be ready to be resented; peacemakers often are. And know your limits: serious conflict, especially where there is abuse or law-breaking, belongs with elders and sometimes with the authorities. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God (Matthew 5:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thrust him aside. The word (apōtheō) is a key one: Israel will thrust Moses away again (v. 39).

Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Stephen has included the question for a reason, and the reason arrives eight verses later. At verse 35 he says: this Moses, whom they rejected, saying, Who made you a ruler and a judge, this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer. The question receives its answer in its own words. Israel demanded to know who had made him a ruler. The answer, which took forty years to become visible, was God (Exodus 2:14).

The question asked again. Stephen leaves its third instance unspoken. Men of this same council had put the identical question to Jesus in the temple courts: tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority (Luke 20:2). God has since answered it for them, in Peter’s words at Pentecost: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (2:36).

Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday? The second half of the taunt is the sting, and a threat. Moses had looked round and seen nobody. Somebody had seen. And the man who tells him so is one of the two he has just tried to reconcile: the secret is out, and it is out through the people he was trying to help.

Israel had some reason. In fairness, consider how it looked from the labour camp. A man who has spent forty years in the palace, who has never carried a brick, turns up, kills an Egyptian, and expects to be recognised as the nation’s deliverer. The reprisals would fall on them. Their failure was genuine, but it was not stupidity. It was the ordinary difficulty of recognising a deliverer who does not look like one, the very difficulty the men listening had lately failed to overcome with a carpenter from Nazareth.

How do I respond when my help is thrown back at me? First, do not be surprised; Moses was rejected for trying to make peace, and Jesus for far more. Second, examine yourself honestly, as Moses had reason to: was there something in my manner or method that made the help hard to receive? Third, do not retaliate or become bitter; commit the matter to God, who sees. And fourth, do not conclude that you must never help again. Moses was rejected at forty and sent back at eighty. Sometimes the timing was wrong, not the love. Keep your heart soft, and wait to see whether God reopens the door.

parallels.desc: who made you a prince and a judge over us?

verseByVerse.quote: "At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses fled. Forty years disappear into one sentence. Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba. Exile (paroikos) is a sojourner, a resident alien, like Abraham.

Three forties. Only this speech gives Moses’ age when he fled, setting his hundred and twenty years in three forties: Egypt (v. 23), Midian (v. 30; Exodus 7:7), the wilderness (v. 36). Two-thirds of that life was over before God said anything to him at all.

What the middle forty contained. He kept another man’s sheep in another man’s country and named his first son Gershom, which Exodus explains as I have been a sojourner in a foreign land (Exodus 2:22), and a man who names his child after his own homelessness is telling you how the years were going. Nothing in the record suggests he expected to go back.

God waited for the second man. At forty he was a prince with an education, a position and a plan, convinced that God was going to save Israel by his hand and that everyone would see it. At eighty he was a shepherd standing before a burning bush producing five separate excuses why God ought to send somebody else. God waited for the second man.

The fallow years. This is the passage for a reader in a long fallow stretch, after the plan that came to nothing. Scripture shows the shape repeatedly, as with David between the anointing and the throne. But the pattern is easily turned into a promise it does not make. Not every fallow decade is preparation for something visible, and telling somebody in year twelve that God is getting them ready is a guess dressed up as a word from the Lord. Moses did not know. What can be said is that the desert was not wasted and God had not finished, and nobody in Midian could have told you either thing at the time.

The rejected one who went away. The deliverer is refused, goes away into a far country, and comes back with God’s authority to the people who refused him. It is the shape of what Peter had preached in the temple: the Jesus they denied, God has raised, and heaven must receive him until the time for restoring all things (3:13–15, 21). In the long middle the deliverer is not idle. Christ, risen and ascended, is gathering his flock from every nation, and he will come back.

Is it wrong to run from danger? No. Moses fled for his life, and so did David, Elijah, Joseph and Mary with the infant Jesus, and Paul over the Damascus wall. Jesus told his disciples, when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Fleeing is not cowardice when it preserves life and does not require denying Christ. What a Christian must not do is run from a clear duty, or deny the Lord to save his skin. Where faithfulness and safety can go together, take the safe road with a clear conscience. Where they cannot, stand.
verseByVerse.note: Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When forty years had passed. Stephen puts the silence in first: four decades in which, so far as we are told, God said nothing to the man he intended to use (Exodus 3:1–2).

What stopped Moses was not the fire. In the Sinai, among bare rock and thorn scrub, a dry bush that caught fire would be a handful of ash a minute later. Exodus tells us what arrested him: I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned (Exodus 3:3). It was the duration.

As he drew near to look. Exodus gives the order: when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush (Exodus 3:4). God spoke to a man who had stopped. This is not a technique; God was in that bush whether Moses looked or not. But much of what God does is available to anybody prepared to stop and look twice, and a life can be spent walking briskly past.

Was it an angel or God himself in the bush? Exodus says the angel of the LORD appeared, and then that God spoke from the bush, saying, I am the God of your father (Exodus 3:2–6). The angel of the LORD speaks as God and is called God. Many Christians, from the early church onward, have understood him as the Son of God appearing before his incarnation, and that is a reasonable reading. What is certain is that Moses met the living God himself, and that the God who spoke from the bush is the God revealed in Jesus Christ (John 8:58).

In the wilderness. This is Stephen’s real interest: not in Egypt nor in Canaan, but in desert belonging to nobody, with one man and a flock of sheep for a congregation.

Should I expect God to speak to me in a burning bush? No; the bush was a unique moment in the history of redemption, when God was giving new revelation. Now God has spoken to us by his Son, and his word is complete in Scripture (Hebrews 1:1–2). But the lesson of turning aside still holds. God speaks to us whenever we stop and attend to his word, and he often draws our attention through ordinary things: a verse that will not let go, a sermon that lands, a providence that makes us look twice. Do not rush past. Make room in your day to stop, read, and listen.

For worship. The bush was not consumed, because the God in it needs nothing to keep him burning. After forty years of silence he still knew the name of a fugitive shepherd, and he called it twice (Exodus 3:4). The God who spoke from that fire came nearer still in his Son, and the sinners he came among were not consumed: he ate with them, touched them, and gave himself for them.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.' And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, 'Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of your fathers. The first thing God says is that he is the same (Exodus 3:6). No explanation of the delay; he names himself by three men dead for centuries, and so tells Moses that nothing has been dropped: the promise made in Mesopotamia to a childless man is being kept this morning in a desert. And Jesus would later draw out of this very sentence the proof of the resurrection: he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him (Luke 20:37–38).

Moses trembled. At forty he was ready to take on Egypt single-handed; at eighty he cannot raise his eyes to a bush. This is the man God has decided to send.

Holy ground. This (Exodus 3:5) is the first time in the Bible that any ground is called holy, and it is a patch of dirt in a foreign desert with a thorn bush on it: no altar, no priest, no temple. When Moses walked back to his sheep, it was scrub again. What made it holy was that God was there, and nothing else ever has.

The sandals. In that world a man took his shoes off at the door of a house, and by long tradition the priests served barefoot in the sanctuary. God is telling Moses that this hillside is his house. Against the charge sheet, Stephen has shown out of the law they revere that the first ground God called holy was unmarked desert, and Moses wrote it down.

Where God now stands. If ground is holy only because God is there, then the holiest place on earth in Stephen’s lifetime was wherever Jesus stood, for in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). This council had condemned the one who was God with us, after witnesses accused him of saying he would destroy the temple made with hands and build another not made with hands (Mark 14:58). Within minutes Stephen will see where he stands now, at the right hand of God (7:56).

Is my church building holy ground? Not in itself. No place under the new covenant is holier than another; Jesus said that true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on this mountain or in Jerusalem (John 4:21–24). A church building is a useful room, to be cared for well and used reverently, but it is not a temple. What is holy is the presence of God among his gathered people, and that is why public worship should be reverent: not because of the bricks, but because the Lord is in the midst of his assembly (Matthew 18:20). Wherever God’s people meet in his name, whether a cathedral, a school hall or a living room, take off your sandals in your heart.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; take off your sandals

verseByVerse.quote: "'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have surely seen. Seen, heard, come down (Exodus 3:7). The first is doubled in the Hebrew: seeing I have seen, steadily, every year of it.

God hears groaning. Exodus, describing the same moment, does not say that Israel prayed. They groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help, their cry rose up to God, and God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant (Exodus 2:23–24). No petition properly worded: a noise made by people at the end of their strength, and God treats it as a communication. That is worth knowing by anyone for whom the words would not come. Paul says that when we do not know what to pray for as we ought, the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). Whatever reaches God, it is not the wording.

I have come down. God does not explain the timing or answer the question every Hebrew slave must have asked in the dark. Israel received a rescue and never an explanation. Scripture’s most sustained example of a long silence ends without a reason. What was given instead was God himself, in motion, on the way.

I will send you. The last clause turns the whole thing over. God says he has come down to deliver them, and then sends a man. The coming down and the sending are one act. And the men listening to this speech had lately watched him do it in a form so complete that they killed the messenger, for the true coming down of God was in his Son, and they are about to kill the next messenger too.

How can God come down, if he is everywhere already? God is everywhere present, filling heaven and earth (Jeremiah 23:24). When Scripture says he came down, it means he acted in a new and particular way: he drew near in saving power to a specific people in a specific place. It is language suited to us, but it describes something real. And it reaches its full meaning in the incarnation, when the eternal Son literally came down from heaven and became flesh (John 6:38; 1:14). The God who said, I have come down, in Exodus, said it again in Bethlehem, and this time he stayed.

parallels.desc: I have surely seen the affliction of my people

verseByVerse.quote: "This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This Moses, whom they rejected. Stephen begins hammering the same word: this Moses, this man, this is the one (vv. 35–38). He has stopped narrating and is pointing, and the portrait is of Jesus.

This man God sent as both ruler and redeemer. Israel demanded to know who had made Moses a ruler and a judge; God made him a ruler and a redeemer. The office they refused him is the office he was given. So with Jesus: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (2:36); the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (4:11).

Redeemer. Redeemer (lytrōtēs), found nowhere else in the New Testament, is the one who buys a man out of slavery or debt: a word his hearers cannot keep at a comfortable distance.

Wonders and signs. Signs confirmed Moses, as they confirmed Jesus (2:22), and Luke uses the phrase of the apostles (5:12) and of Stephen himself (6:8). Moses, the Twelve and the man now on trial are being set in a single line: all sent, all attested, and all disbelieved by the same institution.

The pattern fully drawn. Stephen still refuses to name the pattern. Joseph, sold by his brothers, fed them. Moses, thrust aside by his people, brought them out. Twice God sent Israel a deliverer, twice Israel refused him at first sight, and twice God sent him anyway.

What does it mean that Jesus is my redeemer? It means you were a slave, and he paid to set you free. Not with silver or gold, Peter says, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). You were in bondage to sin, under the law’s curse and the fear of death (Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 2:15), and you could not buy yourself out. Christ had the right, as your kinsman in our flesh, and the resources, as the Son of God, and he paid it all. So you belong to him now, not as a slave in fear but as a ransomed child, and the life you have is no longer yours to spend as you please, because it was paid for (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.' This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet like me. The promise (Deuteronomy 18:15) is the text Peter preached from in the temple courts (3:22), and Stephen means Jesus, as Peter did. It goes straight at the second charge: Moses himself told Israel to expect somebody else and to listen to him. To honour Moses is to listen to Jesus.

The congregation in the wilderness. The word for congregation is ekklēsia, the Old Testament’s term for the assembly of Israel and the New Testament’s word for the church. Israel in the wilderness was God’s assembly, the church of the old covenant.

With the angel. Stephen says the law came through angelic mediation, as the New Testament says elsewhere (v. 53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). He is not diminishing the law; at verse 53 he uses it as the aggravating factor in the charge he brings against them.

He received living oracles to give to us. Living oracles: not a dead code or an antique, but words of God with life still in them, still speaking. It is said by the man on trial for despising the law. And not to you but to us: he claims the law as his own inheritance, in a hearing convened on the charge that he has thrown it away. (A few early manuscripts read to you here; most modern Bibles, like the KJV, read to us.)

A demonstration, not a denial. Denial always sounds like a man on the back foot. Stephen states what he actually believes, in terms so high that the accusation collapses. The best answer to being misrepresented is usually not a correction but a demonstration.

Is the Old Testament still for Christians? Entirely. It is the Bible Jesus read, quoted and called the word of God, and he said it bears witness about him (John 5:39). Paul says the Scriptures, meaning the Old Testament, are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and that all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable (2 Timothy 3:15–16). We read it through Christ, so that its sacrifices point us to his cross and its ceremonies are fulfilled in him rather than kept by us. But its stories, laws, psalms and prophets remain living oracles for us. If you have neglected it, start with Genesis, the Psalms or Isaiah, and read looking for Christ.

For worship. The living oracles given at the mountain were never meant to stay on stone. The God who spoke through angels and through Moses has now spoken in a Son, who is himself the Word, full of grace and truth, and whose words are spirit and life (John 6:63). At Sinai the congregation begged not to hear the voice again (Deuteronomy 18:16), and the promise of a prophet like Moses was God’s answer: he now speaks through one of our own brothers.
verseByVerse.note: “The congregation” is the same word as “church.”

parallels.desc: a prophet like me

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, 'Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our fathers refused to obey him. Thrust aside is the word of verse 27. Israel pushed Moses aside before the exodus and again after the sea had opened: the rescue made no difference to the reflex.

In their hearts they turned to Egypt. Within weeks of the sea they were longing for Egypt (Numbers 14:3–4), because it was familiar and the food arrived. Numbers records what they missed: the fish, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic (Numbers 11:5). They remembered the menu and forgot the whips. The heart turned back before the feet did.

The homesickness of the redeemed. This is not about somebody else. A man is genuinely delivered and would not go back if asked outright, yet there is a homesickness in him for the country he was rescued from: not for its misery but for its familiarity, the not having to trust anybody for tomorrow. Egypt fed you every day and asked nothing of you except your life.

Make for us gods. They gave Moses about forty days on the mountain before replacing him (Exodus 32:1). Idolatry is wanting a god you can see and control, one who goes where you want to go. And the complaint is contempt: this Moses, of whom we do not know what has become.

The mediator out of sight. The calf was made while Moses was out of sight, doing for the people what they could not do for themselves. Our mediator has gone up, out of sight, and the world asks what has become of him. He is not idle: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). And the comparison runs deeper. When Moses came down he offered to be blotted out of God’s book for the people’s sin, and God would not accept the offer (Exodus 32:30–33). Christ’s offering was accepted. He became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and bore the sin of the very people who were so quick to replace him.

A trap closing. These people had eaten manna that morning, so witnessing miracles does not make anybody faithful, and a Christian who assumes he would have done better is the sort of person Stephen has in front of him. Every man on that council would have agreed that their ancestors were a disgrace. That is the trap, and it closes in twelve verses.

What do I do with the longing for my old life? Name it honestly, and do not be shocked by it; Israel felt it, and so do most believers at some point. Then remember accurately. Egypt was not garlic and melons; it was whips and dead babies. Ask God to show you the truth about what you were rescued from. Feed on what he has given now: his word, his people, the manna of each day’s grace. Remove what makes the road back easy. And look forward, as Moses did, to the reward (Hebrews 11:26). The longing for Egypt fades fastest when the heart is fixed on the promised land.

parallels.desc: make us gods who shall go before us

verseByVerse.quote: "And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: "'Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The works of their hands. This phrase helps explain why Stephen dies (Exodus 32:4–6). Its twin arrives at verse 48: the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. In the Greek Old Testament, made by hands is very largely a word for idols, the contemptuous term for things people carve and then bow down to (Isaiah 46:6).

The temple in the same category. So when Stephen applies it to the temple, a Jewish ear does not hear a remark about architecture. It hears the temple put into the same category as the golden calf. That is the offence. Even a God-given building can become an idol when it takes God’s place.

God gave them over. He did not strike them; he let them have it. Paul uses the language three times in Romans 1: God gave them up (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). From the inside it feels like nothing happening at all. A man insists on his idol, and God stops arguing with him.

Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? The clause that carries the rest of Stephen’s case, quoted from Amos (Amos 5:25). It is a rhetorical question, and an extraordinary thing to ask, because of course they did. The wilderness generation sacrificed constantly; the book of Leviticus is the paperwork for it. Amos is not denying that the ritual happened. He is denying that it arrived. This is religion as a bargain: doing the right things in God’s direction, so that God will owe us and leave us alone, while the heart stays with the calf. Forty years of offerings, and God asks whether one of them was ever truly brought to him.

Who is hearing this. Before the men who run the sacrificial system, Stephen puts the offerings themselves in question. And the question reaches anyone who does religious things: not whether the activity is happening, or correct, or sincere-feeling, but whether it is being brought to God or merely performed in his vicinity.

The one offering that arrived. The New Testament answers Amos’s question. It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). But one offering did arrive. Christ, through the eternal Spirit, offered himself without blemish to God (Hebrews 9:14), and God accepted it, as the empty tomb and the ascension declare. The men who run the altar have condemned the one sacrifice to which every altar pointed.

Could God give me over like that? If you are worried that he might, that worry is good evidence he has not. Those whom God gives over do not tremble about it; they rejoice in the works of their hands and want nothing more. The believer who sins and is grieved, who wants to be rid of his idol and cannot yet see how, is being pursued by God, not abandoned. God disciplines the children he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and his discipline hurts precisely because he has not let go. The danger is not in the struggle. It is in the settled, contented refusal to be turned. If you can still hear his objection to your idol, thank him, and listen.

For worship. The most terrible judgment is to be handed over to what we wanted. The wonder of the gospel is that God handed someone else over: he did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), so that people who had rejoiced in the works of their own hands might rejoice for ever in the work of his.

parallels.desc: did you bring me sacrifices forty years in the wilderness?
the host of heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "'You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tent of Moloch. Amos (5:26) means that Israel in the wilderness had two tents: the tent of witness, and the tent of Moloch, carried through the same camp by the same people. From the first generation the sanctuary had a rival in the baggage. And note again: the images that you made.

Who were Moloch and Rephan? Moloch (or Molech) was a pagan deity, named as the abomination of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:7) and notorious across the region for child sacrifice: children were made to pass through the fire to him (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 32:35). The tent of Moloch is a portable idol shrine carried in procession, a grim parody of the tabernacle. Rephan is the star of your god: an astral deity, probably the planet Saturn worshipped as a god. This is star worship, the bowing to the host of heaven that Scripture repeatedly condemns (Deuteronomy 4:19; 2 Kings 21:3–5).

An honest word on the names. Stephen is quoting the Greek Old Testament of Amos 5:25–27, and its wording differs from the Hebrew, which at this point is genuinely obscure. Where the Hebrew has Sikkuth and Kiyyun, probably names of Mesopotamian astral gods (Saturn again), the Greek rendered them Moloch and Rephan. So the exact identifications are the best scholarly reconstruction, not certainty; but the sense is plain, and it is Stephen’s point. Even in the wilderness, the very generation that carried God’s tabernacle was also carrying the shrines of pagan star gods.

Beyond Babylon. Amos wrote beyond Damascus; Stephen presses the prophecy to the exile that actually came. The land did not protect them, and Stephen places the court inside the same sentence.

Exile borne for us. The prophets also promised a return from exile, and the New Testament shows how God brings home a people who deserve to be sent away. Christ was cut off out of the land of the living (Isaiah 53:8), carrying the banishment that idolatry earns, so that those whose fathers had carried Moloch’s tent could be brought near.

Do people still worship Moloch and the stars? In other forms, yes. Moloch was the god to whom children were sacrificed for the sake of prosperity and security, and every age finds its own ways of sacrificing children to the adult’s comfort, career or convenience. The star of Rephan is the old ancestor of astrology, the belief that our lives are ruled by the heavens rather than by the God who made them. Horoscopes may seem harmless fun, but Scripture treats looking to the stars for guidance as turning from God (Isaiah 47:13–14). The Christian looks past the stars to their Maker, who calls them all by name (Isaiah 40:26), and who holds our times in his hand.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen quotes Amos from the Greek Old Testament; Moloch was the god of child sacrifice, and Rephan probably an astral god (Saturn). Amos said “beyond Damascus”; Stephen says “beyond Babylon,” where the exile actually went.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tent of witness. Stephen first defends the sanctuary: God ordered it. The tent of witness is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the law, the testimony (Exodus 25:16; Numbers 17:7). The fathers carried the tent of Moloch; God gave them the tent of witness.

A tent. Not a house: a tent, struck in a morning and standing by evening. The one dwelling God designed for himself was portable, its furniture fitted with rings for carrying poles.

According to the pattern. So even the tent was a copy, a model of something Moses was shown on the mountain (Exodus 25:40), a copy and shadow of heavenly realities (Hebrews 8:5). Hebrews says what it pointed to. Christ is a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man (Hebrews 8:2). He entered through the greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands, not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood, securing an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:11–12).

With Joshua. And it kept moving, to Gilgal, Shiloh, Nob and Gibeon. For Greek readers there is a glint of something more: the name Joshua in Greek is Jesus (Iēsous), which is why the KJV actually prints Jesus in this verse. The first Jesus brought the tent into the land; the second would bring the true dwelling of God among men.

Until the days of David. That is the hinge, and everything after it concerns what happened when somebody decided the arrangement ought to be permanent.

Then should churches not own buildings? They may, and many should; a building is a tool, and a good one. Stephen thought the tabernacle mattered enormously, and God designed it. The question is not whether a church has a building but whether it could lose one and still be a church. The early Christians met in homes, in rented halls (19:9) and in the open air, and the church grew. A congregation that would collapse if its building were taken away has put its weight on the wrong thing. Use your building gladly, keep it modest and useful, and keep your heart in the people and the word.
verseByVerse.note: The “tent of witness” is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: "who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A dwelling place for the God of Jacob. David comes off well (Psalm 132:5). He wanted to build God a house, having noticed he lived in cedar while the ark sat under canvas (2 Samuel 7:2), and Scripture never suggests the motive was wrong.

But it was Solomon. The little word but carries what God said through Nathan. Would you build me a house to dwell in? I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt, but I have been moving about in a tent. Did I ever ask any of the judges of Israel why they had not built me a house of cedar? (2 Samuel 7:5–7).

I will build you a house. When David offered, God turned the offer round. You will not build me a house; I will build you a house, a dynasty (2 Samuel 7:11–13). David offered God a building and God gave David a dynasty.

The greater Son of David. God promised David a son whose throne would be established for ever (2 Samuel 7:13). Solomon’s kingdom was torn in two soon after he died. The promise was waiting for a greater Son. The angel told Mary that the Lord God would give her child the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32–33). The house he builds is not cedar but living stones, his people (1 Peter 2:5). And the heir of that dynasty is the one these men had lately helped to nail to a cross outside the city wall.

Even the builder knew. None of which makes the temple illegitimate: God filled it with his glory, and Jesus called it his Father’s house. And the man who built it said at the dedication, before the whole nation, that heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built (1 Kings 8:27). Even the builder knew.

A short and nearly invisible step. David’s desire was good. But there is a step from I want to honour God with this to God requires this, and must be honoured here, and the step is short and very nearly invisible. A thousand years after Solomon, a man is on trial for his life because a building God never asked for had become the thing his people could not imagine him without.

How do I know whether my good plan for God is what he wants? Hold it with open hands, as David did. David told Nathan, and when God said no, he did not sulk; he sat before the LORD and gave thanks for what God would do instead (2 Samuel 7:18–29). So test your plan against Scripture, pray over it, ask the counsel of godly people, and watch how God opens or closes the way. Above all, notice if the plan has become something you cannot imagine God without. That is the sign a good desire is turning into an idol. God may give you something better than you asked: not the house you wanted to build him, but the house he builds you.

For worship. David wanted to do something for God, and God answered by doing something for David that made the offer look small: not a building for a season but a house for ever, a Son on the throne whose reign will not end. Every believer gathered into the house of David’s Son is part of the overflow.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Houses made by hands. Made by hands (cheiropoiētos), the idol word whose twin Stephen used of the golden calf (v. 41), is now fastened onto the temple. His point is not that the temple was wrong, but that treating it as the place where God was contained was idolatry. Paul says the same in Athens (17:24).

The Most High. The Most High is a title outsiders often use, from Melchizedek to a fortune-telling slave girl (Genesis 14:18–20; Acts 16:17): the God of Israel described from beyond the boundary, and exactly the right title for a speech about a God who declines to be kept inside one.

Heaven is my throne. So that nobody can accuse him of inventing the idea, he quotes Isaiah (Isaiah 66:1): God seated with the sky for a chair and the planet under his feet for a stool.

What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? Now, says the prophet, describe the building. Give the dimensions. Say where the resting place is to go. It is God asking a builder for a specification, and the question answers itself the moment anybody tries. No house can hold him. Now he dwells in Christ, the true temple (John 2:19–21), and in his people (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22).

The throne Stephen is about to see. Within minutes Stephen will look into that heaven and see who stands at the right hand of God (7:55–56). The man they condemned for threatening their temple is at the right hand of the only throne Isaiah says God has. No house can hold the Most High; but the Most High has a Son, and in him God came close enough to be crucified and has been raised high enough to rule.

The line he leaves out. His hearers knew the passage well enough to supply Isaiah’s very next sentence: but this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isaiah 66:2). So Isaiah does say where God dwells: not in a structure but in a certain sort of person. Stephen stops one line short, and the line describes precisely what the men in front of him are not. Many in the room would hear the missing sentence, which is worse.

If God is everywhere, why should I go to church? Because the church is not a building but a people, and God has promised to be present among his gathered people in a special way (Matthew 18:20; 1 Corinthians 14:25). Scripture commands us not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25), because we need the preached word, the Lord’s Supper, the prayers and the fellowship of the saints. You can pray alone anywhere, and you should. But the living stones are meant to be built together into one house, not scattered across the field. Going to church is not visiting God’s building; it is joining God’s temple.

parallels.desc: heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool

verseByVerse.quote: "'Did not my hand make all these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Did not my hand make all these things? Eight words close the argument (Isaiah 66:2). The temple was built by human hands, and human hands were made by God. The stone came out of ground he made, cut by men whose lungs he kept full while they worked. A man cannot house his maker in materials his maker supplied. The Creator cannot be confined by what creatures make.

A question to end on. Stephen ends with a question: the last thing the council hears before he turns and faces them is God’s own voice asking whether they had ever stopped to consider who made the quarry.

A question to put to oneself. It is possible to know perfectly well that God is not contained in a building and to have quietly relocated him somewhere just as manageable: a style of service, an hour of the week, a way of feeling when the music is right. The test is what a man would have left if the thing were taken away.

What does it mean to tremble at God’s word? Not to be terrified of the Bible, but to take it with utter seriousness, as the voice of the living God. The one who trembles at God’s word lets it correct him rather than correcting it. He reads it expecting to be addressed, obeys what it says even when it costs, and is moved by its promises as well as its warnings. Josiah tore his clothes when he heard the law read (2 Kings 22:11–19), and God looked on him with favour. Trembling at the word is the opposite of the council’s stopped ears. It is a soft heart that hears God speaking and bows.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The defence becomes a charge. Stephen tells the council that they resist the Holy Spirit as their fathers did, and that they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One whom the prophets foretold. Furious, they rush at him, and he sees heaven opened and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. They stone him outside the city, and he dies praying for them. A young man named Saul looks after the coats.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stephen and the pattern of martyrdom

The Greek word for a witness is martys, and it came to mean someone killed for the faith only after enough witnesses had been. Stephen’s death has the shape the church has recognised ever since: the truth told without softening, Christ seen at the moment of dying, the killers prayed for. It earns nothing: Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit, so the courage, the vision and the forgiveness were all given to him. And martyrdom is nowhere in the New Testament something to be sought. Stephen did not go looking for it. He was preaching, and it was done to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's last recorded words asked that God not hold this sin against the men throwing the stones. A few feet away, minding their coats and approving of the execution, stood the man who never, to the end of his life, stopped mentioning that he had been there (22:20; 26:10). Now: The church lost its most gifted man and gained nothing visible; the persecution that followed scattered most of the Jerusalem church; and between them those two disasters put the gospel into Samaria, into Antioch and eventually into Rome. It is worth remembering on a day when a loss looks total.

verseByVerse.quote: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You stiff-necked people. The turn lies in a single pronoun. Again and again Stephen has said our fathers, arguing as a member of the household. Now he says your fathers, and says it again in the next verse. The defence has become a prosecution.

A farming word. Three charges, each a quotation. Stiff-necked describes an ox that sets its neck against the driver’s hand: not bolting, simply refusing. It is the word God himself used of Israel at Sinai after the golden calf (Exodus 32:9; 33:3, 5).

Uncircumcised in heart and ears. To that audience this is a cutting insult: telling circumcised men, in the covenant’s own vocabulary, that the mark cut into their bodies never reached the place it pointed to. And it is not his coinage: Moses and Jeremiah said it (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 9:26), and the Scriptures do the accusing. Their fault was this: they carried the outward sign of belonging to God, but what they loved and chose had never been given to him, and their ears took in his words without ever letting them in.

You always resist the Holy Spirit. To resist is to shove back against something coming toward you. The Spirit is the one who spoke through the prophets, against whom Israel rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit (Isaiah 63:10). And always is the sting: a habit running from the wilderness into this room.

The Spirit of Christ in the prophets. Whom were they resisting? Peter says that the Spirit who spoke through the prophets was the Spirit of Christ in them, predicting the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow (1 Peter 1:10–11). So to resist the Spirit in Moses and the prophets was already to resist Christ, and when the Son came, anointed with that same Spirit (Luke 4:18), the old resistance found its final object.

A word of care. Sentences like this have been used as a weapon against Jewish people for the better part of two thousand years, and that must be named. This is a Jew, in the Jewish council, quoting Moses and the prophets, saying to the leadership of his own nation what Isaiah and Jeremiah had said to the leadership of theirs. It is prophetic speech inside a family. A man does not get to borrow Stephen’s sentence unless he is standing where Stephen was standing, and almost nobody who has quoted it has been.

If the Spirit can be resisted, is grace not irresistible after all? Both truths are taught in Scripture, and they fit. The Spirit’s outward call through the preaching of the word comes to many, and those left to themselves resist it, always, as Stephen says; that is what fallen hearts do. But when God effectually calls his elect, he does not merely invite; he gives a new heart that gladly comes (Ezekiel 36:26; John 6:44; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.1 and the Westminster Confession 10.1). This is what is meant by an effectual call: a call that does what it says, as the voice of Jesus at the tomb brought Lazarus out alive (John 11:43–44). The resistance is real, and God overcomes it, not by forcing an unwilling man but by making him willing. The proof is standing at the edge of this very scene, holding coats. Saul resisted the Spirit as hard as any man in Jerusalem, until the risen Christ called him by name, and he could resist no longer.

On a Tuesday. The resistance Stephen names is the ordinary daily possibility of setting the neck against something true from God. Is there a word of God you are resisting? Ask the Spirit who raised Jesus, and now lives in you, to soften your neck, and listen, today. And if that question troubles you, take heart: the trouble is itself the Spirit at work, for a hardened neck does not worry about being stiff.
verseByVerse.note: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears” is the prophets’ language for stubborn refusal to listen.

parallels.desc: a stiff-necked people

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? A question with no available answer. Jeremiah was imprisoned and dropped into a cistern; Isaiah, by tradition, was sawn in two; Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:21). It was not the pagans who did it: the men who suffered most at Israel’s hands were the men God sent to Israel. Jesus had said the same (Matthew 23:29–37; Luke 11:47–51).

The Righteous One. The Righteous One is the title Peter used in the temple courts (3:14), the one Paul will hear applied to Jesus at his conversion (22:14), and it reaches back to the righteous Servant of Isaiah (Isaiah 53:11). The supreme court of the nation is told that it condemned the one genuinely innocent man in its history.

Betrayed and murdered. The Greek calls them betrayers and murderers: nouns hung round their necks as titles.

Did not keep it. On trial for speaking against the law, Stephen closes by saying that it came to them by the hand of angels, an honour he praised at verse 38, and that they broke it. He never denies the charge; he changes who is being examined.

The most conservative accusation. He does not say the law is finished: they had it and did not do it, the most conservative accusation available and the hardest to answer. The last word on the law of the first Christian to die for the faith was not an attack on Israel’s Scriptures but a charge that Israel’s leaders had not obeyed them.

Was Stephen being unloving? No. Love sometimes has to say the hardest thing, and Stephen said it as a member of the family, in the words of the family’s own prophets, to people he wanted to see saved. His last breath proves it: he prayed for these very men. The prophets spoke like this because they loved Israel, and Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the same week he pronounced its judgment (Luke 19:41–44). We should be slow to imitate Stephen’s sharpness, because we rarely have his clarity, his Spirit-filled courage or his love. But when the truth must be spoken, it is not unloving to speak it plainly, as long as we would gladly die for the people we are speaking to.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ground their teeth. The council is enraged, the word Luke used at 5:33 of this same body hearing Peter: cut to the quick, sawn through. Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury (Psalm 35:16; 37:12), and Jesus uses the phrase of the lost in outer darkness (Matthew 8:12). Fury has gone past words.

He gazed into heaven. While they glare at him, he looks up with the fixed gaze (atenizō) the council turned on him in 6:15, and what he is looking at is not in the room.

Full of the Holy Spirit. Luke has used the phrase of Stephen before (6:3, 5). At this moment it brings two things. First, sight: the Spirit gives eyes for the unseen, for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:10). Second, strength for the supreme test, so that he dies like his Lord, committing his spirit to Jesus and forgiving his killers. It is what Jesus promised witnesses dragged before councils: the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say (Luke 12:11–12). Luke does not say Stephen was filled afresh (as Peter in 4:8) but that he was full: the settled state carries him through.

The glory of God. The God of glory who appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia (v. 2) now appears to the first martyr in Jerusalem, and in the middle of the glory stands a man, Jesus, at God’s right hand, the place of honour and power.

Can I be filled with the Spirit? Yes; every Christian is commanded to be: do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). The tense of the verb suggests keep on being filled. It is not a one-off experience for the spiritual elite, but the ordinary Christian life lived under the Spirit’s control. And its truest evidence is not ecstatic feeling but a man who sees Christ clearly and lives and dies like Christ graciously. Paul follows the command with singing, thanksgiving and humble submission to one another (Ephesians 5:19–21). So ask God for it daily, feed on his word, confess sin quickly, and obey what you know. The Spirit did not spare Stephen the stones. He filled him to face them.
verseByVerse.note: Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I see the heavens opened. As at Jesus’ baptism (Luke 3:21), the barrier is drawn back, and a dying man is allowed to see.

The Son of Man. Two things are extraordinary, and the first is the title. Son of Man is how Jesus habitually spoke of himself, and outside the Gospels almost nobody else uses it. Stephen calls Jesus what Jesus called himself, before the very council to which Jesus had said: from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God (Luke 22:69). Stephen says: I see him. They have now heard the claim twice, before the same council, and the second time they do not wait for a verdict.

Standing. The second is the posture. Elsewhere Christ at the Father’s right hand is seated. Psalm 110 says sit, and Hebrews builds an argument on the fact that this priest sat down, because his work was finished (Hebrews 10:12). Stephen sees him standing. Why? Perhaps to welcome his servant home; or as a witness standing to testify for him in the heavenly court, as Stephen testifies for him on earth; or as a judge rising to pass sentence. All may be true.

Two courts. Two courts are sitting that day. In the lower one a man is tried on the evidence of witnesses put up to lie, the outcome settled before he opened his mouth. In the higher one, as the accused is about to be condemned, his advocate rises to his feet. Jesus had promised it in Luke’s first volume: everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God (Luke 12:8). Stephen is acknowledging him before men at the highest cost, and Luke shows the promise being kept while it is still being paid for.

The court at three in the morning. Most Christians will never stand before a council, and will nevertheless be judged: by an employer, a family, a country, or their own conscience convening a court at three in the morning with the evidence stacked and no defence prepared. This verse says there is another court in session, and it never lets the testimony go unanswered. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Christ Jesus is the one who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us (Romans 8:33–34). To justify is a courtroom word: God the Judge declares the sinner righteous, because Christ has borne his sin and Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Will I see heaven opened when I die? Scripture does not promise every believer a vision like Stephen’s, and many faithful Christians die without one, some peacefully and some in confusion or pain. What it promises is better than a vision: presence. To depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23); to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Whether your eyes see anything at the end or not, the Lord Jesus will be there to receive you. Stephen was allowed to see beforehand what every believer will see immediately afterwards.

For worship. The Son of Man whom the council condemned is the one to whom the Ancient of Days has given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him, with a dominion that will never pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). The council had the last word on earth for about an hour. And the King of that everlasting kingdom is on his feet for one servant about to die outside Jerusalem, because no one who confesses him is too small for him to rise for.
verseByVerse.note: Elsewhere the Son of Man is seated at God’s right hand; here he stands — perhaps to welcome Stephen or to plead as his witness.
