parallels.desc: I will acknowledge him before the angels of God

verseByVerse.quote: But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They stopped their ears. The most dignified men in the nation, with their fingers in their ears, shouting so as not to hear. It is the exact fulfilment of Stephen’s charge six verses earlier: he said they were uncircumcised in their ears, and they stopped them with their hands.

With one accord. With one accord (homothymadon) is the word Luke used of the church’s unity, with one accord in prayer and in the temple (1:14; 2:46). Now it describes a mob’s rage. There is a unity of the Spirit, and there is a unity of the mob, and they look alike for a moment from a distance.

Why would learned men refuse even to listen? Because to listen was to lose too much. Their standing, their power and their whole religious identity rested on being right about God, and to hear Stephen out was to admit that they had handed God’s Messiah to death. It is easier to stop your ears than to lose yourself. Every heart has the same reflex when the truth threatens what it lives for. Yet the grace of this chapter reaches even here: the young man holding the coats had his ears stopped as firmly as any, and Christ opened them.

A lynching by a court. No verdict, no sentence, no vote; they simply rushed at him. Rome reserved capital punishment (John 18:31), so it was probably a lynching. Luke is describing a proceeding that had stopped being a proceeding.

Out of the city. Yet they cast him out of the city, because the law required a stoning to take place outside the camp (Leviticus 24:14). They keep the geography of Leviticus and abandon everything else in it.

Outside the gate with his Lord. Jesus had been led out of Jerusalem to die, suffering outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12), and false witnesses had stood up at his trial too (Mark 14:56–57). Stephen’s death has the shape of his Master’s because he belongs to him. But the likeness stops at the decisive point. Stephen’s blood sanctifies no one. He goes outside the camp bearing the reproach that Christ endured (Hebrews 13:13), because Christ had already gone there bearing his sin.

The witnesses laid down their garments. The law of Moses required that in a stoning the witnesses throw first (Deuteronomy 17:7), so that any man who had sworn a life away had to be the one to take it. These are the planted witnesses of chapter 6: the men who lied about Stephen are the men who killed him with their own hands, and they took their coats off in order to do it properly.

At the feet of a young man named Saul. With no introduction, Luke brings in the most important man of his second half. A young man (neanias), minding the coats: the respectable part, the part that gets no blood on it, the part a man can afterwards tell himself was not really participation. Paul never let it go (22:20; 26:10). Every man who threw a stone is anonymous. The one Luke names is holding the coats.

Is holding the coats really so bad? Yes, and that is why Paul never forgot it. Most of us will never throw a stone, but most of us have held a coat: laughed along with the cruel joke, stayed silent while someone was slandered, approved in our hearts what we would never have done with our hands. Scripture treats approval as participation; Paul says those who give approval to evil share in its guilt (Romans 1:32). The good news is in the same verse. The man who held the coats became the apostle who wrote, Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost (1 Timothy 1:15). There is forgiveness for the coat-holders too.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning took place outside the city; the witnesses threw the first stones. This is the first mention of Saul, later Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Two prayers. The first is for himself, and it is a quotation. Psalm 31:5 says into your hand I commit my spirit, and it is addressed to God. Jesus prayed it from the cross, addressed to the Father: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46). Stephen prays it to Jesus.

Dying on the assumption of his deity. A Jewish man, being killed for blasphemy by the highest religious authority in Israel, spends the last moments of his life praying a psalm addressed to the God of Israel, and addresses it to Jesus of Nazareth. He is not arguing for the deity of Christ; he is dying on the assumption of it, treating Jesus as God, the one into whose keeping a human spirit goes, though Scripture says the spirit returns to God who gave it (Ecclesiastes 12:7). No faithful Jew would commend his soul to a mere creature.

Falling to his knees. A man under a hail of stones does not kneel by accident. He knelt because he was going to pray.

Lord, do not hold this sin against them. The request for his own soul was spoken; the request for his murderers was shouted. He spent his last breath on the men who were taking it. It is Jesus again: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). (Those words of Jesus are missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, but many scholars judge them genuine and most Bibles print them.)

The order reversed. Jesus prayed first for his killers and then committed his spirit; Stephen reverses the order. The first Christian death is shaped like Christ’s, with the sequence turned round.

What it does not mean. This verse has been used to lay a burden Scripture does not lay. It is not a rule that a Christian must feel forgiving at the moment of injury, or that failure to produce this prayer at the graveside of a murdered child is a failure of faith. Luke has already told us where it came from: Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit. The forgiveness in this verse is not an achievement modelled for imitation by willpower. It is a gift being reported. What is asked of ordinary Christians is that they should want to get there, and be willing to be taken there slowly, which for most people is the work of years and not of minutes.

Must I forgive someone who is not sorry? Stephen prayed for men who were still throwing stones, so the heart of forgiveness does not wait for an apology. It lets go of revenge, hands the wrong to God, and genuinely desires the other person’s good, even their salvation (Romans 12:17–21). But full reconciliation, the restoring of trust and relationship, does require repentance (Luke 17:3–4), and forgiveness never means pretending a wrong was not wrong, or staying exposed to someone dangerous, or not reporting a crime. You can forgive an abuser in your heart and still go to the police. Begin, as Stephen did, by praying for them. The feelings often follow the prayers, slowly.

He fell asleep. A gentle verb for a violent death, and neither euphemism nor sentiment. It is the New Testament’s word for the death of believers (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 1 Corinthians 15:18, 20), a statement about what death now is for those who belong to Christ: sleep, from which the body will wake in resurrection.

Does fell asleep mean the soul is unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes the body, which lies in the grave and will be woken. Stephen’s spirit did not sleep. He had just prayed, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, and the Lord did. Jesus promised the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Paul says that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). The souls of believers at death are made perfect in holiness and pass immediately into glory, while their bodies rest in their graves until the resurrection (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1; Westminster Confession 32.1).

The prayer answered. Stephen asked that this sin not be held against them. A few feet away, holding the coats and approving, stood a young man who would be struck down on the road to Damascus, would one day call himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15), and would write more of the New Testament’s letters than any other man. Augustine is said to have put it this way: if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul. The prayer was answered first in the man who would have been the last to expect it.

In the flow. Stephen’s death closes the Jerusalem chapters of Acts, and Luke at once tells us what God does with it: the persecution that follows scatters the believers, and they preach the word as they go, first in Judea and Samaria (8:1, 4), exactly the next steps Jesus named in 1:8. The stones meant to stop the word are the means of its spread.

On a Tuesday. Learn to die as Stephen did: each night as you lie down, commend your spirit to the Lord Jesus, so that when the last night comes, the words are already familiar.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen’s last words echo Jesus’ words on the cross. “Fell asleep” is the Christian way of speaking of a believer’s death.

7.theology: Rejected, then vindicated. Stephen’s survey shows a pattern in God’s ways: the one God sends is rejected first. Joseph, Moses, the prophets and at last the Righteous One himself were refused, and each time God vindicated the rejected one and used the rejection to rescue his people. It is the pattern of the cross, and Stephen shares it. He is killed by men and received by Christ, and his prayer is answered in the conversion of the young man who watched him die.
7.examples:
Then: Stephen stands before the council in Jerusalem and preaches to them from their own history.

Now: Where Christians cannot be answered by argument, they are sometimes silenced by force. Stephen did not meet that day in his own strength. Full of the Holy Spirit, he looked up, saw Christ, commended his spirit to him and prayed for his killers. The same Spirit is given to every believer, and the same Lord stands at God’s right hand for them.

8.title: The Scattered Gospel
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. <sup>2</sup>Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. <sup>3</sup>But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. <sup>4</sup>Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. <sup>5</sup>Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. <sup>6</sup>And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. <sup>7</sup>For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. <sup>8</sup>So there was much joy in that city. <sup>9</sup>But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. <sup>10</sup>They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” <sup>11</sup>And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. <sup>12</sup>But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. <sup>13</sup>Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. <sup>14</sup>Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, <sup>15</sup>who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, <sup>16</sup>for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>17</sup>Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. <sup>18</sup>Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, <sup>19</sup>saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” <sup>20</sup>But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! <sup>21</sup>You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. <sup>22</sup>Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. <sup>23</sup>For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.” <sup>24</sup>And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” <sup>25</sup>Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. <sup>26</sup>Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. <sup>27</sup>And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship <sup>28</sup>and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. <sup>29</sup>And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” <sup>30</sup>So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” <sup>31</sup>And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. <sup>32</sup>Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. <sup>33</sup>In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.” <sup>34</sup>And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” <sup>35</sup>Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. <sup>36</sup>And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” <sup>38</sup>And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. <sup>39</sup>And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. <sup>40</sup>But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
8.overview:
Stephen’s death sets off the first great persecution, led by Saul, and the scattered believers preach wherever they go. So the second stage of Jesus’ plan in 1:8 begins: Judea and Samaria. The Samaritans claimed the God of Israel but kept only the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim, and Jews and Samaritans had despised each other for centuries (John 4:9). Philip, one of the seven, preaches Christ there, and many believe, including a magician named Simon. The Spirit is given when Peter and John come and lay hands on the new believers, a sign that Samaritans and Jews are one church, and when Simon tries to buy that power, Peter calls him to repent.

Then an angel sends Philip to a desert road, where an Ethiopian official, a eunuch returning from worship in Jerusalem, is reading Isaiah 53. Philip begins with that passage and tells him about Jesus, baptises him at the roadside, and is taken away. The Ethiopian goes home rejoicing, and the gospel is already on its way to the end of the earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Persecution, Scattering, and the Gospel in Samaria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The persecution that begins with Stephen’s death scatters the church, and Saul goes from house to house arresting believers. Philip takes the gospel to Samaria, where signs and great joy follow. Peter and John come from Jerusalem and lay hands on the Samaritans, who receive the Spirit, and when Simon offers money for the same power, Peter tells him that God’s gift cannot be bought.
verseByVerse.theology:
The scattering as mission

God’s purposes are not only unharmed by human wickedness but advanced through it. Jesus had said the witness would go to Judea and Samaria (1:8), and so far the church had stayed in the city. It took a murder and a persecution to send it out. That does not mean the suffering was anything less than real: Luke records men weeping loudly over a grave in the same breath. It means that the man leading the destruction was, without knowing it, spreading the gospel across two regions.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jews had no dealings with Samaritans, and the quarrel was not a misunderstanding: it had a ruined temple on Mount Gerizim in it, pulled down by a Jewish army. The gospel crossed that line before anybody had written a word of argument about whether it should. Now: The barrier a congregation is least likely to cross is never the one it debates. It is the one it has stopped noticing, because everyone it knows is on the same side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 8 is the turning point when the gospel leaves Jerusalem. Persecution scatters the church, and the scattered believers carry the gospel to the half-Jewish Samaritans and then to an African official, as Jesus said it would go (1:8). The chapter that opens with a grave ends with a man going home rejoicing.

Saul approved. The chapter division cuts a sentence in half: this line is Luke’s last word on the stoning. The young man holding the coats was not a bystander. The word (syneudokōn) means he consented, thought well of it, was pleased; and Paul spends the rest of his life saying so, with shame (22:20).

A great persecution. On that day. Stephen’s death was the starting gun of the first general persecution, aimed probably at the Hellenists, Stephen’s circle. Once somebody had been killed and nothing happened to the killers, the restraint was gone.

All scattered, except the apostles. The church had not left Jerusalem by choice; God used persecution to push them out. The word for scattered (diesparēsan) is built on the verb for sowing: seed thrown across a field. Yet the twelve, already arrested twice and flogged once, stayed in the city everybody else was fleeing; Luke does not say why. The consequence is clear: the people who took the gospel to Samaria were not the apostles but the ordinary members who ran.

Devout men buried Stephen. The burial is braver than it looks. Jewish law as later recorded in the Mishnah withheld public mourning from a man executed by the court, and the custom was probably older. These men did the opposite, loudly, on the day a persecution began. They may have been believers, or devout Jews who would not let the man be shovelled away. Either way, somebody with something to lose stood at that grave and wept aloud on purpose.

Grief is not a lapse. Christians are sometimes given the impression that a believer with a firm grasp of the resurrection should bury somebody without much noise. The first Christian response to the first Christian martyrdom was a great lamentation, and Luke records it without a word of correction. Paul tells a grieving church not that they should not grieve but that they should not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Jesus himself wept at a graveside he was about to empty (John 11:35).

The Lord who stood for Stephen. Stephen’s last sight on earth was the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (7:56), and what follows is not the collapse of Christ’s cause but its next step: on the day of the first martyr’s death he begins to send his witnesses out, using the stones as his means. Luke also shapes the burial to recall another, when a good and righteous man laid in a tomb a body the council had condemned (Luke 23:50–53). The servant is buried as his Master was. But the Master’s tomb was empty on the third day, and that is why devout men can weep loudly over Stephen and still not weep without hope.

Why does God allow his church to be persecuted? Scripture gives us part of the answer, though not all of it. Persecution purifies the church, as fire refines gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). It joins us to Christ, who was persecuted first (John 15:20; Philippians 3:10). And, as here, God uses it to spread the gospel: the seed is scattered and grows in new fields. Tertullian’s old saying, that the blood of the martyrs is seed, could have been written over this verse. None of that makes persecution good, and we should pray for persecuted believers and work for their relief (Hebrews 13:3). But it means that no persecution is outside God’s purpose or beyond his power to turn to good.
verseByVerse.note: The scattering fulfils Jesus’ plan in 1:8: Judea and Samaria come next.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ravaging the church. Luke picks a violent word deliberately. Ravaging (elymaineto) is the word the Greek psalm uses of a wild boar getting into a vineyard and wrecking it (Psalm 80:13), ruining in an afternoon what took years to grow. Saul later admitted it all, calling himself a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent (22:4; 1 Timothy 1:13).

House after house. There were no church buildings; the church met in people’s homes. So persecuting the church meant going through front doors: men coming into a kitchen where a family has been praying, and taking people out of it, women too. Dragged off is the word Luke will later use of Paul himself being dragged out of a city and left for dead (14:19).

Every door he broke was Christ’s. Saul thought he was clearing heretics out of Israel’s vineyard. In fact he was laying hands on the Lord himself, who will ask him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (9:4). The Lord counts his people’s injuries as his own. And the psalm whose word Luke borrowed already pointed to the remedy: after the boar has ravaged the vine, Israel prays, let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself (Psalm 80:17). Stephen had just seen that Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. The vine had a keeper, and the ravager was about to meet him.

Zeal without God. Saul was not irreligious. He did all this out of zeal for God, as blameless as a man could be in keeping the law (Philippians 3:6). That is the warning for religious people: when religion becomes a way of proving that we are the righteous ones, it can make us hard and even cruel, certain that we are serving God while we are fighting him. Saul’s cure was not more zeal. It was meeting the Lord he was persecuting, and learning that his own righteousness was loss compared with knowing Christ (Philippians 3:7–9).

Grace did not give him amnesia. The man who went door to door arresting mothers later wrote that love is patient and kind (1 Corinthians 13:4). Some thirty years on he still calls himself the foremost of sinners, in the present tense (1 Timothy 1:15). Grace did not erase his memory. It let him carry an accurate, unbearable memory without despair, which is more remarkable than forgetting.

Not a guarantee. Saul’s story is no pledge that every persecutor will be converted; most of the men who arrested Christians in the first century, as far as we know, died as they had lived. It is a demonstration that nobody is disqualified by the record, which is what Paul himself says it was given for: that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16).

How should I pray for those who persecute Christians today? As Jesus told us: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44). Pray for their conversion, by name if you know them, remembering Saul. Pray that God would restrain their violence and protect his people (4:29–30). Pray for justice, for governments to protect religious freedom, and for persecuted believers to stand firm and be comforted. It is not wrong to ask God to stop evil men, as the psalmists did. But let the first prayer be Stephen’s: Lord, do not hold this sin against them. God has answered that prayer before.

verseByVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. The scattering that looked like defeat is the next stage of the plan Jesus gave in 1:8. Stephen had just argued that God was never confined to one building or one land (7:48–50), and the scattered church now proves the point on foot. Luke will open the next great advance with the same words (11:19).

The ordinary word. The verb Luke chooses (euangelizomenoi) is not the herald’s word, which he uses of Philip in the next verse, but the word for telling good news. When people in strange towns asked why they had left Jerusalem, they told them. The first missionary expansion of the church was carried out by amateurs, under duress, with no strategy, because they could not stop talking about the reason they had been driven out.

Philip went down. This Philip is one of the seven (6:5), not the apostle: one of the men appointed to make sure the widows were fed. It is the table-servants who are breaking the boundaries in this book while the apostles hold the centre.

A feud centuries old. Samaria was not simply an unevangelised region. After Assyria deported the northern tribes, it resettled the land with foreign peoples, and the mixed population claimed the God of Israel, kept only the five books of Moses, and worshipped at a rival temple on Mount Gerizim (2 Kings 17:24–41), which a Jewish army had pulled down about a hundred and fifty years before. Calling a man a Samaritan was an insult (John 8:48).

Proclaimed to them the Christ. Philip walks into that, and he preaches a person. He does not open with an argument about which mountain was the right one or whose copy of the law was correct. The Samaritans expected a Messiah too, the restorer (John 4:25), and Philip tells them he has come. The quarrel that centuries of argument had not settled was left where it was, and something was announced that made it irrelevant.

Am I meant to share my faith if I am not a pastor? Yes. The people in this verse had no office at all, and they spread the gospel across two regions. Pastors are called to preach and teach publicly, and that is a particular calling (Ephesians 4:11). But every Christian is a witness to what Christ has done, and every Christian can tell someone why he believes. You do not need to preach a sermon. You need to be ready to give a reason for your hope when asked, gently and respectfully (1 Peter 3:15), to invite people to hear the word, and to speak naturally of Christ in the places where life has put you. The gospel has always travelled furthest in ordinary conversations.
verseByVerse.note: This Philip is one of the seven, not the apostle. Samaritans were a mixed people despised by Jews; they also expected a coming deliverer.

parallels.desc: Philip the evangelist

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With one accord. It is the phrase Luke used of the disciples praying in the upper room (1:14), now used of a crowd of Samaritans, a small shock deliberately given. And the signs are in the sentence in second place. The miracles got Philip a hearing; the message held the crowd.

Unclean spirits. Unclean spirits are demons, and here they cry out as they did before Jesus (Mark 1:26). The list ties Samaria to Jerusalem on purpose: spirits coming out, the paralysed and the lame healed, chronic and visible ailments a whole town could verify (3:1–10), now in a despised city through a man appointed to hand out bread. There is no reduced edition of the kingdom for people on the wrong side of a border.

Many, not all. One small honesty in the wording belongs to anybody who has prayed a long time and not been healed. Even at the height of an outpouring, Luke writes that unclean spirits came out of many, and that many were healed, a word that may leave somebody still on the mat. He does not explain it and he does not hide it.

The lame walk. These are not random wonders. When John the Baptist asked from prison whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus pointed to exactly these things: the lame walk (Luke 7:22), as Isaiah had said when God came to save, the lame man would leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:4–6). So when paralysed Samaritans stand up under Philip’s preaching, the answer Jesus gave John is being given again. The healer has gone up to heaven, and his work goes on in Samaria under his name (1:1).

Philip was not an apostle, so why could he do signs? Like Stephen, he was one of the seven on whom the apostles had laid their hands (6:6), and his signs belong to the same founding ministry. Even so, the Samaritans received the Spirit only when the apostles came (vv. 14–17), which shows how closely these gifts were tied to the apostles. On the cessationist reading, held charitably, such sign gifts belonged to the foundation age and are not a standing pattern for today. The reason is that the New Testament ties such signs to the apostles’ founding witness (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, often called continuationists, believe these gifts continue today, and they are brothers to be loved, not dismissed. God still heals in answer to prayer; what has ceased is the apostolic sign gift attesting new revelation.

Why does God not heal everyone I pray for? Scripture does not give us a full explanation, and we should beware of anyone who claims to. It is not because your faith was too small; Paul prayed three times for his own thorn to be removed, and God said no, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God heals some now as a foretaste of the new creation, and he will heal all his people in the resurrection, when there will be no more pain (Revelation 21:4). Until then, keep praying, use the means he gives, and trust that his no is never a lack of love.

For worship. In the city Jerusalem despised, men carried for years on mats walked home, and the demons went out shrieking at the name of Jesus. That name has lost none of its authority. The King who healed many in Samaria has promised a day when those of every century who prayed and still sat on the mat will rise whole, to walk with him in a city with no sickbed in it.

verseByVerse.quote: So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So there was much joy in that city. Joy in a city, not merely in individuals: something had changed in the public atmosphere of the place (13:52; 16:34). Luke will use the same note at the end of this chapter of a single man on a desert road, the same fact at a different scale.

A man named Simon. Luke introduces the man who will show what the gospel is not. Magic (mageuōn) was not entertainment or conjuring. A practitioner claimed real access to powers, and people paid him for results: a curse on a rival, a charm against illness. The man who could operate that machinery was feared, consulted and rich. Later Christian writers regarded this Simon, often called Simon Magus, as the father of heresies, and Justin Martyr, himself born in Samaria, wrote that the Samaritans honoured him as the first god.

Somebody great. Luke’s summary of Simon’s message is telling. That is the entire content. Not a doctrine, not a God, not a promise: a claim about the speaker. Everything Simon offered was ultimately about Simon. Few of us have ever claimed to be the power of God, but the craving underneath is common: to be admired, to be thought somebody. Christ frees us from it, because the one who matters most has already loved us at our worst, and we have nothing left to prove (Romans 5:8; Galatians 1:10).

The one who is great. Simon’s claim has an answer in the one Philip preached. Luke recorded an angel’s word about Mary’s son: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High (Luke 1:32). The greatness Simon claimed for himself God had already given to someone else, and the one who truly is great said, I am among you as the one who serves (Luke 22:27), and the next day died for the people he served. Simon took a city’s worship and gave it nothing. Christ takes nothing from us and gives himself.

The test of a ministry. The collision is not between power and no power; Philip has just been healing paralytics. The difference is what the power points at. Simon amazed people, and they concluded that Simon was great. Philip did signs, and the crowds ended up listening to a message about somebody else. The test in any century is what the watchers end up attached to. If a ministry produces crowds who are knowledgeable about the minister, something has gone wrong that no orthodox statement of faith will correct.

Is magic real, and is it harmless to dabble? Scripture treats sorcery and the occult as real and as forbidden, not as harmless fun (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Galatians 5:20). Some of it is trickery and some of it may involve real spiritual powers, and both are dangerous: the one deceives, the other enslaves. So a Christian should have nothing to do with fortune-telling, séances, spells, tarot or any attempt to gain hidden knowledge or power apart from God. If you have been involved, confess it, renounce it, get rid of the objects, as the Ephesians burned their magic books (19:19), and rest in Christ, who has disarmed every power (Colossians 2:15). You do not need to be afraid. You need to be finished with it.
verseByVerse.note: Later Christian writers regarded this Simon (often called Simon Magus) as an early false teacher; from his name comes “simony,” the buying of church office.

verseByVerse.quote: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the least to the greatest. The whole social range: the labourer and the magistrate, the servant girl and her mistress. Simon’s hold was not confined to the credulous poor, the comforting assumption people make about this kind of thing. It reached the top.

The power of God that is called Great. The odd, half-technical phrase shows that Simon had supplied the city with a theology: they thought him a divine power flowing out from God. He was not a street performer but a religious institution with a creed.

For a long time. Luke gives the mechanism, and neither ingredient is truth: amazement, and the sheer weight of years in which everybody grew up with it. That is how most religious authority that does not come from God keeps its hold. Nobody has to be persuaded of anything, only unable to explain what is happening, for long enough that it becomes normal.

The stronger man. Jesus once described his own work in words that fit this city: when one stronger than the armed strong man attacks and overcomes him, he takes away the armour he trusted in and divides the spoil (Luke 11:21–22). Samaria had been held a long time by fear and wonder. Jesus does not send a cleverer magician against those powers. He comes in his word, by an ordinary preacher, and takes his spoil: men and women set free and baptised into his name.

How was anyone to tell the difference? That raises the question a reader is entitled to ask, since Philip’s ministry looks, from outside, remarkably similar: crowds, signs, amazement. Luke’s answer is not about the phenomena. The Samaritans turned when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Simon offered an experience and a claim about himself; Philip offered a message about a King, and people believed it. The signs got him a hearing. The content held them, and the content was somebody else’s name. Signs alone do not prove truth; the message must be tested (Deuteronomy 13:1–3).

Can Satan really do miracles? Scripture warns that he can produce counterfeit signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9; Revelation 13:13; Matthew 24:24), though his power is limited and always under God’s control (Job 1:12). That is why a miracle is never enough by itself to prove a message true. Moses told Israel that if a prophet gave a sign that came to pass but led them to other gods, they were not to listen (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). So the question to ask of any wonder is not merely whether something happened, but what it is being used to teach, and whether it leads you to the Christ of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they believed Philip. What displaces Simon is not a stronger performance. A city held for years by amazement is released by a message, given in two phrases: the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ.

What is it to preach the kingdom of God? The kingdom is God’s saving reign, his kingly rule breaking in through Jesus the Messiah to rescue and to rule. Philip preached the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ in one breath: you cannot proclaim the kingdom without the King. To preach it is to announce that God’s long-promised reign has arrived in Christ, who died, rose and reigns, and to call people to repent, believe and bow to him as Lord, entering his kingdom now and for ever (28:31). Why is the phrase on page after page of Matthew, Mark and Luke, and rare in John and the letters? Not because the truth fades, but because the vocabulary shifts. Jesus preached the kingdom to Jewish hearers, steeped in Israel’s hope (Matthew 4:17; Daniel 7:13–14). John says the same thing with a different word, eternal life (John 3:3, 5). The apostles, writing after the resurrection, put the focus on the reigning King: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9). Same kingdom throughout.

Both men and women. They believed, then were baptised, the order this commentary follows (see vv. 36–38). And both men and women: in a world where a woman’s religious standing often travelled through her husband, Luke records the women being baptised on their own faith.

Even Simon himself believed. Luke states it without qualification: he believed, he was baptised, he attached himself to the preacher. A reading which has Simon play-acting from the start reads something Luke has not written. Like the seed on rocky ground that believes for a while (Luke 8:13), he believed something, for a time, without new birth, which is God giving a new heart from above, so that a person loves God instead of using him (John 3:3–8; Ezekiel 36:26). Simon’s belief changed his opinions, not his heart.

He was amazed. Simon amazed the Samaritans, and now the amazer is amazed. He has changed places in the sentence without changing his interest. He was drawn by power, not by Christ, and five verses later he will try to buy it.

Was Simon truly saved? Luke says he believed and was baptised, and some take him as a true believer who fell into serious sin. But Peter’s words say his heart was not right before God, that he was in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, and that he had neither part nor lot in this matter (vv. 20–23). The more likely reading is that his faith was the kind that is impressed by miracles but has never turned from self. That fits what Scripture teaches about perseverance: those whom God truly saves, he keeps, and those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

Can I be baptised and still not be a Christian? Yes, sadly; Simon was. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, commanded by him, and believers should be baptised. But the water does not save. What saves is Christ himself, received by true faith, which the Spirit works in the heart (Ephesians 2:8–9). So the question is not, was I baptised, but, do I trust Christ, love him, and want to turn from my sin? If you find those things in yourself, however weakly, they are the marks of the new birth. If you do not, do not rely on your baptism. Come to Christ today.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles at Jerusalem heard. The sentence is remarkable for what is not in it: no debate, no committee, no summons for Philip to explain himself, though nobody had authorised a food-distributor to evangelise the far side of an old quarrel. The response is to send two men down to pray for them, and their first act is to ask God to give those people more.

Peter and John. John is the best thing in the verse. When a Samaritan village refused Jesus hospitality, James and John asked whether they should call down fire from heaven to consume them, and were rebuked (Luke 9:52–55). Now the same man walks into the same territory to put his hands on Samaritans and ask God to give them the Holy Spirit. What grace had done to John in the intervening years is described nowhere; it is visible in the fact that he made the journey.

Reaping where Jesus sowed. At a well outside Sychar, Jesus had told the disciples that the fields were white for harvest: I sent you to reap that for which you did not labour (John 4:35–38). He had sown in Samaria himself, with one woman. The harvest the apostles came to bless was the Lord’s before it was anyone else’s.

In the flow. Jerusalem’s response sets a pattern: when Gentiles believe in Antioch, the church again sends someone (11:22–23), and when Peter baptises Cornelius, Jerusalem glorifies God (11:18). Each time the point is one church, not a cluster of rival ones.

How can I lose a prejudice I have had all my life? Probably not by arguing yourself out of it in an afternoon. John’s instinct about Samaritans was to incinerate them. The instinct was not argued away. It was replaced, slowly enough that nobody recorded the process, by walking with Jesus. So bring the prejudice to Christ honestly, as sin. Pray for the people you find it hardest to love. Get to know some of them as people, especially fellow believers from that group. Serve them. And remember that Christ died for them as he died for you, and that they will share heaven with you (Revelation 7:9). Feelings follow faithfulness, and the Spirit who changed John can change you.

For worship. John once asked for fire from heaven on Samaria, and Jesus said no. Now John asks heaven for a gift on Samaria again, and this time what comes down is the Spirit. Between the two prayers stands a cross, where the judgment those villages deserved, and John deserved, fell on the Son of Man himself. That is why heaven can send blessing where it might have sent fire.
verseByVerse.note: John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village.

verseByVerse.quote: for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not yet fallen on any of them. Luke states the anomaly flatly. These people had believed and had been truly baptised, and the Spirit had not come. Normally the Spirit comes with faith (2:38); in chapter 10 he comes before anybody has been baptised at all (10:44). Here there is a gap.

They laid their hands on them. The answer that best fits Luke’s narrative is that this was a hinge in the history of salvation rather than a pattern for individuals. After centuries of rival temples there was a real danger of two churches, a Jewish one and a Samaritan one. God held back the Spirit until the apostles came, so that Samaritans received the Spirit through Jewish hands and the church remained one. Something visible probably happened, since Simon saw it (v. 18).

The great crossings. The pattern across Acts supports this. As the gospel crossed each great barrier, God marked the crossing with a visible coming of the Spirit: on Jews at Pentecost, on Samaritans here, on Gentiles in Cornelius’s house (chapter 10), and on the disciples of John at Ephesus (chapter 19), once-for-all moments in the spread of the one church to all peoples (1:8).

The gift of the ascended Christ. Whoever lays hands on whom, the giver in this scene is the Lord Jesus, who, exalted at the right hand of God, had poured out the promised Spirit (2:33). The Samaritans had not been baptised into a lesser Lord. The apostles prayed; Christ answered. And receiving the Spirit is not a feeling or an impersonal force, but God himself coming to live in a person: he joins him to Christ, assures him that he is God’s child, and begins to make him holy (John 14:16–17; Romans 8:15–16).

Where Christians differ: a second blessing, or a sacrament? Pentecostal and charismatic brothers often see here a two-stage pattern: conversion, then a distinct baptism in the Spirit, and they read Acts 19 the same way. Roman Catholics and others see the basis for confirmation, a sacrament in which a bishop’s hands confer the Spirit. This commentary’s view: this was a unique moment in salvation history, as the gospel crossed a great barrier, like the Gentiles in chapter 10 and John’s disciples in chapter 19. It was a once-for-all bridging, not the normal pattern. Romans 8:9 says anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion, without a second stage or an apostle’s hands. This is said with real respect for brothers who differ, many of whom love the Spirit and the Scriptures deeply.

The apostles’ hands. The same reading explains why no one today should claim to give the Spirit by laying on hands. The gift came through the apostles because it was their foundational work to join each new people into the one church (Ephesians 2:20), and that role was not passed on. The letters teach the regular way: when you believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13).

Do I need a second experience of the Spirit? No. If you belong to Christ, you already have the Spirit, all of him, from the moment you believed (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). You are not a half-Christian waiting for a second gift. What you do need, every day, is to walk by the Spirit and be filled with the Spirit (Galatians 5:16; Ephesians 5:18): to yield more of yourself to the one who already lives in you. Many believers have seasons when God makes his presence and love unusually vivid, and those are precious gifts. But they are fresh fillings of the Spirit you have, not the arrival of a Spirit you lacked.

Should I seek to speak in tongues as proof that I have the Spirit? No. Even in the apostolic church, Paul asked, do all speak with tongues? and expected the answer no (1 Corinthians 12:30). The proof of the Spirit’s presence is that you confess Jesus as Lord, cry to God as Father, and bear the Spirit’s fruit (1 Corinthians 12:3; Romans 8:15; Galatians 5:22–23). Many Reformed Christians believe the gift of tongues ceased with the apostolic age; continuationist brothers disagree, and we hold our view charitably. But on any view, no believer should be told that he lacks the Spirit because he has not spoken in tongues.

On a Tuesday. A Samaritan and a Jew under the same apostolic hands: that is what a church is. The believer of another background or style whom you pass in the car park on Sunday has the same Spirit you have, all of him, and God means you to be one.
verseByVerse.note: The apostles’ presence tied the Samaritan believers to the church in Jerusalem, with one Spirit in one church.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He offered them money. Simon saw something. Whatever happened when Peter and John laid hands on those Samaritans was visible; Luke declines to say what. Then the offer, the first attempt in Christian history to purchase a spiritual gift.

Give me this power also. He does not ask to receive the Spirit, but for the power to lay his own hands on somebody else and have the Spirit come. He is not applying for a blessing. He is applying for a franchise, to be somebody great again (v. 9).

Doing business the only way he knew. By the standards of Simon’s old profession the request is reasonable, even courteous. Names, formulas and techniques were commodities, bought at the going rate. He has failed to notice that he has changed worlds: in this one there is no going rate, because the thing on offer was never for sale, and the men holding it did not buy it either. Simon thinks the Spirit is a power to be bought and used. But the Spirit is God. Three chapters earlier money and the Holy Spirit had already met, when Ananias and Sapphira lied not to men but to God, and fell dead (5:3–5). Simon is standing nearer to the fire than he knows.

The Spirit for the asking. Simon wanted to buy what Jesus had promised to give for the asking: how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13). And the one who dispenses the Spirit is the Son, who received him from the Father without measure (John 3:34). Simon wanted to stand where only Christ stands, and Christ gives freely to beggars, never to buyers.

Simony. His name has been attached to the sin ever since. Simony, the buying and selling of church office and spiritual privilege, became a great scandal of the medieval church, and every tradition since has found its own way of putting a price on something God gives away.

The quieter modern shapes. The modern forms are quieter: the giving that expects a return in blessing, the service undertaken with an eye on what it buys, the prayer offered as a lever. In each the assumption is Simon’s: that there is a rate, and a man who pays it is entitled to the result. It is how nearly everything else in life works. It is not how this works.

Is it wrong to pay ministers, or to give expecting God to bless me? Paying ministers is right: the labourer deserves his wages, and those who preach the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Timothy 5:18; 1 Corinthians 9:14). That is support for work, not a purchase of grace. And God does promise to bless generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:6–11). What is wrong is giving as a transaction to obtain spiritual power or material reward, the seed-faith teaching that a gift to a preacher will make God pay you back with money or healing. That is Simon’s error dressed up as faith. Give because God has given to you, freely and cheerfully, and leave the blessing to him.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
May your silver perish with you. It is among the harshest things Peter says to anybody; J. B. Phillips rendered it, to hell with you and your money. Yet Peter is naming the direction the man is travelling, your money is going to destruction and you with it, because he wants it changed, and he goes on to tell Simon to repent.

The gift of God. Then the theology of the whole passage in one clause. It is the word Peter used at Pentecost, the gift of the Holy Spirit (2:38). A gift is not a cheap kind of purchase but a different kind of thing: the moment a price is paid, it has stopped being a gift. Grace is God’s undeserved kindness, and if it could be earned, grace would no longer be grace (Romans 11:6). If it were available on Simon’s terms, nobody in that room would have had any, Peter included.

Not with silver. Years later the same Peter wrote that we were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). The gift is not free because it is cheap; it is free because the whole price was paid by another. To offer money for it treats the blood of Christ as a deposit that needs topping up. Peter’s horror is the horror of a man who knows what the Spirit cost.

You have neither part nor lot in this matter. The phrase echoes the law of Moses, where the Levite has no portion or inheritance when the land is divided (Deuteronomy 12:12): when the ground is measured out, Simon’s name is on none of it. Then the diagnosis, echoing Psalm 78:37, their heart was not steadfast toward him: outward faith, inward crookedness.

Simon believed and was baptised, so could that be me? Verse 13 said Simon believed and was baptised; verse 21 says he has no share in this at all. Scripture is not embarrassed by the category. It says the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). It records a crowd who believed when they saw the signs, to whom Jesus did not entrust himself, for he knew what was in man (John 2:23–25). And John, writing to a church that had watched people walk out, says they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Some believing is real as far as it goes and never goes as far as Christ. Simon is its portrait: gripped, impressed, attached to the preacher, and interested from first to last in what he could get. But the reader who finds this passage frightening, who has read verse 13 and thought, that could be me, is displaying the one symptom Simon never displays anywhere in this story. Simon is not worried about his heart. He is worried, as his reply to Peter shows, about what might happen to him. A man anxious about whether he truly loves Christ is asking a question that never entered Simon’s head, and the anxiety is itself evidence of an interest Simon did not have. God gives his children assurance through his promises, the inner witness of the Spirit, and the fruit of a changed life (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2; Westminster Confession 18.2).

parallels.desc: Gehazi takes silver for Elisha’s healing
give without pay

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repent and pray. Having said one of the severest things he ever says, Peter immediately tells the man what to do about it. The prescription follows the diagnosis in the same breath, which is what distinguishes a rebuke from a dismissal. Some say the hard thing and leave the man standing in it; others will not say it at all and call the omission kindness. Peter does both inside two sentences, and the second is the reason for the first.

If possible. Read carelessly, the phrase sounds as though Peter were unsure whether God would forgive a sin of this size. But the uncertainty attaches to Simon, not to God’s willingness. It is the difference between saying, God may not forgive you, and saying, you may not repent, and the distinction matters to anyone carrying something he fears is too large.

Pray to the Lord yourself. Not, ask me to pray. The man who has just tried to buy access through an intermediary is told to go directly and ask for himself, and to repent, which is a change of mind that becomes a change of direction, turning from sin to God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). In one sentence Peter refuses both the money and the role of broker.

The gall of bitterness. The diagnosis is built from two Old Testament phrases. The gall of bitterness reaches back to Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit (Deuteronomy 29:18): a thing growing out of sight, exactly right for a man whose problem nobody could see until money was mentioned. The bond of iniquity is the language of chains, from Isaiah’s call to loose the bonds of wickedness (Isaiah 58:6). Simon is not a believer who has slipped but a man still tied up, and a man in chains cannot untie himself.

The chains Jesus came to loose. That second phrase has a history in Luke’s Gospel. At Nazareth Jesus read from Isaiah a line drawn from this same passage: to set at liberty those who are oppressed (Luke 4:18), and said the Scripture was fulfilled that day. So when Peter tells a man bound in iniquity to pray to the Lord, he is sending him to the one person who announced, as the programme of his ministry, that he had come to undo exactly this kind of knot. The chains are real. So is the Liberator.

Is there any sin too big to be forgiven? No sin is too big for the blood of Christ, which cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). Jesus does speak of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as unforgivable (Mark 3:28–30), but that is the settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ, calling his work the devil’s, not a single terrible act a person regrets. Those who have committed it do not fear they have; they do not care. If you are troubled that your sin may be too great, that very trouble shows the Spirit is still at work in you. Do what Peter told Simon: repent, and pray to the Lord. Whoever comes to Christ, he will never cast out (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: “Gall of bitterness” echoes Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray for me. Simon’s answer is a small masterpiece of missing the point. Peter had named a crooked heart and a bond of iniquity; Simon asks about the consequences. He is not asking to be changed; he is asking not to be hit. That is the difference between a man who is sorry and a man who is frightened, and the two make very similar noises. It is Pharaoh asking Moses to plead with the LORD to take away the frogs (Exodus 8:8).

Whom he asks. Peter had told him to pray to the Lord himself. Simon replies, you pray for me. He is still in his old trade, assuming that the power belongs to the practitioner. Rebuked for treating the Spirit as a commodity, his instinctive next move is to treat Peter as one.

The prayer behind Peter. Simon wanted Peter to stand between him and God. Peter knew what he himself stood on: Simon, Simon, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31–32). Peter denied his Lord three times, and his faith did not fail, because the prayer that held him was Christ’s. That intercession is not for hire. The risen Jesus always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and the way to be covered by it is to come to him oneself.

Luke stops. We hear no more of Simon in Scripture; the later legends about Simon Magus are lurid and none of them in Scripture. Luke leaves him under a question mark: a warning delivered, a door held open, no answer recorded. A resolved ending would let the reader off, relaxing either at the long reach of grace or at not being like him. Left open, the question was never really about Simon.

Many villages of the Samaritans. Sent to look into a revival in one city, the apostles went home seeding a whole region on foot, having become part of what they came to see.

Is it wrong to ask others to pray for me? Not at all. Scripture tells us to pray for one another (James 5:16), and Paul constantly asked churches to pray for him (Romans 15:30; Ephesians 6:19). The problem with Simon was not that he asked for prayer but that he asked for it instead of repenting, and instead of going to God himself. Ask your friends to pray for you, and pray for them. But never let someone else’s prayers become a substitute for your own coming to Christ. No one can repent for you, and no one needs to stand between you and God: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

On a Tuesday. Fear of consequences is not repentance. Next time you are sorry for something, ask yourself honestly: am I sorry I did it, or sorry about what it might cost me? Take the real thing to God. Even our best repentance is mixed, and we stand not on its purity but on Christ, who obeyed perfectly in our place (1 John 2:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An angel sends Philip from the revival in Samaria to a desert road, where an Ethiopian official is reading Isaiah aloud in his chariot. Philip begins from Isaiah 53 and tells him the good news about Jesus, and at the first water the official asks to be baptised. Then the Spirit takes Philip away, and the Ethiopian goes on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the death of the Servant

Philip began with this Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus, and the Scripture was the last of Isaiah's Servant Songs. It is the Old Testament passage that comes nearest to explaining what a cross is for: the Servant is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him, and with his wounds we are healed. The transgressions are ours, the wounds are his, and the exchange is the whole point. He is not merely an instance of innocent suffering but a substitute, the guiltless one bearing the penalty the guilty deserved, so that the guilty go free. From Isaiah 53 the road to Christ was short.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A man barred from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1 was reading a scroll which, three chapters past where he had it open, promised eunuchs a name in God's house better than sons and daughters. He was reading his own exclusion, and without knowing it his own invitation. Now: The people most certain the door is shut to them are often the ones who know the rules best. It was not a careless man who needed telling that nothing prevented him. It was the man who had read the regulation and accepted it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
verseByVerse.commentary:
Toward the south. Consider the timing. Philip is in the middle of what may have been the most fruitful work of his life, and an angel tells him to leave and stand on a road. The road to Gaza, the last town of any size before Egypt, ran south-west through empty country: no town, no crowd, no synagogue, and no word on how long he is to wait.

He rose and went. There is not a question in it. He does not ask what for, or whether the Samaritan work will survive without him. Everything that follows depended on a man being willing to leave something that was going extremely well.

Why did God guide so directly then but not now? First, a correction: angelic appearances were never everyday, even in Scripture. They cluster at a few pivotal moments: the patriarchs, the exodus, the prophets here and there, the birth of Christ, the empty tomb, the launch of the church. Most godly saints never saw an angel. Acts is exactly such a turning point, the once-for-all launch of the gospel to Samaria, to Ethiopia, to Cornelius, to the end of the earth, and for that foundational breakout God used extraordinary steering: angels, visions, the Spirit speaking by name (10:3; 13:2; 16:9). Like the signs that authenticated the apostles’ message, this belonged to the laying of the foundation (Ephesians 2:20). Today God guides by settled and sufficient means, and we are not less supplied but more: the completed Scripture, a lamp to my feet (Psalm 119:105), able to equip us for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17); the indwelling Spirit who illumines it; prayer, wisdom, godly counsel and providence. Scripture even warns against craving angelic encounters (Colossians 2:18; 2 Corinthians 11:14; Galatians 1:8). God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and to ask for an angel when we hold the word of the Son is to ask for something lesser. Two honest qualifications: angels are not idle, but remain ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1:14), often unseen; and no verse says outright that angels stopped speaking. That they no longer do so as our normal guidance is a fair inference from the foundational character of the Acts era and the sufficiency of Scripture, held charitably.

An Ethiopian, a eunuch. Ethiopia here is the ancient kingdom of Cush, south of Egypt, in modern Sudan, with its capital at Meroë; to Greeks and Romans it was the end of the earth. Royal courts employed eunuchs in the household, since a man who could father no children posed no dynastic threat, and they often rose to the highest posts of trust. The word could be a looser title (Genesis 39:1), but here he is most likely a literal eunuch.

Candace. Candace was a title, like Pharaoh, for the queen, or queen mother, who ruled Meroë, and this man is her finance minister: powerful, wealthy, trusted with the treasury of a kingdom.

He had come to Jerusalem to worship. Here is the poignancy. Under the law, no one whose male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1). Here is, most likely, a God-fearing Gentile (one who worshipped Israel’s God without becoming a full convert) who has travelled more than a thousand miles to worship, only to be shut out at the door. Yet he is reading Isaiah, the book in which God promised the eunuch who holds fast his covenant a name better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isaiah 56:3–5).

A house of prayer for all peoples. Two verses later God says his house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7), the verse Jesus quoted when he cleared the outer court where foreigners like this treasurer were allowed to pray (Mark 11:17). That same week he was crucified, the temple of his body destroyed and raised on the third day (John 2:19–21). In him the house Isaiah promised was built. The eunuch had gone to Jerusalem to find it and been held at the door. On the road home, the door came to him.

Was it not cruel of the law to shut a eunuch out? It was hard, and it was meant to teach something. Under the law bodily wholeness was a picture of the wholeness God requires of those who come near him, which is why even a priest with a blemish could not offer the sacrifices (Leviticus 21:17–23). The rule was not a verdict on the man’s worth or sincerity. It was a lesson in God’s holiness: no one is fit by nature to walk into his presence. And the law was never God’s last word. Isaiah promised its end for eunuchs (Isaiah 56:3–5), and Christ, the only truly unblemished one, was cut off so that the shut-out could be brought in (Hebrews 10:19–22).

In the flow. Samaritans were half-insiders who shared Moses with Israel; this treasurer comes from the end of the earth (1:8), a step beyond Samaria and a step short of Cornelius in chapter 10. One conversion at a time, Luke shows that no one is too far off for Christ.

Why would God take Philip away from a revival to reach one man? Because God values the one as well as the crowd. The Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one (Luke 15:4). And God sees what we cannot: this one man may well have been the gospel’s door into Africa. We tend to measure ministry by numbers, and God measures it by faithfulness and by his own purposes. If you are called from something fruitful to something small and hidden, it is not demotion. It may be the most important work you will ever do.
verseByVerse.note: Gaza was the last town on the road to Egypt. “Ethiopia” here is the kingdom south of Egypt (in modern Sudan); Candace was the title of its ruling queen. The law barred eunuchs from the assembly, but Isaiah promised them a place.

parallels.desc: to the eunuchs … a name better than sons and daughters
Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God

verseByVerse.quote: and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seated in his chariot. A covered carriage, moving slowly, with a driver, and he was reading aloud, as ancient readers usually did, so that Philip could hear him. A hand-copied scroll of Isaiah was a serious purchase. The treasurer has spent real money on the sacred book of a religion that will not fully admit him, probably in Greek, a language not his own, and is reading it in the desert on the way home from a pilgrimage that ended at a barrier. He was seeking.

The man in the scroll. He had bought a book whose central figure he could not yet name, though Jesus said of the Scriptures, it is they that bear witness about me (John 5:39). Barred from the temple courts, he was carrying home the Servant whose soul would be made an offering for guilt (Isaiah 53:10), in whom every sacrifice in that temple was fulfilled. The Spirit who sends Philip to the chariot is sending him to finish a sentence Isaiah began.

Go over and join this chariot. The angel sent him to the road; the Spirit sends him to the chariot. The verb (kollaō) means to be glued to something, the word used of Saul later trying to attach himself to the disciples (9:26). Philip is told to fasten on.

The division of labour. The work is shared, and it takes an enormous weight off the messenger. The Spirit arranged the road, the timing, the scroll and the passage. What was left for Philip was to walk over. Most Christians will never receive an audible sentence like Philip’s, but much of his obedience was doing something small and mildly awkward with a situation already in front of him, and much of what looks in retrospect like guidance was, at the time, a nudge toward a conversation already available.

How do I know when God wants me to go over to someone? Usually not by a voice, but by an opportunity you can see and a love you already have. Pray each morning that God would put people in your path and give you courage. Then watch for the openings: the colleague who mentions a crisis, the neighbour who asks why you go to church, the friend reading something spiritual. Scripture has already told you to love your neighbour and to be ready to speak (1 Peter 3:15). You do not need special guidance to obey that. If an opportunity is in front of you and nothing forbids it, take it. You may be walking toward a man God has been preparing for years.
verseByVerse.note: People usually read aloud. A scroll of Isaiah was a costly possession.

verseByVerse.quote: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip ran to him. A grown man jogging along a desert road beside a state official’s carriage, out of breath. Eager obedience, and not a dignified picture.

Do you understand what you are reading? Then the opening line, a beautifully judged sentence for a stranger to speak. In Greek it is a play on words: do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)? It is a light touch, and exactly right. Not a challenge, not a sermon, not a change of subject. Philip begins with the thing the man is already doing and asks a question about it. That is worth taking seriously by anyone who dreads these conversations, because the dread is nearly always about having to introduce a subject out of nothing. Philip introduces nothing. He notices what is in the man’s hands and asks how he is getting on with it. A simple, direct question: a good way to start a conversation about the Bible.

How can I, unless someone guides me? And the answer is a wonderfully teachable sentence, as humble as any in Acts. Consider who says it: a man of rank, in his own carriage, with a driver, replying to a stranger who has just run up out of the desert on foot. He does not bluff. He does not say he has his own view of the passage, or that he was only reading out of interest. He admits at once, to an obvious inferior, that he is out of his depth. The word for guide (hodēgēsei) means to lead on the way, the word Jesus used of the Spirit guiding into all the truth (John 16:13).

Two errors ruled out. Two errors are ruled out. The first is that Scripture is so plain nobody ought to need help with it: this intelligent, serious man cannot get through Isaiah 53 alone, and the God who inspired the text also gave the church teachers (Ephesians 4:11; Nehemiah 8:8). The second is that Scripture is so difficult ordinary people had better leave it to the qualified. Nobody suggests the eunuch should stop reading. The answer to his difficulty is not less Bible. It is a man in the carriage.

The key is a person. The passage stays locked until you know whom it describes. The apostles themselves had not understood the suffering Servant until the risen Jesus opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45–46). What Philip brings to the carriage is not superior scholarship but the name that turns a riddle about a silent lamb into good news.

He invited Philip. An open door, opened by the man himself: the teacher is asked to sit beside him, not to stand over him.

What if someone asks me a question I cannot answer? Say so honestly; the eunuch’s humility is a good model for the teacher as well as the learner. You might say, that is a good question, and I do not know, but I would like to find out with you. Then do: ask your pastor, read a good book, and come back. Most people are not looking for a Christian who knows everything. They are looking for one who is honest and who cares about the truth. And you can always tell what you do know: who Jesus is, what he did, and what he means to you. Philip did not need to answer every question about Isaiah. He needed to get to Jesus.

For worship. The God who breathed out Isaiah 53 did not leave a seeking man alone with a scroll he could not read. He sent a runner along a desert road. It is the way of our God to come near: he wrote the book, he sends the guide, and by his Spirit he opens the eyes, until the reader sees that the page he has been puzzling over is about the one who loved him.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: “Do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The passage. By God’s providence the scroll is open at Isaiah 53:7–8, in the fourth of Isaiah’s Servant Songs, poems about a mysterious Servant of the LORD who will bring God’s salvation to Israel and the nations (Isaiah 42:1–9; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12). The wording differs a little from our Old Testament because the eunuch was reading the Greek translation, but the sense is the same: an innocent sufferer led to death and cut off.

Like a lamb before its shearer. Anybody who has watched shearing knows the detail Isaiah is reaching for: the animal is turned over and held, and it goes completely still. The prophet is describing a man who did not resist, and the Gospels record exactly that: Jesus was silent before his accusers (Mark 14:61), and before Herod he answered nothing (Luke 23:9).

Justice was denied him. Not merely that he suffered, but that the courts failed. Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus, and then delivered him over to their will (Luke 23:4, 14, 22, 25).

Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth. The line is genuinely difficult, and readers have taken it two ways: either that nobody could describe the wickedness of the men among whom he lived, or, more probably, that nobody could number his descendants. The second fits the paragraph, because a few lines later Isaiah says of this same Servant that he shall see his offspring (Isaiah 53:10), an extraordinary thing to say of a man just described as cut off and buried. He dies without descendants, and yet he will have countless spiritual children.

His own biography. Now put that before the man in the carriage. He is a eunuch: no children, no name carried forward, and in the ancient world that was not a private sorrow but the erasure of a man from the future. The law that shut him out of the assembly had shut him out on precisely that ground. And he is reading aloud about a man cut off from the land of the living, who would somehow see his offspring after all. He was reading his own biography and could not work out whose it was. His question to Philip is a man asking who this is, because whoever it is, is standing exactly where he is standing.

What does Isaiah 53 offer someone who feels cut off? Everything. The Servant was cut off so that the cut-off could be brought in. He was despised and rejected, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3), so he knows from the inside what it is to be excluded, shamed and alone. If you feel shut out, by your body, your past, your singleness or childlessness, your illness or your story, look at him. He bore our griefs and carried our sorrows, and by his wounds we are healed (53:4–5). In him you have a family, the church, and a name better than sons and daughters. No one who comes to the Lamb is left outside.
