On a Tuesday. Read Isaiah 53 slowly this week, all twelve verses, and every time it says he, put Jesus’ name; every time it says we or us, put your own.

parallels.desc: like a sheep he was led to the slaughter

verseByVerse.quote: And the eunuch said to Philip, "About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else? It is the right question, and not a naive one. The identity of Isaiah’s Servant was genuinely disputed. Interpreters, Jewish and later Christian, have proposed the prophet himself, or Hezekiah, or Israel as a nation, or a faithful remnant within the nation, or a Messiah still to come. The eunuch has read the passage carefully enough to see that it is about a person, and honestly enough to admit that he cannot tell which.

Beginning with this Scripture. Then Philip opened his mouth, a solemn phrase for an important speech (10:34; Matthew 5:2). Philip does not change the subject or produce an outline. The man had a question about a text; Philip answers it, and keeps going until he arrives at Jesus, the move the risen Christ made on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:27). The instinct in these conversations is to steer onto ground where we know the material. Philip does the opposite.

He gospelled Jesus to him. Literally, he announced Jesus as good news. Jesus is not a topic within the message. He is the message, and Jesus himself said Isaiah 53 was written of him (Luke 22:37).

How can I be sure Isaiah 53 is really about Jesus? Look at where the question arises. The eunuch is reading the passage and asking who it is about before Philip arrives. The text raised the question by itself, in the mind of a foreigner with no Christian instruction, on a road in the desert. Christ is not being imported into Isaiah; he is being identified in it. And the fit is exact: a Servant who suffers not for his own sins but for the sins of many, who is silent before his accusers, who is condemned unjustly, who dies, is buried with the rich, and then sees his offspring and is exalted (Isaiah 52:13–53:12). Christians are convinced that no one else in history fits. Many Jewish readers today take the Servant to be Israel, but Isaiah’s Servant suffers for the transgression of my people (53:8), and is innocent, as no nation is. Nor did Christians write Jesus into the text: the great Isaiah scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, copied more than a century before he was born, contains this chapter much as we read it. Jesus said it was about him, and the apostles preached it so (1 Peter 2:22–25).

For worship. The Lamb opened not his mouth before his shearers, and so Philip could open his. The Servant kept silent under judgment so that good news could be spoken about him on every road on earth. He is not one subject among many in the Scriptures. He is their meaning and their joy.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some water. In a desert, a stream or pool, there by providence when it was needed.

See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized? He asks it; Philip does not suggest it. What was said in the carriage had evidently included baptism, and the Ethiopian connects it to the water they are passing. And his question (ti kōlyei) is the word he has carried his whole life. What prevents me? He knows the answer, confirmed at the end of a journey of over a thousand miles: his own body, the law in as many words, and a temple that would not let him past the outer court. What he is really asking is whether the barrier is still there.

He is inhabiting Isaiah 56. Three chapters after the Servant’s suffering, the book in his hands promises eunuchs a place within God’s house and his walls (Isaiah 56:3–5). The excluded man is holding the prophecy of his own gathering.

The curtain and the water. What had prevented him was a temple, and its barriers marked a real distance between sinners and a holy God. When Jesus died the curtain of the temple was torn in two (Luke 23:45), and we now have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). The barriers were not swept aside as though they had never mattered. They taught that sinners cannot walk into God’s presence uncleansed, and Christ has done the cleansing, once for all (Hebrews 10:10). So when the eunuch asks what prevents him, the honest answer is nothing, any longer, because the Servant was cut off in his place.

Textual note: verse 37. Your Bible may not have it, though the KJV and NKJV print it. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says that if he believes with all his heart he may, and the eunuch confesses that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. It is not in the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added later, perhaps from an early baptismal liturgy. The words are old; Irenaeus quotes them before the end of the second century. It reflects true early practice, since baptism followed faith, but it was likely not part of what Luke wrote.

Nothing is lost. Nothing is lost if it goes. The eunuch plainly did believe, and every word the verse contains is taught openly elsewhere in the same book (2:38; 8:12; 16:31–33). The words may be a later copyist’s. The practice they describe is apostolic.

Does this show that baptism is for believers? Yes. The order here, as in verse 12, is hearing, believing, then baptism, and that is the order in every baptism in Acts where the order is described. Christians who baptise infants agree that adult converts must believe first, but hold that the children of believers may also be baptised, and we honour their sincere conviction. The more likely reading, given every example in Acts, is that baptism is for those who have come to faith (1689 London Baptist Confession 29.2).

I was baptised as a baby. Should I be baptised now? On the believer’s baptism view, which this commentary holds, yes, and that is no criticism of your parents, who very likely acted in love and faith; talk with your pastor, with humility and a desire for peace. (See Ephesians 4:4–5 for the fuller answer.)

On a Tuesday. If you have believed in Christ and not been baptised, ask the eunuch’s question: what prevents me? Speak to your pastor this week.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says “If you believe with all your heart, you may,” and the eunuch replies, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: can anyone withhold water for baptizing?

verseByVerse.quote: And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He commanded the chariot to stop. In this whole passage the powerful man gives exactly one order, and it is to halt his own carriage in the middle of a desert so that a stranger can baptise him. Went down into, and came up out of, the water: the language suggests immersion, the ordinary meaning of baptizō, to dip or plunge.

One of the Servant’s offspring. An hour earlier he had been reading about a Servant cut off, who would yet see his offspring (Isaiah 53:8, 10). Now he comes up out of the water as one of them. The burial and rising the water pictures are not his own achievement but Christ’s, shared with him (Romans 6:4). He went down into the water as a man whose line ended with him. He came up in Christ, in a family that will never end.

Where Christians differ: the mode and subjects of baptism. Some sprinkle or pour; some baptise infants. The words down into and up out of could, taken alone, describe a man wading into a stream. This commentary’s view: the pattern here is a believer, confessing faith, baptised by immersion. This is the New Testament norm. Christians who sprinkle or baptise infants hold their views sincerely, and we hold ours with charity, but the credobaptist practice (baptising those who profess faith) best fits passages like this. Immersion shows most clearly what baptism means: dying to the old life, buried with Christ, and rising to walk in newness of life.

The Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away. The verb means snatched (harpazō), as of a man caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2), a sudden removal like Elijah’s (1 Kings 18:12). Whether miraculous transport or simply a sudden leading, Philip’s work there was done.

On his way rejoicing. Now stand where the Ethiopian is standing. He has been a Christian for perhaps ten minutes. He is wet, on a desert road, and the man who explained everything to him has gone without a goodbye. Ahead is a journey of a thousand miles and more, to a court where he may be the only believer, with no church and no Bible in his own language. And he went on his way rejoicing. He did not need Philip; he had Christ. The joy is not bravery under adverse conditions. It is the ordinary result of the gospel.

Not a case against the church. The verse is occasionally used to argue that a Christian does not really need the church. Luke has spent seven chapters describing a community that ate, prayed and grieved together, and the eunuch’s isolation is a circumstance, not a recommendation. What the verse establishes is narrower and more comforting: a believer who has nothing but Christ has enough to be going on with, in a hospital, a prison, or a country where the nearest congregation is far away.

Toward the end of the earth. Later tradition holds that the Ethiopian church traces itself to this man; Luke does not say so. What can be said is that a man went south that afternoon with the good news about Jesus, toward the end of the earth (1:8).

What if I am the only Christian where I am? Then you are in the eunuch’s company, and Christ is enough for you. Hold on to him through his word: read it daily, and memorise some of it. Pray, and pray aloud if you can, as this man read aloud. Look for even one other believer to pray with, in person or at a distance. Find a church online to listen to if you have none near, while you pray for one. Live your faith openly and kindly among the people around you; you may be the beginning of a church, as he may have been. And remember that you are never really alone: you belong to a body that spans the earth, and the Lord has promised, I am with you always (Matthew 28:20).

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD caught him up

verseByVerse.quote: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Philip found himself at Azotus. Azotus is Ashdod, one of the old Philistine cities, some twenty miles up the coast from Gaza. Then, without pausing, he does what he has been doing all chapter: a coastline of towns, one after another, all the way to Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea.

In the flow. Philip settles in Caesarea, the city where Peter will open the door to the Gentiles (chapter 10). Before that, Luke turns back to Saul, the ravager of verse 3, and shows the risen Lord meeting him on another road.

The king who comes to Ashdod. Zechariah said that God would take the abominations from Philistia’s teeth until it too became a remnant for our God, like a clan in Judah (Zechariah 9:6–7), and two verses later announced the coming king, righteous and having salvation, humble and mounted on a donkey (9:9; Matthew 21:5). Philip, preaching town by town up the coast, is the herald of that King, and Israel’s old enemies are hearing that he has come.

Twenty years later. Philip reappears once, some twenty years later: we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him (21:8). Look at the word we. Luke stayed several days under Philip’s roof, and much of chapters 6 and 8 very likely came across a table from the man it happened to.

Still the evangelist. He is still called the evangelist two decades on, and he has four unmarried daughters who prophesied (21:9), quietly fulfilling Joel’s promise that sons and daughters would prophesy (2:17). He settled in a port city, raised a family, and went on being the man who tells people about Jesus.

What if my Christian life feels ordinary? Then it may be exactly what God intends. Most of Scripture’s faithful people spent most of their lives doing ordinary things faithfully: working, raising children, opening their homes, speaking of Christ to whoever was near. Philip had one dramatic afternoon and twenty years of ordinary faithfulness, and the twenty years were not the lesser part. God does not grade us by the drama of our stories but by faithfulness (1 Corinthians 4:2). Keep your door open, raise your children in the Lord, speak of him in your town. Nothing done for Christ is ordinary to him.

For worship. Philistia and Cush were named long ago among the peoples of whom the Lord would one day say, this one was born in Zion (Psalm 87:4–6). In a single chapter a treasurer of Cush is born again on the road south and the towns of Philistia hear the gospel on the road north. He saw Philip’s famous afternoon and his twenty quiet years alike, and he will gather the fruit of both before his throne.
verseByVerse.note: Azotus is Ashdod, on the coast. Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, became Philip’s home.

8.theology: The gospel crosses its first barriers. In Acts 8 the gospel crosses from Jews to Samaritans, and then to a man from Africa, as Jesus said it would (1:8). The Ethiopian, kept out of the temple’s inner courts, is reached on a desert road through the passage he happened to be reading: God’s call that brings a person to faith at work, as the Spirit directs the preacher, opens the Scriptures and draws the seeker. The God who gathers a people from every nation does it through ordinary means: a man, a chariot, a scroll.
8.examples:
Then: Scattered believers, fleeing for their lives, who could not stop talking about Christ. A table-server taken from a city-wide revival to one man on a road. An African official who came to Jerusalem seeking God and found him on the way home.

Now: In Acts 8 God works through disruption: a persecution that scatters, a command that redirects, a passage that raises exactly the right question. Planning is not wrong, but our plans should be held loosely enough that we will go over to the person God puts in front of us.

9.title: The Road to Damascus
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest <sup>2</sup>and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. <sup>3</sup>Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. <sup>4</sup>And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” <sup>5</sup>And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. <sup>6</sup>But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do.” <sup>7</sup>The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. <sup>8</sup>Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. <sup>9</sup>And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. <sup>10</sup>Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” <sup>11</sup>And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying, <sup>12</sup>and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.” <sup>13</sup>But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” <sup>15</sup>But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. <sup>16</sup>For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.” <sup>17</sup>So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized; <sup>19</sup>and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.” <sup>21</sup>And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” <sup>22</sup>But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. <sup>23</sup>When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, <sup>24</sup>but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him, <sup>25</sup>but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. <sup>26</sup>And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. <sup>27</sup>But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. <sup>28</sup>So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. <sup>29</sup>And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him. <sup>30</sup>And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. <sup>31</sup>So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. <sup>32</sup>Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. <sup>33</sup>There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. <sup>34</sup>And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. <sup>35</sup>And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. <sup>36</sup>Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. <sup>37</sup>In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. <sup>38</sup>Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.” <sup>39</sup>So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. <sup>40</sup>But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. <sup>41</sup>And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. <sup>42</sup>And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. <sup>43</sup>And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
9.overview:
Acts 9 tells the most important conversion in church history. Saul of Tarsus, the church’s fiercest enemy, sets out for Damascus with letters to arrest believers, and the risen Jesus stops him on the road. Blinded, he is led into the city; three days later a frightened disciple named Ananias is sent to him, and he receives his sight, the Spirit and baptism, and at once preaches that Jesus is the Son of God.

The persecutor becomes the persecuted: he escapes Damascus in a basket, is received in Jerusalem only because Barnabas vouches for him, and is sent home to Tarsus. Luke then returns to Peter, who heals Aeneas at Lydda, raises Tabitha at Joppa and lodges with a tanner, which sets the scene for chapter 10.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Jesus stops Saul on the road to Damascus, sends Ananias to restore his sight and baptise him, and turns the persecutor into a preacher. Soon hunted himself, he is sent home to Tarsus, and the church has peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of Grace in Conversion

Saul's conversion shows grace that does not wait to be wanted. He was not seeking Christ; he was hunting Christians, with an arrest warrant in his bag. Paul never describes his conversion as a search that ended, but as being laid hold of. Reformed theology reads it as the pattern rather than the exception: the difference between Saul and a quieter case is one of speed and lighting, not of mechanism. It also makes despair about anybody unreasonable: the church's most violent enemy went on to write a great part of its Scriptures.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ananias was sent to the man carrying a warrant that covered Ananias himself. He told God plainly what he thought of it, and then he went, and the first word out of his mouth was brother. Now: The church's most persuasive argument has always been the people in it who ought, by every reasonable calculation, to be enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 9 tells the most important conversion in church history, and Luke tells it three times (here, 22:3–16 and 26:9–18). The chapter shows sovereign grace: Christ saves whom he chooses, even his enemies, and he does it in person. The man who set out to put the name of Jesus out of the world ends the chapter as the one who will carry it to the end of the earth.

Still breathing threats. Still tells us this was not a passing fit of temper but the settled condition of his life. The participle empneōn, breathing in, describes the atmosphere he lives in: his very breath is hostility. And murder means murder: when believers were put to death, Paul says years later, he cast his vote against them (26:10). Stephen was not the only one.

Letters to the synagogues. Then the machinery, which tells you what kind of man this was. He does not gather a mob. He goes through the proper office. Damascus lies about a hundred and thirty-five miles north-east of Jerusalem, a week on foot, and it is outside Judea altogether, a different province under a different administration. Letters from the high priest carried great weight in the synagogues of the Diaspora (the Jewish communities scattered outside the land), and Rome generally let Jewish authorities deal with their own people in religious matters, though how far such letters could be enforced in a foreign city is uncertain. So what Saul is carrying is not a licence to riot. It is paperwork, obtained through proper channels. He was organised, funded and legal, and he believed with his whole heart that he was doing God’s work (22:3; Galatians 1:13–14).

Synagogues and prisons, as he said. None of this took the Lord by surprise; he had described it in advance. Before his death Jesus warned his disciples: they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name’s sake (Luke 21:12). Saul’s letters are addressed to synagogues, and his purpose is prisons. The persecutor is fulfilling, item by item, the word of the man he thinks a false prophet. And the last clause of that prophecy has a further irony waiting in it: the man carrying these warrants will himself be brought before governors and a king, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, for that same name.

Why Damascus? Because there was a large and ancient Jewish community there, and because the believers scattered by the persecution of chapter 8 had gone somewhere. Saul is not opening a new front. He is pursuing refugees he had himself created, a week’s journey from home, to bring them back in chains.

Belonging to the Way. This is one of the earliest names the Christians had for themselves, and Luke uses it half a dozen times in this book (19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). They did not call themselves a school, a party, a sect or a synagogue. They called themselves a road, hē hodos. Whether the name came from the Lord’s own words, I am the way (John 14:6), or from the prophet’s cry to prepare the way of the LORD (Isaiah 40:3), or from both, the effect is the same: it is a word about travelling, and it describes a manner of life rather than a set of opinions. Christianity is not first a society you join but a road you walk, behind someone who has gone ahead. It is also, as it happens, precisely the wrong kind of thing to try to stamp out. You can shut a building. A road runs.

Men or women. It is the second time Luke has said it about Saul in two chapters (8:3), and he will not let the reader make this abstract. Whatever else was in those letters, they authorised the arrest of somebody’s mother.

How could a man so devout be so wrong? Because sincerity is not the same as truth, and zeal is only as good as what it is aimed at. Paul later said of his own people what had been true of himself: they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Romans 10:2). Saul knew his Bible, prayed daily, and lived strictly. What he did not know was who Jesus was, and that one error turned all his devotion into a weapon against God. It is a sobering warning for religious people. Being earnest, disciplined and certain does not make us right; only the truth about Christ does. The safeguard is not less zeal but zeal held open to Scripture, and a readiness to be corrected by it.

On a Tuesday. A way is something you are either walking or not. Ask what in this week’s diary is on the road behind Christ and what is simply parked beside it: the conversation you have put off, the generosity you mean to start.
verseByVerse.note: Damascus lay about 135 miles north-east of Jerusalem and had a large Jewish community. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian movement.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He approached Damascus. A week’s journey, and the city was in sight; the arrests were perhaps a few hours away. God does not stop men only at the beginning of their sins. Sometimes he lets them get to the very edge of the thing they meant to do.

A light from heaven. The verb is built on the word for lightning: it flashed, and it enveloped him. Paul later adds that it happened at midday, and the light was brighter than the sun (22:6; 26:13). A Syrian noon, and something outshone it. It was the glory of the risen Christ, the glory Isaiah saw in the temple, which John says was the glory of Christ (John 12:41).

Three tellings of one event. The differences between Luke’s three tellings are sometimes produced as evidence of invention, so they repay an honest look. The first is about posture. Here the men with him stood speechless (v. 7); before Agrippa, Paul says we had all fallen to the ground (26:14). A likely resolution is simple: everyone went down, and then the escort got up while Saul stayed where he was.

The commission on the road. The second difference is larger. In this chapter Saul is told simply to go into the city, where he will be told what to do, and the commission arrives later through Ananias. Before Agrippa, the commission is spoken by Christ on the road itself, at length, with the Gentiles named. But Paul is then in the dock before a king and a Roman governor, to whom a Jewish disciple’s testimony from a back street in Damascus is worth nothing. So he compresses, folding what he was told into the encounter that authorised it. Before a Jerusalem crowd, by contrast, Ananias is the point, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews (22:12), exactly the credential that mattered there. The three tellings are best read as the same event addressed to three rooms, which is how truthful people ordinarily retell things.

Falling to the ground. The man who had been dragging others to the floor of their own houses is on the floor of the road. When the glory of God comes near, men do not stand and assess it; they go down, as Ezekiel did by the river Chebar and John did on Patmos.

Saul, Saul. Then the voice, and the first word is the man’s name, said twice. Scripture does that sparingly, and usually at a hinge: Abraham with the knife raised (Genesis 22:11), Jacob on the way down to Egypt (Genesis 46:2), Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:4), Samuel in the dark (1 Samuel 3:10), Martha in her busy kitchen, Simon on the last night. It is the address of somebody who knows the person and is about to change his life. It is tender as well as urgent. And Paul notes, when he tells it later, that it came in the Hebrew language (26:14), so the risen and glorified Christ speaks to him in his mother tongue and uses his Hebrew name, not the Greek one the world would come to know him by.

Why are you persecuting me? Saul had never met Jesus of Nazareth; what he had done was drag Christians out of houses. Yet the voice does not say my people, or my church. It says me. (See Acts 22:7 for the fuller answer.)

The body in a pronoun. Everything Paul later wrote about the church being the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 1:22–23) is already lying in that pronoun, and he heard it before he had a theology to put it in. It is the same truth the Lord taught on the Mount of Olives: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). It cuts two ways and both of them matter. It means that the way a Christian treats another Christian is not a matter of church politics; Christ files it under his own name. And it means that whatever has been done to a believer, the exclusion, the cruelty, the years of it, the thing nobody else noticed, has not gone unrecorded, because it was not finally done to him alone. The Lord takes it personally, and he says so in the first sentence he ever speaks to Paul.

Does this mean Jesus is still suffering in heaven? No. He is risen and glorified, beyond pain and beyond the reach of any persecutor; death no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:9). What the word me teaches is union, not fresh suffering. Christ is so joined to his people, the Head to the body, that what is done to them is counted as done to him, and he feels it with them in sympathy. Hebrews says we have a high priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). So when you are wronged for his sake, you are not suffering in a corner of the universe he has forgotten. The one who reigns at the Father’s right hand regards the wound as his own, and he will answer for it.

On a Tuesday. Think of the Christian you find hardest to bear. The way you speak about that person this week, and to him, Christ files under his own name.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who are you, Lord? He says Lord before he has any idea who is speaking. The word kyrios could mean no more than sir, and a man flat on a road addressing a voice out of a light might reasonably reach for it. But this is a vision from heaven, the fall has already done its work, and Saul knows he is facing a divine being. By the end of the answer the word will mean everything it can mean.

I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Six words which cost Saul everything he had. Take the two halves separately, because each is a demolition. I am Jesus: so the body is not in the tomb, the disciples were not lying, the movement is not a fraud, and the man Saul thought a deceiver justly hanged on a tree and cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23) is alive, glorified and speaking from heaven. Everything Saul has done for these past months has been done to the Messiah of Israel. Gamaliel, his own teacher, had warned the council that they might be found opposing God (5:39). Saul had been doing exactly that. Whom you are persecuting: present tense, still going on, as of this morning. He is not being told about a mistake he once made. He is being interrupted in the middle of it, with the warrants still in his luggage.

Rise and enter the city. Not a word of rebuke, nothing about Stephen. He is told to get up and wait for instructions, like a man just taken into someone’s service, which is exactly what has happened. His first act of obedience is to be led somewhere he did not choose.

Where Christians differ: how does conversion happen? Many earnest Christians in the Arminian tradition (which holds that God’s grace enables everyone who hears, but each person’s free choice decides whether he believes) see Saul’s conversion as untypical, and they rightly insist that people must truly repent and believe. This commentary’s view: the details were unique, but in every believer Christ takes the initiative, overcomes the sinner’s resistance and makes him willing (Galatians 1:15–16); every conversion is a Damascus road, whether quiet or dramatic. (See 2 Corinthians 4:6 for the fuller answer.)

Must every Christian have a dramatic conversion like this? No. Saul’s experience was unusual in form, because he was being called as an apostle and witness. But its substance is the same for every believer: Christ seizes a sinner by grace. Many come to faith gradually, like Timothy, who knew the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15), and cannot name a day. What matters is not the drama but whether one now trusts Christ.

Does God force people to believe against their will? No, and the difference matters. God does not drag an unwilling man into the kingdom kicking and screaming. He changes the will itself, so that the man who would not come now wants to come. Saul was not overpowered into a faith he resented; he got up from that road asking what his new Lord wanted of him. The Westminster Confession puts it well: God draws his people to Jesus Christ, yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace (Westminster 10.1). The Second London Confession of 1689 says the same (10.1). Grace does not cancel our freedom. It rescues it from bondage to sin, which is why everyone who has been called this way describes it afterwards not as captivity but as release.

A note on the older Bibles. The King James adds a sentence here: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks, with Saul’s trembling question about what the Lord would have him do. Jesus really did say them, and Luke records them when Paul retells the scene before Agrippa (26:14), but they are not in the Greek manuscripts at this point; copyists of the Latin Bible filled them in from chapter 26. Nothing has been lost from Scripture. And the image is worth keeping: an ox that kicked back at the farmer’s spiked goad only drove the point deeper. Stephen’s face, Stephen’s prayer: the goads had perhaps been at work on Saul long before the light.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person you consider least likely ever to become a Christian, and bring that name to God, not vaguely, and not with your expectations already lowered. If Christ could stop Saul, he can stop anyone.

For worship. I am Jesus. The whole of the Christian faith turns on the fact that the Crucified is not dead but speaking, and that he speaks first. Saul did not find Christ; Christ found Saul. And he did not answer the persecutor’s hatred with a word of revenge. He said his own name, and gave him something to do.

verseByVerse.quote: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stood speechless. A party of armed men on the Damascus road with nothing to say, and their leader on the ground unable to see. They came out of Jerusalem as an escort. They go into the city leading a blind man by the hand.

Hearing the voice but seeing no one. This half-verse is a favourite of sceptics. Luke says here that the men heard the voice; later Paul says they did not hear the voice of the one speaking (22:9, as the King James renders it).

A sound, not the words. There is a difference between hearing a sound and hearing with understanding: the men heard a noise but could not make out the words, as when the Father spoke from heaven and the crowd said it had thundered (John 12:29). The ESV renders 22:9 did not understand the voice, and the difficulty largely eases. Likewise they saw the light but not the person who spoke. The event was real and public. The revelation was for Saul.

Proximity is not reception. The men beside him experienced the identical event and went away with nothing but a story about strange weather. Saul went away with a Lord. People can sit under the same sermon for years, a pew apart, and one hears a noise and the other hears the voice of Christ.

Eyes opened and seeing nothing. The irony is not lost on Paul, who spent his life writing about veils and blindness and light shining into hearts (2 Corinthians 3:14–16; 4:4–6). Here was a man who had never been in any doubt about what he was looking at. His eyes are open and there is nothing in them.

That those who see may become blind. Jesus had said this would happen, and said it to Pharisees: For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind (John 9:39). Saul was a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees (23:6), as certain of his sight as any man in Jerusalem, and on this road that word comes true in his own body. And because the same Lord came to make the blind see, the darkness on the road is not the last word over him. It is the first stage of the miracle.

Led by the hand. The last time we saw Saul he was dragging people through doorways. He meant to lead prisoners out of Damascus; he is led into it, helpless, in the position of the people he came to arrest.

Was the blindness a punishment? It was more a mercy and a sign than a penalty. A punishment would have fitted the crime, and nothing in this chapter does. The blindness was the natural effect of the glory he had seen, and it gave him three days in which the whole world he had lived in could be taken down. It was also a living picture: the man who had been spiritually blind was made to feel his blindness so that he would know his sight, when it came, was a gift. Compare the sorcerer Elymas, who is struck blind for a time as a judgment for opposing the gospel (13:11). Saul was blinded on the way into the gospel, and his sight was given back with the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Pride is the feeling of seeing perfectly well. If there is a subject on which you are completely certain and have stopped listening to anyone, ask God whether that is where you are blind, and ask without dread: the Lord who opened Saul’s eyes gives sight as a gift.

For worship. Christ did not argue Saul out of his blindness; he shone on him, and had him led by the hand into the city like a child. That is how the God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, shines in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). It is hard to believe Paul wrote that sentence without remembering this road.
verseByVerse.note: In 22:9 Paul says his companions did not understand the voice; they heard a sound but not the words.

verseByVerse.quote: And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days without sight. No sight, no food, and, the detail people skim, no water. In that climate three days without drinking is the edge of what a body will take. This is not a man keeping a fast. It is a man who has stopped functioning, in shock, in repentance, and, as the Lord will tell Ananias, in prayer.

The room in the dark. He is in a strange city, in a borrowed house, with arrest warrants in a bag that nobody is going to use. Every certainty he possessed on the morning he left Jerusalem is gone, not weakened but gone, and the one thing he now knows for certain is that the people he was travelling to imprison were right about everything, and that he has spent his best years and his considerable gifts hunting the Messiah of Israel. And what he did with the time was pray: not, one imagines, in the well-formed manner of a Pharisee who had prayed every day of his life, but in a dark room, with no idea what to say.

A death and a rising. Luke does not press the number, and we should not build on it. But the shape is unmistakable: he goes into darkness, everything he was dies there, and then a man comes and he is raised up and washed. It is the shape of the gospel itself, the death and resurrection of the Lord into which every believer is baptised. Paul would spend the rest of his life writing about being buried with Christ and raised with him (Romans 6:4), about the old self having been crucified, and about a new creation in which the old has passed away (2 Corinthians 5:17). He had lived it before he wrote a word of it, on the floor of somebody’s guest room. What does dying and rising with Christ actually mean? When Christ died and rose, he did it as the representative of his people, so God counts the believer as having died to his old life in Christ’s death and as living a new one by his life (Romans 6:4–11). It is why a Christian can say, I have been crucified with Christ, yet Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20).

For anyone in a collapse of certainty. There is something here for the person whose faith has come apart in his hands, or who has been shown something about himself he cannot unsee. Saul’s three days were not the end of him, though they cannot have felt like anything but an end. Scripture’s most spectacular conversion has a dark room in the middle of it.

Does God always bring people through darkness before conversion? No. Some, like Saul, are broken before they are healed. Others are drawn quietly: of Lydia Luke says simply that the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said (16:14), and the Ethiopian went on his way rejoicing on the very day he met Philip (8:39). The darkness is not a stage that has to be passed through, and nobody should feel his conversion is suspect because it lacked one. What every conversion has in common is that the old self is put to death and a new one is raised by Christ. In some lives that takes three days on a floor; in others it happens over a cup of coffee and an open Bible.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a dark room of your own just now, do what Saul did: pray, even if the prayer has no shape. And if you know someone in that room, do not rush him out of it with explanations. Be the person who brings food on the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A disciple named Ananias. One of the most important minor characters in the New Testament, in a single plain sentence. No office, no title: a Christian who lives in the city, handed one of the most consequential errands of the first century. (He is not the Ananias of chapter 5; the name was common.) Paul adds that he was a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there (22:12), a man with a standing the errand would end.

Here I am, Lord. It is the answer of Abraham, of Samuel and of Isaiah (Isaiah 6:8). Ananias has not been told what the thing is, and he will argue about it once he hears. It is the reply of a man who is available before he knows the assignment, and that is rarer than being willing once the details are known.

The street called Straight. The ordinariness is the point. It was a real road, the long thoroughfare through Roman Damascus, and it runs through the old city to this day. A street, a householder, a name and a home town, Tarsus, a proud city of learning (21:39): God’s guidance in this passage has an address on it.

For behold, he is praying. What is not said matters. Not, he is safe now; not, he has repented and you will find him much changed. The single credential given for the most dangerous man in the province is that he is praying, which from anybody else would prove nothing. From the Lord who is speaking, that is the whole case. A man who has begun to pray to Christ is a man Christ has already taken hold of.

Does God still guide his people by visions like this? God is free to do as he pleases, and Christians who believe he still sometimes speaks in dreams and visions are our brothers. But even in Acts such visions were rare and came at turning points in the founding of the church, and the more likely reading is that this kind of direct revelation belonged to that apostolic age. Ananias’s vision was not the normal way God guided his people then, and it is not the normal way now. We are guided by Scripture, which is sufficient for everything we need for faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17), and by prayer, wise counsel and the ordinary providences that open and close doors. Any impression that pulls against the plain teaching of Scripture is to be refused, however vivid. And the good news is that we do not need a vision to obey. Ananias’s great act was simply going to a house and loving a man. That is guidance anyone can follow today.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary believers for extraordinary tasks, and almost always the task is a person at an address: the neighbour who has just lost her husband, the colleague who asked about church and was never followed up, the young man at the back who has stopped coming. The Shepherd who sends you already knows the door.
verseByVerse.note: Straight Street still runs east–west through the old city of Damascus. Tarsus was a major city in Cilicia, known for learning.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has seen in a vision. God has been at both ends of this the whole time. While Ananias is being given a street name, Saul has already been shown a man called Ananias coming through a door. Neither arranged it, and when Ananias walks into that room, the blind man will have been expecting him by name, just as God will prepare both Peter and Cornelius in the next chapter. For Saul it is the first concrete thing he has been given; for Ananias, it means he is not walking in cold.

The door opened from the inside. The Lord is reasoning with a frightened man, and his argument is that the door has already been opened from the inside. The same is often true of the conversation a Christian quietly dreads, the apology owed, the subject that has to be raised. That is no guarantee that obedience will always be safer than it looked; Ananias’s errand was genuinely dangerous and he was right to say so. But the God who sends people is already at work on the far side, and the messenger is very rarely the first one there.

Why did the Lord not simply heal Saul himself? He could have, of course. The light that blinded him could have restored him on the spot. But Christ chose to give Saul his sight, his welcome and his baptism through a member of the church he had been persecuting. Saul needed to receive mercy from the hands of the people he had hunted, and to be taken into their family, not merely converted on his own. That is how the Lord ordinarily works still. He saves people by himself alone, but he brings them to faith through the word spoken by other believers (Romans 10:14), and he gathers them into a church. Nobody is meant to be a Christian by himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have heard from many. Ananias argues with God, and Luke reports it without a syllable of disapproval. He is stating the case as any sane member of that congregation would. Some of the refugees who had run to Damascus were sitting in his own meetings, and Saul’s reputation had arrived well before Saul.

Your saints. It is the first time in Acts that Christians are called this: the holy ones, hagioi, set apart for God. It is not a special class but the ordinary name for all of them (Romans 1:7). Your saints: they belong to Jesus, which is why harming them is harming him (v. 4). The man Ananias is sent to will later use the same word of ordinary congregations of fishermen and slaves, and of himself, the very least of all the saints (Ephesians 3:8).

All who call on your name. All: Ananias is describing a warrant with his own name inside it, and he is being asked to identify himself, as a Christian, to the officer sent to arrest him. And those who call on your name was the mark of a Christian from the beginning (1 Corinthians 1:2). The phrase comes from Joel, everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved (Joel 2:32), and Peter and Paul both apply it to Jesus (2:21; Romans 10:9–13). The name on which Israel called for salvation is now the name of Jesus.

Arguing with God. Moses produced five objections at the bush, and God dealt with each; Jeremiah said he was too young. What distinguishes Ananias from Jonah is not that he kept his doubts to himself but that he raised them in God’s presence and then did what he was told. A piety that suppresses the objection and calls the suppression faith is usually fear wearing better clothes.

Where Christians differ: who are the saints? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches use “saints” mainly for specially holy people, canonised after death, whose prayers are sought. This commentary’s view: in the New Testament every believer is a saint, set apart by God in Christ (Ephesians 1:1; Philippians 1:1). Holiness of life should follow, but the title is given by grace, not earned. We pray to God alone, through Christ alone.

Is it right to pray to Jesus himself? Yes. The usual pattern of Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18), and that is how Jesus taught us to pray. But the first Christians also called directly on Jesus, as Stephen did while the stones were falling: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (7:59). Ananias is talking to Jesus in this very verse. That is one of the clearest signs in the New Testament that the church worshipped Jesus as God, because a devout Jew would never pray to anyone less. So you may speak to the Lord Jesus freely, as to the Father, and you are not praying to a different God when you do. The three persons are one God, and every prayer offered in Christ’s name reaches him.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, you are a saint, not because you feel holy but because he has set you apart for himself. Live like one, in the ordinary places where nobody calls you anything.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chosen. God answers the objection, and the answer is not reassurance but information. The word for chosen, eklogē, is the word of election, God’s choosing of particular people to belong to him and serve him, out of his free love and not because of anything he saw in them (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11). Saul was chosen before he was born, and long before he deserved anything except judgment: by the grace of God I am what I am, he would write (1 Corinthians 15:10).

A chosen vessel. The word behind instrument, skeuos, is the ordinary one for a container: a jar, a pot, the sort of word that turns up in an inventory. Saul is not described as a hero but as a receptacle picked out, and the value is entirely in what it is for and who chose it. Paul never forgot the word: we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7).

Gentiles and kings. The destinations are the table of contents for the rest of the book: the Gentiles named first, an extraordinary thing to say in those first years (13:46–48); kings, Agrippa and, in prospect, Caesar (27:24); and the synagogue in every city. And he is to carry the name, as one carries something precious through a crowd. It is the name, not his own, that he is entrusted with.

A share in the Servant’s work. Isaiah’s Servant was to be a light for the nations, that God’s salvation might reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6); Simeon called the infant Jesus exactly that (Luke 2:32), and Paul and Barnabas quoted the same verse to explain their turning to the Gentiles (13:47). Saul is not sent on an errand of his own beside Christ’s. He is drawn into the Servant’s own mission, as a vessel through which the light of the nations will shine.

How much he must suffer. And then the sentence which is the reason this passage cannot be preached as a success story. It is joined to the commission by a conjunction, not separated from it by a paragraph. The calling and the cost arrive in the same breath, spoken to a third party before the man himself has been told anything. The little word must, dei, is Luke’s word for divine necessity, the word Jesus used of his own suffering (Luke 9:22). And there is an exchange in it that is hard to miss: Saul had spent months making people suffer on account of that name, and the first thing said about his future is how much he will suffer for it. Not as punishment, because his sins were forgiven, but as the cost of carrying the name of a crucified Lord.

What that meant in practice. Paul eventually listed it (2 Corinthians 11:23–28): five times thirty-nine lashes, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, a night and a day adrift at sea, and the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches. That is the career being announced here.

What it does not mean. Not every calling carries this measure of suffering, and a Christian whose life has been comparatively gentle has not been given a second-rate commission; Scripture nowhere makes hardship the proof of authenticity. But the verse is a permanent corrective to the presentation of Christ as the route to a better, smoother, more successful version of the life one already has.

Was Saul chosen only for service, or for salvation too? Both, and they cannot be pulled apart. In this verse the emphasis falls on service: Saul is chosen as an instrument for a task. But Paul himself traced his salvation back to the same choosing grace. God set him apart before he was born and called him by grace (Galatians 1:15), and he received mercy so that Christ might display his perfect patience in him as an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16). The same is true of every believer: chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), and created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:10). You were not chosen because you were useful. You were chosen in love, and then made useful.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ is costing you something this week, a friendship, a promotion, a reputation, do not conclude that you have taken a wrong turning. The cost was in the calling from the start, and your Lord said so.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ananias departed. A plain sentence for the bravest thing anybody does in this chapter. He had said what he thought, been answered, and gone.

Brother Saul. Ananias lays his hands on him, and the first word out of his mouth is brother. In the room is a blind man from Tarsus who arrived in Damascus with a warrant that covers Ananias and everyone like him. Ananias belongs to a congregation swollen with refugees who ran from this man, some of whom may have lost somebody. He has every reason to open with a question, or a condition, or at the very least a wary silence. He opens with a family word, and he uses it before Saul has said anything at all. He can say it because Christ had said it first: the one who sanctifies is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

On the road by which you came. Ananias names the road, so that Saul knows he is not being humoured, and names the one who met him there.

Filled with the Holy Spirit. It is not an apostle who does this. The man who restores Paul’s sight and very probably baptises him is a disciple in a provincial city about whom nothing else is known (22:12). Paul would insist that he had not received his gospel from any man (Galatians 1:11–12), and that is consistent, because what Ananias gave him was not a gospel. It was his eyes, a welcome, and water.

Was this a second blessing after conversion? No. The filling with the Spirit came as part of Saul’s conversion; Ananias came to him within days of the road, and the Spirit came with the restoring of his sight and his baptism. It was not a later stage that every Christian must seek. Paul himself later taught that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), so every believer has the Spirit from the first day. What Christians rightly go on seeking afterwards is to be filled with the Spirit more and more, day by day (Ephesians 5:18). Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians teach a later baptism in the Spirit, and their hunger for more of God is right; we differ from them, as brothers, on whether Scripture makes it a second stage.

Something like scales. Luke the doctor (Colossians 4:14) marks it as a comparison: something like. We still say the scales fell from my eyes. And at Nazareth Jesus had read out his own programme, including recovering of sight to the blind (Luke 4:18); here the risen Lord keeps that word for the man who had fought him hardest.

Then he rose and was baptized. No interval, no probation: baptism follows faith, at once.

Was Saul converted on the road, or at his baptism? He was Christ’s from the road: he called Jesus Lord, he prayed, and Ananias greets him as Brother (v. 17). Baptism was the outward sign and public confession. When Ananias later says be baptized and wash away your sins (22:16), he joins the sign to what it signifies, as Scripture often does; the washing is by faith in Christ, calling on his name.

Should we baptise people as quickly today? In Acts, those who professed faith were baptised promptly, usually the same day (2:41; 8:38; 16:33), and that pattern should shape us: baptism belongs at the beginning of the Christian life, not as a reward at the end of a long course. We hold, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2), that baptism is for those who profess repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, because in the New Testament it is those who hear, repent and believe who are baptised (2:38, 41; 8:12), so a church rightly asks for a credible profession first and takes time to hear it. Our paedobaptist brothers baptise the children of believers as well, and we honour them as faithful Christians while we differ. If you were baptised as a baby, this is something to talk over with your pastor without fear, and without contempt for the church that baptised you. But no one should be kept waiting for years to prove himself. If you trust Christ and have not been baptised, speak to your pastor this week.

How could God forgive a man like this? Saul had approved of murder and dragged families to prison. Many people quietly wonder whether some sins are too great. Paul answered the question himself: though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent, I received mercy, and Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost (1 Timothy 1:13–15). He adds that he was shown mercy precisely as an example, so that no one would ever think himself beyond it (1:16). The blood of Christ is enough for the worst thing you have done. The only sin that is never forgiven is the one never brought to him.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you find it hard to call brother or sister: a person who hurt you, a new convert with an ugly past? Grace calls you to say the family word first. That does not mean pretending nothing happened or setting aside wise safeguards. It means meeting a person Christ has received as Christ received you.

For worship. Brother Saul. In those two words the whole gospel stands in a doorway. The Lord Jesus had forgiven his persecutor before a single apology was offered, and sent one of the persecuted to say so. That is what the risen Christ does with his enemies: he gives them eyes, his Spirit, and a family.

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking food. Luke has not forgotten that this man has not eaten for three days. Before the theology there is a meal, and the people he came to arrest became his family: he sat at their tables and slept under their roofs, perhaps among the very refugees he had hunted.

In the synagogues. Saul had carried letters to the synagogues at Damascus, authorising him to search them. He now walks into those same synagogues and preaches the thing he came to stamp out.

He is the Son of God. What he preaches matters, because of how soon it is. Not: this man was a prophet, or a teacher, or even the Messiah; that comes two verses later. The very first recorded sermon of the apostle Paul, preached within days of his baptism by a man who had spent his adult life defending the oneness of God against every blasphemy, is that Jesus of Nazareth is God’s Son. (The King James reads that he preached Christ; the earliest manuscripts have Jesus.) It is the only time in Acts that the title is used in preaching like this (but compare 13:33; the King James also has it at 8:37, a verse missing from the earliest manuscripts and so given only in a footnote in most modern Bibles), and it is exactly the claim for which the council had condemned Jesus (Luke 22:70–71). Whatever else his conversion did, it did not leave him working his way toward that conclusion gradually. He had met the person and drawn the only possible inference on the road (compare Galatians 1:16; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

What did Saul mean by “Son of God”? The title gathers up two streams of Scripture into one confession. First, it is a claim to full deity. To call Jesus God’s own Son, in the unique sense, is to say he shares the very nature of God, which is exactly how his hearers understood it: Jesus was charged with “making himself equal with God” because he called God his own Father (John 5:18; 19:7). “Son” here speaks not of a beginning or of a lesser rank but of sameness of nature and eternal relation: as an earthly son shares his father’s humanity, the divine Son shares the Father’s deity, eternally, of one substance with him, “begotten, not made.” Second, “Son of God” was a royal, messianic title: the promised king of David’s line was called God’s son (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), so to say “Jesus is the Son of God” is also to say he is the Christ, the anointed King, which is just where Saul’s preaching goes next, “proving that Jesus was the Christ” (v. 22). In Christ the two meet: the true Davidic King who is himself truly God.

One guard against misunderstanding. Scripture calls angels and even believers “sons of God” (Job 1:6; John 1:12), but those are sons by creation or by adopting grace. Jesus is the only Son (monogenēs, John 3:16: the one-of-a-kind Son, which older Bibles render only begotten), Son by eternal right and by nature, not made a son and not adopted. We become sons only through him. So this short sentence is the gospel in miniature: the man Jesus, crucified and risen, is God the Son and the royal Messiah, worthy of all trust, worship, and obedience, and it is the very confession that saves, “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31; compare 1 John 4:15).

Should a new believer start speaking about Christ straight away? Yes, in the sense Saul did: telling people who Jesus is and what he has done. You do not need a theology degree to say that Jesus is the Son of God and that he has changed your life; the man born blind in John 9 had known Jesus for less than a day when he said, I was blind, now I see. What a new believer should not do is rush into teaching or leading others, and the church kept that distinction even with Saul, who spent years out of the limelight before he was given leadership. Speak of Christ freely and early. Take on responsibility slowly.

On a Tuesday. If someone asked you today who Jesus is, what would your first sentence be? Saul’s was not about himself or what Jesus could do for his listeners. It was about the person. Practise saying it plainly, in your own words.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says he also went to Arabia (the Nabataean kingdom) before returning to Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? All who heard him were amazed, and the synagogue’s reaction is one of the more understandable in Scripture. They know exactly who this is and exactly what he came for, because the letters had been announced in advance and arrangements had presumably been made. And here he is, in the seat, saying the opposite of what he was sent to say. The word they use of his career, porthēsas, is a violent one: made havoc, the language of sacking a city or laying waste to a country. It is not their invention either. Paul takes the same word and uses it of himself, twice, when he writes to the Galatians (Galatians 1:13, 23). He never softened the vocabulary. Whatever else he became, he did not become a man who described his past in careful language. That is what grace does. A man trying to justify himself has to manage his record. A man justified by God, that is, declared righteous by God for Christ’s sake and not for his own deeds, can tell the truth about his past, because his standing no longer rests on it (Philippians 3:9).

Increased in strength. The verb is the one behind I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:13). Not natural confidence returning: something was being supplied.

Proving that Jesus was the Christ. The Greek word for proving, symbibazōn, means to bring things together, to knit or join them side by side; the image is of laying two things next to each other until the fit is obvious. That is precisely what Paul does in every letter and every sermon recorded of him: this text and that event, laid alongside one another, the promise beside the fulfilment, until the listener can see they belong together. And the hardest piece he now fitted was the one that had kept him from Christ: a Messiah hanged on a tree, under the curse of the law (Deuteronomy 21:23). He had thought the cross disproved Jesus. He came to preach that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The method of a lifetime was operating from the first days, because a first-class rabbinic training in the Scriptures was now pointing the other way. God does not throw away the gifts and training of the people he converts. He turns them round.

Ability arrived at once; deployment did not. Saul is formidable immediately, and within a few years he is sent quietly home to Tarsus for a long, largely unrecorded season. The New Testament warns against putting a recent convert into leadership, lest he become puffed up with conceit (1 Timothy 3:6), and even this gifted convert waited years.

How can I show someone that Jesus is the Christ? Do what Saul did, on a smaller scale: lay the Scriptures and the facts side by side. Read Isaiah 53 with a friend and ask whom it describes. Read Psalm 22 next to the crucifixion. Show how the promises to Abraham and David land on Jesus, and how the empty tomb holds it all together (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). You do not need to win every argument, and you will not convert anyone by cleverness, because only the Spirit opens blind eyes. But God uses honest explanation of his word, and it is far better to open the Bible with someone than to argue round it.

On a Tuesday. God can use your training, your mind and your past for his glory, including the parts of your past you are ashamed of. Somewhere in what you know and what you have lived is something that could serve Christ’s people, and he does not waste it.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When many days had passed. Laid against Paul’s own account, those days include a departure into Arabia and a return to Damascus, about three years in all (Galatians 1:17–18). Luke is writing the story of a movement and moving at its pace.

The Jews plotted to kill him. The hunter becomes the hunted. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas, the Nabataean king, was guarding the city in order to seize him (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). Religious objection supplied the charge and the state supplied the soldiers, as with Jesus before Pilate and later at Thessalonica (17:5–9).

Watching the gates. A watch on all the gates of a walled city, around the clock, is not a gesture. Three years earlier Saul was the one with the authority, the letters and the men; now he cannot use the gates, and depends on a handful of disciples to get him out alive. For the next thirty years Paul is on the receiving end of precisely what he used to administer.

Why did God let his new servant be hunted so soon? Because this is what the Lord had said would happen (v. 16), and because the servant is not above his master (John 15:20). Persecution was not a sign that something had gone wrong with Saul’s conversion; it was a sign that it was real. And the plot became known to Saul. God did not prevent the danger, but he watched over his man in the middle of it and kept him until his work was done. That is how he usually protects his people: not always from trouble, but always through it, and never one day beyond his appointed time.

On a Tuesday. If you are opposed for your faith this week, do not take it as proof that you have failed. Ask instead whether you have given offence by Christ or only by your manner. If it is by Christ, rejoice quietly. You are in good company.
verseByVerse.note: “Many days” probably covers about three years. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lowered in a basket. Perhaps the best-known escape in the New Testament, and it is entirely undignified. The future apostle to the Gentiles, the man who will stand in front of kings, is folded into a large woven hamper and let down over a wall in the dark by people hoping the rope holds, like the spies Rahab let down at Jericho (Joshua 2:15).

The boast of a basket. He never forgot it. Writing to Corinth about men undermining him with their credentials, he says that if he must boast he will boast of the things that show his weakness, lists labours, imprisonments, beatings and shipwrecks, and ends the catalogue on the basket (2 Corinthians 11:30–33). Of everything in a life that included being caught up into the third heaven, he selected as his boast the night he was lowered out of a window like a sack of figs.

Strength in weakness. That is not false modesty. He had understood something his rivals had not: my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Those words were the risen Christ’s, and they describe Christ before they describe Paul: he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). The basket was where the servant began to learn the shape of his Master’s glory.

Is it cowardly to run? One thing should be said plainly, because it releases a great many people from an unnecessary burden. Saul ran away. He did not stay and preach and take what came; he went over the wall at night and left the city. There is no hint of reproach in the text, and the Lord himself had told his disciples that when they were persecuted in one town they should flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Courage in Scripture is not the refusal to leave. Paul stood his ground on plenty of occasions and left quietly on others, and he seems to have had no rule about it beyond the work continuing.

So when should a Christian flee, and when stay? A rough guide from Scripture: it is right to flee when staying would achieve nothing but your death or imprisonment and the work can go on elsewhere, as here, and as when Jesus himself withdrew from those who sought to kill him before his hour had come (John 8:59; 10:39). It is right to stay when leaving would mean denying Christ, or abandoning people in your care who cannot leave with you; a shepherd who runs and leaves the sheep is a hired hand (John 10:12–13). Between those two, pray, take counsel from your church, and do not despise yourself for choosing life. The Lord wants living witnesses as well as faithful martyrs.

His disciples. He has been a Christian for perhaps three years and there are already people in Damascus who are his. (Most modern Bibles follow the earliest manuscripts in reading his disciples; the King James has the disciples.) They held the rope.

For worship. The Lord who would one day send Paul before Caesar first sent him over a wall in a basket, and both journeys were equally in his hand. The disciples held the rope; Christ held the man.

parallels.desc: let down in a basket through a window in the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All afraid of him. It is the loneliest sentence in the chapter. The people now shutting their doors are the ones who got away, or whose relatives did not. Their fear is not weak faith. It is arithmetic: a man with his record claiming to be one of them is exactly what an informer would do. So here is Saul, three years after the road, unwelcome in the synagogue and not admitted by the church. For a man once praised above his contemporaries (Galatians 1:14), it was a hard lesson in where his standing now came from: not from the approval of any room in Jerusalem, but from the Lord who had received him.

Barnabas took him. Then one man crosses the room. Took him means took hold of him: he laid hands on the man everybody else was backing away from, walked him in, and vouched for him out loud. Barnabas was a respected believer, a Levite from Cyprus whose name meant son of encouragement (4:36), and it is the second time Luke has shown us this man doing the same kind of thing. The first was a field sold and the money laid down without a speech; this is a reputation put at risk on behalf of somebody with none. If Barnabas was wrong, he had just introduced an assassin to the entire leadership of the church. Years later he would take the same kind of risk on John Mark (15:37–39), and be proved right again (2 Timothy 4:11).

The door the Gentile mission came through. Nobody else moved. One man with no office beyond a nickname believed a story everybody else found incredible, and Paul’s whole mission to the Gentiles came through that door.

He had seen the Lord. Barnabas tells the two things that mattered: that Saul had met the risen Lord, and that his life since had matched his claim. Paul would later rest his whole apostleship on that sight (1 Corinthians 9:1).

The apostles, or two of them? Set this beside Paul’s own account of the same visit and a question surfaces. Luke says Barnabas brought him to the apostles. Paul says that when he finally went up to Jerusalem he saw Cephas, and stayed fifteen days, and saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:18–19). Plural in one, and pointedly not plural in the other. They fit well once you see what each writer is doing. Luke is describing Saul’s reception, that the church’s leadership received him, which is the whole point of the paragraph, and uses the collective term for that body, as we might say a man was taken to meet the board when in fact two directors were in the office that week. Paul is under oath, so to speak: he is arguing to the Galatians that he did not get his gospel secondhand from Jerusalem, so he counts heads with deliberate precision and keeps the number as small as honesty allows.
