His case depends on it having been a short and limited visit; Luke’s case depends on it having happened at all. And Paul’s two names are exactly the two who mattered for the introduction: Peter, the leading apostle, and James, the head of the Jerusalem church. Barnabas got him in front of the men whose word would settle it.

How can I be a Barnabas without being naive? Barnabas did not simply feel generous; he knew the facts. He seems to have heard Saul’s story, learned what had happened in Damascus, and judged it true before he put his name to it. So take time to listen to the person others are wary of, find out what has actually changed, and then speak up for him. At the same time, welcoming a repentant sinner never means ignoring real dangers. Where someone has abused or harmed others, a church must keep proper safeguards in place and protect the vulnerable, while still offering the gospel and fellowship. Grace and wisdom are not opposites. Barnabas had both, and the church was safer for it, not less safe.

On a Tuesday. You were brought into God’s house because Christ vouched for you, so be a Barnabas. Think of the newcomer at church whom nobody quite knows what to do with, the person with the awkward history. Find out his story. Sit with him. Introduce him to someone.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas was a respected believer from Cyprus.

parallels.desc: Paul visits Cephas and James

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In and out among them. An Old Testament way of describing ordinary comings and goings (1 Samuel 18:16): he was part of the household now, no longer at the door. And he was bold, with parrēsia, plain and fearless speech, Luke’s mark of the Spirit-filled witness (4:13, 31).

Disputed against the Hellenists. These are the Greek-speaking Jews of the Jerusalem synagogues, the circle Stephen had argued with, who could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke and had him killed. Saul had held the coats (7:58). Now he has walked back into the room where it happened and taken up Stephen’s argument, on Stephen’s side. Stephen’s mantle has fallen on the man who held the coats.

A word on who the Hellenists were. The term (the King James has Grecians) names a person’s language and culture, not his faith: Jews of the diaspora raised in Greek, with synagogues of their own in Jerusalem, whose circle included men from Cilicia (6:9). In 6:1 it labels Greek-speaking believers; here, unbelievers. Saul of Tarsus came from that world himself.

Seeking to kill him. The second organised attempt on Saul’s life in one chapter, and he has been a Christian for about three years.

Was Stephen’s death wasted, then? It looked like it at the time: a brilliant preacher silenced in his first public season, and the church scattered. But Stephen died praying for the men who stoned him, Lord, do not hold this sin against them (7:60), and one of those men is now preaching Stephen’s message in Stephen’s synagogue. Augustine is often quoted as saying that if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul. Whether or not one can draw the line so straight, the pattern is plain: no faithful witness for Christ is ever wasted, even when it seems to end in failure. God answers prayers in ways the one who prayed may never see this side of glory.

On a Tuesday. Is there a place, a family, an old circle of friends, where you used to stand on the other side? That may be exactly where God wants you to speak now, not with superiority, but as one who knows from the inside what they believe and why.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews — the group that had opposed Stephen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sent him off to Tarsus. The church takes charge of him and removes him, down to Caesarea and home to Cilicia, and he goes where the brothers put him. Paul later adds that the Lord himself had told him in a vision in the temple to leave Jerusalem quickly (22:17–21). The church’s decision and Christ’s command pointed the same way.

The hidden years. And then the narrative simply stops carrying him. Saul does not appear again until chapter 11, when Barnabas travels to Tarsus to look for him and brings him to Antioch (11:25–26), and depending on how the years are counted, the gap is something in the region of eight to ten. Luke covers a decade of Paul’s life with half a sentence. For anyone who measures his worth by being seen to be useful, that decade is a quiet rebuke: Christ valued the servant long before anyone valued his work.

What was he doing? Not nothing. Paul says in his own account that he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia, and that the churches of Judea kept hearing that the man who used to persecute them was now preaching the faith he had once tried to destroy (Galatians 1:21–23). Several of the beatings in his later catalogue probably fall in these years, and so, very likely, does the vision he describes as having happened fourteen years before he wrote about it (2 Corinthians 12:2). He was working. Nobody was writing it down.

Thirty years in Nazareth. Saul’s hidden decade follows the shape of his Lord’s life. Of Jesus’ first thirty years the Gospels tell us almost nothing (Luke 3:23), yet at the end of them, before he had preached a sermon, the Father said: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (Luke 3:22). The years nobody wrote down had pleased God.

Was the church wrong to send its best preacher away? No. They were protecting his life, and the Lord himself had told him to go (22:18). There is no failure here, either of courage on Saul’s part or of love on the church’s. Sometimes the wisest thing a church can do for a gifted and endangered young man is to take him out of the spotlight. And if you are the one who has been moved on, out of a role, a city or a ministry you loved, it may not be a demotion. It may be the Lord’s way of preparing you for the work he actually has in mind.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a season where nothing you do seems to be noticed, do the work in front of you as though Christ were watching. He is. What you do for him that nobody else will ever know about is not lost; he receives it, flawed as it is, for the sake of his own perfect obedience.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea was the port; Tarsus was Paul’s home city.

parallels.desc: the regions of Syria and Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church had peace. One of Luke’s hinge sentences, with a quiet irony in its placing: the church gets its peace in the paragraph after its chief persecutor has been converted and shipped home. And church is singular (the King James, following later manuscripts, reads churches): one people across three regions under one Lord.

The peace Christ made. The church’s peace did not come from a change of policy in the council. It came because the risen Lord had gone out to meet the man driving the persecution and made him his own: the enemy was not pacified but converted. And the building that follows is the work of the same hands: I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18).

A target hit. Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria: the second and third stages of the commission (1:8) have now happened, not by any plan of the church, but through a persecution nobody wanted. Only the end of the earth is outstanding, and the man who will take it there has just gone home to Tarsus to wait.

The comfort of the Holy Spirit. The fear of the Lord is the reverent awe that draws near to God in love while never trifling with his holiness, like a man who loves the fire and pulls his chair close, yet would never put his hand in it. Its companion is richer than our word comfort suggests. Paraklēsis belongs to the same family as paraklētos, the name Jesus gave the Spirit: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever” (John 14:16). In use the word means coming alongside to help, and it sounds three notes at once: to console the troubled, to encourage the faint-hearted, and, as the old English word from the Latin for with strength reminds us, to make strong. It is God’s own Spirit coming alongside his people to console them, embolden them and strengthen them to stand.

Fear and comfort together. Fear and comfort are partners, and out of the two together the church was built up and multiplied (Ephesians 4:12–16). A church with fear and no comfort becomes harsh and anxious. A church with comfort and no fear becomes careless and soft.

Does a church grow only when there is no persecution? No. The church had grown explosively under persecution too: those who were scattered went about preaching the word (8:4). God uses both seasons. Persecution scatters the seed; peace lets it root and be built up. Neither is a sign of his absence. If your church is in a quiet season, the question is not whether God is at work but whether you are using the peace to be built up in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Spirit, or simply to rest.

On a Tuesday. Take the two phrases as a check on your own walk this week. Where have you been treating God casually? Where have you been carrying anxiety alone, as if there were no Helper beside you? Neither lack is mended by trying harder. The Helper is already given to every believer, and his power, not your resolve, is what makes a holy and unafraid walk possible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Luke returns to Peter, visiting the churches of the coastal plain. At Lydda the paralysed Aeneas is healed, and at Joppa Tabitha is raised from death, and in both towns many turn to the Lord. Peter then lodges with Simon the tanner, where chapter 10 begins.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha deliberately recalls the raising of Jairus's daughter: the mourners put outside, the command to rise, the girl presented back to her people. Peter does what he had watched being done, in the name of the one who did it, and that is why he kneels first. Every healing and raising in Acts is a sign rather than a policy: a small sample, given in advance, of the day when everything sin and death have broken is put right for good. A sign that happened every time would not be a sign but the arrangement, and the arrangement is still to come.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Tabitha died, the widows stood in the room holding up the coats and dresses she had made while she was with them. That was her ministry, and it was what the church had to show for her. Now: It is worth asking what would be held up for you: not what would be said at the service, which is easier, but what could be carried into the room and shown. And whatever it is, Christ counts the smallest of it as done for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here and there among them all. The apostle out of Jerusalem, going round from congregation to congregation on the coastal plain: the first glimpse in this book of what most Christian ministry actually consists of, visiting believers in unremarkable towns. Peter the fisherman has become Peter the shepherd: feed my sheep (John 21:17). And he did not plant these churches. Philip had preached his way through this plain (8:40), and the saints are the fruit of a persecution and of refugees who could not stop talking.

He went about doing good. Peter’s circuit has a model, which he would soon describe in Cornelius’s house: Jesus went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him (10:38). The healing about to happen in Lydda is the same Jesus still doing good, now from heaven. The ministry of Acts is not Peter’s ministry replacing Christ’s. It is Christ’s, continued.

The saints at Lydda. Lydda is the old town of Lod, about twenty-five miles north-west of Jerusalem, a market town on the main road down to the sea, where whatever happened would be discussed by travellers within a day.

Bedridden for eight years. Peter found him, which is what you say about somebody you were not looking for. Eight years is long enough that everybody in a town that size knows the house and has stopped expecting anything. Somebody had been washing him and turning him for eight years, and had long since stopped mentioning it.

Mercy before confession. Aeneas matters because of where this book is going. Luke says nothing whatever about his faith. He is not called a disciple, not said to have believed, and not recorded as speaking. He is simply a man Peter found. In two verses the mercy will arrive before any confession does, and in the next chapter Peter will be standing in a Gentile house watching the same thing happen on a very much larger scale.

In the flow. Luke now leaves Saul in Tarsus and takes up Peter again (8:25), moving him town by town from Lydda to Joppa, where chapter 10 opens.

On a Tuesday. Christ had not forgotten Aeneas. Somewhere in your church or street is someone who has been housebound so long that people have stopped calling; go this week. And remember the carers, who have been doing the lifting and washing for years without anyone mentioning it.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda (modern Lod) lay about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem, on the road to the coast.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. The tense is present: is healing you, now. Not I heal you: Jesus Christ heals you. Peter had learned at a temple gate to tell a staring crowd it was not by his own power or piety that the lame man walked (3:12–16), and he does not wait to be misunderstood a second time.

Rise and make your bed. The Greek can also mean, spread your own table. Either way it is the first command given to a man who has not stood up for eight years: do for yourself what others have done for you all these years. It is the ordinary domestic gesture by which a man signals that the illness is over.

Lydda and Sharon. Sharon is the whole fertile coastal plain. Luke is describing a movement across a region, not conducting a census, but the mechanism is easy to see: everybody had known about Aeneas for eight years, and he was standing in the street. The sign led to faith, and the faith was in the Lord, not in Peter.

Does Christ still heal like this through his ministers? Christ still heals and answers prayer as he wills. But healings like Aeneas’ and the raising of Dorcas at Joppa were apostolic signs confirming the gospel as it spread. Many Christians believe such gifts continue; the more likely reading is that they belonged to the apostolic age, and that no minister today may claim them. Those who believe the gifts continue are our brothers, and the question between us is not whether Christ heals today, which he plainly does, but whether he now gives anyone the power to heal at will, as he gave it to the apostles as the signs of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12).

A word to the reader still on the mat. A passage like this can be quietly cruel if it is left to speak alone. Aeneas was healed after eight years; a great many faithful people are not healed after eighty. Paul left a colleague behind ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and carried a thorn that was never removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Nothing suggests that Aeneas had more faith than anybody else on the plain. What the passage establishes is not a method but an authority, and the authority has not diminished. The timing is not ours to hold, and the day is coming when the whole plain of Sharon gets up.

Then should I still pray for healing? Yes, and boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them (James 5:14–15), and God often heals in answer to prayer, sometimes through doctors and medicine, sometimes beyond them. What we may not do is claim a guarantee, or tell a sick believer that his illness continues because his faith is weak. Pray as Jesus did in the garden: ask plainly for what you want, and add, not my will, but yours, be done. If healing comes, give Christ the glory. If it does not, he has promised grace sufficient for the weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9), and a resurrection body that will never be ill again.

On a Tuesday. When something good happens to you, a recovery, an answered prayer, a crisis averted, say out loud whose doing it was, as Peter did. Jesus Christ did this.
verseByVerse.note: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A disciple named Tabitha. Luke calls her a disciple using the feminine form of the word, mathētria, which appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Tabitha in Aramaic and Dorcas in Greek both mean gazelle: a woman known in both halves of a mixed port town, Joppa, modern Jaffa.

Full of good works. Full of is the phrase Luke used of Stephen: full of faith and of the Holy Spirit (6:5). He now uses it of a woman whose recorded output is coats. Luke evidently did not consider these to be different orders of achievement: faith working through love (Galatians 5:6).

In those days she became ill and died. In half a sentence she is gone, in a chapter full of healings, with an apostle eleven miles away. Luke does not soften it or account for it.

Her Lord’s compassion, stitched. Tabitha’s needle was doing in Joppa what her Lord had done in Galilee. Luke’s Gospel is full of Jesus’ care for widows (Luke 21:1–4; 20:47), and the God of Israel had always called himself protector of widows (Psalm 68:5). Her coats were not a side-activity of discipleship. They were the likeness of Christ, made in cloth.

Laid her in an upper room. The last detail matters most. In that climate burial usually followed death within the day; washing the body and laying it out was the first act, and interment ordinarily came next. They did the first and stopped. They put her upstairs, and they sent two men down the road. Nobody says why, but it is not hard to guess. They were hoping.

Why does God take his most useful servants? Scripture does not give us the reason in Tabitha’s case, and it would be presumption to invent one. What it does tell us is that our days are written in God’s book before one of them comes to be (Psalm 139:16), and that usefulness is not a shield against death. Godly people die young, and wicked men sometimes live long. The comfort is not that we can explain it but that the one who holds the days is good, and that for the believer, to die is gain (Philippians 1:21). The church in Joppa grieved as people who loved her, and they were right to. But they did not grieve as those who have no hope.

On a Tuesday. Be full of good works: not famous ones, but the kind that can be held up in a room after you are gone, the meal, the coat, the visit, the note. Ask what one thing you could make or do this week for someone who has no one to provide for them.

For worship. Christ sees the needle and thread. The Lord who will judge the world by what was done for the least of his brothers counted every garment Tabitha stitched as made for him, and he names a seamstress in a port town in the same breath as the first martyr.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the port from which Jonah sailed. Tabitha (Aramaic) and Dorcas (Greek) both mean “gazelle.”

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sent two men. Eleven miles: a long day’s round trip, and a body upstairs in a warm climate.

Please come to us without delay. The message does not say what for. It does not ask Peter to raise her or even name the woman. They have washed a corpse, declined to bury it, and sent for an apostle with an urgent request that says nothing about what they want. They had heard of Aeneas.

How people pray at the worst moments. Not with a clear petition properly framed, but with an urgent, half-formed sentence that cannot bring itself to ask for the thing it wants, because the thing is too large to say out loud. Come quickly is very often the whole of it. God is not put off by a badly drafted request. He had already told Moses that he heard the groaning of people who had not managed to compose a prayer at all (Exodus 2:23–25), and Paul says the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). What these disciples had was a dead friend, a road, and a conviction they could not articulate that it was worth fetching the man who knew Jesus. That turned out to be sufficient.

Joppa again. Joppa is the port where a prophet, ordered to preach to Gentiles, took ship in the opposite direction. On a roof in that town Peter will be told three times to take and eat what he has spent his life refusing, and will then go to a Gentile house. The call to the nations comes a second time at Joppa, and this time the man goes.

Something greater than Jonah. What makes the difference is not that Peter is braver than Jonah. It is that the greater Jonah has come. Jesus called himself the sign of Jonah to his generation and said, something greater than Jonah is here (Luke 11:29–32). The prophet who sailed from Joppa went down into the deep against his will, came up, and preached to Gentiles grudgingly. The Son of Man went down into death willingly, rose on the third day, and sent his own message to the nations with joy. The call that goes out from Joppa a second time is his call, and the one who now gives it has already been to the depths and back for the people he is calling.

On a Tuesday. In your grief, send for help. Do not wait until you can pray properly or explain what you need. Call a friend, call your pastor, call on the Lord with the six words you have.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda was about 11 miles from Joppa.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Showing tunics and other garments. Upstairs they are holding up the clothes, one after another, while they cry. It reads like the memory of somebody who was in that room (Luke 1:2). Her love had been made visible in cloth.

Who these women were. A widow without a son often had nothing between her and destitution but charity. These are the people whose neglect had caused an early dispute in the church (6:1). Luke recorded the failure. He records the remedy too, and the remedy has a name.

Put them all outside. Every move Peter makes is one he has seen before. His Lord had cleared a house in Galilee where a twelve-year-old girl lay dead (Mark 5:40), and Peter was one of only three disciples allowed in.

Tabitha, arise. What he said, very likely in Aramaic, was Tabitha, koum, one letter away from Talitha koum, the words Jesus had said to Jairus’s daughter with Peter in the room (Mark 5:41). He is reaching for the only precedent he has, because he was there when it worked.

Knelt down and prayed. But one thing he does that his Lord did not. Jesus took the child’s hand and told her to get up; there is no prayer because there did not need to be. Peter kneels beside a dead woman and asks for something he has no power to perform, and only then speaks. The words are nearly identical and the authority is entirely borrowed.

She sat up. The first face she sees is not the one she might have expected, and Luke lets us see it through her eyes.

On a Tuesday. Before you try to help anyone in a crisis, kneel. Whatever room you are walking into this week, a hospital ward, a grieving home, pray first and speak second, and remember that every good thing you bring is borrowed.

parallels.desc: “Talitha cumi”

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gave her his hand. The last thing Peter does is the most ordinary, what he did for the lame man at the temple gate (3:7) and what Jesus did for his mother-in-law (Mark 1:31).

Presented her alive. They had been put outside a few minutes earlier in tears with an armful of clothes. Presented her alive is the language Luke used of Jesus presenting himself alive to his apostles after his suffering (1:3): a picture of resurrection, and of whose resurrection lies behind this one.

The hard thing. Something has to be said, or the passage becomes an instrument of cruelty. Tabitha was raised. Every other Christian who died in Joppa that year stayed dead. Luke records two resurrections in the whole of Acts (here and Eutychus, 20:9–12) and the deaths of many believers, including James, one of the Twelve, executed by Herod with no rescue, in the same chapter in which prayer brought Peter out of prison (12:1–11). Whatever this passage is, it is not a description of what God routinely does when his people ask, and no one should be handed it as though it were.

A sign, not the destination. What it is, is a sign: not the destination but a board at the roadside with the destination’s name on it. Tabitha herself proves it, because she died again, and at her second funeral nobody sent to Lydda. What she was given was not immortality. It was a few more years of making coats, and a demonstration, in one upper room on one afternoon, of what the God of the resurrection intends to do universally and at once.

Where the comfort lies. The point is not that God might do this again for the person you have lost. The point is that he has announced, in a room in a port town, in front of witnesses whose story reached Luke, what he means to do for everybody who belongs to him. The widows got their friend back for a while. They will get her back for good.

Will we know our loved ones again? Scripture gives good reason to think so. Paul comforts grieving Christians not with a vague hope but with a reunion: the dead in Christ will rise, and we will be caught up together with them, and so we will always be with the Lord, therefore encourage one another (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). That comfort would mean nothing if we did not know each other. Moses and Elijah were known on the mount of transfiguration, and the risen Jesus was recognised by his friends. We will be changed, made like Christ, but not made into strangers. The widows of Joppa will hold Dorcas’s hands again, and they will know whose hands they are.

Can a modern person really believe this happened? The question is not whether dead people normally get up. Everyone in Joppa knew they do not, which is why they wept and washed the body. The real question is whether God exists and whether he raised Jesus. If the tomb in Jerusalem was empty, as the first witnesses insisted at the cost of their lives (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), then the raising of a seamstress in Joppa is not a strange exception to how the world works. It is a small sign from the One who made the world and has already begun to remake it. Luke, a careful historian who checked his sources (Luke 1:1–4), records it plainly, names the town, the woman and the house, and says that all Joppa knew. Some suggest such stories grew in the retelling; but Luke wrote within living memory, about a named town where people could still ask.

On a Tuesday. If you are grieving a believer who has died, do not let this story become a reproach, as though you had not prayed hard enough. Let it become a promise. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 aloud this week, and say the name of the one you have lost alongside it.

verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many believed in the Lord. The pattern of the whole section: the sign is not the point, the sign gets a hearing, and what people believe in is the Lord rather than the apostle.

Simon, a tanner. A tanner turned the hides of dead animals into leather, in solutions that included urine and dung. The work brought constant contact with carcasses, which under the law made a man unclean (Leviticus 11:39–40), and later Jewish law required tanneries to stand well outside the town (Mishnah, Bava Batra 2:9). And Peter, who will shortly say he has never eaten anything common or unclean (10:14), moves in and stays for weeks.

The touch that cleanses. Jesus touched a leper (Luke 5:13) and the bier of a dead young man (Luke 7:14), and the uncleanness did not pass to him; his cleanness passed to them. Peter, lodging among carcasses, is following the Holy One who came to the unclean, and who is about to send him into a Gentile house to do the same.

The house before the roof. On the roof of that house, over that smell, Peter will see the sheet let down (10:6). The vision that opens the door to the Gentile world is given to a man already sleeping under a roof no scrupulous Pharisee would have entered.

Whose house would you not stay in? It is worth asking. Not in theory, where everybody is generous, but in practice: the address that would need explaining, the household whose habits or history or trade would make it awkward. Peter had not yet worked out his theology of clean and unclean; he had merely accepted an invitation from a man who worked with dead animals. The theology came later, on the roof, and it came to a man who was already in the building.

Does this mean every scruple is just prejudice? No. Some lines are drawn by God’s word, and those we must keep whatever it costs: Christians may not join in idolatry or sexual sin, however welcoming the house. But many of our lines are drawn by custom, class, culture or temperament, and Christ is constantly stepping over them. The test is to ask, honestly and with an open Bible, whether a thing you avoid is forbidden by God or merely unfamiliar to you (Romans 14:1–4, 14). Peter’s food laws had once been God’s command, and in Christ they had been fulfilled and set aside (Mark 7:19). How much more should we hold loosely the barriers that were never commanded at all.

For worship. The bodies of the animals whose blood was brought into the holy place were burned outside the camp, and so Jesus also suffered outside the gate, to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:11–12). The Son of God went to the place where the town ended, the place of carcasses and shame, and made it the door into the household of God. Blessed be the one who went outside so that outsiders could be brought in.
verseByVerse.note: Tanners handled the skins of dead animals, a trade many Jews regarded as unclean — a hint of the lesson Peter is about to learn.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest picture of unconditional election and effectual calling. There was nothing in Saul to attract God’s grace (Philippians 3:4–6); God chose him according to his own purpose. Paul later wrote that his conversion was meant as a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. Election is not a closed door; it is the ground of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother, and they were afraid. It took Barnabas, the son of encouragement, to vouch for him.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person most openly opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to stop. That is a reason for prayer, and for being ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>7</sup>When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, <sup>8</sup>and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>21</sup>And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” <sup>22</sup>And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>30</sup>And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing <sup>31</sup>and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. <sup>32</sup>Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ <sup>33</sup>So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
This is one of the turning points of Acts, so important that Peter retells it in chapter 11 and again at the Jerusalem council (15:7–11). The gospel has reached Samaritans and one Ethiopian; now it reaches Gentiles as Gentiles. Cornelius, a Roman centurion at Caesarea, is a God-fearer: a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God but had not become a Jew by circumcision. God prepares both men, Cornelius by an angel and Peter by a vision on a rooftop in Joppa, and brings them together.

Peter goes to Caesarea and preaches Jesus, Lord of all, through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles as he did at Pentecost, and Peter has them baptised. The chapter settles that Gentiles are welcomed into God’s people by faith in Christ, without becoming Jews first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God prepares a Roman centurion by an angel and a Jewish apostle by a vision, and brings them together in Caesarea. Peter preaches Christ to a Gentile household, the Spirit falls on them while he is still speaking, and they are baptised.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean, and What the Food Laws Were For

The sheet is full of animals and the argument is about people, and Peter himself makes the translation at verse 28. The food laws had never been about digestion. They kept Israel visibly distinct from the nations at every meal. The vision retires a shadow rather than repealing a word: the separation was always temporary and always pointing forward, and its purpose was fulfilled when the dividing wall of hostility came down in Christ (Ephesians 2:14). And Peter did not reason his way from doctrine to table fellowship: he obeyed a command he found repellent and worked out the theology afterwards.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter needed a vision repeated three times, a word from the Spirit and the Spirit falling in front of witnesses before he would accept what he had been told plainly at the ascension. Now: The instinct to take the gospel only to people like ourselves is seldom held as a conviction; it is held as an assumption, which is why it survives so much preaching against it. Peter had a lifetime of habit, and God was patient enough to take three goes.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 10 is the great turning point of the book: the gospel goes to the Gentiles. Peter retells it twice (11:1–18; 15:7–11), because it settles for ever that Gentiles are welcomed into God’s people by faith in Christ, without becoming Jews first. Over the whole chapter stands one sentence of Peter’s: Jesus Christ is Lord of all (v. 36).

A man named Cornelius. Luke introduces the man carefully, and every detail makes the same double point: this is a most admirable man, and the hardest possible case for a Jewish church to welcome. Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea, built by Herod the Great with a harbour, a theatre and a temple to the emperor, and named after Caesar Augustus. Pilate governed from there; a stone bearing his name was found in its theatre in 1961. It was the most Roman city in the land.

A centurion of the Italian Cohort. A centurion commanded about eighty men, the professional backbone of the Roman army. Cornelius is the Roman occupation in person, the man who enforces the taxes and the crucifixions. And yet the centurions of the New Testament are almost always portrayed well, like the one whose faith astonished Jesus (Luke 7:2–10).

A devout man. He is devout, and he has brought his family and servants with him into the fear of God. His alms go to the people, which in Luke means the Jewish people, so a Roman officer was funding the poor of the nation he garrisoned. And he prays continually.

A God-fearer. What he is not is a convert. The God-fearer attached himself to the synagogue, believed in the God of Israel, kept what he could of the moral law, but had not been circumcised and so remained formally outside: too Jewish for his Roman friends, never quite Jewish enough for the congregation.

The best Gentile in the empire. If moral seriousness and religious sincerity were enough, this is the man they would be enough for. Yet the angel does not tell him he is fine. He tells him to send thirty miles down the coast for a fisherman with something to say. That cuts two ways at once. Nothing Cornelius had done had earned him anything, and yet God had noticed every bit of it and was already moving.

The rank that stood at the cross. Luke’s readers have met this rank before, at the foot of a cross. A centurion oversaw the crucifixion of Jesus, watched him die, and praised God, saying, Certainly this man was innocent (Luke 23:47). Now, in the capital of the province that executed him, another centurion is praying to the God of Israel without knowing the name of the man his fellow officer saw die. Before the chapter ends he will hear that the man hanged on a tree is Lord of all, Judge of the living and the dead, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness (vv. 36–43). The best Gentile in the empire needed exactly what the worst needed: not more devotion, but Christ.

On a Tuesday. God sees those who seek him outside the church: the colleague who asks careful questions, the decent man who gives more to charity than you do. Do not assume they are fine, and do not assume they are far away. Be ready to be the one God sends.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. A centurion commanded a company of about eighty soldiers. “God-fearers” were Gentiles who worshipped Israel’s God without becoming full converts.

parallels.desc: another centurion who loved the Jewish nation

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About the ninth hour of the day. Three in the afternoon, the hour of the evening sacrifice and of prayer (3:1). A Roman officer was keeping Jewish prayer times, and the angel arrived while he was doing it. Cornelius’s reaction is terror, as people in Scripture usually feel when they meet an angel.

As a memorial before God. The message has been misread in both directions. The vocabulary is taken from the sacrificial system. A memorial, mnēmosynon, was the portion of the grain offering that the priest burned on the altar, the token by which the whole offering came before God (Leviticus 2:2). So the angel tells an uncircumcised Roman soldier, who could not have carried a sacrifice past the outer court, that his prayers and his money have gone up like an offering God has noticed. The psalmist had prayed that his prayer would be counted as incense before God (Psalm 141:2). Cornelius’s had been.

The hour Jesus died. The ninth hour had gained a new meaning, though Cornelius did not know it. A few years earlier, about the ninth hour, Jesus had cried out with a loud voice and breathed his last outside Jerusalem (Luke 23:44–46). So a Gentile was keeping the hour of the evening sacrifice without knowing that the true sacrifice had already been offered. His prayers rose like the memorial portion; but a memorial is only a token, and it is the sacrifice that atones. The angel sends him to a man who will tell him of the Lamb whose once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:10) is the reason any sinner’s prayer can be welcome before God.

What it does not mean. His prayers and alms did not earn salvation: he still had to send for Peter to hear the message by which he would be saved (11:14). But neither is God indifferent to the groping of an honest man. The prayers of a Gentile who did not know the gospel were noticed and remembered, and God answered them by arranging a journey. That is a comfort to anyone praying for someone nowhere near the faith.

Does God hear the prayers of people who are not yet Christians? The Bible says plainly that no one comes to the Father except through Christ (John 14:6), and that the prayer of one who turns his ear from God’s law is an abomination (Proverbs 28:9). But God is not deaf to the cry of a person whom he is drawing to himself, and this verse shows him hearing such a cry and answering it, by sending the gospel. He does not answer it by saving the man without Christ; he answers it by bringing him to Christ. So if you are not yet a believer and have been praying in the dark, keep seeking. The answer God gives to that kind of prayer is himself, in his Son, through his word.

For worship. God remembers. The God who heard Hagar in the wilderness and Hannah at the tabernacle kept every prayer of a Roman soldier, and his answers are better than the prayers that asked for them. Cornelius asked for light. God sent him Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the hour of afternoon prayer. A “memorial” offering was one that brought the worshipper to God’s remembrance.

parallels.desc: the memorial portion

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Send men to Joppa. A genuine messenger from heaven, speaking to a man who wants God, does not preach the gospel. He gives a name, a town, a householder and a street.

On human breath. Angels in Scripture announce, warn, guide and rescue; they told shepherds of Christ’s birth (Luke 2:10), but in Acts they never preach the gospel to anyone. God’s settled arrangement is that the news of salvation travels on human breath, from someone who has it to someone who has not (Romans 10:14). It would have been simpler to let the angel say it; instead the whole apparatus of heaven is deployed to get a fisherman onto a road. We have this treasure in jars of clay (2 Corinthians 4:7). That is a great dignity conferred on ordinary Christians, and a great responsibility.

The name Jesus gave him. The angel uses the name Jesus had given. Simon was called Cephas, Peter, the rock, by Christ at their first meeting (John 1:42), and to this man, after he confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, the Lord promised the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 16:16–19). Those keys are turned by the preaching of the gospel. Peter turned them for Jews at Pentecost (2:14–41), and he is about to turn them for Gentiles in Caesarea. So even the address points to Christ: Cornelius is to send for the man whom Jesus named and commissioned, and what that man carries is the confession on which Christ builds his church.

A house by the sea. The angel distinguishes the two Simons, knows the second one’s trade, and knows the house is by the sea, as tanneries often were. Heaven gives its directions down to the street. And Cornelius is not told why, or what Peter will say. Most obedience arrives in that condition: enough instruction to act on and no explanation at all. (The King James adds that Peter would tell him what he ought to do; those words are not in the earliest manuscripts, and the angel’s fuller message is given at 11:14.)

Why did God not just let the angel tell him the gospel? Because God has chosen to spread the news of his Son through people who have received it themselves. A preacher who has been forgiven speaks of forgiveness as no angel can, for angels have never needed a Saviour. And the message binds the church together: the Gentile is brought in by the Jew, the hearer by the speaker, so that no one can boast of having found the way alone. It also means the job is yours. If an angel would not do it in Caesarea, an angel will not do it in your street.

parallels.desc: Simon the tanner

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He called two of his servants. Immediately, action. Cornelius does not wait to see whether the impression fades by morning. And the soldier he sends is devout, corroborating verse 2: a man under his command shared his faith closely enough to be trusted with this.

Having related everything. He sent them not with an instruction but with the whole story: a senior officer in a rigidly hierarchical profession sat his subordinates down and told them what had happened to him while he was praying. It explains the welcome Peter gets four days later, a room full of relatives and friends already assembled and briefed.

As the other centurion sent. At Capernaum a centurion with a dying servant sent elders to Jesus, saying he was not worthy to have him under his roof (Luke 7:3–7). Cornelius sends for the same reason: he needs what only Jesus can give. But Jesus is now risen and reigning, and he comes to a Gentile house in the word his servants preach.

On a Tuesday. When God speaks to you through his word, do not delay, and do not keep it to yourself. Tell the people closest to you what he has been showing you. Obedience that is spoken about tends to spread.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day. Luke cuts between the two ends of the story and lines up the timing: the messengers are perhaps an hour away, and Peter’s vision comes just as they arrive. God’s timing is not approximate.

On the housetop to pray. The flat roof, reached by an outside stair, was the coolest and most private place in the house, where a man went to be alone. The sixth hour is noon; the devout also prayed at midday (Psalm 55:17; Daniel 6:10).

He became hungry. Luke refuses to leave out the unspiritual detail. It is noon, the meal is cooking downstairs, and in the gap between the hunger and the food, God speaks to a hungry man in the language of food.

He fell into a trance. Ekstasis, a state in which ordinary perception is suspended and God communicates directly (22:17). The vision that opens the church to the whole non-Jewish world is given to a man on a roof, in a borrowed house that smelt of tanning. He had simply gone up to pray.

What Jesus went on doing. Luke called his Gospel an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (1:1), so Acts is what he goes on doing from heaven. The Lord who said his witnesses would go to the end of the earth (1:8) is now moving the last stage himself, setting a hungry apostle on a roof as the Gentiles reach the gate.

On a Tuesday. Peter was praying when God spoke. Keep your times of prayer, especially the unremarkable ones in the middle of a working day. You are not waiting for a vision; you are keeping company with the God who speaks through his word.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon. Flat roofs were used for prayer and rest.

verseByVerse.quote: and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavens opened. Luke uses the phrase sparingly and always when something changes permanently: at the Jordan (Luke 3:21), and when Stephen saw the Son of Man standing (7:56). The boundary has been crossed from the other side.

Something like a great sheet descending. Something like is Luke’s honesty when a witness describes an unfamiliar thing by the nearest familiar one: a large square of cloth, or a sail like those in the harbour below.

By its four corners. The prophets speak of God gathering the outcasts of Israel from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:12). Peter is watching something held at the four points of the compass, full of every kind of living creature. The shape of the vision announces its subject before a word is spoken: all nations.

It comes down. Peter does not go up. Heaven descends to where he is standing, which is what the rest of the chapter is about: God moving toward people who could not have come to him, on their own roofs, at lunchtime.

Why heaven stands open. Every other opened heaven in Luke’s two books has Jesus at its centre: the Spirit descending on him at the Jordan, the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand for Stephen. Jesus had told Nathanael that he would see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man (John 1:51). He is Jacob’s ladder, the one way between heaven and earth. So when heaven opens over a roof in Joppa, it is open because of him. The barrier between a holy God and the unclean nations was not lifted by a change of policy. It was removed by the Son who came down, died and ascended, and the sign that the nations are now to be gathered comes down by the way he opened.

parallels.desc: the heavens were opened

verseByVerse.quote: In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All kinds of animals. The categories are those Leviticus uses when it draws the lines (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14), and the sheet is not a selection: clean and unclean together, the pig beside the sheep, the vulture beside the pigeon. Contact with unclean creatures defiled a Jew; eating them was unthinkable.

Rise, Peter; kill and eat. Kill: do the butchering yourself, from the mixed sheet, out of creatures he had been taught before he could walk were an offence to God.

What martyrs had died for. And it was not a marginal scruple. Under the Greek king Antiochus two centuries earlier, a mother had watched her sons killed rather than eat pork, and the books of the Maccabees that recorded it were treasured. Refusing unclean food was what martyrs had died for, and everybody knew the stories. So the command is an instruction to do the very thing faithful Israelites had gone to their deaths refusing to do, and it comes from heaven, from a voice Peter will call Lord. That is why the next verse holds one of the most understandable refusals in Scripture, and why God has to say it three times.

The one whom uncleanness could not touch. The command makes sense only because of who had come. Under the law, uncleanness spread: touch a leper or a corpse and you were defiled. Then Jesus touched a leper, and the leprosy left him (Luke 5:13). He took a dead girl by the hand, and she rose (Luke 8:54). A woman unclean for twelve years touched his garment, and she did not make him unclean; he made her whole (Luke 8:43–48). In him holiness ran the other way. The food laws had trained Israel to guard the clean from the unclean. Now the Holy One himself had come, and his cleanness was the stronger.

The animals were the vehicle; the freight was people. One guard, because this passage is pressed into service for arguments it was not given for. It does bear on what Christians may eat: the New Testament is clear that no food is unclean in itself, and Mark says so in an aside (Mark 7:19). But Peter himself tells us what the vision was for, and it is not a menu: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean (v. 28). The passage is used most faithfully when it dismantles the habit the food laws had come to enforce, the sorting of human beings into those one can sit down with and those one cannot. That habit long outlived the dietary code, and it has never needed a Bible verse to keep it going.

For worship. The God who drew the lines in Leviticus is the God who erased them in Christ, faithful in both. He kept Israel distinct until the promised Seed came, and then lowered a sheet over a roof in Joppa. His purposes were always heading for a table with every nation at it.
verseByVerse.note: The sheet held both clean and unclean creatures together, all of which Peter is told to eat.

parallels.desc: clean and unclean animals

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By no means, Lord. Two words that will not go together: absolutely not, and Lord. The sentence contradicts itself before he has finished it. He stands where Ezekiel stood when he protested against eating defiled food (Ezekiel 4:14).

A recognisable habit. It is not the first time: Depart from me (Luke 5:8); You shall never wash my feet (John 13:8); Far be it from you, Lord (Matthew 16:22). He is the disciple who tells Jesus what will not be happening, and calls him Lord while doing it.

Jonah’s port. Joppa was where Jonah took ship the other way when God sent him to Gentile Nineveh (Jonah 1:3). Centuries later a Jewish prophet in Joppa is again told to go to the Gentiles, and again his first word is no. What lies between the two men is Christ, the greater Jonah who has already been through the deep for the nations (Matthew 12:39–41), so this reluctant prophet needs no storm and no fish, only a word repeated three times.

Common or unclean. Common means ritually unfit, for ordinary use rather than for God. Peter’s lifetime record is to his credit: he has never once done it. He is defending God’s own law, kept at cost, and he is defending it against God.

Holding the scaffolding. What Peter cannot let go of is not a sin but an obedience, a genuine one, kept faithfully for decades. God has not grown lax; the command had a purpose, the purpose has arrived, and Peter is holding on to the scaffolding after the building is up. Christians who are stuck are often stuck on something that was once right, was kept at cost, and has quietly become the thing they will not let God touch. Peter’s by no means, Lord is not a rebel’s sentence. It is a good man defending a good thing at the moment God is moving past it. And there is a quieter danger in a long record of obedience: it can become the thing we stand on before God, and then the people who lack that record begin to look unclean to us. Peter’s clean record could not save him any more than Cornelius’s alms could save Cornelius; both men needed the same Christ (v. 43).

How do I tell a good conviction from a scaffold I should take down? Ask where it comes from and what it is for. If a conviction rests on a plain command of Scripture that still applies to Christians, keep it, whatever it costs: no vision overturns the moral law. But if it rests on a custom, a tradition, or an Old Testament ceremony that the New Testament says has been fulfilled in Christ, hold it loosely, and be ready to let it go when it starts to keep people at a distance whom Christ has welcomed. Peter did not change his mind because he felt like it; he changed because God himself spoke. We have the finished word of God for that, not new visions, and the New Testament is clear on which lines have been taken down (Colossians 2:16–17).

For worship. Peter put never and Lord into one sentence, and the Lord answered the second word, not the first. He hears our protests and outlasts them, not by crushing the protester but by speaking again.
verseByVerse.note: “Common” means ritually unfit, profane.

parallels.desc: “I have never defiled myself”

verseByVerse.quote: And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What God has made clean, do not call common. Note the tense and the agent: the thing has already been done, and Peter’s part is to stop describing it wrongly. A fact has altered and his vocabulary is out of date. And the correction is aimed at his speech: do not call. Within thirteen verses he will make the translation himself: I should not call any person common or unclean (v. 28).

Made clean at Golgotha. The tense is past because the work is finished. The food laws had separated Israel from the nations (Leviticus 20:24–26), and Paul says that Christ abolished the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, to create in himself one new man in place of the two, and to reconcile both to God in one body through the cross (Ephesians 2:14–16). The line was not worn away by time or repealed by a council. It was fulfilled and taken down by a death, and what it had pictured is now the substance, which belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). The voice on the roof is announcing an accomplished fact, and the fact has a name: Jesus Christ crucified.

Heard but not grasped. Jesus had already declared all foods clean (Mark 7:18–19), and Peter had been standing there. He had heard it and not drawn the conclusion, a sobering thought for anyone who assumes that hearing good teaching is the same as being changed by it.

This happened three times. Three denials by a charcoal fire, three questions on a beach (John 21:15–17), and now three times the vision comes. God appears to know exactly how many repetitions this particular man requires.

Taken up at once. The vision does not end with an application. It leaves a man on a roof with a command he has refused and no idea what it is for. A great deal of Christian experience happens there: the instruction received and the meaning not yet arrived, and nothing to do but wait until somebody knocks at the gate.

Where Christians differ: are the food laws binding today? Some groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists and some Messianic Jews, still keep the Old Testament food laws, often out of an earnest wish to honour all of Scripture. This commentary’s view: Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19); this vision confirms it; Paul teaches that food is a matter of freedom (Romans 14:14, 20; 1 Timothy 4:3–5). The food laws were shadows fulfilled in Christ. Christians are free to eat anything with thanksgiving, though they should be considerate of the weaker conscience (Romans 14:15).

Then why did God give the food laws at all? Not because pork was wicked or sheep were holy, but to teach and to protect. Day by day, at every meal, the food laws taught Israel that she was set apart for a holy God, and that holiness means distinction (Leviticus 11:44–45; 20:25–26). They also kept her from being swallowed by the nations around her until the Messiah came. When Christ came, the true holiness they pictured arrived in him, and the people of God was no longer to be marked by a diet but by faith in him, gathered from every nation. The laws were not a mistake that God corrected. They were a signpost, and Peter was standing at the place it pointed to.

On a Tuesday. Do not call unclean anyone God has made clean in Christ. Think of a Christian whose background or past makes you uneasy, and do one concrete thing about it: an invitation, a phone call, a seat beside him on Sunday.

parallels.desc: he declared all foods clean

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Inwardly perplexed. Thoroughly at a loss, and Luke says it twice. The apostle received a revelation from heaven, repeated three times, and did not know what it meant. The vision was about food and not about food, and there was no way to get from the sheet to the Gentiles by thinking harder.

Perplexed before. It was not the first time. Luke’s Gospel records the disciples failing again and again to understand what Jesus told them about his death: the saying was hidden from them (Luke 9:45; 18:34). The women at the empty tomb were perplexed (Luke 24:4), and the meaning came only when the risen Lord opened the disciples’ minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). The same Lord is at work on this roof. He does not leave his servants holding riddles. He explains himself in his own time, and the explanation always leads back to him: the sheet will make sense in a Gentile house, while Peter is telling them about Jesus.

Stood at the gate. While the vision is still unresolved, its answer is standing in the street asking for Peter by name.

Understood by obeying. The meaning comes not by further revelation but through events: Peter will understand the sheet by obeying the knock. Some things are understood only when they are acted on, and God often explains his word by his providence.

verseByVerse.quote: And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit said to him. Three parties are being moved in this chapter, and none can see the others: Cornelius has an angel and an address, the messengers a road, Peter a sheet of animals. Here the wiring becomes visible, and it is the Spirit himself who speaks, a person who directs, sends and commands.

Three men are looking for you. The number is exact, two servants and a soldier (v. 7), and without hesitation does more than steady Peter’s nerves. The Greek, mēden diakrinomenos, can also be rendered making no distinction. The verb means to divide, to sort one thing from another, and it is the verb Peter uses in his report at Jerusalem (11:12) and the idea he returns to at the council, where he says God made no distinction between us and them (15:9). So the Spirit’s word is not merely do not dither. It is do not sort these men into a category, and it forbids the reflex before it can operate.

For I have sent them. That last clause governs the whole chapter. Peter is not told who Cornelius is or what the vision meant. When the Jerusalem church calls him to account, this is what he produces: the Spirit told me to go with them (11:12).

The Spirit of Jesus. The Spirit who speaks on the stairs is not a free-floating influence. Jesus, exalted, had poured him out (2:33), and Luke will call him the Spirit of Jesus (16:7). The Spirit sends Peter to Gentiles because Christ has already claimed them, and his work, as Jesus promised, is to bear witness about Christ (John 15:26).

How does the Spirit lead Christians today? Here the Spirit spoke directly to an apostle at a turning point in the founding of the church, and we should not expect such words as our normal guidance. Today the Spirit leads us chiefly through the Scriptures he inspired, which are complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17), by opening our understanding of them, by working in our hearts a desire to obey, and by ordering our circumstances in his providence. And the direction he gives in Scripture is unmistakable on this very point: we are to make no distinction among those Christ has received. You do not need a voice on the stairs to know you should welcome the stranger at the gate.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter went down to the men and said, "I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?" And they said, "Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the one. Peter goes down and opens with a flat, practical sentence. The Spirit gave him the instruction and withheld the explanation, and he is about to get it from three strangers at a gate.

Upright and God-fearing. Their answer is a small masterpiece of diplomacy. They lead with the awkward fact, a centurion; then what a Jewish hearer would most want to know, upright and God-fearing; then well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation; and the clincher, directed by a holy angel to send for you. They had probably rehearsed it on the road, knowing how unlikely their errand sounded.

To hear what you have to say. That is the whole invitation: not to be healed or impressed, but to hear. Most preachers spend their lives trying to get people to listen; here is a man who sent servants on a journey of days to secure a hearing for a message he could not yet describe.

The voice of the Shepherd. What Peter has to say is not a set of ideas but a person. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), and Peter’s message will be a man: anointed, crucified, raised, appointed Judge, offering forgiveness in his name (vv. 38–43). Jesus had said that he had other sheep, not of this fold, whom he must bring also, and that they would listen to his voice, so that there would be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16). Some of those sheep were waiting in Caesarea. The servants at the gate were fetching more than a preacher. They were fetching the voice of the Shepherd.

On a Tuesday. The world around you is often more ready to hear about Christ than you think, and what people need from you is not your opinions but his word. If someone asks you a question about your faith this week, do not change the subject. Say what you have to say, simply and kindly.

verseByVerse.quote: So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His guests. Peter takes two Gentile servants and a Roman soldier into the house for the night. That means beds and a meal, and a meal means a table, precisely what a devout Jew did not share with Gentiles and precisely what the vision had been about. The man who had said by no means, Lord before lunch had Gentiles eating in his lodgings by supper. He did not resolve his theology first; that comes in verse 28. He obeyed one step at a time, and the first step was having them in the house.

The table Jesus kept. Peter had learned this from his Master. He had watched Jesus go in to Zacchaeus while the crowd grumbled that he had gone to be the guest of a sinner (Luke 19:5–7), and recline at Levi’s feast among tax collectors, saying, I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Luke 5:29–32). Hospitality in the church is not good manners added to the gospel; it is the gospel acted out, because Christ welcomed us when we were strangers to God (Romans 15:7). Peter had sat at those tables as a guest. Now he was laying one.

The next day. Joppa to Caesarea is about thirty miles and the men had already walked it. He gave them a night’s rest first, a small kindness Luke did not have to record.

Some of the brothers. At Jerusalem we learn there were six of them (11:12), because Peter had them beside him when the church demanded an explanation. A man does not take six witnesses on a pastoral visit. Whatever happened in Caesarea would be examined and possibly disbelieved, and it is a leader making his account checkable before anyone has asked.

Why does it matter that Peter brought witnesses? Because the gospel is not a private experience but public truth, and God wanted the church to receive the Gentiles on the basis of evidence, not on one man’s say-so. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Peter brought six. There is wisdom here for any Christian or leader involved in something sensitive: act in the open, bring others with you, keep your conduct checkable. Integrity that welcomes scrutiny protects both the leader and the people he serves.

On a Tuesday. Hospitality often comes before the gospel. Open your home this week to someone outside your usual circle: a meal, a coffee, a bed for the night. Christ welcomed you first.

For worship. Christ is the host of a supper so large that his servants are sent into the roads and lanes to compel people to come in, until his house is filled (Luke 14:23). Two servants and a soldier asleep in a tanner’s house were among the first guests brought in from the lanes of the Gentile world.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa to Caesarea was a journey of about 30 miles.

parallels.desc: six brothers accompanied me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Expecting them. Cornelius has spent four days on this, and meanwhile has been going round Caesarea inviting people to hear a man he has never met. A serving officer has told his family and friends, probably brother officers too, that an angel told him to send for a Jewish fisherman; if nothing came of it he would look ridiculous for years. That is faith expecting something, and love too: he wanted the people he loved to hear.

He filled a room. The first thing this man does with something from God is gather a congregation. The Gentile mission begins in a house full of somebody’s relatives, because a Roman soldier could not think of a reason to hear this alone.

Fell down at his feet. Then Peter arrives, and Cornelius does the wrong thing. The verb, prosekynēsen, means to prostrate oneself in reverence, the ordinary word for worship. Be fair to him. Four days ago an angel stood in his house and told him to send for this man, and in the world Cornelius grew up in, when something from heaven turns up you get on the floor. His is an error of reverence, made by a man who does not yet know what he is dealing with, and it is corrected in the next verse, immediately and kindly.

A light for the Gentiles. Simeon, waiting in the temple, called the infant Jesus a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32). Now, in the most Gentile house in Judea, a room full of people is waiting for the same light. Cornelius goes to the floor because he takes the messenger for the thing itself. But something worthy of worship has indeed come to his door, carried in Peter’s mouth.

parallels.desc: “You must not do that”

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter lifted him up, saying, "Stand up; I too am a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I too am a man. Not, you are embarrassing me. I too am a man: on the same side of the floor, made of the same material. And he reaches down, takes hold of a Roman centurion and puts him back on his feet. The first thing Peter does in the first Gentile home to hear the gospel is pick a man up off the floor.

Two scenes in Caesarea. Two chapters later a king in this same city will accept exactly the acclaim Peter refuses, the voice of a god and not of a man, and Luke records his end in one unsparing verse (12:21–23). Paul and Barnabas will refuse worship at Lystra (14:14–15), and the angel refuses it from John (Revelation 19:10).

Harder than it looks. Cornelius’s reverence was genuine, and refusing it risked chilling the room. There is a false humility that deflects with one hand and enjoys the compliment with the other. Ministries that last are built on Peter’s refusal, and many that collapse stopped making it somewhere.

What Jesus did not refuse. The apostles and angels refuse worship. Jesus accepted it, from the disciples in the boat (Matthew 14:33), and from Thomas, who called him my Lord and my God (John 20:28). He never once said, Stand up; I too am a man. Either he was the most dangerous blasphemer who ever lived, or he is God.

Where Christians differ: veneration of saints and leaders. Some traditions bow before popes, saints or images; Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians distinguish that honour from the worship due to God alone, and many are sincere in it. This commentary’s view: Peter, whom Rome calls the first pope, refused to let anyone bow before him. No servant of Christ should receive the reverence due to God.

Is it wrong to honour Christian leaders? No. Scripture tells us to respect and esteem those who labour among us and are over us in the Lord, very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13), and to remember our leaders and imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7). The line is crossed when honour becomes reverence, when a leader is treated as beyond question, his words as equal to Scripture, or his presence as bringing us nearer to God. Healthy honour says, thank God for this man. Idolatry says, I cannot do without him. A good pastor will do what Peter did and lift you back on your feet.

For worship. There is one before whom falling down is right, and he too lifts the fallen. When John fell at his feet as though dead, the risen Christ laid his right hand on him and said, Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one (Revelation 1:17–18). Glory to the one at whose feet it is safe to fall.

parallels.desc: we also are men, of like nature with you
