verseByVerse.quote: And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many persons gathered. Peter walks into a Gentile house, sees a room full of Gentiles, and opens by naming the barrier, to the people it applies to. He does not begin with something warm and general and hope nobody raises it. The word athemiton means taboo, not done, and the God-fearers in that room had felt it most: welcome at the synagogue door and not past it.

Two things about the barrier. The law of Moses nowhere forbids a Jew to enter a Gentile house. What had grown up was a dense hedge of custom around the purity laws, until strict Jews would not enter Gentile homes or eat with Gentiles (John 18:28; Galatians 2:12). And it had once had a real purpose: a people surrounded by empires that swallowed nations whole survived by not eating with them.

God has shown me. The vision was about animals; Peter says it was about persons, and nobody had told him that. On the coast road with three Gentiles for company, he worked out what he had been shown: no human being is unclean in God’s sight because of race or nation.

The doorway Jesus was led through. John’s Gospel gives this custom a sharp edge. On the morning of the crucifixion the chief priests would not go into the Roman governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled but could eat the Passover (John 18:28). They stood outside. Jesus was taken in. The true Passover Lamb was led across the threshold they would not cross, condemned in a Gentile house by a Gentile judge, and crucified by Gentile soldiers, for Jew and Gentile alike. Peter steps through a Roman doorway now because his Lord went through one first, and went through it to die.

Naming the barrier. Peter’s honesty is part of why the room could trust him. He had not come to tell them the division never existed. He had come to tell them who had ended it.

Does this mean every human being is already clean before God? No. Peter is speaking about race and nation, not about sin. No one is unclean because he is a Gentile, a Roman, or anything else he was born. But every one of us, Jew and Gentile alike, is unclean because of sin, and needs to be washed (Romans 3:23). That is why Peter goes on to preach forgiveness through Christ (v. 43). The barrier of nationality has been removed so that the gospel can reach everyone; the barrier of sin is removed only by the blood of Christ, received by faith. Both truths have to be held together, or we end either with racism or with universalism.

On a Tuesday. Name your own barrier. Is there a group of people you were raised to look down on, or simply to avoid? Say it honestly to God, and then cross the room. Christ broke the wall down at the cross; walk through the gap, beginning with the wall nearest you.
verseByVerse.note: The law did not forbid visiting Gentiles, but Jewish custom treated a Gentile home as unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without objection. It is not quite the whole truth: he had said by no means, Lord, until God repeated himself three times. But once he was sent for, he raised nothing. The arguing was finished on the roof.

The one who came without objection. Peter’s journey, made after three refusals, sits inside a far longer journey made with none. The Son of God came from the Father’s side into a world that was not merely unclean but hostile, and the letter to the Hebrews gives his words on coming as, Behold, I have come to do your will, O God (Hebrews 10:7). He needed no vision repeated three times. He came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10), and he went further than any centurion’s parlour: to a cross. Every servant who goes without objection follows, at a great distance, the Lord who came without one.

Why you sent for me. He has a vision, a word from the Spirit and the authority of an apostle, and the first thing he does in that house is ask and wait. Cornelius’s account of the angel, told to a room that has waited four days for it, establishes that the meeting was arranged from heaven at both ends. Peter could have asserted that. He asked, and let his host establish it.

On a Tuesday. Ask before you tell. The next time you have a conversation about faith, begin by asking the other person what has been happening in his life, and listen properly before you speak.

For worship. The Lord who turned Peter’s by no means into without objection is the God who works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). He does not merely command; he changes the heart that hears the command.

verseByVerse.quote: And Cornelius said, "Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four days ago. The angel’s message appears twice in one chapter and a third time in the next. Luke repeats what matters. (The King James has Cornelius say he was fasting; the earliest manuscripts do not mention it.)

In bright clothing. Two men in dazzling apparel stood by the women at the empty tomb (Luke 24:4), and two in white robes at the ascension (1:10); in each the news is about Jesus. This angel has only an address to give, but he belongs to the same story: the crucified man is alive, and he is Lord.

Your prayer has been heard. Neither telling in this chapter gives the angel’s message more than that, and the order to send for Peter. Reporting to Jerusalem, Peter adds the clause the reader has not yet been given: the angel said Peter would declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household (11:14).

The question the third telling settles. That clause settles the question this chapter otherwise leaves open, and it is the question every thoughtful reader asks about Cornelius. He was devout, God-fearing, generous and prayerful, and his prayers went up before God like an offering. Was he then already saved, and was Peter merely bringing information? The angel’s own words say no. He was told to send for a man who would tell him how to be saved, which means that on the day the angel appeared, with all that piety behind him, he was not.

Hard and kind. It is a hard sentence and a kind one. Hard, because it will not allow the comfortable conclusion that sincerity is enough and the gospel an optional refinement. Kind, because of what God did about it. He did not leave the honest seeker to his sincerity. He sent an angel and a vision, and moved an apostle down the coast against every instinct he had, to get the message to one Roman officer and his household. God is so far from indifferent to the man reaching after him in the dark that he will rearrange the church to reach him.

On a Tuesday. Tell what God has done for you. Your story, told simply and honestly, can open hearts that an argument would close: what you were, how Christ met you, what he has done since. It need not be dramatic to be his.

verseByVerse.quote: "Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.' So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Kind enough to come. A courtesy a Roman officer did not owe a Jewish fisherman: Cornelius recognises that Peter crossed something to get here.

In the presence of God. Cornelius’s last sentence is worth learning by heart. We are all here: nobody is missing. In the presence of God: they are not primarily aware of Peter; they know whose house this has become. To hear all: not the parts that suit them, all of it. That you have been commanded by the Lord: they do not expect Peter’s opinions. They assume he is under orders and that they are about to hear what the orders were.

Commanded by the Lord. Peter had indeed been commanded, by the risen Lord who sent the apostles to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19–20), and within minutes he will say so (v. 42). The preacher stands under the Lord Jesus, and the sermon is Christ’s own message about himself.

A model congregation. Few preachers have ever walked into a better room, and it did not happen by accident: behind it lie four days of telling a garrison town, and years of praying and giving (v. 2). Many of us hear preaching expecting some of it to be interesting, and respond by assessing it. Cornelius’s household came expecting to be commanded by God through a man, and the Holy Spirit fell on them before he had finished. Those two facts are probably connected.

What if the preaching at my church is poor? Then pray for your preacher, and come anyway in the presence of God. Cornelius’s words do not depend on the preacher’s eloquence but on the hearer’s expectation that God will speak through his word. Where a sermon faithfully opens Scripture, God is speaking, even if the delivery is plain. You can help by preparing: read the passage beforehand, pray for the preacher, arrive in time, and listen for what God is commanding rather than for what entertains. If the preaching is not faithful to Scripture, that is a different and more serious matter, to be raised lovingly with the elders. But most of us need to bring more to church before we complain about what we take away.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter opened his mouth. The formula for a weighty speech (8:35), and this is the first sermon ever preached to a Gentile household. Its first words are an admission: not, as I have always taught, but, I am now getting it.

The face-receiver. The Greek word, prosōpolēmptēs, is a vivid compound meaning one who receives the face: who judges by who somebody visibly is. It is courtroom language for a judge who decides by looking at the parties. The compound first appears here, but the picture behind it is Old Testament: Moses says that God is not partial, literally that he does not lift faces (Deuteronomy 10:17). He is exactly the magistrate who does not take the face. And Peter says it while looking at a room of faces he had been raised to sort. He had known the principle all his life; he is saying that he has finally seen where it goes. Paul builds on the same truth: God shows no partiality (Romans 2:11), and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28).

Even his enemies said it. Peter had watched this impartiality walking about. In the last week in Jerusalem, spies sent to trap Jesus opened with flattery that was nonetheless true: Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality (Luke 20:21). He had touched lepers and dined with Pharisees, healed a centurion’s servant and a synagogue ruler’s daughter. The God who does not take the face had shown his own glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and that face turned toward the poor, the foreign and the despised as readily as toward anyone. What Peter now understands about God, he had watched for some three years in the Son.

In the flow. Peter states his thesis here, and the sermon supplies the ground: God shows no partiality because Jesus Christ is Lord of all (v. 36), and everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness (v. 43). The sermon opens with the open door and closes with the only way through it.

Acceptable to him. Acceptable, dektos, means welcome. Nationality is no barrier. God welcomes the one who fears him, from any nation.

Where Christians differ: are sincere seekers saved without the gospel? Inclusivists, Christians who believe that Christ’s death can save some who never hear of him, read this verse to mean that people who fear God and do right, in whatever religion, may be saved through Christ without knowing his name. They hold it out of real compassion for those who never hear. This commentary’s view: Cornelius was not yet saved: the angel said Peter would bring a message by which he would be saved (11:14). “Acceptable” means acceptable as a candidate, someone God welcomes to hear the gospel, regardless of nation. The verse removes ethnic barriers, not the need for Christ. Peter goes straight on to preach that forgiveness comes through faith in Jesus (v. 43).

What about those who never hear? It is the question behind the question, and it is asked with real anguish. Scripture is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (4:12; Romans 10:13–17), and that everyone has enough light in creation and conscience to be without excuse (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). It also tells us that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), and that infants dying in infancy who are among God’s elect are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest their grief on that good and merciful Judge. What Scripture never does is offer the unevangelised as a reason for the church to relax. Its answer to the question is this chapter: God moved heaven and earth to get the gospel to one man. The right response to the question is not speculation but mission.

On a Tuesday. God did not choose you by your face, and neither should you sort others by theirs. Notice this week whose company you seek out and whom you dismiss, and ask whether the face is deciding for you.

parallels.desc: God is not partial

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the word that he sent to Israel. Peter begins the story where it began. The gospel came to the Jews first, and he states it in a Gentile drawing room without embarrassment: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16).

Good news of peace. The phrase is out of Isaiah, where a runner comes over the hills with news that the war is over: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace (Isaiah 52:7). Peter stands before a professional soldier using the vocabulary of a herald announcing the end of hostilities. And the peace is double: peace with God for sinners who were his enemies, his just anger turned aside because Christ bore it (Romans 5:1, 9–10), and peace between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14–17).

He is Lord of all. Then, dropped into the sentence like a bracket, the largest claim in the chapter. The Greek puts all first: of all, he is Lord. Peter is speaking to an officer of an empire whose creed was that Caesar is lord, in a city named after Caesar, and he says it in an aside (Romans 10:12).

Why it matters here. Peter has just said that God shows no partiality, and here is the ground. The gospel cannot be kept inside one nation, not because God has become broad-minded, but because the man at its centre owns everything. A local Lord may have a local people. A Lord of all has no outsiders, only subjects who have not yet been told. Peter was brought to a house he would never have entered, because the one who sent him already owned the address.

What does it mean in practice that Jesus is Lord of all? It means there is no part of the world, and no part of your life, outside his rule. He is Lord of the nations, so no people is beyond the reach of the gospel. He is Lord of governments, so rulers are accountable to him and Christians obey them under him, not instead of him (4:19). He is Lord of your work, your money, your body, your evenings and your relationships. The confession Jesus is Lord was the earliest Christian creed (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3), and it was dangerous precisely because it left Caesar no room to be ultimate. It still leaves nothing else room: not career, not comfort, not self.

Is it arrogant to call Jesus Lord of all, as Peter does in a Gentile house? Only if Christians had invented him or earned their place under him. But the claim is not that Christians are better than other people; Peter has just admitted, in front of Gentiles, that God had to correct him. The claim is about Jesus, and it stands or falls with the resurrection Peter is about to describe (vv. 40–41). If he rose, he is Lord whether anyone likes it or not, and keeping quiet about it would be the unkind thing. And look at the terms of his welcome: the respectable and the outcast come in exactly the same way, as people who receive forgiveness, not as people who have earned it (v. 43). A message that humbles everyone equally is the opposite of arrogance.

For worship. The Lord of all could have come to Caesarea as Rome had come, with standards and a garrison. He came preaching peace, and paid for it himself, making peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). Every other lord of the earth has made his peace by killing his enemies. This one made it by dying for them.

parallels.desc: who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: "you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beginning from Galilee. The story of a Galilean preacher had been talked of in the province for some three years and had ended in a public execution sixty miles away. So Peter starts where the public record starts: not a philosophy but an account of what a particular man did, within living memory, offered to people who could check it. His outline is the very shape of Mark’s Gospel, and early tradition says that Mark wrote down Peter’s preaching.

Anointed with the Holy Spirit. Anointed is the verb behind Christ, so Peter is explaining the title to a room that has not grown up with the vocabulary. Kings and priests were anointed with oil; this one with the Spirit, at his baptism (Luke 3:22; 4:18): the Father anointing the Son with the Holy Spirit.

Oppressed by the devil. To be oppressed is to be tyrannised, held down under a cruel power. Peter sums up Jesus’ whole ministry of healing and deliverance as a rescue operation, prising people loose from the devil’s grip. The phrase reaches wider than open demon-possession, though not every illness is a direct demonic act. It gathers up all whom the devil’s dark dominion held, for behind the reign of sickness, bondage and death in a fallen world stand “the works of the devil,” and “the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy” them (1 John 3:8). Jesus himself called a crippled woman one “whom Satan bound for eighteen years” (Luke 13:16).

The great Liberator. So every healing was a liberation and a preview of total victory. Jesus came as the stronger man who binds the strong man and plunders his house (Mark 3:27): “if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). And he pressed it to the end: at the cross he “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15), and through death destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). Whatever cruel power has held a person down, Jesus is mightier, and he rescues us “from the domain of darkness” into his own kingdom (Colossians 1:13; Acts 26:18).

For God was with him. Peter speaks here of Jesus’ true humanity: a man anointed by the Spirit, in whom the Father was at work. In the same sermon he calls him Lord of all and Judge (vv. 36, 42). The eternal Son did not lay aside his deity; he lived his human life in dependence on the Spirit, which is why he can be our pattern as well as our Saviour.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit who anointed Jesus now lives in you, so go about doing good today, as he did. Not grand deeds, but the next good thing: the visit, the repair, the meal, the word of comfort.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s outline of Jesus’ life resembles the shape of Mark’s Gospel.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me

verseByVerse.quote: "And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are witnesses. Peter says it before he says anything about the cross, and again in the next verse. Everything rests on the claim that the men saying it were there (1:8; 2:32).

Hanging him on a tree. Then the death, and the way he puts it would have made a Jewish hearer flinch. He does not say crucified, which is the ordinary word and the one Cornelius would have expected from a Roman perspective. He reaches instead for a phrase out of Deuteronomy, a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23): the law about a body left on a tree, which every Jew knew and which was the standing objection to the whole Christian claim. A crucified Messiah was a cursed Messiah, and that was the end of the argument.

The objection as the description. Peter does not avoid the scandalous word; he puts it in the sermon. Paul later takes the same verse and shows what it is for: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). So the church understood from very early on that the worst thing about the crucifixion was the point of it. He bore the curse that was ours.

But God raised him on the third day. One conjunction carries the whole gospel. They put him to death; God raised him. Two subjects, two verbs, and the second reverses the first. In these early sermons the resurrection is consistently something done to Jesus by God. Not only that he rose, though that is true, but that God raised him, which is the language of a verdict. A court had ruled; a higher court has set the ruling aside. What men called a curse, God called his Son, and said so by emptying the grave. And he made him to appear, literally gave him to become visible: real appearances, to real people, which leads straight into the strangest sentence in the sermon.

What does it mean that Jesus became a curse for us? The curse is God’s just sentence on sin, the opposite of his blessing (Deuteronomy 27:26; Galatians 3:10). Everyone who breaks his law is under it. On the cross, Jesus, who had never sinned, took that sentence in our place: God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is penal substitution: the penalty was real, the substitute was Christ, and the debt was paid in full. So if you trust in him, there is no curse left for you. It fell on him at Golgotha, and the empty tomb is God’s announcement that it has been exhausted.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to think that God is against you because of your sins, look at the tree and say slowly: he became a curse for me.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chosen by God as witnesses. It is an unlikely thing for an inventor of a story to include. A man fabricating a resurrection would hardly concede that the risen figure was not shown to the general public. Peter raises the difficulty himself, unprompted.

Why not to everybody? Scripture does not fully explain it, and it is honest to say so. But the logic is not hard to see. A public appearance in the temple courts would have compelled belief of a kind, the kind a man cannot get out of, and God’s consistent way is to give sufficient evidence to those who will testify rather than overwhelming evidence to those who will not. And there was to be a definite, nameable, countable body of witnesses, so that the church’s claim would rest on people who could be found and questioned rather than on a rumour that everybody had heard from somebody (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). God chose to spread the news by witness, not by spectacle, because faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (John 20:29).

Who ate and drank with him. Then the proof Peter chooses: not we saw him, but we had meals with him. A hallucination shared by a dozen men does not take bread and hand it round. The risen Christ ate broiled fish in front of them (Luke 24:41–43) and made breakfast on a beach (John 21:12–13). Ghosts do not eat, and no lash or sword could talk the apostles out of what they had seen.

Does it matter whether the resurrection was physical? Everything depends on it. If Christ was raised only as a spirit, then death has not been defeated, only survived, and our bodies have no future. But the New Testament insists that the same body that was laid in the tomb came out of it, transformed and glorified, with the marks of the nails still in its hands (John 20:27). That is why Christians bury their dead in hope, and why Paul could say that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). Because he rose bodily, we will too.

On a Tuesday. When doubts come, go back to the evidence the chosen witnesses gave: read Luke 24 or 1 Corinthians 15 this week, slowly, as testimony from men who had breakfast with the risen Lord.

For worship. The Lord of glory kept the habits of friendship on the far side of the grave. His resurrection is not a rumour of survival but a body at a table, and the table is not finished: he will drink the fruit of the vine new with his people in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29).

verseByVerse.quote: "And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge of the living and the dead. Peter’s last two sentences hold the whole of what the church has to say, and the first is the harder: this man will judge the human race (17:31; John 5:22). The living and the dead closes every exit: nobody is too long buried to be included and nobody too much alive to be exempt.

Good news, not only threat. This is presented as part of the good news, and it is, when you consider the alternative: a universe in which nothing is ever finally called what it is, where the killer and the killed go into the same silence. A judgment guarantees that the accounts will be settled. What makes it terrifying is not that there is a judge; it is that we are in the dock. Judgment is not God losing his temper. It is the holy God refusing to call evil good, and that same holiness is why the forgiveness offered in the next sentence could only be paid for by a cross.

To him all the prophets bear witness. Which is why the second sentence comes immediately. The whole Old Testament points to Christ (Luke 24:27).

Forgiveness of sins through his name. The judge and the Saviour are the same person, the only arrangement under which anybody could survive the first sentence. The one appointed to assess the living and the dead is offering forgiveness now, in a front room in Caesarea, before the bench is ever taken. This is the answer to Cornelius’s prayers.

Every word chosen. Look at the width of the last sentence. Everyone: not every Jew, not every circumcised person, everyone. Who believes in him: not achieves, not qualifies, not is born into; faith alone, not circumcision, law-keeping or good works. Receives forgiveness of sins: a gift received, not a wage earned. Through his name: on his account and not on ours. Paul’s word for it is justification: the verdict of the Judge that a guilty person stands forgiven and in the right with him, not because he has become good, but because Christ’s death has paid for his sin and Christ’s righteousness is counted to him (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). That word everyone is very nearly the last thing Peter says before the Holy Spirit interrupts him, and the interruption is God’s way of saying that the word meant what it said.

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Some teach that forgiveness comes through faith plus sacraments or works, and many who hold this love Christ sincerely. This commentary’s view: forgiveness is received by everyone who believes, and here the Spirit falls before any baptism or work is done (v. 44): justification by faith alone, through Christ alone, by grace alone. (See Luke 18:14 for the fuller answer.)

How do I know if I have really believed? Believing in Christ is not a feeling to measure but a trust to place. Ask yourself: Do I rely on Jesus alone, and not on my goodness, to be accepted by God? Do I believe he died for my sins and rose again? Am I turning from sin to follow him, however falteringly? If the answer is yes, then the promise of this verse is yours: everyone who believes receives forgiveness. Assurance does not rest on the strength of your faith but on the faithfulness of the one you trust. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves as surely as strong faith does. And the evidence that it is real will grow: love for Christ, a hatred of sin, and a desire to obey him (1 John 5:13).

On a Tuesday. When you are careless about sin, remember that Jesus is the Judge. When you are crushed by guilt, remember that the Judge is the one who forgives, and that what he counts to you is his own perfect obedience, not your uneven record.

verseByVerse.quote: While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was still saying these things. A momentous sermon is cut off in the middle by the Holy Spirit. As soon as they heard that everyone who believes receives forgiveness, they believed, and God sealed it.

The Holy Spirit fell. No appeal, no prayer to repeat. Nobody is baptised first; the water does not appear until Peter asks for it. Nobody is circumcised or has agreed to keep the law. God simply does not wait (Galatians 3:2).

Sealed in his name. The Spirit fell at a precise point in the sermon: the moment the name of Jesus had been offered to everyone who believes in him. Jesus had sent his apostles to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations (Luke 24:47), and had said that the Spirit would glorify him, taking what was his and declaring it (John 16:14). In Caesarea the two promises met. Forgiveness was offered in Christ’s name to Gentiles, and Christ’s Spirit, poured out from his throne (2:33), came down on them before the sentence was finished. The interruption was the risen Lord setting his own seal on his own gospel. A seal is an owner’s mark: it says this is genuine and this is mine. By giving the Spirit, God marked these Gentiles as his own and guaranteed their inheritance with him (Ephesians 1:13–14).

Amazed. The six Jewish Christians Peter brought as witnesses are beside themselves. They had believed for some time that Jesus was the Messiah. They had not remotely believed this.

Even on the Gentiles. Unthinkable, but undeniable: God accepted them as they were, uncircumcised. It is a mercy that Luke left it in. The first Christians did not arrive at the inclusion of the Gentiles by reflection; their Scriptures had foretold it and their Lord had sent them to the ends of the earth, and when God did it in front of them they stood with their mouths open. That is a comfort to anybody whose first reaction to a work of God was bewilderment, not faith. It neither stopped God nor disqualified the six; they went back to Jerusalem and told what they had seen.

Is this a second experience after conversion? The Spirit fell while Peter was still speaking, the moment they believed; there was no second step. This was the Gentile Pentecost, the moment God showed the church that Gentiles too received the Spirit on believing, and as an event it was unrepeatable. Pentecostal Christians read it as a pattern for a later baptism in the Spirit; but Peter himself later says that God gave them the same gift when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ (11:17). They are our brothers, and their longing to be filled with the Spirit is right; the question between us is only whether Scripture makes it a separate, later step.

In the flow. The Spirit came on Jewish believers in Jerusalem (2:1–4), then on Samaritans (8:14–17), and now on Gentiles, with Peter present each time the gospel crossed a new boundary. That is why Peter rests his defence in Jerusalem on this moment: God gave them the same gift he gave us (11:17).

On a Tuesday. Expect God to be at work when his word is spoken, even before the speaker has finished. When you share the gospel, you are not the one who makes it effective; the Spirit is.

For worship. The Father promised through Joel that he would pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and in a Roman parlour all flesh came to include soldiers, servants and a centurion’s relatives. He gave the gift before anyone could earn it or argue about it, and it leaves the most careful believers in the room standing amazed.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speaking in tongues. How did anybody know the Spirit had fallen? The sign is the same as in Jerusalem (2:4, 11), recognisable at once by a man who had been there. Peter will tell the church that the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning (11:15), and the council that God made no distinction (15:8–9).

The demonstration was for Jerusalem. God could have converted that household quietly. Instead he gave a sign describable only in the words already used of Pentecost, in front of six Jewish witnesses. And it settled the question before the argument began: there was no case left for Gentile believers as associate members, conditional on circumcision, at a separate table. God had decided publicly, and the church spent years catching up.

Were these tongues real languages, and is speaking in tongues the evidence of the Spirit? Peter says the Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning (11:15), so they were likely the same as at Pentecost. The tongues were a sign for the Jewish believers that God had accepted Gentiles; they are not presented as the proof of the Spirit for every later Christian. Many Christians believe the gift continues today, and they are our brothers; the more likely reading is that it belonged to those foundational moments, because in Acts tongues accompany the gospel’s crossing of new boundaries, and the New Testament presents such signs as God’s confirming of the apostles’ message (Hebrews 2:3–4).

Extolling God for his Son. Megalynontōn means magnifying, as at Pentecost. Moments earlier this household had heard that a man hanged on a tree had been raised and appointed Judge, and that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness. Their first praise, in languages nobody had taught them, was praise for that, as Mary had magnified the Lord for the same Christ (Luke 1:46).

Then how do I know I have the Spirit if I have not spoken in tongues? By the signs Scripture gives every believer, not the special sign given at this turning point. The Spirit is present wherever a person confesses from the heart that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), cries out to God as Father (Romans 8:15–16), loves other Christians (1 John 4:13), and bears his fruit: love, joy, peace, patience and the rest (Galatians 5:22–23). Paul asks the Corinthians, do all speak with tongues? and expects the answer no (1 Corinthians 12:30). If you trust Christ, you have the Spirit. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), so the reverse is also true: if you belong to him, the Spirit is yours.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit’s gift always leads to praise. Take five minutes today simply to tell God what he has done, without asking for anything.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have? The question is addressed less to the room than to the six men behind Peter, and through them to the church in Jerusalem, and it is unanswerable. Withhold, kōlysai, means prevent, hinder: the word of the eunuch’s question by the roadside, what prevents me from being baptized (8:36). The argument runs back from a fact nobody can dispute: these people have received the Holy Spirit just as we have. No second-class Gentile believers. If God has given the reality, who can refuse the sign?

Not more cautious than God. Peter does not send to Jerusalem for a ruling, impose a probationary period, or require circumcision, which the whole church will argue about for years. He watches what God has plainly done and refuses to be more cautious than God.

He commanded them to be baptized. The language of an order, which the head of that household would have recognised. Baptism follows faith and the Spirit.

In the name of Jesus Christ. This is no contradiction of Jesus’ command to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), and no support for the teaching (sometimes called Jesus Only) that treats the phrase as a rival formula and denies the Trinity. Luke is describing the baptism’s character: Christian baptism, which marks a person out as now Jesus’ own, as distinct from John’s. To be baptised into his name is to be baptised into the whole triune God, and this very scene shows the Father anointing (10:38), the Son saving, and the Spirit falling (10:44). So we baptise with the Lord’s own words, as the church has from the earliest days (the Didache, an early Christian manual from around AD 100, already prescribes them).

The Spirit before the water. These people received the Spirit before they were baptised, so the Spirit and forgiveness come by faith, and baptism follows as the sign and the Lord’s command, not as the means. Luke gives no one fixed order (compare 2:38; 8:16–17; 19:5–6), but here the Spirit did not wait for the water.

Does the baptism of a whole household support infant baptism? The household here were those who heard the word, received the Spirit and spoke in tongues (vv. 44, 46), so all were believers. Christians who baptise infants see in household baptisms a covenant pattern including children, reasoning that as Israel’s sons received circumcision, the children of believers should receive the covenant sign; but this household, at least, was made up of believers. That is why the church baptises those who profess faith, while honouring the paedobaptist brothers who read the household texts differently.

Under a new name. Roman soldiers swore their oath in the name of the emperor, and Cornelius had served for years under Caesar’s name. Now he went down into the water under another, and came up owned by a better Master, who had bought him with his own blood (20:28).

Remain for some days. The quiet triumph of the chapter: a Jewish apostle who days earlier would never have entered a Gentile house stays on as a guest, eating at that table. Jerusalem will complain of exactly this (11:3). The wall is truly down.

If baptism does not save, why does it matter so much? Because Christ commanded it, and obedience to him is never optional (Matthew 28:19). Baptism is his appointed sign of union with him in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4), a public confession that you belong to him, and the doorway into the visible fellowship of his church. It does not make you a Christian; it marks you as one. Peter did not treat it as a formality to be skipped once the Spirit had come. He commanded it at once. A believer who has never been baptised is not lost, but he is living in disobedience to a plain command of his Lord, and missing a means of grace by which Christ strengthens faith.

On a Tuesday. If God has accepted someone, so must you. Refuse to create second-class Christians in your church by look, tone or seating plan.

For worship. The promise to Abraham, that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed, was kept that afternoon in one Gentile family, and it has been kept in every family gathered in since. Every believer from every nation stands in a line that runs back through that house by the sea, and the God who swore an oath to Abraham kept it in Abraham’s greater Son.

10.theology: Election and the Nations. Acts 10 is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham: “in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). Acts 10 shows the means: the preaching of Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and the sovereign gift of the Holy Spirit to all who believe. The Gentile mission is not an emergency plan devised when Israel rejected the Messiah. It is the ancient plan of the God who chose Abraham in order to bless the world through him, and in Cornelius’s house that intention breaks into history.
10.examples:
Then: A Roman soldier who prayed toward Jerusalem and a Jewish fisherman who would never have entered a Gentile home were brought together by two visions thirty miles apart.

Now: Every generation of the church is tempted to rebuild walls that God has torn down. The divisions that feel most natural (racial, cultural, economic) are the likeliest new versions of the old divide between Jew and Gentile. What God has made clean, do not call common.

11.title: The Church at Antioch
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. <sup>2</sup>So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him, saying, <sup>3</sup>“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.” <sup>4</sup>But Peter began and explained it to them in order: <sup>5</sup>“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. <sup>6</sup>Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>7</sup>And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ <sup>8</sup>But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ <sup>9</sup>But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’ <sup>10</sup>This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven. <sup>11</sup>And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. <sup>12</sup>And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house. <sup>13</sup>And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; <sup>14</sup>he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’ <sup>15</sup>As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. <sup>16</sup>And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ <sup>17</sup>If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” <sup>18</sup>When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” <sup>19</sup>Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews. <sup>20</sup>But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. <sup>21</sup>And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. <sup>22</sup>The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, <sup>24</sup>for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord. <sup>25</sup>So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, <sup>26</sup>and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. <sup>27</sup>Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. <sup>28</sup>And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius). <sup>29</sup>So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. <sup>30</sup>And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
11.overview:
When Peter returns to Jerusalem, Jewish believers who insist on circumcision criticise him for eating with uncircumcised men, for a shared table meant full acceptance. Peter tells the story in order, with six witnesses: God gave the Gentiles the same Spirit he gave the apostles. The critics fall silent, then praise God for granting the Gentiles repentance.

Meanwhile believers scattered after Stephen’s death reach Antioch in Syria, the third city of the empire, and some of them begin preaching the Lord Jesus to Greeks. Barnabas comes from Jerusalem, rejoices at what he finds, and fetches Saul; after a year of teaching, the disciples are first called Christians there. When Agabus foretells a famine, the young Gentile church sends relief to the believers in Judea.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter, criticised for eating with Gentiles, answers with a plain account of what God did, and the church ends by praising God that the Gentiles too have been granted repentance that leads to life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel’s Reach and the Church’s Lag

This passage shows not a wicked church being corrected but a devout one being overtaken. The men who met Peter were holding to a boundary God himself had drawn, which had done its work and been retired, and they had not yet seen it. God settles the question not by a new decree but by doing the thing in public, before witnesses who could be questioned, and letting the church draw the conclusion. It is also a warning about the gap between conviction and conduct: the church conceded the principle in verse 18 and was still arguing about the practice at a council years later, and Peter, who won this argument, later behaved as though he had lost it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter answered a hostile hearing by telling what had happened, including the parts against himself, with six men present who had seen it. He pulled no rank. Now: In a disputed matter that is still the strongest thing available. A man who tells the story straight, admits where he resisted, and brings witnesses is hard to answer; a man who says only that God told him, with nothing checkable attached, has given nobody anything to test.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Over both halves of this chapter, Peter’s defence in Jerusalem and the new church at Antioch, stands the same truth: the turning of a sinner to God is God’s own gift, and he gives it to whom he pleases, from every nation, so that his people come to be known simply by the name of his Son.

News travels. The news travelled faster than the man. Six men had walked home from Caesarea with a story, and by the time Peter came up to the city the whole province had heard a version.

The circumcision party. Luke names a group, literally those of the circumcision. In 10:45 the same phrase simply meant the Jewish believers who had come with Peter; here it marks out those Jewish believers in Jerusalem who hold that Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God’s people (15:1, 5). Paul uses the same phrase of the men whose arrival at Antioch made Peter get up from a Gentile table (Galatians 2:12).

The verb Luke chooses. They criticised him, diekrinonto, took issue with him. At root the verb means to separate or to sort one thing from another, and Peter will use it again in a moment when he reports that the Spirit told him to go with the three men making no distinction (v. 12).

Being fair to them. These men were not inventing a prejudice. They were defending a boundary God had drawn himself, in writing, which faithful Israelites had died rather than cross. Their instinct was not that of small men but of serious ones who had not yet been told what God had decided.

The circumcision made without hands. Their question is answered, in the end, by Christ himself. Circumcision was the sign that a man belonged to the covenant people. Paul would later tell Gentile believers that in Christ they had been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him and raised with him (Colossians 2:11–12). What the knife marked on the outside, Christ accomplishes within every believer. The Gentiles in Caesarea were not lacking what the sign pointed to: they had been given Christ.

Is it wrong to question a Christian leader? No, and this passage shows it can be right. The Jerusalem believers did not gossip about Peter behind his back or split the church; they raised the matter with him directly, and he answered them patiently. The Bereans were praised for checking even Paul’s teaching against the Scriptures (17:11). What matters is the spirit and the standard. Question openly, not in whispers. Question by Scripture, not by preference. And be ready, as these men were in the end, to be persuaded and to praise God when you are shown to be wrong.

For worship. The word of the Lord ran from a front room in Caesarea to every town in Judea faster than the apostle who had preached it, and no faction could call it back. His word is never bound (2 Timothy 2:9), and it does not return to him empty but accomplishes what he purposes (Isaiah 55:11). He spoke Christ into a Gentile house, and the house believed. He is speaking him still into houses the church has argued about.
verseByVerse.note: The circumcision party were Jewish believers who held that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge. They do not say, you preached to Gentiles, or, you baptised uncircumcised men, which is the far larger question and the one that will dominate the council in chapter 15. The complaint is about a meal.

Eating as a verdict. That looks trivial to a modern reader, and it was nothing of the sort. In the ancient world a shared table was the plainest public statement two people could make about each other. A Jew could trade with a Gentile, serve under one and argue with one; sitting down to supper said, in front of everybody, that you belonged to one company. Preaching to Gentiles could be a mission. Eating with them is a verdict. If Peter can sit at Cornelius’s table, the wall is down, and everything else follows.

The charge laid against his Master. Peter had heard the complaint before. The Pharisees and scribes grumbled at Jesus in almost the same words: this man receives sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:2). Jesus answered with three parables about a shepherd, a woman and a father who go after what is lost and rejoice when it is found. So the charge brought against Peter is the charge brought against his Lord, and it is the best thing that could be said of either. A church that is never accused of this has stopped doing what Jesus did.

The same man, later. Peter wins this argument completely; the room falls silent and praises God. Some years later, at Antioch, he is eating with Gentile believers as a matter of course when men arrive from this same party, and he gets up from the table. The other Jewish believers follow, even Barnabas, until Paul confronts him in front of everybody because his conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).

Where Christian failure lives. A conviction can be argued to a conclusion, defended in public, praised by the church, and still not have reached the part of a man that decides where he sits at dinner. Peter’s theology was right in chapter 11 and his feet were wrong in Galatians, and the gap between the two is where most Christian failure actually lives. Paul names what moved Peter’s feet: he was afraid of the circumcision party (Galatians 2:12). The good opinion of the right people is one of the oldest idols of the religious heart, and the only cure for it is a heart more sure of Christ’s approval than of anyone else’s (Galatians 1:10): an approval won by his perfect obedience and counted as ours (Romans 5:19), which no failure at a table can undo.

If Peter could fail like that, how can I hope to stand? By the same grace that restored Peter every time he fell. He denied Christ three times and was restored; he withdrew from the Gentiles and was corrected, and years later he calls Paul our beloved brother (2 Peter 3:15). Your standing does not depend on never failing, but on Christ, who keeps those the Father has given him (John 10:28–29). What you can do is close the gap between belief and practice deliberately: notice where your table, your friendships and your diary contradict what you say you believe, and let a faithful friend tell you when they do.

On a Tuesday. Who would you be uncomfortable being seen eating with? Not in theory, but in your actual town, with your actual friends watching. That is the person to invite.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together meant full acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter began and explained it to them in order: "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In order. The word kathexēs is the one Luke used of his own orderly account (Luke 1:3). Peter tells it as he lived it, from the roof onwards. He does not quote Scripture or appeal to his office. He is not making a case. He is giving evidence.

Why an account works better than an argument. An argument meets a counter-argument, and both sides go home unmoved. An account of events, given in order, with witnesses present, must be either accepted or called a lie, and with six men from Joppa in the room the second is not available. The best answer to criticism is often a patient, honest account.

A witness, not an advocate. Peter is doing exactly what Jesus appointed him to do. You will be my witnesses, the Lord had told him (1:8), and a witness does not argue a case; he says what he saw. All through Acts the apostles’ authority rests on that: they testify to what the risen Christ has done, so that their hearers must deal with him and not with them. Even this report, though it begins with a sheet, ends with the Lord’s remembered word (v. 16), with faith in the Lord Jesus Christ (v. 17), and with Gentiles given repentance that leads to life.

Where it began. Not with an idea of Peter’s, which the circumcision party would be entitled to object to, but on a roof at midday, when the whole thing came down on him from outside.

Something like a great sheet. He uses the same phrase Luke used in chapter 10 (10:11). Even before a hostile room, Peter will not describe it more definitely than he saw it. And he adds: it came down to me.

For worship. The Lord comes down. He came down to a roof in Joppa with a vision Peter had not asked for, as the Son once came down to a manger and a cross, unbidden and unearned, and every work of grace since has had the same direction. Sinners do not find him by searching the heavens. He finds them where they are, praying or not praying, and leaves them with nothing to say for themselves except to tell, in order, what he has done.

verseByVerse.quote: "Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beasts of prey. Peter’s retelling is harder than Luke’s own account of the vision, which in the earliest manuscripts listed animals, reptiles and birds (some later ones, followed by the KJV, add wild beasts at 10:12 too). Reporting to law-observant Jews already angry with him, Peter names beasts of prey, wild carnivores, the creatures furthest from anything a Jew would put on a plate. And looking at it closely: he did not glance at the sheet and recoil. He examined it item by item, and knew exactly what he was being asked to do before he refused.

Making his own case worse. Every instinct would shade the account. Peter tells them precisely how offensive the command was, because his case rests on its having come from God, and a softened command is no longer the one that came. The offensiveness of the instruction is part of the evidence that it was not his idea.

The hardest fact in the apostles’ message. Peter had done this before, in a far greater matter. Preaching in Jerusalem, he did not soften the death of Jesus into a misfortune. He told the crowd that they had crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men, and that God had made him both Lord and Christ (2:23, 36). The apostles always led with the most repellent fact in their message, a Messiah executed on a tree, because it was the fact that saves, and no one inventing a religion to please Jews or Greeks would ever have chosen it.

Should we soften the hard parts of the gospel to make it easier to accept? No. The gospel has an offence that cannot be removed without destroying it: the cross is a stumbling block and folly to the world (1 Corinthians 1:23). We should remove every unnecessary offence, our rudeness, our jargon, our cultural baggage, so that the only stumbling block left is Christ himself. But we may not trim what God has said about sin, judgment, the uniqueness of Christ or the call to repent, because it is the very hardness of these truths that shows they did not come from us. People are not won by a gospel made comfortable. They are won by a gospel made clear.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.' But the voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By no means, Lord. The shrewdest thing in the speech is simply honesty. Peter puts his own objection into the record in the words he used, the words every man in that room would have used. When God gave him this command, his first reaction was theirs.

What it does to the argument. They came believing Peter had gone soft on the law, and here he is testifying that he defended it to God’s face. He was the man who said no; whatever changed his mind was not in him. Peter shows that he held their position and stated it more strongly than they had, and only then says what happened next.

With the blood of a spotless lamb. Peter would come to say how God makes people clean. At the council he said that God had cleansed the Gentiles’ hearts by faith (15:9), and in his first letter he told Gentile Christians that they had been ransomed from their futile ways not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). The voice on the roof was not announcing a relaxation of standards but that the Lamb had been sacrificed, and his cleansing reached Gentiles too. Clean means fit to come near the holy God. The food laws had been given with the words, be holy, for I am holy (Leviticus 11:44–45), and every meal taught Israel that the holy God is not approached on our terms. Christ did not lower that standard. He met it for us, so that a Gentile washed in his blood may draw near with a true heart (Hebrews 10:22).

Does the vision abolish the Old Testament food laws? Its first point is about people: Peter concludes that he should not call any person common or unclean (10:28). But it also reflects what Jesus had already declared (Mark 7:19, where the KJV’s purging all meats is generally read today as Mark’s comment that Jesus declared all foods clean): the food laws, which separated Jew from Gentile, are fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and Christians are free to eat any food (Romans 14).

For worship. The voice from heaven had the last word, and it always will. God does not need our permission to cleanse what he chooses to cleanse, and his declaration over a sinner washed in Christ cannot be overturned by any accuser. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33).

verseByVerse.quote: "This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times. Peter produces it as evidence, and in that room it was strong. A single experience can be doubted; a thing repeated three times has moved out of the category of impressions.

The Lord who asks three times. Three is Peter’s number. Three denials by a charcoal fire; then, on a beach, the risen Jesus asked him three times, Simon, son of John, do you love me? and three times gave him his sheep to feed (John 21:15–17). The Lord did not restore him with one question and leave him to wonder whether it had taken. Now the same Lord speaks three times on a roof, with the same kindness, not exasperation. He knew how many times this man would need to hear it, and said it that many times. Christ’s patience is measured not by what we deserve but by what we need.

Drawn up again into heaven. Then it stopped, with no application attached. The application was already walking up the road and would be at the gate within the hour. Peter did not have to work it out. He had to answer the door.

verseByVerse.quote: "And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that very moment. The sheet has just gone back up, and at that instant three strangers are at the door, sent the day before the vision was given. Nobody arranged that.

Making no distinction. The whole defence turns on that phrase, mēden diakrinanta, the verb Luke used in verse 2 of the men now questioning him. Peter quotes it back to a room doing the very thing it forbade, and does not point it out.

All authority, down to the minute. The Lord who sent Peter had told his apostles on what ground he sent them: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me; go therefore and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:18–19). The risen Christ who upholds the universe (Hebrews 1:3) also governs the pace of travellers on a coast road, so that his word and his messengers meet at a door. And the Spirit’s instruction to make no distinction is the same commission in its plainest form: all nations, without exception.

These six brothers. These: they are in the room. Peter brought his witnesses back to Jerusalem and up to this meeting. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). He has brought double. Ask them, Peter is saying.

The foresight. On the morning he left Joppa (10:23), Peter took along men who could later say what they had seen. Being right is not the same as being believed, and the honest way to handle a claim nobody wants to hear is to make it checkable. And then, plainly: we entered the man’s house. The very thing he is accused of, he states as a fact.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit makes no distinction among those who believe, and neither should the church. Look around your congregation and ask whether any group is quietly treated as second-class: the poor, the new, the foreign, the young, the old. Then do something to bring them in.
verseByVerse.note: Six brothers made seven witnesses with Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel in his house. Here Peter supplies Cornelius’s side of the story, and with it a piece of information that Luke’s earlier account twice held back (10:4–6, 30–32). Both times the angel’s message ran the same way: your prayers and alms have been remembered; send to Joppa for Simon called Peter. Both times it stopped there.

A message by which you will be saved. Now Peter finishes the sentence, and that clause is the whole reason he can stand in that room. Before the vision on the roof, before the knock at the gate, God had already told a Gentile that a message was coming by which he would be saved. Peter did not go to Caesarea and then decide that Gentiles could be saved. He was sent as the delivery of a promise that had already been made without him.

What the message was. Peter had preached Jesus, hanged on a tree, raised, appointed Judge, through whose name everyone who believes receives forgiveness (10:38–43). Cornelius’s prayers could reach God’s notice; only Christ could reach his guilt. Peter had already told the council in Jerusalem that there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (4:12).

It settles the question about Cornelius. Cornelius was devout, generous and prayerful, and God had noticed all of it. He was also, on the day the angel came, not saved, because the angel told him a message was coming by which he would be. No reading of that sentence allows the gospel to have been an optional enrichment for a man already safe. Sincerity does not save. Salvation comes through the gospel (Romans 1:16; 10:14–17).

Is it not unfair that a sincere man like Cornelius still needed the gospel? It would be unfair only if salvation were a prize for the most sincere, and it never is. Peter, a lifelong keeper of the law, was saved in exactly the same way as Cornelius, by a gift he had not earned (15:11). So the gospel does not shut out the sincere. It shuts out boasting, for the devout and the careless alike. And look at what God actually did. He did not leave a seeking man to his seeking. He moved an angel, a vision and an apostle up the coast to bring him the one message that could save him. That is not a God looking for reasons to keep people out. It is a God going to great lengths to bring them in.

You and all your household. The promise arrives with a family attached to it, the servants, the soldiers, the relatives Cornelius had gathered (compare 2:39). The whole household heard and believed (10:44), and household salvation in Acts follows household hearing and believing (16:31–34; 18:8).

Does you and all your household mean that a family is saved together, or support infant baptism? Cornelius’ household heard the word, received the Spirit and spoke in tongues (10:44–46), so they were believing hearers. The verse does not teach that faith passes to children automatically; each was saved by hearing and believing. Christians who baptise infants (paedobaptists) see a covenant pattern in household baptisms, like circumcision given to Abraham’s sons; but the households in Acts are described as hearing and believing. That is why this commentary holds believer’s baptism, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2), while gladly honouring the many faithful brothers and sisters, perhaps including you if you were baptised as a baby, who read these households the other way.

Can I trust God for my family’s salvation? You can pray for it with great confidence, because God loves to work in families and has often saved whole households. But Scripture does not promise that every member of a believer’s family will be saved, and each person must come to Christ himself. What you can do is what Cornelius did: bring your family under the word, gather them where the gospel is preached, live the faith in front of them, and pray for each of them, every day. Then leave them in the hands of the God who is more willing to save than you are to ask.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I began to speak. Peter is being precise, and the precision is his argument. Luke’s account in chapter 10 says the Spirit fell while Peter was still speaking; Peter’s own account says it happened as he began. He had not finished or called for a response. God did not wait for the rest of it.

Just as on us at the beginning. Not a lesser gift or a partial one, but the same thing, and the apostles in that room had been there for the first one and could judge for themselves. Peter calls Pentecost the beginning, the start of a new era, and he is saying that what happened in a Roman officer’s front room was the beginning happening again to different people.

I remembered the word of the Lord. The theology arrived as a memory. Watching Gentiles speak in tongues, Peter did not reason his way to a conclusion; a sentence came back to him, spoken by Jesus just before the ascension (1:5). It had sat in him for years, and it came up at the exact moment it was needed and explained everything he was seeing. The words of Jesus interpret events, and not the other way round. Peter could not have looked it up. What he had was what he had heard and kept, as Jesus had promised: the Spirit will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (John 14:26).

What is the baptism with the Spirit? It is Christ’s act of pouring out his Spirit on his people, uniting them to himself and to one another. John the Baptist could only apply water to the outside; Jesus gives the Spirit himself, who cleanses and renews from within. Paul says that in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free (1 Corinthians 12:13). So every believer has been baptised with the Spirit, and the proof is not a particular experience but faith in Christ and a life being changed by him. If you trust in Jesus, the promise of Acts 1:5 has been kept in you.

On a Tuesday. A verse learned years ago can surface in a hospital corridor or a hard meeting, uninvited and exactly right. You do not know when you will need what you have stored, but the Spirit does.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same gift. The gift came with faith, not with circumcision or law-keeping.

When we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. Peter gives the full title. The one thing the apostles and Cornelius’s household had in common was not a nation, a law or a history, but a Person believed in. Men who had walked with Jesus for three years and Gentiles who had first heard of him that afternoon received the identical gift, because it comes not from the believer’s past but from the Lord he trusts. To refuse those who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ would be to refuse the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who had given them his Spirit.

Who was I that I could stand in God’s way? It is the last sentence of the defence, and it is worth noticing what kind of sentence it is not. Peter does not say he was right. He does not say he had authority, or that he had weighed the matter and reached a considered view, or even that he had obeyed. He pleads incapacity. The leading apostle of the church, answering the church, says in effect: what was I supposed to do, stop him? Stand in God’s way is kōlysai, hinder, prevent: the same word as withhold the water (10:47). To refuse those whom God has accepted is to fight God (5:39).

What it does not mean. This verse is quoted in church disputes far more often than it is examined, and in the wrong hands it becomes a way of ending discussion rather than resolving it. It is not a formula for winning arguments by asserting divine backing. It works in this passage because of everything attached to it: a vision repeated three times, an independent vision given to a man thirty miles away, three messengers who arrived at the precise moment, an explicit word from the Spirit, six witnesses who can be questioned, and a public sign identical to the one the apostles had seen at the beginning. Peter has just spent thirteen verses laying out the evidence, and only then does he draw the conclusion. A man who says God told him and produces none of that has said something quite different. And today, with the apostolic witness complete, the test of any claim is the written word of God.

So is the baptism with the Spirit a second stage after conversion? Peter equates what Jesus promised (1:5) with what Cornelius received when he believed: the same gift. Pentecostal Christians point to the Samaritans (8:14–17) and the Ephesian disciples (19:1–7), who received the Spirit after believing. But those were moments when the gospel crossed new boundaries, and Paul teaches that every believer has been baptised in the one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). The more likely reading is that the baptism with the Spirit is given to every believer at conversion. Many Pentecostal believers are earnest and fruitful Christians, and the disagreement is about how to read these chapters, not about whether the Spirit is real and powerful today.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They fell silent. Silence first, and the order matters. The objection simply runs out.

God has granted repentance. Then the praise, from criticism to worship, the best possible response to correction. Not, the Gentiles have repented, but God has granted. Repentance is God’s gift (2 Timothy 2:25), not something we produce, and what they praise him for is not that a barrier fell but that people were given eternal life.

The gift from the throne. Peter had told the Sanhedrin that God exalted Jesus at his right hand as Leader and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins (5:31). Now the church hears that the exalted Christ gives the same thing to Gentiles. Repentance that leads to life is not a mood a sinner works up. It is a gift given from a throne by the Saviour who died, and the life it leads to is his own risen life.

One part for the whole. Only repentance is named, not faith; yet faith is plainly implied, for these Gentiles had believed (vv. 17, 21). Scripture often names one part of a thing for the whole. Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning to Christ: repentance turns from sin, faith turns to the Saviour, and you cannot truly do one without the other. So Scripture sometimes names both, “repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15), “repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20:21); sometimes only repentance (here; Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19); and sometimes only faith (“believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved,” Acts 16:31; John 3:16). Never build a doctrine on the absence of a word: it would be a serious mistake to read this verse as though faith were unnecessary, or Acts 16:31 as though repentance were. And the turning itself is God’s gift, as faith is also called “the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8; compare Philippians 1:29).

Those who were scattered. Luke drops the scene, goes back several years to the persecution that killed Stephen, and picks up a thread left in chapter 8 (8:1–4). The scattered believers travelled as far as Phoenicia, the coast around Tyre and Sidon, and Cyprus, and Antioch in Syria, the third city of the empire, with a large Jewish community.

No one except Jews. After verse 18 it lands like a cold draught. The church has just agreed, with praise, that God has granted repentance to the Gentiles, and Luke’s next sentence reports that for some time believers had carried the gospel across three regions and told nobody but their own kind. The gap measures how long it takes a settled conviction to reach the street.

If repentance is God’s gift, what am I supposed to do? Repent. God’s gift of repentance does not happen around you but in you: he gives it by working in your heart so that you yourself turn from sin, freely and genuinely. You are never told to wait passively until you feel repentant. You are commanded to repent and believe (17:30), and the very desire to obey that command is the first sign that God is granting it. And if you are praying for someone who shows no sign of repentance, this verse is your warrant. You cannot argue anyone into it, but you can ask the God who grants it to grant it to them.

For worship. The tears a sinner sheds over his sin, the first turn of his face toward Christ, the whole road from death to life: all of it is granted, from the throne of the one who died. He gave it in Jerusalem, and in Caesarea, and soon in Antioch, and he is giving it still. There is no heart so hard that he cannot give it repentance, and no nation he has not purposed to give it to.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenicia was the coastal region north of Galilee. Antioch in Syria was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Antioch unnamed believers tell Greeks about the Lord Jesus and many turn to him. Barnabas and Saul build up the church, the disciples are first called Christians, and the church sends famine relief to Judea.
verseByVerse.theology:
Antioch and the Shape of a Sending Church

Antioch is the New Testament’s picture of a missionary congregation, and almost nothing about it was planned. It began with ordinary believers doing the obvious thing; it was recognised rather than authorised; it was built up by a year of ordinary teaching; and its first act as a church was to send money to a church that had been suspicious of people like them.
