Within two chapters it will give away its two finest teachers. A church is not measured only by what it gathers but by what it is prepared to give away.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The step that opened the gospel to the Gentile city was taken by men from Cyprus and Cyrene whose names nobody recorded. Now: Much of the work that matters most in any generation is done by people who will never appear in an account of it, who simply speak of Christ to whoever is in front of them.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But there were some of them. The whole future of the church is in this exception.

Nameless men. Luke tells us where they came from and not who they were: Greek-speaking Jews from the island of Cyprus and from Cyrene in North Africa, used to living among Gentiles and less scandalised by them than a man raised in Judea. Lucius of Cyrene (13:1) may have been among them, but Luke, who names dozens of minor figures, leaves these men unnamed.

Cyrene again. Men of Cyrene had a synagogue in Jerusalem and were among those who argued with Stephen and could not withstand him (6:9–10). Luke does not say these are the same men, and it would be wrong to assert it. But the city that supplied some of Stephen’s opponents also supplied some of the first men to do what Stephen had been killed for pointing toward.

The Hellenists also. The manuscripts divide between Hellenists, Greek-speaking Jews, and Greeks, Gentiles proper. The sense requires Gentiles, since this sentence is the contrast to verse 19.

Preaching the Lord Jesus. To Gentiles they did not start with Jesus is the Messiah, a Jewish title that meant little in a Greek city, but with Jesus is Lord, which every Greek understood and which claimed everything. Antioch was full of lords: Apollo at Daphne, the mystery cults, the emperor himself. Jesus went there in the mouths of his people, and was with them as he had promised (Matthew 28:20). Wise evangelism adapts its words, not its message.

No vision, no angel. Peter needed a sheet let down three times before he would enter a Gentile house. These men talked to Greeks because there were Greeks there. They already had their commission (1:8), and they obeyed it.

The hand of the Lord. An Old Testament phrase for God’s power actively at work (Isaiah 59:1). And the pairing matters: they believed and turned, faith and repentance together, as in verse 18. Heaven’s verdict on the initiative of unnamed men was to bless it enormously.

Do I need a special call to tell people about Jesus? No. Every Christian already has one. The command to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19) and the promise of the Spirit for witness (1:8) belong to the whole church, not to apostles alone. Some are called and gifted to preach and to lead, and the church should recognise them. But speaking of Christ to your neighbour needs no ordination. These men had no title, no training we know of and no instructions, and they started the church that sent the first missionaries into the Gentile world.
verseByVerse.note: “Hellenists” here seems to mean Greek-speaking Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sent Barnabas. As with Samaria (8:14), news of an irregular advance produces a delegation, and the choice settles the outcome. Others would have arrived looking for a fault. They sent Barnabas, a Cypriot like some of the evangelists, and the son of encouragement (4:36).

He saw the grace of God. What did he actually see? A room full of uncircumcised Greeks with pagan backgrounds and no synagogue training, worshipping the God of Israel, taught by nobody in particular. Barnabas looked at an untidy crowd of new believers and identified the one thing really going on.

Glad. Not relieved, not cautiously satisfied: glad, a word from the same family as the grace he saw (chairō, charis). He had earned his name twice already, selling a field for the poor and vouching for Saul when nobody else would go near him. Here he earns it a third time simply by being pleased, and a great deal turned on it. The Gentile mission survived its inspection because the inspector was a man capable of being delighted.

With steadfast purpose. Then he does the work. Exhorted, parekalei, is the root of his nickname: he encouraged them. With steadfast purpose is literally with purpose of heart, a settled inward intention. He does not begin by correcting them, but tells a young church the one thing it will most need.

Holding fast to the Lord. The Lord they are to remain with is the Lord Jesus they had just turned to (v. 21), and the charge is the one Jesus gave his own disciples: abide in me, and I in you, for apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:4–5). Barnabas does not give a young church a programme. He points it to a Person and tells it to hold on.

How do I see the grace of God in other Christians? Look for what only God could have done. A new believer’s doctrine may be muddled and his habits rough, but if he loves Christ, wants to hear the word, is beginning to hate his sin and loves God’s people, you are looking at the grace of God. Name it to him, and thank God for it aloud. Then, when correction is needed, it will come from someone he knows is on his side. Barnabas did not ignore what needed teaching; he and Saul spent a year teaching (v. 26). But he started with gladness.

verseByVerse.quote: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good man. Luke stops the narrative to explain the previous verse, and the explanation is a character reference. Not brilliant or well connected. The sentence sits between a man rejoicing over somebody else’s work and going to fetch somebody better at teaching than himself: a man with no jealousy in him.

Full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. Luke uses the phrase not for a momentary filling for a single task (Acts has those too, 4:8, 31; 13:9) but for a settled condition: a man so yielded to the Spirit that the Spirit governs his character, words and deeds, and the church can see it in the fruit. The same is said of Jesus himself (Luke 4:1) and of Stephen (6:5), so to be full of the Spirit is simply to be deeply like Christ. In Barnabas it is concrete: the giver who sold his field (4:36–37), the big-hearted man who vouched for the feared new convert Saul (9:27), the encourager who was glad to see God’s grace in Antioch (11:23).

Borrowed from the Good Shepherd. Every goodness Luke can find in Barnabas is borrowed. Jesus called himself the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and the marks of Barnabas’s goodness are the marks of that Shepherd in miniature. He gave away what he owned (4:36–37), went after a man everyone else avoided (9:27), and rejoiced over sheep he had not gathered himself. That is why his goodness added people to the Lord rather than to himself.

Not a rare distinction. Every believer is commanded to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), a continuous filling sought by yielding to him: letting the word of Christ dwell richly (Colossians 3:16), praying, obeying, walking by the Spirit rather than grieving or quenching him (Galatians 5:16; Ephesians 4:30; 1 Thessalonians 5:19).

Is goodness enough to make a person a Christian? No. Barnabas was good because he was full of the Spirit and of faith, not the other way round. No one is good enough by nature to be accepted by God; Jesus said that no one is good except God alone (Mark 10:18). The goodness Luke praises here is the fruit of grace: the Spirit producing in a forgiven sinner the likeness of Christ. That is why it is open to every believer. You cannot make yourself good by effort. But if you belong to Christ, the Spirit who made Barnabas good is at work in you, and you can ask him daily to fill you.

For worship. Christ is the fountain, and every saint ever called good is a cup filled from it. The Lord who makes sinners good does not make them proud of it. He makes them glad over others, quick to fetch help and content to be forgotten, so that the people they serve look past them to him.

verseByVerse.quote: So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To look for Saul. The verb, anazētēsai, means to search hard, to hunt up and down. It had been years since Saul was sent to Tarsus (9:30). Barnabas travelled a hundred miles on the strength of remembering a man, and then had to look for him. He knew whom God had called to the Gentiles (9:15), and he did not try to keep the work for himself.

The second time. The first was in Jerusalem, when every Christian in the city was frightened of the man and Barnabas took him by the arm and walked him in to the apostles (9:27). The second is this: years of obscurity ended because one man could not leave him out there. The two acts between them are the reason there is a Pauline half to the New Testament.

Making room for a greater man. Barnabas is the recognised leader of the most promising church in the world, and he goes and fetches a teacher who will eclipse him. Within two chapters Luke writes Paul and his companions (13:13). He went anyway, in the spirit of John the Baptist: he must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

For a whole year. A year in one place, with one congregation, teaching. Not a campaign. The church which becomes the launching point for the entire Gentile mission was built by twelve months of ordinary instruction from two men who stayed put.

First called Christians. Christianos is a Greek stem with a Latin ending, the form used for the followers or partisans of somebody, as people spoke of Herod’s men as Herodians (Mark 3:6). It means Christ’s people, Christ’s lot. It was very probably a nickname coined by outsiders, perhaps in mockery. The believers came to wear it gladly (26:28; 1 Peter 4:16).

What the neighbours had concluded. Not that these people were strange, or a philosophy, but that they were somebody’s: outsiders could not describe them without using his name. And Christ is not a surname. It is a title, the Greek for Messiah, the Anointed One, the King God had promised (2:36), so the nickname meant, in effect, the King’s people. A church of Jews and Gentiles needed a new name: neither Jew nor Gentile, but Christ’s.

What makes someone a Christian? Not a family, a culture, a church membership or a moral code, but belonging to Christ by faith. The name means Christ’s person, and that is the heart of it: you are a Christian if you have trusted Jesus Christ as your Saviour and Lord, and he has made you his own. Many people call themselves Christian because of where they were born; the neighbours in Antioch used the name because of how people lived and whom they talked about. The question to ask yourself is not whether you have the label, but whether you have the Lord.

For worship. They were called by his name. The Son of God has given his name to a people from every nation, and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). There is no higher title in the universe, and he gives it freely to sinners.
verseByVerse.note: “Christians” means “Christ’s people” — probably a nickname given by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophets came down. Luke mentions them without explanation. Prophets were a recognised ministry in the early church (13:1; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11), part of the foundation era (Ephesians 2:20).

Agabus. He appears again in 21:10–11, foretelling Paul’s arrest. All the world means the Roman world. What Agabus supplies is not doctrine but information: a specific, checkable warning, given so that the church could act.

In the days of Claudius. The emperor Claudius ruled from AD 41 to 54, and ancient historians record a series of severe grain shortages in his reign; a famine struck Judea around AD 45 to 48, severe enough that Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism, bought grain in Egypt and had it shipped to Jerusalem, as Josephus tells. Luke ties his story to history that can be checked.

Jesus had said there would be famines. Jesus had told his disciples that there would be great earthquakes, and in various places famines, and that such things were not to terrify them, for the end would not come at once (Luke 21:9–11). The ascended Lord who gives prophets to his church (Ephesians 4:11) was now, through one of them, giving notice of one of the troubles he had foretold, and his people answered it not with panic but with love.

What the warning was for. Not so that they could fill their own storehouses: what follows is a collection, a chance to be generous early.

Do men like Agabus exist now? Christians differ about it, and the difference is real and held in good faith on both sides: some hold that gifts of this kind ceased with the apostolic foundation, others that they continue in some form. The first is the better view, since the signs and revelatory gifts of Acts accompanied the apostles as the credentials of their foundational witness (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4).

The continuationist case and the better reading. Continuationist Christians (those who hold that all the gifts continue today) believe that prophets like Agabus still speak in the church, pointing to 1 Corinthians 14 and to Christ’s giving of prophets in Ephesians 4:11–13. The more likely reading is that New Testament prophecy, as revelation from God, belonged with the apostles to the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and that what Agabus foretold, the famine, came to pass, as true prophecy always did.

The boundary. What both sides agree on is the boundary. Whatever Agabus was, he was not adding to Scripture and nobody treated him as if he were; his contribution was a piece of practical information which the church then acted on with its own judgment. Any claim in any century that would correct, supplement or override what is written is a different thing altogether.

How should I respond if someone tells me he has a word from God for me? Kindly, and carefully. Do not mock him, for he may be a sincere brother who holds a different view of the gifts. But test what he says by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). If it contradicts the Bible, reject it. If it simply repeats what the Bible already says, receive it as a reminder of God’s word, not as new revelation. If it claims to tell you something the Bible does not, a person to marry, a job to take, a date something will happen, you are not bound by it. Make your decisions by Scripture, prayer, wise counsel and the providence of God, and you will not go astray.

For worship. Nothing in his world takes the Lord of history by surprise, not famines, not emperors, not the price of grain in Egypt. As through Joseph, the warning became a means of feeding the hungry.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor Claudius ruled AD 41–54; ancient historians record severe famines in his reign, including in Judea.

parallels.desc: Agabus again

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Relief to the brothers in Judea. Watch which way the money goes: the new Gentile church, argued about in Jerusalem, pays for the mother church’s food. Relief is diakonia, ministry, service: the new unity in Christ expressed in money.

Unasked. No request came from Jerusalem. The response to prophecy was not speculation but generosity.

Every one according to his ability. Not a flat rate or an equal share: each gave in proportion to what he had, the New Testament’s settled pattern for giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:11–12). Not equal amounts, but equal sacrifice. Money promises security, and a hand that opens for a hungry brother belongs to someone who has found his security somewhere else (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

To the elders. This is the first mention of elders in the Christian church. The Jerusalem church now had elders alongside the apostles (15:2), men entrusted with its care.

By the hand of Barnabas and Saul. This is the first joint mission of the partnership that will take the gospel across the empire, and it is not a preaching tour: their first work together was delivering money to hungry people. They were trustworthy men to carry it, as Paul would later insist such gifts require (2 Corinthians 8:20–21).

Bread for the Lord he had persecuted. The money goes to some of the very believers Saul had dragged from their houses. On the Damascus road the risen Lord had asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (9:4). Christ counts what is done to his people as done to himself, and he says the same of kindness: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). So when Saul walks into Judea with famine relief for the believers he once hunted, he is bringing bread to the Lord he once persecuted.

How does this visit fit with Paul’s account in Galatians 2? The more likely reading is that Galatians 2:1–10 describes this famine visit, a private meeting with the leaders, before the public council of Acts 15. Others equate Galatians 2 with Acts 15. The first fits better, since Paul, arguing about circumcision, never mentions the council’s decision. That is partly an argument from silence, and good scholars weigh it differently, but it is a weighty one.

The collection never stopped. Paul spends years of his later ministry organising exactly this: a fund gathered from Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He explains the theology of it in a sentence: if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings (Romans 15:27). It began here.

How much should I give when a need like this famine comes? Scripture gives no fixed percentage for Christians, but it gives principles that are more searching than any percentage. Give regularly (1 Corinthians 16:2), in proportion to what God has given you (2 Corinthians 8:12), cheerfully and not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7), and sacrificially, as the Macedonians gave beyond their means (2 Corinthians 8:3). Many Christians find a tenth a helpful starting point, and many who can give more should. Give first to your own church, which feeds you, and then to believers in need and to gospel work. And remember that the measure is not the amount but the cost, and the motive is the grace of Christ, who though he was rich became poor for your sake (2 Corinthians 8:9). The disciples at Antioch answered the question in one line: each according to his ability (11:29).

parallels.desc: remember the poor

11.theology: Repentance as Gift. “God has granted repentance that leads to life” (11:18). Repentance is not a human achievement that God rewards; it is itself his gift. That does not remove human responsibility: the Gentiles really repented and believed. But behind their turning was God’s giving. This is the order of all true conversion: God grants, the sinner turns, and God receives the glory.
11.examples:
Then: Unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene crossed a boundary and began the church in Antioch.

Now: Antioch is a picture of a healthy sending church: mixed in its people, taught by gifted teachers, quick to meet need, and willing to send its best people out. A church may fairly ask whether it looks more like the anxious critics in Jerusalem or the glad, generous church at Antioch.

12.title: The Prison and the Providence
12.text: <sup>1</sup>About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. <sup>2</sup>He killed James the brother of John with the sword. <sup>3</sup>And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. <sup>4</sup>And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. <sup>5</sup>So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. <sup>6</sup>Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison. <sup>7</sup>And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his hands. <sup>8</sup>And the angel said to him, “Dress yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so. And he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” <sup>9</sup>And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. <sup>10</sup>When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him. <sup>11</sup>When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting.” <sup>12</sup>When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. <sup>13</sup>And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. <sup>14</sup>Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate. <sup>15</sup>They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!” <sup>16</sup>But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed. <sup>17</sup>But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. <sup>18</sup>Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. <sup>19</sup>And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. <sup>20</sup>Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. <sup>21</sup>On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. <sup>22</sup>And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” <sup>23</sup>Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. <sup>24</sup>But the word of God increased and multiplied. <sup>25</sup>And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
12.overview:
A new persecution comes from the top. Herod Agrippa I has James the brother of John executed, the first apostle to be martyred, and, seeing that it pleases the Jewish leaders, arrests Peter at Passover. While the church prays, an angel wakes Peter on the night before his trial, the chains fall off, and he walks out through the iron gate.

Peter goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where the church is praying, and is left knocking at the gate while they tell the servant girl Rhoda she is mad. Then he leaves for another place. At Caesarea, hailed as a god, Herod is struck down, as Josephus also records, and the word of God keeps growing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Herod's Persecution and God's Deliverance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Herod kills James and imprisons Peter; the church prays; an angel brings Peter out, and the praying church can hardly believe it. Then Herod, hailed as a god at Caesarea, is struck down, and the word of God goes on growing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Praying Church, the Sovereign God, and the Grave of James

Here a teaching about prayer either becomes honest or becomes cruel. The church prayed earnestly and Peter was delivered; it very likely prayed for James too, and James was buried. Luke gives no reason, and we must not supply one. Prayer is not a mechanism that produces outcomes in proportion to fervency. Prayer is the appointed way a dependent people bring their case to a sovereign God, who answers according to his own good purposes and does not always explain them. And God answered people who did not expect him to: the power lies not in the praying but in the God prayed to.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rhoda’s news was met with you are out of your mind by the very people who had been up all night asking for it. Luke records it without rebuke, and the deliverance stood. Now: Many Christians pray while quietly not expecting, and feel like frauds. This chapter is kind to them.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 12 sets two kings side by side. Herod kills, imprisons and is worshipped as a god; the church has no weapon but prayer. Over the chapter stands the other King, unseen and unnamed in most of its verses, who sends an angel to wake a prisoner and an angel to strike down a tyrant, and whose word no throne can stop.

Herod the king. This is Herod Agrippa I. His grandfather, Herod the Great, tried to kill the child at Bethlehem; his uncle, Herod Antipas, beheaded John the Baptist and put a robe on Jesus to mock him. Raised in Rome among emperors, he was made king of all Judea in AD 41, and he worked hard to please the Jews. This is the first persecution of the church by the state rather than by the religious leaders.

James the brother of John. Ten words, and one of the Twelve is dead, probably beheaded, around AD 44. Luke gave Stephen a chapter and a half; he gives James, one of the inner three, half a sentence. The brevity is not carelessness; Luke wants the reader to feel it.

In the flow. Between Barnabas and Saul setting out with famine relief (11:30) and their return (12:25), Luke sets Herod’s attack: while a Gentile church was feeding Judea, Judea’s king was killing an apostle. Peter, the leading figure since chapter 1, then leaves the story. Herod’s sword fell just as the mission to the world was about to begin, and it could not stop it.

Was nobody praying for James? Four verses later the church is praying for Peter, and Peter walks free. And the question that raises has to be asked out loud rather than stepped around, because every reader asks it. Luke does not say, but it is hard to imagine otherwise. This is the same church, in the same city, in the same weeks, and James was an apostle they had known for more than a decade. They very likely prayed for James as earnestly as they prayed for Peter, and James was executed and Peter was delivered, and Luke offers not one syllable of explanation for the difference.

Respecting the silence. That silence must be respected rather than filled. There is no suggestion anywhere in the text that the prayers for James were less fervent, or that his faith was weaker, or that God had a lesson for him that Peter did not need. Every one of those explanations has been offered to grieving people, and all of them are inventions.

What can be said. What can be said is smaller and truer. First, Jesus had told James this was coming: when James and John asked for the two best seats, he asked whether they could drink the cup he was about to drink, and said they would (Mark 10:35–39). James drank it first; John drank it slowly and died old. Second, Peter’s deliverance is the exception Luke records, not the rule he teaches. By early and consistent tradition Peter was executed in the end, in Rome (compare John 21:18–19), and no angel came to that cell. Third, a book which recorded only the deliverances would be a lie, and useless to most of its readers.

The cup with the wrath drained. When Jesus told James he would drink his cup, he did not mean that James would help to pay for sin. The cup Jesus dreaded in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36) was the wrath of God against sinners, which he alone could drink, and drank to the bottom. What James drank under Herod’s sword was suffering for his Lord’s name, with every drop of judgment already drained out of it. Herod could strike a body on earth. The Head sat at the right hand of God, beyond any king’s reach, receiving his servant home.

No replacement. When Judas fell, a replacement was chosen to make up the Twelve (1:21–26). When James dies, nobody is appointed in his place. Judas had abandoned his office; James finished his. The Twelve were witnesses of the risen Lord for a generation, not an office to be handed down, and their foundation, once laid, did not need relaying (Ephesians 2:20).

Why does God rescue some of his people and not others? Scripture does not give us the reasons in particular cases, and we must not invent them. But it tells us enough to trust him. Both James and Peter were equally loved, equally prayed for and equally safe in Christ. God’s purposes for each were different, and both were good: James was taken home to glory, Peter was given more years of work. Neither outcome was a failure of prayer or of love. Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15), and nothing, not even the sword, can separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39). When you cannot see why, you can still see who: the Father who did not spare his own Son.

For worship. James had stood on the mountain when the Lord’s face shone and his clothing became dazzling white (Luke 9:29), and in the garden when that same face was pressed to the ground (Mark 14:33–35). He had seen the glory and the agony. Herod meant the sword as an ending; in the hand of the Lord Jesus it was only the usher, bringing a friend home to the face he had seen shining on the mountain.
verseByVerse.note: This Herod is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as king from AD 41 to 44. James is the first of the Twelve to die for his faith.

parallels.desc: the cup that I drink you will drink

verseByVerse.quote: and when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It pleased the Jews. There is the motive, stated by Luke without embarrassment. Herod killed an apostle not out of conviction but because it went down well, and moved on to a second for the same reason. Approval is the idol here, and it is a cruel god: it asked Herod for one apostle, and then for another. By the Jews Luke means the leaders and people of Jerusalem, not every Jew; the church itself was still almost entirely Jewish.

The days of Unleavened Bread. Holding the execution until after the feast is religious tact: he will not spoil Passover, and he will have a larger crowd. And there is an irony: Passover celebrates the night God brought his people out of the house of bondage, and the king is holding an apostle in one, waiting for the celebrations to finish before killing him.

Four squads of soldiers. Four squads of four, sixteen men, one squad for each watch of the night: two chained to the prisoner, two at the door, relieved every three hours. Sixteen men for one fisherman, and there is a reason for it. The authorities in this city had put these men in prison before, and had come in the morning to find the cell locked, the guards at their posts and the prisoners gone (5:19–23). Luke sets the arrangements out in detail so that the reader knows precisely what was in place before the chains fell off.

To bring him out to the people. More than ten years earlier, in this same week, another prisoner was held under guard in Jerusalem and brought out to the people, and the crowd asked for Barabbas and shouted for the cross (Luke 23:18–21). But the two prisoners do not stand in the same place. Jesus went out to that crowd as the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), whose blood is why God passes over his people, and no angel came for him, because he had come to die. Every rescue in this chapter, and every mercy his people have ever received, comes through the one prisoner who was not rescued.

Should Christians expect hostility from governments? Sometimes, yes. Scripture teaches us to honour and obey the governing authorities as God’s servants for our good (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17), and many governments have been kind to the church. But it also warns that rulers may rage against the Lord and his Anointed (Psalm 2:1–3; Acts 4:25–27), and Jesus said his followers would be brought before kings for his sake (Luke 21:12). The Christian’s posture is respectful submission in everything lawful, prayer for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and quiet refusal when commanded to disobey God (5:29). We neither idolise the state nor fear it. We fear God.

On a Tuesday. Herod’s sin starts very small in all of us: the joke told because the room will like it, the opinion softened because the boss holds another. Most days the question is quietly there, whom am I trying to please?

For worship. Sixteen soldiers, two chains, an iron gate and a date fixed for after the feast: Herod had arranged everything except the Lord. He who sits in the heavens laughs at the plans of kings (Psalm 2:4), because he holds the calendar on which they pencil them, and he had already written in a different date for Herod. Herod needed sixteen men where the Lord needed one angel.
verseByVerse.note: Four squads of four soldiers took turns to guard him through the night watches.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But earnest prayer. Luke sets the entire apparatus of the state against a prayer meeting and joins them with but, and by the end of the chapter one of the two is dead.

Earnest. The word ektenōs means stretched out, at full reach; Luke uses a form of it of Jesus praying in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). And the praying is corporate: the church, continuous, fervent and united, which had already buried James and knew perfectly well what a Herod does with an apostle.

Sleeping between two soldiers. On the last night before the execution, chained by each wrist to a soldier, Peter sleeps soundly enough that an angel has to hit him to wake him.

Where the peace came from. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8). The peace did not come from confidence about the outcome; Peter had no reason to expect an angel, and James had not got one. It came from the Lord himself, in whose hands both outcomes lay.

Another prayer for Peter. The church was not the first to pray for this man. On the night of his arrest Jesus had told Peter that Satan wanted to sift him like wheat, and then, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31–32). That prayer carried Peter through his denial and back, and it had not lapsed. The Lord who prayed for him in the upper room always lives to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25), and the prayers rising from Mary’s house went up to a Father already listening to his Son.

How can I have that kind of peace? Not by persuading yourself that everything will turn out as you want, but by entrusting yourself to the one who holds the outcome. Paul gives the pattern: do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God, and the peace of God will guard your hearts (Philippians 4:6–7). Name the fear to God in so many words. Remind yourself of what is true about him: his love, his power, his promises. Remember that your life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), so that the worst that can happen cannot touch what matters most. Then lie down. Peace is not the absence of danger; it is the presence of the Lord in it.

For worship. The keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4), and so a fisherman chained between two soldiers can. The Lord who once lay asleep on a cushion in the stern while the storm broke over the boat (Mark 4:38) shared his own rest with Peter on the last night. And the same Lord, in Gethsemane, did not sleep. He prayed more earnestly, in agony, while his friends slept around him. He kept that vigil so that his people may lie down.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell off his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel of the Lord stood next to him. As with the shepherds (Luke 2:9), no approach is described. A light fills the cell, and none of the soldiers wakes.

He struck Peter on the side. Hold on to that verb, patassō, because Luke uses it twice in this chapter. Here an angel of the Lord strikes a man to wake him; at verse 23 an angel of the Lord strikes a man and he dies: one blow to rouse a sleeping prisoner and one to end a king who thought he was a god. There is something almost comic here: the light has not worked, so the angel gives Peter a dig in the ribs.

Free before he knows it. The chains fell off: not unlocked, not struck off. They come off first, while Peter still thinks he is dreaming. It is the shape of the gospel. At Nazareth Jesus read that he had come to proclaim liberty to the captives (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 61:1), and Luke now shows the risen Lord doing to one prisoner’s wrists what he does to every sinner’s heart: the chains come off by a power not his own, and the understanding follows the freedom. No sinner first understands the gospel and then frees himself. God makes him alive while he is still dead in his sins (Ephesians 2:4–5), and only then does he begin to see what has been done for him.

Does God still send angels to rescue his people? Scripture says the angels are ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and the angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him (Psalm 34:7). So we may be sure that God uses his angels for our protection, mostly unseen and unknown. But visible angelic rescues like this one are rare even in the Bible, clustered at turning points in redemption, and we are never told to expect them, to seek them, or to pray to angels. Pray to God. How he answers, by angels, by people, by ordinary means or by none that you can see, is his business, and every answer is from his hand.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those in chains, literal and spiritual: persecuted Christians in prison today, and friends bound by addictions or despair. Name one of each before God this week.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to him, "Dress yourself and put on your sandals." And he did so. And he said to him, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me." And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dress yourself. A being from the presence of God has just dissolved Roman iron, and he is now telling a fisherman to put his shoes on.

God and the practical. Somebody has thought about the cold. God does not find the practical beneath him; the risen Christ cooked breakfast on a beach. And there is a division of labour. God does the impossible, the chains; he leaves Peter to do the possible, the sandals.

Follow me. Peter had heard those words from Jesus, by the lake at the beginning and on the beach at the end (Mark 1:17; John 21:19), and Luke may well want us to hear the echo. On the beach they came straight after Jesus told him that when he was old another would dress him and carry him where he did not want to go (John 21:18). Tonight Peter is in chains, and he is not old. Herod has fixed a date, but the Lord had fixed Peter’s days long before, and no king could bring the last of them forward by an hour.

He thought he was seeing a vision. Peter is not being obtuse: since the roof at Joppa (10:10), visions were a category he had, and he walks out of the prison in complete confusion.

Nobody believes it. Peter does not believe what God is doing while he is doing it, and in a few verses the church will tell a servant girl she is raving. God did it anyway.

Does God only act when we have enough faith? No. Faith is the hand that receives God’s gifts, and Scripture calls us to pray believing (James 1:6). But God is not bound to the size of our faith; he answers out of his own goodness. Here nobody, not Peter, not the church, believed the rescue was happening, and it happened. The man who cried, I believe; help my unbelief, received what he asked (Mark 9:24). So do not despair because your faith is weak. Bring the weak faith to a strong Saviour, and let him do far more abundantly than all that you ask or think.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first and the second guard. Luke dismantles Herod’s arrangements one at a time, and says nothing about how the guards were passed.

The iron gate. The last obstacle is the outer door of the fortress. The Greek for of its own accord, automatē, gives us our word automatic; the New Testament uses it only here and of the earth that produces a crop by itself (Mark 4:28). No lock is picked and no guard overpowered; the gate behaves as though it had been asked.

The Lord of the doors. This gate belongs to a pattern that runs through Acts. Prison doors open for the apostles (5:19) and for Paul and Silas (16:26); a door of faith opens to the Gentiles (14:27); the Lord opens Lydia’s heart (16:14). It is the work of God under the reign of the risen Christ, who calls himself the one who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut (Revelation 3:7). His sovereignty reaches every barrier between his word and his people, the hard heart included.

Immediately the angel left him. One street, and the angel is gone, leaving Peter alone in the dark in a city where a king wants him dead. He was sent to get him through a gate. God is not sparing with his help; he is exact with it.

Why does God sometimes seem to leave us just when we need him? He does not leave us, though his extraordinary help may be withdrawn. The angel left Peter, but the Lord did not: Peter’s first thought in the next verse is that the Lord had rescued him, and his feet took him straight to the house where the church was praying. God often gives remarkable help to bring us through a crisis and then returns us to the ordinary means: our own legs, our own judgment, the fellowship of other believers. That is not abandonment. It is the Father treating us as sons who can walk. He has promised, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

For worship. The angel who opened Herod’s gate had a forerunner. Matthew tells us that on the first Easter morning an angel of the Lord came down, rolled back the stone from the tomb and sat on it (Matthew 28:2). He did not roll it away to let the Lord out, but to let his people look in. Because the grave could not hold him, no prison, no iron gate and no grave will hold those who are his.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter came to himself, he said, "Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting." When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Peter came to himself. The phrase is like the one Luke used of a young man sitting among pigs in a far country who suddenly saw his situation for what it was (Luke 15:17). It is the moment the fog clears.

Now I am sure. Until this moment he was not. He does not describe his own part, because he had none. The whole sentence has one subject, and it is not Peter.

Whose angel. At Pentecost Peter had told this city that God had made the crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ (2:36), and Jesus had spoken of the angels as his own (Matthew 24:31). And consider who is saying it. The last time Peter stood in a Jerusalem courtyard at night, he said he did not know the man (Luke 22:57). Now he stands in a dark street and confesses that the man had come for him. The Lord who answered that denial with a look and a restoration has answered these chains with an angel.

The house of Mary. Mary has a house with a gateway and a servant, and she is named in her own right, which suggests a widow of means who had put her property at the church’s disposal. That it was the house of the upper room cannot be proved. Her son John Mark, a cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), has a long road ahead of him, and Peter will one day call him my son (1 Peter 5:13).

Many were gathered together. With Peter under sentence and James freshly buried, the church is in a house in the dark, in numbers, still praying, which took nerve, and is why Peter knew which door to knock on.

On a Tuesday. If you have a room and a table, offer them to your church for a prayer meeting or a small group, and be the Mary of your street.
verseByVerse.note: John Mark later wrote the Gospel of Mark; he was a cousin of Barnabas. His mother’s house was large enough to hold a gathering.

parallels.desc: God sent his angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Recognizing Peter's voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A servant girl named Rhoda. Luke does not name the soldiers or most of the church in that room, but he names a slave girl who answered a door. Rhoda means rose: a servant of no standing in a house she did not own, whose one recorded action was a mistake.

Recognizing Peter’s voice. She knew it through a closed door at night: a household slave had been in the room often enough while the apostle taught to know his voice. The church apparently did not send the staff out.

In her joy. It is one of the rare sentences in Scripture that is plainly funny. The most wanted man in Jerusalem is left standing in the street because the girl who found him was too happy to let him in. An angel opened the iron gate; a joyful girl kept the wooden one shut. Luke reports it with affection; the people who come off badly in the next verse are the ones who were praying.

Like the women at the tomb. In Luke’s Gospel the first news that Jesus was alive came at dawn from women who had been to the tomb, and to the apostles their words seemed an idle tale, and they did not believe them (Luke 24:10–11). Peter was one of those apostles, though he got up and ran to the tomb (24:12). Now he is the one standing outside, and a servant girl carries the news nobody will credit. The God who raised Jesus delights to put the news of his life-giving power first into the mouths of those the world does not count as witnesses, so that the power is plainly his (1 Corinthians 1:27–29).

The one who believed and was glad. She is the only one in that house who at once both believed it was Peter and was glad (the prayer meeting managed neither), and her error was one of excitement. Of all the things to get wrong on the night God answered, hers is the one to be caught doing.

Does God notice people as ordinary as Rhoda? He notices nobody else. Every person in God’s story is ordinary until he notices them, and Scripture is full of servants, widows, children and slaves whom the world never named and God did. Rhoda was a slave in someone else’s house, and her name is in the Bible. If you feel invisible in your church or in your life, remember that the Lord who numbered the hairs on Peter’s head knew the name of the girl who answered his door. Your faithfulness in small places is seen, and your joy in his works delights him.
verseByVerse.note: Rhoda means “rose.”

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "You are out of your mind." But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, "It is his angel!" But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are out of your mind. It is said by people who have spent the night asking God for precisely what the girl has just announced.

She kept insisting. She stood her ground against a room of her betters, and they kept saying: it is his angel.

It is his angel! That was a current belief, and Luke reports it without endorsing it: the idea that a person had a guardian spirit which might appear looking and sounding like him, and which might turn up at the moment of a death. The prayer meeting has produced, on the spot, a theological explanation for why the answer to their prayers cannot be the answer to their prayers.

They thought they saw a spirit. On the evening of the first Easter, when the risen Jesus stood among the disciples, they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit, and even when he showed them his hands and feet they disbelieved for joy (Luke 24:36–41). Peter had been in that room; now he is the one outside, and the church reaches for the same explanation. The answer to that unbelief, then and now, was a real body: a Lord who ate broiled fish before their eyes, a fisherman knocking with real knuckles on a real gate.

Do believers have guardian angels? Scripture says angels serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and Jesus says of his little ones that in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father (Matthew 18:10). But no text clearly teaches that each person has one assigned angel, and Luke records the disciples’ belief without endorsing it. We may be sure that God sends his angels for his people, and we are never to pray to them.

Not casual people. Contempt would be a mistake: they were meeting at genuine risk to pray for a condemned man. Their problem is a common one: they prayed without expecting, and when the answer knocked, they could think of every explanation but the true one. Meanwhile Peter kept knocking.

They were amazed. The lesson here is far kinder than the rebuke this scene usually gets turned into: God answered anyway. The deliverance did not wait on their expectation and was not withdrawn when they called the messenger mad. Their faith was real but weak, and God answered beyond it, as he is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20). This chapter does not shame such people. It brings the answer to their gate and lets them be amazed.

Is it wrong to pray when I do not really expect an answer? It is far better to pray weakly than not to pray at all, and this church is proof that God hears such prayers. But we should ask him to grow our expectation, because he invites us to come boldly (Hebrews 4:16). One practical help is to keep a record of what you ask and how God answers, so that your memory of his faithfulness grows. Another is to pray Scripture’s promises back to him, so that your expectation rests on what he has said rather than on how you feel. Expectation is not presumption: it is trusting that God hears and will answer in his way and time, even if the answer is not the one you pictured.
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews believed each person had a guardian angel.

verseByVerse.quote: But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, "Tell these things to James and to the brothers." Then he departed and went to another place. Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Motioning to them to be silent. A fugitive in a courtyard at night has to quieten a houseful of astonished people before the street hears them.

How the Lord had brought him out. The subject of that sentence is the point of it. He tells them not how he got out but what the Lord did, the only version he is in a position to give.

Tell these things to James. This is not the James who was killed fifteen verses ago. This is James the Lord’s brother, who did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5), saw the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 15:7), and is generally held to have written the letter of James. James is now the man you send word to in Jerusalem, a quiet change of leadership: from here on he presides at the council and receives Paul’s reports (15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9).

Another place. Luke does not say where, perhaps to protect him. Peter appears once more in Acts, at the council (15:7), and then leaves the narrative with no farewell. Luke opened this book by calling his Gospel an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (1:1), and Acts is what Jesus went on doing from the throne, by his Spirit and his word. Peter can walk off the stage because he was never its centre. The Lord who had just brought him out of prison stays on it to the last page.

Where Christians differ: did Peter go to Rome? Some Roman Catholic tradition says Peter went to Rome at this point and was bishop there for twenty-five years. This commentary’s view: there is no evidence that Peter went to Rome now; he is in Jerusalem a few years later (15:7). Paul’s letter to the Romans, written around AD 57, greets many people in Rome but never mentions Peter. Peter probably did go to Rome late in his life and died there under Nero, as early tradition says. But the New Testament never presents him as bishop of Rome or head of the church.

No little disturbance. Luke’s driest sentence: he means there was uproar.

Why tell the story to the church? Because what the Lord does for one of his people belongs to all of them. Peter could have slipped away without a word; instead, at real risk, he stopped to tell the praying church what God had done and to send word to James and the brothers. Testimony strengthens faith, answers prayer publicly, and gives God the glory. The Psalms are full of it: come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul (Psalm 66:16). When God answers your prayers, tell the people who were praying with you. It is part of the answer.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, who became leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put to death. Under Roman practice a guard was answerable for his prisoner: a man who lost one could expect the penalty the prisoner would have received (16:27; 27:42). So Herod does the thing the system provided for, and men die because an angel opened a gate.

The shadow in the verse. Luke reports it without comment, and it would be dishonest to supply the comfort he withholds. Peter’s deliverance cost other men their lives. Deliverances happen inside a fallen world, and the Bible reports the price rather than tidying it, which is one reason it can be trusted about the rest.

A keeper who loses none. Set beside Herod’s rule the keeper the gospel describes. On the night of his arrest Jesus told the Father that he had guarded those given him, and not one had been lost but the son of destruction (John 17:12); in the garden he told the soldiers, if you seek me, let these men go (John 18:8). He was answerable for his people and paid with his life, not because he had lost them but so that he never would. Herod’s guards died for a prisoner they could not keep. The Good Shepherd died for sheep he will not lose, and rose to keep them for ever.

Down to Caesarea. Herod leaves Jerusalem and never comes back. His final recorded act in the holy city, where he had been so careful to appear devout, was to have his own men executed for something none of them had done.

Was God unjust to let the guards die? No. God did not kill the guards; Herod did, and Herod answered for it. God is under no obligation to prevent every evil act of wicked men, and he often allows them to show what they are before he judges them. His ways in such things are often hidden from us, and Scripture does not invite us to explain them all. But it assures us that the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), that no innocent blood is forgotten by him, and that every tyrant will give account. The cross itself is the ultimate proof: the most unjust act in history, done by wicked men, was the means by which God saved the world, and the men who did it will answer to him.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who live under cruel rulers today, and for those who serve them in fear. And pray for rulers themselves, that they would come to fear God before it is too late.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman practice a guard who let a prisoner escape could suffer the prisoner’s penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king's country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Angry with Tyre and Sidon. We are not told why Herod was angry, but the leverage is plain. The Phoenician ports had almost no farmland and had imported their grain from Galilee since Solomon’s day (1 Kings 5:11). Herod could not conquer them. He could starve them, and they knew it.

Blastus. The chamberlain controlled access to the king. Two ancient cities had to win over a courtier, very possibly with money, to get permission to eat.

Access without a chamberlain. Set that beside the throne the gospel opens. Through Christ we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18), and the one who brings us in is not a courtier to be bought but the King’s own Son, who paid the cost of entry himself: we enter by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way he opened through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). Tyre and Sidon pleaded with a king who used hunger as a lever. The Father of Jesus gives his children their daily bread for the asking (Luke 11:3), and no Blastus stands at his door.

On an appointed day. We have a second account of this occasion from outside the New Testament. The Jewish historian Josephus, with no interest in defending Luke, describes Agrippa at Caesarea at games for the emperor, entering the theatre at daybreak in a robe woven of silver that blazed in the sun, and flatterers calling out to him as a god. He records that the king was seized almost at once with violent pain in his belly, was carried out, and died after five days.

Two independent witnesses. Two writers, independently, describe the same king, occasion, acclamation and sudden illness. Luke says an angel of the Lord struck him and Josephus does not, exactly the difference one would expect.

Why does it matter that Josephus confirms Luke? Because the Christian faith rests on things that really happened, not on myths or private visions. Luke told Theophilus he had written so that he might have certainty concerning the things he had been taught (Luke 1:4), and he wrote as a historian, naming rulers, cities and dates that could be checked. Again and again, outside sources and archaeology have confirmed his accuracy in detail. Not every detail has been confirmed, and a few, such as the timing of Theudas (5:36), are still debated, but the overall pattern is strong. That does not prove every miracle, but it shows that Luke was a careful and truthful witness, and it gives good reason to trust him when he tells us what only the eyewitnesses saw: an empty tomb, an angel in a cell, and a church that turned the world upside down.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon, on the coast, depended on Galilee’s farmland for grain.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were shouting, "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice of a god! It is flattery from men who had just won over a courtier and needed the grain to keep coming, and Herod knew exactly what it was worth. Ancient rulers were often hailed as gods. The point is that he did not correct it.

Two scenes in Caesarea. Two chapters earlier, in this same city, a Roman centurion fell at Peter’s feet, out of genuine reverence rather than calculation, and Peter pulled him up and said, Stand up; I too am a man (10:26). Same town, same kind of moment, opposite responses, and only one of the two men is alive at the end of this chapter. Paul and Barnabas will do as Peter did at Lystra (14:14–15).

Two robes. Luke has set another scene beside this one, in his Gospel. On the day Jesus was condemned, Herod Antipas, this king’s uncle, mocked him, dressed him in splendid clothing and sent him back to Pilate (Luke 23:11). The uncle put a fine robe on the one man who truly was God, to laugh at him; the nephew put on silver and let a crowd call him what he was not. The cry was a lie about Herod. About Jesus the truth is greater still: in him the voice of God and the voice of a man are one voice.

Because he did not give God the glory. The reason given is not the one a reader expects. Not because he executed James, imprisoned Peter or killed his own guards: none of that is cited. The charge is that a man let himself be called divine and did not hand the honour back. I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other (Isaiah 42:8). To give God the glory means to acknowledge, in the heart and aloud, that he alone is God and that every good thing we have comes from him.

The sin underneath the others. The murders were real. But the thing named in the indictment is the theft of something that belongs to God alone, which is the sin underneath all the other ones. A man who is willing to be worshipped will do anything at all to the people underneath him.

Is it not vain of God to insist on the glory? In us it would be, because we are not worthy of it: a man who demands praise is claiming what he does not deserve. With God it is the reverse. He alone is supremely worthy, and wanting us to see him as he is means wanting what is true and what is best for us, since we were made to find our fullest joy in him (Psalm 16:11). A God who let creatures be worshipped in his place would be leaving them to a lie. And this God does not guard his glory from a distance. He gave his Son, who shared that glory before the world existed (John 17:5), to die for people who had stolen it.

Eaten by worms. Josephus, independently, records five days of agonising pain in his belly before his death in AD 44. Luke gives it a single sentence: the grandson of Herod the Great, in silver, on a platform, with a crowd calling him a god, and within the week a burial. Pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18), as Nebuchadnezzar learned when he boasted on his palace roof and was driven out to eat grass like an ox until he acknowledged that the Most High rules (Daniel 4:30–37).

What it does not mean. This is not a template for reading illness or sudden death as divine judgment, and it has been misused that way with great cruelty. Luke tells us the reason here because it was disclosed to him. In almost every other case nobody has been told, and the man who claims to know why somebody is ill has appointed himself to a bench he has not been called to. Jesus himself warned against the assumption that those who suffer disaster were worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1–5).

How do I give God the glory when I am praised? Receive the kindness graciously, without false modesty, and then turn it quickly toward God, in your heart and, where it is fitting, in your words. You might say, thank you, God has been very kind, or, I am grateful it helped. More important is what happens inside: remind yourself that every gift you have was given (1 Corinthians 4:7), and refuse to feed on the praise in private afterwards. Herod’s danger was not that people admired him but that he kept what belonged to God. The test is whether, when praised, you feel larger, or more grateful.

On a Tuesday. Watch the subtler forms of Herod’s sin: the secret pleasure in being thought indispensable, the irritation when someone else gets the credit. Bring them to God as soon as you notice them. None of us hands the glory back perfectly; the Son did, glorifying the Father on earth in our place (John 17:4), and for his sake even proud hearts are forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus also records Agrippa’s sudden death at Caesarea after being hailed as a god, in AD 44.

parallels.desc: my glory I give to no other

verseByVerse.quote: But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the word of God increased. A king hailed as divine is dead and buried, and the next thing Luke writes is a message spreading. This is the point of the whole chapter.

The language of living things. Increased and multiplied is the language Genesis uses of creatures filling the earth (Genesis 1:22). Luke’s progress reports (6:7; 9:31) mark the close of a movement. The movement Herod set out to destroy wrote him into its records as an illustration. The grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of our God will stand for ever (Isaiah 40:8; 1 Peter 1:24–25).

The child Herod’s grandfather hunted. Herod the Great sent soldiers to Bethlehem to kill a child; his son Antipas mocked the man that child became, and stood with Pilate against him (4:27); his grandson killed one of that man’s apostles and now lies dead at Caesarea. Jesus has outlived them all, not by escaping them but by dying and rising. The kings of the earth set themselves against the Lord and his Anointed (Psalm 2:2; Acts 4:26), and the Anointed has the last word. In Acts the word of God is the news of Jesus Christ, Lord of all (10:36), and its growth is his doing: it is the risen Lord who adds to his church (2:47).

When they had completed their service. The famine money from Antioch has been delivered (11:29–30), and the two of them turn for home. The manuscripts differ between to and from Jerusalem, but either way they are going back to Antioch.

John, whose other name was Mark. He is Mary’s son, very likely in the house the night Rhoda left Peter at the gate.

The boy in the luggage. He is now going to Antioch, and from there on the first missionary journey (13:5). In Pamphylia he will turn back and go home (13:13), which will later cause a sharp quarrel that splits Paul from Barnabas (15:37–39). Years later Paul will write from prison asking for him, because he is useful to him for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11), and by the church’s earliest tradition he wrote down the recollections of Peter, which the church has read ever since as the Gospel of Mark. Here he is a name added to somebody else’s luggage.

If a Christian has failed badly, can God still use him? Mark is the answer. He deserted the mission, became the cause of a painful split, and might easily have been written off for good. Barnabas did not write him off, and in the end neither did Paul, who came to count him useful. And God used him to write what was probably the earliest Gospel. Failure is not the end of usefulness for a believer who repents and keeps going. The same is true of Peter, who denied his Lord and was restored to feed his sheep. If you have failed, confess it, receive Christ’s forgiveness, accept the consequences humbly, and get back to work. The Lord is not finished with you.

On a Tuesday. When the news is full of powerful people doing terrible things, read Acts 12 again, and remember who has the last word. Then do something small for the word of God this week: give to a missionary, invite a friend to church, teach a child a verse.

For worship. The verbs God spoke over the first living creatures, increase and multiply, are spent in this verse on a message, because the message gives life. Herod’s body went to the worms, and the word of the risen Christ went on making dead hearts live in lands Luke never heard of. Nothing that word has brought to life will ever die: not the church it gathers, and not one soul it has made alive.

12.theology: Providence, Prayer, and the Sovereignty of God over Kings. Acts 12 shows a God who governs kings and councils, who opens prison gates and strikes down tyrants, and who is not moved by the calculations of the powerful. James dies and Peter lives, both by God’s appointment. The church prays, and the answer still takes them by surprise. Herod grasps at divine honour and is given worms. The fitting response is not to explain his ways but to pray, to trust, and to keep speaking the word that outlasts every king.
12.examples:
Then: A church under a murderous king, with no legal protection and no army, met in a house and prayed with everything they had. They were answered in a way they did not expect.

Now: Where power is set against the gospel, the church’s answer is neither despair nor political scheming but earnest, persistent prayer to the Lord who made heaven and earth. And when the knock comes at the door, to open it.

13.title: The First Missionary Journey Begins
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. <sup>2</sup>While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” <sup>3</sup>Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off. <sup>4</sup>So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. <sup>5</sup>When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them. <sup>6</sup>When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. <sup>7</sup>He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. <sup>8</sup>But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. <sup>9</sup>But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him <sup>10</sup>and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? <sup>11</sup>And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. <sup>12</sup>Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. <sup>13</sup>Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup>but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. <sup>15</sup>After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.” <sup>16</sup>So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. <sup>17</sup>The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it. <sup>18</sup>And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. <sup>19</sup>And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance. <sup>20</sup>All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. <sup>21</sup>Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. <sup>22</sup>And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ <sup>23</sup>Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. <sup>24</sup>Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. <sup>25</sup>And as John was finishing his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’ <sup>26</sup>Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation. <sup>27</sup>For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. <sup>28</sup>And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. <sup>29</sup>And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>But God raised him from the dead, <sup>31</sup>and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. <sup>32</sup>And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, <sup>33</sup>this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’ <sup>34</sup>And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ <sup>35</sup>Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see corruption.’ <sup>36</sup>For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, <sup>37</sup>but he whom God raised up did not see corruption. <sup>38</sup>Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, <sup>39</sup>and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. <sup>40</sup>Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: <sup>41</sup>‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’” <sup>42</sup>As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. <sup>43</sup>And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. <sup>44</sup>The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. <sup>45</sup>But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. <sup>46</sup>And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. <sup>47</sup>For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” <sup>48</sup>And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. <sup>49</sup>And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. <sup>50</sup>But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. <sup>51</sup>But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium. <sup>52</sup>And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
13.overview:
The third stage of Acts 1:8, “to the end of the earth”, begins. While the Antioch church is worshipping and fasting, the Holy Spirit tells them to set apart Barnabas and Saul, and they send them off with John Mark. On Cyprus the sorcerer Elymas, opposing the gospel, is struck blind for a time, and the governor Sergius Paulus believes.

Mark turns back at Perga, and the two cross the Taurus mountains to Pisidian Antioch. There, in the synagogue, Paul preaches his first recorded sermon: God’s promises to Israel are kept in Jesus, crucified and raised, and through him everyone who believes is freed from everything the law of Moses could not free them from. A week later the whole city comes; jealous leaders oppose; Paul turns to the Gentiles, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believe. The missionaries are driven out, and the new disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The First Missionary Journey Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From worship and fasting at Antioch the Spirit sends Barnabas and Saul to Cyprus. At Paphos a sorcerer opposes them and is struck blind for a time, and the Roman governor believes, amazed at the teaching of the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missionary Call and Corporate Discernment
