The Spirit speaks not privately to Barnabas and Saul but in the assembly, and the church fasts, prays and lays hands on them before letting them go. An individual sense of call is confirmed by a congregation, and the congregation’s judgement by the Spirit, with neither acting alone. A church’s seriousness about mission is measured not only by what it gives for it but by whom it is willing to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The leaders listed in verse 1 came from Cyprus, North Africa, Cilicia and a royal court, and most of them were in Antioch because persecution had scattered them there. Now: Antioch did not set out to be diverse; it set out to preach to whoever was in front of it, and this is what its leadership looked like a few years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 13 begins the third part of the book: the gospel to the ends of the earth (1:8). Behind every step stands the risen Christ, sending his Spirit, keeping his ancient promises to David, and gathering a people he chose before they had heard his name.

Prophets and teachers. These are the leaders of the church: prophets who brought a word from God before the New Testament was written, and teachers who explained the Scriptures.

The five names. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus. Simeon who was called Niger: Niger is Latin for black or dark, very likely a description rather than a family name, so Simeon may well have been from Africa; some suggest he was Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus’ cross (Mark 15:21), though no one can be sure. Lucius of Cyrene, from North Africa (compare 11:20). Manaen, a syntrophos of Herod the tetrarch, brought up with him at court: he had very likely shared a nursery with the Herod who beheaded John the Baptist. And Saul, last on the list, the former persecutor.

What a church looks like. Very likely an African, an aristocrat and a former persecutor, and not one of them one of the Twelve. It is what a church looks like when it has stopped asking who is allowed in. Two boys grew up in the same palace; one became the murderer of the Baptist and the other a teacher of the church of Christ. Grace took one and passed the other by. Election, God’s free choice of those he will save, is exactly this: God did not find something better in Manaen; he set his love on him freely, before he had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11; Ephesians 1:4).

Worshiping the Lord and fasting. The word for worshipping (leitourgountōn) is the word for priestly service, ministering before God; it gives us our word liturgy. The church’s great missionary step came out of worship and prayer, not out of a planning meeting.

Set apart for me. The pronouns matter. For me: they belong to him before they belong to Antioch. I have called: the call had already been given; the church only recognises it. The Holy Spirit speaks in the first person, as one who claims servants for himself: the voice of God, not of a force (compare Romans 1:1). And the church is asked for its best two leaders, not those it can spare.

Whose work it is. The risen Jesus had promised that the Spirit would make his followers witnesses to the end of the earth (1:8), so the voice in Antioch is Christ keeping his word from the throne. And the man asked for is Saul, his chosen instrument to carry his name before the Gentiles (9:15). The Lord they were worshipping had named this day a dozen years before it came.

What is fasting? Fasting is worth pausing on, since many believers today have never done it. To fast is voluntarily to go without food (for part of a day, a day, or longer) to seek God. It is not dieting, nor a hunger strike to twist God’s arm, nor the self-punishment Scripture warns against (Colossians 2:23). The empty stomach drives the soul to God, saying with the body what the heart means: Lord, I want you more than my daily bread. In Scripture it goes with earnest prayer and attends the great seekings of God: guidance and the sending of missionaries (here; 13:3; 14:23), repentance (Joel 2:12; Jonah 3), grief (2 Samuel 1:12), crisis and intercession (Esther 4:16; Ezra 8:21–23), and steady devotion (Anna, Luke 2:37). Jesus himself fasted forty days (Matthew 4:2).

Is it commanded of Christians, and is it in the Epistles? Honestly, no: fasting is nowhere laid on believers as a law, and the letters mention it barely (2 Corinthians 6:5; 11:27 may even be involuntary hunger). Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add fasting at 1 Corinthians 7:5 and in a few Gospel verses (such as Mark 9:29); the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it there. So no one sins by not fasting, and no one earns anything by it. And yet Jesus plainly assumed his people would fast: when you fast, he said (not if), warning only against doing it for show (Matthew 6:16–18); and asked why his disciples did not fast, he said the wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, but the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast (Matthew 9:15), this present age between his ascension and return. So fasting is not a rule to keep under compulsion, but a privilege and means of grace the Lord expects his church to use.

How did the Spirit say this? Luke does not say. The likeliest answer is through one of the prophets named in v. 1, speaking in the gathered church (compare 11:28). Today, with the Scriptures complete, the Spirit guides churches through his word, prayer, and the wisdom of the church and its elders, not by new revelations. Many faithful Christians believe the Spirit still speaks through prophecy, and they are brothers; this commentary holds that revelation of this kind belonged to the apostolic foundation, because the written word is now complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

How does a person know whether he is called to such work? The call here was heard by the church, not by Barnabas and Saul alone, and confirmed with fasting, prayer and the laying on of hands (v. 3). A call to missionary or pastoral work is not a private impression; it is tested by gifts, character, the desire to serve, and the recognition of the church and its leaders.

So should you fast? Gently, yes: not from guilt or to score points, but as a gift worth taking up; you are missing a help your Master meant you to have. Why? Because in some seasons, a weighty decision, a heavy burden in prayer, sorrow over sin, a longing to seek God afresh, setting aside even food to give that time and hunger to God focuses and humbles the heart and intensifies prayer; and the very hunger preaches that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4). How? Start small: skip a meal or a day, and spend the time in prayer and the Word; always tie the fast to a purpose and to prayer (fasting without praying is merely going hungry); keep it secret, never paraded (Matthew 6:17–18). Two cautions: guard against pride, for the Pharisee boasted that he fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12), and Isaiah 58 shows God despising a fasting joined to hard-heartedness; and use ordinary wisdom about health (the unwell, pregnant, or medicated should take care, and abstaining from water is only ever brief). Fasting earns nothing; but as a humble, hungry way of seeking the God who satisfies, it is worth recovering, for out of one such fast at Antioch the Spirit launched the gospel to the nations.

Does the Holy Spirit still call particular people to particular work? Yes, though not usually by a voice in a meeting. He still gives gifts, lays burdens on hearts, opens doors and moves churches to recognise and send. What has changed is the means, not the Sender. If you sense a pull toward some work for Christ, do not keep it private and do not wait for a voice. Tell your elders, serve where you are, let others test whether the gifts are there, and pray with them. The Spirit who called Barnabas and Saul called them in company, and he still does.
verseByVerse.note: Niger is Latin for “black,” so Simeon may have been from Africa, like Lucius of Cyrene. Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas. Here begins Paul’s first missionary journey (13–14).

parallels.desc: set apart for the gospel of God

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After fasting and praying. Four verbs make a sending: they fasted, prayed, laid hands on them and let them go. Having heard the Spirit, they fast a second time, which is not doubt but what serious people do before an irreversible step.

They laid their hands on them. This is not ordination to an office and does not confer anything Barnabas and Saul did not have; the Spirit had already called them, and both had been in ministry for years. It is the congregation’s public act of identification and blessing, as with the seven (6:6): these are our men, this is our work, and we are putting our hands on it in front of everybody.

Sent them off. The verb means literally they released them, let them go. The Spirit sent them (v. 4); the church released them. They are the two most valuable men the congregation possesses, and it lets them both go at once.

The Sender behind the senders. The rarer test is a congregation giving away the people it can least afford to lose, to work it will not see. A church can make an idol of its own stability, keeping its gifted people close because it needs them in order to feel safe. And this is the shape of the gospel itself. The Father did not send what he could spare; he sent his only Son, the one he loved before the foundation of the world, into a world that would kill him (John 3:16; 17:24). And the Son, sent, now sends: as the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you (John 20:21). A church that releases its best is not being generous beyond the gospel. It is being drawn into it.

Does laying on of hands give the Spirit or special power? Not here. Sometimes in Acts the apostles laid on hands and the Spirit came in a special way (8:17; 19:6), marking key moments as the gospel crossed new boundaries. But this act at Antioch is done by the church, for men who already had the Spirit and the call. It is a solemn, prayerful setting apart, much as a church today commissions missionaries or ordains elders. Nothing magical passes through the hands. What passes is the church’s blessing, its recognition and its pledge to stand behind those it sends.

What does it mean to share in a missionary’s work? It means more than an occasional prayer. Antioch put its hands on these men, and that meant owning them: praying by name, sending money, writing, welcoming them back and hearing their report (14:26–27). Paul calls such churches partners in the gospel (Philippians 1:5). In practice, know the names of the missionaries your church supports, pray for one of them each week, find out what they actually need, and when they come home, give them a meal and an evening, not a five-minute slot.
verseByVerse.note: Laying on hands commissioned them for the task.

verseByVerse.quote: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sent out by the Holy Spirit. The church sent them off; the Spirit sent them out: one act described from two sides.

To Cyprus. Seleucia was the port for Antioch, sixteen miles down the Orontes, and Cyprus lay a day or two’s sail across open water. The first missionary journey begins with a sail to the island where Barnabas grew up (4:36), where there were contacts and believers already (11:19).

In the synagogues of the Jews. In Salamis they establish the pattern of the next fifteen years: to the Jew first (Romans 1:16), in every city, even after the last synagogue had thrown him out.

What the synagogues heard. Luke calls it the word of God, and he has already shown what that meant on Saul’s lips: in the synagogues of Damascus he proclaimed Jesus, saying that he is the Son of God (9:20). Barnabas was a Levite, born into the tribe set apart to serve the sanctuary, and he came home to tell his own people that the sacrifice the sanctuary pointed to had been offered. Two men stood up to announce the one Moses wrote about (John 5:46).

John to assist them. The word (hypēretēs) is the assistant who does the practical work. John Mark is carrying things, and Luke mentions him so that we notice his absence eight verses later.

Why go to the synagogue first if they were sent to the Gentiles? Because God’s promises came through Israel, and the gospel is the fulfilment of those promises. It would have been strange to announce that Israel’s Messiah had come and skip Israel. The synagogue was also where people already knew the Scriptures, and where God-fearing Gentiles gathered, so it was the natural first door. Paul never saw Jew and Gentile as rival audiences. One Christ, promised to the one and given to both.

Is it wrong to start where you have connections? No. Barnabas began on his own island, among his own people, and Luke records it without a hint of reproach. God usually spreads the gospel along existing lines: families, friendships, workplaces, home towns. Andrew brought his brother; the Samaritan woman told her village. Start with the people God has already put near you. Just do not stop there. The same journey that began in Cyprus went on over the Taurus mountains to towns where they knew no one.

On a Tuesday. If your part in the work is carrying the bags, there is honour in it: John Mark’s first job was luggage, and the Spirit wrote him into Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: Seleucia was Antioch’s port. Cyprus was Barnabas’s home island; Salamis was its main city in the east. John is John Mark.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first

verseByVerse.quote: When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As far as Paphos. A hundred miles on foot, covered in a clause. Paphos was the Roman capital, and what they find there is a study in contrasts.

A Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. A Jew, with the Scriptures, trading in magical arts they forbid (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), attached to a Roman household. His name means son of Joshua, or son of Jesus.

A man of intelligence. On the other side, the proconsul: shrewd, perceptive, a man who understands things. And what this shrewd man does is send for two travelling Jewish preachers, because he wants to hear the word of God. Not all the powerful are closed to the gospel.

The proconsul and Luke’s accuracy. The title is one of the small marks of Luke’s accuracy that has been tested and held. Cyprus became a senatorial province, governed by a proconsul, in 22 BC, and Luke uses the correct term; one or two inscriptions naming a Paulus who may be this proconsul have been found, though scholars debate the identification.

Kings shall see. Paul will close this chapter by quoting Isaiah’s words about the Servant of the Lord, a light for the Gentiles to the ends of the earth (13:47; Isaiah 49:6). The next verse of that prophecy says that kings shall see and arise, and princes shall bow down, because of the faithful LORD who has chosen his Servant (Isaiah 49:7). The Servant is Jesus, and in Paphos the prophecy begins to come true in a Roman governor’s house. And there is somebody at his elbow whose whole position depends on his not hearing them.

Is magic or the occult real, and should Christians be afraid of it? Scripture treats the occult as real enough to forbid and false enough to despise. Behind it stand real spiritual powers (Ephesians 6:12), but they are creatures, and they are defeated ones: Christ disarmed them at the cross (Colossians 2:15). So a Christian should neither dabble nor dread. Keep away from horoscopes, mediums, spells, charms and anything that promises hidden power or knowledge apart from God. But if you belong to Christ, you are not at the mercy of any of it. The one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

On a Tuesday. Do not assume that the clever, successful or powerful person in your life is closed to Christ. Pray for one person in authority you know.
verseByVerse.note: Paphos was the Roman capital of Cyprus, at the western end. A proconsul governed a province for the Roman Senate. Bar-Jesus means “son of Joshua.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elymas the magician. Elymas may come from a word for a wise man or sorcerer, more a title than a name. Like Simon in Samaria (8:9–11), he sold access to power.

Opposed them. Elymas’s motives were not purely theological. He is the resident authority on the invisible in the household of the most powerful man on the island, and two Jewish preachers have just been invited in to talk about God. If the proconsul believes them, Elymas is finished: not damned, merely unemployed. A great deal of opposition to the gospel has looked like this, without announcing itself. And behind the man’s interests stood darker powers (Ephesians 6:12).

Seeking to turn the proconsul away. He does not attack the doctrine. The work is done sideways, through the relationship he already has. The gospel is rarely refuted in front of the person who was about to believe it. It is undermined afterwards, quietly, by somebody they trust. And the phrase tells you how close the proconsul was: on the edge of believing, and Elymas could see it.

The stronger man. Jesus had described this moment. In the parable of the sower some of the seed falls along the path, and then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved (Luke 8:12). But Jesus also said that when a strong man guards his palace his goods are safe only until one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him (Luke 11:21–22). The risen Christ is that stronger one, and Sergius Paulus is about to be carried out of the strong man’s house.

What if someone close to the person I am praying for is working against the gospel? Expect it, and do not be thrown by it. Pray specifically, both for your friend and for the one turning him away, because Elymas too was within reach of mercy (v. 11). Keep the conversation open and honest, so that quiet undermining has something plain to be measured against. And remember that no adviser, spouse or friend can finally keep away from Christ someone God is drawing. The proconsul believed with Elymas standing in the room.

On a Tuesday. Turn the light on yourself: is there anyone whose drift toward Christ, or toward deeper obedience, you are quietly discouraging because it would cost you something if they changed? A raised eyebrow, a joke at the right moment, a warning about getting too religious. That is Elymas’s method. If you find it in yourself, bring it to the Lord who forgave Saul for standing in the gospel’s way.

parallels.desc: the magicians of Egypt oppose Moses

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul, who was also called Paul. Luke never explains it. This is not a conversion souvenir; like many Jews of the Diaspora he simply had two names, as John Mark did (12:12): a Hebrew one for the synagogue and a Roman one for everywhere else, and Paulus was a common Latin family name. What changes is his world: from now on his life is spent among Gentiles.

Paul now leads. From here on it is Paul and Barnabas, not Barnabas and Saul (v. 13). And there is one further touch, either a coincidence or a very dry joke: the proconsul’s name is Sergius Paulus. Some note that the Latin name means small, and the man who called himself the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9) carried it well.

Filled with the Holy Spirit. The steady gaze is Spirit-given discernment. The words that follow are ferocious, and they echo what Jesus said to those who opposed him (John 8:44).

Will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? And then the charge itself, which echoes Scripture. The prophet’s cry was to make straight in the desert a highway for our God (Isaiah 40:3), and Luke’s Gospel tells us whose road that was: John the Baptist went before the Lord to prepare his ways (Luke 1:76; 3:4–6), and the Lord who came along them was Jesus. The straight paths of the Lord are the roads by which Christ comes to people. Elymas has been doing the reverse, putting bends in a road God was building toward a man’s soul. And the man bending them is named Bar-Jesus, son of Jesus, a name that means the LORD saves. He wears the Saviour’s name and fights the Saviour’s approach to a man’s soul. Paul’s words strip the name off him: not son of Jesus, but son of the devil.

Not a model for ordinary conversation. This is not temper but a prophetic sentence, spoken to a man who had a governor’s ear and was using it to shut a door; Paul himself tells Timothy to correct opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25).

So when, if ever, should a Christian speak this sharply? Rarely, and almost never in our own cause. The ordinary pattern is gentleness, patience and respect (1 Peter 3:15–16), even with people who mock. Scripture keeps its severest words for those who deliberately twist God’s truth to keep others from it, false teachers and spiritual manipulators, and even then they are spoken to protect the vulnerable, not to win an argument. Paul here was filled with the Spirit and spoke with apostolic authority. An ordinary believer’s plain duty, when someone is leading others astray, is usually to say clearly that it is false, warn those at risk, and leave the judgment to God.
verseByVerse.note: Saul was his Jewish name, Paul (Paulus) his Roman one; from here on, in the Gentile world, Luke calls him Paul.

parallels.desc: the ways of the LORD are right

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time." Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hand of the Lord is upon you. It is a hand of judgment: the mighty hand that brought his people out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 26:8; compare the uplifted arm of 13:17), and it is the Lord’s hand, not Paul’s. Then remember who is pronouncing it. A dozen years earlier a light had struck him blind on the Damascus road, and he had gone into the city led by the hand (9:8). Paul is not enjoying it. He is recognising it.

For a time. A sentence with an end date, a judgment with mercy in it. Paul had been blind for three days, and at the end of them a man had put hands on him and called him brother (9:17). The hand that struck Saul down was Christ’s, and so was the hand that lifted him. Nothing in this passage puts Elymas beyond hope, and the one man in the room who knew that darkness is the one who set a limit on it. Luke never tells us what became of him.

Mist and darkness. Mist first, then darkness: the man who had been leading a governor by the ear now needs a stranger to lead him by the hand.

Astonished at the teaching. Luke is clear about what actually converted the proconsul. He was astonished not at the miracle but at the teaching. The sign opens the door and the word does the work, and a man who believes only because he was impressed has not yet believed the gospel itself. Sergius Paulus is the first named Gentile ruler in Acts to believe.

Did the proconsul really become a Christian? Luke says plainly that he believed, and in Acts that word means saving faith, not polite interest. Some have doubted it because Luke does not mention his baptism, but Luke often leaves such details out, and his point is clear: the governor of Cyprus put his trust in the Lord Jesus. It is a fine thing to notice that the first convert of Paul’s Gentile mission was a Roman of the highest rank, and that at Philippi the same gospel would reach a businesswoman and a jailer, and set a slave girl free from the spirit that enslaved her (16:14–34). The gospel came for the highest and the lowest alike.

Why are such miracles not common today? Signs like this blindness accompanied the apostles, marking them out as Christ’s authorised messengers while the new covenant word was being given (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). With the apostles gone and Scripture complete, that particular ministry has ceased. Christians differ here, and many who expect such signs today love the Lord deeply; this commentary’s view rests on the link Scripture itself draws between the signs and the apostles. God has not changed, and he still answers prayer, heals and judges as he wills. But the ordinary means he now uses to astonish people is the one that did the real work in Paphos: the teaching of the Lord, faithfully spoken.

Was it not cruel to strike a man blind? It was a judgment, and Scripture does not apologise for God’s judgments, because he is holy and Elymas was doing grave harm, trying to keep another man from eternal life. But look at its shape. It was limited, for a time; it stopped the harm at once; and it gave Elymas the very experience by which God had once brought Paul to himself. A God who never opposed evil would not be kind, only indifferent. This God judges, and even his judgment leaves a door open.

For worship. The teaching that astonished a Roman governor astonishes still: the Judge of all became the one judged, and the Light of the world went into the dark at Calvary, where the sun’s light failed at noon while he hung there (Luke 23:44–45). Elymas could not see the sun for a time. The Son of God went under the darkness of judgment itself, so that the blind could be led by the hand into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9).

parallels.desc: Paul himself led by the hand

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–52 — Paul's Sermon in Pisidian Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Pisidian Antioch Paul preaches in the synagogue: the story of Israel leads to Jesus, the promised Son of David, crucified and raised, through whom forgiveness and justification are offered to all who believe. The response divides the city: jealous opposition from the synagogue’s leaders, joy among the Gentiles, and the missionaries driven out, leaving behind disciples full of joy and the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith in Paul’s First Sermon

Verses 38–39 are the first explicit statement in Acts of justification by faith. Freed can be rendered justified, a courtroom word. The law cannot give that verdict; faith in the crucified and risen Jesus receives it. And it is not preached softly: the same sermon that announces the amnesty ends with Habakkuk’s warning to scoffers (vv. 40–41).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A city hungry for the word was met by jealous opposition from the synagogue’s leaders. Now: Those who have long been near the things of God are sometimes the slowest to welcome his work among newcomers, while outsiders receive it gladly; it is a warning for insiders in every church.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul and his companions. From here on it is Paul, and the man who fetched him from Tarsus and vouched for him in Jerusalem has become part of the phrase and his companions.

Overtaken and content. There is no meeting, no vote. Barnabas, who had every reason to mind, appears not to have minded: a man overtaken by somebody else’s growth, who goes on walking beside him. Barnabas could bear it because his worth did not lie in his place in the phrase; his name was already written in heaven (Luke 10:20).

John left them. No reason given, and we do not know why. Homesickness, danger, malaria (compare Galatians 4:13), a cousin slipped to second place, a mission turning to Gentiles too fast: all are guesses, and none is in the text.

What it cost. Luke does record the cost. Two chapters on, this departure, which Paul regards as desertion (15:38), breaks up the partnership. The two men who walked out of Antioch together separate over it (15:36–41).

Failure need not be final. In what was probably the last letter Paul wrote, from a Roman prison with his own execution close, he asks for Mark by name: Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11; see also Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24). The record of the desertion is in Scripture for ever. So is the request for him at the end.

Another road to Jerusalem. Luke’s Gospel turns on a journey in the other direction. When the days drew near for him to be taken up, Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), knowing what waited there, and he did not turn back when the road grew hard or his friends fell away. Mark went back to Jerusalem because the road ahead was too much. Jesus went up to Jerusalem because the road ahead was the cross. That is why the story of a deserter does not end at Perga. The one who never left the road walked it for those who do, and a Saviour who finished his work can restore a young man who did not finish his.

Antioch in Pisidia. The two who remain go up. Pisidian Antioch, a Roman colony, lay a hundred miles inland and three and a half thousand feet up, over the Taurus mountains: danger from rivers, danger from robbers (2 Corinthians 11:26).

They sat down. This was Paul’s usual practice (17:2). Two travel-stained strangers sat down like anybody else and waited to see whether they would be asked. Paul’s first recorded sermon begins with two men sitting down and keeping quiet.

I gave up on something God gave me to do. Can I come back? Yes, and Mark is your proof. His failure was real, it was public, and it hurt people he loved. Scripture does not pretend otherwise. But the same Scripture shows him restored, trusted and useful. Coming back usually means owning the failure honestly, without excuses, and then simply taking up faithful work again, often smaller work, alongside people who will help you. You will not undo Perga. You do not need to. The Lord who restored Peter after his denials restores deserters still.

How should I treat someone who let the team down? Paul and Barnabas both had a point. Paul saw that the work needed reliable men; Barnabas saw that a young man needed a second chance. In the end both were vindicated, and Paul himself came to value Mark. So take failure seriously, and do not pretend it does not matter, but do not write the person off. Give him a smaller task, an older friend, and time. Many of the most useful servants in the church were once somebody’s disappointment.

For worship. The Lord wastes nothing, not even a desertion. The young man who turned back at Perga lived to write a Gospel, by the church’s early testimony, and its great sentence is about the one who never turned back: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Mark could not finish one journey. He was given the honour of telling the world about the one who finished everything.
verseByVerse.note: Perga was in Pamphylia on the south coast of Asia Minor; Pisidian Antioch lay about 100 miles north, up in the mountains. Mark’s departure later divided Paul and Barnabas.

parallels.desc: Mark is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the reading. Then the rulers of the synagogue, lay leaders who organised the service, notice the two visitors and send a message down to them; visiting teachers were often invited to speak (Luke 4:16–17).

The reading and its history. The service centred on two readings: one from the Law, the five books of Moses, and one from the Prophets, like the passage Jesus stood to read from Isaiah at Nazareth (Luke 4:16–20). After them came a word of exhortation, open to any competent man present, exactly the door opened to Paul. The roots run to Moses (Deuteronomy 31:10–13) and Ezra (Nehemiah 8:8); the synagogue itself probably grew up in the exile.

And do Jews still do this? Yes, with striking continuity. To this day the Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll on the Sabbath (and Mondays, Thursdays, and festivals), on the annual cycle that ends and begins again each year at Simchat Torah (rejoicing in the Torah; in ancient Israel the cycle probably took about three years), still paired with a prophetic reading and a teaching: the very practice Luke describes, kept now as two thousand years ago. And it is the church’s inheritance too: the public reading of Scripture followed by exposition is the pattern Paul charged Timothy to keep, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching (1 Timothy 4:13), the shape of Christian worship ever since. The deep irony here: the Law and the Prophets had just been read aloud, and Paul rises to show that every line was pointing to the Jesus he is about to preach (Luke 24:27, 44). The reading set the table; Paul served Christ from it.

Any word of encouragement. In Greek a logos paraklēseōs, the phrase the writer to the Hebrews uses of his own long letter (Hebrews 13:22): a word that comes alongside and strengthens, the ancestor of the sermon. What they will get is the consolation itself. Luke used the same noun of what old Simeon was waiting for in the temple, the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25), and Simeon found it in a baby in his arms. Paul is about to tell this synagogue that the comfort every Sabbath reading had promised has a name, and has risen from the dead.

They have no idea what they have asked for. By the next Sabbath the whole city will be at the door. A polite formality is what the whole chapter turns on, which is very often how God opens a door.

Is a sermon really encouragement, even when it is hard? Yes. The word Paul was invited to give was a word of encouragement, and the sermon that followed contained a sharp warning (vv. 40–41). Biblical encouragement is not flattery. It is the word that comes alongside you and puts strength into you, and sometimes that strength comes through a rebuke, sometimes through comfort, always through Christ. A sermon that only made you feel good about yourself would not have encouraged you; one that brought you to Christ always does, even when it hurts on the way.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stood up. In a synagogue the teacher normally sat to expound (Jesus sat down in Nazareth before he began, Luke 4:20), and Paul stands, motioning with his hand, the posture and gesture of a public speaker in the Greek world. Luke notices that hand twice more (21:40; 26:1). This is his first recorded sermon.

In the flow. This sermon is Luke’s fullest sample of Paul’s preaching in a synagogue, as the speech at Athens (17:22–31) will be his sample of Paul’s preaching to pagans. It moves from Israel’s history (vv. 17–22), to the promise kept in Jesus (vv. 23–37), to the offer and the warning (vv. 38–41). Peter preached the same gospel at Pentecost (2:14–36): the apostle to the Gentiles has no different message from the apostle to the Jews.

You who fear God. His first sentence names two congregations, not one. The God-fearers were Gentiles who had attached themselves to the synagogue. They worshipped the God of Israel but had not been circumcised. Picture a man who has heard the promises to Abraham read aloud perhaps a thousand times, each time understanding that they were addressed to somebody else’s family. Cornelius was one (10:2), and Lydia (16:14). So the Gentile response in verse 48 is not a sudden lurch. The ground had been ploughed for years by the synagogue itself.

Chose our fathers. The sermon opens on God’s choosing. Israel was chosen not for its greatness but because the LORD set his love on them (Deuteronomy 7:6–8). It will also end on God’s choosing: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (v. 48). Every man in that room would have said amen to the first. What split the congregation a week later was not whether God chooses. It was whom.

Made the people great in Egypt. The multiplying of the promised family did not happen in the promised land. It happened in a foreign country, under a king who was trying to stop it: the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied (Exodus 1:12). God’s promise to Abraham made its greatest visible progress during the centuries that looked, from the inside, like the promise having been forgotten.

The exodus he accomplished. With uplifted arm (Exodus 6:6): Paul starts with the exodus because the gospel is a second one. On the mountain of transfiguration, Luke tells us, Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31), and the word Luke uses is exodos. Isaiah, looking ahead to the greater deliverance, asked to whom the arm of the LORD had been revealed, and answered with the Servant despised, pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities (Isaiah 53:1–5). The arm raised over Egypt was bared again at Golgotha, not to strike Israel’s enemies but to take the blow itself, and lead a people out of a worse slavery than Pharaoh’s.

Why does Paul start so far back? Because he wants them to see that Jesus is not a new idea but the point of the whole story. Every hearer knew this history; Paul retells it so that, when he reaches Jesus, they will see the story landing where it was always heading. It is also a lesson in how to read the Old Testament. It is not a collection of moral examples; it is one long account of God choosing, rescuing, enduring and promising, all of it leading to his Son (Luke 24:27).

On a Tuesday. If you are in an Egypt of your own, a job, a family situation, an illness you would never have chosen, do not conclude that God’s purposes for you have stalled. His people grew most where it looked least likely.
verseByVerse.note: “You who fear God” are Gentile worshippers of Israel’s God.

parallels.desc: with an outstretched arm

verseByVerse.quote: "And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He put up with them. The word (etropophorēsen) means he bore with their ways. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read he carried them (etrophophorēsen, a difference of one letter), and points to what Moses said of these same forty years: the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son (Deuteronomy 1:31). Both are true of that wilderness, and neither flatters Israel: either God spent forty years enduring them or forty years carrying them, and the reason he had to do either is the same.

Measure the forty years. Within weeks of Sinai they were dancing round a golden calf, and soon proposed choosing a leader to take them back to Egypt (Numbers 14:4). God’s own summary is that they put him to the test ten times (Numbers 14:22). The generation that saw the sea open died in the sand.

He did not leave, and he did not pretend. He put up with them. If you have ever suspected that God stays with you only because he has not looked closely, this verse is better news than that. He has looked, the assessment is in, and he is still walking at the pace of the slowest man in the column.

As an inheritance. Then, in the next breath, a gift, not an achievement. Nobody in Scripture earns an inheritance; it comes to you because of who your father is. Moses made sure they could not misunderstand it: not because of your righteousness (Deuteronomy 9:5).

Seven nations in Canaan. Paul passes over it in a phrase (Deuteronomy 7:1), but an honest reader feels its weight: how could a good God order the destruction of the Canaanites? We must not be glib; the loss of life is real and grievous. But several truths, held together, show this is not the arbitrary cruelty it is often imagined to be.

First, it was judgment, not ethnic hatred. Israel had no general warrant to harm Gentiles; she was even to offer peace to distant cities (Deuteronomy 20:10). This was a bounded act of justice on particular nations for particular, appalling sin. God held back judgment four hundred years, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (Genesis 15:16). And the sin? Among other things, burning their own children alive in sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31; Leviticus 18:21), with entrenched idolatry and cultic prostitution, until the land itself, defiled, vomited out its inhabitants (Leviticus 18:24–25). This is the wrath of a holy God against great and violent evil, long endured.

Second, it was not favouritism toward Israel. God twice tells them this is not because of your righteousness but because of the wickedness of these nations (Deuteronomy 9:4–6), warning that if Israel does the same, the land will vomit them out too (Leviticus 18:28), and centuries later it did, in the exile. The standard is God’s holiness applied impartially, not ethnic preference. And mercy stood open throughout: Rahab the Canaanite was spared through faith and stands in the Messiah’s own bloodline (Joshua 6:25; Matthew 1:5). The issue was never race but allegiance.

Third, underneath the objection lies a question it skips. We assume the Canaanites had a right to life that God violated. But Scripture holds that God is the Author and rightful Lord of all life (Deuteronomy 32:39), and that every one of us has already forfeited life through sin (Romans 6:23). On that reckoning, what needs explaining is not that God judges sin, but that he is so patient, and that anyone is spared at all. (On the hardest part, the children, Scripture gives no glib answer; we rest in the One of whom Abraham asked, Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Genesis 18:25), trusting his mercy toward little ones, as David did for his own child (2 Samuel 12:23), and refusing to pretend we see more than we do.)

And finally, a unique event. It is emphatically not a model for today. Jesus refused the sword (my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would have been fighting, John 18:36); the church’s weapons are not of the flesh (2 Corinthians 10:4); we love our enemies and leave vengeance to God (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:19). No one may invoke Joshua to justify violence in Christ’s name. The conquest is a sober preview of the final judgment, and at the cross the judgment we all deserve fell on Jesus. The same holy God who judged Canaan did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32) but laid our condemnation on him, so that wrath and mercy met. The only refuge, as for Rahab, is faith in the God of Israel, now revealed in Christ.

Does God still put up with his people today? Yes, and every honest Christian depends on it. The patience that bore with Israel in the wilderness bears with the church now: our grumbling, our forgetfulness, our small idolatries. But patience is not approval. The wilderness generation also shows that God’s patience is meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), and Hebrews uses this very forty years as a warning not to harden our hearts (Hebrews 3:7–19). So take comfort that he bears with you, and take care not to treat his bearing as permission.

For worship. For forty years the Holy One walked through the sand with a complaining people and did not walk away. He fed them bread from heaven and gave them water from the rock, and Paul says that the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4): the Son of God was already among them, bearing with them, struck so that they might drink.

parallels.desc: seven nations greater than you

verseByVerse.quote: "All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The difficulty. About 450 years is a well-known chronological knot. If the 450 years covers the period of the judges, as the older printed Greek text and the King James read it, then the sum will not come out. First Kings 6:1 puts 480 years between the exodus and the fourth year of Solomon, and 450 years of judges alone leaves no room for the wilderness, the conquest, Samuel, Saul, David, and the first four years of Solomon on top.

The better reading. The better attested reading, which is what the ESV translates, attaches the number to what has just been said rather than to what follows: all this, the growth in Egypt, the exodus, the wilderness, the dividing of the land, took about 450 years. Then the sum works neatly: about four hundred years in Egypt (Genesis 15:13; Acts 7:6), forty in the wilderness, and roughly seven to ten to take and divide the land. And Paul says about.

He gave them judges. The judges were God’s gift of deliverers, and consider what that word means, given what the book of Judges actually contains. It is one of the bleakest stretches in Israel’s history, a spiral of idolatry, oppression and rescue, until the book’s own closing verdict is that everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25). And God’s response, through three centuries of it, was to go on giving.

Look at what he gave. It is not a roll of heroes. A left-handed assassin. A woman, with a general who would not go without her. A frightened man threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the enemy. The son of a prostitute, thrown out by his own family. A strong man who could not govern his own appetites and ended blind, grinding grain in his enemies’ prison. He was not doing his best with poor material. He was demonstrating, over three hundred years, that the deliverance never depended on the deliverer.

The Judge who did not die. The recital is running toward one name. Judges keeps raising up saviours (the LORD raised up a deliverer, Judges 3:9, 15) and keeps watching each rescue wear off, because whenever the judge died, they turned back (Judges 2:19). The cycle could only be broken by a deliverer who did not die, or who died and did not stay dead. That is exactly where this sermon is going: God raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption (13:30–34). His rescue does not wear off.

Does a chronological puzzle like this undermine the Bible’s reliability? No. A difficulty is not a demonstrated error. Here the problem disappears once you notice which clause the number belongs to, and that Paul says about. Many such puzzles have clear answers; a few still lack a certain one, and an honest reader can say so without alarm. Scripture is true in all it affirms, and our understanding of ancient numbering, manuscripts and summaries is what needs patience. A book that had been tidied up by later hands would have fewer such knots, not more.

On a Tuesday. Look at the imperfect people God has put over you, your pastor, your parents, your manager, and thank God for one specific good he has done you through one of them.
verseByVerse.note: The 450 years probably cover the stay in Egypt, the wilderness and the conquest.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked for a king. The older account tells us that the asking was itself the sin: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Samuel 8:7). Samuel told them what a king would cost, and they said: no, we will have a king. Underneath the demand was a hunger to be like everyone else; they wanted a king like all the nations (1 Samuel 8:5, 20).

Answered prayer is not always approval. He gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Psalm 106:15): the psalm is speaking of the quails in the wilderness, but the principle is the same. Scripture will not let us read every answered prayer as a divine endorsement. Some doors open because you leaned on them.

For forty years. The forty is Paul’s, not the Old Testament’s. The text of 1 Samuel 13:1 is incomplete, as the ESV’s footnote there shows, and gives no reliable figure for Saul’s reign. Josephus, writing a generation after Paul, gives forty in one place (though twenty in another), so Paul is repeating a received figure of his day rather than inventing one.

A Saul of the tribe of Benjamin. Standing in front of them is another Saul of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5), removed from his old course on a road. He does not draw the line.

He raised up David. The commendation Paul quotes joins Scriptures: a man after his own heart from 1 Samuel 13:14, I have found David, my servant from Psalm 89:20, and the words about doing all my will echo what God says of Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28. And it raises a question.

How can God call David a man after his own heart? This is the man who took another man’s wife; who, when the pregnancy could not be hidden, tried to manoeuvre the husband home to cover it; and who, when the husband proved too loyal to go, had him posted where the fighting was heaviest and the line pulled back from him. Adultery finished off by murder by memorandum. And this is God’s man? Three things, and they matter.

First, the sentence describes God’s choice. It was spoken long before Bathsheba, and it is not a character reference. God says it in 1 Samuel 13, at the moment Saul is rejected, and its emphasis falls on the seeking rather than on the man found: the LORD has sought out a man after his own heart.

Second, what each did when he was caught. What actually separates the two kings is not that one sinned and the other did not. Saul, confronted over Amalek, argued: the people did it, the animals were meant for sacrifice, and in any case he had obeyed. When at last he said I have sinned, he asked in the same breath to be honoured before the elders of the people (1 Samuel 15:24–30). David, confronted by Nathan with a story and one sentence, you are the man, answered: I have sinned against the LORD (2 Samuel 12:13). No lawyer, no context, no blame shifted. And then he wrote it up, set it to music, and handed it to the choirmaster, so that the whole nation could sing his worst hour back to him forever (Psalm 51). That is a man who cared more about being right with God than about being thought well of.

Third, the direction of a life. Who will do all my will is measured against the man he replaced. Saul had one plain instruction at Amalek and kept the best of the livestock. David’s life, for all its wreckage, ran in the direction God pointed; he never went after other gods, and that is precisely the measurement the books of Kings apply to every later king in the line.

God’s man cannot stay down. If you are afraid your failures have disqualified you, remember that God’s chosen king has a murder in his file. If you are tempted to use that as cover, remember what it cost him: a dead child, a fractured house, a son in armed rebellion, and a psalm he had to sing in public for the rest of his life. God’s man is not the man who never falls. He is the man who cannot stay down, because God will not leave him there.

The Son who did all his will. Read honestly, the commendation is bigger than the man. David did not do all God’s will; Bathsheba and Uriah are in the record. Only one son of David has ever been able to say, I have come to do your will, O God (Hebrews 10:7, from Psalm 40), or that his food was to do the will of the one who sent him and to accomplish his work (John 4:34). And his perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19), which is why a sinner can afford to be as honest as David. God raised up David, and the same verb is used of raising Jesus from the dead (vv. 30, 37), not to a throne in Jerusalem but from the grave.

What does it actually mean to be after God’s heart? It means to want what God wants and to love what he loves. In David’s case that showed in his delight in God’s presence, his hunger for God’s honour, his refusal to touch the Lord’s anointed even when Saul hunted him, and his readiness to be broken over sin. It is not a temperament or a talent. It is a direction of the heart that only grace produces, and it is visible most clearly not in success but in repentance. You can ask God for it today: create in me a clean heart, O God (Psalm 51:10).

On a Tuesday. The last time you were confronted with a fault, by your spouse, a friend, your own conscience, did you argue like Saul or confess like David? If it was Saul, go back to that person this week and say the plain words: I was wrong.
verseByVerse.note: The Old Testament does not state Saul’s reign clearly; the historian Josephus also gives forty years.

parallels.desc: a man after his own heart

verseByVerse.quote: "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise made. As he promised: the last three words carry the weight. David is settled at last: the wars are over, he is living in a house of cedar, and it strikes him that the ark of God is still under canvas. He proposes to build a temple. That same night God’s answer comes through Nathan; it declines the offer and returns it multiplied: you will not build me a house; I will build you one. I will raise up your offspring after you, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever; your throne shall be established forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16).

The promise buried. Four hundred years after Nathan, Nebuchadnezzar’s army broke into Jerusalem. The last king of David’s line, Zedekiah, was caught fleeing; they killed his sons in front of him and then put out his eyes, so that the last thing he saw was the end of the dynasty (2 Kings 25:7). No son of David sat on a throne in Jerusalem again. Some six hundred years, and the royal line had run down into a carpenter’s shop in a village in the hills of Galilee.

Not as we still hope. Any reasonable observer would have called that promise dead. It had been publicly falsified for two dozen generations. And a travelling tentmaker stands up and says: as he promised. Not as we still hope. As he promised, and here he is.

God has brought. He did not make salvation available in principle. He led a Saviour in, in a body, to a particular people, at a particular date, under a named governor.

A Savior. The word (sōtēr) means rescuer, deliverer, and it had a rival in that town. In a Roman colony of old legionaries, Saviour was the empire’s word for its emperor, and Paul hands the title to a crucified Galilean. Every heart still has its candidate for the title: a career, a marriage, a political cause, a bank balance. Each of them asks to be served and none of them can save. The Saviour God brought gives himself for those he saves.

What exactly does Jesus save us from? From the guilt of our sin and the wrath of God it deserves, from the power of sin that enslaves us, and in the end from the very presence of sin and death. Matthew puts it plainly: he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). He is not first a helper for people who are mostly managing; he is a rescuer for people who are lost. That is why the name and the title belong together: Jesus means the LORD saves, and the Saviour is the LORD himself come to do it.

On a Tuesday. Name the promise of God you have quietly written off: not denied, just shelved, because of how long it has been. Then look again at how late this one was, and how completely kept.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John had proclaimed. Why John, five hundred miles from the Jordan? Because they had heard of him: John’s movement had travelled into the Dispersion without its ending (18:25; 19:1–7). So Paul is closing a real gap: yes, John, and here is what John himself said he was for.

Finishing his course. The word is dromos, a runner’s track, the distance a man has been set to cover. Paul will use it of himself twice: if only I may finish my course (20:24), and at the very end, I have finished the race (2 Timothy 4:7). John’s course finished in a cell, cut short because a girl danced well at a birthday party (Mark 6:21–28). By every measurement we normally use, it was a humiliating end. Scripture calls it finishing his course. God does not measure a life by where it stopped. He measures it by whether the ground assigned to you was covered.

I am not he. At the height of his influence, with crowds coming out to him and delegations sent to ask who he was, John refused to be thought the Messiah (John 1:20). He spent his greatest capital on a denial.

Not worthy to untie. Untying sandals was a slave’s job (Luke 3:16). A later rabbinic saying excused a disciple from this one slave’s task; John says he is not fit even for it.

The pattern for preparatory work. This is the pattern for nearly everybody: the parent whose child will go further, the teacher whose pupil will be the better preacher. I am not he is accuracy, and it is liberating, because the moment you stop being the point you stop having to be impressive. John was told that his whole value lay in making somebody else visible, and he called it his joy (John 3:29–30).

What was John’s baptism, and how is it different from Christian baptism? John’s baptism was a sign of repentance, preparing Israel for the coming Messiah. Christian baptism is baptism into the name of the Lord Jesus, after he has come, died and risen, and it signifies union with him and the gift of the Spirit. That is why the men at Ephesus who knew only John’s baptism were baptised again in Jesus’ name once they believed (19:4–5). John pointed forward; Christian baptism looks back to a finished work and confesses it. And repentance, in both, means more than feeling sorry: it is a change of mind that becomes a change of direction, turning from sin to God, and John told the crowds what that looked like in their own jobs and homes (Luke 3:8–14).

For worship. The greatest man born of woman knelt in his mind before the sandals of Jesus. And the One whose sandals he was not worthy to untie took off his own outer garment, knelt, and washed the feet of his disciples, and then went to the cross to wash them entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers. Here the sermon stops being a history lesson: Paul names Jews and God-fearing Gentiles inside a single word.

To us. Not to them, back there, but to the people in this room, this morning. Every sermon has to make that turn or it is a lecture. To a God-fearer, years a guest at somebody else’s family reading of a will, a visiting rabbi says: not you may listen, but sent to us.

Has been sent. The message was not discovered by clever men. It was dispatched, deliberately, to a particular address; the word behind our word apostle is inside that verb.

The message and the Sent One. Hebrews calls Jesus the apostle of our confession (Hebrews 3:1), the one sent from the Father, and Jesus said that whoever receives the one he sends receives him (John 13:20). So the message of this salvation is not a report about a Saviour who stays at a distance. It is the way the sent Son himself arrives in a synagogue in Pisidia, and whoever receives the word receives him.

This salvation. Not salvation in general, but the specific thing that happened to a named man under a named governor. Christianity is not a theory about how people get saved. It is a report of something done.

How can I know the message is really for me? Because it is addressed to everyone who hears it, without exception and without a qualifying test. You do not need first to prove that you are chosen, or good enough, or sorry enough. The gospel comes to you as a sinner and says: this is for you; come. Election is God’s secret business, and it is discovered by believing, not before believing. If you have heard this message, it has been sent to you, and the right response is not to wonder whether you are allowed to take it but to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read every Sabbath. The prophets had been read aloud in that synagogue not long before (v. 15). The men who missed the Messiah did exactly what this congregation had done before Paul stood up. Paul later describes it as a veil lying over the heart whenever Moses is read (2 Corinthians 3:14–15).

Fulfilled them by condemning him. Their blindness did not frustrate the Scriptures. It carried them out. They were not derailing God’s plan but were the instrument of it, and they did not know.

No guilt worthy of death. If they were fulfilling prophecy, were they guilty? Paul answers in this very breath, and the answer is yes. This was a court that got it right and asked for the execution anyway. Luke’s Gospel has Pilate say three separate times that he finds no guilt in the man (Luke 23:4, 14, 22).

Ignorant and answerable. So both things stand: they acted in ignorance, and they are answerable. Peter had already held those two together in Jerusalem itself, telling the crowd that they and their rulers had acted in ignorance and yet had killed the Author of life (3:15–17). Paul lets the two stand side by side without softening either.

Would we have known better? Now the part aimed at us. It is natural for any of us to assume quietly that we would have known better. It is very hard not to; we have the end of the story and they did not. So be exact about who these people were. They were the most Scripture-soaked population on earth. Many of them could read it in the language it was written in. They had it read publicly every week of their lives. They lived in the city where it was kept and worked in the building where the promises were housed. And they looked straight at the fulfilment and saw a blasphemer. Familiarity with the Bible is not the same thing as recognition of Christ. You can read a chapter every morning for thirty years and be no nearer. That is not an argument for reading less; it is a reason to pray before you read, because the difference between them and us was never that we are cleverer. And if you do read, asking him to show you Christ, that very asking is a sign that he is already opening your eyes (Luke 24:45).

If God planned it, how can people be blamed for it? Because God’s plan does not force anyone to act against his own will. The rulers did exactly what they wanted to do, from motives that were their own: envy, fear, the love of power. God, in his wisdom, ruled over their wickedness and turned it to the salvation of the world (2:23; 4:27–28). Scripture never lets God’s sovereignty excuse human sin, and never lets human sin escape God’s sovereignty. Both are taught; we are to believe both, and to be glad that even the worst crime in history could not slip out of the hands of a good God.

On a Tuesday. The rulers had a reason to misread the prophets: recognising this man would have cost them their standing, their income and their control of the temple. So ask what a plain reading of Scripture would cost you, and whether that happens to be a passage you have found unusually difficult to be sure about. Then ask the Lord who opened the disciples’ minds to open yours.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that was written of him. All of it (John 19:28, 30): thirty pieces of silver (Zechariah 11:12–13), silence before his accusers (Isaiah 53:7), hands and feet pierced and clothing divided by lot (Psalm 22:16–18), numbered with transgressors (Isaiah 53:12), not a bone broken (Psalm 34:20), and a grave with a rich man (Isaiah 53:9). They were in the scrolls in that synagogue’s own cupboard, and Paul is preaching to men who could go and check him.

Who laid him in a tomb. In fact it was Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council who had not consented, who laid him in a tomb (Luke 23:50–53). Paul is compressing, speaking of Jerusalem as a single actor, the way we say that a city did something.

Do not hurry past the burial. It is in Paul’s summary of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4) and in the creed, because the burial is the notary’s seal on the death. Every theory that Jesus merely fainted on the cross and revived in the cool of the tomb has to explain how a man in that condition, sealed behind a stone he could not have reached from the inside, presented himself three days later as the conqueror of death. The stone was moved from the outside.

Why the tree here, and not the cross? The word is xylon, which means simply wood or timber: a beam, a stake, a tree. The apostles use it of the cross on purpose (also 5:30; 10:39; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24), to sound a deliberate echo of the Law: if a man is hanged on a tree, his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). To call the cross a tree is therefore to load the word with meaning: Jesus hung where the accursed criminal hung, bearing the curse of God in our place, as Paul spells out: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). And see the precise fit right here: they took him down from the tree and buried him at once, fulfilling that very command not to leave the body on the tree overnight. The word is no loose synonym; it preaches the heart of the cross: he took our curse. To be cursed by God means to stand under his judgment, cut off from his blessing; Jesus took that place so that those who trust him might receive the blessing promised to Abraham instead (Galatians 3:14). (Some also hear a quiet echo that the curse which entered the world by a tree in Eden was undone on a tree at Calvary, a lovely thought, though the plain reference is Deuteronomy’s curse.)

Why does it matter so much that prophecy was fulfilled in detail? Because it shows that the cross was not an accident God later made the best of. It was the plan, announced centuries ahead and carried out to the letter. That matters for your faith: Christianity rests on events God foretold and then did, which you can check. And it matters for your comfort: if God kept every word about his Son’s suffering, down to the dice and the vinegar, he will keep every word about your salvation and your future too.

For worship. He who laid the foundations of the earth was laid in a hole cut in its rock. The hands that formed Adam from the dust were wrapped in linen and folded still. He went all the way down, so that nothing in that darkness would be strange to him when he comes to raise his people out of it. A borrowed grave was enough. He needed it only until the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: "But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God raised him. In verses 27 to 29 the subject is they, and what men do ends in a sealed tomb. Then the subject changes, and the direction of the whole history reverses, as in apostolic sermon after apostolic sermon in this book (2:24; 3:15; 4:10).

For many days he appeared. He does not say the resurrection was felt. He gives duration and witnesses: forty days (1:3), not one moment at dawn that could be put down to grief and poor light. And to those who had come up with him from Galilee: the same men, the whole way, there when it went wrong.

Now his witnesses. Present tense: fifteen years on, the men he cites are alive and can be questioned. It is exactly the move he makes in writing to Corinth: more than five hundred saw him at one time, most of whom are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:6). That is a strange sentence to write unless you positively want your readers to go and check.

Witnesses rather than experience. Paul does not use his own encounter, which Luke tells three times. He rests the resurrection on the testimony of those who had followed Jesus from Galilee, people he had been hunting at the time. That is the right way round, and it is the opposite of how most of us argue for our faith.

My own experience of God feels thin. Is my faith on weak ground? No. Your assurance does not stand on the vividness of what happened to you. It stands on what happened to Jesus, in public, in front of people who could be named, in a city where the authorities had every motive to produce a body and never did. Feelings rise and fall; the empty tomb does not. Experience matters, and the Spirit does give his people a living sense of God, but the foundation is history. On grey days, go back to the witnesses, read the resurrection chapters, and stand where they stood.

On a Tuesday. Write down the two words but God, and put them where you will see them today, over the thing that seems finished: a marriage, a prodigal, a diagnosis, your own sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We bring you the good news. Not advice or a technique for living better: a report that a promise has been kept.

To us their children. The fathers were given the promise. The children were given the thing. Hebrews puts it exactly: these all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13, 39–40). The gospel is not a new religion, but the completion of the old.

In the flow. Verses 32–37 rest on three texts: Psalm 2, who the risen Jesus is; Isaiah 55, what his rising brings; Psalm 16, why it can never be lost. A living King can give what a dead one never could.

The second Psalm. Psalm 2 is a coronation psalm for the king of David’s line, on the day he was enthroned. Paul applies it to the resurrection: the day God installed Jesus as king, declaring him Son with power (Romans 1:4; Hebrews 1:5; 5:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus became God’s Son at the resurrection, as if he were not his Son before. He is the eternal Son (John 1:1, 18; 17:5). The idea that God adopted a man on Easter morning (adoptionism) is wrong, for four reasons.

First, look at the psalm Paul is quoting. Its today is the day of enthronement, not of anybody’s conception. Israel’s kings were addressed as God’s son at their accession: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Samuel 7:14); I will make him the firstborn (Psalm 89:27). The language is throne language from the start.

Second, declared, not created. Paul says elsewhere precisely what the resurrection did to Jesus’s sonship: he was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). The resurrection published a fact; it did not manufacture one.

Third, the Son before the raising. God has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world (Hebrews 1:2), and Hebrews then quotes this very psalm three verses later (Hebrews 1:5) without the least embarrassment.

Fourth, the same guard at Pentecost. The identical guard is needed at Peter’s Pentecost sermon, where God has made him both Lord and Christ (2:36): there too the eternal Son is installed in the office he came to fill, not turned into something he was not.

So what changed on the third day? Not who Jesus is. What changed is who knows it. On the Friday the public verdict on him was that he was a blasphemer, justly executed, and heaven had said nothing. On the Sunday God said something, and what he said was: this is my Son, here is the proof, and I am putting him on the throne. If you have ever wondered what God thinks of Jesus, you are not left to guess. He said it out loud, in an empty tomb, in a way that cannot be argued with, and the sentence he used was: You are my Son.

What does this mean for me if I am in Christ? It means you belong to a King who is already reigning, not to a cause that might one day win. Psalm 2 goes on to promise the Son the nations as his heritage and the ends of the earth as his possession, which is exactly what is beginning to happen in this chapter. And because you are united to the Son, the Father’s pleasure in him reaches you too: you are adopted, a child of God (Galatians 4:5–7). The verdict of the empty tomb is the verdict over your life.

parallels.desc: you are my Son; today I have begotten you

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' Therefore he says also in another psalm, 'You will not let your Holy One see corruption.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No more to return to corruption. This phrase separates Easter from every other raising in the Bible: Jesus will never die again (Romans 6:9).

Reprieve or resurrection. The widow’s son at Nain sat up and spoke, and one day was buried again. Jairus’s daughter got up and was given something to eat, and in time she died. Lazarus came out, and somewhere there is dust that used to be Lazarus. Each was a reprieve, a body handed back on loan. Jesus was not resuscitated. He was raised out the far side of death and beyond its reach, into a body that will not wear out and cannot be reclaimed. Death has no second claim on him.

The holy and sure blessings of David. This is Isaiah 55:3, God’s everlasting covenant of steadfast love to David. The two texts share a word. Isaiah promises the holy and sure blessings of David; Psalm 16:10 says you will not let your Holy One see corruption. In the Greek Bible these congregations used, the same root stands behind holy in both places: hosios. Linking two passages by a shared term was a recognised Jewish method; Paul argues as his hearers had been taught to argue.

Sure blessings need a living King. But how sure can a covenant be if the man it was made with is in a tomb, and everyone who inherits it ends in a tomb as well? A dynasty of corpses is not an everlasting kingdom. If the promises to David are to be sure, at some point somebody in that line has to stop dying. That is why Paul reaches for the second text, Psalm 16:10, as Peter had done at Pentecost (2:27).

What are the blessings of David that come to us? Everything God promised to David’s house: a King who reigns for ever, God’s steadfast love that will not be withdrawn, a people secure in his kingdom, and, in Isaiah 55, an open invitation to everyone who thirsts to come and receive it without money. In Christ these become ours: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, an eternal inheritance. They are holy because God gives them, and sure because the King through whom they come can never die again and lose them.

On a Tuesday. At a believer’s graveside, or lying awake thinking of your own death, this is the difference that holds: not a longer loan, but a body given outright, because Christ lives for ever.

parallels.desc: the steadfast, sure love for David

verseByVerse.quote: "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David saw corruption. Psalm 16 cannot be about David, because David decayed, as Peter said at Pentecost (2:29).

A beautiful epitaph. The older versions turn the sentence the other way, that David served his own generation by the will of God. Both readings are true, and either way the boundary in the sentence is the same: in his own generation. Not in every generation. Not in ours.

Enough. David did not fix Israel; he left a divided family and an unbuilt temple. He did what God gave him to do in the years he was given, and then he stopped, and it is recorded as enough. If your own work feels small and local, a congregation of forty, a family, a class of children, one difficult relative, this is the sentence to keep. You are asked to serve the purpose of God in your own generation, the only one you have been issued with. Nobody in Scripture is commended for the size of his sphere.

Fell asleep. The man after God’s own heart rotted in the ground. Jesus did not. Christians call death sleep, and the word is only usable because one body in the history of the world went into a tomb and did not decay. Take verse 37 away and fell asleep is a euphemism. Leave verse 37 where it stands and it is a description.

Does fell asleep mean the dead are unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes how death looks from this side and what it is for the believer: temporary, peaceful, with a waking to come. It does not mean the soul is switched off. Jesus promised the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43); Paul said to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). The believer’s soul goes at once into the presence of the Lord, conscious and at rest, while the body sleeps in the ground awaiting the resurrection (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1; the Westminster Confession 32.1).

What does serving my generation look like in practice? It means taking the people, place and years God has given you as your actual assignment, rather than waiting for a bigger one. Ask: who has God put within my reach that no one else is placed to serve?
