Your children or grandchildren, your neighbours, your colleagues, the congregation you belong to, the needs of your town in your lifetime. Be faithful there, in the ordinary means: prayer, the word, hospitality, honest work, mercy. Then leave the next generation to the God who will raise up its servants too.

For worship. David’s tomb was still pointed out a thousand years later. The Son of David served the purpose of God for every generation at once: in one afternoon outside Jerusalem he did the Father’s will for all his people in every age, and his tomb was empty by the third morning. He holds every small generation of his people, ours among them, inside his everlasting one.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let it be known to you therefore. Everything up to this point has been argument; this is the conclusion.

Forgiveness of sins is proclaimed. Forgiveness is not offered on terms you must first earn, not made available to suitable applicants. Proclaimed: the word for a herald standing in a public square reading out what the king has decided. Paul is not explaining how to apply for a pardon but reading out an amnesty, through Jesus, offered to you.

Freed from everything. The ESV notes that freed can be rendered justified: dikaioutai, Paul’s great word, here for the first time in Acts. It is a courtroom word. To be justified is not to be improved, cleaned up, or given a fresh start. It is to have a judge declare, formally and on the record, that you are in the right. Everyone who believes: by faith alone. From everything: every sin, completely.

The courtroom. A man is in the dock. He did it. And the judge, who has read every page, says: not guilty. The reason is not that the file was thin, and not that the judge is easy-going. The reason is that the sentence has already been served by somebody else, and the court holds the receipt. That is justification. And the verdict is more than a blank slate. Christ’s own obedience is counted to the believer’s account, the way a gift is paid into an empty bank account, so that God regards him as clothed in his Son’s perfect record (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Not by the law of Moses. The law showed sin but could not remove it (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16). The sacrifices could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). But be specific here, because the general answer, that nobody keeps it perfectly, is true and is not the whole of it.

The limit written into the law. The law’s machinery for sin had a limit written into it. The ordinary offerings covered sins committed unwittingly, in ignorance, by mistake; a few deliberate wrongs, such as theft confessed and repaid, had an offering too (Leviticus 6:1–7). But for sin done defiantly, with the eyes open and the hand raised, the law named no personal offering at all: the person who does anything with a high hand shall be cut off from among his people (Numbers 15:30–31). A man could stand in the temple courts with his best lamb and there was nothing in the book that would take it.

David knew. He had committed adultery and arranged a killing, both with his eyes wide open, and when he came to write it up he said so: you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering (Psalm 51:16). He was a king with unlimited access to the altar, saying that the altar had nothing for him. Now they hear a thousand-year-old question answered in their own synagogue.

The high-handed sin. So the offer here is not for tidy people who have fallen a little short. It is aimed at the sin you did not drift into, the one you chose, the one nothing has ever touched: not resolutions, not service, not an unbroken run of Sundays, not a hundred confessions of the same thing. That is what Paul means by everything from which you could not be freed.

Everyone who believes. Not everyone who improves or has the right ancestry: believes. That is the whole entry requirement, and it is deliberately the one thing a beggar can do as easily as a benefactor. This is Galatians and Romans in embryo, before either letter was written.

Where Christians differ: justification. Some teach that justification is a process in which faith and works, or faith and sacraments, together make us righteous. This commentary’s view: Paul says everyone who believes is justified, declared righteous, from everything, through Christ, not by the law. Justification is God’s legal verdict, received by faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness credited to us (Romans 4:5; 5:1; Philippians 3:9). Good works follow as fruit, not as ground.

If I am justified by faith alone, does it matter how I live? It matters enormously, but not as the ground of your acceptance. The faith that receives Christ for pardon also receives him as Lord, and the Spirit who gives that faith begins at once to change the believer (Ephesians 2:8–10). So a justified person will fight sin and grow in good works, not to earn God’s verdict but because he already has it. Someone who says he trusts Christ and is content to go on in deliberate sin should not comfort himself with this verse; he should ask whether he has believed at all (James 2:17). But a believer who hates his sin and keeps fighting it, even after many falls, is not that person: the fight itself is the Spirit’s work in him (Galatians 5:17).

What if I do not feel forgiven? Then rest on what has been proclaimed rather than on what you feel. A herald’s announcement is true whether or not the prisoner believes it at first; the gates are open either way. Feelings of guilt often linger after a sin has been forgiven, especially for the high-handed sins. Take them back to the word: everyone who believes is freed from everything. Thank God for it in so many words, even before the feelings follow. They usually do, but your pardon does not wait for them.

On a Tuesday. Name the sin nothing has ever touched, and bring it, by name, to the One through whom forgiveness is proclaimed. Then, when the memory of it accuses you this week, answer it with this verse rather than with a promise to do better.

For worship. David stood at the altar with nothing to bring, and the law of Moses had nothing to give him. A thousand years later his Son stood in Jerusalem as the offering the law had never contained, and was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of his people (Isaiah 53:8), the deliberate sins among them included. He is just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26), and he sends a herald to read out two words of the decree: from everything.

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: 'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beware, therefore. He has just announced an amnesty. He ends by telling them what happens to men who laugh at one, as Peter did (3:23).

You scoffers. The quotation is Habakkuk 1:5, and its original setting is what gives it teeth. Habakkuk had complained that God was doing nothing about Judah’s corruption, and God’s answer was this verse: the work was Babylon, an answer that appalled him. The unbelievable work in the original was a judgment nobody would credit until the siege ramps were up against their own walls.

Paul’s use of it. God has done another unbelievable thing in your days, this time a rescue and not a ruin: a crucified man raised and forgiveness proclaimed in his name. The warning is: your fathers were told in advance about a work of God they refused to credit, and it arrived anyway, and it flattened the city. Do not assume that because this word is good news it can safely be laughed at. (Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament his hearers used, which reads you scoffers.)

The one who wept over the city. Some fifteen years earlier Jesus had come over the Mount of Olives, seen Jerusalem and wept over it, because it did not know the time of its visitation, and he told it that its enemies would set up a barricade around it and tear it down (Luke 19:41–44). Habakkuk’s siege ramps would rise again. The Lord whose resurrection Paul has just proclaimed is not a stranger issuing threats. He is the Saviour who weeps over scoffers and then dies for them, among them a man from Tarsus who had once been a blasphemer and a persecutor (1 Timothy 1:13). Paul’s warning carries Christ’s tears in it.

Perish. That is where Paul’s first recorded sermon lands. A gospel that has lost the ability to say that word is not the gospel Paul preached, and the kindness of a warning is exactly proportional to the danger it names. Nobody shouts at a man about a fire that is not burning.

Who the warning is aimed at. But the wrong reader will take it home. It is a warning to scoffers: men who hear, understand, and treat the thing as beneath serious attention. The frightened Christian who reads this verse at midnight and wonders whether it describes him should notice something simple: a scoffer is not troubled by warnings. The alarm you feel is itself evidence that the description has not fastened on you. The real question the verse puts is whether you have been told and are declining to act on it.

Is it loving to end a gospel message with a warning? Yes. Jesus warned about judgment more often than almost anyone else in Scripture, and he was love made visible. A warning is not the opposite of good news; it is what makes good news urgent. If perishing is real, then a preacher who never mentions it is not being kind, only quiet. The aim is never to frighten people away but to frighten them toward the only refuge. Paul’s warning comes straight after the widest offer imaginable, and that order is the pattern: the door first, then the reason to go through it now.
verseByVerse.note: Habakkuk warned of God’s astonishing judgment by the Babylonians.

parallels.desc: I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people begged. What they asked for was the same thing again next week.

They could not take a copy home. They had heard the most important thing they would ever hear, once, and had seven days to hold it with nothing but memory and each other. We carry more sermons in our pockets than we will ever listen to, and it is worth asking honestly which of us is in the worse position.

One week apart. This is the same congregation that will be filled with jealousy two verses from now. Between the begging and the jealousy lies one week, and Luke does not tell us what happened in it. Enthusiasm for the word of God and hostility to it can live in the same building seven days apart, and sometimes in the same person.

Many Jews and devout converts. Some did not wait: born Jews and proselytes, circumcised converts. The first fruit comes out of the synagogue, not around it.

Continue in the grace of God. The first pastoral instruction in that city was not do more. It was: stay. The Christian life begins and continues by grace (Galatians 5:4; Colossians 2:6). And grace in the New Testament is not a substance but a Person’s kindness, the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 13:14), poured out at the cross and given at the door. To continue in it is to stay near him.

What does it mean to continue in the grace of God? Grace is God’s free, undeserved kindness to sinners in Christ: salvation as a gift, never a wage, never earned. To continue in it, to remain, to abide, to hold fast, is to go on living every day on that same footing of free grace on which you first came in. You were welcomed home freely, with empty hands; continuing in grace means staying there: not slipping back onto the treadmill of trying to make God love you by being good enough, and not despairing when you fail, as though grace had run out. It is the very thing Paul urges on the Colossians: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him (Colossians 2:6). The way in is the way on.

Picture the prodigal son. He came home expecting to earn his keep as a hired servant, and instead the father ran to him, put the robe on him, and welcomed him as a beloved son. Now imagine that son, a week later, quietly slinking off to the servants’ quarters to start earning his place after all. That is what it looks like to drift out of grace. To continue in the grace of God is to stay at the Father’s table as a freely loved child, to keep coming to Christ with empty hands and drawing on his daily mercy for strength, forgiveness and growth (2 Peter 3:18). And lest this make you anxious about whether you can hold on: the call to continue is real (Colossians 1:23), yet the God who began this grace is the one who keeps us in it. We persevere because he preserves us.

How can I tell if I have drifted onto the treadmill? Watch for the signs. You feel closer to God on days you performed well and distant on days you failed. You put off praying after a sin until you feel you have done enough penance. You resent other Christians who seem to get away with less effort. You serve out of fear of disapproval rather than gratitude. The cure is not to try less but to go back to the gospel: confess the sin, receive the forgiveness Christ has already won, and serve from his acceptance rather than toward it.
verseByVerse.note: Converts to Judaism are proselytes.

verseByVerse.quote: The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Almost the whole city. Nobody organised this. What there very likely was, all week, was God-fearers going home to Gentile neighbours and relatives and saying: you will not believe what a man said in the synagogue on Saturday.

Filled with jealousy. Two things must be said about that sentence, and neither cancels the other. The first is that Luke cannot possibly mean the Jewish people as such. The preacher is a Jew, and so are most of the Christians in the story so far. Luke means the Jewish leaders of that synagogue and those under their influence, in that city, on that morning. The church’s long and shameful habit of reading sentences like this one as a verdict on a race is a misuse of Scripture that has cost innumerable lives, and the man speaking here is the man who wrote that he could wish himself accursed for the sake of his own people (Romans 9:3).

The jealousy is not alien to us. The second is that the jealousy is not hard to understand. These men had kept a minority faith alive in a pagan colony, at real cost, for generations. Last Sabbath the synagogue was theirs; this Sabbath it is full of people who have come to hear two strangers. And consider what they were jealous of. Not error: Luke records no answer to Paul’s argument. Luke says precisely what set it off: they saw the crowds.

The jealousy Jesus met first. When the crowds followed Jesus, the Pharisees said to one another, look, the world has gone after him (John 12:19), and Pilate could see that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed him over (Mark 15:10). A servant is not greater than his master (John 15:20). And the Master’s answer to envy was not to shrink the crowd. He went on welcoming outsiders to the end, and the envy that sent him to the cross became the means by which the door was opened to every Gentile in that Pisidian street.

Reviling him. Watch how the opposition degrades. First they contradict: that is at least an argument, and an argument can be answered. Then they are reviling him (blasphēmountes, blaspheming, slandering): the tearing down of a man instead of an answer to what he said. When a case moves from the argument to the man, the argument has been lost. And when it is your own tone that has moved from the argument to the man, it is worth asking what you are actually defending.

Why would religious people oppose a work of God? Because religion can become a possession rather than a surrender. When people come to feel that God’s work belongs to them, his blessing on outsiders feels like a loss. That is how the elder brother felt when the prodigal was welcomed (Luke 15:28–30). The danger is greatest for those who have served longest. The protection is to remember that we were outsiders too, brought in by grace, and that the work was never ours to own.

On a Tuesday. Recall the last time God did something obviously good through somebody whose success made your own work look small: the neighbouring church that grew while yours did not, the younger man who preaches better than you. What was the first thing you felt, before you corrected it? Confess it to the Saviour who was handed over out of envy and died for the envious; then pray for that church, that person, and ask God to bless them more.

verseByVerse.quote: And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spoke out boldly. Boldness is the great Acts virtue, prayed for and given (4:29–31). It does not mean loudly. It means without editing.

First to you. This order was not tact. It was owed: the promises were made to this people. It is what Paul later compressed into a single phrase: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16).

You judge yourselves unworthy. Thrust aside is the word Stephen used of Israel rejecting Moses (7:27, 39). Nobody said, I am unworthy of eternal life. They said: not from him; not on those terms. Paul tells them that is the same sentence. A refusal is a verdict, and the man who gives it has passed it on himself.

Polite refusals. Most refusals of Christ are not defiant. They are polite, reasonable and postponed. And the politeness does not alter what has been decided. If a man is handed the only bread there is and says, thank you, not just now, he has settled the question of whether he will eat, however courteously he put it.

We are turning to the Gentiles. A guard is needed here, because these words have been read for centuries as though God had finished with Israel on that Sabbath in Pisidia. He had not, and Paul demonstrates it with his feet: in the next city, they go to the synagogue again (14:1). He says it again in Corinth (18:6) and Rome (28:28), and goes first to the synagogue in each new city. Each time it was a local verdict on a local refusal, not a final verdict on a people. His own answer to the question is flat: has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite (Romans 11:1). What God intends for Israel’s future Christians have read in more than one way, and Romans 11 is the place to weigh them; but no reading permits a Christian to treat the Jewish people as written off.

A light for the Gentiles. That is Isaiah 49:6, and in Isaiah it is spoken to the Servant, that is, to the Messiah. Simeon understood it so (Luke 2:32). Paul takes a text about Christ and says the Lord has commanded us, not confusing himself with the Messiah. The church’s task is not a separate assignment running alongside Christ’s. It is a share in his. What the Servant was sent to do, his people are now doing in him, which is why Paul can call himself an ambassador and say that God makes his appeal through us (2 Corinthians 5:20).

Too light a thing. The full sentence runs: it is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob; I will make you as a light for the nations. God himself says that restoring Israel alone would be too small a commission. Paul is turning from the synagogue, and to some it will look like abandoning his people’s hope. He answers by producing the one verse in which God calls that hope, taken by itself, not big enough.

If God appoints people to life, how can people judge themselves unworthy? Both are true, and Luke sets them two verses apart on purpose. Those who reject the gospel do so freely and are fully responsible; no one is lost who wanted Christ and was refused. Those who receive it do so because God has worked in them (v. 48). Unbelief is ours; faith is God’s gift. We do not need to explain how the two fit to believe both, and we must not let either cancel the other.

On a Tuesday. If you have been saying not now to Christ, hear Paul: a polite postponement is still a verdict. Settle it today.

For worship. The Servant was given a commission so large that restoring Israel was too light a thing for it, and he fulfilled it by being lifted up on a cross outside Jerusalem. From a shut synagogue in Pisidia the beam swung out across the nations, and it has not stopped moving. The prophet whose warning closed Paul’s sermon saw where it ends: the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea (Habakkuk 2:14).
verseByVerse.note: The Servant’s calling to be a light to the nations is now carried out through the apostles.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gentiles began rejoicing. The door stood open to them, from a Jewish prophet, on the very morning the leadership was shutting them out.

Glorifying the word. Not Paul, whom they had every reason to make much of: the word of the Lord. Glorifying is normally kept for God himself, and Luke lets it fall on the message. When people are genuinely converted, the thing they cannot stop praising is what they heard, not the man they heard it from.

As many as were appointed. One of the clearest statements of election in Scripture. Appointed means ordained, assigned. Luke does not say as many as believed were appointed, but as many as were appointed believed. God’s appointment came first; their faith followed as its result.

Why is this one of the strongest verses in Scripture for election? Three things give it force. Appointed (tetagmenoi) is a perfect passive participle, a completed action done to them by another, and the unnamed agent, as so often, is God (the divine passive): as many as had been appointed by God to eternal life believed. The order is decisive: the appointment comes first and the believing follows; faith is the fruit, God’s prior choice the root. And the context sharpens it: two verses earlier the unbelieving Jews judge themselves unworthy of eternal life (v. 46), rejection at their own door, while the believing Gentiles are those appointed to eternal life. Luke sets the two side by side without embarrassment: responsibility in unbelief, grace in belief. It fits a steady pattern: all that the Father gives me will come to me (John 6:37); you do not believe because you are not among my sheep (John 10:26); the Lord opened her heart (Acts 16:14); Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 8:29–30.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians (Christians who hold that God’s choice responds to faith he foresees) read this as disposed to eternal life, by their own inclination, or say God appointed those he foresaw would believe. This commentary’s view: the passive voice points to an outside agent, God; and the word is used elsewhere of being appointed by authority (Romans 13:1, “instituted”). God’s sovereign choice is the cause of faith (Ephesians 1:4–5; John 6:37). It is a reason for joy and humility, not pride: they believed because grace chose them. And it fuels mission: God has his people in every city, waiting to hear (18:10).

How do our non-Reformed brothers read it? Godly, Bible-loving Christians who are not Calvinist (that is, not Reformed in their view of election) honour this verse and read it mainly two ways. First, some take the participle as middle voice, as many as had disposed themselves toward eternal life, describing the people’s own receptivity rather than a prior decree. (The form can be middle or passive; Reformed readers answer that, given Luke’s usage and the contrast with v. 46, the passive with God as agent is far more natural, but the middle is honestly held.) Second, the classic Arminian reading affirms a genuine appointing grounded in God’s foreknowledge: foreseeing who would freely believe, God appointed those to eternal life (Romans 8:29). Election is real, but conditioned on foreseen faith, so free will is preserved. A few read it corporately: the destiny of the believing people as a body, entered by faith.

And it must be held in charity. What unites us comes before what divides: every side believes salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, that God is sovereign and good, that sinners are truly responsible, and that the gospel must be freely offered to all, exactly what Paul is doing here. The difference is over how God’s sovereignty and our believing fit together. This is an in-house disagreement among brothers who love the same Lord and Bible, to be carried with humility, not point-scoring. And the verse does not make God the author of anyone’s unbelief (v. 46 lays that on the rejecters), nor does it dampen evangelism; in Acts, election runs right alongside tireless preaching. Rightly held, it humbles the believer, banishes boasting, and turns assurance into worship.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God chose these Gentiles because he saw something good in them, or because he foresaw their faith; the faith itself is the fruit of the appointing (Ephesians 2:8). It does not mean anyone who wants to come to Christ will be turned away for not being on a list; Jesus says whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). And it does not mean we can know in advance who is appointed. The list is God’s, and it is read only in the believing.

How can I know if I am one of those appointed to eternal life? By looking where Luke looks: as many as were appointed believed. You do not discover your election by peering into God’s secret counsel but by trusting Christ. If you have come to him, resting on him alone for forgiveness, that faith is the evidence of your appointment, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). If you are not sure you have come, do not puzzle over decrees; come now. No one who comes is ever told he was not chosen.

Then why preach or pray, if God has already appointed? Because God appoints the means as well as the end. He has chosen to bring his people to faith through the preaching of the word and the prayers of his church (Romans 10:14–17). Look at this very verse: the appointed believed when they heard. Paul was told later in Corinth to keep speaking precisely because the Lord had many people in that city (18:9–10). Election does not make evangelism pointless; it makes it hopeful. We go knowing that God has people out there who will believe.

Is it unfair that God chooses some and not others? Fairness would leave us all under judgment; election is God showing mercy to guilty people who deserved none. (See Romans 11:5 for the fuller answer.)

The word was spreading. Election never stops evangelism; it powers it. In two verses Paul and Barnabas are expelled; the gospel reached the upland villages anyway, carried by people whose names nobody wrote down. The missionaries were removed. The word was not.

On a Tuesday. If you believe, thank God today, in so many words, that your faith was his gift and not your achievement. Then let it make you humble toward those who do not yet believe, since you were no better, and bold to speak to them, since God has his people still waiting to hear.

For worship. Before Pisidian Antioch was founded, before Abraham was called, before the world was made, the Father set his love on a people and wrote their names in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8). The book is the Lamb’s because every name in it was bought with his blood. On one ordinary Sabbath in an upland colony some of those names heard the gospel for the first time, and believed, and rejoiced.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devout women of high standing. The synagogue could not touch them directly, so the pressure went round another way: women of rank, the synagogue’s own God-fearers, some very likely married to the men who ran the colony.

Influence, not a mob. A word in the right drawing rooms, and the missionaries were put out of the district by due process. That is what much opposition to the gospel has looked like: not violence but influence, applied quietly by people who never have to raise their voices. And there is a hard irony in it. The women are called devout. They were the fruit of the synagogue’s own patient work among the Gentiles, and they were used to expel the men who had just told them the promises were theirs.

Drove them out. Perhaps this is when Paul was beaten with rods (2 Corinthians 11:25), and this town stayed with him. In his last letter he lists it by name: my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra (2 Timothy 3:11). He never forgot it. He also never once suggested it had been a mistake to go.

They shook off the dust. This is not a gesture Paul invented in temper. It is an instruction, given by Jesus to his own men when he sent them out (Luke 9:5; 10:11). It was a sign that a town was being left to its own responsibility. And it carried a meaning everybody present would have caught. A devout Jew might shake off the dust of Gentile lands; to do it to a Jewish community was to say: in this matter, you are the ones on the outside.

What the shaken dust does not license. It is not permission for an ordinary Christian to write people off in a huff. It was done by apostles, under an explicit command from Christ, after a full and public hearing, and only when the answer had become a settled and organised refusal. And look at what they did not do. They did not curse anybody. They did not organise resistance, appeal to Rome, or stay to have the last word. The gesture is not revenge; it is a transfer of responsibility: you have been told, and it is now yours.

And went to Iconium. Eighty miles or so east down the road, and they start again. Persecution moves the gospel on (8:4). That is the answer to the question of what a Christian does when a door is shut in his face. You do not stop; you relocate.

When should I stop sharing the gospel with someone who keeps refusing? Rarely, and usually not at all in the sense of giving up on them. Paul left a city, not a person, and only after an organised, public rejection. With family, friends and neighbours, keep loving them, keep praying, and keep the door open, even if you stop raising the subject for a season because it has become an argument. Jesus told us not to throw pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6), but he also kept eating with sinners. Change your approach if you must; do not change your love.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment. Iconium lay about 80 miles to the east.

parallels.desc: persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples were filled with joy. The chapter’s last sentence is about the disciples left behind, converts of a few weeks whose teachers have been expelled. There is no building, no elder and no New Testament. They have a few weeks of teaching, each other, and God.

Filled. Not coping. Not bearing up. Filled, and the tense says they went on being filled, not that it happened once on the day the apostles left. The apostles left, but the Spirit stayed.

Joy with a source. The Spirit is the source of the joy; if joy were a mood produced by circumstances, this verse could not exist. The joy arrives with a Person.

Whose joy it is. That last evening Jesus told his friends that he had spoken so that his joy might be in them and their joy might be full (John 15:11), and promised that their sorrow would turn into a joy no one would take from them (John 16:20–22). He endured the cross, Hebrews says, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). The gladness of a handful of converts in a hostile colony is a share of that joy, poured out by the Spirit he sent. They were filled with the joy of a Saviour who had looked past the cross and seen them.

In the flow. The chapter’s pattern repeats at once in Iconium and Lystra (14:1–20), and Paul and Barnabas will come back to strengthen these very disciples (14:21–23). The joyful church in Pisidian Antioch is the sign that the risen Christ had not left with his preachers.

What it does not mean. This is not a command to feel cheerful, and it is not a denial of grief. Paul knelt and prayed with the Ephesian elders, and they all wept (20:36–38). Jesus wept at a grave (John 11:35). The Christian position is not joy instead of sorrow but, as Paul put it, sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10): two things at once; and anyone who has buried a believer knows exactly what that means and how it is possible.

What if I am a Christian and do not feel this joy? Then you are not alone, and you are not disqualified. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit, and fruit grows; it is not switched on. Seasons of depression, grief, illness or spiritual dryness come to genuine believers, as the Psalms show again and again (Psalm 42; 88). Do not try to manufacture joy; go to its source. Keep near the means God uses: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the company of his people. Tell a mature Christian how you are. And if your low mood is deep or long, seek medical help too; that is not a lack of faith.

parallels.desc: joy of the Holy Spirit in much affliction

13.theology: Election and Evangelism. Acts 13:48 states plainly that the believing of the Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch rests on their prior appointment to eternal life. This is not fatalism: it does not stop preaching but undergirds it. Paul and Barnabas preach to everyone who will listen, not knowing who is appointed, and through the preaching God brings to faith those he has appointed. Election is the ground of missionary confidence in every hostile city.
13.examples:
Then: Barnabas and Saul, sent from a worshipping, fasting church, arrive in city after city with nothing but the word and the Spirit; the appointed believe, and the disciples are filled with joy even when their teachers are expelled.

Now: The Antioch church was not looking for a missionary project; it was seeking God, and God spoke. A congregation’s mission grows out of its worship and prayer, and when the Spirit calls, it must be ready to send its best.

14.title: Suffering and Strengthening
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. <sup>2</sup>But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. <sup>3</sup>So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. <sup>4</sup>But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. <sup>5</sup>When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them, <sup>6</sup>they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, <sup>7</sup>and there they continued to preach the gospel. <sup>8</sup>Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. <sup>9</sup>He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, <sup>10</sup>said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and began walking. <sup>11</sup>And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” <sup>12</sup>Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. <sup>13</sup>And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds. <sup>14</sup>But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, <sup>15</sup>“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. <sup>16</sup>In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. <sup>17</sup>Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.” <sup>18</sup>Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them. <sup>19</sup>But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. <sup>20</sup>But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. <sup>21</sup>When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, <sup>22</sup>strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. <sup>23</sup>And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. <sup>24</sup>Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. <sup>25</sup>And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia, <sup>26</sup>and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled. <sup>27</sup>And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. <sup>28</sup>And they remained no little time with the disciples.
14.overview:
The first missionary journey runs on through the cities of southern Galatia, in the heart of modern Turkey. At Iconium many Jews and Greeks believe, the city divides, and a plot to stone the apostles drives them on to Lystra and Derbe. At Lystra a man lame from birth is healed, and the crowd takes Paul and Barnabas for Zeus and Hermes. The two tear their clothes, rush into the crowd, and preach to pagans with no Bible the living God who has never stopped giving rain, harvests and gladness.

Then Paul is stoned and left for dead, and he gets up and walks back into the town. Instead of taking the short road home, the missionaries go back through the cities that had persecuted them, telling the believers that tribulation is the road into God’s kingdom and appointing elders in every church. At Syrian Antioch they report how God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The First Journey Continues and Returns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter follows Paul and Barnabas from a divided Iconium to Lystra, where a healed lame man and a crowd ready to worship them lead to a sermon on the living God who gives rain and harvests, and then to a stoning. The missionaries retrace their route, strengthening the disciples and appointing elders, and return to Syrian Antioch.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as the path into the kingdom

The must of verse 22 is not pessimism but theology. Suffering is not a sign of God’s absence: the servant who shares his Lord’s cross will share his Lord’s resurrection, and the pattern of dying and rising is the pattern of life in the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked back into the city where he had just been stoned. Now: Those whose life is secure in the risen Christ can go on witnessing after suffering for it, because their hope is his resurrection, not this world’s preservation of their lives.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 14 completes the first missionary journey: a divided city, a crowd that tries to worship two preachers, a stoning survived, and young churches strengthened and given elders. It is a chapter about the living God who will not share his glory with idols or with preachers, and who keeps the churches his Son has bought.

Now at Iconium. Iconium (modern Konya) was a city in the Roman province of Galatia, a substantial Greek-speaking city about ninety miles east of Pisidian Antioch. Paul’s letter to the Galatians was probably written to these churches.

They entered together into the Jewish synagogue. They have just been driven out of Pisidian Antioch, where Paul announced that he was turning to the Gentiles (13:46, 50), and in the next city the first building he walks into is a synagogue. That is what the turn to the Gentiles meant in practice: not a resignation from his own people.

In such a way. Luke does not say they spoke faithfully, or at length, or with power, but in such a way: a comment on how the thing was put. There is such a thing as saying true things badly, and these two did not.

Jews and Greeks believed together. In one synagogue in Iconium, Jews and Greeks believed the same message in the same weeks, and in the same breath Luke calls them simply the brothers. That is what Christ died to do: he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). The slander of the next sentence was aimed at a peace that had been made at the cross, and it could not unmake it.

Poisoned their minds. Poisoned (ekakōsan) means embittered, made hostile: an audience worked on, over time, by people with access to them. Slander does not answer the preaching. It goes round it, to people who have not heard it yet, and gets there first.

The injury of slander. It does not happen where you are, so there is no defence against it. You discover it only in its effects: rooms that go quiet, an invitation that stops coming. You cannot answer a charge that was never put to you, and trying makes you look exactly like the man they were warned about.

Outliving it. So what did these two do about it? Nothing, so far as Luke records: no defence, no letter to the synagogue. They stayed and went on speaking for a long time. Some slander can only be outlived, by going on doing the work in front of everybody until the account people were given stops matching the man they can see.

If faith is God’s gift, why does it matter how we speak? Because God gives faith through means, and our words are among them. Faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:17), and the Spirit is pleased to use speech that is clear, honest, warm and well put. Careless, confusing or unkind speech can put real obstacles in a hearer’s way. None of this means clever words can produce faith; only God opens hearts (16:14). But it does mean we should take care to understand the gospel, explain it plainly, answer questions honestly and speak with love. Paul asked for prayer that he would make it clear, as he ought to speak (Colossians 4:4).
verseByVerse.note: Iconium (modern Konya) was a city in the Roman province of Galatia; Paul’s letter to the Galatians may be to these churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they remained for a long time. Luke joins the two sentences with the word so, meaning therefore: the poisoning of the city is given as the reason they stayed. When a place goes cold on us we start looking at the timetable. These men treated the hostility as evidence that something was happening worth opposing, and dug in.

Who bore witness to the word of his grace. Their bold speech is the open, unguarded speech the church had prayed for in Jerusalem (4:29, 31). The sentence runs the other way round from what we expect: not the apostles bearing witness to the Lord, but the Lord bearing witness to the word they were preaching. And the gospel is the word of his grace (20:24, 32): God giving what nobody has earned.

The Lord who works from heaven. In Acts the Lord is the risen Jesus, and this verse is part of what he goes on doing (1:1). The ascended Christ is not a retired founder whose followers carry on in his absence. From the right hand of God he takes the words of two hunted men in a provincial town and signs them as his own, and the grace they spoke of is the grace he showed when he gave himself for sinners. The preacher speaks of Christ, and Christ speaks for the preacher.

Signs and wonders. Signs confirmed the apostles’ message (Hebrews 2:3–4), and Paul reminds these same churches of the miracles worked among them (Galatians 3:5). The signs authenticate not the men but the word of his grace: a signature at the bottom of a particular document.

Should we expect signs and wonders in ministry today? Here the Lord granted them to confirm the word of his grace through the apostles (v. 4). Continuationist Christians (those who believe all the gifts of the early church continue today) believe such signs continue as the gospel goes to new places, and many of them are earnest, godly brothers. The more likely reading is that these signs belonged to the apostolic witness of the founding era: Paul calls them the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12), and Hebrews speaks of them as God’s confirmation of those who first heard the Lord (Hebrews 2:3–4). God remains free to heal and to answer prayer in remarkable ways. What continues as the ordinary pattern is the Lord bearing witness to his word as it is preached.

How does the Lord bear witness to his word now? By the Holy Spirit, who takes the preached word and presses it home to the conscience: convicting of sin, opening blind eyes, giving faith, changing lives (1 Thessalonians 1:5). That is still a wonder, and in some ways the greater one. A man whose bitterness melts, a family that begins to pray, an addict who walks free, a proud heart that bows to Christ: these are the Lord’s signature on his word today. So when you speak the gospel, you are not on your own. The same Lord stands behind it.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the people of the city were divided. Two good men preached the gospel in Iconium with great effect, and the measurable outcome was that the town split in half. Jesus said it would: do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division (Luke 12:51). Not because Christians are quarrelsome, but because a man can be neutral about most claims, and cannot be neutral about the claim that a particular executed Jew is the Lord of his life.

With the apostles. Luke calls Paul and Barnabas both apostles here and again at verse 14; everywhere else he keeps the word for the Twelve. Here they are men sent out on mission by the church in Antioch.

Two senses of apostle. The word does two different jobs in the New Testament. In its strict sense an apostle is one who had seen the risen Christ and been commissioned by him personally as an eyewitness and a layer of foundations: the Twelve, with Paul added as one untimely born (1 Corinthians 15:8). That office cannot be repeated: the man had to have seen him (1:21–22), and a foundation is laid once (Ephesians 2:20). In its wider sense the word simply means one who is sent, as of Barnabas here and of the messengers of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23). In that sense the church has always had them, and mostly calls them missionaries, the same word arriving through Latin instead of Greek. Behind both stands the apostle and high priest of our confession (Hebrews 3:1), the Son sent by the Father, who sends his people as the Father sent him (John 20:21).

When someone claims the title today. Then ask which of the two things is being claimed. A sent one, yes, and thank God for them. A man whose word stands beside Scripture because he saw the risen Christ, no. That door closed when the last of them died, and it is a mercy that it did: a church that can still be given new foundational revelation is a church that can be told anything.

Both Gentiles and Jews. Two communities that agreed on almost nothing found something they could agree on. It is the pattern of the trial itself, where Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day (Luke 23:12). Opposition to Christ unites people who would not otherwise sit in the same room, a strange backhanded testimony to who he is.

What if following Christ divides my own family? Then you are walking a road Jesus described in advance, and he walked it first: even his brothers did not believe in him for a time (John 7:5). Do not provoke division needlessly; be the kindest, most honest and most dependable member of your family. Honour your parents in everything that does not require disobeying Christ. Keep loving those who disapprove, and keep praying. But do not buy peace by denying him. Many families that were split by the gospel have later been reunited in it, as Jesus’ own brothers were (1:14).
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Barnabas are both called apostles — men sent out on mission.

verseByVerse.quote: they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They learned of it and fled. Somebody probably told them. A plot involving the rulers of a city was known in advance to two travelling preachers, which suggests that someone on the inside got word out. Luke does not say who. This book is quietly full of people like that.

Fleeing is not cowardice. And they ran. Jesus commanded it: when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Leaving is not always weakness, nor staying always faith. The mission is the point, not the missionary’s reputation for nerve.

The hour that could not be fled. Jesus did it himself. At Nazareth he passed through the middle of a crowd that meant to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:30), and in the temple he hid himself when they picked up stones (John 8:59), because his hour had not yet come. Then the hour came, and he set his face to go to Jerusalem, and in the garden he walked out to meet them. He fled until fleeing would have abandoned the work, and then he stayed, for us. That is why his servants are free to run from Iconium. The one death that had to be faced to save the world has been faced, by him.

What decides it. Hold verse 6 next to verse 20, where the same man, stoned and dragged out of Lystra for dead, walks straight back into the town. What decides it in both places is the work: he leaves Iconium because staying would end the preaching; he re-enters Lystra because new disciples need to see him on his feet. So if you are weighing whether to leave something hard, the question is not whether you would be braver to stay, but what happens to the work if you go and if you do not. Nobody grades his own courage accurately anyway.

To Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia. Lystra and Derbe were smaller towns to the south and south-east. Lystra is only about twenty miles from Iconium, but it was over a boundary, in Lycaonia, and outside the reach of the Iconian magistrates. Lystra was a Roman colony, and probably Timothy’s home town (16:1).

They continued to preach. It is a step down in the world: a small colony in rough hill country whose people still shouted in Lycaonian when they were excited. They arrive as fugitives in a backwater whose language they do not speak, and they start again. Not recovered, and then preached. Fled, and preached.

Is it ever right for a Christian to flee persecution today? Yes. Believers in hostile countries sometimes face a real choice between staying and leaving, and Scripture gives freedom for both. Joseph took Mary and the child to Egypt; the church scattered from Jerusalem (8:1–4); Paul was let down the wall at Damascus (9:25). What is never permitted is to deny Christ to stay safe. So pray, seek counsel, think of those who depend on you and of the work, and then act in faith. And churches in safer places should pray for, welcome and support those who have had to flee.
verseByVerse.note: Lystra and Derbe were smaller towns to the south and south-east, in the region of Lycaonia.

parallels.desc: Timothy of Lystra

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Could not use his feet. Luke gives three descriptions where one would have done: he could not use his feet, he was crippled from birth, and he had never walked. Not injured, not declining: a man who had never in his life taken a step. The healing closely resembles Peter’s in 3:1–10: Paul’s ministry has the same marks as Peter’s. He had been listening in a town where Luke mentions no synagogue and most people had never heard the Scriptures.

Seeing that he had faith. This sentence has done a great deal of damage in the church. Read carelessly, it says the healing happened because the man’s faith was sufficient, from which it follows, with awful logic, that where healing does not happen the faith was not sufficient. That is told at bedsides, and it is not what this verse says.

Who is doing the seeing. Paul is looking intently, the verb Luke used of him staring at Elymas, and seeing. Most likely it was not printed on the man’s face but shown him. This is not an apostle grading a candidate’s spiritual performance; it is an apostle being given to know what God intended to do. And the faith he sees is itself something God has been producing through the preaching.

Faith to be saved. Made well (sōthēnai) is the ordinary word for being saved, and it points to what the man’s faith was faith in: Jesus, crucified and raised, through whom forgiveness is proclaimed (13:38). His faith was not a strength of his own that qualified him. It was a lame man’s empty hands held out to the Christ he heard about, and the healing was Christ’s (9:34). If faith were a power, the weak would be lost. Because faith only receives, everything rests on the one received, and he is able for the weakest grip that ever reached for him.

Test it against the rest of the book. The man at the temple gate asked for money and expected nothing else, and was healed anyway (3:6). Dorcas was dead (9:40). The high priest’s servant was helping to arrest Jesus when his ear was healed (Luke 22:51). If healing ran on the sufferer’s faith, half the healings in Scripture could not have happened. And Paul asked three times to be relieved of his thorn and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9), and he left Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). The apostle who read this man’s faith in a Lystran street could not read his own way out of a thorn.

So if you are ill. If you are ill, or someone you love is, and you have been made to feel that the failure is yours, pick this verse up the other way round. It does not say that faith produces healing. It says that on one particular afternoon in one particular town, God let his apostle see what he was about to do. Your not being healed is not a report card on your faith. If it were, Paul failed his.

Should I still pray for healing? Yes, gladly and boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14–15), and God often answers, sometimes through doctors and medicine, sometimes beyond them. Pray as a child asks a father, honestly naming what you want, and then rest the answer in his wisdom, as Jesus did in Gethsemane: not my will, but yours. If healing comes, give thanks. If it does not, his grace is sufficient, and the full healing is certain at the resurrection, when the lame will leap and the body will be raised imperishable.
verseByVerse.note: The healing closely resembles Peter’s healing of the lame man at the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: said in a loud voice, "Stand upright on your feet." And he sprang up and began walking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stand upright. Consider what is being asked of the man. He has never stood. He has none of the ten thousand small corrections a body makes without being told; walking is a skill, and this man had never had the skill to forget.

He sprang up. Sprang up (hēlato) means leapt, like the lame man of 3:8. Not stood carefully, not helped upright between two men. He jumped: everything a person normally acquires over the first two years of life, handed over complete. It is Isaiah 35:6: then shall the lame man leap like a deer. The prophet promised it of the days when God comes to save, the time of the promised King who would put right everything sin had broken, and at last death itself (Isaiah 35:5–6; 25:8).

The sign Jesus pointed to. When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus answered with Isaiah’s list: the lame walk (Luke 7:22). The leaping lame were his credentials. So when a man in Lystra jumps to his feet, it is not Paul’s power on display. It is the Messiah of Isaiah 35, risen and reigning, still doing the work that identified him, in a town that had never heard his name until that week.

What is not in the sentence. Peter at the temple gate said, in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk (3:6), and when the crowd came running and stared at the apostles as though they had done it by their own power, Peter at once pointed them to the God of Abraham (3:12–13). Here Luke records no name at all (a few later manuscripts add one, but the earliest do not), and a crowd that had never read the Scriptures is left to interpret what it has seen out of the only religious vocabulary it possesses.

A miracle by itself teaches nobody anything. That is why what follows goes so badly wrong. A miracle compels attention, and then people explain it with whatever they already believe. Jerusalem had the Scriptures, and even there the crowd needed Peter to tell them it was the God of Israel. Lystra had Zeus and reached for him. The apostles never treat a sign as self-explanatory; where nobody says what it meant, the crowd supplies its own meaning, and this crowd is already sending for oxen. So when God does something good in your life, say plainly, to yourself and to others, who did it: unexplained blessings drift into being called luck.

How should I respond to stories of miracles today? With openness and with care. God is able to do anything, and he does answer prayer in ways that leave doctors puzzled. But a remarkable event does not interpret itself, and it does not prove the teaching of whoever was standing nearby. Ask what is being taught, and whether Christ and his gospel are being honoured, because Scripture warns that false teachers can come with signs (Matthew 24:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:9). The test of any ministry is not whether wonders are reported but whether it agrees with the word of God.

For worship. The Christ who will raise his people imperishable gave one pagan town a glimpse of that morning: legs that had never borne weight, steady in a second. He does not repair what is broken a little at a time, as we do. He gives whole what was never whole. On the last day all who are his will rise like that man, at once and complete, and the first thing they do with their new feet will be to run to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!" Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saying in Lycaonian. They cried out in Lycaonian, the old country language, not the Greek Paul had been preaching in, and Paul and Barnabas probably did not understand it. Under strain people revert to the tongue they think in. The detail explains the delay: the two go on standing there while a sacrifice is organised around them, and they find out when the animals appear.

The gods have come down. The reaction looks wild until you know the local story. The Roman poet Ovid, a generation or so before Paul, had written up a legend set in neighbouring Phrygia. Zeus and Hermes came through the country disguised as travellers and were turned away from a thousand doors. One poor old couple, Philemon and Baucis, took them in. The gods turned the couple’s cottage into a temple and drowned the district that had refused them.

Fear with a long memory. When two strangers turn up and something impossible happens, you do not want to be the household that got it wrong. So the shouting is not simple enthusiasm. It is fear with a long memory, and it explains why the priest comes at a run with cattle.

Zeus and Hermes. Zeus was the chief god; Hermes was his messenger, the god of speech. Inscriptions linking the two have been found near Lystra. So the man doing the talking is taken for the junior deity, and the quiet one beside him for the god. Luke, who has recorded Paul taking over the leadership of this mission, does not comment.

Sized up wrongly. The people of Lystra got both men wrong, in opposite directions, on the same afternoon, and neither verdict survived the week. It is the oldest mistake of all. When God himself came among us in a man, he had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2), and the crowds looking for greatness looked straight past him to the cross.

How is the incarnation different from the Lystrans’ idea of gods coming down? Utterly. In the myths the gods only looked human for a while, in disguise, to test people and then punish them. In Jesus the eternal Son truly became man, taking a real human body and soul, permanently, without ceasing to be God (John 1:14). He did not come to inspect our hospitality but to receive our rejection, and instead of drowning those who turned him away, he died for them. The Lystrans feared gods who came down to judge. The true God came down to save.

For worship. Lystra called the quiet man Zeus and the talker Hermes. In Jesus the God who sends and the Word who is sent meet in one person, and neither is a disguise: the Father has spoken to us in his Son (Hebrews 1:2), who keeps our nature still, glorified, at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.note: A local legend told of Zeus and Hermes visiting the region in human form unrecognised. Hermes was messenger of the gods, so the speaker, Paul, was taken for him.

parallels.desc: they said that he was a god

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priest of Zeus. Literally the phrase means Zeus-before-the-city: the town’s own guardian, whose shrine stood outside the walls, the local authority for the weather and the harvest.

Brought oxen and garlands to the gates. Oxen were the most expensive offering the town could make, and the garlands were wound about the animals’ heads before they were killed. This is not under discussion. It is under way: the grandest religious act in the town’s calendar, arranged in honour of two preachers, with the whole population delighted.

Why this moment is dangerous. It is dangerous because it is flattering, and because it is sincere. These people are grateful and frightened, and they have brought the best they have. That is the easiest thing in the world to let run: not to endorse it, simply to be slow about correcting it, reflecting that the crowd is finally listening. Many a scandal of Christian celebrity has begun in a version of this room: not a man claiming to be more than a man, but a man declining, for a while, to interrupt people who were treating him as though he were.

Religion as a bargain. The oxen also show what religion at Lystra was: a bargain. Feed the god and he sends rain; refuse him and the district drowns. It survives in church clothes: I pray, I give, I behave, so God owes me a good year. The living God had been sending rain to people who never thanked him (v. 17), and in Christ he gives himself to people who have nothing to offer. Grace is not a better deal with God. It is the end of dealing.

The one man who may be worshipped. When Cornelius fell at Peter’s feet, Peter lifted him up: I too am a man (10:26). When John fell before an angel, he was told not to (Revelation 19:10). Here two apostles are about to tear their clothes rather than accept a garlanded ox. Yet when the disciples in the boat worshipped Jesus (Matthew 14:33), and when Thomas called him my Lord and my God (John 20:28), he did not stop them. Every true servant of God refuses worship, and Jesus received it. Either he was the worst of blasphemers, or he is what Thomas said; and within about twenty-five years of the cross Paul was already praying to him in Aramaic, Our Lord, come (1 Corinthians 16:22). What the apostles will not accept at Lystra is the very honour that belongs to their Master.

Is it wrong to admire or thank a pastor or Christian leader? No. Scripture tells us to esteem our leaders very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13), and gratitude is right. The danger begins when admiration turns into dependence or exemption: when a leader is treated as beyond question, when his words carry more weight than Scripture, or when his failings are hidden to protect his image. Thank your leaders, pray for them, and hold them to account. And leaders should be quick, like Paul, to deflect the glory to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Garlands were wreaths placed on sacrificial animals.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, "Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They tore their garments. Tearing your clothes was a Jewish sign of grief and of horror at blasphemy: it is what the high priest did at what he took to be blasphemy from Jesus (Mark 14:63). That is what they thought of the honour being offered them. And they rushed out into the crowd: not onto a platform, and not away, but into it, to get physically between the people and the altar.

We also are men, of like nature with you. The Greek is homoiopatheis, of the same feelings, the same sufferings and passions, the word James uses of Elijah (James 5:17): the same aches, the same fears, the same capacity to be hurt. Before long Paul will be lying outside that same gate under a heap of stones, and the town will have its proof.

Men like you, and the Man who is more. The apostles’ protest is the exact reverse of the news they have come to bring. They insist they are only men, so that the crowd will look past them. The message they carry is about one Man who is truly of like nature with us and is also infinitely more: the Son who had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest (Hebrews 2:17), and through whom all things were made (John 1:3). Lystra tried to turn men into gods. The gospel announces that God has become a man without ceasing to be God: a man who wept and was weary, and the one who could say, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58).

Harder than Caesarea. King Herod in Caesarea let the crowd hail his voice as a god’s and was struck down because he did not give God the glory (12:22–23). What makes Lystra harder is sincerity. Herod’s flatterers depended on his country for their food (12:20). These people mean it. It is far easier to refuse worship from a man working an angle than from a man who simply wants to say thank you in the only currency he has, and who will be hurt when you will not take it.

Preaching with no Bible to quote. This is the first sermon in Acts addressed to people with no Bible at all: no Abraham, no Moses, no prophets, not even one God to start from.

In the flow. Set beside the synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch (13:16–41) and the later one at Athens (17:22–31), this short word shows that the gospel never changes while the starting point does: Scripture for those who have it, creation and the God who gives rain for those who do not. It also raises the question chapter 15 must settle: when pagans like these turn to God, on what terms are they welcomed?

Vain things. Vain things (mataiōn) are empty, hollow, worthless, the Greek Old Testament’s word for idols (Jeremiah 2:5); compare turning to God from idols in 1 Thessalonians 1:9. The gods of Lystra had to be fed by a priest. The living God, against dead idols.

All that is in them. That last phrase is straight out of Scripture (Exodus 20:11; Psalm 146:6), and they do not say so, because saying so would have meant nothing here.

Where they start, and what they demand. They did not open with justification or with Genesis 12. They took the one real point of contact a pagan farming town had, the sky, the fields, the food on the table, and they used it. And having found the point of contact, they did not soften the demand by a syllable: turn. It is the same word Peter used in Jerusalem. The starting place moved. The call did not.

How do I talk about Christ with someone who knows nothing of the Bible? Start where Paul started: with what they already know and experience. Creation, conscience, the goodness of ordinary life, the longing for meaning, the reality of death. Speak of the God who made all this and who is not like the idols of our age, money, success, pleasure, image. Then move to the heart of it: he has come in Jesus, died and risen, and calls us to turn to him. Avoid church jargon, explain terms, ask questions, and be patient. The starting point can change. The message and the call to turn must not.

For worship. The god of Lystra stood in a temple by the gate and waited for his priest to feed him. The living God has never waited on anyone, and he needs nothing from our hands. Idols must be carried by their worshippers, as Isaiah mocked them, while the LORD carries his people from the womb to grey hairs (Isaiah 46:1–4). So name the vain things you look to for security or joy, your bank balance, your reputation, a screen, and turn from one of them today: at the cross the living God carried his people’s sins, and bore away the very guilt of having bowed to vain things.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: turned to God from idols

verseByVerse.quote: "In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In their own ways. That is a stark sentence, and it raises the question this whole scene has been circling: what about all the people who never heard? Before Christ, God let the nations go their own way, as he gave his law only to Israel (Psalm 147:19–20). Not that he approved, but that he was patient (17:30). Now the times of ignorance are over: God calls all to repent.

Patience paid for at the cross. Why could a holy God let the nations go their own way for so long? God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, to show his righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins (Romans 3:25). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger against sin by bearing that anger in the sinner’s place. The centuries of patience were not God shrugging at idolatry. They were patience on credit, drawn on a cross that had not yet been raised. That is why the patience could end in a summons rather than a sentence: the man who brought the summons was preaching the very death that had made the waiting just.

Not an abstract question. It is one of the questions most likely to be put to a Christian by somebody he loves. Take what Scripture says, and refuse both comfortable answers.

First, nobody is judged against a light he was never given. Gentiles who do not have the law are judged by what they did have: the work of the law written on their hearts, their conscience accusing or else excusing them (Romans 2:14–16). God is not weighing a man against a revelation he withheld from him. That is worth saying to anyone whose real fear is that God is unfair.

Second, they are not innocent. What can be known about God is plain from what has been made, so that people are without excuse, and the charge is not ignorance but suppression: knowing something of God and not honouring him or giving thanks (Romans 1:19–21). Paul says it here in kinder language: God had been sending Lystra rain the whole time.

Third, the Judge is good. Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Genesis 18:25) is answered in the asking. You are not being asked to certify the eternal state of people you have never met. You are being asked whether the God who did not spare his own Son can be trusted with them.

Refuse the false comfort in both directions. This verse gives no ground for supposing the nations are safe in their ignorance: the era of overlooking has ended and a summons has arrived (17:30). Nor does it allow us to speak as though God owed the nations more than he gave, or as though we could pronounce on each individual. Scripture does teach that there is salvation in no one else (4:12), and that salvation comes through conscious faith in Christ. Those who die in infancy are a separate case, and we rest the elect among them in the mercy of the God who saves them in Christ. Parents who have lost a little one need not fear that God will judge a child by a gospel the child could never hear; David’s hope for his infant son, I shall go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), has comforted many. For the rest, God has put a job in our hands: how are they to hear without someone preaching? (Romans 10:14).

Then can someone be saved by following his conscience and the light he has? No. Conscience and creation show enough of God to condemn, never enough to save, because no one lives up to the light he has; all have sinned (Romans 3:23). Salvation comes only through Christ, received by faith, and faith comes by hearing his word. That is precisely why Paul walked into Lystra, and why the church sends missionaries still. The right response to the question of those who have not heard is not speculation but sending, giving and going.

parallels.desc: the times of ignorance God overlooked

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness." Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet he did not leave himself without witness. Even without Scripture, God left evidence of himself in creation and providence (Romans 1:19–20; Psalm 19:1). Speaking to farmers on the Anatolian uplands, Paul does not reach for the stars or the moral law within. He reaches for rain, harvest, dinner, and being glad.

Rains and fruitful seasons. The rain fell on the fields of a town that had built a temple to Zeus at its gate, and God sent it anyway, season after season. The people now leading oxen up to the wrong god had eaten every day of their lives at the table of the right one.

Food and gladness. The last item is the surprising one. God’s witness to himself in a pagan town included gladness: the pleasure of a good meal, the ease of a year that has gone well. Paul tells idolaters that their happiness was evidence.

Whose hand sent the rain. Paul does not name Christ in this short speech, but all things were created through the Son, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17). The rain on Lystra’s fields fell at the word of the one Paul had come to preach. So common grace is not a separate religion of nature with its own road to God. It is the same Lord being kind to his enemies before they know his name, and the kindness on the farm points to a greater kindness: the one who had fed them all their lives would give himself for them.

Common grace. Common means not cheap but given to all in common: the goodness God shows believer and unbeliever alike, the rains and food and gladness here, and beyond them life and breath (17:25), the restraint of evil, the skill and beauty found even among those who do not know God, and the patience that delays judgment. God makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good (Matthew 5:45).

Two things must be kept clear. First, common grace is not saving grace: it is undeserved kindness, but it blesses this life without, by itself, reconciling anyone to God. Second, it is a witness (v. 17), leaving people without excuse (Romans 1:20) and meant to lead you to repentance (Romans 2:4). The tragedy is to take the gifts and ignore the Giver (Romans 1:21).

Where Christians differ: can creation save? Some Christians (often called inclusivists) argue that those who respond to God’s witness in nature may be saved without the gospel. This commentary’s view: God’s witness in creation is real, and leaves everyone without excuse (Romans 1:20), but it is not enough to save. It shows God’s power and kindness, not his way of salvation through Christ. That is why Paul and Barnabas came to Lystra with the gospel. General revelation (what God shows of himself to everyone through creation and conscience) points to God; special revelation, the gospel, brings us to him.

Scarcely restrained. Then verse 18, deliberately anticlimactic. An apostle at the top of his powers, in an emergency, got the sacrifice stopped by the skin of his teeth; Luke does not even say the crowd was persuaded, only restrained.
