The best answer, given at the right moment by the right man, may only just hold. If you have said the true thing as well as you knew how and watched it barely land, you are in good company.

Is it right for Christians to enjoy food, harvests and ordinary pleasures? Yes, and to enjoy them as from God. Paul tells Timothy that God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and that everything created by God is good if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). The sin is not enjoyment but ingratitude, or making the gift into a god. So eat, laugh, delight in a good harvest or a good holiday, and say thank you to the one who gave it. Gladness received from God and returned to him in praise is part of worship.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium. Iconium is some twenty miles from Lystra; Pisidian Antioch is more than a hundred. Somebody organised this: a journey of several days made deliberately over hill roads to finish in this town what they had started in their own. Hatred will make an effort that indifference never makes.

They stoned Paul. The people who not long before had to be physically restrained from worshipping this man now throw stones at him until he stops moving. Nothing had changed except who had been talking to them: Hosanna, then Crucify.

What a crowd’s approval is worth. A reputation handed to you by people who do not know you can be taken back by people who do not know you, and the same afternoon’s excitement supplies both. And these were not monsters by the standards of their town. They were ordinary, frightened, easily led people who had just been told a persuasive story, which is worth knowing about ourselves.

Supposing that he was dead. A stoning is not a beating; it is an execution, and this one was carried far enough that the men doing it concluded the job was finished. Paul later lists it: once I was stoned (2 Corinthians 11:25). And writing to these very churches he says he bears on his body the marks of Jesus (Galatians 6:17). Some of them were made here.

How much he must suffer for my name. None of this took the Lord Jesus by surprise: I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name (9:16). The man who had kept the coats while Stephen was stoned now lies under stones himself. It is the same Lord in both scenes: he received Stephen home, and he lifted Paul back onto his feet. The stones of Lystra were part of the commission Christ had given him, and the risen Christ was with him under them.

He rose up. Luke does not say that Paul was raised from the dead, only that the crowd supposed he was dead and that he got up. Luke, who readily reports a raising when one happened (9:40; 20:9–12), declines to say. And there were disciples in Lystra: a small group of brand-new believers stood in a ring round the body of their teacher outside the wall, which took some nerve.

Timothy, perhaps. One of them may well have been Timothy. Lystra was probably his town (16:1–2), and writing to him for the last time Paul names the persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra as though Timothy needs no explanation (2 Timothy 3:10–11). The young man who had to be told more than once not to be afraid may have begun by watching his hero dragged out of town as a corpse, and signed on anyway. And the hero set out for Derbe the very next day, some sixty miles on foot.

Why does God let his servants suffer like this? Scripture gives no single answer, but it gives several true ones. Suffering conforms us to Christ, who suffered first (Philippians 3:10). It proves that the message is believed, not merely sold, since nobody is stoned for a sales pitch. It strengthens other believers, who see that faith survives the worst (Philippians 1:12–14). And it is temporary and outweighed: this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). God does not waste a single stone thrown at his people.

What should I do if I am mistreated for my faith? Do not retaliate; bless (Romans 12:14). Do not be ashamed; rejoice that you are counted worthy to suffer for his name (5:41). Use proper protection where you can, as Paul later used his citizenship. Tell other believers and let them gather around you, as the disciples did here. And keep going, even if, like Paul, it is the next day and you are still bruised. The Lord who stood by Paul stands by you.

For worship. There are scars in heaven. The risen Lord showed his hands and his side to his friends, and the wounds he took for us are the only wounds in the universe that heal. Paul carried away from Lystra the marks of Jesus, and got up off the ground because the Lord who had been put to death outside a city wall had already risen. The stones could leave him for dead. They could not reach the life that was hidden with Christ in God, and they cannot reach ours.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch was about 100 miles from Lystra.

parallels.desc: once I was stoned

verseByVerse.quote: When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many disciples. Read verse 21 as a route. Derbe is the far end of the journey. From there a road ran east through the Cilician Gates to Tarsus, Paul’s home town, and on to Syrian Antioch: the shorter way home, familiar, and safe. And instead they turn round.

What is a disciple? Made many disciples is worth pausing on, because we easily lose the very idea of a disciple. It is the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19): not just converts, but disciples. The word (mathētēs) means a learner, an apprentice: not one who collects information but one who attaches his whole life to a master, learns his teaching and his way of living, and sets out to become like him: everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher (Luke 6:40). Jesus made it costly and total, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me (Luke 9:23), yet also the ordinary identity of every believer: disciple was the word for a Christian before the name Christian existed (Acts 11:26).

Where the modern church stumbles. We can reduce the faith to a single decision and forget that the commission is to make disciples, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you (Matthew 28:19–20). Paul and Barnabas did not count converts and move on; they came back to strengthen them.

They returned. Back through Lystra, where Paul had been stoned; Iconium, where a plot to stone him had united the town; Antioch, where the leading families had had them expelled: in reverse order, deliberately, to care for the new believers.

Strengthening the souls. The preaching has been done. They are going back to make sure that what they started can stand without them, and the reason Paul walks back into the town where he was stoned is in what he told them.

Through many tribulations. Every convert in those cities was facing the obvious question: is this what following Jesus is going to be like? And Paul’s answer, delivered on legs that had recently been stoned, was yes. Must (dei) means it is necessary: not optional, not a sign of failure (John 16:33; 1 Peter 4:12–13). That exposes a quiet hope many of us carry: that if we follow Jesus well enough, life will run smoothly, and that if it does not, God has failed us. Paul promises the kingdom, not comfort, and the kingdom is worth far more.

The same must. On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus asked, Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26). Necessary there is the same dei. The road Paul describes is the King’s own road. He entered his glory through the cross, and those joined to him enter the kingdom through tribulation behind him. The hardship does not mean the road has gone wrong; it is the sign that they are following the right Master.

We, not you. He says we, not you: he is describing a road he is standing on, to people who had seen him on it. He does not tell them it will get easier. He tells them the difficulty is the road and not a diversion from it, which is the only comfort that survives real trouble, because it removes the second wound. Suffering hurts. Suffering plus the suspicion that it means God has gone is unbearable, and it is the second half Paul is taking away.

Did we not already enter the kingdom? You may be puzzled. Paul says God has transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13, past tense), yet here entering is still future. Both are true; this is the already and not yet. God’s saving reign in King Jesus comes in two stages. It already arrived at his first coming (the kingdom of God has come upon you, Matthew 12:28), and every believer is already under its reign, enjoying its blessings (forgiveness, the Spirit, sonship). And it is not yet consummated: its full glory waits for his return, when he reigns openly and makes all things new, and in that sense we will yet enter or inherit it (Matthew 25:34; 1 Corinthians 15:50; 2 Timothy 4:18). The kingdom here is the future kingdom, entered fully at Christ’s return. Same kingdom, two stages: the already real but partial, the not yet full and final.

Two ways of speaking. To assure us, Paul says we have been placed in the kingdom; to press us on in hope, as here, he points to the kingdom we have yet to enter, as a decisive battle may be won while the victory parade still lies ahead. The many tribulations are the appointed road into its fullness, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17).

Does this mean every Christian will be persecuted? Every Christian will face tribulations, though not all in the same form. For some it is prison or violence; for others it is mockery, lost opportunities, family pressure, illness, grief, or the long fight against sin. The word covers the whole pressure of living for Christ in a fallen world. So do not seek suffering, and do not be ashamed if yours seems small compared with others’. But when it comes, do not be surprised, as though something strange were happening (1 Peter 4:12). It is the road, and the King has walked it.

On a Tuesday. Think of a newer Christian you know and strengthen them this week: a message, a coffee, a prayer, an honest word that following Jesus is hard and worth it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Appointed elders. Cheirotoneō originally meant to vote by a show of hands, and by the first century it had come to mean simply to appoint. It may suggest the congregation took part, but a single verb will not settle a system of church government. What the sentence plainly says is that Paul and Barnabas did the appointing, in every church without exception. Elders were leaders appointed in each church, as in the synagogue.

In the flow. This verse completes the pattern of the first journey: preach the gospel, make disciples, go back and strengthen them, and leave them under elders and committed to the Lord. A mission that only gathered converts would have died with its missionaries; one that left shepherds could outlast them. Paul’s farewell to the elders of Ephesus (20:17–35) will show what such men were for: to keep watch over the flock Christ bought with his own blood.

The timing. These churches were probably only months old, every member a recent convert, with no training college and no New Testament to study. Paul did not conclude that it was too soon. He concluded that a church without elders was a church he could not leave, and raised leaders out of the material in front of him. Keeping the churches dependent on himself would have felt safer and would have been fatal.

Was this simply what these two men happened to do, or a mandate? That they appointed elders in every church shows it was fixed practice, and the rest of the New Testament confirms it: Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders in every town (Titus 1:5), a church without them being not yet in order. Every church we meet has them: Ephesus (Acts 20:17), Peter’s readers (1 Peter 5:1), James’s (James 5:14), Philippi’s overseers and deacons (Philippians 1:1). Two things. First, three words name the same office from different angles: elder (presbyteros, maturity), overseer or bishop (episkopos, oversight), and pastor or shepherd (poimēn, care), all used of the same men (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5, 7; 1 Peter 5:1–2). Second, it is always elders, plural: a team, not a lone ruler. Shared leadership is the apostolic norm.

Where Christians differ: church government. Episcopal churches have bishops over many churches; Presbyterians, elders gathered in courts; Congregationalists and Baptists, congregations governed by their own members and elders. This commentary’s view: the New Testament pattern is a plurality of qualified elders in each local church, recognised with the congregation’s involvement, with deacons serving alongside (1 Timothy 3). Elder and bishop (overseer) are the same office in the New Testament. Christ alone is head of the church.

What authority does that give them, and what does it not? Elders have real, God-given authority: to lead or rule (1 Timothy 5:17), to teach and guard sound doctrine (Titus 1:9), to shepherd and watch over souls (Acts 20:28); and the flock is to obey your leaders and submit to them (Hebrews 13:17). But it is strictly bounded. It is derived: they are under-shepherds serving the Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4), tending the church of God, not their own (Acts 20:28). It is Word-bound: they minister Scripture’s authority, so they may not bind consciences with rules God has not given (the error of Colossians 2); they declare God’s Word, they do not legislate. And it is not the right to dominate: not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3); they lead as servants, not lords (Mark 10:42–45), and will give an account to God (Hebrews 13:17). Real authority, but servant-authority: Christ-derived, Scripture-limited, accountable, never tyrannical. The elders are no little popes.

So how should churches choose elders today? Here the apostles appointed elders as they founded churches, with prayer and fasting; in Acts 6 the congregation chose and the apostles appointed. The more likely pattern for churches now is that the congregation recognises men who meet the qualifications Paul lays down (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9), and that existing elders confirm and set them apart. And every church had elders, plural.

And what qualifies a man for it? The two lists (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9) stress character, not talent. The umbrella is above reproach: a life giving no just handle for accusation. Under it: faithful in marriage (a one-woman man), self-controlled, sober-minded, gentle and not violent, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, hospitable, upright, holy, not a recent convert (mature, lest he be puffed up). He must manage his own household well, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church? (1 Timothy 3:5), and be well thought of by outsiders. Only one item is an ability, not a trait: he must be able to teach, holding firm to sound doctrine to give instruction and also to rebuke those who contradict it (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:9), the chief thing distinguishing an elder from a deacon. The lesson humbles: an elder is not the most gifted or successful man in the room, but a man of proven Christlike character who knows and can teach the truth; nearly everything on the list is simply the mature Christian life, on display in one fit to model it.

Then why does Paul say an elder must not be a recent convert, when these men were all new? Because circumstances differed. In a brand-new church there was no one else, and the apostles, with apostolic discernment, chose the most mature men available and kept up close contact through return visits and letters. Some may have been Jews or God-fearers who had known the Scriptures for years. Later, in established churches like Ephesus, where mature men were available, Paul could and did insist on it (1 Timothy 3:6). The principle is the same in both: appoint the most mature, tested men God has given, and do not leave a church without shepherds.

They committed them to the Lord. The word behind committed is used of depositing something valuable with somebody else for safekeeping. It is the word Jesus used from the cross: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46). Paul and Barnabas are handing over something that was never theirs to keep, to the only one who can keep it, and they do it fasting, as serious men did before a step that could not be taken back.

And then they walked away. They left new believers, in hostile towns, under brand-new elders, with no means of finding out for months how any of it was going. What made that bearable is in the last clause: the Lord in whom they had believed.

No one will snatch them. That Lord had already said what he would do with such people: I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18); no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). The elders were real shepherds, but they were not the reason the flock would survive. The reason was a Shepherd who had laid down his life for these sheep and taken it up again. Paul and Barnabas were not leaving the churches alone. They were leaving them with their owner.

Resignation or entrusting. Anyone who has had to hand something over, a work, a child, a parent, knows the difference. Resignation lets go because it has run out of options. Entrusting lets go into hands it can name. So pray for your elders, and name the person or thing you are most anxious about, and hand it over today, in words, into the hands of the Lord in whom you believe.
verseByVerse.note: Elders were leaders appointed in each church, as in the synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perga. Perga is where the journey went wrong: the town where John Mark left them and went home (13:13). On the way out they had passed straight through it, a man short, with nothing planted. Now, coming back, they stop and preach. Much of God’s work is done on the second pass. The place where you failed, or were failed, is very often the place you are brought back to with something to give.

They went down to Attalia. Attalia was the port on the south coast, modern Antalya, some twelve miles from Perga, where they wait for a ship going east. It is unglamorous, and it is the actual substance of the mission.

To the other towns as well. When the crowds at Capernaum tried to keep Jesus, he said, I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose (Luke 4:43). The risen Lord is still going from town to town, now on the feet of his servants, and a town like Perga, passed over once, does not stay passed over.

Most of a life given to God. In two chapters: well over a thousand miles, probably the best part of two years, a string of cities evangelised, one man stoned. Most of a life given to God looks like these two verses: getting to the next place, speaking there, and going on.

My Christian life feels ordinary and repetitive. Is that a problem? Not in itself. Most faithfulness is ordinary: daily prayer, steady work, the same church on Sundays, the same family needs, kindness repeated. God values it and writes it down, as he did these two verses. The danger is not routine but drift, going through motions with a cold heart. So keep the routine and warm it: ask God each morning for one person to serve and one word to speak. Plodding with Christ is still walking with Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Attalia was the port on the south coast.

verseByVerse.quote: and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sailed to Antioch. Home to Syrian Antioch, perhaps two years after setting out, and Luke identifies home by what had happened there: the place where they had been commended to the grace of God.

Commended to the grace of God. A congregation had fasted and prayed and laid hands on two of its leading teachers and let them go (13:1–3), and then there was nothing else it could do. It had no way of knowing whether the two were alive. To commend them to the grace of God was to put two people somewhere it could not follow them, and go on praying. It is what a parent does at a door, and what any of us does with somebody we love and cannot help, a child abroad, a friend in hospital, and this verse says it is not a gesture. The ship came in, and both men were on it.

The work fulfilled. Not attempted, not begun: fulfilled. The commission of 13:2, the work to which I have called them, is closed out here with the same word. Between those two sentences lie hundreds of miles of mountain road, a stoning, and churches in city after city. Grace sent them, kept them, and finished the work through them.

Because another work was finished. Before the cross Jesus said to his Father, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4), and on the cross, It is finished (John 19:30). Paul and Barnabas added nothing to Christ’s saving work; they carried its news. A mission can have edges, a beginning and an end, because the work that saves has nothing left undone.

How do I know when a piece of work for God is finished? Ask what you were actually given to do, rather than everything that could be done. A teacher for a term, a carer for a season, a role in a church for a few years: when the task God assigned is done, it is right to lay it down with thanks, even if needs remain. Seek counsel from others who know you, pray, and look at whether the door is closing. Finishing well is not doing everything; it is doing the given thing, and then handing over without guilt.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained no little time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that God had done. The grammar of the report is the whole point. Not what they had done for God, nor even what they had achieved with his help: God is the subject of the sentence. Luke has bracketed the journey with the same claim: commended to the grace of God at one end, all that God had done at the other. That is not modesty; it is accuracy. A congregation that hears what its missionaries have accomplished will begin, quietly, to assess them. A congregation that hears what God has done will begin to pray.

What Christ has accomplished through me. Years later Paul summed up his whole ministry the same way: I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience (Romans 15:18). The one at work in Cyprus, Antioch, Iconium and Lystra was the risen Christ, gathering the nations promised to him (Psalm 2:8). The missionaries came home as witnesses, not heroes.

A door of faith. The image stayed with Paul: a wide door for effective work at Ephesus, with many adversaries (1 Corinthians 16:9); a request from prison that God would open to us a door for the word (Colossians 4:3). God opened it; they had walked through a door, not made one. And it is a door of faith: Gentiles could come in on the same terms as anyone else, by believing, without first becoming something they were not. A Greek in Lystra did not have to become a Jew first, by circumcision and keeping the law of Moses, to belong to God’s people. He had only to trust Christ (Romans 10:12–13).

A door that would soon be challenged. Within a short time men would come down from Judea to say that the door had been opened too wide, and that these Gentiles must be circumcised (15:1). It is a pattern worth expecting rather than being wounded by: the clearest work of God tends to be followed, quite soon, by an argument about it inside the church.

No little time. Luke’s understatement: a good long while. The record of the church’s first great missionary journey ends with two tired men staying put for months with their own congregation. There is a permission in that for anyone who believes faithfulness means never stopping. Rest, in this book, is not a lapse in obedience. It is part of the shape of it.

How can my church support missionaries when they come home? Do what Antioch did: gather to hear them, and listen for what God has done, not only for statistics. Give them time and real rest, not just a slot in a service. Ask about their struggles as well as their successes, and pray with them. Help with practical needs: housing, transport, medical care, the children’s schooling. Returning missionaries are often exhausted and out of step with home. A church that welcomes them well is sharing in the work as truly as when it sent them.

For worship. The door of faith was opened by God, and the risen Christ holds its key: he opens and no one will shut (Revelation 3:7). The men from Judea would soon try to narrow it, and could not. Through it have come Gentiles from every nation, at length us, all on the same terms, with empty hands and believing hearts, and he will not close it until the last of his people has come in.

parallels.desc: a wide door for effective work

14.theology: Suffering as the path into the kingdom. Acts 14:22 says plainly that tribulation is the road by which God’s people enter his kingdom. The cross was not a detour on the way to the resurrection; it was the way, and the church that follows a crucified Lord walks the same road. Paul speaks of filling up in his flesh “what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body” (Colossians 1:24): not that Christ’s atoning work was incomplete, for nothing was lacking in it, but that his sufferings are reproduced in his body, the church, as the gospel goes out into the world.
14.examples:
Then: Paul, stoned and left for dead outside Lystra, got up, walked back into the city and went on to Derbe the next morning. Later he returned through the cities that had tried to kill him to strengthen the believers and appoint elders.

Now: Many Christians quietly expect the Christian life to be comfortable, and when it is not, they assume something has gone wrong. Acts 14 says tribulation is the appointed road, and the Lord who walked it first walks it with his people. A suffering church is not a failing church.

15.title: The Jerusalem Council
15.text: <sup>1</sup>But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” <sup>2</sup>And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. <sup>3</sup>So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. <sup>4</sup>When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them. <sup>5</sup>But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.” <sup>6</sup>The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. <sup>7</sup>And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. <sup>8</sup>And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, <sup>9</sup>and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith. <sup>10</sup>Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? <sup>11</sup>But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” <sup>12</sup>And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. <sup>13</sup>After they finished speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me. <sup>14</sup>Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name. <sup>15</sup>And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, <sup>16</sup>‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it, <sup>17</sup>that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things <sup>18</sup>known from of old.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, <sup>20</sup>but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood. <sup>21</sup>For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.” <sup>22</sup>Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, <sup>23</sup>with the following letter: “The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings. <sup>24</sup>Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, <sup>25</sup>it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, <sup>26</sup>men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>27</sup>We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth. <sup>28</sup>For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: <sup>29</sup>that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.” <sup>30</sup>So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. <sup>31</sup>And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement. <sup>32</sup>And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. <sup>33</sup>And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them. <sup>35</sup>But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also. <sup>36</sup>And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.” <sup>37</sup>Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. <sup>38</sup>But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. <sup>39</sup>And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, <sup>40</sup>but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. <sup>41</sup>And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
15.overview:
The success of the Gentile mission raises a question the church could not avoid. Men from Judea arrive in Antioch teaching that Gentile converts cannot be saved unless they are circumcised and keep the law of Moses: in effect, Gentiles must become Jews to become Christians. It was not an odd idea, for circumcision was the covenant sign God gave Abraham. Paul and Barnabas dispute it fiercely, and the church sends them to Jerusalem to settle it with the apostles and elders.

At the council Peter reminds everyone that God gave the Spirit to Cornelius’s household and cleansed their hearts by faith, and that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus. James, the Lord’s brother, shows from Amos that God always meant to gather Gentiles into the rebuilt house of David, and proposes that Gentile believers carry no burden of the law, but avoid four things that would make shared tables impossible. A letter goes to Antioch with Judas and Silas, and the church rejoices. The chapter ends with a painful quarrel: Paul and Barnabas part over John Mark, and two teams set out.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teachers from Judea unsettle Antioch, and the church sends Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem. After long debate, the testimony of Peter, Paul and Barnabas and James’s reading of Amos lead the apostles, elders and whole church to lay no burden of the law on the Gentiles, asking only four abstentions for the sake of fellowship. A letter goes with Judas and Silas, and Antioch rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by faith alone: the council’s verdict

Peter’s speech (vv. 7–11) is the plainest statement in Acts that Gentiles are saved the same way Jews are: by grace through faith, not by keeping the law. The council confirms together what the Spirit had already shown in Cornelius’s house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The council produced a pastoral letter rather than a treatise: practical guidance that let Jew and Gentile live together in one church. Now: Churches still face questions about what may be required of believers. The council’s way of handling them, hearing what God has done, testing it by Scripture, debating openly and deciding together, remains a good pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 15 stands near the centre of the book: must Gentiles be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved? The Jerusalem council answers no, and asks only that Gentile believers avoid what would make fellowship with Jewish believers impossible. Over the whole chapter stands the God who knows the heart, who cleanses it by faith, who planned from of old to take a people for his name from every nation, and who will not let anyone add a single step to the work of his Son.

But some men came down from Judea. They may be connected with the men of Galatians 2:12 who came from James, but Luke does not say so; what the council’s letter does say is that they went out with no instructions from Jerusalem (v. 24).

In the flow. God has just opened a door of faith to the Gentiles (14:27); this verse asks on what terms they may come through it. Peter speaks here for the last time in the book, and from here on Paul’s mission fills the story, so the council is the hinge on which the book turns.

You cannot be saved. Almost everything in that sentence is right. It assumes Jesus is the Messiah, that he died and rose, and that these Gentiles must be saved. It is not the sentence of an unbeliever. What it does is add one condition, and that is all it takes. Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17); the question was whether Gentile believers must receive it, and with it keep the whole law (Galatians 5:3): Christ plus circumcision. Paul called it a different gospel (Galatians 1:6–9).

The most dangerous kind of sentence. Christians tend to picture false teaching as a denial. Often it is not. Much of the most harmful error is an addition, made by sincere people, to a set of true statements. The most dangerous kind of sentence is not one that contradicts the gospel but one that agrees with it and then says and.

Why does one word matter so much? Because of what it does to the whole. Suppose salvation is ninety-nine parts God’s grace and one part your compliance. That one part is now the part everything hangs on, the joint that can fail, and your standing before God rests, in the end, on you. Paul saw this at once and wrote to the Galatian churches in some of the sharpest language he ever used: if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you; you are severed from Christ (Galatians 5:2–4). Not damaged. Severed. A gift with a condition attached is not a gift, and a rescue you have to help with is not a rescue.

Then Christ died for no purpose. Underneath the argument about a rite lies a question about the cross: if justification were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose (Galatians 2:21). To be justified is to hear God the Judge pronounce you in the right with him, pardoned and accepted as righteous, on the strength of Christ alone. If something must be added to Christ for a sinner to be saved, then his death was not enough. The whole chapter is a defence of the sufficiency of Jesus: what he did on the cross either saves completely or does not save at all.

No small dissension and debate. Luke is being dry; he means a furious row. On this question Paul would not give in even for a moment (Galatians 2:5). The Christian instinct that peace is the higher value is usually a good one, but on the gospel itself, refusing to fight is not gentleness; it is desertion.

Aimed precisely. But watch how precisely Paul aims. In the very next chapter he circumcises Timothy himself (16:3), yet he would not let Titus be circumcised (Galatians 2:3–5). Same rite, opposite decisions, because in one case it was a free choice made for the sake of the mission, and in the other it was demanded as a condition of salvation. That is the whole of Christian wisdom about secondary things: what you may cheerfully do for love, you must refuse absolutely the moment somebody makes it necessary.

Appointed to go up. The verb is passive; the church did the appointing. The man who insists his gospel came to him from no human being (Galatians 1:11–12) goes anyway, because being right on your own is not the same as the church being settled.

What does Jesus plus look like today? Rarely circumcision. It is any requirement added to faith in Christ as the ground of acceptance with God: you must be baptised in our church, speak in tongues, keep the Saturday Sabbath, perform certain rituals, reach a certain level of holiness, or belong to the right group, before God will really accept you. Many of these things may be good, or debatable, in their place. But the moment they are made conditions of salvation, the gospel is changed. Ask of any teaching: does it leave Christ’s finished work sufficient, received by faith alone, or does it add a step?

For worship. The Son of God did not lay the foundation of our salvation and leave us to build the last storey. He cried, It is finished, and the Father raised him: nothing can be added to a work that God himself has declared complete. Blessed be the Lord who lets no one, Pharisee or apostle or our own anxious hearts, add a condition to his grace.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham; the question was whether Gentiles must become Jews to be saved. This meeting in Jerusalem, about AD 49, is often called the Jerusalem Council.

parallels.desc: Paul’s account of a Jerusalem meeting

verseByVerse.quote: "So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being sent on their way by the church. The New Testament’s phrase for helping travellers on with what they need (compare 3 John 6). They go as the congregation’s representatives, with the congregation behind them.

Describing the conversion. They are travelling to a hearing about whether the Gentiles they have converted are really saved, and they spend the journey telling the story of those conversions in every church they pass. Not marshalling arguments. Men on the way to a tribunal turned the trip into a preaching tour, which is worth copying on the way into any hard meeting.

Great joy. Those churches had been founded by the scattered believers (8:4–14; 11:19), and had themselves been outside the circle most recently. People who have just been let in are rarely the ones who want the door narrowed.

The map Jesus drew. You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). Now two men walk back to the centre of that map, through Samaria, carrying news from its far edges. The delegation goes up to Jerusalem not to ask permission for something new, but to report that the plan Christ announced is being carried out, by him.

They were welcomed. Warmly, by the church and the apostles and the elders. The men of verse 1 were a faction, not Jerusalem’s voice (v. 24), which is worth remembering before writing off a whole church because of who turned up from it.

Is this the visit of Galatians 2? One question hovers over this visit and is worth settling honestly, because a reader with a study Bible will meet it. Is this the visit Paul describes in Galatians 2, where he went up to Jerusalem, laid his gospel before the pillars, and they added nothing to it? Many think so: the cast is much the same (Paul, Barnabas, Peter, James), the issue is identical, and so is the outcome. Others place Galatians 2 at the earlier famine visit (11:30), chiefly because Paul is listing his Jerusalem visits precisely in order to prove his independence, and it would be odd for him to skip one, which would also mean Galatians was written before this council rather than after it. The honest position is that it is not certain, and that very little rests on it. On either reading the two accounts say the same decisive thing: Paul submitted his gospel to the Jerusalem leadership, and they added nothing to it. (Their later clash at Antioch, Galatians 2:11–14, was over Peter’s conduct, not a different gospel.)

Why should news of conversions bring such joy? Because heaven rejoices over it first. Jesus said there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10). A conversion is a dead person brought to life, an enemy made a child, a captive set free. If we hear such news coolly, it may be a sign that we have forgotten what it meant for us. The churches of Phoenicia and Samaria rejoiced because they remembered. Joy at others’ salvation is one of the surest marks of a heart that has tasted grace.

For worship. The God who saves is the God who delights in saving. The gladness that ran from church to church began in the Son, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2): out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied (Isaiah 53:11), and every story told in Phoenicia and Samaria was part of his reward coming in.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, 'It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers and Pharisees. Luke puts together two words most of us keep apart. These are not opponents who have infiltrated the church. They are converted men, inside it, who love the God of Israel and now trust his Messiah, and they are the crisis.

Feel the case from where they stood. These men were raised to believe that the boundary of God’s people was marked in the flesh, by God’s own command to Abraham, never once withdrawn. They had kept the law at real cost, and are now asked to receive as full members men who had lately been sacrificing to idols. Their objection is not malice. It is a lifetime of conviction meeting a new fact.

The man who had been one of them. The man who will argue hardest against them had been a Pharisee, son of a Pharisee (23:6; Philippians 3:5), which is why he refutes the position so exactly and with so little patience.

It is necessary. Necessary (dei) is Luke’s word for divine obligation, the must that stood over the cross. They are saying God requires Gentiles to become Jews, keeping the whole law, to belong to his people. Nothing smaller would have needed a council.

Circumcised in him. The New Testament’s answer is not that circumcision never mattered, but that it has been fulfilled in a person. Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), born under the law to redeem those under it (Galatians 4:4–5), and Gentile believers already bear the mark: in him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11). To ask the Gentiles for the knife now is to ask for the shadow after the body has come, for circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter (Romans 2:29).

A test, and a guard. Think of the marker you privately treat as necessary, and picture meeting, in heaven, somebody who trusted Christ and got that thing wrong all his life. If you hesitate, you have found the mark you have quietly added to Christ, and the cure is to look again at him. And a guard: this does not mean nothing matters. The council will lay down four things (v. 29). The chapter turns on keeping two questions apart: what is required in order to be saved, and what is required in order to live together. Collapse them in either direction and you get a false gospel or a lawless church.

Why would sincere believers want to add a condition? Because a condition gives us something to hold. Grace leaves us with nothing to point to but Christ, and that feels exposed. A rule we can keep feels safer: we can check it, measure ourselves by it, and see at a glance who is in and who is not. Underneath lies an old desire to keep some control over our standing with God, and some credit for it. The religious moralist and the irreligious rebel are closer than they look: both want to be their own master, one by breaking the rules and the other by keeping them. The gospel takes control out of both their hands and gives them Christ.

Can a real Christian hold a seriously wrong view? Yes, as these men show. Being born again does not make anyone instantly correct on everything, and believers can hold errors, sometimes serious ones, out of old habits of thought. That is why the church needs teaching, patience and correction. But an error about the way of salvation is not a small matter: if it hardens into a settled rejection of grace, it becomes another gospel. So treat brothers in error as brothers, reason with them from Scripture, and do not give way on the gospel itself.

parallels.desc: as to the law, a Pharisee

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gathered together. The first church council, and the whole church was involved (vv. 12, 22).

Much debate. Open, honest discussion, not a decree from above: a council on the gospel itself, with apostles in the room, and it was a long argument. Luke records no voice from heaven settling it at the outset. Yet this same meeting produced the sentence it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us (v. 28). The Spirit’s verdict came at the end of a hard debate rather than instead of one.

Peter stood up. This is his last appearance in Acts. The man who has carried the first half of this book goes out not with a miracle but with an argument for somebody else’s freedom.

When you have turned again. On the night of his denial Jesus told this man, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32). The man who denied by a fire that he knew Jesus now stands before the whole church to defend Gentiles who know Jesus and nothing of Moses. The best argument for grace in the room was the man making it.

God made a choice among you. In the early days: Cornelius was perhaps ten years earlier (chapter 10), and the Jerusalem church had given its verdict then: to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life (11:18). They had already settled this, and here they are arguing about it again. Hearing and believing: that is how Gentiles came in, and nothing was said about circumcision.

Agreement that never reached the heart. A church can formally agree something, mean it, and discover ten years later that the agreement never reached the place where convictions live. What is resisted here is not new information but the cost of what they already believed.

By my mouth. God chose; Peter’s mouth was the instrument. He has the strongest personal precedent in the room and takes no credit for it, which is why the precedent carries.

Is it wrong for Christians to argue? Not if it is the right kind of argument about the right kind of thing. The apostles debated at length, openly, and the church was the better for it. What Scripture forbids is quarrelsomeness, harshness, pride, and fighting over trivia (2 Timothy 2:23–25; Titus 3:9). Healthy debate keeps to the question, listens to the evidence, goes to Scripture, assumes good faith, and aims at agreement in the truth rather than victory. If you find you enjoy winning more than finding the truth, step back.

verseByVerse.quote: "And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, who knows the heart. The word is kardiognōstēs, heart-knower, found only twice in the New Testament: here, and at 1:24, when the eleven prayed, you, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen. Both times the church has to decide who is in, and reaches for the same name for God: men see the outside and God sees the rest. In a debate about a mark in the flesh, Peter names God by the attribute that makes the flesh irrelevant.

Just as he did to us. Then the evidence, which is a fact. He saw their faith and gave them the Spirit, before any circumcision: not a lesser measure, not a provisional instalment. The same. You may debate whether these people qualify, but God has already moved in.

No distinction. It is the verb of 11:12, making no distinction, and the tense matters: it is done. The question before the council is whether to reimpose a distinction God has already removed.

Cleansed their hearts. Then the clause that wins the argument. The verb echoes the sheet let down from heaven: what God has made clean, do not call common (10:15). The heart is the place that needs cleansing, and faith is the means; what faith lays hold of is the blood of Christ, which purifies the conscience (Hebrews 9:14).

The heart was always the problem. That is the organ the Old Testament always named. Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart (Deuteronomy 10:16); the LORD your God will circumcise your heart, so that you will love the LORD your God (Deuteronomy 30:6); I will give you a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26). The party of the Pharisees is asking for the sign; God has already given the thing the sign pointed at.

The gift of the ascended Christ. At Pentecost Peter had explained the outpouring: being exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this (2:33). So when Peter says God made no distinction, the council is being asked whether it will refuse those whom the risen Lord himself has already filled.

By faith. Not by ritual, descent, effort or a probationary period of good behaviour. The instrument by which a heart is made clean is empty-handed trust, which is why it is available to a Roman centurion, and to you tonight, and why no committee has ever been able to add a step to it.

How does faith cleanse the heart? Not by its own power, as if believing were a kind of moral detergent. Faith cleanses because it joins us to Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7), and because through faith we receive the Spirit, who makes the heart new. Faith is the empty hand; Christ is what fills it. So the cleansing is both a once-for-all washing of guilt, when we first believe, and a continuing purification, as the Spirit works holiness in a heart that keeps trusting. If you feel your heart is still far from clean, keep looking to Christ. The cleansing is his work, and he does not leave it half done.

On a Tuesday. Look at the Christian you find hardest to accept: if God has given him the Spirit, what right have you to make a distinction?

For worship. God knows the heart, and he does not stop at knowing it. He looked into the hearts of a Roman centurion and his household and saw everything there was to see, and he did not turn away; he made them clean and came to live in them. The one from whom nothing is hidden is the one who loves without reserve, and no one is a second-class member of a family where the Father has made no distinction.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test? That is a serious charge, aimed at the most orthodox men in the room. The phrase belongs to the wilderness: it is what Israel did at Massah, demanding that God prove himself after he had already shown them his power (Exodus 17:7; Psalm 95:8–9). Peter tells the party of the Pharisees that they are repeating it. That is no small charge: of the generation that tested him in the wilderness, God swore that they would not enter his rest (Psalm 95:11). The holy God is not to be told how he ought to have saved people. To put God to the test is to demand that he do it your way after he has shown you his. God has already acted: he gave the Spirit, he cleansed the hearts, he made no distinction. To require circumcision now is to inform God that his method was insufficient, and to do it while calling yourself a defender of his law.

By placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? Then the image. A yoke joined animals together for work; teachers spoke of the law as a yoke to be taken up. Consider who is speaking and where. Peter is an observant Jew, standing in Jerusalem, in front of Pharisees, and he says: none of us has ever managed it. Not our fathers. Not us. Not me. He does not say the law is bad; he says it is a weight no one in the history of his nation has carried, and that the honest record of Israel is a thousand years of proving it. No one kept the law perfectly (Galatians 3:10; James 2:10). The generation that received it broke it before Moses got down the mountain; the nation that was given the land was deported out of it for the same reason.

The inside. You can manage the outside. You cannot manage the inside, and the law asked for the inside, which is what makes it unbearable. A rule about murder can be kept. A rule about what you want cannot. So the Pharisees propose to lay on these Gentiles a burden that has crushed everyone who tried to carry it. Jesus offers an easy yoke (Matthew 11:29–30).

Just as they will. Then the sentence that turns the council over. Peter does not say that the Gentiles will be saved the way we are, by becoming Jews. He says that we Jews will be saved the way they are, by grace. The Gentiles have become the standard. Every advantage of Israel still exists (Paul will list them in Romans 9), and not one of them contributes anything at the point of being saved.

One low door. That cuts both ways, and the second is the comfort. If everything that makes you a better candidate counts for nothing here, then everything that makes you a worse candidate counts for nothing either. The Christian of forty years and the convert of last Tuesday are saved the identical way. There is one door, it is very low, and everybody goes through it on the same terms.

The yoke he carried. The yoke that neither the fathers nor Peter could bear was borne by one. The Son of God was born under the law (Galatians 4:4) and loved God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself every day of his life. Then he took the curse the law pronounced on its breakers (Galatians 3:13). So grace does not mean God has quietly dropped his demands. They were met in full by Jesus, and the penalty paid in full. His perfect obedience is counted as ours, so our best obedience, never perfect, is accepted for his sake, and our failures do not undo our standing.

Then is God’s law useless for Christians? No. The law is holy, righteous and good (Romans 7:12). It cannot save, because no sinner can keep it, but it does three things still: it shows us our sin and drives us to Christ; it restrains evil in the world; and for the believer, its moral commands, summed up in love for God and neighbour, show the shape of the life the Spirit is producing in us (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.6; the Westminster Confession 19.6). What is gone is the law as a yoke to earn acceptance, and the ceremonies that pointed forward to Christ. The Christian obeys not to be saved but because he has been.

Will I be saved through grace, or am I already saved? Both. Peter speaks here of the future, we will be saved, because salvation reaches its completion at the last day. But Scripture also says believers have already been saved (Ephesians 2:8) and are being saved (1 Corinthians 1:18). The point is that from first to last it is the same grace: the grace that forgave you when you first believed is the grace that will keep you and bring you safe to glory. You will never graduate from grace to something else.

On a Tuesday. If you are tired from carrying a yoke of trying to earn God’s favour, lay it down today. Say to God, in words: I will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, and nothing else.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke joined animals together for work; teachers spoke of the “yoke” of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. After they finished speaking, James replied, 'Brothers, listen to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the assembly fell silent. Five verses earlier there had been much debate. Now nobody speaks: the argument has run out of road, and the men who were shouting are listening.

They listened to Barnabas and Paul. Since Paphos it has usually been Paul first. In Jerusalem the old order comes back, because there Barnabas is the trusted man: the Levite who sold his field for the church (4:36–37), the one who vouched for Saul (9:27), Jerusalem’s own emissary to Antioch (11:22).

Signs and wonders among the Gentiles. The two of them do not argue theology; Peter has done that. They report facts, laid before the assembly as evidence that God had confirmed the Gentile mission with signs.

The council’s method. That gives a model worth keeping. Testimony first: what has God actually done? Then Scripture: the prophets agree with it (v. 15). Then judgment (v. 19). Experience is admitted as evidence and never made the authority. That order guards a church against deciding doctrine from stories, and against being so afraid of stories that it cannot see what God is plainly doing in front of it.

James replied. Not James the brother of John, executed at 12:2, but the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church (12:17), remembered for strict law-keeping, whose judgment would carry weight with conservative Jewish believers.

The brother who did not believe. He grew up in the same house and did not believe: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). Then Jesus was crucified, and then, Paul tells us in a bare line, he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). The brother who did not believe now presides over the decision that his brother is the Saviour of the world.

For the family you pray for. If you are praying for somebody in your own family who knows the Christian at close quarters and is unimpressed, James is your verse. It took a resurrection. But it happened, and he was in the house the whole time.

Peter speaks, James rules. In this room the summing-up belongs to the head of the local church, and the decision is taken by the apostles and elders with the whole church (v. 22). It is worth noticing, and not worth quarrelling over.

How should a church weigh experience in a disagreement? Listen to it carefully, and then test it by Scripture. Stories of what God is doing matter: they may show you that your theory was too small. But experiences can be misread, exaggerated or counterfeited, and feelings are not revelation. So ask: does Scripture teach this? Does it honour Christ and the gospel of grace? Do the fruit and the doctrine agree? The council heard the reports with respect, and then let the prophets decide.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon has related. Three things in one sentence. First, the name: Simeon is the Hebrew form of Simon (compare 2 Peter 1:1). In a room debating whether Gentiles must become Jews, James refers to the man who argued for Gentile freedom by his most Jewish name, perhaps signalling that the case did not come from an outsider.

How God first visited the Gentiles. Second, the verb. In Scripture it is what God does when he comes to rescue: he visited his people in their slavery (Exodus 4:31); Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people (Luke 1:68). It is the homecoming word, and James puts it on the nations.

The visit was a person. In Luke that verb has a face. At Nain the crowd cried, God has visited his people! (Luke 7:16), and Jesus wept over Jerusalem because it did not know the time of its visitation (Luke 19:44). The visit Israel’s prophets longed for came in the person of the Son, and has now reached Lystra and Antioch by his Spirit and his word.

To take from them a people for his name. Third, and most provocative. The Greek Old Testament keeps laos, the people, meaning Israel, apart from ethnē, the nations. James has taken the word reserved for Israel and applied it to men taken out of the nations: a people for his name, God’s own treasured possession, showing the world what he is like (Deuteronomy 14:2; 1 Peter 2:9–10). It would have been hard to say anything more inflammatory to the men of verse 5, and he says it gently, in their own vocabulary, from their own Scriptures.

From them. Not all of them. God is taking a people out of the nations, which is remnant language (the part God keeps and calls for himself out of a larger whole), and it guards two errors: that everyone is swept in regardless, and that the church has simply replaced Israel. The church is God’s one people, from Jews and Gentiles: very likely what Paul means by the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16).

So are Gentile Christians now part of Israel? In this sense, yes: they are grafted into the one olive tree of God’s people (Romans 11:17–24), heirs of Abraham through faith (Galatians 3:7, 29), fellow citizens with the saints (Ephesians 2:19). There is one people of God, not two, gathered around one Messiah. That does not erase the difference between Jew and Gentile as peoples, or settle every question about Israel’s future; Christians read Romans 11 in more than one way. But no believer is a guest in someone else’s family. Every one who trusts Christ is a full member of God’s people.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon is the Hebrew form of Simon (Peter).

verseByVerse.quote: "And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, "'After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of the prophets agree. James does not say the prophets predicted this and therefore we must accept it. The Scriptures are the fixed point, and what Peter, Barnabas and Paul have reported is measured against them. Had Amos not agreed, no number of signs and wonders would have settled the matter.

The tent of David. James quotes Amos in its Greek form. The tent of David is David’s dynasty and kingdom, fallen into ruin (Amos 9:11), and Amos calls it not the house or the throne but the booth of David: a temporary shelter of branches in a vineyard at harvest, and a collapsed one.

I will restore it. God’s answer is not to replace it with something grander. He goes back to the fallen shelter and puts that up again. James says this is being fulfilled now: in the resurrection and enthronement of Jesus, David’s son (2:30–36; 13:34), and in the gathering of the Gentiles into his kingdom.

The Hebrew and the Greek. Now the difficulty, which the honest reader will meet the moment he turns to Amos, and which is worth facing squarely rather than stepping over. James is quoting the Greek Old Testament, and at the crucial point it does not read like the Hebrew. Amos 9:12 in our English Bibles, translated from the Hebrew, says the purpose is that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name. James quotes it as that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord. Edom has become mankind, and possessing has become seeking.

Three things help. First, the differences are exactly the kind that arise between two ancient copies rather than the kind a translator invents: in Hebrew written without vowels, Edom and mankind differ by at most one easily missed letter, and possess and seek differ by a single letter. The Greek translators were probably working from a Hebrew manuscript and read the consonants one way; the text behind our Old Testament read them another. Second, the Greek Old Testament was the Bible most of the church actually read, Antioch included, and the quotation comes in the form those readers knew, as Paul’s did in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch (13:41) and as any preacher’s does. Third, and most important: the argument survives on either text. Even in the Hebrew, the restored kingdom of David includes all the nations who are called by my name: Gentiles bearing God’s name inside David’s rebuilt house, which is precisely the point in dispute. The council did not smuggle the Gentiles in through a variant. Both texts have them there; the Greek simply says it more warmly. Some details of how the two texts came to differ remain uncertain, and believers can admit that honestly while holding that Scripture speaks truly.

Where Christians differ: when is David’s tent rebuilt? Dispensationalists see the rebuilding of David’s tent as a future millennial kingdom for Israel, after the church age. This commentary’s view: James says the conversion of the Gentiles agrees with Amos now. David’s fallen tent is rebuilt in the risen Christ reigning on David’s throne, and in his church of Jews and Gentiles. The promise is fulfilled in the gospel age. This is the amillennial reading, which follows the apostles’ own use of the prophets.

How our dispensational brothers read it. Dispensational brothers (who see God as keeping distinct purposes for Israel and for the church) generally take the rebuilt tent to await a future restoration of national Israel and David’s throne, and read James as showing only that the present Gentile ingathering is in harmony with the prophets. Both readings rejoice that Gentiles are saved by grace without becoming Jews, the very point of the council, and the difference should be carried with charity.

Is it legitimate for the New Testament to use the Greek Old Testament? Yes. The apostles quoted Scripture in the form their hearers knew, as we quote a familiar translation. Where the Greek differs from the Hebrew, the apostles never build a doctrine on a mistake; they use wording that faithfully carries the meaning, often drawing out what the Hebrew implies. And because the apostles wrote under the Spirit’s inspiration, their use of the Old Testament is itself the authoritative guide to its meaning. When James says Amos is being fulfilled, that is how we should read Amos.

For worship. God does not abandon the ruins of his promises. David’s house fell to a garden hut, and then to nothing, and God raised it up again in a Son who will never fall. Every Gentile who seeks the Lord is a sign that the shelter is standing again, and the One who promised it is the One doing it.
verseByVerse.note: James quotes Amos in its Greek form. “The tent of David” is David’s fallen royal house.

parallels.desc: I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The remnant of mankind. Why is the tent of David rebuilt at all? Not so that Israel may have a king again for its own sake, but that the rest of humanity might seek the Lord. If the King was raised up for the sake of the nations, then requiring the nations to become Israelites first has the prophecy backwards.

Called by my name. Amos does not say the Gentiles will become Jews; he says they will bear God’s name, literally that his name has been called over them. It is what is said of the temple, this house that I have built is called by your name (1 Kings 8:43): to be publicly marked as his property, the way a name over a door tells you whose house it is.

The name called over you. James uses the same idiom in his letter: the honourable name by which you were called (James 2:7). In Acts the name is always the name of Jesus (2:38; 4:12). So the name God has placed over the Gentiles is the name of his Son. They do not need to be marked as Jews. They carry the name of the Son of David himself, and his rebuilt house is full of people who answer to it.

Says the Lord, who makes these things. James is about to hand down a ruling, but he does not finish on his own authority. The last voice in his quotation is God’s.

What if I do not feel that I belong? There is a word here for the Christian who does not feel that he belongs: who sits in church suspecting he is tolerated rather than wanted, or who came in late, or from the wrong background, or with a history he would rather nobody knew. Belonging, in this verse, is not established by how you feel about the family. It is established by whose name has been called over you. That was done to you; you did not do it, and you cannot undo it by feeling unworthy of it. The Gentiles in Amos are not told to earn the name. They are told it is already on them.

Does seek the Lord mean people find God by their own searching? No. Scripture says plainly that no one seeks God on his own (Romans 3:11). When people truly seek the Lord, it is because he has first sought them and drawn them. Here the seeking is the result of God’s rebuilding: the Lord does these things, and the nations seek him as a consequence. So if you find yourself seeking God, take it as a sign that he is already at work in you, and keep seeking, for he is found by those who seek him with all their heart.

parallels.desc: all the nations who are called by my name

verseByVerse.quote: "'known from of old.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Known from of old. If you grew up with the King James, verse 18 is a whole sentence: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world. The ESV gives a few words and attaches them to the end of Amos’s quotation, which is worth explaining.

A textual note. The longer sentence stands in the mass of later Greek manuscripts, the text the King James translators worked from. The shorter reading is in the oldest and best copies we have. On the shorter reading, the words are still part of what God says through the prophet; on the longer, they become a separate remark of James’s own about God’s omniscience in general. And this ought to be reassuring. The shorter reading, the one the modern versions print, is actually the stronger one for James’s argument. A general statement that God knows everything he does would be true but loose. What the better text says is sharper: God makes these things known from of old. This particular thing. The ingathering of the nations was published centuries in advance, and the council is not deciding a new policy but catching up with an old announcement.

Nothing is at stake. God’s eternal knowledge of all his works is taught plainly elsewhere (Isaiah 46:10; Ephesians 1:4). Whichever reading is in your Bible, the doctrine stands; only the address of the proof text moves. Most textual variants are like that, and the footnotes exist because translators are being honest with you.

Not plan B. From of old: this was not a change of plan. The inclusion of the Gentiles was God’s purpose all along, made known to Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and announced through the prophets (Isaiah 45:21–22). Jerusalem had condemned Jesus because it did not understand the prophets it read every Sabbath (13:27); this time the men in the room see what had been written down.

The mystery hidden for ages. Paul calls it the mystery hidden for ages in God: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel (Ephesians 3:6, 9). The plan known from of old was never a plan about circumcision. It was a plan about a person: to gather a people from every nation into his Son, the seed in whom all the families of the earth would be blessed.

If God planned everything from of old, do my choices matter? Yes. God’s eternal plan includes our real choices and actions, and works through them, not around them. The council still had to debate, decide and write; the missionaries still had to walk. God’s purpose is the reason our obedience is not wasted, not a reason to sit still. We act responsibly, praying and choosing as wisely as we can, and rest in the knowledge that a wise and good God has woven even our mistakes into a plan that will not fail (Romans 8:28).

On a Tuesday. The parts of your life that look like improvisation, the detour, the years that came to nothing, the door that shut, are being handled by someone who does not improvise. Name one of them to God today and thank him that he knew it from of old.

parallels.desc: who told this long ago?

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
My judgment. Summing up the council, the word carries the weight of a ruling, and the first thing the ruling does is take something away: no circumcision, no burden of the law. Before one requirement is named, the ruling is: stop making it hard for them. The verb (parenochlein) means to harass, to pile on difficulties: the Gentile converts were being harassed by some within the church, and it must stop.

Harassing people toward Jesus. A church can easily attach to the gospel a cloud of expectations, about dress, vocabulary, background, politics, a conversion story of the right shape, none of them stated as conditions, all of them functioning as conditions, and then wonder why people who genuinely turned to God do not stay. The first ruling the church ever issued about new believers begins: we should not trouble.

Burdens hard to bear. James’s own brother had said as much: you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers (Luke 11:46); Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them (Luke 18:16). The Christ who kept his sharpest words for those who made coming to God hard is the Christ whose brother now says: we should not trouble them. The church was not being lenient. It was being like Jesus.

Those who turn to God. Turn is the conversion word, and James uses it as settled fact before he says anything about their behaviour. The order is the gospel in miniature: they are in, and then we talk about how to live.

Four abstentions. Having lifted the burden, James lays down four things, probably echoing the law’s rules for foreigners living among Israel (Leviticus 17–18): food offered to idols; sexual immorality (perhaps including marriages within forbidden degrees, Leviticus 18); meat from animals strangled rather than drained of blood; and eating blood (Genesis 9:4). These would deeply offend Jewish believers and make table fellowship impossible.

If the food laws are abolished, why forbid blood and strangled meat? First, hold on to what the council had just decided: Gentiles are saved by grace, not by keeping the law (15:11), so these are not kosher rules smuggled back in, nor conditions of salvation. Why ask them, then? For love and unity. Jewish believers were revolted by these things: meat offered to idols, and the eating of blood (which strangled meat retains). Scripture had forbidden blood since Noah, long before Moses (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17), out of reverence for the life in it. For Jew and Gentile to sit at one table and be one church, the Gentiles, free in conscience, were asked to surrender a few things that would deeply wound their brothers: liberty limited by love (Romans 14). And all four cluster around the pagan temple (idol-meat, blood, strangled animals, ritual immorality were the stuff of idol-feasts), so the decree also keeps new converts clear of their old idolatry. It is not back to the law; it is: love your brother, and stay clear of idols.

But does not Paul later allow food offered to idols? No contradiction (1 Corinthians 8–10), once two questions are distinguished.
