(1) Eating as an act of worship, at a temple feast: Paul forbids it as flatly as the council: flee from idolatry; you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons (1 Corinthians 10:14, 21). On idolatry, Paul and James are identical. (2) Eating meat that had merely passed through a temple and is now sold in the market or served at a private meal: this Paul treats as neutral (an idol has no real existence, 8:4; eat whatever is sold in the meat market, 10:25), permitted, governed only by love: do not eat if it would wound a weaker brother (8:9–13). So Paul is not overturning the decree but applying its same two principles, flee idolatry, let love limit liberty, with more nuance. The ruling was a wise unity measure for a raw Jewish and Gentile church; its permanent heart, no idolatry, no sexual immorality, freedoms surrendered for love, never changes, even as the specific abstentions from blood and strangled meat are generally understood to belong to that moment (most Christians today do not observe them, seeing the reverence for blood fulfilled in the blood of Christ once shed). The thread from James to Paul is one: keep clear of idols, and love your brother more than your dinner.

Where Christians differ: are these rules binding today? Some groups hold that Christians must still avoid blood, for example in black pudding, or even (Jehovah’s Witnesses) blood transfusions. This commentary’s view: these were not conditions of salvation (that was settled in v. 11), but practical rules for fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers at that time. Paul later teaches that food is a matter of conscience and love (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8–10). The rule against sexual immorality is permanent moral law; the food rules applied the principle of not offending a brother. Blood transfusions have nothing to do with eating blood.

Why is sexual immorality in a list about food? Because in the pagan world it was bound up with idol worship and temple feasts, and because Gentile culture treated it as ordinary, much as many do today. Jewish believers were horrified by it, and rightly, for it is not a matter of custom but of God’s moral law, forbidden again and again in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 6:18; 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5). Its place on the list warned new Gentile converts that turning to God meant a break with the sexual habits of their old life. That part of the decree has never expired.
verseByVerse.note: The four requirements probably echo rules the law gave for foreigners living in Israel (Lev 17–18), and would let Jewish and Gentile believers eat together.

parallels.desc: sacrifices, blood, and what dies of itself
sexual relations

verseByVerse.quote: "'For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read every Sabbath. This is James’s reason for the four abstentions, and one of the more puzzling sentences in Acts. Careful readers have taken it three ways.

Three readings. Some read it as being about the Jewish believers: Moses is preached in every city, so in every city there are Christians of Jewish background with these scruples, and the four abstentions are the minimum floor on which a mixed congregation can eat together. Some read it as being about the Gentiles: anyone who wants the law of Moses can hear it any Sabbath, so the church has no need to impose it. And some read it as a reassurance to the Pharisees’ party that the ruling does no dishonour to Moses, who goes on being read every week.

For the sake of brothers. The first reading fits the ruling’s stated purpose best and is the one most take. On any of the three, James grounds the abstentions not in the Gentiles’ own holiness but in other people: believers, in towns these Gentiles will never visit, who could not sit at a table where blood was served. Not because those men are right; the council has just declared they are not right about circumcision. Because they are brothers.

The hardest form of love. Surrendering a liberty you are entitled to, for somebody whose scruple you do not share and privately think mistaken, is the hardest form of Christian love and much the commonest (Romans 14). It costs more than the grand sacrifices because nobody notices you doing it.

Moses wrote of me. And Moses, read every Sabbath, was writing about Christ: if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me (John 5:46; compare Luke 24:27). The scrolls read every week in Iconium were witnesses for the very Messiah the Gentile believers trusted, and nothing should be put in the way of one hearer who is on that road.

How do I know when to give up a freedom and when to stand on it? Give it up when using it would genuinely harm a brother’s conscience or faith, cause him to stumble into sin, or block someone from hearing the gospel (1 Corinthians 8:13; 9:19–23). Stand on it when someone demands it as a condition of being right with God, because then the gospel itself is at stake (Galatians 2:4–5). The difference is between a weaker brother who is hurt and a false teacher who is imposing. With the first, love limits liberty. With the second, liberty must be defended for the sake of the gospel.

For worship. The Gentiles of Antioch were asked to give up a dish for brothers they would never meet. For Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:3): he had every right to the glory of heaven and laid it aside, and to his own life and laid that down too, for the weak, the scrupulous and the wrong. Every small freedom surrendered at a shared table is a faint reflection of that Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, with the following letter: "The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the whole church. Agreement, after great debate: apostles, elders and the whole church named together in the sending. Luke does not explain the mechanics, but the decision was not simply handed down from a room upstairs.

To choose men. They had a letter, and instead of simply sending it, they chose men and sent them with it. A ruling that arrives as a document is a verdict; you are left alone with your questions and whatever tone you imagined in it. A ruling that arrives in the hands of two respected men who will stay and answer anything you ask is a pastoral act. Antioch had been unsettled by men who came with words. Jerusalem answers with men who came with words, and the difference is that these were sent.

Not only a letter. That instinct runs back to the way God himself has spoken: in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14): he came, and stayed, and answered questions. Sending Judas and Silas with the letter is a faint copy of that.

Leading men. Both Jerusalem men, both, so far as we can tell, Jewish: the delegation carrying a verdict for Gentile freedom is drawn from the side that had most to lose by it, so nobody could say the Gentiles had voted themselves a privilege.

Remember the second name. Silas is the Silvanus of Paul’s letters (2 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Thessalonians 1:1), who carried, and perhaps helped to write, Peter’s first letter (1 Peter 5:12). He has come to Antioch to deliver a letter and go home. Within twenty verses he will be Paul’s partner, and before long singing in a Philippian cell at midnight (16:25). Men are forever setting out on errands that turn into their life’s work.

Brothers to brothers. The letter’s first word settles the question it was written to answer. Brothers to brothers, on both ends of the address: Jewish and Gentile believers are one family. Before a single clause of argument, the salutation has conceded everything the Judaizers (those insisting that Gentile believers must live as Jews) were contesting.

Does the Council set a pattern for church government? Apostles, elders and the whole church took part (vv. 22–23), and the decision was reached by appeal to Scripture (vv. 15–18) and to what God had done. It bound the churches beyond Jerusalem because the apostles were present and the decision agreed with Scripture. Churches today may meet together to settle questions, as Presbyterian synods do, and congregations take part in decisions; but no later council carries apostolic authority, and none can bind the conscience beyond what Scripture says.

A fingerprint. The Greek word for greetings here appears as a letter’s greeting in only three places in the New Testament: this letter, a Roman officer’s despatch (23:26), and the letter of James. The man who drafted this one seems to have written another.

Why does it matter that we call other believers brothers and sisters? Because it is true, and because truth spoken shapes how we treat one another. In Christ we have one Father and one elder Brother, and so we are family, not members of a club or customers of a service. Families eat together, bear with one another, tell the truth, share burdens, and stay together through quarrels. The word brother in this letter was a healing word to Gentiles who had been told they were outsiders. It can still be one: say it, and mean it, to the believer who feels least at home.
verseByVerse.note: Silas is the Silvanus of Paul’s letters; he became Paul’s travelling companion.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gone out from us. The mother church puts it in writing that men who had used its name had no authority to do so. And the wording is honest: from us is conceded in the same breath as the disowning.

Although we gave them no instructions. What they deny is the commission. That is the right shape for an institution that has been misrepresented, and it is rarer than it ought to be: the temptations are to defend your own because they are your own, or to pretend they were never anything to do with you.

Unsettling. The word (anaskeuazontes) is used of dismantling a building or plundering a house: they took your minds apart. The injury was not immorality or a split but unsettled minds. People who had been sure they belonged to God were no longer sure, and that is the characteristic wound of adding anything to the gospel. An uncertain Christian cannot love, give or speak of Christ freely, because part of him is permanently occupied with checking whether he is in.

The peace he left. Paul uses the same word for the same kind of men: there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ (Galatians 1:7). The cure for a distorted Christ is Christ undistorted. In the upper room Jesus said, Let not your hearts be troubled. Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you (John 14:1, 27). His peace rests not on our reaching some further standard but on what he did the next day, on the cross.

Having come to one accord. Luke’s word for the church’s Spirit-given unity (1:14; 4:24), placed eighteen verses after much debate (v. 7). They did not reach one accord by leaving the subject alone. The unity is on the far side of the argument, which is the only kind that holds.

With our beloved Barnabas and Paul. The two men the circumcision party had been quietly undermining are named in an official document with an adjective of affection, and Barnabas first: in a Jerusalem letter, the Jerusalem order.

How can I have assurance if my mind has been unsettled? Go back to the gospel itself, not to your feelings or your record. God promises that whoever believes in the Son has eternal life (John 3:36), and he cannot lie. Your assurance rests first on that promise, then on the Spirit’s inner witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16), and then on the fruit of a changed life, which will be imperfect but real (the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession, both 18.2). If someone has told you that you need something more than Christ, test it by Scripture as Antioch did. And talk to a mature pastor or friend; unsettled minds are often settled in conversation.

parallels.desc: some who trouble you

verseByVerse.quote: "'men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Risked their lives. The Greek (paradedōkosi) is stronger than risked: they have handed over their lives, as at the stoning in Lystra (14:19). Jerusalem is not saying these are sound men whose theology we have checked. It is saying: these are the men who have already paid for this gospel with their bodies, and the people telling you they are wrong have paid nothing like it.

For the name. Not for a mission strategy, but for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The name runs through the chapter: a people for his name (v. 14), called by his name (v. 17), lives handed over for the name. The council exists to answer whether that name is enough by itself.

By word of mouth. Two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), the written word and the living voice sent together. A letter can be read with a hostile tone supplied by the reader or explained away by whoever gets to it first, so they sent two men who could be asked follow-up questions.

Does suffering prove that someone’s teaching is true? Not on its own. People have suffered and died for false beliefs too. But suffering does show sincerity: it is hard to believe that someone is in it for gain when he keeps being stoned for it. And in Scripture faithful suffering is one of the marks of true servants of Christ, in contrast to false teachers who look for comfort and profit (2 Corinthians 11:23–29; 2 Timothy 3:10–12). So the test of teaching is always Scripture; but a teacher’s willingness to suffer for Christ rather than profit from him is a good reason to listen carefully.

On a Tuesday. Find out about a persecuted church or a believer imprisoned for their faith, and carry them to God in prayer this week.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the Holy Spirit and to us. One of the boldest sentences any church body has written about its own decision, and quoted ever since to justify a great deal that it will not bear. The Spirit led the council through Scripture, through what God had done, and through the agreement of the church.

He will guide you into all the truth. Jesus promised that the Spirit of truth would guide them into all the truth, and he will glorify me (John 16:13–14). Watch him do precisely that: he guarded the sufficiency of Christ, nothing added to the grace of the Lord Jesus. Whenever the Spirit truly leads the church, Christ is made larger and the burdens on his people smaller, and that is one sure way to tell his leading from a committee’s preferences.

Three things stand under it. The Spirit had already acted publicly before any of them voted (v. 8). Scripture agreed (v. 15). And apostles were in the room, holding a commission that is not repeatable. A committee with none of those three has no business borrowing this sentence.

The order of the words. The guard is in the order: to the Holy Spirit and to us. They do not write: we have decided, and we trust the Spirit approves. Nor do they write: the Spirit has spoken and we merely wrote it down, which would have sounded more impressive and been a lie, because they had argued at length. Christians ever since have wanted to delete one half or the other: some claiming a directness God did not give them, others reducing the church’s decisions to human management with a prayer at the start. These men were willing to put their names next to the Spirit’s, which is a far more sobering thing than claiming a private impression.

No greater burden. They admit the four things are a burden. What they promise is that nothing further will be added, which was the whole anxiety of the Gentile churches, and remains the anxiety of anyone who suspects the requirements will keep coming.

Three versions of the decree. Luke gives the decree three times: James speaks it (v. 20), the letter writes it (v. 29), and years later James quotes it back to Paul (21:25). The letter tightens things polluted by idols, broad enough to cover almost anything connected with a temple, into what has been sacrificed to idols, a specific and checkable thing. It also moves sexual immorality to last, so that the three food matters stand together, and that is the order James uses at 21:25. So the decree did not quietly lapse once feelings cooled.

You will do well. Not you will be saved, but you will do well: advice for fellowship, not a condition of salvation. And it ends gently, with no threat and no penalty. Farewell.

Where Christians differ: the authority of church councils. Some see this council as the model for later councils whose decisions bind the church infallibly. This commentary’s view: this council included apostles, and its decision became Scripture. Later councils have no such authority. They are valuable and to be respected when they agree with Scripture, as Nicaea and Chalcedon do, but they can err (Westminster Confession 31.4). Scripture alone is the final authority. This is sola Scriptura, Scripture alone.

May a church today say it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us? Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that the great councils of the church carry the Spirit’s guarantee and bind the faithful. Reformed churches hold that councils can err, and that their decisions bind only as far as they agree with Scripture. Here the apostles were present, and their judgment became part of Scripture itself. Churches may pray for and follow the Spirit’s guidance, but they cannot claim this sentence for their own decisions.

Are these four requirements binding today? Two of them, avoiding idolatry and sexual immorality, are permanent moral commands repeated throughout the New Testament. The food rules, about blood and strangled meat, were given so that Gentile believers would not needlessly offend their Jewish brothers in that setting; Paul later treats food offered to idols as a matter of conscience and love (1 Corinthians 8; 10:25–29). The principle that lasts is to use our freedom with love for others.

How should I seek the Spirit’s guidance in my own decisions? Follow the council’s pattern on a small scale. Start with Scripture: what has God already said that bears on this? Look honestly at the circumstances God has arranged. Pray, and ask counsel of wise believers, especially if the decision affects others. Weigh the options in the light of love for God and neighbour. Then decide, and own the decision humbly, without claiming that God spoke to you directly. The Spirit usually guides through his word, prayer, wisdom and the church, not through private voices, and he is no less present for that.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They delivered the letter. It was read to the whole church, at once, out loud. The people whose minds had been unsettled heard the answer with their own ears at the same moment as everyone else.

Stand in that room. This is where a doctrine becomes a person’s own relief. You are a Gentile in Antioch. Not so many years ago, perhaps, you were sacrificing to the gods you had grown up with, and then you heard about Jesus and believed, and something in you came alive. Then men arrived from Jerusalem, from the church of the apostles, and said you were not, in fact, saved: there was a further thing, and until it was done you were outside. You have spent months not knowing whether you belong to God. And now a letter is read aloud, and its first word is brothers, and it says the men who unsettled you were never sent, and that nothing further is required of you.

They rejoiced. They were saved by grace, as they were. The gospel of grace brings joy; legalism brings fear.

Joy by subtraction. Nothing was added to these people to produce that joy: no new experience, gift or vision. Something was taken away, a doubt. Most of the deepest joys of the Christian life are like that: the removal of something that had been standing between you and what you already had.

Nailed to the cross. And what was removed had a destination. The demand laid on Antioch was a legal debt the Gentiles were told they still owed. Paul tells Colossae where every such demand has gone: cancelling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The letter read in Antioch did not cancel anything. It announced a cancellation already made, on a hill outside Jerusalem.

Why does legalism produce fear? Because if acceptance with God depends even partly on your performance, you can never be sure you have done enough. Every failure becomes a threat, every rule a test you might fail, and every other Christian a rival or a judge. That is why legalistic churches are often anxious, harsh and joyless, even when they are very busy. Grace produces a different kind of obedience: glad, grateful and secure, because it flows from acceptance rather than toward it. Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

On a Tuesday. You may be carrying an unsettled mind of your own: some question about whether God has really accepted you that you have never put into words. Open the New Testament today at Romans 8 and read it aloud, as Antioch heard its letter.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Themselves prophets. Jerusalem sent not two couriers but two prophets, and they did not hand over the letter and catch the next ship. They stayed.

Encouraged and strengthened. One of the plainest descriptions in the New Testament of what a prophet in the early church did with his time. There is prediction in Acts (11:28; 21:11), but here, where Luke tells us what two named prophets did in a local church, they talked to people for a long time and left them stronger. Paul’s definition matches: the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation (1 Corinthians 14:3).

With many words. Luke’s cheerful admission that it took a while: hours of talking to frightened people, probably repeating themselves. That is a comfort to anybody who suspects his own ministry is unremarkable.

A bruised reed he will not break. That patience has a source: a bruised reed he will not break, and a smouldering wick he will not quench (Matthew 12:20). Antioch was a reed bent by a false gospel. Its Lord did not answer its weakness with a sharp word and a deadline. He gave it two men and many words and as long as it took: the Servant still binding up the bruised through those he sends.

Sent off in peace. The chapter began with no small dissension and debate (v. 2), and now men are sent home in peace. It is not the peace of a subject nobody raised, but what was left when the thing was fought out properly and settled.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 34: that it seemed good to Silas to remain there. It is probably a later addition to explain why Silas is in Antioch in v. 40. Silas may have gone back to Jerusalem and later returned, or stayed.

Are there prophets like Judas and Silas today? In the sense of men receiving new revelation from God to stand alongside Scripture, no: that foundational gift belonged to the apostolic age, when the New Testament was not yet complete (Ephesians 2:20), and the canon is now closed. But the work Judas and Silas are described as doing here, strengthening and encouraging believers with many words drawn from the truth God has given, goes on in every faithful pastor, teacher and friend who opens the word to a troubled soul. Many Christians hold the gift of prophecy continues in some form, and they are brothers; but none should claim for any word today the authority of Scripture.

On a Tuesday. Christ has dealt gently with your bruises, so think of one shaken believer you know, and give them not a single sentence but an hour: listen, then speak the truths of the gospel to them, even the ones they have heard before.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 34: “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teaching and preaching the word of the Lord. Your Bible goes straight from verse 33 to verse 35, and the footnote is a small, unusually clear window on how we came to have the New Testament we have.

The missing verse. Verse 34 exists in the King James (Notwithstanding it pleased Silas to abide there still) and in the manuscripts behind it. The modern versions put it in the margin, noting that some manuscripts insert: but it seemed good to Silas to remain there, because it is absent from the oldest and best copies we have. Now ask why anybody would add such a sentence, because the answer is disarming. Look at verse 33: Judas and Silas were sent off, back to the men who had sent them. Then look at verse 40: Paul chooses Silas and departs. A copyist reading those in sequence sees a snag (how can Paul take a man who has gone home to Jerusalem?) and supplies a line to keep Silas in Antioch.

How variants usually arise. That is the shape of the great majority of textual variants, and it should steady rather than alarm you. The scribe was not inventing doctrine, or protecting a party, or smoothing away something inconvenient. He was tidying a narrative wrinkle, in good faith. And we can see him doing it, because the copies without his tidy-up have survived; the evidence is all still on the table, which is precisely why the footnote is there. Nothing whatever is at stake in verse 34: Luke was quite capable of leaving a gap between a departure and a return, and Silas may simply have gone and come back, or delayed his going.

Councils are rare; teaching is daily. One of the gravest crises in the church’s history has just been resolved, and the next sentence is that two men stayed in their own congregation and taught.

With many others also. The ministry of the word was shared by many, and Luke names none of them. If you have measured your own service against the people whose names are known and concluded that yours does not count, Luke puts the many others in the same clause as Paul and Barnabas, with the same verbs. The distinction is ours, not his, and not God’s.

Gifts of the ascended Lord. Where did Antioch get so many teachers? When Christ ascended on high he gave gifts to men: the shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints (Ephesians 4:8, 11–12). The many others were presents from the throne, given by the risen Jesus to a church he had just defended at Jerusalem.

The last time together. This is the last time Paul and Barnabas appear together as partners. Soon they will part over Mark.

Does every Christian have a part in the ministry of the word? Yes, though not all in the same way. Some are called and gifted to preach and teach publicly, and the church should test and recognise them. But every believer is to let the word of Christ dwell richly, teaching and admonishing one another (Colossians 3:16): parents with children, friends over coffee, older women with younger, a word of Scripture in a hospital ward. The many others of Antioch were probably a mixture of all these. Ask where God has given you people to share his word with.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — The Parting of Paul and Barnabas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul proposes going back to visit the churches of the first journey. Barnabas wants to take John Mark, who had left them in Pamphylia; Paul refuses. After a sharp disagreement they part: Barnabas sails with Mark to Cyprus, and Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
verseByVerse.theology:
God’s rule over his servants’ conflicts

Luke does not approve the quarrel, and something real was lost when these two partners parted. Yet God worked through it: two teams went out instead of one, and John Mark, the cause of the dispute, later proved his worth, so that Paul himself asked for him (2 Timothy 4:11; Colossians 4:10). God does not waste the failures of his servants; he works through them, and despite them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Barnabas took Mark back to Cyprus, over the ground where he had failed, to restore him. Paul took Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Both bore fruit. Now: When Christians disagree on something that does not touch the gospel, they can still each go on with the work, speak well of one another, and leave room for God to heal the break in time.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, 'Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.' Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See how they are. The last clause is the whole man: the daily pressure of his anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28). He has been driven out of most of those towns, and what is on his mind is whether the people he left behind are all right. Keep that in view, because the quarrel is about to make both men look small.

In the flow. The plan to revisit becomes the second journey, which carries the council’s decisions to the very churches whose freedom it defended (16:4), and then into Europe. And it begins with a sharp quarrel, so that we learn that the gospel goes forward through forgiven and imperfect servants.

John called Mark. The John Mark who had turned back (13:13). Barnabas, the encourager, wanted to give him a second chance, and any reader who has been paying attention knows at once what is coming.

The whole life of Barnabas. He first appears selling a field, nicknamed son of encouragement (4:36–37). When the church was afraid of a recently converted persecutor, Barnabas brought him to the apostles (9:27), and later went to Tarsus to find him (11:25–26). Barnabas’s entire biography is taking a chance on somebody other people had written off.

The irony. The man refusing to take a chance on Mark is a man whose ministry exists because Barnabas took a chance on him (9:27). That is not said to convict Paul, whose case was serious: Mark had abandoned the mission. It is said because it is one of the most human things in the New Testament: to have been rescued by a kindness, to be grateful for it all your life, and to be unable to see the same situation when it turns up with somebody else’s name on it.

An honest complication. Mark was Barnabas’s cousin (Colossians 4:10). It does not make Barnabas wrong (a man may be right about somebody and partial to him at the same time), but it is part of the picture.

Tell his disciples and Peter. Paul would come round: get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). It is the pattern of the Lord Jesus with deserters. On the morning of the resurrection the message at the empty tomb, as Mark’s own Gospel records it, singled out the worst of them by name: go, tell his disciples and Peter (Mark 16:7). The Christ Paul and Barnabas preached takes runaways back into his service, and the young man at the centre of this quarrel would live to prove it.

How do I care for people I helped bring to faith? Keep in touch, as Paul wanted to: ask how they are, not only spiritually but in life. Pray for them regularly and specifically. Read the Bible with them, or put them in touch with someone who will. Help them find a church and settle there. Be honest about your own struggles, so they do not think the Christian life should be easy. And do not take it personally if they need others more than you; your aim is their growth in Christ, not their attachment to you.

On a Tuesday. Look for the person in your church whom others have quietly written off, and take a chance on them, as Barnabas did for Saul and Christ did for you.

parallels.desc: Mark the cousin of Barnabas

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Withdrawn from them. Now Paul’s case, which is stronger than usually allowed. The verb Luke chooses is not left, as at 13:13, but a heavier word (apostanta): to stand off from, to desert, the verb from which the noun apostasy comes. It suggests how Paul had come to see it since. He saw it as abandoning the work, and he needed reliable companions for dangerous journeys.

To the work. Look at how precisely he states the charge. He says Mark had not gone with them to the work, the word the Holy Spirit used when it all began: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them (13:2). Paul’s objection is not that a young man let him down personally. It is that a man walked out on a commission the Holy Spirit had named, and that the same commission is now being proposed again.

No one who looks back. Paul’s seriousness came from his Lord: No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). The Christ who welcomed sinners also spoke with great severity about the cost of following him, and had set his own face toward Jerusalem to finish his work. Paul could not treat the commission lightly, because his Master never had.

Two men looking at two things. So the two of them are not looking at the same thing at all. Barnabas is looking at a person, and asking what will become of him. Paul is looking at a commission, and asking what will become of it. Both objects are real, both men are right about the object they are looking at, and neither can see why the other will not be reasonable.

Luke declines to judge. Anyone who has sat on a church committee, or in a family, where two people of unquestioned goodwill could not be reconciled, has watched this exact thing. Scripture does not tell you which of them was right. Our instinct is that one party must be the problem, and Luke will not let us have it.

Each right about something. What we do get, later, is that each of them turned out to be right about something. Barnabas was right about Mark, as Paul himself later said (2 Timothy 4:11). And Paul was right that the second journey would need men who would not go home: within a chapter Silas is in the inner cell of a Philippian prison with his feet in the stocks.

When two good Christians disagree, must one of them be sinning? Not necessarily. Two believers can look at the same situation, both seeking God’s glory, and weigh different goods differently, as Paul and Barnabas did. There may be sin in how they disagree, in harsh words, pride or refusal to listen, and there often is. But the disagreement itself may simply reflect the limits of our wisdom. So when you are in one, examine your heart before your opponent’s, assume the other person may see something you do not, and ask God to show you what each of you is rightly guarding.

For worship. Barnabas held on to the person and Paul held on to the work, and neither could hold both. In Christ the two meet perfectly: he guards his work with a holy jealousy, and he restores deserters with a tender patience. He did not drop Peter after the denials, and he did not let the work of the gospel fail either. Only he holds the commission and the person in one hand without losing either.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sharp disagreement. Luke’s word is paroxysmos, from which we get paroxysm: irritation, provocation, a violent flaring, a fit. He does not soften it or apologise for it: Christians, even apostles, can disagree strongly.

The other place the word appears. The noun appears once more in the New Testament: let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works (Hebrews 10:24). The word behind stir up is this one. The same heat that tears two missionaries apart in Antioch is the thing Christians are commanded to provoke in each other. Passion is not the problem in either verse; what it is aimed at is.

They separated. The common comfort is that God used the quarrel to double the mission, and Luke does let us see both men going on to fruitful work. But it must not become approval. Two men who had faced mobs together never appear working side by side again in this book. Something real was lost. A reader estranged from a Christian brother is helped by seeing that the Bible records one that hurt, and does not tidy it.

Not permanent. And then the hope, which rests on evidence. Years afterwards Paul writes, Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living? (1 Corinthians 9:6): a throwaway line that puts their two names in one clause and treats Barnabas as a fellow worker in good standing. And he introduces Mark to the Colossians, warmly, as the cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10). A real break, and not a permanent one.

Barnabas took Mark. Cyprus is Barnabas’s own home (4:36), and the first leg of the very journey Mark abandoned. Barnabas takes him back over the ground where it went wrong and walks it again with him, at cost to himself. That is what restoring somebody looks like. It worked: Mark became Paul’s fellow worker (Philemon 24), and by early tradition he wrote the Gospel that bears his name.

Commended to the grace of the Lord. The church at Antioch did not treat the quarrel as disqualifying, and it sent Paul with its blessing, using the same words over him as when he first went out (14:26): it put him where it could not follow, into the keeping of God’s grace.

Sent out on grace, not on being right. Paul was not commended to his own judgment, which had just been in a furious argument, nor to his record, but to the grace the council had just said saves Jew and Gentile alike: My grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). The grace that saved us is the grace that sends us, and it is the only thing that covers what we bring with us onto the road.

The camera angle. This is Barnabas’s last appearance in Acts. Luke follows Paul from now on. That is the shape of Luke’s narrative, which is travelling toward Rome; it is not a verdict on the man. Do not mistake the camera angle for the assessment of God: a great deal of the best work in the church is done by people the story stops following.

What should I do if I have fallen out with a fellow Christian? First, own your part honestly before God, without waiting for the other person to own theirs. Then do what you can to seek peace (Romans 12:18): a humble message, an apology for what you got wrong, an offer to meet. If agreement on the issue is impossible, you may still be able to part without bitterness and speak well of each other, as Paul later spoke of Barnabas. Do not gossip about the quarrel. Pray for the other person’s blessing. And leave room for God to heal over years what cannot be healed in a week.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Mark were later reconciled.

parallels.desc: get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: "And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Syria and Cilicia. Cilicia, whose chief city was Tarsus, was Paul’s home province, where he had worked during his hidden years (Galatians 1:21), and this verse and the council’s letter (v. 23) are the only places in Acts that mention churches there.

The hidden years. Acts never records their founding. When the believers sent Saul off to Tarsus (9:30), he disappears until Barnabas fetches him (11:25): perhaps the best part of a decade. This verse is the trace: no account of the preaching, only churches on the ground. That is worth having if the most obscure stretch of your own life is the one you cannot see any fruit from. Paul’s years in Tarsus were not a holding pattern before the real ministry started.

The hidden years at Nazareth. Of Jesus between his boyhood and his baptism Luke gives one sentence: he increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:52). Yet before he had preached a sermon, the Father said: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (Luke 3:22). The unrecorded years of his servants are lived in the footsteps of a Lord whose own were precious to his Father.

Strengthening. Luke’s third use of the word in quick succession (14:22; 15:32): plainly something the church needs more of than it gets. Part of it was the council’s letter, delivered as he went (16:4). The theology of chapter 15 arrives in the churches on foot.

How the second journey begins. The journey that will plant the churches to which many New Testament letters were written begins not with a vision but with a man who has just parted from his oldest partner, walking through his home province, propping up small churches nobody has heard of.

What does it mean to strengthen a church? It means helping believers stand firmer in Christ: teaching them the truth so they are not tossed about by every new idea (Ephesians 4:14), encouraging them in trials, reminding them of the gospel of grace, correcting error gently, and building up love among them. Every member can do some of it. A word of Scripture to a struggling friend, faithful attendance that encourages others, prayer for the leaders, a meal for a family under strain, patience with a difficult member: all of these strengthen a church.

15.theology: Saved by grace alone, through faith alone. Peter’s summary, “we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will”, is the heart of what the Reformers later contended for. The men who demanded circumcision were sincere believers, but sincerity does not make a false gospel true. The law cannot save and never could; it shows our need of grace rather than offering another way. The cross of Christ is sufficient, and anything added to it as a condition takes away from it.
15.examples:
Then: A church divided over what a person must do to be saved was settled not by compromise but by clarity: Scripture (James’s use of Amos), tested alongside what God had plainly done.

Now: The same error keeps coming back in new clothes: grace plus something, whether baptism, church membership, moral effort or a particular practice, as the ground of salvation. The church’s task in every generation is to say the council’s answer clearly, defend it firmly, and live it gladly.

16.title: Into Macedonia
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. <sup>2</sup>He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. <sup>3</sup>Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. <sup>4</sup>As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily. <sup>6</sup>And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. <sup>7</sup>And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. <sup>8</sup>So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. <sup>9</sup>And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” <sup>10</sup>And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. <sup>11</sup>So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, <sup>12</sup>and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days. <sup>13</sup>And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. <sup>14</sup>One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. <sup>15</sup>And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us. <sup>16</sup>As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. <sup>17</sup>She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.” <sup>18</sup>And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour. <sup>19</sup>But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. <sup>20</sup>And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men are Jews, and they are disturbing our city. <sup>21</sup>They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.” <sup>22</sup>The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. <sup>23</sup>And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely. <sup>24</sup>Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks. <sup>25</sup>About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, <sup>26</sup>and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened. <sup>27</sup>When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. <sup>28</sup>But Paul cried with a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.” <sup>29</sup>And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. <sup>30</sup>Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” <sup>31</sup>And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” <sup>32</sup>And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. <sup>33</sup>And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds, and he was baptized at once, he and all his family. <sup>34</sup>Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God. <sup>35</sup>But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, “Let those men go.” <sup>36</sup>And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.” <sup>37</sup>But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.” <sup>38</sup>The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. <sup>39</sup>So they came and apologized to them. And they took them out and asked them to leave the city. <sup>40</sup>So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.
16.overview: Acts 16 tells how the gospel crossed into Europe. At Lystra Paul takes on Timothy, the son of a Jewish believer and a Greek father. The Spirit shuts the way into Asia and Bithynia, and at Troas a vision calls the team over to Macedonia; here Luke’s narrative changes to we, as he joins them. In Philippi, a proud Roman colony, the gospel reaches three very different people: Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened by the river; a slave girl set free from a spirit of divination; and the jailer of the prison where Paul and Silas are put after a beating without trial. At midnight they sing, God shakes the prison, and the jailer asks how to be saved: believe in the Lord Jesus. Before leaving, Paul uses his Roman citizenship to protect the young church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Timothy, the Macedonian Call, and Lydia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul takes Timothy with him and delivers the Jerusalem decisions. Then the Spirit closes two doors, a vision at Troas sends the team into Macedonia, and at Philippi Lydia, the first convert in Europe that Luke records, opens her house to the church.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit directs the mission

The Holy Spirit kept the team from preaching in Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them into Bithynia; the door to Europe opened only after those two had closed. The Spirit is not only the power behind the church’s plans but the one who sets the mission’s course. The church’s part is to obey both the open doors and the closed ones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Lydia’s household became the first church in Europe that Luke records, gathered in a businesswoman’s home around the word of God. Now: The church is still built wherever the Lord opens hearts, in homes as often as in church buildings, and through work and friendship as often as through programmes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 16 tells how the gospel crossed into Europe: a young helper gained, doors closed and one opened, and in Philippi three very different people reached, a businesswoman, a slave girl and a Roman jailer. Every kind of person, every kind of bondage, and one answer: Believe in the Lord Jesus. The risen Lord steers his own mission, opens hearts, breaks chains, and gathers into one house people the world would never have put in one room.

Back to Lystra. A crowd there tried to sacrifice oxen to Paul and, a few days later, stoned him and dragged him out for dead (14:19). He walks back into it on purpose, and what he collects there is the best thing he ever got out of any city.

A disciple was there, named Timothy. He is already a disciple, probably converted on the first journey, and he knew at first hand what Paul had suffered at Lystra (2 Timothy 3:10–11). His mother is a Jewish believer; Paul later names her and her mother, Eunice and Lois, in whom his faith dwelt first (2 Timothy 1:5), and from childhood he had been acquainted with the sacred writings (2 Timothy 3:15). He became Paul’s closest co-worker, his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2).

A Greek father. The father, a Gentile, perhaps dead by now, is never called a believer, and he had probably not allowed his son to be circumcised. So Timothy grew up in a home divided down the middle, belonging fully to neither community.

One new man in a divided house. Timothy is the shape of the church Paul is building. Jew and Greek had met in his home and stayed apart there. They met again in Christ, who came to create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace (Ephesians 2:15–16). What a marriage could not reconcile, the cross did. If you have grown up between things, a divided home, two cultures, a family where the faith came down one side only, Timothy is in Scripture partly for you. The thing that made him awkward is the thing Christ made useful.

Well spoken of. Two churches, eighteen miles or so apart, volunteered the same verdict, and a good reputation is a qualification for ministry (1 Timothy 3:7). That is still the soundest way to identify a man for ministry: not what he says about himself, but what those who have known him for years say when asked.

I am the only believer in my home. Is there hope for my children? Yes, and Timothy is one of the Bible’s answers. His father did not believe, yet a mother and grandmother quietly taught him the Scriptures, and God made him a pastor. Paul tells a believer married to an unbeliever that the children are not shut out but set in a place of blessing (1 Corinthians 7:14). Read the Bible with your children, pray with them and for them, take them to church, and live the faith gladly in front of them. You cannot convert them, but you can put the word in front of them, and God is pleased to use exactly that.

For worship. The God who shepherds the generations was at work in a divided house in Lystra, in a grandmother’s faith and a mother’s teaching, long before Paul came back down the road. He wastes nothing: not the stones of Lystra, not the awkwardness of a mixed home, not the quiet years of Bible reading at a kitchen table.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s mother was Eunice and his grandmother Lois. He became Paul’s closest co-worker.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He circumcised him. Read with chapter 15 still open, the act looks impossible. Paul has just won a public fight against men who said Gentiles must be circumcised, and is carrying the letter that settles it. The contradiction dissolves once you see two things, and the second is the one usually missed.

First, the principle. What may never be conceded as a condition may be freely chosen as a courtesy. Because Jerusalem has ruled that circumcision saves nobody, Paul is free to circumcise a man without the act meaning anything about salvation at all. Settle the doctrine and you are at liberty in the practice: Paul would never circumcise anyone to help him be saved, but he could circumcise a Jewish colleague to help him be heard.

Second, Timothy was not a Gentile. By the Jewish reckoning that later became the rule, and may already have been common, a child’s standing followed the mother. In Jewish eyes Timothy was a Jew, and an uncircumcised Jew was a standing scandal, one his own town knew about. To the synagogue he would look like an apostate.

The difference with Titus. Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation (Galatians 2:3–5). Titus was a Gentile, and the gospel was at stake. Timothy was ethnically Jewish, and circumcision removed an obstacle.

Because of the Jews. The reason is missional. Paul starts in the synagogue in every town, and an uncircumcised companion would have ended that conversation in five minutes over a distraction. He became a Jew to the Jews to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

What it cost Timothy. It was an operation on an adult: no anaesthetic, days of pain, some risk, and then a long walk. His first recorded act as a missionary is to submit to that, to get a hearing among people who had looked down on him his whole life, who had not asked it of him and would probably never know.

How do I know when to adapt for the sake of the gospel and when to refuse? Ask two questions. First, would doing this compromise the gospel or require me to sin? If someone says you must do it to be right with God, or if Scripture forbids it, refuse. Second, would it remove an unnecessary obstacle for the people I want to reach? Then you are free to do it, even at cost. So a missionary may learn a language, change his diet, dress modestly by local standards, or give up a legitimate habit. But he may not join in idolatry, hide the cross, or add conditions to grace. Freedom in practice; firmness in the gospel.

Born under the law. Timothy’s wound has a pattern older than Paul’s strategy. God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5), and on the eighth day the child was circumcised (Luke 2:21). He who owed the law nothing kept every word of it, and became a servant to the circumcised so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy (Romans 15:8–9). That is the mind Timothy is learning: the free man who makes himself a servant for the sake of others (1 Corinthians 9:19), because his Master did it first and at far greater cost.

On a Tuesday. Look for the small, unremarked cost that would remove an obstacle between somebody else and the gospel. Most such costs are never noticed by anyone but God, and that is enough.
verseByVerse.note: Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation; Timothy, with a Jewish mother, was circumcised to remove an obstacle among Jews.

parallels.desc: to the Jews I became as a Jew

verseByVerse.quote: As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The decisions. Here is what happened to the Jerusalem Council: it went into a bag and was carried around Galatia on foot, and read out in one small congregation after another. Decisions (dogmata) are the council’s decrees.

When doctrine is settled. We think of doctrine as settled when the argument is won. It was settled in Iconium when a handful of frightened Gentile believers watched Paul unfold a document from the apostles telling them they were already in. If Galatians was written to these very churches, as many think, men like those of 15:24 had already unsettled them (Galatians 1:6–7), and the letter is carried to the places that most needed it.

Strengthened, then increased. One of Luke’s progress notes (6:7; 9:31), and the order is an argument: strengthened first, then grown, and the so ties both to the decrees. A church that does not know where it stands cannot grow, because its members are too busy checking their own footing to look outward.

Through the grace of the Lord Jesus. What did the letter tell those frightened Gentiles? That nothing could be added to Christ (15:11). Jesus had not done most of their salvation and left the knife to finish it; he had done all of it. And the growth has the same author: the Lord added to their number day by day (2:47). Christ guarded the truth about himself, and then he filled the churches that held it.

Is doctrine the enemy of evangelism? So if you have wondered whether doctrinal precision is the enemy of evangelistic warmth, whether time spent getting the gospel exactly right is time stolen from telling people about it, here is Luke’s answer in one sentence, and he puts the causal word in the middle of it. Churches that know clearly that they are saved by grace alone are freed to love, to welcome and to witness. Churches that are vague about it either harden into legalism or drift into having nothing to say. Good doctrine is not the opposite of warm evangelism; it is its fuel.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forbidden by the Holy Spirit. Two closed doors in two verses, both shut by God. Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, populous and full of great cities, with Ephesus its capital. These men are doing what they were commissioned to do, and there is no suggestion of sin or rebuke. Two good men with a right aim are stopped.

We are not told how. It may have been a prophecy, an inner conviction, circumstances; every theory is a guess. Luke’s silence stops us turning the episode into a method and grading each other on our ability to detect the same signal.

The Spirit of Jesus. Bithynia was a rich province in the north, on the Black Sea. Then the phrase, which is unusual enough to have been noticed for centuries. Luke has called him the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Lord, and simply the Spirit; this is the only place in Acts where he is called the Spirit of Jesus. (The KJV reads simply the Spirit, following later manuscripts; the earliest read the Spirit of Jesus, as most modern Bibles do.) The phrase shows that the Spirit is the Spirit of the risen Jesus, sent by him and acting for him. Paul will use close relatives of it: the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9), the Spirit of his Son (Galatians 4:6), the Spirit of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:19). And it appears exactly where the direction of the mission is being taken out of the missionaries’ hands. The one who is steering is the same Jesus who said you will be my witnesses to the end of the earth, and he is doing the steering personally. The men on the road are not executing a strategy they devised and asking God to bless it. They are being moved.

Closed doors. They did not sit and wait; they kept moving, and the Spirit closed doors. God guides moving feet, and a good plan that has failed is not evidence that God has stopped paying attention.

They did not know at the time. We read these refusals already knowing about the vision at Troas. Standing on that road, they had two refusals and no explanation. They found out later. Almost everybody finds out later, and a good many never find out at all.

Was the ban on preaching in Asia permanent? No. It was for that time and that journey; within a few years Paul spent more than two years in Ephesus, in Asia, and all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord (19:10). God was ordering the mission, not shutting a door for good. Not that God did not care for Asia; it was not yet the time.

Not every closed door has a Macedonia behind it. Some closed doors are simply closed, and Scripture does not promise you the explanation. What it shows is that the Lord of the mission can steer by refusal.

How can I tell whether a closed door is God’s guidance or an obstacle I should push through? Often you cannot tell at once, and that is all right. Some obstacles are meant to be overcome by perseverance, as Paul kept preaching through opposition; others are God’s no. Pray, look honestly at your motives, ask counsel of mature believers, and check that you are not running from duty or toward mere comfort. If the way stays shut after reasonable effort, accept it without bitterness and look for the open path. God holds both the doors and you, and he is not offended by sincere mistakes made in obedience.

For worship. The risen Jesus is not an absent founder. He steers his church by his Spirit, closing what he will close and opening what he will open. His refusals are as loving as his permissions: the Lord who stopped Paul at the border of Bithynia was already preparing a riverbank in Macedonia and a woman’s heart to hear.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its chief city. Mysia and Bithynia lay in the north-west.

parallels.desc: all the residents of Asia heard the word

verseByVerse.quote: "So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Down to Troas. A few words cover a long, dispiriting walk, through country Luke does not say they preached in, until they run out of land. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy, and three men with no commission for anywhere they can reach on foot are standing on a beach.

The Lord who walked the road of defeat. The one steering them was not guessing. Luke has just called the Spirit who stopped them the Spirit of Jesus, and Jesus knows from the inside what it is to walk a road that looks like the end. He set his face to Jerusalem, and to every eye at the time the journey finished in failure: friends scattered, the Teacher dead, two disciples walking home saying, we had hoped (Luke 24:21). Yet Peter would preach that he was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (2:23). The greatest dead end in history was the hinge of the world’s salvation. A Lord who turned a cross into a crown can certainly turn a beach at Troas into a door, and the missionaries on that shore were being led by one who had already walked further into the dark than they ever would.

What Troas actually was. They could not see it, but Troas was the crossing point between two continents, the place from which any ship for Macedonia would sail. Every refusal had been moving them toward the one town from which Europe was two days away. And Troas is where Luke appears to join them: soon the narrative changes from they to we, and the man who wrote more than a quarter of the New Testament walks into the story at the town they reached because everywhere else was forbidden. The two refusals put an apostle and a historian in the same room, and neither of them chose it.

What should I do when I have reached the end of my road and can see nothing ahead? Do what Paul did: keep doing the next faithful thing where you are, and wait for God to show the next step. Troas was not wasted time; it was where Luke joined and the call came. Keep up the ordinary means of grace: prayer, Scripture, the company of believers. Be honest with God about your confusion, as the psalmists were. Do not force a door just to end the uncertainty. And remember that the God who brought you to the shoreline knows exactly where the boat is.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy.

verseByVerse.quote: And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Help us. After two refusals, a vision in the night, and it is a request: not an order, not a rebuke. A man asks for help. Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece, and this is the first entry of the gospel into Europe that Luke records.

Concluding. Concluding (symbibazontes) means putting things together, reasoning to a conclusion, working it out. Even after a night vision of a man pleading with him, Paul did not simply know what to do. The vision had to be interpreted, and the team did it together (note the plural), and what they arrived at was a judgment, not a certainty handed down. The man in the dream had not said preach the gospel. He had said help us. Working out that the help meant the gospel was the missionaries’ own conclusion. The closed doors, the vision and the team’s discernment together showed God’s will. Even this, one of the most dramatic pieces of guidance in the New Testament, required sanctified reasoning in the morning. If Paul had to conclude, you are not failing when you have to conclude.

In the flow. Here Acts changes direction: the word crosses from Asia into Europe (1:8), not because Paul planned it but because the Lord shut two doors and opened a third. Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens and Corinth (16:11–18:17) all flow from this night at Troas.

Immediately. Having reasoned it out, they moved the same day. Deliberation and instant obedience are not enemies; here they are consecutive.

We. The first of the we passages (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), where Luke joins the story as an eyewitness, perhaps as Paul’s doctor (Colossians 4:14), and says so by changing a pronoun and nothing else.

Does the Spirit still guide like this, through visions and direct prohibitions? This was part of the founding of the church, when God gave the apostles direct revelation. Today, with Scripture complete, God guides his people through his word, prayer, wise counsel, the needs before us and the doors he opens and closes in his providence. He may still use circumstances to close a way, as here; but we do not wait for visions to know what to do. Many faithful Christians, especially in Pentecostal and charismatic churches, believe God still gives such dreams, and some missionaries report them; they too insist that any impression must be tested by Scripture. This commentary holds the more cautious view because the New Testament ties such revelation to the apostles’ founding work (Ephesians 2:20), while gladly owning those who differ as brothers and sisters.

A pronoun. From here on, large stretches of Acts are the report of somebody who was in the boat, and his unshowy way of reporting himself (he never names himself in either of his books) is part of why he is believed. He stayed with Paul to the last cold months in Rome: Luke alone is with me (2 Timothy 4:11). And in his own account he is a pronoun, a gentle rebuke to the way most of us tell the story of what God has done with us.

The help was Christ. Who answered that cry? Paul crossed the sea, but Paul knew whose help he carried. He would later say he dared speak only of what Christ had accomplished through him to bring the Gentiles to obedience (Romans 15:18). And before Agrippa he would say that the risen Christ himself would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles (26:23). The man in the vision asked for help, and what came to Philippi was the Helper of the helpless, the Lord Jesus, speaking through the mouths of his servants and opening hearts by his Spirit. Luke began his history with all that Jesus began to do and teach (1:1). Here is the continuation: the ascended Lord, crossing into Europe in the persons of four men in a boat.

Who is crying out for help today? Everyone who does not know Christ, whether or not they put it that way. The cry rarely sounds like a request for the gospel. It sounds like loneliness, anxiety, addiction, a marriage falling apart, a question about death at a funeral, a teenager’s despair, a refugee’s need for a friend. The man in the vision asked for help; the missionaries understood that the deepest help was the gospel. Meet real needs with real kindness, and do not stop there: the greatest help you can give anyone is Christ.

For worship. Long before a man of Macedonia stood in Paul’s dream, a whole lost world stood before the Father with no voice to plead for itself. And the Son came over, from heaven to earth: he took hold not of angels but of the offspring of Abraham, and was made like his brothers in every respect (Hebrews 2:16–17). Every crossing of the gospel since is an echo of his.
verseByVerse.note: Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece — the gospel’s first step into Europe. Here “we” appears: Luke, the author, joins the journey.

parallels.desc: further “we” passages

verseByVerse.quote: "So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A direct voyage. Straight across, probably with a following wind, two days; the same crossing the other way later takes five (20:6), the kind of detail that fits a writer who was there. Neapolis was Philippi’s port.

A Roman colony. Philippi was named after Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great. A colony was a piece of Rome transplanted: settled with discharged legionaries, governed under Roman law, its citizens holding Roman citizenship, and immensely proud of it. It was, in its own estimation, Italy in Macedonia.

Why Luke mentions it. The gospel’s first European address is the proudest, most Roman town in the province, entered through a women’s prayer meeting outside the gate. The story turns on that standing twice: in the charge, customs that are not lawful for us as Romans (v. 21), and when it costs the magistrates their dignity in the street (v. 39).

Citizens of heaven. A Philippian lived in Macedonia but belonged to Rome, kept Rome’s laws and took his identity from a city he might never have seen. So when Paul later told this church that our citizenship is in heaven, they understood: they were a colony of heaven on earth.

Every knee in the colony. From heaven, Paul later told them, we await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ (Philippians 3:20–21), and in a town that hailed Caesar as lord and saviour, those were not neutral words. He set before them the one who emptied himself and became obedient to the point of death on a cross, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Philippians 2:7–11). The colony that boasted of Rome was about to receive a church that boasted of Christ, the Lord before whom the emperor himself would one day kneel.

Some days. There is no synagogue to preach in, and for several days the mission to Europe consists of a few men walking round a strange town waiting for the Sabbath.

What does it mean in practice to be a citizen of heaven? It means your deepest loyalty, identity and hope belong to Christ’s kingdom, while you live as a good resident where God has placed you. You obey the laws of the land unless they command sin, work honestly, seek the good of your town (Jeremiah 29:7), and pray for those in authority. But you do not take your values from the surrounding culture, you are not crushed when it rejects you, and you do not set your hope on its success. Like a Philippian veteran, you live by the customs of home, and you wait for your King to come from there (Philippians 3:20).
verseByVerse.note: Neapolis was Philippi’s port. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with army veterans, governed like a little Rome.

parallels.desc: our citizenship is in heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Outside the gate. Every clause is a step down. Foreign cults were often kept beyond the walls of a Roman colony. Where we supposed: they were guessing where a handful of Jews might gather. The riverside was probably the River Gangites, west of the city. By the rule in later Jewish writings it took ten Jewish men to form a synagogue, and the leading city of the district apparently could not produce ten.

We sat down. So Christianity arrived in Europe: not in the forum, but by a few travellers who walked out of a side gate on a Saturday morning, found women praying by a river, sat down on the bank, and started talking. Paul, trained as a Pharisee, sat down and taught women, the ordinary posture of a Jewish teacher, where at Pisidian Antioch he had stood like a public speaker (13:16).

The Teacher who sat by a well. Paul learned that posture from his Lord, who wearied from his journey sat beside a well in Samaria and spoke of eternal life to a woman nobody else would have stopped for (John 4:6–7). When his gospel reached Europe it came, as he had so often come, to the people the world overlooked, sitting down beside them.

The women at the river. Out of that conversation came the church at Philippi, which alone supported Paul when no other church did (Philippians 4:15–16), and which he called his joy and crown. Perhaps the warmest letter Paul ever wrote went to the people who started as the women at the river.

Does Paul’s practice here mean women may preach in church? Paul taught the gospel to these women, which shows how highly the gospel values women as hearers, disciples and partners in the work; women like Lydia, Euodia and Syntyche laboured beside him (Philippians 4:2–3). That is a different question from who should preach and exercise authority in the gathered church, which Paul addresses elsewhere, reserving the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the congregation to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). Both truths stand: women are equal heirs of grace and indispensable in gospel work, and the church’s pastoral oversight is entrusted to men who serve with self-giving love. Many faithful Christians read those passages differently and welcome women as pastors; this commentary holds the view above because Paul grounds it not in local custom but in the order of creation (1 Timothy 2:13), while honouring brothers and sisters who disagree.

On a Tuesday. The apostles did not decide that a handful of women was too small a return on a sea crossing. If your own service feels absurdly small for the effort it took, this verse is the shape of most of what God actually does. Go to your small meeting this week as though it mattered, because it does.

For worship. Those women by the river were praying to the God of Israel without yet knowing the name of his Son, and the Son had already sent his answer across the sea. He hears prayers that have not yet learned his name.
verseByVerse.note: There was apparently no synagogue; Jews met to pray in the open, by the river.

verseByVerse.quote: One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay." And she prevailed upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lydia. Luke tells us four things about the first person in Europe whose conversion he records. She is a woman, in a world where her name would not normally appear in a history. She is from Thyatira, in Asia, the province the Spirit had just forbidden them to preach in: they were stopped from going to her country, and she had already come to theirs. She is a seller of purple goods, the luxury trade that clothed magistrates and emperors, and so a person of means, with a house big enough for a household and, shortly, for a church (v. 40). And she is a worshiper of God: a Gentile who had attached herself to the God of Israel without becoming a Jew. No strategist would have picked her: the vision showed a man of Macedonia, and the first person helped is a foreign businesswoman.
