The Lord opened her heart. Paul spoke; the Lord opened. Paul could reach her ears; only the Lord could open her heart (2 Corinthians 4:6). Lydia did pay attention, really, freely; but she did so because the Lord opened her heart. And she was already religious: a worshipper of God, at a prayer meeting, on the Sabbath. Religion can bring a person to the riverbank; only Christ can bring her to life, which is good news for the devout and the careless alike.

Effectual calling. Here is one of Scripture’s clearest pictures of what Reformed Christians call effectual calling: God’s call that does not only invite but brings the hearer to faith. Lydia believed because God first opened her heart, grace the cause, faith the fruit (compare 13:48). Other Christians hold that grace enables every hearer but can be refused. For the believer it is pure comfort and humility: if you believe, it is because God opened your heart, so no boasting, all thanks.

The risen Lord who opens. The verb is a deliberate echo. At Emmaus the risen Jesus opened the eyes of the two, and they said their hearts burned while he opened to them the Scriptures (Luke 24:31–32); then he opened their minds, that repentance and forgiveness should be proclaimed in his name to all nations (Luke 24:45–47). By a river in Macedonia the same Lord does to a Gentile woman what he did in the upper room: his own commission fulfilled, one opened heart at a time.

Her household. In the first century a household was far larger than our nuclear family: servants and slaves, employees, dependants, sometimes extended kin. Lydia seems to head her own house (no husband is mentioned), so her household likely means her servants and dependants, perhaps children, though Luke gives no roster.

And did they all believe, or were they simply baptised? Honestly, the text does not say: Luke records that Lydia believed (the Lord opened her heart) and that her household was baptised, but nothing explicit about the household’s faith. That silence is why this is one of the household baptism texts in the friendly baptism disagreement. Believer’s-baptist readers fill the gap from the other households Luke describes (the jailer’s, where the word was spoken to all in the house, v. 32; Crispus’s, which believed, 18:8), concluding Lydia’s household believed and were baptised as believers, Luke compressing. Paedobaptist readers (who baptise the infants of believers) note that only Lydia’s faith is mentioned, yet the whole household is baptised on the head’s faith, the old covenant pattern (Genesis 17), including dependants and any little ones. Scripture leaves the gap; each side fills it from its view of the sign. The first is the more likely, since in the other households Luke describes, hearing and faith are explicit (v. 32; 10:44; 18:8). What is beyond dispute, and a comfort, is that God loves to save not lone individuals but whole households: the conversion of one is so often the open door of grace to a home (compare v. 31). Pray, then, for your whole household.

Where Christians differ: household baptisms. Paedobaptists see household baptisms as including infants, and so supporting infant baptism. This commentary’s view: no infants are mentioned in any household baptism in Acts. In the jailer’s case, the word was spoken to all who were in his house (v. 32), and the whole household rejoiced with him that he had believed (v. 34): people old enough to hear the word and to share the joy. In Cornelius’s, all heard and received the Spirit (10:44). The households baptised were households who heard and believed. Credobaptists hold this charitably, respecting brothers and sisters who read it differently.

Honouring our paedobaptist brothers. Many of the most godly and learned Christians in history, Calvin among them, have baptised the infants of believers out of a sincere conviction that God’s covenant embraces the children of his people, as in Abraham’s day. They do not think baptism saves the child. We differ on who should receive the sign, but share the same gospel, the same Saviour, and the same hope for our children.

Come to my house. The first recorded act of any Christian in Europe. She puts her new standing on the table and dares them to say that her conversion was real and then decline to eat with her. Within hours she has understood that being received by Christ means being received by his people.

And she prevailed upon us. The word means she pressed until they gave way, which suggests they hesitated: Paul was careful about being kept at anybody’s expense (compare Philippians 4:15). It is one of the very few places in Acts where somebody argues Paul down and wins, and it is a convert of a few hours. Anyone who thinks they have no ministry because they cannot teach or lead should notice that Lydia’s contribution to the New Testament is a room: the church at Philippi first gathered in her house.

If God must open the heart, is there any point in my praying and speaking? Every point. Lydia’s heart was opened while Paul was speaking, not instead of his speaking. God uses the very means he commands: the word spoken, and prayer for those who hear. So pray before you talk to someone about Christ, asking the Lord to open their heart. Then speak as clearly and kindly as you can. If they do not respond, you have not failed, and they are not beyond hope. You did your part; leave the opening to the only one who can do it, and keep praying.

On a Tuesday. With Lydia the house followed the heart. Whom could you invite to your table this week for the sake of Christ: a missionary, a new Christian, a lonely member of your church, a neighbour who has never been in a Christian home?
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira, in Asia, was famous for its purple dye; purple cloth was a luxury. A “worshiper of God” was a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–40 — Prison and Earthquake in Philippi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Freeing a slave girl from a spirit of divination costs her owners their income and Paul and Silas a beating and a night in the stocks. At midnight they sing, an earthquake opens the prison, and the jailer believes with his household. In the morning Paul turns the magistrates’ quiet release into a public apology, encourages the believers at Lydia’s house, and leaves.
verseByVerse.theology:
Praise at midnight

Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight, after being stripped and beaten with rods, and the other prisoners listen. Their praise is not in spite of the suffering but in the middle of it, and it comes from Christ, not from their circumstances, which had not changed. Paul later wrote that we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance (Romans 5:3). Not every believer can sing on such a night, and Scripture also gives words for lament, but the songs in that cell were a witness the prisoners heard.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The jailer asked what he must do to be saved, the question of Pentecost (2:37) asked again in a Philippian prison, and the answer had no doing in it: believe in the Lord Jesus. Now: The answer is still the same: not circumcision, not ritual, not moral achievement, but trust in the Lord Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and us, crying out, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. Lydia was a respectable, devout woman whose heart the Lord opened quietly; this girl is a slave in the grip of a demon, freed by a word of command, and a Roman jailer will follow: every kind of person and every kind of bondage. Freeing the girl is also what lands Paul and Silas in prison (vv. 19–24).

A slave girl. Luke gives her no name and three kinds of ownership: she is a slave, she is possessed, and she is an income. Few people in Acts are more thoroughly owned.

The python spirit. The Greek is pneuma pythōna: literally a Python spirit, as the ESV notes. The Python was the serpent that guarded Delphi before Apollo killed it; Delphi’s priestess, the Pythia, then spoke Apollo’s oracles, the most prestigious in the ancient world, and by Paul’s day a python meant a soothsayer thought to be inspired by him. A slave girl believed to have such a spirit was a commercial oracle of the highest value. In truth she was possessed by a demon.

Servants of the Most High God. Her testimony is formally true, but its source is demonic, as demons spoke true words about Jesus (Mark 1:24; 5:7): accurate content, corrupt source. An oracle endorsing Paul would tie the gospel to the very system it was displacing.

How the crowd heard it. To a Greek ear the Most High God was a title people used of Zeus, and the Greek has no article: a way of salvation, exactly what every cult in a Roman town claimed to offer. Heard by the crowd, she was endorsing two more travelling holy men with one more route to blessedness for sale. Every word could be agreed to by a pagan without changing a thing he believed.

Neutralised by agreement. That is the commonest way the gospel is neutralised now: not by contradiction but by warm agreement on slightly different terms. Christ is affirmed as one of the great spiritual teachers. Nothing is denied and nothing is left.

No other name. Paul is doing what his Lord did. A demoniac cried out, Jesus, Son of the Most High God (Luke 8:28), and Jesus rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ (Luke 4:41). Nor is he a way of salvation among many: there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (4:12). Christ will be known as he is, or not at all.

Is it wrong to consult horoscopes, tarot or mediums just for fun? Yes. Scripture forbids every attempt to gain hidden knowledge or guidance from sources other than God (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), not because they are always effective, but because they are a turning away from him to rival powers, and some of those powers are real and dark. Treating them as harmless fun trains the heart to look elsewhere for direction and may open doors that should stay shut. A Christian has something far better: a Father who knows the future and holds it, a Saviour who guides, and a word that is a lamp to his feet.

For worship. The powers of darkness can borrow true words, but they cannot borrow him. Delphi’s oracle sold the future by the hour. The Lord Jesus holds the future and gives it freely, and the girl who had been made to speak for darkness was about to be set free by the Light.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the Greek reads “a spirit, a python” — linked to the oracle at Delphi, where Apollo was said to have slain a serpent called Python.

parallels.desc: no one who practises divination

verseByVerse.quote: "And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many days. Paul did not act at once. Day after day this girl trailed the missionaries through the streets shouting after them, and day after day he let it run.

Paul, having become greatly annoyed. Greatly annoyed (diaponētheis) means troubled, worn out, exasperated: perhaps at the confusion she caused, perhaps in distress for the girl herself. This is not a serene apostle exercising cool authority at a chosen moment. It is a tired man who has finally had enough, and God used it, and Luke recorded it without tidying it. We imagine God only works through us when our composure is intact; here the best-known exorcism in Acts is done by a man at the end of his temper.

In the name of Jesus Christ. Paul speaks to the spirit, not the girl, and by Christ’s authority. He does not bargain with it or require anything of the girl. He names a name, and the thing that had held her for years leaves within the hour. When the seventy-two reported that even the demons were subject to them in his name, Jesus said he had seen Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:17–18). The name Paul speaks is the name of the stronger man who overpowers the strong man and carries off the people he held (Luke 11:21–22). The New Testament is never uncertain about the outcome of that collision.

That very hour. What became of her? She is not said to have believed. So far as the text goes, she is still a slave the next morning, now one who has stopped earning, owned by furious men. Perhaps she joined the church at Lydia’s; we do not hear. She was the one person in the story who was not consulted about anything, and her ending is withheld.

Resist closing the story. A reader who has watched a real deliverance leave someone with a harder life afterwards, the addiction broken and the debts still there, needs to know that Scripture is not embarrassed by that. The spirit came out; everything else about her was still difficult. So if you have helped someone out of a bondage, do not walk away when the dramatic part is over.

Exorcism today. Demons are real, personal and evil, the name of Jesus has all authority over them, and the Christian’s ordinary weapons are the gospel, prayer and the armour of God. The Reformed position is cautious, for scriptural reasons. (1) The dramatic commanding of demons clusters in the era of Christ’s ministry and the apostolic founding. (2) The Epistles, which teach the church to fight the devil, never establish an office of exorcist or give a ritual of deliverance; they give ordinary weapons: resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7); put on the whole armour of God (Ephesians 6:10–18). (3) A true believer, indwelt by the Spirit, cannot be possessed: he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4); harassed from without, but not inhabited. (4) Blaming sins on demons evades repentance, when Scripture lays sin at our own heart (James 1:14; Mark 7:21–23). So deliverance comes through the gospel (Colossians 1:13), prayer, and Christ’s authority humbly invoked when needed: never a technique, a specialist, or a spectacle.

Other views, answered kindly. Some churches keep a formal rite of exorcism, and much of the charismatic world practises deliverance ministry, often for Christians; we honour the seriousness and the zeal to help, but find no such office in Scripture and hold that a believer cannot be possessed. Others reduce possession to ancient mental illness; Scripture distinguishes the sick from the demonised (Mark 1:32–34). The two ditches: do not deny the demonic, and do not see a demon behind every sin and sickness.

For you, then. You need not fear demons, nor go hunting for a deliverance minister. If you are in Christ, the strongest Being in the universe lives in you, and at the cross Christ has already disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15). Fight your sins as your own, by the Spirit, resting in your Lord’s finished victory. Where missionaries meet overt occult darkness, the remedy is the same: the gospel and the name of Christ, humbly.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, 'These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their hope of gain was gone. There is the motive, stated before any charge is laid. Gone (exēlthen) is the verb of v. 18 when the spirit came out: their hope of gain went out of her when the spirit did.

Funded, not argued. This is the shape of a great deal of opposition to Christianity. It is not usually argued; it is funded. When the gospel changes what people do with their money, their bodies or their time, somebody’s revenue falls, and the objection will be dressed in principle and never mention the accounts. At Ephesus the silversmith says, before he mentions the goddess, that from this business we have our wealth (19:25–27).

They seized Paul and Silas. The leaders, and both Jews. Timothy, whose father was Greek, and Luke, almost certainly a Gentile, are left alone, and Luke’s we drops out of the narrative until Paul comes back through Philippi years later.

These men are Jews. Not a word about the girl or the money. The ethnic charge was an appeal to live prejudice: Claudius had recently expelled the Jews from Rome (18:2), and a town full of veterans was in the mood to hear it. The men who had been living off a possessed child reached for the nearest prejudice to hand.

Disturbing our city. And the civic charge will be used against Christians for centuries: not that the message is false, but that things were quieter before. It never has to prove anything, and the gospel really does disturb a city where a girl can be owned and worked.

Treated as their Master was. When Jesus freed the man at Gerasa and the pigs were lost, the people asked him to depart from them (Luke 8:37): a man restored was worth less to them than a herd. At his trial the charge was that he was misleading the nation and stirring up the people (Luke 23:2, 5). If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). The men dragged into the market are walking in their Lord’s footprints, and the trouble they cause is the trouble he caused, by setting a captive free.

Should Christians challenge industries that profit from evil? Yes, wisely and lawfully. The gospel sets people free, and freedom often costs someone their profit: traffickers, pornographers, exploitative lenders, gambling and drug trades. Christians should refuse to profit from such things themselves, help their victims, speak for them, and support just laws. Expect resistance, often disguised as concern for jobs, tradition or freedom. But remember Paul’s order: he did not set out to reform Philippi’s economy; he preached Christ and set one girl free. The deepest change in any city begins with the gospel changing people.

For worship. Her owners counted her in coins, and when the coins stopped they had no further use for her. The Lord Jesus counts his people in blood: redeemed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). Men sell what they own; he bought what he loves, and nothing he has paid for will ever be put up for sale again.

parallels.desc: profits threatened again at Ephesus

verseByVerse.quote: "'They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For us as Romans. In Philippi it was the one sentence guaranteed to land. Rome generally tolerated Judaism as an ancient national religion. What it did not tolerate was a foreign cult recruiting Roman citizens out of their own religion. You could be a Jew; you could not make a Roman into one. Tell veterans in their own square that two foreigners are undermining Roman custom and you will not need evidence. And nobody could see the irony: the two men in the dock are Roman citizens themselves.

The charge was, in its way, accurate. Christianity did advocate customs a Roman could not simply add to his existing life, because of who Jesus is. Pilate had heard the same fear: everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar (John 19:12). Jesus did not deny being a king; his kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). A man who confessed Jesus is Lord in a colony where the loyal formula was Caesar is lord had changed allegiance, and everything from his household gods to his guild dinners would feel it. The gospel is welcome as long as it is one more thing a person has. It becomes intolerable when it starts reorganising what he already had.

Does following Christ make me a bad citizen? No; it makes you a better one, but never a worshipper of the state. Christians are to pray for rulers, pay taxes, obey the law and seek the good of their nation (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2). But when any authority demands what belongs to God alone, worship, ultimate loyalty, or disobedience to his commands, we must obey God rather than men (5:29), respectfully and without violence. Many of the best citizens in history have been Christians precisely because their conscience was bound to a higher King.

On a Tuesday. Christ has claimed the whole of you, and his Spirit is at work reorganising what you already had: ask which arrangement in your life you have not yet let him touch.

verseByVerse.quote: "The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd joined in attacking them. Mob justice, and fast. Nobody calls a witness; the prisoners are not asked to answer. Between the accusation and the flogging there is nothing at all.

Beaten with rods. The clothes are ripped away in the market square. Then the rods, wielded by the lictors, the magistrates’ officers who carried bundles of rods as the sign of their power to punish. A Roman flogging with rods opened the back, and men died of it.

Many blows. Paul refers to this day twice: three times I was beaten with rods (2 Corinthians 11:25); and though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict (1 Thessalonians 2:2). He walked from this to Thessalonica and preached there with the marks still on him.

Shamefully treated. The word is not injured but outraged: the public stripping of two men who had done nothing, by officials who never asked them a question. The text treats it as injustice: Paul will protest that they were beaten publicly and uncondemned (v. 37). God used this night magnificently, but the earthquake does not make the flogging right.

Granted to suffer for his sake. Jesus too was stripped in public and scourged on the order of an official who had found no guilt in him (Luke 23:14–16; John 19:1). Paul regarded this day as fellowship with Christ. Years later he told this very church that it had been granted to them for the sake of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for his sake, engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had (Philippians 1:29–30); some of them may have watched these rods fall. The stripes on Paul’s back were the marks of belonging to a crucified Lord.

Into prison. No charge recorded, no sentence, no term: two bleeding men put away with an instruction about security and nothing else.

If God brings good out of injustice, does that make the injustice less wrong? No. God’s sovereignty over evil never turns evil into good. Joseph’s brothers meant it for evil, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20): both are true, and the brothers were still guilty. So when you have been wronged, you may grieve it, name it, and seek lawful justice, while trusting that God will not waste it. Do not let anyone hurry you past the wrong in the name of his providence. Scripture never does.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for Christians who are beaten, imprisoned or shamed for their faith: find one specific name or country, and pray for them as you would want to be prayed for in the inner prison.
verseByVerse.note: Beating with rods was done by the magistrates’ officers, the lictors.

parallels.desc: three times I was beaten with rods
shamefully treated at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: "Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He put them into the inner prison. Told to keep them safely, the jailer slightly exceeds his orders: the innermost cell, and the stocks as well. The inner prison is the windowless interior room: no light, no air moving, the floor filthy.

The stocks. A heavy timber with a row of holes, in which the legs could be fixed, sometimes forced wide apart: hours in it produced cramp that became agony, with no way to lie down or reach your own torn back. Luke builds the picture deliberately, backs untreated, legs clamped, the dark, no charge, to make what these two men did next almost unbelievable.

I was in prison. There is someone else in that cell. On the Damascus road the risen Lord had asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (9:4): what was done to his people he counted as done to himself. So the jailer who clamped those feet was, without knowing it, doing it to the Lord. I was in prison and you came to me (Matthew 25:36): before morning this same jailer will wash the wounds he left untended, and so become the first in Philippi to visit Christ in prison.

What if I am in my own inner prison right now? Then you are in a place God knows well. Joseph was in the pit and the prison; Jeremiah in the cistern; Paul and Silas in the stocks; and the Lord Jesus in the darkness of Gethsemane and the cross. Your inner prison may be illness, depression, grief, a trapped situation at home or work. Do not pretend it is not dark. Tell God plainly how it is, as the psalmists did. Ask a friend to come and sit with you. And hold on to this: no cell is so deep that Christ is not there, and none is so locked that he cannot open it in his time.
verseByVerse.note: Stocks were wooden blocks that clamped the feet.

verseByVerse.quote: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praying and singing hymns. Joy in suffering, as when the apostles left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (5:41). Both verbs are continuous: not one defiant snatch of a psalm, but long enough to be noticed down the corridor. What they sang was probably the psalms: men in the dark asking how long, and then turning to praise before anything has changed. They had a hymnbook written for nights like this one.

The prisoners were listening. The tense suggests they went on listening. Consider what those men were used to hearing at midnight in that room, and then consider hearing this.

A guard. This verse is regularly used as a stick. It is not a command to feel like singing, nor a measurement you have failed. Paul himself writes elsewhere that he was so utterly burdened beyond his strength that he despaired of life itself (2 Corinthians 1:8), which is the same apostle describing the opposite experience without any embarrassment. Scripture gives you Philippi at midnight and it also gives you Gethsemane, and the psalm that ends with darkness as the only companion (Psalm 88:18). If tonight you can only manage the praying half of verse 25, you are still inside the verse.

Where the joy was anchored. Nothing in their circumstances had improved, and they did not know the earthquake was coming. So the gladness came from somewhere the magistrates could not reach.

The Lord who sang on the way to Gethsemane. That somewhere was a Person: Rejoice in the Lord always, Paul later wrote to this church from another prison (Philippians 4:4). On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:26), probably the closing Passover psalms (Psalms 113–118). He sang on the way to his arrest, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). Paul and Silas were following a Lord who had sung first and gone further into the dark than they would ever go.

A great earthquake. God answered, as he had once shaken the room where the church prayed (4:31), and the surprise is in the last clause: every door, and every chain on every prisoner. God’s reply to the two who prayed was wider than the two who prayed (Luke 4:18).

Does God always deliver his people from prison like this? No. Sometimes he does, as here and with Peter (12:6–11). Sometimes he does not: James was killed (12:2), Paul spent years in custody and, as the early church remembered, was eventually executed, and many believers today remain in prison for Christ. The earthquake at Philippi shows that God can deliver; it does not promise that he always will in this life. What he always does is stand by his people (2 Timothy 4:17), give them grace to endure, and bring them through death itself into his presence. Final deliverance is certain even when earthly release is not.

On a Tuesday. Learn one psalm of lament and trust by heart this week, Psalm 42, 46 or 130, so that you have something to sing, or at least to pray, when the night comes. Others notice how you handle trouble.

parallels.desc: at night his song is with me

verseByVerse.quote: When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He drew his sword. He reaches for his own sword before he reaches for a light. It looks like panic, and it was arithmetic: a guard who lost his prisoners could face their penalty himself (compare 12:19), and falling on his own sword was the respectable Roman way out. For a Roman of his kind, honour was worth more than life, and that is what an idol looks like: something so precious that losing it feels like a reason to die. The gospel was about to give him a worth no magistrate could take away.

Do not harm yourself. Both halves are astonishing. First, Paul knew: from the innermost room he grasped what was happening in the doorway and shouted before the sword went in, paying attention to somebody else at the one moment nobody would have blamed him for thinking about himself.

We are all here. Second, and far harder. Every door was open, every chain off, and they had every legal grievance a man could have. Nobody moved: not Paul, not Silas, and not one of the other prisoners, men with no faith at all and every reason to run. Luke does not explain it, and it is the quietest miracle in the chapter. The first thing Christianity did for the jailer was stop him killing himself.

He saved others. At the cross the rulers scoffed, He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God (Luke 23:35). He could have come down. He stayed, and because he stayed, those who mocked him could be forgiven. Paul’s refusal to walk out of an open prison is a small, true likeness: the man who could have saved himself stayed, and so the man who had chained him lived. Christ would not save himself, and therefore he saves us.

What should I do if I, or someone I love, is thinking of suicide? Treat it as urgent, as Paul did: speak up at once, and do not leave the person alone. Tell them plainly that their life matters to God and to you. Get help immediately: call emergency services or a crisis line, involve a doctor, tell a trusted pastor or friend. If it is you, tell someone today. Despair lies; it says there is no way out, but the jailer’s worst night became the night of his salvation. Christ came to give life, and there is no shame, sin or loss so great that he cannot meet you in it.

For worship. A bleeding prisoner shouting through the dark to spare the man who had clamped his feet: that love was learned from the Lord who prayed from the cross, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34; some early manuscripts of Luke lack the prayer, but many scholars judge it genuine, and Stephen’s prayer echoes it, 7:60). The sword never fell in Philippi because grace reached the jailer first, and the sword of God’s justice never falls on Christ’s people because it fell on him.
verseByVerse.note: A guard who let prisoners escape could face their penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trembling with fear. A few hours ago this man locked two prisoners in the dark; now he is on the floor in front of them. He did not tremble at death a moment earlier. Sinners who sense the nearness of the holy God have always shaken (Isaiah 6:5), and the wonder of this night is that the God who shook the prison sends the jailer a word of mercy.

Then he brought them out and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? There is no greater question anyone can ask, and it is worth asking honestly what he meant by it, because the answer he gets is bigger than the question he asked. On the face of it he may have meant something quite immediate. Saved was an ordinary word: saved from drowning, from illness, from a sentence. He is a man whose prison has just fallen down around him, who was seconds from suicide, and who may simply have been asking how he gets out of this alive. But his prisoners are all present, so his immediate danger has passed. And these are the men a slave girl had been following through the streets announcing that they proclaimed the way of salvation (v. 17), the men whose singing had filled his prison at midnight while their backs were in ribbons. The earthquake had shaken more than the prison. He knew he needed saving from more than Roman punishment, and a man who had never asked anything of the sort found the words in his mouth in the middle of the night.

What must I do? The form of the question is the instinct of every religious person who has ever lived, and it is the instinct of every irreligious one too the moment he is frightened. Tell me the task. Give me the requirement and I will meet it. It is the same question the crowd asked at Pentecost (2:37) and the rich young ruler asked Jesus, and it is the question the Jerusalem council had just fought over. He is a practical man in a uniform, and he wants the procedure. What he is about to be handed has no procedure in it at all.

Not these lords but the Lord. He calls them Sirs, kyrioi, lords, on his face before them. The answer moves the word to where it belongs: believe in the Lord Jesus. As at Lystra (14:14–15), the servants will not stand in the place of the one they preach. The earthquake was not theirs, and every knee that bends in fear before his servants is meant to rise and bow before him.

What did the jailer need saving from? From the wrath of God against sin, which is the deepest danger any person faces, deeper than any prison or sentence. Scripture says that all have sinned and that the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; 6:23), and that those who die without Christ face a just and conscious judgment that does not end (Matthew 25:46). To be saved is to be rescued from that, forgiven, reconciled to God, given his Spirit, and brought at last into his presence. The jailer may not have grasped all of that at midnight. He grasped enough to know that he needed it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. This answer is the summit of the chapter. Chapter 15 settled that Jew and Gentile alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus (15:11); here that ruling is spoken to a pagan Roman in one sentence, with nothing added. The slave girl had shouted a way of salvation (v. 17); now the way is named, and it is a person.

Believe in the Lord Jesus. He asked what he must do, and the answer contains no doing at all. One verb: believe. Not believe and be circumcised; not believe and make restitution to the men you flogged; not believe and reform your life first, which is what most people privately assume. Salvation is by faith alone, in Christ alone. Paul’s word for it is justification: God, the holy Judge, declares the sinner righteous in his sight, not because he has become good, but because Christ’s obedience and death are counted to him, received by faith (Romans 4:5; 5:1).

Believe in a person. Believe in the Lord Jesus, not believe that something is the case: the difference between knowing a bridge will hold and standing on it.

The Lord Jesus. Jesus is the man from Nazareth executed some twenty years before. Lord is a word this man had heard used of Caesar all his working life, and the confession will cost Christians in this colony their standing and sometimes their lives. He is being told to transfer his allegiance, by a man with the magistrates’ rod marks on his back.

And you will be saved. The promise is future and certain: not you may be, but you will be.

Is that not too easy? It is easy to receive because it was costly to give. Believing is not a small effort that God kindly accepts in place of a large one; it is giving up every effort to save yourself and putting your whole weight on Christ, which proud hearts find the hardest thing of all. The religious man wants to contribute something, the irreligious man wants to stay his own master, and believe in the Lord Jesus refuses both. Nor does it leave a life unchanged: that same night this jailer washed the wounds he had caused (v. 33). Salvation is free to us because it cost Christ everything: he loved us and gave himself for us (Galatians 2:20).

You and your household. This man’s first coherent thought after his own rescue was his house. The offer arrives at the door of the whole household in the same sentence as it arrives at him, and that same night the missionaries speak the word to every person under that roof.

Does you and your household promise that if I believe, my family will be saved? No. Salvation is not passed from one person to another; Luke goes on to show that Paul spoke the word to all who were in his house (v. 32), and that the whole household rejoiced with him (v. 34). The promise is that the same way of salvation is open to all of them. A parent whose grown child does not believe has not been failed by this verse. He may pray for his child, speak and live the gospel, and trust the God who saves.

The household texts. The household’s baptism in v. 33 is another of the household texts in the friendly baptism discussion (see v. 15). The promise reaches as wide as faith reaches, and those baptised in this house were those who heard the word and believed.

What does it actually mean to believe in the Lord Jesus? It means to trust him: to rely on him alone for forgiveness and acceptance with God, and to receive him as your Lord. It includes knowing who he is and what he has done (he is the Son of God who died for sinners and rose again), agreeing that it is true, and then resting your whole weight on him, the way you rest on a chair. It is not a feeling, though feelings may come with it, and it is not a work that earns anything; it is the empty hand that receives a gift. If you are unsure whether you have ever believed, you can do it now: tell him that you have no hope but him, and that you trust him to save you.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to measure your standing with God by what you have done, come back to this verse: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, and his obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19). And pray by name for each member of your household who does not yet believe.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word spoken to all. It is the middle of the night, with an earthquake’s damage still on the floor and two men who ought to be lying down, and everybody under that roof is woken and gathered to hear the gospel explained more fully. Nobody is told they can hear about it in the morning.

What is the word of the Lord? The word of the Lord is the gospel message: the good news about the Lord Jesus (who he is, his death and resurrection, the call to believe, v. 31), and from the Lord, carrying his own authority. When Paul and Silas spoke it, the jailer was not hearing two men’s opinions but the Lord’s word delivered through his messengers (as Paul says elsewhere: when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, 1 Thessalonians 2:13).

But how can an ordinary reader be confident of what it means? Three things give solid confidence. First, God made the saving word clear (what theologians call the perspicuity of Scripture): the central message is plain enough that a rough jailer and his household heard it at midnight and were rejoicing in God before dawn (vv. 32–34). The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple (Psalm 119:130); God speaks to be understood, not to be decoded by experts. Second, he does not leave you to puzzle it out alone: the same Spirit who gave the word opens the heart and mind to receive it (the Lord opened Lydia’s heart, 16:14; the Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth, John 16:13; 1 Corinthians 2:12). Third, the word proves itself: it does what no mere human word can, converting and transforming (a jailer is a new man by dawn), and we test it against the rest of Scripture, as even the apostle Paul was tested by the Bereans (17:11).

One honest limit. Not every passage is equally easy (even Peter said some of Paul’s writing is hard to understand, 2 Peter 3:16); the clarity is chiefly of the things needful for salvation and life. So you may hold the heart of it, how to be saved, how to live, with real confidence, while reading the harder edges humbly, in the church, under faithful teaching. Your assurance rests not on your own cleverness but on God’s clarity and the Spirit’s witness.

Washed their wounds. Consider whose wounds those were. This man had put the two of them in the inner cell with their backs already opened and fixed their feet in the stocks without a thought, because they were only prisoners. The blood had been drying on them for hours while he slept. Now he is kneeling on the floor with water, cleaning the injuries he had been content to ignore.

That is repentance. Nobody asked him for it. He simply cannot leave those backs untended now. That is what conversion does before it does anything else: it changes who a person is able to walk past.

Baptized at once. In the middle of the night, with no delay. And Luke’s word order is surely deliberate: he washed their stripes; they washed him in baptism. Two cleansings in one sentence, and the man doing the first is the man receiving the second. The faith was already working before the sign was given to it.

Washed in the name of the Lord Jesus. The jailer could wash blood off a back. He could not wash a single sin off his own soul, and the water did not pretend to. In Acts believers are baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus (2:38; 10:48; 19:5), and the sign directs every eye to him: Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name (22:16). All who were baptised into Christ Jesus were baptised into his death, buried with him and raised to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:3–4). So the jailer’s baptism tells the whole night’s story in water: the old man who drew a sword on himself died with Christ, and a new man rose with him before dawn. The water did not change him; by faith he had been joined to Christ.

Does this household baptism support infant baptism? Christians who baptise infants see in it a pattern of whole families brought into the covenant. But Luke says the word was spoken to all who were in his house (v. 32) and that the whole household rejoiced with him (v. 34). The more likely reading is that those baptised were those who heard and believed. That is the credobaptist conviction (baptism for believers) this commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession: baptism is for those who profess repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus. Our paedobaptist brothers, who love the same Lord and the same gospel, read the household pattern through the covenant promise to believers and their children; we honour their conviction, while believing the text points to a household that heard, believed and was baptised together.

Should new converts be baptised as quickly as this? In Acts baptism normally followed conversion closely, often the same day (2:41; 8:38; 9:18; 10:48), because it was the public confession of faith in Christ and the sign of entry into his people. There was no long waiting period. Many churches today rightly take a little time to make sure that a profession is credible and that the person understands what baptism means. That is wise, especially where people have little Christian background. But the aim should be to baptise believers without needless delay, not to make baptism a reward for maturity.

For worship. Hours before his arrest the Lord of glory tied a towel round his waist, poured water into a basin and knelt to wash the feet of men who would desert him within hours (John 13:4–5). That same Lord, risen and reigning, reached into a Philippian prison and taught a jailer’s hands to kneel with water. He washed the man inwardly before the man washed anyone, and he does not leave hard hands as he finds them. Grace stoops lower than we ever can, and then it teaches us to stoop.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He set food before them. From the innermost room to the jailer’s own table in one night: it is probably the first thing they have eaten since before the flogging, and the man serving it is the man who locked them up. It is hospitality like Lydia’s: fellowship at table between a Roman jailer and two Jewish prisoners.

The first meal. One of the first Christian meals recorded in Europe: not in a hall, not on a Sunday, but in the small hours, in a prison official’s kitchen, with the plaster down off the walls.

He rejoiced. The word is a strong one: exulted, was overjoyed. Between the sword at midnight and the joy before dawn nothing has improved in his circumstances. He still has to explain a wrecked prison to the magistrates in the morning. Yet everything in him has changed. He had been God’s enemy and was now forgiven and welcomed as a son; he had been ready to throw his life away and now had eternal life (John 5:24).

Today salvation has come to this house. In Luke’s Gospel a chief tax collector who had made his living off other people received Jesus joyfully into his house and promised to put right his wrongs, and Jesus said, Today salvation has come to this house, for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:6–10). Now an official who had made his living holding people down has washed the wounds he caused, opened his house and rejoiced. It is the same Saviour doing the same thing, his seeking that found this man in the dark.

Can I really be joyful when my circumstances are still hard? Yes, though it will not be a joy that ignores the hardship. Christian joy is gladness in God himself, in what he has done for you in Christ and promised you, and none of that is touched by your circumstances. It sits alongside sorrow rather than replacing it (2 Corinthians 6:10). It grows as you dwell on the gospel, pray, sing, and spend time with God’s people. Do not wait for your situation to change before you rejoice; the jailer did not. Begin by thanking God for one thing that is true of you in Christ today.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, 'Let those men go.' And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, 'The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let those men go. Luke does not tell us why. Perhaps the flogging looked worse in daylight, or the earthquake had unsettled a superstitious town, or they thought a night in prison was enough. What is certain is the shape of what they do: no summons, no hearing, no finding, no record. Just a message, early, by a subordinate: let them go.

An institution that knows it has done wrong. Nothing is admitted or written down; the problem is removed from the premises before anybody important asks about it. And police (rhabdouchous) means rod-bearers, very likely the same officers whose rods had been used the day before.

Go in peace. The man delivering this message is a Christian of a few hours’ standing, and he is delighted: a warm send-off, spoken as a brother. He has no idea that Paul is about to refuse.

A kind person who wants it to stop. A new believer, out of sheer goodwill, urges a course that would leave an injustice standing and a young church unprotected. Sometimes the pressure to let a thing drop comes not from your enemies but from a kind person who wants the unpleasantness to stop. If you are newer, be slow to urge an older Christian to let something go until you understand why he is standing firm; if you are older, explain, gently, what you are protecting.

A peace the magistrates could not give. Go in peace is the word Jesus spoke to the forgiven woman: your faith has saved you; go in peace (Luke 7:50). The jailer has that peace now, and it did not come from the magistrates: since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). That is why Paul can refuse the magistrates’ quiet without losing anything. Their peace, a problem removed from the premises, is the peace the world gives; Christ’s was already settled in that house (John 14:27).

How do I know when to let something drop and when to pursue it? Ask who is affected and what is at stake. If only your own comfort or pride is involved, letting it go is usually the way of Christ (1 Corinthians 6:7; 1 Peter 2:23). If others, especially the vulnerable, will be harmed by silence, or if the honour of the gospel is at stake, love may require you to pursue it, lawfully and without vindictiveness. Seek wise counsel, especially if you are hurt or angry. And remember that wanting peace is good; the question is whether the peace offered is real or only quiet.

For worship. The officers who carried the rods at dusk carried the release at dawn, and had no idea whose errand they were running. The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD (Proverbs 21:1). The risen Christ, head over all things for the church, sent the earthquake at midnight and the messengers in the morning with the same hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said to them, 'They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beaten publicly, uncondemned. Why did he not say this yesterday? Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial, and the claim would normally have stopped the rods. In Jerusalem he speaks up before the whipping (22:25).

Why not earlier? Luke does not tell us, and honest answers are limited. It may be that in the uproar of verse 22 (a shouting crowd, clothes being torn off) nobody was listening; perhaps he did say so, and was not heard. Luke is careful to record that the magistrates never asked them anything. It may be that he chose to suffer for Christ first. What we can say is that he did not use his rights to protect his own back, and he did use them the next morning. The difference between those two moments is the key to the whole verse.

And do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out. Because look at what he actually demands, which is not compensation and not an apology for himself. He demands that the thing be undone publicly. The offence was committed in the market square in front of the town, and a private release leaves the town’s last memory of these two men as the morning they were flogged as criminals. And Paul is not going to be in Philippi to correct that impression. Lydia is. Her household is. The jailer is, and he has to go on working for these same magistrates. There is a church of a few weeks’ standing in that colony, and it will live or die partly on whether the authorities believe they can treat its founders as vermin without consequence.

Why do you strike me? Paul’s Master had walked this line before him. Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), and still handed him over to be scourged: beaten publicly, uncondemned, in the fullest sense. Jesus went to the cross willingly and opened not his mouth to save himself. Yet when an officer struck him at his hearing before the high priest, he answered, If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me? (John 18:23). The Lamb who would not resist his death still named injustice as injustice. Paul does the same here. He bore the rods without a word for himself, and he will not let a lie about Christ’s servants stand in the square where Christ’s little church must live.

In the flow. Paul’s protest also serves one of Luke’s steady purposes. Again and again Roman officials who look at the facts find that the Christians have broken no Roman law (18:14–16; 19:37; 26:31–32). Here the pattern begins, and it is the magistrates who turn out to be the lawbreakers: the gospel is not a crime.

Not pride or revenge. This is not a man standing on his dignity but one securing, on his way out of town, the only legal protection his converts are ever going to have. Christians may use their legal rights for the sake of the gospel and the church (22:25; 25:11).

When should a believer insist on his rights? This answers a question Christians genuinely struggle with: when should a believer insist on his rights, and when should he absorb the wrong? Paul does both in this chapter, and the line between them is not comfort but other people. He took the beating without invoking the law when the only person who would have benefited was himself. He invoked it the moment the beneficiaries were the church he was leaving behind. It is the same principle he presses on the Corinthians, who were suing each other and to whom he says: why not rather suffer wrong? (1 Corinthians 6:7), because there the only thing at stake was their own advantage. So the test is not whether you are entitled. You may well be. It is whether the person protected by your insisting is you.

Is it unspiritual for a Christian to go to the police or the courts? No. The governing authorities are God’s servants for our good, to restrain wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and Paul used Roman law repeatedly. Crimes such as assault, fraud or abuse should be reported to the authorities; abuse in particular must never be hidden or tolerated, in the church or anywhere else, and victims should be protected first. What Paul discourages is believers suing one another over private disputes before unbelievers, when the church could help them settle it (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). Using the law to protect others and to see justice done is a proper Christian act.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial.

verseByVerse.quote: "The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. So they came and apologized to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were afraid. The chief magistrates are as afraid in the morning as the jailer was at midnight, and rationally: ordering a Roman citizen flogged without trial was an offence that could end a career, and a colony that allowed it could lose its privileges.

The irony completed. The charge was that they advocated customs not lawful for us as Romans. The only people in the story who broke Roman law were the Romans, in the act of defending it, against two men who held the citizenship the accusers were so proud of.

They came and apologized. They came, which is what Paul had required: the men who had ordered the public stripping walked down to the prison in daylight, where everyone would see them go. Asked to leave, not ordered: they were in no position to order anything.

Two things, pulling opposite ways. God vindicated his servants publicly, and it is right to be glad about it. But Luke chooses his words: they were afraid. Nothing suggests these men were sorry or thought better of the gospel; they wanted the problem gone politely. An apology extracted by fear is not repentance. The vindication was real, and it changed nobody’s heart, and a Christian who has finally been proved right about something will need both halves of that sentence.

The verdict reversed. The rulers of Jerusalem had condemned Jesus, and God overturned their verdict on the third day: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (2:36). The magistrates at the prison gate are a small picture of that. But here the reversal changed no one, and when God vindicated his Son, three thousand were cut to the heart: the vindication of Christ is also the salvation of sinners.

What if I am never vindicated in this life? Many faithful believers are not. Stephen was not vindicated before the Sanhedrin; countless martyrs died with their names blackened. Scripture promises that God will vindicate his people, but often on the last day rather than this one (Romans 12:19; 2 Thessalonians 1:6–10). Commit your cause to him who judges justly, as Jesus did (1 Peter 2:23). Do what is right, speak the truth where it helps, and then leave your reputation in his hands. The verdict that matters most has already been given: there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

For worship. Two frightened magistrates came down to a prison gate, and one day every magistrate and emperor who has ever held a rod will stand before the one they condemned. The rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory, and he is coming as Judge. On that day the servants who were stripped and shamed for his name will not need anyone to escort them out. He will bring them in himself, and show before all the world that they are his.

verseByVerse.quote: "So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They visited Lydia. Publicly vindicated and asked to leave, they could have gone straight to the gate. Instead the last thing they do in Philippi is walk across town to the church in Lydia’s house.

They encouraged them. Two men whose backs were opened by rods the day before encourage the church rather than the other way round.

An unlikely founding membership. Count the church they leave behind. A foreign businesswoman in the luxury trade, with her household. A jailer, with his. A slave girl, if she came, and Luke will not tell us. And the brothers: a word that appears here without introduction, which suggests there were others by now whom Luke has not named. Set those people beside each other. At the top of the town, a woman of means. At the bottom, a girl who had been owned and worked. In between, a man employed to hold people down. In a Roman colony obsessed with rank, the one place in Philippi where those three could sit in the same room was a house church.

The mind of Christ in Lydia’s house. What held such a room together? Not class, race or taste. Paul later set before this church Christ: have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5–7). The businesswoman and the jailer had nothing in common except a Lord who had come down further than either of them and made himself the servant of both.

A church Paul loved. The church at Philippi became one of Paul’s most loving and generous churches (Philippians 1:3–5; 4:15–16), and the word joy runs through the letter he later sent them from beginning to end. He wrote it in chains, to the church that had been born in a jail. Luke seems to have stayed behind: the we stopped after verse 17 and resumes at Philippi in 20:5.

What it cost. Add up what it cost to plant this church: two provinces closed, weeks of walking toward nothing, a sea crossing, days in a strange city with no way in, a public flogging, a night in the stocks, and an expulsion. What was gained was a room in a woman’s house, a jailer’s household, and a letter we still read.

In the flow. The Philippian story closes where the church began, with Lydia, and sets the pattern for the journey: a church born, persecution driving the missionaries on, every expulsion carrying the gospel further (17:1–10).

How can I encourage others when I am the one who is hurting? Often your hurt is exactly what makes your encouragement believable. People listen to someone who has suffered and still trusts God. You do not need to pretend you are fine; Paul’s back was visibly torn. Tell honestly what God has been to you in the trouble, point others to the same Lord, and keep it simple. Comfort received from God becomes comfort you can give (2 Corinthians 1:4). And let others encourage you too: a church is a place where the wounded take turns.

On a Tuesday. The Christ who made himself the servant of both the businesswoman and the jailer still gathers that kind of room. Look around your church for the people who would never meet anywhere else, the wealthy and the poor, the respectable and the rescued, and make sure they are sitting at the same table.

parallels.desc: your partnership in the gospel from the first day

16.theology: Effectual calling and the opened heart. At Philippi Paul preached and the Lord opened Lydia’s heart (16:14). Both are real and both are needed: without the preaching she has nothing to believe, and without the Lord’s work the words stay outside her. The Reformed call this effectual calling: God’s call through the gospel that brings a person to faith. It is why prayer goes with every act of evangelism: we can speak, and only God can open a heart.
16.examples:
Then: A dealer in purple cloth, a slave girl and a Roman jailer, as different in rank, race and circumstance as three people could be, were met by one gospel in one city, and the church at Philippi was born from them.

Now: The Lord who opened Lydia’s heart still opens hearts, and still steers his church by closed doors as well as open ones. The answer to the jailer’s question has not changed: believe in the Lord Jesus.

17.title: Athens and the Unknown God
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. <sup>2</sup>And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, <sup>3</sup>explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.” <sup>4</sup>And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. <sup>5</sup>But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar, and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd. <sup>6</sup>And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, <sup>7</sup>and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.” <sup>8</sup>And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things. <sup>9</sup>And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. <sup>10</sup>The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. <sup>11</sup>Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. <sup>12</sup>Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men. <sup>13</sup>But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. <sup>14</sup>Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there. <sup>15</sup>Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed. <sup>16</sup>Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. <sup>17</sup>So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. <sup>18</sup>Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, “What does this babbler wish to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities”—because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. <sup>19</sup>And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? <sup>20</sup>For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.” <sup>21</sup>Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new. <sup>22</sup>So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. <sup>23</sup>For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you. <sup>24</sup>The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, <sup>25</sup>nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. <sup>26</sup>And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, <sup>27</sup>that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us, <sup>28</sup>for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’ <sup>29</sup>Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. <sup>30</sup>The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, <sup>31</sup>because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.” <sup>32</sup>Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” <sup>33</sup>So Paul went out from their midst. <sup>34</sup>But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.
17.overview: Acts 17 follows Paul through three very different cities. In Thessalonica he reasons in the synagogue from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Messiah; a church is born, and jealous opponents raise a mob and accuse the believers of proclaiming another king. In Berea the Jews receive the word eagerly and test it daily against the Scriptures. In Athens, the old intellectual capital of the Greek world, crowded with idols, Paul speaks before the Areopagus council, a model of preaching to people without the Bible: from their altar to an unknown god he moves to the Creator who needs nothing, who now commands all people to repent and will judge the world by the man he raised from the dead. Some mock, some put it off, and a few believe.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Thessalonica Paul shows from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and a church is born among Jews, God-fearing Greeks and leading women. Jealous opponents raise a mob, and the believers are charged with proclaiming a rival king. Sent away by night, Paul finds in Berea hearers who receive the word eagerly and test it against the Scriptures, until opponents follow and he is sent on to Athens, leaving Silas and Timothy behind.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Berean pattern

The Bereans received the word eagerly and examined the Scriptures daily (17:11). That is neither credulity nor scepticism, but eager hearing joined to careful testing by Scripture: sola Scriptura practised in the ordinary work of hearing sermons.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Thessalonian accusers said these men had turned the world upside down, and they were right that the gospel had rearranged households, loyalties and a synagogue. Now: The gospel still unsettles whatever opposes Christ’s kingdom. The question for a church is whether it is unsettling the right things, sin, death and injustice, or only offering comfortable religious experience.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. One gospel is adapted wisely to Jews, God-fearers and pagan philosophers, and under all three scenes runs one thread: the risen Jesus is Lord of synagogue, marketplace and council alike, and none of them can keep him out.

To Thessalonica. Two towns are passed through in half a verse, on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road from the Adriatic to Byzantium. From Philippi to Thessalonica is about a hundred miles, and Paul walked it with a back opened by rods a few days earlier. Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a busy port, a city from which a message could travel in every direction; within months Paul could tell the church there that the word of the Lord had sounded forth from them everywhere (1 Thessalonians 1:8).

As was his custom. The last time he entered a public place in this province he came out stripped and flogged. His custom did not change. It was his settled practice to go to the synagogue first in each new city, taking the gospel to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16), and showing those who already held the Scriptures that the Christ they hoped for is Jesus. The synagogue’s service of reading and teaching, at which visitors could be invited to speak, was the very platform he used.

As his Lord had done. Luke has used this phrase once before. When Jesus came to Nazareth, as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, read Isaiah’s promise of the Spirit-anointed one who would proclaim good news to the poor, and said, Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (Luke 4:16–21). His hearers were amazed, then furious, and drove him out of the town. Paul’s custom is his Master’s custom, and so is the result: the same Scriptures, the same claim that they are fulfilled in Jesus, and he will be driven out the same way. The risen Christ is still going to the synagogue on the Sabbath, in the person of his apostle.

Three Sabbath days. This is often read as meaning Paul was in Thessalonica for only three weeks, and that is very unlikely, because his letters point to a longer stay. He worked night and day with his hands so as not to burden anyone (1 Thessalonians 2:9); the Philippians, a hundred miles away, sent him help there more than once (Philippians 4:16); and the congregation had turned to God from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9), which is not a description of synagogue Jews.

Which three weeks Luke is counting. Luke says three Sabbaths in the synagogue. That is the length of the synagogue phase, not of the mission. When the synagogue closed to him, Paul went on working among Gentiles for a good while longer, and they make up most of the church he writes to. Where a reader is told there is a contradiction, there is a summary and a letter, and they fit.

He reasoned with them. The word is dialegomai, from which we get dialogue: he discussed, argued, took questions. For three Sabbaths men who knew the Scriptures put their objections and he answered them out of the Old Testament, which both sides owned. Christian preaching is reasonable. It appeals to the mind as well as to the heart, and it is not afraid of a question.

Is it right to argue about the faith? Yes, if by arguing you mean what Paul did: giving reasons, from Scripture, with patience, and listening to the objection before answering it. Peter tells every believer to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). What Scripture forbids is quarrelling: the point-scoring, the raised voice, the need to win (2 Timothy 2:24–25). The test is simple. If you are still listening, still gentle, and still praying for the person, you are reasoning. If you are enjoying his defeat, you have stopped.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a port on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia. Amphipolis and Apollonia were stops along that road.

verseByVerse.quote: "explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Explaining and proving. Explaining is dianoigō: to open up, to prise apart. Luke keeps this word for remarkable company: it is what Jesus did on the Emmaus road, when he opened to them the Scriptures and their hearts burned (Luke 24:32), and that evening when he opened their minds to understand them (Luke 24:45); and it is what the Lord did to Lydia, when he opened her heart to pay attention (16:14). Paul opens the Scriptures; only God opens the person.

Setting it on the table. Proving is paratithemenos, the ordinary word for setting food before somebody, as the jailer at Philippi did (16:34). Paul lays the evidence out where people can reach it. He is not performing over their heads. He is serving.

Necessary for the Christ to suffer. Here is the whole quarrel between the church and the synagogue in one sentence. Most Jews expected a conquering Messiah, the son of David who would break the oppressor and reign; a crucified Messiah was not a disappointing version of the hope but a contradiction of it. Paul knew how that sounded: Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Where did he prove it from? He does not tell us here, but the trail is not hard to follow, because the risen Christ had already walked two disciples through the same argument, and asked the same question in almost the same words: was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory (Luke 24:26)? The texts are the ones the apostles use everywhere: the servant who was pierced for our transgressions and numbered with the transgressors, and who afterwards shall see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53); the sufferer of Psalm 22, whose hands and feet are pierced and his garments divided (the Hebrew of the word pierced is uncertain, but the ancient Greek translation and most English Bibles read it so), and whose psalm ends with all the ends of the earth turning to the LORD; the Holy One whose body will not see corruption (Psalm 16); the Anointed One who is cut off (Daniel 9:26); the pierced one they will look upon and mourn (Zechariah 12:10). The suffering was never an accident that theology had to be rearranged around. It was in the book the whole time, and had been read aloud in that synagogue for generations.

This Jesus is the Christ. The argument has two steps, and most people collapse them. First, from the Scriptures: this is what the Christ must be like, one who suffers and rises. Second, from history: and here is the man who matches. He suffered and rose; therefore he is the Messiah. Paul does not begin with Jesus and search for texts to fit him. He establishes the pattern first and then produces the person. It is a model of preaching for every age: from Scripture to Christ.

How can I read the Old Testament and see Christ without forcing it? Read a passage first for what it meant to its first hearers. Then ask where it is heading: which promise it carries forward, which pattern it sets up (the lamb, the priest, the king, the temple), which longing it leaves open that only Christ answers. You are not hunting for secret codes in every tent peg. You are following roads that the New Testament itself has already walked, and Acts gives you the map: the apostles return again and again to the same psalms and prophets. Start with Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and Psalm 16, read them slowly beside the Gospel accounts of the cross and the empty tomb, and you will be doing in your own chair what the Bereans did in theirs.

For worship. The cross was not God’s rescue of a plan gone wrong. It was necessary, written into the Scriptures long before a nail was forged, because the Father had determined to save sinners through the suffering of his Son, and the Son had agreed to it gladly. Every lamb on every altar pointed to him, every psalm of the righteous sufferer was rehearsing his lines, and the empty tomb was promised before Bethlehem was a village. He suffered because it was written, and it was written because he loved us before the world began.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some were persuaded. God uses argument: the Spirit does not bypass the mind; he opens it, and then the reasons do their work. And the proportions are the story. Of the Jews, some. Of the God-fearing Greeks, a great many. Of the leading women, not a few. The synagogue produced a handful; the Gentiles attached to the synagogue came in crowds. Paul’s letters show that many more were Gentiles converted straight from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

But the Jews were jealous. That imbalance is what lights the fuse. These God-fearers were the synagogue’s own fruit, Gentiles it had taught at cost over years, and they are walking out of it behind two visitors after three weeks. It had happened before, at Pisidian Antioch, when the crowds gathered to hear Paul and the synagogue leaders were filled with jealousy (13:45). What is new here is the method.

Wicked men of the rabble. Luke’s word is agoraioi, marketplace men: the idlers of the public square, loafers and thugs for hire, who could be had cheaply by anyone wanting a crowd in a hurry. This is not a spontaneous outbreak of civic feeling; somebody put it together, out of men who neither knew nor cared what the argument was about.
