Manufactured opposition. Respectable people who would not have thrown a stone themselves used men whose only interest was the day’s pay. It was done before, to the Lord himself: Pilate knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered Jesus up, and the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas instead (Mark 15:10–11). The stirred-up crowd got its way, and God raised him from the dead. A crowd is not always what it seems, and it never has the last word.

The house of Jason. Jason was probably Paul’s host, a local who has done nothing except offer a spare room. When the missionaries move on, and they will move on tonight, he stays, with his door broken, his name on a charge sheet, and his money posted as a bond. Luke tells us nothing else about him, unless he is the Jason Paul later greets as a kinsman in Romans 16:21, which would mean he came through it and was still standing years later.

The cost nobody writes down. This is the part of the cost of the gospel that gets least attention, because the people who bear it do not write the letters. The visiting preacher is beaten and moves on. The local believer who housed him has to go on living in the town afterwards, among the neighbours who watched. If you have ever quietly paid for somebody else’s ministry, in your family, your workplace or your street, Jason is in Scripture for you, and Luke thought his name was worth keeping.

Why would religious people be so jealous of the gospel? Because the gospel takes away the one thing religious pride lives on: being the ones who are in, by the right birth, the right effort, the right observance. When outsiders come in freely by grace, without going through the long apprenticeship, those who trusted in their apprenticeship feel robbed. It is the elder brother’s complaint in the parable (Luke 15:28–30). The cure is not to have less religion but to remember that we too came in by grace alone. A Christian who catches himself resenting how easily someone else was welcomed has found the same jealousy in his own heart, and should take it to the cross.
verseByVerse.note: Jason was probably Paul’s host.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city authorities. They were called politarchs, a title almost unknown in the surviving literature but found in more than a dozen inscriptions from Thessalonica alone. Luke uses exactly the right local title, the kind of small thing that fits a historian who was there or who asked people who were.

Turned the world upside down. It is a famous compliment paid to the church by its enemies, and it is usually quoted more cheerfully than Luke meant it. The verb is anastatoō, and it is not a gentle word: to unsettle, to throw into disorder, to drive out of house and home. Luke uses it once more in this book, of an Egyptian who stirred up a revolt and led four thousand assassins into the wilderness (21:38). The charge is not that these men are exciting. It is that they are insurgents. And yet the charge is also a compliment, for the gospel turns the world the right way up.

Another king, Jesus. This is the accusation that could actually kill: treason. Thessalonica was a free city, self-governing, exempt from a Roman garrison, allowed to keep its own assembly and its own magistrates. That freedom was a gift from Rome and could be taken back. A city that harboured men who proclaimed a rival king would not stay free for long. So the charge is aimed with real skill. It is also, in the sense intended, false. Paul was not organising a revolt; he had spent three weeks in a synagogue arguing about Isaiah, and his settled instruction to Christians was to pay their taxes and honour the authorities (Romans 13:1–7).

Not simply untrue either. Jesus is King of kings: not a political rival to Caesar in the world’s way (John 18:36), but Lord over Caesar too. Paul really was announcing round the empire that a man had been raised from the dead and made Lord, and that a day of judgment had been fixed with him as judge; within months he wrote to this church about the Lord descending with a cry of command (1 Thessalonians 4:16), in words also used when an emperor visited a city. The early Christians would not say Caesar is Lord; they said Jesus is Lord. The mob was wrong about the method and right about the collision: no political arrangement in the world is finally neutral about him.

Does “another king” make Christians political revolutionaries? No. Christ’s kingdom does not advance by the sword or the ballot box but by the word and the Spirit, and his subjects are commanded to pray for rulers, pay their taxes and do good (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2; 1 Peter 2:13–17). But it does mean no ruler is ultimate. When a government commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, a Christian must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), respectfully and accepting the cost. A Christian can be the best citizen in the town precisely because Caesar is not his god: he serves him honestly, and he will not worship him.
verseByVerse.note: The “city authorities” were called politarchs, a title found in inscriptions from Thessalonica. Claiming another king could be treated as treason against Caesar.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rumour and a calculation. The crowd has a rumour of sedition in their own town; the politarchs are frightened of Rome. Thessalonica held its freedom at Rome’s pleasure, and a city that could not keep order would have order imposed on it, as the town clerk at Ephesus says out loud: we really are in danger of being charged with rioting (19:40). These men are not weighing a theological claim. They are calculating what a report to the governor would cost them.

The pattern of the authorities. The pattern repeats through the whole book and most of history: the authorities never actually rule on the truth of the matter. Gallio will refuse to hear it (18:15). Felix will keep Paul two years and decide nothing (24:27). Festus will find nothing deserving death, and send him to Rome only because Paul has appealed to Caesar (25:25). Here the magistrates take a bond and make the problem go away. Institutions are not usually in the business of deciding whether something is true. They are in the business of keeping things quiet, and a church that pins its hopes on being officially found innocent will wait a long time.

What is truth? The pattern began at the trial of Jesus. Truth itself stood in front of a Roman governor and said, Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice, and Pilate asked, What is truth? Then he went out without waiting for a reply (John 18:37–38). He found no guilt in him, and then gave the crowd what it wanted to keep the peace. The magistrates of Thessalonica, taking a bond and closing the file, are doing on a small scale what Pilate did on the largest: managing a disturbance instead of weighing a King. And the King was not diminished by it. The verdict Pilate would not give, God gave on the third day. Every court that has since declined to ask whether Jesus is Lord has been ruling, without knowing it, in a case already decided.

Should we not want the gospel to have a fair hearing in public? Yes, and Paul used every legal right he had, as later chapters show (16:37; 25:11). It is good to seek justice and freedom of worship and to pray for them (1 Timothy 2:2). But the church does not depend on them. The gospel spread fastest in this book in cities where the authorities were indifferent or hostile. So work for fairness, and do not be crushed when it does not come. The verdict that matters has already been given, in the resurrection, and no magistrate can overturn it.

For worship. The rulers took counsel together against the Lord and against his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens was not disturbed (Psalm 2:2–4). Cities rage, magistrates calculate, crowds are bought and sold, and the Son reigns on, unthreatened, setting his own times. Our peace is not that the world is quiet; it is that the throne is occupied.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Money as security. Jason and the others put up a bond, forfeit if the trouble recurred, which in practice meant that the men who caused it would leave and not come back. So Jason bought Paul’s freedom to leave with his own money, and the price was that Paul could not return without putting Jason’s property, and probably Jason, at risk.

Satan hindered us. A few months later Paul writes to this church that he wanted to come to them again and again, but Satan hindered him (1 Thessalonians 2:18). We are not told what the hindrance was and should not pretend to certainty, but a bond that would cost a friend everything if Paul walked back through the gate is a natural candidate, often proposed. If so, what Paul calls Satan’s work was a piece of ordinary municipal paperwork nobody could appeal.

Ordinary obstacles. Not every obstacle to God’s work is dramatic; some of it is a condition attached in an office by men who were only trying to get home. Paul does not pretend it did not hurt, yet he did not sit still: he wrote letters, he sent Timothy (1 Thessalonians 3:1–2), and the church he could not visit became one of the great joys of his life.

Away by night. By night, as at Damascus, when Paul was let down the wall in a basket (9:25), then about fifty miles south-west, off the main highway, to a quieter town. And straight into the synagogue: after two cities in a row had ended in violence, they changed the address and nothing else.

Imitators of the Lord. Paul himself tells us how he read this flight by night. Writing to the church he had just been torn from, he says: you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit (1 Thessalonians 1:6). And he sets their suffering beside the Lord’s own: they had suffered from their own countrymen, as the churches in Judea had, where the Lord Jesus himself was killed (1 Thessalonians 2:14–15). Paul, a Jew writing about his own people with grief, is not blaming a race; he is tracing one road. The Lord was rejected and killed; his apostles were driven out; his young church suffered; and all of them were following the same Lord down the same road, toward the same resurrection.

Is it cowardly for a Christian to run from persecution? No. Jesus told his disciples that when they were persecuted in one town they should flee to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul did so repeatedly, though never by denying Christ. Fleeing is wrong when it means abandoning the faith or deserting people who depend on you; it is wise when staying would only waste a life the Lord can still use elsewhere. Here the local believers made the decision, and Paul accepted it. He did not run from the work. He ran to the next synagogue.
verseByVerse.note: Berea lay about 50 miles west of Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
More noble. The word is eugenesteroi: better born, of finer stock. It is a class word, and Luke applies it to a country-town synagogue by comparison with that of the provincial capital, redefining it under everybody’s nose. Nobility here is character, measured by what a man does when he is handed something new that he did not ask for.

With all eagerness. Luke tells us exactly what they did, in two halves that have to be kept together. This is the first half, and it is not the cautious half. They were not braced against it. They wanted it, and received it gladly, before they had checked it.

Examining the Scriptures daily. That is the second half, and the verb, anakrinontes, is a legal one: to sift evidence, to conduct a judicial examination, as in a court. And daily, which means this went on well past the Sabbath. Men who had a living to earn went home from a synagogue meeting, opened the scrolls, and worked through Isaiah and the Psalms to see whether a visitor had told them the truth.

Neither credulous nor cynical. Take either half on its own and you get something the Bible does not commend. Eagerness without examination is how people are swept into every enthusiasm that has ever damaged a church; a congregation that receives everything gladly will receive the next thing gladly too. Examination without eagerness is the other disease, and it is the more respectable one: the hearer who arrives armed, whose Bible is open to catch the preacher out, and who has not been moved by anything in twenty years. Luke praises the men who did both at once, which is much harder than either.

Where Christians differ: the final authority. Some say the church or tradition must interpret Scripture for the believer, and that individuals should not test teachers. This commentary’s view: the Bereans tested an apostle by Scripture, and Luke calls it noble. Scripture is the final authority by which every teaching is tested (Isaiah 8:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1). This is sola Scriptura (Latin for Scripture alone): not that teachers and tradition are useless, but that Scripture judges them all. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, who love the Scriptures, hold that the church’s tradition and teaching office share that authority; we answer them gently from this very verse.

Many of them therefore believed. “Therefore”: the daily examination did not produce sceptics who could never be satisfied; it produced faith, and more of it than the city up the road had managed. Rigour was the road to belief, for these are the Scriptures that bear witness about him (John 5:39). Day after day they found him in the scrolls they had owned all their lives, the pierced servant of Isaiah and the Holy One who would not see corruption. The Bereans did not believe in spite of their Bibles. They believed because their Bibles were about him.

Does sola Scriptura make every Christian his own pope? No. The Bereans examined Scripture together, in a synagogue, under teaching, not alone against everybody. Sola Scriptura means Scripture is the only infallible rule, not the only help. God gives the church pastors and teachers (Ephesians 4:11–12), the wisdom of the centuries, and confessions that summarise what Scripture teaches; all of these are valuable and all are under the Bible, to be corrected by it. A believer who thinks he has found something no Christian has ever seen should be humble and slow. A believer who hears something from the pulpit that the text plainly does not say should open his Bible, and then go and talk to his pastor.

How do I actually examine the Scriptures when I hear a sermon? Keep it simple. Open the passage the preacher is using and read the verses around it: does the point come from the text, or is the text just a launching pad? Look up the cross-references he gives. Ask whether what was said fits the rest of the Bible’s teaching on the subject. If something puzzles you, write it down and ask, kindly. And make the daily part real: a regular, unhurried reading of the Bible for yourself is what gives you the ear to notice when something is off, and the joy to notice when something is gloriously right.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came there too. Fifty miles. On foot or by mule, over two or three days, for no purpose except to break up a meeting in a town they did not live in. Acts has shown this before, when men followed Paul from Antioch and Iconium to Lystra and got him stoned (14:19): hatred will spend an effort that indifference never will.

The target. On arrival they did not preach against him; they agitated and stirred up, the same trade as at Thessalonica. And the target was not the synagogue, where the Bereans were examining the Scriptures daily and would not be hurried, but the crowds. When a case cannot be won in the room where the evidence is, it gets taken outside to people who have not seen any.

Silas and Timothy remained. This is easy to miss and is the more important detail. Silas and Timothy stay, in a town just stirred up against them, to strengthen a young church. The work at Berea did not require Paul. It required somebody. Paul had learned that from his Master, who spent some three years making men who could carry the work, and then told them it was to their advantage that he go away, because he would send the Helper (John 16:7). The Lord of the church withdrew his visible presence and his church grew. A Paul who thought the mission stood or fell on his own presence would have misunderstood the Lord he served.

How do I know when to stay and when to step back? Ask whose presence is the problem and whose is needed. Paul’s presence was drawing fire onto the believers; Silas’s and Timothy’s was building them up. Sometimes love means staying when it would be easier to leave; sometimes it means stepping out of the way so that others can do the work without you. Take counsel from mature believers, as Paul accepted the brothers’ decision. And be willing to be the one who is not the centre of the story.

verseByVerse.quote: "Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As far as Athens. The escort goes home, and Paul is left in Athens on his own. Athens had long been the intellectual centre of the Greek world, home of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle; by Paul’s day it was past its political glory, but still a famous university city, full of philosophers and temples.

Alone in Athens. Paul almost never worked alone; his letters are full of names. This is the one extended stretch in Acts where he is by himself, and we know how he felt about it. Writing to the Thessalonians a few months later, he says that when he could bear it no longer, he was willing to be left behind at Athens alone (1 Thessalonians 3:1). It is his own word, alone, and he uses it about one of the most celebrated cities in the world.

Not a machine. There is a picture of Paul as indestructible and self-sufficient that Scripture will not support. The man who sang at midnight in a Philippian cell sends an urgent message from Athens asking his friends to hurry. The loneliness was not a failure of faith; the Areopagus address was preached out of it.

Is it wrong for a Christian to feel lonely? No. Being alone and finding it hard is not a sign that something has gone wrong in your Christian life. It is a thing that happened to the apostle Paul, in writing, and he did not apologise for minding. God himself said it was not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18), and our Lord in Gethsemane asked his friends to watch with him. Loneliness is not sin; it is a need. Bring it to God honestly, as the psalmists did, and do what Paul did: ask for company. Send the message. Tell a friend or your pastor you are struggling. The body of Christ exists partly so that no member has to carry that alone.

The Lord stood by me. Paul was alone, but he was not left alone. At the very next stop, in Corinth, with this loneliness still fresh, the Lord spoke to him in a vision by night: Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you (18:9–10). And at the end of his life, writing from another prison, Paul would say, At my first defence no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed (2 Timothy 4:16–17). That is the pattern of Athens. The friends are hundreds of miles away, the city is indifferent, and the risen Christ stands beside his servant, so that the sermon preached out of loneliness becomes one of the most famous ever given.

The unnamed escort. These Bereans, converts of a few weeks, travelled several hundred miles to see Paul safely to Athens and went home. Nobody records their names, and without them the next scene does not happen.

In the flow. Here the chapter changes ground. Thessalonica and Berea were synagogue cities; in Athens the gospel walks into the heart of Greek learning and religion, where most hearers had no Bible at all, and the word reaches the city that thought itself the centre of the world (1:8).

On a Tuesday. Look round your church for someone who is in their Athens at the moment, new to the area, recently bereaved, or carrying a ministry by themselves, and be the answer to their message before they have to send it.
verseByVerse.note: Athens had long been the intellectual centre of the Greek world, though no longer politically powerful.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Alone in Athens, Paul is distressed by the city’s idols and reasons daily in the synagogue and the marketplace. The philosophers take him to the Areopagus to explain his talk of Jesus and the resurrection. Starting from an altar to an unknown god, he preaches the Creator who needs nothing, the unity of all nations from one man, the command to repent, and the coming judgment by the man God raised. Some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe, among them Dionysius of the council and a woman named Damaris.
verseByVerse.theology:
What creation can and cannot tell

At the Areopagus Paul uses what can be known of God through creation, often called natural theology: God has not left himself without witness (14:17), and every nation lives within boundaries he has set (17:26). But creation cannot tell anyone the gospel. To move from the God who made everything to the man he has appointed takes the Word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some mocked the resurrection, some said they would hear Paul again, and some believed: dismissal, deferral and faith. Now: The gospel still divides its hearers along much the same lines. The church cannot prevent the first two responses; its task is to preach so plainly that the third is open to all who will receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His spirit was provoked. The word is parōxyneto: stirred, distressed, angered. Luke used its noun for the sharp disagreement that broke up Paul and Barnabas (15:39). The fierceness that cost him something at Antioch now drives him into the marketplace at Athens. Our strongest traits show up in our best moments and our worst alike; grace does not hand us a new temperament, it makes the one we have holy.

Full of idols. Luke’s word is not found in any earlier surviving Greek writing and may be his own coinage: something like idol-infested, the way you would describe a house overrun. Ancient visitors remarked on how crowded the city was with statues and shrines, and a Roman satirist joked of one region that it was easier to meet a god there than a man; Athens would have qualified at least as well.

Every one a masterpiece. Many of those idols were works of art, in one of the great collections of sculpture in the ancient world. Paul walked through some of the finest art the human race had yet produced, and what he felt was grief and anger, because he was not looking at the workmanship but at what it was for. The thing that moved him was not first the immorality of Athens or its arrogance. It was that the glory belonging to God was being handed to objects, beautifully (Romans 1:23).

Zeal and tears. Paul felt two things at once, for God’s honour and for the people, and he learned both from his Lord. When Jesus found the temple turned into a market, his disciples remembered that it was written, Zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17). And when he came near Jerusalem and saw the city, he wept over it, because it did not know the things that make for peace (Luke 19:41–42). The Son of God was jealous for his Father’s glory and broken-hearted for the people who were robbing it. Neither cancelled the other. The cold zealot who does not weep and the soft sympathiser who is never provoked have both lost half of Christ. In the streets of Athens his apostle has both halves, and so he does what his Lord did: he goes in among them and speaks.

In the synagogue and in the marketplace. He did not withdraw from the city or stand in the street shouting at it. He talked to people: first, as usual, those who had the Scriptures, and then in the agora, the centre of public life where Socrates had taught, among shoppers, loafers, philosophers and slaves sent on errands. One message, two doorways, and he used whichever was open on the day. That is what to do with the thing that grieves you about the place you live: not a post, not a private lament, but a conversation with somebody who is in it.

How can I be grieved by idolatry without becoming self-righteous? Remember that the idols of Athens are in your own heart too. Calvin called the human heart a factory of idols, and every Christian was rescued from some version of that city. Paul’s grief was for God’s glory and for the people, not against them; that is why it sent him into the marketplace to reason, not out of it to sneer. Today’s idols are rarely statues: money, success, the body, a romance, a political cause, comfort. When you see them ruling the people around you, let it move you to pray and to speak, gently and with reasons, as one beggar telling another where the bread is.
verseByVerse.note: The marketplace (agora) was the centre of public life, filled with statues and shrines.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, 'What does this babbler wish to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities' — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, 'May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epicureans and Stoics. These were the two live schools in Athens. The Epicureans held that the gods exist but are serene, remote and uninterested in us; the world is atoms falling, there is no providence, and death is simply the end, which is the good news of the system, because it means no afterlife and no judgment. The aim of life is pleasure, understood as tranquillity, the absence of pain and fear.

The Stoics. The Stoics held nearly the opposite. The divine is the rational principle running through all things, so everything is ordered; the aim of life is to live in harmony with nature, accept fate calmly and endure what comes without complaint. God is not remote but diffused, and in some sense is the universe. Paul’s sermon will agree with each school about something and disagree with both about God.

What does this babbler wish to say? Luke preserves two reactions. The first word is spermologos, a seed-picker. It began as a name for a bird hopping about pecking up scraps, passed into slang for the men who scavenged the market floor for what fell off the carts, and ended as an insult for someone who picks up bits of ideas and passes them off as learning. It is the sneer of the professional at the amateur, and it is the first thing the philosophers of Athens said about the apostle to the Gentiles.

Foreign divinities. That sentence has a shadow over it that any educated Athenian would have felt at once. Introducing new divinities was the charge on which Athens had tried and executed Socrates, four and a half centuries earlier, in this city. Luke does not need to say so.

Jesus and the resurrection. It is quite possible they misheard him. Jesus and Anastasis, the Greek word for resurrection, which is a feminine noun, sound to a pagan ear like a pair of names, a god and his consort, a new divine couple, which would explain the plural divinities exactly. If so, the cleverest men in Athens listened to the gospel and concluded that Paul was recommending two new gods, one of them called Resurrection.

I am the resurrection. The mistake was nearer the truth than they knew. Jesus and the Resurrection are not two deities but one person. Standing at the tomb of Lazarus, Jesus said, I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live (John 11:25). The resurrection is his own deed and his own life, which he laid down and took up again by his own authority (John 10:18). Paul was not offering Athens a pair of new gods to add to its collection. He was offering them the one Lord who has death in his hands.

The Areopagus. The Areopagus, the Mars Hill of the older English Bibles, was both a rocky outcrop north-west of the Acropolis and the venerable council named after it, Athens’s supreme authority in matters of religion, morals and education, which by Paul’s day may often have met down in the marketplace. To be brought before it was not a formal trial so much as an examination by the gatekeepers of what ideas and gods Athens would entertain.

Do I need to understand philosophy to share the gospel? No, but it helps to understand the person in front of you. Paul knew what Epicureans and Stoics believed because he had listened in the marketplace. Your neighbours are rarely trained philosophers, but they all have working beliefs: that this life is all there is, that God is distant, that everything happens for a reason, that you should just be true to yourself. Learning to hear those beliefs, and kindly showing where they fall short and where Christ answers what they were reaching for, is what Paul is doing here. It takes curiosity and love more than a degree.
verseByVerse.note: Epicureans taught that the gods were remote and the aim of life was a calm, untroubled pleasure; Stoics taught living by reason and duty. “Babbler” is literally “seed-picker” — like a bird pecking up scraps of learning. The Areopagus was the city’s ancient council, named after the Hill of Ares.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strange things. It is a courteous sentence and also a summons. Strange (xenizonta) is the word for foreign, alien, surprising, belonging somewhere else. They are not saying the message is offensive; they are saying it does not fit any of the shelves they own. A crucified Jewish workman raised bodily from the dead and appointed judge of the world does not correspond to anything in Greek philosophy or Greek religion, and the philosophers were quite right to find it foreign.

We wish to know. Curiosity, at least, and an open door. Paul takes it at face value: he does not complain about their motives or demand a better attitude before he will speak.

Interest is not yet obedience. But Luke’s very next remark is that the Athenians spent their time on nothing except telling or hearing something new. That is not cynicism; two of them are named as converts by the end of the chapter. It means Luke knows the difference between an appetite for the interesting and a willingness to be changed.

A distinction to turn on ourselves. A person can consume a great deal about God, sermons, books, podcasts, with genuine interest, and let the interest stand in for obedience. If you fear that this describes you, bring your interest to Christ as it is: he does not turn away those who come wanting to want him (John 6:37).

Herod was glad to see him. Luke has shown this curiosity before, aimed at Jesus himself: Herod was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him and was hoping to see some sign done by him (Luke 23:8). Jesus made him no answer. Now the risen Christ, through his apostle, answers another audience that wants to know, fully and plainly, down to the day of judgment and the empty tomb. That is grace. But the answer is not a curiosity to be enjoyed. It ends with a command to repent.

What should I do when a friend is curious about Christianity? Treat the curiosity as an open door, and walk through it gladly, as Paul did. Answer the question actually asked, simply and honestly, and if you do not know the answer, say so and find out. Offer to read a Gospel together; Mark can be read in an evening. But do not confuse interest with faith, theirs or yours. Gently, at the right moment, make it personal: what would it mean for you if this were true? Curiosity can lead to Christ, but only if the conversation eventually reaches him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something newer. Luke steps aside to describe the city, because everything on the Areopagus depends on it: Athens loved ideas as entertainment. The comparative, something newer, pictures an appetite not for novelty as such but for the next one, which can never be satisfied, only fed. Athens had lost its politics to Rome and its trade to Corinth; what remained was its reputation and its conversation. And Luke includes the foreigners: a culture forms its residents more quietly than they realise.

Investigation or entertainment. This is a description and not a denunciation. Curiosity is not a sin; Luke has just praised the synagogue at Berea for examining the Scriptures daily. The difference between Berea and Athens is not how much they liked ideas. It is what they thought ideas were for. Berea tested a claim to find out whether it was true, because if it was true something would have to happen. Athens sampled a claim to see whether it was interesting. The first is investigation. The second is entertainment with a serious face on. It is a danger for every generation: always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth, gathering teachers to suit itching ears (2 Timothy 3:7; 4:3).

The one thing that cannot be sampled. When Paul reaches the resurrection, the city that would listen to anything discovers it has a limit. An audience open to every idea is usually open only to ideas that ask nothing of it, and Athens is about to be handed something that cannot be tasted and put down, because it is not an idea at all. It is a man, raised from the dead and appointed to judge the world, and he will not stay on the shelf. The newest thing that ever happened in history happened to the one who is older than history (Hebrews 13:8). Athens wanted something newer. It was offered someone eternal.

Is it wrong to enjoy new ideas and learning? Not at all. Every true discovery is a glimpse of God’s world and God’s wisdom, and Christians have been among the most curious people in history. The problem is curiosity that never commits, that treats God as a topic rather than as the Lord. So enjoy learning, and let it end in worship. When you meet something new about God, ask not only whether it is interesting but whether it is true, and if it is, what it requires of you. Old truths, rightly heard, are often the newest thing a person can learn.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown god." What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Very religious. The opening word is deliberately double-edged. Deisidaimonesterous can mean religious, careful about the gods, or it can mean superstitious, and Paul’s hearers would have heard both. It is a compliment they could accept and an accurate diagnosis at the same time. (The KJV’s too superstitious takes the word in its harsher sense.) Paul starts respectfully, without mocking them but without approving either, because the ambiguity is the truth about them. These people genuinely are reaching for God. They are also getting it comprehensively wrong.

In the flow. Here one of the most carefully built speeches in Acts begins. It moves from their altar (v. 23) to God the Creator who needs nothing (vv. 24–25), humanity made from one man to seek him (vv. 26–28), idolatry and the command to repent (vv. 29–30), and judgment by the man God raised (v. 31): from what they half knew to what they could not know without being told.

As I passed along. The sermon was not brought in his luggage; it was written in the streets by a man paying attention to what the people in front of him actually did.

An altar to the unknown god. Ancient writers mention altars to unknown gods in Athens, set up so that no god was offended or left out. Diogenes Laertius tells how, centuries earlier, during a plague which no sacrifice would lift, the Athenians sent for Epimenides of Crete, the poet many think Paul quotes in a moment, and on his advice turned sheep loose on the Areopagus and built an altar wherever one lay down, to whatever god was responsible and had not yet been named. The altar was not humility. It was insurance.

What you worship as unknown. A great deal is built on this sentence that it will not carry. It is sometimes read as though Paul were saying that the Athenians were worshipping the true God all along under another name, and that all sincere religion arrives at the same place. He does not say that. He says they worship in ignorance (the KJV’s whom follows later manuscripts; the earliest read what, which fits his point that they did not know the one they reached for), and within seven verses he tells them that the times of that ignorance are over and God now commands them to repent. You do not summon people to repentance for worshipping the right God correctly.

A confession filled. What he does say is subtler and better. Their altar is an admission, carved in stone in the middle of their own city, that their religion is incomplete and has not reached the end of the matter. There is a God they have not named. Paul does not baptise their worship; he takes their confession of ignorance and offers to fill it. He will make the unknown God known.

What could the Athenians know of God? Paul says elsewhere that God’s eternal power and divine nature have been clearly perceived in creation (Romans 1:20), and that the work of the law is written on every heart (Romans 2:14–15). The altar to an unknown god shows a people who knew there was more than their idols. But that knowledge left them without excuse, not without need; it could not tell them who God is or how a sinner may be reconciled to him. That is why Paul proclaims what they did not know.

Do people of other religions worship the true God without knowing it? No. This verse is often used to say so, but Paul says the opposite: the Athenians worshipped in ignorance and needed to repent. Every person knows something of God from creation and conscience, and many religions contain true and beautiful insights. But no one is reconciled to God by sincere worship of a god they do not know. Salvation comes through conscious faith in Jesus Christ, the one mediator between God and men (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5). That is not narrowness; it is why Paul crossed the sea to tell them. If they could be saved without hearing, Paul’s urgent journey to the Areopagus would hardly have been needed.

He has made him known. How will Paul make the unknown God known? Not by a better argument about altars, but by a man. The sermon that opens at this altar closes with the man God raised from the dead, and the whole distance between them is the distance the Son came. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known (John 1:18). Jesus told Philip, Whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9). The Athenians had built an altar to the edge of their knowledge and left it blank. God has written on that blank space a name, Jesus, and a face that can be known.

Every person’s unknown altar. Here is a model for beginning with somebody who does not want a lecture. Paul does not open with their sin, though he will reach it. He opens with the thing in their own life that does not add up, and which they have already half-admitted. Every person has an altar to an unknown god somewhere: a longing they cannot account for, a standard they hold others to and cannot meet, a fear of death they do not discuss. The question is not whether they have one. It is whether you have been paying attention as you passed along.
verseByVerse.note: “Very religious” could be a compliment or mean “very superstitious.” Ancient writers mention altars at Athens dedicated to unknown gods.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who made the world. He begins at the beginning, with creation, because this audience has no Bible. There is no point saying as it is written to men who do not accept the writing. So Paul starts with the one thing every human being has in front of him: the world exists, and it did not make itself.

Being Lord of heaven and earth. In one clause he has already parted company with both schools in the room. God made the world, so he is not the indifferent absentee of the Epicureans. And he is Lord of it, over it, distinct from it, so he is not the Stoics’ divine reason diffused through everything. He is personal, and other than what he has made: against pantheism, which says everything is God, and against materialism, which says there is nothing but matter.

Does not live in temples made by man. If the council met near the Areopagus, Paul had the Parthenon in view over his shoulder: one of the most beautiful buildings in the world, holding a statue of Athena some forty feet high in gold and ivory, the pride and the treasury of the city. And he says, to the men responsible for all of it, that the God who matters does not live in any of them. It is close to what Stephen said about the temple in Jerusalem shortly before he was stoned (7:48), and Paul is saying it in Athens about theirs. The argument cuts both ways and always has: a God who can be housed is a God who can be managed.

A temple not made with hands. And yet God has chosen to dwell with men, in a way no architect could have designed. Jesus’ accusers quoted him: I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands (Mark 14:58), and he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:21). The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9): not a part of God or a likeness of him, but God himself living in a human body. Athens had built the most beautiful house on earth for a goddess who was not there. God built his own temple, in the person of his Son, and it is the only one that has ever been truly filled.

Not served by human hands. Athens ran on the assumption that the gods required feeding: sacrifices, festivals, a priesthood, and the meat trade that went with it. Religion was a transaction in which the gods got what they needed and the city got protection. Paul says God is self-sufficient. He does not need our sacrifices, our worship, or anything (Psalm 50:9–12), and therefore the entire arrangement is upside down. Many people keep the same bargain in Christian clothes: if I pray, give and behave, God owes me a quiet life. Paul’s God cannot be put in anyone’s debt (Romans 11:35–36), and that ends the bargain.

He himself gives. Then a clause of enormous kindness: the traffic runs the other way. They have been carrying things up the hill to a God who has been supplying them the whole time, including the men on the council who are about to laugh.

A comfort for the useless. If God needed nothing from Athens, he needs nothing from you either. Your service, your giving, your usefulness are not contributions to a God who was running short; he asks for them for your sake. Which means the day you can do none of them, through illness, age or exhaustion, you have not become a worse investment. You were never an investment. You were always a child being given things.

If God needs nothing, why should I worship, pray or serve? Because he is worthy, and because it is good for us. A father does not need his child’s drawing, yet he delights in it and puts it on the wall. God does not need our worship, but he is glorified in it and delights in it, and we were made for it: we find fullness of joy nowhere but in his presence (Psalm 16:11). Prayer does not inform God or supply him; it is how he has chosen to give us what he has promised, and how we learn to depend on him. Service does not add to his wealth; it shares in his work, as a privilege. Nothing we do makes him more. Everything we do for him makes us more fully what we were made to be.

On a Tuesday. Try counting the gifts of one ordinary day, from breath on waking to sleep at night, and thank him for each by name.

parallels.desc: who gives breath to the people

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
From one man. The Athenians held that they were autochthonous: sprung from the soil of Attica itself, not migrants like everybody else. The orators repeated it at public funerals, and it grounded their conviction that they were better than the rest of the world: Greeks above barbarians, and Athenians the truest of the Greeks because they alone had grown where they stood. And Paul, standing in front of the council of that city, says every nation on earth came out of one man.

Every race of one blood. All humanity comes from one man, Adam (Genesis 1–2; Romans 5:12). If that is true, the Athenian in the front row, the slave carrying his shopping and the Scythian on the edge of the world are relatives, and the distinction the city rested on does not exist. Every scheme that has ever ranked human beings by descent contradicts this verse, and Paul preached it to the people most invested in the opposite. (The KJV and NKJV read of one blood, following later manuscripts; the earliest read simply from one, and most modern Bibles say from one man.)

Where Christians differ: one man. Some today regard Adam as a symbol rather than a historical person. This commentary’s view: Paul here, and in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, treats Adam as a real man from whom all nations descend, and whose sin and death spread to all. The unity of the human race, and the gospel of the second Adam, rest on it. Christians who read Adam otherwise often do so from a sincere wish to honour both Scripture and science, and they deserve a patient hearing; the reason for this view is that Paul’s parallel between Adam and Christ (Romans 5:12–19) needs both to be real men, and Adam and Eve to be real people, specially created by God (Genesis 2:7, 22).

Periods and boundaries. God has fixed for every nation its times, the rise, fall and duration of every people, and its places, the borders of its lands. Determined (horisas) means marked out, decreed: not blind chance, the Epicurean view, nor impersonal Fate, the Stoic one, but the appointment of the living, personal God, who removes kings and sets up kings (Daniel 2:21). A humbling word to proud Athens, and a steadying one for us when the headlines look out of control.

Feel their way toward him. The arranging has a gracious aim. Feel their way (psēlaphēseian) means to grope, as a blind man in the dark. And it lands personally: your century, your country, your town, the family you were born into were set on purpose, that you would seek him and find him (Psalm 139:16). Where and when you live is not an accident; it is an appointment, a kindness designed to bring you home to the God who is near.

Does this mean that unbelievers really seek God? Paul says no one seeks for God (Romans 3:11). Here he states God’s purpose in arranging the nations, that people should seek him, and his phrase feel their way toward him pictures the groping of the blind, who may not find. Fallen humanity gropes for God but cannot find him by its own search. Left to themselves, people turn away from the God they half know. Those who truly find him do so because he first seeks them (18:10; Luke 19:10).

Not far from each one of us. The problem is not his distance but our blindness. God is not spread thinly through everything; there is simply no place where he is absent and no one he is far from (Psalm 139:7–10; Jeremiah 23:23–24), and Paul preaches it to a city full of shrines built on the opposite assumption.

One man and the Man. Paul’s sermon is bracketed by two men: the one man from whom God made every nation, and the man whom God has appointed to judge the world and raised from the dead (v. 31). Paul explains the pairing elsewhere: As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive (1 Corinthians 15:22). From the first, every nation inherited its life, its scattering and its death. In the second, a new humanity is being gathered from all those nations, one by one, through faith.

Does one human race mean ethnic and cultural differences do not matter? No. They matter, and they are God’s good gift: he made the nations and set their places, and in the end people from every tribe and language will stand before the throne, recognisably themselves (Revelation 7:9). What this verse forbids is ranking them. No nation is nearer to God by birth, and no race is lesser. In a church that means the stranger is welcomed as family, prejudice is repented of rather than excused, and the fellowship around the Lord’s Table is the clearest picture on earth of the one blood and the one Saviour.

parallels.desc: he fixed the borders of the peoples

verseByVerse.quote: "'for "In him we live and move and have our being"; as even some of your own poets have said, "For we are indeed his offspring."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him we live. Paul quotes two pagan poets to a pagan audience, and both lines probably come from poems about Zeus. The first is traditionally credited to Epimenides, the Cretan sage of about 600 BC.

His offspring. The second is from the Phaenomena of Aratus, a Stoic poet of about 270 BC from Cilicia, Paul’s own home region. Paul knew Greek literature and used it as common ground. So what is he doing, and how far does it license us to go?

A true sentence in a false frame. First, what he does not do. He does not say the poets were right about Zeus. He does not treat their religion as another road to the same place; he is two verses from telling them to repent. He takes a true sentence out of a false frame and puts it in the true one. Pagans said something accurate about the dependence of every living thing on God, and got the name of the God wrong, and Paul keeps the accurate part and corrects the address. He does it elsewhere too. Writing to Titus about Crete, he quotes Epimenides again, and this time the line is an insult about Cretans, and Paul says flatly that this testimony is true (Titus 1:12–13). He is quite willing to say that an unbeliever has told the truth.

Two errors avoided. One error is to treat everything outside the church as poison; Paul could not have preached this sermon if he had thought so. The other is quoting whatever is popular in order to seem approachable; Paul uses two lines and then turns them against the whole religious system the poets belonged to. He is not borrowing credibility. He is taking territory.

Total dependence. This is not pantheism; Paul has just insisted God is distinct from what he made. It is total creaturely dependence: the life you are living at this moment is on loan, and so is the breath you are taking while you read the sentence. And the New Testament names the one who holds us so. All things were created through the Son and for him, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17); he upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3). And the wonder is that the Lord who sustains every life entered one, became dependent as a child is dependent, and laid his own life down. The poets glimpsed a God in whom we live. They never imagined a God who would die for those who live in him.

The turn of the argument. And we are indeed his offspring is the pivot of what follows. Paul lets it stand, in the sense that every human being is God’s creature and bears his image, and then he is about to turn it round on them with considerable force. If we are his offspring, then whatever God is like, he is at least as alive as we are. And that is exactly what a statue is not.

If we are all God’s offspring, are we all God’s children? In one sense yes, in another no, and the difference matters. Every human being is God’s offspring by creation: made by him, in his image, dependent on him, and loved by him as his creature. But Scripture keeps the name children of God, in the saving sense, for those who receive Christ and are born of God (John 1:12–13; Galatians 3:26). So we can say to anyone, you were made by God and for God; and we must also say, you need to be adopted into his family through his Son. Both are true, and the gospel needs both.

Can I use films, songs and books in sharing the gospel? Yes, as Paul did, with care. Look for the true thing a story or song has glimpsed: a longing for home, a hunger for justice, a sense of guilt, a hope that death is not the end. Name it honestly, and then show where it is fulfilled in Christ. Two cautions from this passage. Do not endorse the frame along with the line; Paul quoted a hymn to Zeus without praising Zeus. And do not stop at the common ground. Paul spent two lines on the poets and then went straight to repentance, judgment and the resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes Greek poets. “For we are indeed his offspring” comes from Aratus; the first line is often attributed to Epimenides.

parallels.desc: Paul quotes a Cretan prophet

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not like gold or silver or stone. The argument is powerful because it is so simple. If we are God’s offspring, living, thinking, choosing, then God is at least that, and a thing made of metal or rock is not. The child cannot make the parent. A living creature manufactures a dead object and then bows to it. Whatever is true of God, he cannot be less alive than the man holding the chisel.

Art and imagination. Paul puts two words at the end: art and imagination. The idol is not merely stone; it is stone plus a human idea. Somebody decided what the god should look like, and then made it look like that. Which means the worshipper is, in the end, kneeling to his own conception, and the god will never require anything of him that he did not first think of himself.

The modern version. That is why idolatry is so durable, and why the modern version is not statues. The manufacture of a god out of the art and imagination of man is a live industry, generally done in the first person: a God assembled out of the attributes we approve of, who is offended by the sins we do not commit and relaxed about the ones we do. It has exactly the defect Paul names: it cannot say anything to you that you did not put in it.

The times of ignorance God overlooked. Overlooked does not mean excused, and it does not mean God did not care. The word means passed over, let go by without pressing the matter, holding back judgment in patience: the same patience Paul described to the farmers at Lystra, where God allowed the nations to walk in their own ways and yet sent them rain and harvests (14:16–17). This is the other end of that patience. It has an expiry date, and the date has passed.

Why the overlooking could end. God’s patience ends now because of what has happened in the meantime. God put forward Christ Jesus as a propitiation by his blood (a propitiation is an offering that satisfies God’s holy wrath, so that the judgement sinners deserved is spent on the substitute), to show his righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins (Romans 3:25–26). The overlooking was never indifference; God held back the full judgment of the nations’ sins because he had determined to deal with sin justly at the cross. The times of ignorance were the long night before the Son came; the but now of this verse is the daylight of Good Friday and Easter, and that is why the command can go out to everyone.

Were those who lived before the gospel saved by their ignorance? No. Their ignorance was not innocence; they had the light of creation and suppressed it (Romans 1:18–21). Overlooked means that God held back the full judgment their sins deserved, as Paul says God passed over former sins in his forbearance (Romans 3:25). Now that Christ has come and the message is going to the nations, God commands all people everywhere to repent. The reason is the coming judgment by the risen man (v. 31).

But now he commands. Then the words that would have struck this audience hardest. Commands: not a recommendation to those who find it congenial, but an order. And all people everywhere, said to a council that divided the human race into Greeks and barbarians, philosophers included. One man and every nation comes back as a universal summons: if we all came from one, we are all answerable to one.

What repentance is. Repentance is a change of mind about God that turns the whole person round: turning from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). It is not merely feeling sorry, and it is not first giving up a list of bad habits. It is a new verdict on God, that he is real, holy and good, and a new verdict on ourselves, that we have been worshipping what is not God, followed by a turn of the whole life towards him, trusting his mercy in Christ. And this is the first word of demand in the entire sermon: only now, having taken the ground from under the idols, does Paul tell them to turn round.

If repentance is commanded, is it something I do or something God gives? Both, and Scripture says both without embarrassment. God commands everyone to repent, so no one may excuse himself by waiting for a feeling. Yet repentance is also God’s gift: he granted repentance that leads to life even to the Gentiles (11:18), and he opens hearts as he opened Lydia’s (16:14). The two do not compete. When you hear the command and turn to Christ, you are doing what you were told, and you will discover afterwards that it was God working in you to will and to work (Philippians 2:13). So do not wait. Obey the command, and thank him for the gift.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly: when did the God I believe in last contradict me? Then open your Bible at a passage you have tended to avoid, and let God say something you would not have said yourself. Where he contradicts you, that is where repentance begins, and the God who commands it is faithful to forgive all that you find there (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "'because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has fixed a day. To an Athenian every clause here is an impossibility. He has fixed a day: not a cycle, not the endless recurrence of ages the Stoics taught, but an end, a date already set in a diary that is not ours. Nothing about it is contingent on whether the Areopagus finds the idea plausible.

In righteousness. The Epicureans in the audience believed that death ends the matter and there is nothing to fear; that is the comfort their whole system was built to give. Paul removes it in a single clause. God will judge the whole world, justly.

Judgment as hope. Judgment is not only a threat. A fixed day when the world is finally assessed in righteousness is, for anyone who has been genuinely wronged, the only hope there is. Every human court is partial, late or bought; this one will not be. Nothing done in the dark to a person nobody defended will go unaddressed, which is why Scripture speaks of the coming judgment as something the whole creation waits for with longing, and the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth (Psalm 96:12–13).

By a man whom he has appointed. Here the sermon stops being philosophy. God will judge the world not through fate or a principle but by a man, with a name, who lived at a particular address. It is Jesus, though Paul does not name him yet. And there is mercy in that arrangement. The one who will assess a human life has lived one. He knows from the inside what it is to be tired, poor, betrayed and afraid. The judge is not an outsider to the conditions he is judging; the Father has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man (John 5:27).

He has given assurance. The word for assurance is pistis, which usually means faith, but in the courts and the market it meant a guarantee, a proof, the security you offer to make a claim credible. God has posted a bond. The resurrection is offered here not as a comforting doctrine but as the evidence for the appointment, the public demonstration that the man in question is the one. It is good news and also a warning: the risen man will judge you.

In the flow. The whole speech has been heading for this verse, the climax of the great sermons in Acts (2:24, 32; 10:40–42; 13:30–37): whether the hearers are Jews with the Scriptures or Greeks without them, the gospel ends at the empty tomb.

To all. Not to insiders or the initiated: it is a public claim about a real event, open to anyone willing to look into it. So the sermon that began with an altar to a god nobody could name ends with a man everybody can.

Will Christians be judged too? Yes, but not to decide whether we belong to God. That was settled at the cross: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Believers will stand before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), where their lives are opened and what was done for him is acknowledged, but the verdict on their persons has already been given. That verdict is justification: the Judge’s own acquittal of the guilty, pronounced in advance, resting on Christ’s record instead of theirs and received by faith (Romans 5:1). And the Judge is the Saviour who died for them. That is why a Christian can say the last day is a hope: the man appointed to judge is the man who bore our judgment.

Why did Paul not mention the cross in this sermon? Very probably he did, or meant to. Luke gives us a summary, and the speech was interrupted before Paul had finished (v. 32). The resurrection presupposes a death, and Paul everywhere preached Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). With hearers who had no Bible, he had to lay the foundation first: who God is, who we are, and why we need a Saviour, judgment being the reason. That is a wise order for anyone speaking to people with no Christian background. Do not begin with the answer before they know the question; but do not stop before you reach the cross.

On a Tuesday. The only way to be ready for the fixed day is to be found in the Judge himself, trusting him now as Saviour: not with a record of your own, for even your best obedience is flawed, but with his perfect obedience counted as yours (Philippians 3:9). And if you have been wronged and see no justice coming, hand the case to the one who will judge in righteousness. You do not have to settle every account yourself; a day has been fixed.

parallels.desc: he will judge the world in righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this.' So Paul went out from their midst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some mocked. Creation, providence, the unity of the human race, even the summons to repent had been strange but discussable. The resurrection is where an audience that would listen to anything stopped listening.

Why the Greeks laughed. It was not stupidity. Most educated Greeks did not want the body back. Many believed the body was a prison for the soul, and death, on the best Greek view, was the soul’s release from it. To announce that a man had been raised bodily was not to offer them a hope. It was to propose returning a prisoner to his cell. The resurrection was the stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23; 15:12).

On their own hill. There is a line that makes the moment sharper still. In the Eumenides of Aeschylus, a play set at the founding of this very council and known to every educated Athenian, Apollo declares that when the dust has drunk up a man’s blood, once he is dead there is no resurrection. The word he uses is anastasis, Paul’s word. That is the Athenian creed on the subject, spoken on the Areopagus in their own literature. Paul stands on the same ground and contradicts it.

Flesh and bones. Athens was not the first audience to find the news unbelievable: the women’s words seemed to the apostles an idle tale, and they did not believe them (Luke 24:11). What changed their minds was the risen Lord himself: See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have (Luke 24:39). Luke, who wrote both books, knew exactly what the Areopagus was laughing at: not a soul escaping, but a body raised. The mockers on Mars Hill were laughing at a man who had eaten broiled fish in front of his friends.

We will hear you again. The second response is the most common one in any century: not refutation but postponement. Some of them may have meant it, and at least one member of that council came to believe (v. 34). But a subject can be kept permanently open, and Felix will do the same thing to Paul at greater length a few chapters later, sending for him often and deciding nothing (24:25–27).

Paul went out. The speech was interrupted, as speeches often are in Acts. He had reached the resurrection, the thing he came to say, and when it was refused he did not stay to soften it.

Was Athens a failure that Paul learned from? It is often suggested that he over-reached with philosophy and poetry, got a poor return, and afterwards resolved to do it differently, deciding to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2), a resolve he made at Corinth, the very next city. It is a tidy theory and there are reasons to doubt it. Paul did preach Christ risen at Athens; that is precisely what they mocked, and he was not withholding the offensive part. Luke, who chose what to include, gives this speech more space than almost any other and presents it as a model of preaching to people with no Bible. And the contrast Paul draws in 1 Corinthians is not with wise engagement but with polished oratory and human cleverness as a means of persuasion, a warning about method written to a church that was addicted to celebrity speakers. What is fair to say is that Athens was hard ground and Luke does not pretend otherwise. Some places take a long time. That is not the same as having done it wrong.

Is it reasonable to believe in a bodily resurrection today? Yes, and the reason is not that people now know less than the Athenians did. Everyone on that hill knew that dead men stay dead; that is why they laughed. The Christian claim has never been that dead men usually rise, but that this one did. The tomb was empty, and nobody could produce the body. More than five hundred people saw him alive, most of them still living when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Frightened men became witnesses who would die rather than deny it. Sceptics have proposed other explanations, from a stolen body to visions born of grief; Christians answer that none accounts for all these facts together, and the honest course is to read the accounts for yourself. And if God made the world and everything in it (v. 24), raising one body is not beyond him. So the question that matters is what it means for you if it did.

What should I do when people laugh at what I believe? Expect it, and do not take it as the last word. The resurrection was laughed at on the day it was first preached to the clever, and it has outlived every one of the men who laughed. Do not answer mockery with mockery, and do not water down the claim to stop the laughing; Paul did neither. Say the true thing clearly and kindly, and leave it. Then notice the others in the room: the ones who want to hear again, and the quiet one who believes. Mockery is loud, but it is rarely the only response.
verseByVerse.note: Most Greeks found bodily resurrection absurd.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dionysius the Areopagite. He names two people. Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council itself, a man of high standing: one of the men who had summoned Paul to explain himself, sitting in judgment on whether this teaching should be allowed a hearing in Athens. The court examined the gospel and one of the judges came over. Tradition, recorded by Eusebius, says he became the first bishop of Athens.

Damaris and others. We know nothing more of her, and we should not invent her. But Luke keeps her name, in one of the most male settings in the book, and the two converts he chooses to name are a member of the aristocracy and a woman. And others with them: unnumbered and unnamed, and that is the whole recorded harvest of one of the most celebrated sermons in Acts.

The honest figure. At Thessalonica, a great many. At Berea, many. At Corinth, where he goes next, so many that the Lord tells him in a vision to go on speaking because he has many in that city who are his people (18:10). At Athens, two names and some others. And Luke writes it down. He does not pad it or explain it away.

The judge who met the Judge. That morning Dionysius had sat on the council to examine a strange teacher, and heard that God will judge the world by a man he has raised from the dead. He believed it, bowed to the Judge of the world, and found him a Saviour. In the very hour his resurrection was mocked, the risen Christ was already drawing his own to himself, as he had said: I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself (John 12:32).

The apostolic standard. One of the most carefully argued sermons in the New Testament, preached by an apostle in a famous centre of learning, produced a handful of people. If your own work has produced a handful, you are not below the apostolic standard. You are on it. Nobody remembers who mocked. We know who believed.

Why do some believe and others mock at the same sermon? Because faith is God’s gift, not the preacher’s achievement. The same words fell on the whole council; the difference was not in Paul but in what God did in the hearts of Dionysius and Damaris. As Luke said at Pisidian Antioch, as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (13:48). Behind that sentence stands election: God’s choice, before the foundation of the world, of those he would save, made out of his own love and not on the basis of their merit (Ephesians 1:4–5). This is not a reason for careless preaching, for God uses means, and Paul prepared carefully. But it is a great comfort. You are responsible for faithfulness, not for results, and you never know which quiet listener the Lord has already chosen to open.
verseByVerse.note: Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council.

17.theology: General revelation and the need for the gospel. Acts 17 shows what theologians call general revelation: the knowledge of God open to everyone through creation and conscience (Romans 1:18–20). The Athenians are groping toward God, but groping is not finding. Creation raises the question, and only the gospel answers it: the God who made the nations and is not far from any of us has now spoken in a man he raised from the dead, and calls all people everywhere to repent. Without the gospel, general revelation saves no one; it leaves everyone without excuse.
17.examples:
Then: Paul in Athens, his spirit provoked, stood before the city’s learned men with the news of a crucified and risen Jew. Some mocked, some believed, and he moved on, leaving Dionysius, Damaris and a few others behind him.

Now: Many people around us are, like Athens, educated, restless and wary of exclusive claims to truth. The Areopagus speech shows a way to speak to them: begin where they are, own what is true in their searching, and then speak of the risen Christ without apology. The resurrection is still the stumbling block, and still the answer to the altar to an unknown god.

18.title: Corinth
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. <sup>2</sup>And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them, <sup>3</sup>and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. <sup>4</sup>And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. <sup>5</sup>When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” <sup>7</sup>And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. <sup>8</sup>Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. <sup>9</sup>And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, <sup>10</sup>for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.” <sup>11</sup>And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. <sup>12</sup>But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, <sup>13</sup>saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.” <sup>14</sup>But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. <sup>15</sup>But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.” <sup>16</sup>And he drove them from the tribunal. <sup>17</sup>And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. <sup>18</sup>After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow. <sup>19</sup>And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. <sup>20</sup>When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined. <sup>21</sup>But on taking leave of them he said, “I will return to you if God wills,” and he set sail from Ephesus. <sup>22</sup>When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. <sup>24</sup>Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. <sup>25</sup>He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. <sup>26</sup>He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. <sup>27</sup>And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, <sup>28</sup>for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
18.overview:
From Athens Paul goes to Corinth, the wealthy commercial city on the isthmus and capital of the province of Achaia (see the introduction to 1 Corinthians). He lodges and works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews recently expelled from Rome by the emperor Claudius, an expulsion the Roman historian Suetonius connects with riots over “Chrestus”, probably disputes about Christ, around AD 49. Opposed in the synagogue, Paul moves next door; the synagogue ruler believes, and a night vision keeps him in the city for eighteen months.

The proconsul Gallio dismisses the case brought against him as a Jewish quarrel, a ruling that gave the church breathing space; an inscription at Delphi dates Gallio’s year to about AD 51–52, one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life. Paul returns to Antioch, ending his second journey, and sets out on the third. Meanwhile in Ephesus Priscilla and Aquila take aside a gifted preacher from Alexandria, Apollos, and complete his understanding before he goes on to strengthen the church in Corinth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Corinth and the Return to Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s eighteen months in Corinth: work at a tentmaker’s bench, a break with the synagogue, a household and many Corinthians coming to faith, the Lord’s promise in the night, and a Roman governor who refuses to hear the case against him. The section closes with Paul’s journey home by Ephesus, Jerusalem and Antioch.
verseByVerse.theology:
Tentmaking and the support of ministry

Here for the first time Acts mentions Paul’s manual work as a means of supporting his mission.
