Paul’s letters show it was an adaptation, not the only pattern: he worked with his hands so as not to burden new churches and to set an example, but he accepted support from established churches (Philippians 4:15–16), and in Corinth itself the gifts brought by Silas and Timothy from Macedonia freed him to preach full time (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Gallio’s dismissal of the charge against Paul protected his preaching at Corinth by treating it as an internal Jewish dispute. Now: God still uses civil authorities and courts to shelter the preaching of the gospel, even when those in power have no understanding of it or sympathy with it.

verseByVerse.quote: "After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Over the whole chapter stands the Lord Jesus, who comes to a frightened apostle at night, already owns people in the most notorious city in Greece, and turns emperors, proconsuls and tentmakers alike to the service of his gospel.

To Corinth. About fifty miles west, and a complete change of world. Athens was a university town living on its past; Corinth was money. Rome had destroyed the old city and a century later refounded it as a colony for freedmen and veterans. By Paul’s day it was the capital of Achaia and one of the richest ports in the empire, on the isthmus between two seas, with a harbour on each. It was about a hundred years old and behaved like it.

To Corinthianise. Its reputation was appalling and had been for centuries; the Greeks had a verb, to Corinthianise, which meant to live immorally. So Paul walks out of the Greek world’s most famous seat of learning, where he had won only a handful of converts, into one of its most notorious cities, alone and with no contacts. And he tells us how it felt: he came to them in weakness and in fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3).

Aquila and Priscilla. A married couple who became Paul’s close friends and co-workers (Romans 16:3–5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Timothy 4:19). Priscilla (Prisca) is often named first, perhaps because she was more prominent or of higher social standing. Luke never records their conversion, and never calls them converts of Paul’s; they simply appear as believers, which suggests they may already have been Christians from the church in Rome, years before Paul wrote to it.

Claudius’s edict. Here the New Testament and Roman history touch. The Roman biographer Suetonius records that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly rioting at the instigation of Chrestus, probably a garbled form of Christ, an expulsion usually dated to about AD 49. If the gospel had reached the Jewish quarter of Rome, a Roman official would have seen exactly what Acts shows in city after city: a synagogue in uproar over a man called Christ.

A forced removal. If that is right, the edict that threw Aquila and Priscilla out of their home was imperial policy about a quarrel the emperor did not understand, concerning the very gospel about to be preached in Corinth. And it delivered to a lonely and frightened apostle two of the most useful colleagues he would ever have. They will house him, work beside him, teach Apollos, risk their necks for him (Romans 16:4), and host churches in more than one city. One of the most fruitful partnerships in the New Testament began with an expulsion.

Another emperor, another decree. Luke has shown us this before. A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered (Luke 2:1), and it sent a carpenter and his pregnant wife to Bethlehem, where the prophet had said the ruler of Israel would be born (Micah 5:2). Now Claudius signs an order about a riot over Christ, and it sends a tentmaker and his wife to Corinth, where Christ means to build his church. The emperors issue their decrees, and the Son of God moves through them unhindered.

What if my move, job loss or upheaval was forced on me? Then you are in good company, and in good hands. Aquila and Priscilla lost their home, their business and their city by an emperor’s signature, and the Lord used it to put them exactly where his apostle needed them. That does not make the loss painless, and you need not pretend it was. But it means the decision taken over your head was not the last word on your life. The God who works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28) is not waiting for better rulers before he can use you. Ask him, in the new place, whom he has set beside you, and whom he has set you beside.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth, the capital of the province of Achaia, was a busy, wealthy trading city with a reputation for immorality. The Roman historian Suetonius mentions Claudius expelling Jews from Rome over disturbances, around AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: "and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tentmakers. They worked with leather and with the coarse goats’-hair cloth for which Cilicia, Paul’s home province, was known: a trade of the awl and the knife, hard on the hands, and unglamorous. Jewish teachers were encouraged to learn a trade rather than make money from teaching the law, so Paul the Pharisee, trained under Gamaliel, had also been trained to cut leather, and in Corinth it kept him alive.

Six days at the bench. It is easy to read Acts and imagine a full-time evangelist. In the ancient city the working day ran from first light until the light went, and Paul was at the bench for it. He tells this very church that they labour, working with their own hands (1 Corinthians 4:12), and the Thessalonians that he worked night and day so as not to be a burden to any of them (1 Thessalonians 2:9). He supported himself to remove any suspicion that he preached for money, a charge he had to answer more than once at Corinth. His trade was not an interruption of his ministry; it was part of it.

A workshop open to the street. So the church at Corinth was planted by a man who preached on the Sabbath and made tents the other six days, and who may well have done the two things in the same room. A workshop in that world was open to the street; customers came, apprentices worked, neighbours stopped. A great deal of the conversation that founded this church probably happened over the bench, with both men’s hands busy.

The carpenter’s apostle. At the bench Paul is following his Master more closely than it might seem. The people of Nazareth knew Jesus simply as the carpenter (Mark 6:3): the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3) probably made doors and yokes and roof beams for the village. So when the apostle sits cutting leather in Corinth he has not stepped down from his calling. He is walking where his Lord walked first, and in the Lord, he later wrote to this city, your labour is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Where Christians differ: should ministers be paid? Some say ministers should always work a trade like Paul; others that the church must always support them. This commentary’s view: Paul teaches that those who preach the gospel have a right to live by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:4–14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18), and he accepted gifts (Philippians 4:15–16; 2 Corinthians 11:8–9). But he sometimes gave up that right for the gospel’s sake. Both patterns are biblical. Churches should support their ministers generously; ministers may work when the work requires it.

How can my ordinary job serve the gospel? In at least three ways, all visible here. First, the work itself is service to God when it is done honestly and well, as for the Lord and not for men (Colossians 3:23); making a good tent is not spiritually neutral. Second, it puts you among people a pastor may never meet, on their ground and on equal terms, and conversations happen naturally there. Third, it gives you a life that commends the gospel: paying your way, keeping your word, not being a burden. You do not need to preach at the photocopier. Be the kind of colleague whose faith people ask about, and be ready when they do.
verseByVerse.note: Tentmakers worked with leather and cloth. Jewish teachers commonly had a trade; Paul supported himself so as not to burden the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every Sabbath. This was not a campaign but a routine, Sabbath after Sabbath, by a man who spent the other six days cutting leather. The second verb is honest. He tried to persuade. Luke does not say he persuaded them, and the wording leaves room for weeks when nothing seemed to happen.

Occupied with the word. Something changes when the two men arrive. Occupied (syneicheto) means wholly absorbed, held fast: from now on he is not fitting the gospel round the working day. What changed? When he was with them and in need, Paul writes, the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied his need (2 Corinthians 11:9; Philippians 4:15). Silas and Timothy probably brought gifts from the churches there, Philippi above all, and good news from Thessalonica too (1 Thessalonians 3:6), and an apostle put down his tools and preached full time.

What a gift buys. Giving to Christian work can feel abstract. Here it is not. The Macedonians were not wealthy; Paul says elsewhere that they gave out of extreme poverty, according to their means and beyond their means (2 Corinthians 8:2–3). What their gift bought was hours: the hours Paul would otherwise have spent at a bench, converted directly into hours in front of people. The church at Corinth exists partly because Christians in Philippi went without something.

That the Christ was Jesus. Not that Jesus was a Christ, or a good man, or a way, but that the Christ they had waited and prayed for every Sabbath in that building was this particular man. In Corinth Paul decided to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2): not a Messiah who had driven out Rome, but one Rome had nailed up, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Greeks, and yet the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). Everything else Paul preached hangs off that identification.

How much should I give, and to what? Scripture does not set a fixed percentage for Christians, but it gives clear principles: give regularly, in proportion to what you have, cheerfully and not under compulsion, and generously, as those who have received everything in Christ (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:9; 9:7). Your first responsibility is to your own church, so that those who teach you can give themselves to the word (Galatians 6:6). Beyond that, the Macedonians show the joy of supporting gospel work far away. Many Christians find a tenth a good starting point and grow from there. The question is not how little is required but what the grace of Christ moves you to give.

On a Tuesday. If you teach, children, a home group, a Sunday school, take heart that Paul tried to persuade week after week when nothing seemed to happen. Turning up again is part of the work.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.' And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they opposed and reviled him. Reviled (blasphēmountōn) can mean slandering a man or blaspheming God, and here it probably means both: insults against Paul and against the Christ he preached. The argument has stopped being an argument. And to insult the Son is to insult the holy God who sent him (Luke 10:16).

He shook out his garments. He shakes out his cloak, a gesture of breaking off responsibility, the same kind of prophetic sign as shaking the dust from the feet (13:51; Nehemiah 5:13). It says: I have nothing of yours on me, and I carry nothing away.

The watchman. Paul’s words are the language of Ezekiel 33: the watchman on the wall. If he sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, God will require the blood at his hand; if he blows it and the people do not take warning, their blood is on their own heads, and the watchman has delivered his soul (Ezekiel 33:1–9). Paul used the same language to the Ephesian elders (20:26).

The trumpet and the walls. The watchman is responsible for blowing the trumpet. He is not responsible for whether anybody comes inside the walls, and Ezekiel keeps the two rigorously apart. Paul has reasoned in that synagogue every Sabbath for weeks and been reviled for it, and what he says, in effect, is: the trumpet has been blown. His conscience is clear, not because he succeeded, but because he spoke.

For the one who grieves. That distinction matters greatly to the reader who carries a private grief about somebody unconverted: a father, a brother, a child who has heard it all and wants none of it. There is a burden that belongs to you and a burden that does not, and the two get mixed together until a person is worn out praying under the weight of an outcome he was never given charge of. You are answerable for the trumpet. You are not answerable for the walls. Paul could sound the trumpet; only Christ could open an ear, and salvation belongs to the Lord. So lay the weight down in prayer, and keep speaking when you can, loving always.

The watchman who wept. Paul learned this posture from his Lord, who also warned a city that would not listen. How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, Jesus said over Jerusalem, and you were not willing (Luke 13:34). And Ezekiel’s chapter gives the heart behind every warning: God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Christ is that heart in flesh. He did not only sound the alarm; he went outside the gate of the city that rejected him and suffered there (Hebrews 13:12), so that people who had reviled him could be brought home. Paul shakes out his cloak; his Master wept over the city that refused him.

Not a licence to give up. Paul says this to a synagogue that had turned hostile after long patience, not to someone who had said no once. And his resolve to go to the Gentiles holds for Corinth only: in the very next city he goes to the synagogue first again (v. 19).

Next door. A bold choice. He sets up the Christian meeting on the other side of the wall, in the house of a God-fearer who had presumably been sitting in that synagogue listening to him; some identify him with Gaius, Paul’s host in Corinth (Romans 16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14).

Standing where they cannot miss him. There is a certain steel in that, and it is not spite. The congregation that threw him out will have the believers meeting next door, including, in the very next verse, their own ruler. Paul has said he is going to the Gentiles, and he is standing where they cannot miss him: a door of mercy open beside a door of judgement.

When is it right to stop speaking to someone about Christ? Rarely, and never in the heart. Paul stopped arguing in this synagogue after months of open blasphemy, but he did not stop loving its people, praying for them or living in plain view of them; he wrote later that he would wish himself cut off for their sake (Romans 9:1–3). For most of us, with a family member or friend, the lesson is not to walk away but to change the mode: when words are only provoking scorn, keep praying, keep loving, keep living next door, and be ready when the door opens again. Jesus himself told his disciples not to throw pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6), but that was about wisdom in speaking, not permission to stop caring.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking out one’s garments was a gesture of breaking off responsibility.

parallels.desc: his blood shall be on his own head

verseByVerse.quote: "Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crispus believed. Read that immediately after verse 6, because Luke has put it there on purpose. Paul has just shaken out his garments at that synagogue and declared himself clear of it. And the first convert Luke names afterwards is the man who ran it.

Who the ruler was. The ruler of a synagogue was not a rabbi but the official responsible for the building and the services, the man who had been giving Paul the platform and quite possibly had to withdraw it: a person of standing, with everything to lose, and he believes. Years later Paul was thankful he had baptised almost none of the Corinthians, except Crispus and Gaius (1 Corinthians 1:14). And the ruler was not saved by his religion any more than the drunkards of Corinth were saved by turning over a new leaf; he came to Christ by the same door as they did, with empty hands.

Does this household baptism support infant baptism? Luke says the household believed, so this describes believers, as with Cornelius (10:44–48) and the jailer (16:34), though Christians who baptise infants read household baptisms as a covenant pattern. (See Acts 16:32 for the fuller answer.)

Many believed. Hearing, believing, baptism: the order again. Many, in the town whose name was a byword for vice. Paul lists later what some of them had been: idolaters, adulterers, thieves, drunkards, swindlers, a catalogue of the sins that city was famous for. And then he writes a sentence that has carried countless people out of their past. Such were some of you, he tells them, and then come three verbs, washed, sanctified, justified, all of it done in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Were. If you have a history that you assume disqualifies you, that verb was written to the church founded in this verse. Not are; were. And it did not change because the Corinthians reformed themselves, but because of the name in which they were washed: for our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). Washed: made clean of guilt. Sanctified: set apart as God’s own. Justified: declared righteous by God the Judge, not because they had become sinless overnight but because Christ’s righteousness was counted as theirs (Romans 4:5). The past is real, and it is past, because he has dealt with it.

If I was baptised as an infant, should I be baptised now? This is a question to take seriously and kindly. On the view this commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, baptism is for those who have repented and believed, so a believer baptised only as an infant has not yet received believer’s baptism and should ask for it, not as a rejection of his parents’ love or his upbringing but as obedience to Christ’s pattern. Talk it through with your pastor. If your church baptises infants, be honest with its elders about your conscience, and seek peace. Many godly Christians differ here; none of them is saved by water, and all who trust Christ are washed by his blood.

On a Tuesday. Name to yourself the person you have quietly decided will never come to Christ, and pray for him: the ruler of the synagogue in Corinth was converted.

parallels.desc: I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius

verseByVerse.quote: "And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid. You do not tell a man not to be afraid unless he is. He had reason: beaten in Philippi, chased out of Thessalonica and Berea, mocked in Athens, and now in a city where the synagogue had just turned on him. The man who wrote more of the New Testament’s letters than anyone knew what fear was.

Go on speaking. Not rest; not go somewhere safer. The same instruction twice, positively and negatively, as you might speak to somebody on the edge of stopping. The cure for the fear is to keep doing the thing that caused it, with the Lord beside you. And then three reasons.

For I am with you. Not I will protect your reputation, or your comfort. Presence: the promise of God to Joshua, to Jeremiah, to the apostles at the end of Matthew (Joshua 1:9; Jeremiah 1:8; Matthew 28:20). The risen Jesus who promised to be with his church always now comes into one frightened man’s room in Corinth and says it to him alone. The voice Paul had first heard on the Damascus road is the voice beside him in the dark.

To harm you. It does not say nobody will attack him; in two verses’ time he is dragged before the tribunal. What is promised is that no attack will land as harm, which is not a lesser promise but a truer one. Paul was given eighteen months in which what happened to him could not stop what God was doing through him. He was later arrested and, by early tradition, executed elsewhere, which is not a failure of this word, because it was given about Corinth and about now.

When a promise seems to fail. That is worth saying to anyone who has claimed a verse like this and then been hurt by something. God’s particular assurances of protection in Scripture are almost always attached to a work and a season, and they promise that the work will not be defeated. They do not promise that you will not be touched. The promises that cover every believer at every hour are deeper still: that nothing will separate us from the love of God in Christ (Romans 8:35–39), and that not a hair of our head will finally perish (Luke 21:18).

My people. The third reason is the strangest and best of them. Before they believed, they were already the Lord’s people. Corinth, wicked as it was, held many whom God had chosen. Not yet converted, but already his. And it is Jesus who says my people: they were the Son’s before they had heard his name, given to him by the Father, and of all that the Father gives him he will lose nothing (John 6:39). This is election: before the world was made, God set his love on particular people to be his own, freely, with nothing in them to prompt it (Ephesians 1:4–5). Paul preached not knowing who they were; Christ knew. The gospel would find them. No city is too dark for the Good Shepherd who says, I have other sheep, and I must bring them also (John 10:16).

Does this verse teach election? Arminian Christians, who hold that God’s choice rests on his foreknowledge of who will believe, read it as God’s foreknowledge of those who would believe, and many of them are faithful and fruitful evangelists. But the Lord calls them his people before they have believed, and the reason Paul should stay and preach is that they are his. The more likely reading is that God has chosen his people, and calls them through the preaching of the gospel (13:48). Election is the reason mission cannot fail, not a reason to stop.

Where Christians differ: does election discourage evangelism? Some think that if God has chosen his people, there is no need to preach. This commentary’s view: here election is the reason to keep preaching. God has his people; the gospel is the means by which they are called (Romans 10:14–17; 2 Timothy 2:10). Election guarantees that preaching will not be in vain.

How do I know if the person I am speaking to is one of the elect? You do not, and you do not need to. Paul did not know which Corinthians were the Lord’s; he only knew there were many. Election is God’s secret until it shows itself in faith (Deuteronomy 29:29). Our instruction is to offer Christ freely and sincerely to everyone, and to plead with them to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20). Treat every person as someone the Lord may be about to call, and you will speak to them with hope. And if you are worried whether you yourself are chosen, the answer is not to search the hidden decree but to come to Christ: all who come to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

In the flow. The vision stands at the centre of the Corinth story: before it Paul is reviled and leaves the synagogue (vv. 6–7); after it come eighteen months of teaching (v. 11) and an attack that fails exactly as promised (vv. 12–17).

On a Tuesday. Name the fear that has made you quiet: of being mocked, of losing a friendship, of saying it badly. Then hear the three reasons as spoken to you: I am with you; nothing will defeat my work; I have people here. The Spirit who made Paul bold now lives in you (1:8), so have one conversation this week you would otherwise have avoided. And where you have kept silent, as every one of us has, remember that Christ never once withheld his Father’s word, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19).

parallels.desc: do not be afraid, for I am with you

verseByVerse.quote: "And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eighteen months. His longest stay so far. Against the rest of the book the number is extraordinary. A few weeks, perhaps months, at Thessalonica. A few weeks at Berea. Days at Athens. Everywhere in the first two journeys, Paul plants and is moved on, usually by force. Here he stops.

Permission to put down roots. Luke puts the verse immediately after the vision, which is the explanation. The promise was permission to put down roots. A man hunted from town to town does not build; a man told that there are many in this city who belong to God can unpack.

The foundation laid in Corinth. This was sustained instruction, taking a mixed congregation of Jews, God-fearers and converted pagans through the Scriptures. Paul later told this church what those months had been: like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:10–11). The church was not built on Paul’s personality, though some came to talk as if it were, and when the letters came to correct them, Paul did not lay a new foundation. He took them back down to the one already there.

Letters written from Corinth. Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth during this time (1 Thessalonians 3:6), among the earliest of his letters we possess. They were written by a tentmaker to a church he had been driven away from and could not get back to, and they are in every Bible on earth.

Why does solid teaching matter so much if the gospel is simple? Because the gospel is simple enough for a child to receive and deep enough to occupy us for eternity, and Christians who are not taught are easily confused, discouraged or led astray (Ephesians 4:14). The Corinthians had eighteen months of Paul and still went wrong on factions, sex, lawsuits, worship and the resurrection; imagine them without it. Good teaching does not replace faith; it feeds it. So sit under the preaching of the Bible gladly and regularly, join a group that studies it, and be patient. Growth in grace is slow, like a tree, and most of it happens out of sight.

On a Tuesday. If you are tempted to move on from a church because it is not exciting, ask first whether it is feeding you on Scripture week by week. If it is, stay, and put down roots. And thank God for the pastors and teachers who give years, not weeks, to the same people.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth during this stay.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gallio. Luke drops a Roman official’s name into the narrative and hands historians one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for fixing chronology. An inscription at Delphi carries a letter from the emperor Claudius which mentions Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, and it dates his term to about AD 51–52. Proconsuls served, as a rule, for one year. So Paul was in Corinth in the early fifties, and most other dates in his life, his conversion, the Jerusalem council, the letters, are reckoned outward from this verse.

The man on the bench. Gallio was the elder brother of Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and tutor to the young Nero, who dedicated books to him and spoke of his charm as something nobody could resist. That is the temperament on the bench in this scene: cultivated, easy-going, and entirely uninterested in the matter in front of him.

What a proconsul was. Rome’s settled provinces were governed on behalf of the Senate by a proconsul, usually a senior senator sent out for about a year with supreme civil and judicial authority: something like a regional governor who was also the province’s chief judge. Achaia (southern Greece, capital Corinth) was a senatorial province at this time; its status shifted over the years, and Luke names it correctly for this moment.

A united attack. After many months in which the synagogue had lost its ruler and many of its members, the opposition finally coordinates, and chooses its moment: a new governor, freshly arrived, who might be expected to want a quiet province. The tribunal (bēma) was the judgment platform in the city’s forum.

Contrary to the law. That sentence is carefully built, and the ambiguity is the whole strategy. Contrary to which law? Roman law, which permitted Judaism as a legal religion; or Jewish law? If Gallio hears Roman law, then Paul is promoting an unlicensed religion and can be shut down across the province by a single ruling. They probably wanted Rome to rule that Christianity was not Judaism and so had no legal standing. If he hears Jewish law, it is a synagogue quarrel and none of his business. Everything depends on a busy proconsul hearing the word law and reaching for the wrong one.

A charge Luke’s readers have heard before. Luke’s Gospel has shown this strategy already. The leaders brought Jesus to a Roman governor’s tribunal and said, We found this man misleading our nation (Luke 23:2), hoping Rome would do what they could not. Pilate found no crime in him and handed him over anyway. Here the same move fails at once, and the difference is not that Gallio is a better man than Pilate. Pilate’s tribunal stood on the road God had appointed for his Son, the road to the cross (4:27–28). Christ went there alone, and was condemned in the place of his people. Paul, who preaches him, comes to Gallio’s tribunal under a word given to him for Corinth: no one will attack you to harm you (v. 10).

Why does it matter that the Bible gets names and dates right? Because Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas but a report of things that happened: a man was crucified under Pontius Pilate and raised on the third day. If Luke were careless about proconsuls, we might wonder whether he was careless about the resurrection. Instead, again and again, inscriptions and histories confirm his titles, places and dates. That does not prove the gospel by itself, but it means the witness is trustworthy, and Luke wrote, as he told Theophilus, so that we may have certainty concerning the things we have been taught (Luke 1:4). Not every question is settled (the census of Luke 2:2, for instance, is still debated), and believers hold Scripture true while admitting honestly that some such puzzles remain unresolved.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio’s term as proconsul to about AD 51–52 — one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life. The tribunal (bema) still stands in the Corinthian marketplace.

parallels.desc: the judgment seat of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, "If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul never speaks. He draws breath to make his defence and the governor cuts across him and decides the case. It is one of the few hearings in Acts where Paul says nothing at all, and it goes better for him than almost any other.

Wrongdoing or vicious crime. Gallio has seen straight through the ambiguity. A Roman court would hear a case of real wrongdoing or of serious villainy, and this, he observes, is neither.

Words and names. Gallio has concluded that the whole business is a dispute over terminology within a foreign religion: whether a particular Jewish title belongs to a particular dead Jew. He is not entirely wrong about the subject and completely wrong about its weight. The name he waved away is the one name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (4:12). One day the judge of Achaia will give account to the one he would not hear, and the name he could not be bothered to weigh will be the name that weighs him.

Classification. It is the commonest reaction the gospel meets in a comfortable society. Not persecution, and not conversion. Classification. The thing is filed as a matter of words and names, a private religious preference, and set aside without hostility by somebody who has other things to do. Athens laughed; Gallio simply did not think it was about anything.

A crucial ruling. Now the consequence, enormous and entirely unintended. Gallio treated the dispute as an internal Jewish matter, so Christianity was treated, for now, as a form of Judaism, under the legal shelter Judaism enjoyed as an ancient and licensed faith. A senior Roman judge’s refusal to act probably helped to shelter the churches for years, until Nero, and Luke likely records it partly to show Theophilus that Christianity was not a threat to Rome.

Useful indifference. God gave his church a season of legal cover through a man who could not have been less interested in it. Gallio was not being kind or secretly sympathetic; he was declining to waste an afternoon. And the protection was real: Christ had said that no one would harm his servant, and he kept his word through a man who did not care. The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will (Proverbs 21:1).

How should I respond when people treat my faith as just words and names? Without anger, and without accepting the label. Most people in comfortable societies are not hostile to Christianity; they simply file it as a private preference. The answer is not to shout but to show that it is about something: a real man who really rose, a real God to whom every person must give account, a real forgiveness that changes real lives. Your life is often the best argument. Gallio could dismiss a vocabulary; it is much harder to dismiss a neighbour whose marriage, honesty and hope have been visibly changed by Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of the authority over your circumstances who seems most indifferent: the employer, the council, the court, the government. Pray for them, as you are told to (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and then rest. Your safety does not depend on their goodwill. The Lord who used Gallio’s boredom can use their busyness.
verseByVerse.note: Gallio treated the dispute as an internal Jewish matter, not a Roman crime.

verseByVerse.quote: And he drove them from the tribunal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Driven from the tribunal. The verb is not a polite one. He had them driven off, perhaps by his lictors: the case not merely dismissed but swept out. The delegation that came with a coordinated complaint, timed for a new governor and framed to make Rome act, is pushed away from the bench in front of the whole city, told that their religion is not worth a magistrate’s time.

The judgment seat. The tribunal Gallio cleared was the bēma, the raised platform in the Corinthian marketplace from which a magistrate gave judgment; a platform identified as this one still stands. Paul did not forget it. He wrote to these Christians that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), and to Rome that we will all stand before the judgment seat of God (Romans 14:10). The Corinthians had seen their apostle dragged in front of one.

Two judgment seats. Set the two side by side, as Paul may well have meant his readers to. At the first, the judge would not hear the case, the accused was never allowed to speak, and the verdict came from a man who thought the whole matter beneath him. At the second, every case is heard, nothing is dismissed as a quarrel about words and names, and the Judge has taken the trouble to become one of the accused. That should sober us before it comforts us. The holy God hears every case and sees every motive, and no one will file his sins there as a matter of words and names.

Can God really use people who do not know him? Yes, all the time, and Scripture is full of them: Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Cyrus, Caesar Augustus, whose census brought Mary to Bethlehem. God’s providence governs all his creatures and all their actions (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.1; the Westminster Confession 5.1), without making him the author of their sin or excusing them for it. That is why a Christian can pray for unbelieving rulers, employers and relatives with real hope: God can use them for good whether they intend it or not. But do not mistake being used for being saved: Gallio rendered real service to the purposes of God and remained entirely outside them. The only safe place is not on the right side of history, but in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sosthenes beaten. A crowd has watched the delegation thrown out of court, and it does what crowds do with people publicly stripped of protection: it beats their leader where the proconsul can see. Sosthenes had probably led the failed case. Who beat him? Perhaps Greeks, venting anti-Jewish feeling; or Jews, angry at his failure. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, say that all the Greeks seized him; the earliest say only that they all did. Either way, nobody here is defending Paul. The mob is not on the side of the gospel; it simply turns on whoever has just lost.

Gallio paid no attention. The same indifference that had just protected the church now watches a man beaten in front of the bench and declines to intervene. Luke sets the two effects of one man’s temperament side by side without comment. Detachment is not a virtue. It served the gospel in one verse and left a man bleeding in the next.

The Judge who pays attention. Luke’s Gospel has another beaten man in it. On the night of his trial the men holding Jesus mocked him as they beat him, blindfolded him and struck him (Luke 22:63–64), and no one in authority lifted a hand. So the battered ruler of the synagogue, whom Rome would not even look at, is not beyond Christ’s sympathy: we have a high priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). The Lord is the opposite of Gallio in everything that matters. He sees the blow the bench ignores and hears the case the court will not hear.

Who was Sosthenes? The ruler of the synagogue, which most likely means the successor of Crispus, who had believed in verse 8. He may instead have been a fellow ruler, since a synagogue could have more than one (13:15). Then look at the first line of the letter Paul later wrote back to this city: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes (1 Corinthians 1:1). It is not certain that they are the same man, and it should not be asserted. But it is a striking coincidence, and if it is the same man, then the beating in this verse is the last thing the New Testament records about him before he turns up as a Christian standing beside the apostle he had prosecuted.

Many days longer. Paul does not leave in a hurry, a mark of how completely Gallio’s ruling had changed the situation. And when he goes, the couple who took him in go with him, leaving the city and the business they had built after being expelled from Rome.

A vow at Cenchreae. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port, and a church grew there too, served by our sister Phoebe (Romans 16:1), who probably carried Paul’s letter to Rome. There the apostle of justification by faith, the teaching that God declares sinners right with himself through faith in Christ and not by keeping the law, had his head shaved because of a vow. It has the shape of the Nazirite vow, in which a man separated himself to the LORD for a period, drank no wine, let his hair grow, and cut it off at the end (Numbers 6:1–21).

Whose vow was it, and why cut his hair at Cenchreae? The grammar could refer to Aquila, but Paul is the natural subject. It may have been a vow of thanksgiving, perhaps of the Nazirite kind, ended by cutting his hair as he left Corinth, with the hair perhaps offered later in Jerusalem. Luke does not explain, but it shows Paul free to keep Jewish customs where they did not touch the gospel (21:23–26).

May a believer still keep the law? Paul’s vow raises a real question: now that Christ has come, may a believer still keep the law, or parts of it? The Reformed answer distinguishes three strands in the law of Moses. The moral law (the Ten Commandments, summed up as loving God and neighbour) reflects God’s unchanging character and abides always; we are not saved by it, but the believer gladly obeys it as the Spirit-enabled pattern of a thankful life. The ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, temple, feasts, clean and unclean foods, circumcision as rite) was the shadow that pointed to Christ and is fulfilled in him (Colossians 2:16–17); no Christian is bound to keep it. The civil law that governed Israel as a nation expired with that nation, though its underlying justice still instructs (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.3–5; the Westminster Confession 19.3–5). So: the moral law stands; the ceremonial and civil are not binding as obligations.

The careful line Paul walks. Here a Jewish vow, later a temple purification (21:23–26), and Timothy’s circumcision (16:3), yet a flat refusal to circumcise Titus (Galatians 2:3–5) and thunder against anyone who made law-keeping a condition of salvation (Galatians 5:2–4). The difference is always why. Made a means of being right with God, or imposed on others as necessary, a practice denies the gospel and is forbidden. Kept freely, as heritage, devotion, conscience, or love that wins a hearing (to the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews, 1 Corinthians 9:20), it is Christian liberty.

The two cases. So a Jewish believer may in liberty keep ancestral customs, feasts, food traditions, even a vow, as heritage, devotion and witness among his people, as Paul did, provided he never makes them the ground of his standing nor binds them on others. A Gentile believer is under no obligation to the ceremonial law at all (the whole verdict of Acts 15); one person esteems one day as better than another, and each one should be fully convinced in his own mind (Romans 14:5), but he must never put himself under the law as a system, which is to fall from grace (Galatians 5:1–4). The test in every case: am I doing this to be accepted, or because I am accepted in Christ? Whether the fourth commandment continues as a Christian Sabbath is one place believers differ; many, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, hold that it does, kept on the Lord’s Day. This commentary takes the view that the Sabbath is a shadow whose substance is Christ (Colossians 2:16–17): Christ is our rest, and the Lord’s Day is a gift gladly kept, not a law.

Should Christians today make vows to God? Scripture permits them but does not require them, and warns against making them rashly: it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). Jesus forbade the kind of oath-making that treats some promises as binding and others as not, and told us to let our yes be yes (Matthew 5:33–37). A lawful vow is a voluntary promise to God of something good and within your power, made thoughtfully, never as a bargain to get something from him or to earn his favour (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 23; the Westminster Confession 22.6–7). Marriage vows and church membership vows are the most common today, and they should be kept with the seriousness of a promise made before God.
verseByVerse.note: A Sosthenes later appears with Paul as a believer. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port. Cutting the hair marked the end of a vow of special devotion.

parallels.desc: the Nazirite vow
Phoebe of Cenchreae

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Left in Ephesus. Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, where the Spirit had forbidden him to preach at the start of this journey (16:6), and where he would eventually spend three years. Now the door opens, and what he leaves behind is a married couple with a trade. Within a few verses they will finish the education of one of the most gifted preachers in the eastern Mediterranean, and later a church meets in their house (1 Corinthians 16:19). Paul’s strategy for the greatest city in Asia was to leave two tentmakers in it.

As always. Days off the boat, in a city he is only passing through, and he is in the synagogue arguing. There is no version of Paul that takes a week to look round a town.

He declined. After Pisidian Antioch, Lystra, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens and the tribunal at Corinth, here at last is a receptive synagogue in the most strategic city in the province, asking for more. And he leaves. Paul wanted to reach Jerusalem, perhaps for a feast, and there was a sending church to report to.

The one who holds the key. Behind every door on this journey stands one person. The Holy Spirit forbade Asia and the Spirit of Jesus would not allow Bithynia (16:6–7). So when Paul declines an open door here, he is not losing his nerve. He is waiting on the one who calls himself the one who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens (Revelation 3:7). A few years later, writing from this very city, Paul would say that a wide door for effective work had opened to him (1 Corinthians 16:9). The door was the same. The hand on it was Christ’s, and he chose the hour.

An open door is not a summons. Paul had learned that in reverse on the road to Troas, when every door was shut and the shutting turned out to be direction; here every door is open and it is still not the instruction. We are generally taught to read opportunity as guidance. Paul had a genuine opportunity, urged on him by people who wanted the gospel, and he said no and went home to his church. Not every good thing you could do is a thing you are being asked to do. Some of them belong to somebody else, or to a later year.

How do I know whether an opportunity is from God? Ask more than whether it is open and good. Ask whether it fits what God has already given you to do: your existing responsibilities, your church, your family, the work in hand. Ask those who know you well and whose wisdom you trust, as Paul went back to his sending church. Ask whether you can say yes to it without saying no to something God has clearly called you to. Pray, and be willing to wait. Scripture gives no promise of private signals for every choice, but it gives wisdom (James 1:5), and wisdom often sounds like not yet.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia.

verseByVerse.quote: But on taking leave of them he said, "I will return to you if God wills," and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God wills. Three words that Paul evidently meant literally. He uses the same qualification writing to Corinth, that he will come to them soon, if the Lord wills (1 Corinthians 4:19), and James turns it into a settled Christian habit: instead of boasting about tomorrow, you ought to say, If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:13–15). Some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add that Paul said he must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem; the earliest manuscripts do not have the words.

A phrase with teeth. In our mouths it is often a pious formula. In Paul’s it had teeth: on this journey he had been forbidden by the Spirit to speak in Asia, forbidden to enter Bithynia, sent to Macedonia by a vision, and driven out of three cities in succession. And God did will it (19:1): he returned, and stayed. The qualification was not pessimism. It was accuracy about who was arranging the itinerary.

Learned from the Son. Paul learned this posture from his Lord. Jesus said that he had come down from heaven not to do his own will but the will of him who sent him (John 6:38), and on the night of his arrest he prayed, Father, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). The Son of God himself lived every day as one long if God wills, and for him the Father’s will meant a cross. That is why the phrase is not fatalism in a Christian’s mouth. The will we bow to is the will of a Father who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Whatever such a Father wills for our tomorrow, it cannot be against us.

Went up. You always go up to Jerusalem, set among the hills, and down from it; so went up and greeted the church, with no city named, means the mother church in Jerusalem, a visit Luke covers in a handful of words.

Down to Antioch. Home to the sending church that had fasted, prayed and laid hands on Barnabas and Saul (13:1–3), presumably to report as after the first journey (14:27). So ends the second missionary journey, roughly three years and perhaps 2,800 miles: churches in Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea and Corinth, Priscilla and Aquila left in Ephesus, and probably the letters to the Thessalonians written.

Accountable to a local church. Paul had seen the risen Christ and been given the gospel by revelation, and he still travelled hundreds of miles to come back to the ordinary local church that had sent him. The journey that began with a quarrel about John Mark ends in the same city, with the mission enormously enlarged.

Does saying if God wills mean I should not make plans? No. Paul made detailed plans, and Scripture commends the forethought of the ant and the builder who counts the cost (Proverbs 6:6–8; Luke 14:28). What James forbids is planning as if we owned tomorrow, the boast that assumes our lives and diaries are in our own hands. Underneath that boast is a claim to hold the reins of our own lives, and it is a quiet rival to God: it tells us we are safe only when tomorrow belongs to us. So plan carefully and work hard, and hold every plan with an open hand. Say if the Lord wills and mean it: when a plan is overturned, you will be disappointed, but not shaken, because you never thought the itinerary was yours.

On a Tuesday. If you serve in any way beyond your local church, report back to it, as Paul did to Antioch: tell them what God has done, and let them pray and rejoice with you.

parallels.desc: if the Lord wills

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul begins his third journey by strengthening the churches of Galatia and Phrygia. Meanwhile in Ephesus a gifted Alexandrian preacher, Apollos, who knows only the baptism of John, is quietly taught by Priscilla and Aquila and then sent on to Corinth with the church’s recommendation.
verseByVerse.theology:
Complete teaching

Apollos’s knowledge was accurate as far as it went but stopped short of the full apostolic message. Priscilla and Aquila show how to help: receive those whose understanding is incomplete, honour what is genuine in it, and fill in what is missing. That is the work of discipleship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Apollos went on to Achaia and strengthened the believers there by showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. Now: The church is still built by ministers whose gifts complement each other: one plants, another waters, and God gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third journey. Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey, probably around AD 53, centred on Ephesus. No commissioning service, no vision, no laying on of hands: Paul simply leaves and starts walking.

Galatia and Phrygia. Back over the same ground. These regions take in the towns of the first journey, Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, Pisidian Antioch, the places where he was stoned and expelled, and which he had already revisited twice. The phrase from one place to the next suggests an unhurried, methodical circuit rather than a dash through.

Strengthening all the disciples. Nothing about that is new territory or new converts. It is maintenance, and the verb Luke chooses says so: strengthening, making firm what is already standing. He used the same word when Paul went back through those towns the first time (14:22) and when he set out on the second journey (15:41). And the word is all. Not the promising ones, not the strategic ones. All the disciples.

Going back. It is tempting to believe that the real thing is the founding and everything afterwards is administration. Paul spent much of his life going back, and the letters are the same activity conducted by post. If your service to God consists largely of turning up again for the same people, you are doing what the apostle to the Gentiles did with his time.

The chief Shepherd’s rounds. Behind Paul’s long walk stands his Lord’s own care. Jesus told Peter that he had prayed for him, that his faith would not fail, and that when he had turned again he must strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32). Christ does not only plant churches; he keeps them, praying for them and sending his servants back to make them firm. Every return visit to Lystra or Iconium was the risen Christ looking in on his own sheep by the feet of a servant, and no disciple in those small towns was too small for his rounds.

What does strengthening other Christians actually look like? It is mostly ordinary. Turning up. Remembering what someone told you last week and asking how it went. Opening the Bible with them and pointing to a promise that fits their trouble. Praying with them, not only for them. Warning them gently when they are drifting, and reminding them that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (14:22). Sending a message on the anniversary of a bereavement. None of it is dramatic, and almost all of it matters. Paul’s word for it is the same whether he was walking to Lystra or writing a letter.

In the flow. Two journeys meet in this verse: the second has just ended at Antioch (v. 22), and the third begins with Paul going the long way to Ephesus (v. 21) through the churches he already has, while Luke pauses for Apollos (vv. 24–28).
verseByVerse.note: Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From Alexandria. Alexandria explains the man. It was the second city of the empire, the intellectual capital of the Greek-speaking world, home of the great library and of the largest and most cultured Jewish community outside Judea, where by tradition the Old Testament had first been translated into Greek. A Jew educated there could be as well educated as anyone in the empire.

Eloquent and competent. Luke piles up five commendations before he raises any difficulty. Eloquent: learned, articulate. Competent: mighty in the Scriptures, able to use them. Some in Corinth later preferred him to Paul (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4–6), and some, from Luther on, have guessed he wrote Hebrews. And he had been instructed in the way of the Lord.

Fervent in spirit. Fervent (zeōn): the verb is used of boiling water, and here means glowing with zeal, perhaps by the Spirit. Paul uses the identical phrase when telling the Romans how a Christian ought to be (Romans 12:11). And accurately. Luke is not damning him with faint praise and then correcting him; what Apollos said about Jesus was true, as far as it went.

The things concerning Jesus. Luke has used that phrase before, at the end of his Gospel. On the road to Emmaus the risen Lord, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreted to two disciples in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). That is what made Apollos formidable: a man mighty in the Scriptures who read them as the risen Christ taught his church to read them, with Jesus as their subject. The Greek Bible of Alexandria, Moses and the Psalms and Isaiah, opened in his hands onto one face. Whatever he still lacked, he had the main thing.

Only the baptism of John. Here is a man learned, powerful in the Bible, on fire and doctrinally accurate, and then this clause. There is nothing wrong with Apollos: he is not a false teacher, a self-promoter, lukewarm or careless. He is excellent, and he is incomplete, and the two are not in tension. The news had simply not all reached him yet. We tend to sort teachers into sound and unsound, and Apollos will not go in either box.

What does he knew only the baptism of John mean? John the Baptist’s baptism was a preparatory one, a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (Luke 3:3), in which people confessed their sins, turned to God, and got ready for the Messiah who was coming. John pointed beyond himself: he baptised with water, but the one coming after him would baptise with the Holy Spirit (Matthew 3:11). So it looked forward to Jesus; it was the getting-ready baptism, not yet the full Christian one. To say Apollos knew only John’s baptism, then, is to say his grasp of the gospel reached accurately up to that preparatory point. He knew of John’s baptism of repentance and of Jesus as the coming one, perhaps even of his life and death, and proclaimed Jesus as the Messiah truly, as far as it went, but had not yet been brought up to the fuller apostolic message that followed: Pentecost, the outpouring and gift of the Holy Spirit, and baptism in the name of Jesus. His knowledge was real but incomplete, the fault of his teaching, not his heart: he taught what he had been taught, probably away from the centre, before the fuller news reached him.

Apollos and the twelve at Ephesus. His case is close kin to that of the Ephesian disciples of 19:1–7, with a difference: Apollos, already fervent and teaching accurately, is simply taught more accurately (v. 26) and is never said to be rebaptised, whereas those men, who had not even heard that the Spirit was given, are baptised into Jesus and receive the Spirit. And even a brilliant, fervent Bible teacher still had more to learn, and humbly received it from a tentmaking couple.

How should I think of a Christian whose understanding is incomplete? As most of us are, in one area or another. Sorting people only into sound and unsound misses the large company of real believers who love Christ and teach truly but have not yet seen everything clearly, because no one has taught them. Such people need help, not suspicion. Be quick to recognise what is right in them, as Luke did with five commendations, and slow to assume bad motives. And turn it on yourself: there are things you have not yet understood, and the Lord may send a Priscilla to you. Be ready to be taught.

In the flow. Luke breaks off Paul’s travels to set the scene in Ephesus before Paul returns, and because Apollos will go on to water what Paul planted in Corinth (vv. 27–28; 1 Corinthians 3:6).

On a Tuesday. The Spirit of truth delights to lead Christ’s people into all the truth, so keep learning. Choose one area of Christian teaching you know you are hazy on, the Holy Spirit, baptism, the last things, and read one good, clear book or chapter of Scripture on it this month. Boil, by all means. But boil with light.
verseByVerse.note: Alexandria in Egypt was a great centre of learning with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: "He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They took him aside. Not up. Not out. Aside: privately, away from the congregation he had been addressing, perhaps in their home. They heard a brilliant man preaching something short of the full truth in public, and they did not stand up to correct him there. Tentmakers taught a scholar, gently and in private.

The alternatives they declined. They could have corrected him from the floor, which would have humiliated and probably hardened him; warned people about him afterwards, which requires no courage at all; or said nothing, since he was gifted and they were only tentmakers. Instead they took him aside.

More accurately. Luke’s word is not rebuked or refuted but explained: set it out for him. And not accurately, as though he had been wrong, but more accurately, because he had been right as far as he went. That is the whole art of helping somebody whose understanding is incomplete, avoiding both silence, which leaves a man preaching half a gospel, and public correction, which almost always makes him defend the position he was about to abandon. If you need to say something difficult to a Christian you respect, this verse is the method: privately, personally, over a meal, beginning with what is right.

More of the same Christ. What did more accurately add? Luke does not list it, but the gap was most likely the one John’s baptism leaves. John had pointed to one coming after him who would baptise with the Holy Spirit. Priscilla and Aquila could tell Apollos the rest as the apostles preached it: that this Jesus, crucified and raised, had been exalted at the right hand of God and, having received the promised Spirit from the Father, had poured him out (2:33), and that his people are now baptised in his name. More accurately did not mean a new subject. It meant the same Christ seen whole: not only the coming one John announced, but the reigning Lord who had come and was now giving his Spirit to his church.

Priscilla named first. Then there are the teachers themselves: a husband and wife, in partnership, teaching a man privately, probably at home, and Luke names Priscilla first, as the New Testament does in most of the places the couple appear. In the ancient world that order is unusual enough to be deliberate, and a natural explanation is that she took a leading part in this, or was the more prominent of the two.

Where Christians differ: Priscilla and women teaching. Some use this verse to argue that women may serve as pastors or preachers in the church. This commentary’s view: Priscilla, with her husband, instructed Apollos privately, probably in their home; this was not preaching in the gathered church or exercising authority as an elder. Scripture reserves the office of elder and authoritative teaching in the church’s gathering to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while women like Priscilla rightly teach, explain, and serve in many ways. This is the complementarian view, held with deep respect for women’s gifts and ministry.

Held gladly, not grudgingly. Egalitarian Christians point to Priscilla, named first, together with Phoebe, Junia and the prophesying daughters of Philip (21:9), as evidence that women taught men in the early church. But any position on the wider question has to be able to hold this verse comfortably and gladly, because Luke plainly regarded what Priscilla did as one of the most useful things anybody did in this chapter.

And Apollos was taught. Consider what it cost him. He was the most gifted speaker in the room, and he sat down with two tentmakers and let them teach him. The gifted man’s greatest asset here is not his eloquence. It is that he could be taught.

So what may a woman do, on this view? A great deal, and churches holding the complementarian view should be quick to say so and to make room for it. Like Priscilla, a woman may explain the faith to others, privately and in many settings, including to men, as she did here with her husband. She may teach children and other women (Titus 2:3–5), lead Bible studies among women, share the gospel with anyone, pray and serve visibly in the church’s life, counsel, write, and use every gift God has given her. What this view reserves to qualified men is the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church. The aim is never to silence women’s gifts but to honour God’s order while putting those gifts to full and joyful use.

How do I receive correction well? Like Apollos: by assuming the person might be right, and listening before defending yourself. It helps to remember that correction given privately and gently, as Priscilla and Aquila gave it, is a gift of love; faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6). Thank the person, even if you are not yet sure they are right. Then take what they said to Scripture, as the Bereans did. If they were right, change, and do it openly if your error was public. A teachable spirit is not weakness. It is the mark of a man whom God can go on using.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A letter of recommendation. Apollos went with one, the ordinary means by which the early church moved people around a world where nobody could check anybody’s credentials (2 Corinthians 3:1). So the Ephesian church put its name behind a man who, not long before, had been preaching an incomplete gospel in their synagogue. They did not send a warning ahead of him. They sent an endorsement.

Through grace. The Greek could mean that Apollos helped them by grace, but most translations rightly read it as those who through grace had believed. In a passing clause about travel arrangements Luke has slipped in a whole doctrine of how anybody comes to faith. Grace means God’s free kindness to people who have deserved the opposite, and faith itself is its gift (Ephesians 2:8–9; Philippians 1:29). It is the same thing said of Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened (16:14), and of the Gentiles at Pisidian Antioch (13:48). Before Apollos opened his mouth in Corinth, grace had gone ahead of him.

If faith is a gift, why am I commanded to believe? Because God gives faith through the very command and promise of the gospel. When Christ is offered, you are truly called to trust him, and you truly do the believing; God does not believe for you. Yet when you do, you discover that he opened your heart to do it, so that you cannot boast (Ephesians 2:8–9). The doctrine is not a reason to wait passively but a reason for humility and assurance. If you have believed, thank God; your faith is his work in you, and what he has begun he will finish. If you have not, do not wait to feel chosen. Come to Christ now, and you will find that grace brought you.

Showing by the Scriptures. Apologetics from Scripture, the work Paul had done in Corinth, now done by somebody else. Apollos may well have been the more polished speaker; some of the Corinthians certainly thought so, and some of them said so in terms that were less than kind about Paul’s own delivery (2 Corinthians 10:10).

Paul pushed him back. Apollos went to Corinth, Paul’s own church, and was such a success that a faction formed round his name: I follow Paul, or, I follow Apollos (1 Corinthians 1:12). Paul refuses the rivalry: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). And he strongly urged Apollos to go back there (1 Corinthians 16:12), pushing him toward the congregation that preferred him.

One name passed from hand to hand. Priscilla and Aquila, who had worked beside Paul, taught Apollos; Apollos strengthened the Corinthians; Paul urged him back to them. Not one link in the chain was jealous of the next, because what was being passed along was not a reputation but a name: the Christ was Jesus (v. 5). When Christ is the message, his servants can afford to be small. He must increase, John the Baptist said of him, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

What if someone else is more gifted than me in the same ministry? Then thank God for him, and pray for his success, as Paul did for Apollos. Jealousy in ministry is common and deadly, because it makes the work about us. The cure is to remember whose field it is: one plants, another waters, and God gives the growth. If a more gifted person waters what you planted, the harvest is the Lord’s, and you will share the joy (John 4:36–37). Ask yourself whether you would be glad if the church you love grew faster under someone else. If not, take that to Christ, who washed feet and was content to be overlooked.

On a Tuesday. Write a short letter of commendation this week: a note to someone telling them how God has used them, or an encouraging word to a church about a believer moving their way.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia is southern Greece, including Corinth.

parallels.desc: I planted, Apollos watered

18.theology: Election as the ground of courage in mission. The Lord’s word to Paul in the night (v. 10) is the doctrine of election given as a promise to a frightened missionary. Paul admits later that he was afraid (1 Corinthians 2:3). God’s answer is not that people will respond, but that he already has his people in the city and calls them through the preaching of the gospel. So election is no reason for idleness. It is a reason to keep speaking.
18.examples:
Then: Paul in Corinth, afraid, working as a tentmaker, preaching every Sabbath, kept there by a vision and a promise for eighteen months. The church that came out of those months would cause him more trouble than any other, and would receive his letters on the cross, the resurrection and love.

Now: Every city has people God means to save. The church’s task is to be in the city, to preach the word, to stay where the Lord has put it, and to trust that the harvest is his. The believer who speaks of Christ in a hard place is not alone.

19.title: Ephesus and the Power of the Word
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. <sup>2</sup>And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” <sup>3</sup>And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” <sup>4</sup>And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.” <sup>5</sup>On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. <sup>7</sup>There were about twelve men in all. <sup>8</sup>And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. <sup>9</sup>But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. <sup>10</sup>This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. <sup>11</sup>And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, <sup>12</sup>so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. <sup>13</sup>Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” <sup>14</sup>Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this. <sup>15</sup>But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” <sup>16</sup>And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. <sup>17</sup>And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. <sup>18</sup>Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. <sup>19</sup>And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. <sup>20</sup>So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. <sup>21</sup>Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” <sup>22</sup>And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while. <sup>23</sup>About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. <sup>24</sup>For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. <sup>25</sup>These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. <sup>26</sup>And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. <sup>27</sup>And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.” <sup>28</sup>When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>29</sup>So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel. <sup>30</sup>But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. <sup>31</sup>And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater. <sup>32</sup>Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. <sup>33</sup>Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd. <sup>34</sup>But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>35</sup>And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? <sup>36</sup>Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash. <sup>37</sup>For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. <sup>38</sup>If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another. <sup>39</sup>But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. <sup>40</sup>For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.” <sup>41</sup>And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.
19.overview:
Ephesus is the climax of Paul’s free ministry. It was the capital of the province of Asia, a port of perhaps a quarter of a million people, home of the vast temple of Artemis and famous across the empire for magic. Paul stays nearly three years (20:31), longer than anywhere else. A dozen men who know only John’s baptism are brought the rest of the way to Jesus; then three months in the synagogue and two years of daily teaching in a hired hall carry the word through the whole province, and the churches of the Lycus valley and the seven churches of Revelation 2–3 probably date from these years.

The gospel then meets the city’s religion: magic, a borrowed use of Jesus’ name, and finally a trade that lives on the goddess. Paul plans the journey to Jerusalem and Rome that the rest of Acts follows, and a riot in the theatre ends with the town clerk declaring the Christians innocent. Luke’s summary is the key: the word of the Lord kept growing and prevailing (v. 20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole of Paul’s Ephesian ministry: twelve disciples of John receive the Spirit, two years of daily teaching reach the province, extraordinary miracles and a failed exorcism show that Jesus’ name is not a spell, magicians burn their books, Paul sets his course for Jerusalem and Rome, and a riot over the trade in shrines of Artemis ends with the town clerk sending the crowd home.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word of the Lord prevailing over magic and idolatry

The magicians who burned their books did not cut back their practice gradually; they made a clean, costly, public break. That is the shape of real repentance: leaving behind what the gospel has displaced, whatever it costs. Luke’s summary in verse 20 is his verdict on the whole Ephesian story: the word wins, over magic, over money and over the riot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Demetrius’s complaint, that his trade would fall into disrepute and the temple of Artemis be counted as nothing, is an honest statement of why many oppose the gospel: it costs them something they value. Now: The gospel still threatens arrangements that profit from idolatry, and the opposition it meets is often about money before it is about belief.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' And they said, 'No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
