Meaning first. The gospel meets every rival power: incomplete religion, demons, magic, and the money-making idolatry of a whole city. Over it all Luke writes the chapter’s real subject: the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily (v. 20). The risen Christ, by his word and Spirit, takes on the most religious, superstitious and commercial city in Asia, and wins.

To Ephesus. Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis, with perhaps 250,000 people. Paul had promised to return if God willed (18:21), and he has. The inland country was probably the high road across the Anatolian plateau rather than the easier valley route, a journey of several hundred miles on foot.

Some disciples. What he finds is a small puzzle. Disciples is Luke’s ordinary word for Christians, so the first impression is that Paul has walked into a group of the Ephesian church. But verse 3 suggests these were followers of John the Baptist’s message rather than ordinary Christians. Like Apollos, they knew only John’s baptism.

Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? Something prompted that question. Luke does not say what, but Paul was evidently watching. He had perhaps been in the city only days and had already sensed that something was missing. And the question itself assumes a great deal. It takes for granted that receiving the Spirit is what happens to a person who believes, and that it is the sort of thing you would know about. The Spirit is received when one believes, not later. Paul is not asking whether they have had a further experience; he is asking whether the ordinary thing has happened.

Not even heard. Not we have not received him; they had not heard. They cannot mean they had never heard of the Spirit, since John spoke of him plainly (Luke 3:16), but that they had not heard the Spirit had been given, that Pentecost had happened. They were not converts waiting for something more; they were men whose information had run out before the story reached its end.

Because Jesus was glorified. Why had the Spirit not reached them? Because their news stopped short of the thing that sent him. John’s Gospel explains that the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified (John 7:39), and Peter said at Pentecost that the exalted Jesus had received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured him out (2:33). The Spirit is the gift of an enthroned Christ: not a reward we work up to but a gift Jesus gives from his throne, the sign that his death was enough and that the Father has accepted it. These men knew John’s promise of one who would baptise with the Spirit; they did not know that he had died, risen, ascended and kept his word. So Paul’s question was, underneath, a question about Jesus: have you heard what he has done?

One question. These twelve had been in Ephesus, sincere and out of date, and the gap was found because one man asked one question. It is worth asking, of the people in your own congregation whom everybody assumes are fine, whether anybody has ever asked them anything.

The cousin of Acts 8. Like the Samaritans in Acts 8, these men receive the Spirit some time after a baptism. But theirs was only John’s, so they were not ordinary Christians awaiting a second blessing but disciples still at John’s pre-Pentecost stage. What they lacked was the rest of the gospel, not a stage two.

How do I know whether I have received the Holy Spirit? Not first by a feeling or a particular gift, but by the fruit of his presence. The Spirit is the one who makes you confess that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), who makes you cry Abba, Father (Romans 8:15–16), who makes you hate the sin you once loved and fight it (Romans 8:13), and who grows love, joy and peace in you, slowly (Galatians 5:22–23). If you have truly trusted Christ, the Spirit is in you, for anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). The question for most believers is not whether to receive him, but whether to keep in step with him.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis. These “disciples” knew only John’s baptism.

parallels.desc: Apollos, who knew only the baptism of John

verseByVerse.quote: "And he said, 'Into what then were you baptized?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.' And Paul said, 'John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into what then were you baptized? Paul does something wise with a wrong answer. He does not correct them at once, and he does not dismiss them. He asks a second question, and the second question is the diagnostic one: what were you baptised into? Paul connects the Spirit with baptism in Jesus’ name. And that is worth having as a method. He is not trying to establish whether they are in or out. He is trying to find out where the gap is, and he does it by tracing the thing back to its source: what were you told, and by whom, and how far did it go? A great deal of unhelpful conversation between Christians would be avoided if the second question came before the verdict.

Into John’s baptism. A baptism of preparation. These men are not pagans or half-hearted. They had repented, turned from their sins, and were waiting for the one John had promised. Their problem was that they were living some twenty years behind the news.

That is, Jesus. John’s baptism was never a destination; it pointed past itself to a person who had not yet arrived, and these men had stopped at the signpost. Paul closes a twenty-year gap in a clause: the one you were told to wait for has come, and here is his name. Every hope John stirred in them, of sins forgiven and a Spirit poured out, now stands before them in a person, crucified, risen and reigning.

Real and unfinished. There is a particular kindness in this scene. Paul does not tell these men that their repentance was worthless or that their years of waiting were wasted. He tells them that what they had was real and unfinished. That is a rare and difficult combination to hold about anybody’s spiritual history, including your own.

What if I was religious for years before I really understood the gospel? Then this passage is for you. Those years may have taught you real things: that God is holy, that sin matters, that you needed someone to come. Many believers look back on a churchgoing childhood or a sincere but confused search and can see God preparing them, like John preparing the way. But preparation is not arrival. If you now trust Christ crucified and risen, you have reached the destination the signposts were pointing to. Do not despise the road, and do not mistake it for home. Thank God for both.

verseByVerse.quote: "On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their first Christian baptism. Twelve men who had already been baptised are baptised again, the only such case in the New Testament, and it is not a second Christian baptism: they had never received one. John’s rite belonged to the era before the cross, valid in its time but preparatory. There is no record that the apostles, some of whom had come from John’s circle (John 1:35–40), were rebaptised; they had received the Spirit at Pentecost.

On hearing this. And it happens fast. No interval, no long course of instruction, no probation. Luke’s pattern all through the book is that baptism follows promptly upon believing: three thousand on the day of Pentecost, the eunuch at the roadside, Lydia apparently the same day, the jailer in the middle of the night. There is no example in Acts of a believer being made to wait for years. And the order is always the same: hearing, believing, then baptism.

In the name of the Lord Jesus. That phrase is the whole difference between the two baptisms. John’s was into a hope. This one is into a person, and into everything that belongs to him. To be baptised into someone’s name in that world was to be transferred into his ownership and his protection, which is why men who had been waiting on John’s promise are now, in one act, publicly attached to a named Lord.

Where Christians differ: rebaptism. Some use this to justify rebaptising those baptised as infants or in other churches. This commentary’s view: this case was unique, as John’s baptism was not Christian baptism. Where someone was baptised before they truly believed, credobaptists (those who baptise believers only) rightly see believer’s baptism as the first true baptism, not a repetition. But those who were baptised as believers in the name of the Trinity should not be baptised again; there is one baptism (Ephesians 4:5).

Does this license rebaptism today? These twelve had received only John’s baptism, before Christ’s death and resurrection and the coming of the Spirit; this was not a repeat of Christian baptism but their first. Those who hold, as this commentary does with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism belongs to believers will baptise someone who was baptised only as an infant, since they regard that as not yet believer’s baptism. Our paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers) regard any baptism with water in the triune name as valid and not to be repeated, and they hold that view from a sincere reading of God’s covenant promises; we honour them for it, while differing. But all agree that someone baptised as a believer is not to be baptised again.

Does in the name of the Lord Jesus conflict with Matthew 28:19? No. Jesus commanded baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Luke here describes whose name and authority the person comes under, not the exact words spoken at the water. The Oneness Pentecostal teaching, which denies that God is three persons and insists that only Jesus’ name may be used, reads a formula into a description. Christian baptism is into the one name of the triune God, revealed in Jesus Christ.

Why does Luke record such a small episode? Twelve obscure men in a large city, whose names we do not have and who are never mentioned again. He records it because the gospel had reached Ephesus in an incomplete form and God did not leave it there. Somebody had preached a half-message and moved on. Apollos had done the same. And in both cases the correction came, privately, patiently, and without anybody being humiliated.

What if I was baptised before I truly believed? Talk to your pastor, and be honest. If you were baptised as a believer, however young and however little you understood, and you have trusted Christ ever since, your baptism stands; faith grows, and baptism does not need repeating every time it does. If, looking back, you are clear that you had no faith in Christ at all at the time, and were baptised for other reasons, then many credobaptist churches would see a baptism now as your first true baptism, as with these twelve. The aim is not to chase a perfect experience but to obey Christ with a clear conscience.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s hands. As with the Samaritans (8:17), the Spirit came through an apostle’s hands. Why? Perhaps to bring this group of John’s followers fully into the one church, and to show that Paul’s apostleship equalled Peter’s.

Tongues and prophesying. This is the fourth and last time in Acts that the Spirit comes with a public sign, and the four repay being seen together: Jerusalem at Pentecost, Jews (chapter 2); Samaria, a people Jews kept at arm’s length (chapter 8); Caesarea, Gentiles in Cornelius’s house (chapter 10); and now Ephesus, men left over from the old order. (At Samaria Luke says only that the Spirit’s coming could be seen.) Each time the Spirit falls visibly at a frontier, with an apostle present. After this chapter it does not occur again in Acts, and the letters, even where they regulate tongues at Corinth (1 Corinthians 14), never tell believers to seek a later outpouring like this one.

The shape of the evidence. So Luke is documenting not the normal Christian life but the joining up of a divided world: Jew, Samaritan, Gentile and John’s leftover disciples, all publicly given the same Spirit, with apostolic witnesses to certify it.

Where Christians differ: a pattern for today? Pentecostals see a second-blessing pattern here (a distinct experience of the Spirit after conversion). This commentary’s view: these men were not yet Christians in the full sense; they had not believed in Jesus as having come. When they believed and were baptised, they received the Spirit at once. This is not a two-stage experience for Christians, but conversion. The tongues were a sign for a transitional moment in salvation history.

A family disagreement. Many godly Christians read these passages differently and expect the same experience today, out of a real hunger for God’s power. The disagreement is a family one: every side agrees the Spirit is given, and that a Christian without the Spirit is a contradiction (Romans 8:9). This commentary differs because Paul’s question ties receiving the Spirit to believing, which is how the letters speak of it (Ephesians 1:13).

What were these tongues and prophecy, and are they for today? They marked these disciples, who had stood at the edge of the new covenant, as fully part of the church. Many Christians, among them people of deep godliness, believe such gifts continue, and we should honour their love for Christ and their desire for his power. The more likely reading is that tongues and prophecy, as revelatory sign gifts, belonged to the foundational age of the apostles as signs of the Spirit’s coming, and ceased with it, the church being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with the canon of Scripture now complete (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4). This is the cessationist view, held charitably. Nothing here makes tongues the evidence of the Spirit for every believer, and God remains free to answer prayer in wonderful ways.

The map the risen Lord drew. The four frontiers are not random. Before he ascended, Jesus told the apostles that they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came upon them, and be his witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). Jerusalem, Samaria, Caesarea, Ephesus: the outpourings trace that map outward, each one the ascended Christ keeping his word at the next border. John had said that the one coming after him would baptise with the Holy Spirit. Here, in a room in Ephesus, the last of John’s own disciples meet that baptiser. The Spirit falls, and the one pouring him out is Jesus.

About twelve. Perhaps a hint of a renewed Israel, but about twelve is the sort of thing a man writes when he is reporting rather than constructing. In a city of perhaps a quarter of a million, the work begins with a dozen men who had been following an out-of-date sermon. Within three years all Asia will have heard the word of the Lord.

In the flow. Verses 1–7 finish a story that began at 18:24, gathering the last followers of John the Baptist into the church of Jesus, as John wanted (John 3:30). They set the theme of the chapter: nothing incomplete, borrowed or rival can stand beside the risen Lord, whether an out-of-date religion, a stolen name, a library of spells or a goddess.

If I have never spoken in tongues, am I missing something? No. Paul asks, expecting the answer no, whether all speak with tongues (1 Corinthians 12:30). The gifts were distributed as the Spirit willed, never to everyone, and on the view this commentary holds the sign gifts have ceased in any case. What no believer lacks is the Spirit himself, with everything that matters most: union with Christ, adoption, assurance, the power to pray, and the slow growth of love. The greatest gift, Paul says, is love (1 Corinthians 13:13). If you love Christ and are learning to love his people, you are not a second-class Christian. You are filled with the same Spirit who came at Ephesus.

On a Tuesday. Treat the believer from a different tradition, charismatic or not, as one who has the same Spirit you have. The ascended Lord has no first-class and second-class members; there is one body and one Spirit (Ephesians 4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three months. Set beside three Sabbaths at Thessalonica, it is the longest synagogue ministry Luke measures anywhere.

What is Paul doing when he persuades them about the kingdom of God? He is making the case for King Jesus. The kingdom of God is God’s kingly rule, and the great news is that the King has come: Jesus, crucified and risen, now reigns and will one day return to reign in full. So to persuade about the kingdom is to show people from the Scriptures who Jesus is and to urge them to bow to him as Lord, and so enter his kingdom, which a person does the moment he repents and trusts the King. We are brought into it now, and we await its full coming when the King returns.

Reasoning and persuading. He argued and sought to convince, patiently, from the Scriptures. You need not be a clever debater: to persuade about the kingdom is, at bottom, to help people see and trust the King.

Stubborn. Luke describes the ending in three stages. First they became stubborn, the word used of Israel in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:8); then they continued in unbelief; then they began speaking evil of the Way, an early name for the Christian faith (9:2), before the congregation: public disparagement aimed at the people still listening. Paul had put up with the first two for three months. What he will not do is go on providing a platform where the thing is being poisoned for everybody else in the room.

He withdrew. He does not leave Ephesus. In Pisidian Antioch he was expelled from the district; in Thessalonica he was smuggled out at night. Here he simply moves down the street and carries on, and he takes the converts with him, which is one of the clearest pictures so far in Acts of a congregation separating from a synagogue and setting up elsewhere.

The hall of Tyrannus. The hall was probably a lecture hall, a scholē (our word school), a public room with no religious associations; Tyrannus was its owner or the lecturer who normally taught there. Shut out of the sacred space, Paul took the gospel into the ancient equivalent of a rented conference room and taught there daily for two years, alongside his trade (20:34). Some manuscripts (not the earliest, so most modern Bibles leave it out) add that he taught from the fifth hour to the tenth, roughly 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the heat of the day, when the hall stood empty and most people rested. The gospel needs no grand temple.

Is it pushy to try to change other people’s beliefs? Only if Paul were selling his own opinions. But he was reasoning, which treats people as minds to be persuaded, not targets to be pressured, and he did it in the open, where anyone could answer back. Everybody tries to persuade others of what they think is true and good; the only question is whether what we commend is true. If Jesus really rose from the dead, then keeping quiet about him is not humility but a lack of love. And the Christian persuades not as one who is better, but as one who has been forgiven and wants the same mercy for the person in front of him.

When should a Christian leave a church? Not lightly, and not because of preferences, personalities or a dull season; Paul stayed three months in a synagogue that was arguing with him. But there are times when leaving is right: when the gospel itself is denied or ridiculed, when Christ is publicly spoken against and the leaders will not be corrected, when you are prevented from obeying Scripture. Even then, go as Paul went: without bitterness, after patient effort, taking care for others who need help, and joining yourself promptly to a faithful church. Never leave the Way because you left a building.
verseByVerse.note: The hall of Tyrannus was probably a lecture hall. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the residents of Asia. This continued for two years, which with the three months makes nearly three years in Ephesus (20:31). And the second half of the sentence is an extraordinary claim, made flatly. Asia was a Roman province of a great many cities and towns, running down the western seaboard of what is now Turkey and inland for a hundred miles and more. Luke’s all is the broad language of a historian describing a whole region reached, not a head count, but the claim is large, and Demetrius will confirm it (v. 26).

Paul did not travel to them. So far as Acts records, he stayed in Ephesus the whole time, in one room, teaching daily. He seems never to have gone to Colossae; he tells the Colossians that many have not seen his face (Colossians 2:1). He probably never went to Laodicea or Hierapolis. Of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, he is only recorded as visiting one.

The funnel. Ephesus was the greatest port on that coast and the terminus of the roads from the interior; traders, pilgrims, officials and students all came through it, some wandered into a lecture hall in the afternoon, and went home. Churches at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis were probably founded in these years through co-workers like Epaphras (Colossians 1:7; 4:13), a man of Colossae who carried the gospel a hundred miles inland to a town Paul never saw. Paul trained others, who went out.

The strategy of staying still. The most travelled man in the New Testament reached an entire province by staying still and teaching every day for two years to whoever happened to be in the room. That is a considerable comfort for anybody whose service to God is fixed in one place. You do not know who is in the room, or where they are going afterwards.

The Lord who walks among the lampstands. Luke calls it the word of the Lord, and decades later the Lord himself spoke to the churches it planted. In Revelation the risen Christ addresses seven churches of this very province, beginning with Ephesus, as the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand and walks among the seven golden lampstands (Revelation 2:1). That is the deeper story of these two years. Paul taught in a hired room; Christ was lighting lamps across Asia, and he never stopped walking among them, knowing their works, correcting and comforting them. The word that spread from the hall of Tyrannus was his own voice, and the churches it made were his.

Is my work wasted if I serve in one small place where nothing seems to spread? No. You cannot see where the people you teach will go, any more than Paul could see Epaphras walking home to Colossae. The Sunday school class, the youth group, the Bible study in your home, the conversation with a colleague: any of them may contain someone who carries the gospel to a place you will never visit. Your task is to teach faithfully what you have been given, and to entrust it to faithful people who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). The spreading is the Lord’s work, and he has never been short of roads.
verseByVerse.note: Churches such as those at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis probably began in this period through Paul’s co-workers.

parallels.desc: three years

verseByVerse.quote: And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Extraordinary miracles. God was doing, not Paul. Luke’s phrase is odd enough to be deliberate: literally miracles not of the ordinary kind, unusual even by apostolic standards. Coming from the man who has already recorded the lame walking, the dead raised and prison doors opened, that is quite a qualification. In a city famous for magic, God showed his superior power.

Handkerchiefs or aprons. The two items are probably workman’s cloths: the sweatband a labourer tied round his head, and the apron a craftsman wore at the bench. These are not priestly vestments or relics. They are the working clothes of a man who made tents in that city for two years, taken away from his bench. It is like Peter’s shadow (5:15).

What Luke does not say. Luke mentions no one’s faith here, only that the sick were healed, so if superstition was mixed in, God was merciful beyond it. This passage has been put to uses it will not bear, so be exact. He does not say Paul distributed the cloths, blessed them, charged for them or recommended the practice, or a word about how it worked. God is the subject and the cloths are purely passive. Somebody took Paul’s sweatband to a sick relative, and God, who was not obliged to do anything of the kind, healed them.

Power that went out from him. Luke has told a story like this once before, about Jesus. A woman who had bled for twelve years touched the fringe of his garment and was healed, and Jesus said that power had gone out from him (Luke 8:44–46). He would not let her go home thinking the cloth had done it; he told her that her faith had made her well. Ephesus is the risen Lord going on with all that he began to do and teach (1:1), through his apostle. Cloth is only cloth. The healing came from the person of the Lord.

Why God stooped to it. Ephesus was a famous centre of the magical arts; written charms from the city were known across the Mediterranean as Ephesian letters, and its people believed absolutely in power conveyed through objects. God met that city where its convictions were, and then spent the next eight verses demonstrating the difference between his power and magic.

Where Christians differ: prayer cloths. Some ministries today sell or send anointed cloths, promising healing or prosperity. This commentary’s view: Luke calls these miracles extraordinary, done by God through an apostle at a unique time, to confirm the gospel in a city of magic. Nothing in Scripture tells believers to use objects for healing. Paul never sold anything. Seeking power through objects is close to the magic Ephesus was about to renounce (v. 19).

Should we expect miracles like these today? Luke calls them extraordinary, and they confirmed Paul as an apostle: the signs of a true apostle were performed among them, he told the Corinthians, with signs and wonders and mighty works (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). God is still free to heal in answer to prayer, and he often does, but Scripture gives no promise that such miracles will accompany ministry today, and nothing here supports selling healing cloths. So the cloths are not a technique, and it should be said plainly that selling prayer cloths, anointed handkerchiefs and the rest to sick and desperate people is precisely the trade this chapter destroys. The Ephesians who understood this passage correctly did not start a business in it. They lit a bonfire.

So should I pray for healing when I am ill? Yes, without hesitation. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them, and promises that the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick (James 5:14–15), and the Lord often answers by healing, through medicine or without it. Pray to God directly, and ask others to pray. What this passage warns against is not prayer but technique: the idea that healing comes through objects, formulas or special people with a gift for sale. God is not a power to be accessed but a Father to be trusted. If he heals, thank him. If he does not yet, his grace is sufficient for you, and the final healing is certain (2 Corinthians 12:9; Revelation 21:4).
verseByVerse.note: The handkerchiefs and aprons were probably the cloths Paul used while working at his trade.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.' Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Itinerant exorcists. Exorcism was a common, often paid, trade in the ancient world, worked by technique: incantations, formulas, charms, and above all reciting powerful names believed to compel the spirits. Jewish exorcists were especially sought after, because they could invoke the name of the one true God (Josephus describes them, and legend traced their arts back to Solomon). It was all about harnessing power by the right words, not about knowing God. These men added Jesus to the list, as a magic word.

The Jesus whom Paul proclaims. The whole disaster is contained in the formula. Not by Jesus. By the Jesus whom Paul proclaims. Second-hand faith: not my Lord Jesus, but the Jesus Paul preaches. They cannot name him on their own account. They have to route the name through somebody else’s relationship with him, the way you might quote an authority you have never met, and they admit it in the act of trying it.

An honest confession. That is the position of a great many religious people, then and now. They have watched Christianity work in a parent, a spouse or a friend whose faith is obviously real, and they would like the results. What they reach for is not Christ but the effect he has on other people. Yet what they reached for second-hand was on offer first-hand: not a power to be borrowed from another man’s life but a Lord who says to anyone, Come to me (Matthew 11:28). You cannot borrow his authority while keeping him at arm’s length; but he never refuses himself to someone who comes.

Seven sons of Sceva. No Sceva appears in the lists of high priests that we have, and the name is Latin. He may have been from a high-priestly family, or claimed the title, the best possible credential in the exorcism trade. If so, the fraud runs all the way down: a bogus priest’s sons using a borrowed name. Seven of them: a family firm.

Is it wrong to end a prayer in Jesus’ name? Not at all; it is right, and Jesus told us to ask in his name (John 14:13–14; 16:23–24). But praying in his name is not attaching a password to the end of a request. It means coming to the Father on the ground of who Jesus is and what he has done, trusting him as your mediator, and asking what fits his character and purposes. The words matter because the person matters. A child who says please father is not using a formula; he is speaking to someone he knows. Pray in Jesus’ name as one who belongs to him, and you will never be using it as Sceva’s sons did.
verseByVerse.note: Exorcists often called on the names of powerful beings in their spells. No high priest named Sceva is known; he may have been from a high-priestly family, or used the title for show.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the evil spirit answered them, Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you? It is a chilling sentence, and in Greek it uses two different verbs. The first, ginōskō, is the word for knowing a person: Jesus I know. The second, epistamai, is the word for recognising, being acquainted with, having someone on file: Paul I recognise. The change may be partly for variety, but it fits the scene. And then the third clause has no verb of knowing at all: but who are you? The demons believe that God is one, and shudder (James 2:19). They know his true servants. They do not fear people who use his name without knowing him.

Three tiers. There is the Lord, whom hell knows exactly: the Holy One of God (Luke 4:34). There is his servant, known in that world because he has been doing damage in it for two years. And there are these seven men, who are nobody. The middle tier is startling: the powers of darkness take note of people who are actually doing something.

Leaped on them. Luke piles up the verbs, leaped, mastered, overpowered. Seven professional exorcists against one possessed man, and he puts the lot of them into the street.

Naked and wounded. A humiliating, almost comic scene, and the only exorcism in Acts that fails. Luke shows what happens when the name of Jesus is used by men who do not belong to the person they name.

Not a technology. The lesson is not only that the demonic is dangerous to meddle with, true though that is. It is that Christianity is not a technology. There is no formula, no words that work, no transferable method, and this is a mercy, because a faith that worked by technique would be available to the manipulative and the cruel. The authority of Jesus is inseparable from Jesus, and cannot be detached and used by somebody who has not submitted to him. So the question in this verse is worth letting land: if the powers of darkness were asked about you, would the answer be I recognise him, or who are you? If that question unsettles a believer who feels small and unfruitful, take heart: the answer rests not on your usefulness but on whose you are, for the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19).

But did Jesus not say not to stop a man casting out demons in his name? He did (Mark 9:38–40), and he also warned of some who would cast out demons in his name and yet whom he never knew (Matthew 7:22–23). The man in Mark was apparently a genuine follower outside the circle of the twelve, and Jesus would not have him forbidden. The sons of Sceva were different: they used Jesus’ name as a borrowed spell, by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims, with no faith of their own, and the demon knew it.

Should a Christian be afraid of demons? No. A believer belongs to Christ, who disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Do not be curious about the occult, do not dabble, and do not give the devil a foothold through unconfessed sin (Ephesians 4:27). Resist him, firm in the faith, and he will flee (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8–9). The armour God gives is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18), not rituals. If someone seems to be in serious spiritual trouble, go to your pastor and pray together. The name of Jesus on the lips of his own is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Known to all. Consider what got the city’s attention. Not the miracles of verse 11: Ephesus was full of wonder-workers. What went round the city was a story about the name of Jesus refusing to work for people who had no right to it. A humiliating public failure turned out to be some of the most effective evangelism in the chapter, because it told a city of magicians something they could not have learned from a success: this name is not a commodity.

Fear. Not admiration, but the recognition that they were dealing with something real and not manageable. Ephesus had spent centuries handling the invisible world by technique and had discovered a power that could not be handled. That is what holiness feels like from the outside: when Isaiah saw the Lord he cried that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5). The holy God is never anybody’s instrument.

The name extolled. Extolled means made great, magnified. In Acts the name of Jesus is never a label; it is Jesus himself in his saving power, the name by which a lame man walked (3:16). The exorcists treated it as a tool small enough to carry about; the city discovered it was larger than they were. That is how the name of Jesus has always grown great: through humiliation. He was himself mocked and crucified, and therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9).

Confessing and divulging. Now the sting, aimed at the church rather than the city. These are believers, who had kept up their magic secretly. Divulging means disclosing what was hidden; spells were thought to draw their power from secrecy, so to reveal them was to break them. Real repentance brings sins into the light (1 John 1:9; James 5:16).

Keeping one door open. So there were Christians in Ephesus who had been holding on to their charms. Not out of rebellion, most likely, but out of the ordinary human instinct to keep one door open: to trust Christ and also to keep the amulet, in case. The modern version is rarely amulets. It is the habit you have never mentioned to anybody, the arrangement you have not brought into the light, the thing you would not want read out. These people had been genuinely converted and were genuinely holding something back. Luke’s word for the cure is not only repented. It is divulged: they said it out loud, to somebody, and found Christ’s forgiveness already waiting in the light.

Do I need to confess my sins to another person, or only to God? To God always, and to others sometimes. Every sin is against God, and he forgives all who confess it to him through Christ (1 John 1:9); no priest is needed to stand between you and him. But James tells us also to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, that we may be healed (James 5:16). Secret sins grow in the dark, and naming one to a trusted, mature believer often breaks its hold. If you have wronged someone, confess to them. If a hidden sin has its grip on you, tell one wise Christian friend or your pastor. You are not seeking absolution from them; you are bringing it into the light where Christ’s forgiveness already shines.

verseByVerse.quote: And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their books. Every word of that is costly. These were not printed volumes but scrolls of incantations, charms and spells, laboriously copied by hand, the working capital of the trade. A magician’s scrolls were his livelihood, his reputation, and his protection. And nobody raided the houses; the owners went home and came back carrying them.

In the sight of all. Publicly, where the city could watch, which is the one method that leaves no way back. A man who quietly disposes of something can quietly replace it. A man who burns it in the square in front of his neighbours has ended a career.

Fifty thousand pieces of silver. Somebody added it up while the fire burned. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, roughly a day’s wage, so this is well over a century of a working man’s income going up in smoke in an afternoon.

Why not sell them? This is the point. They could have sold them. There was a ready market: every one of those scrolls had a buyer somewhere in Asia, and the proceeds could have gone to the poor, or to the church, or to Paul’s support. It would have looked like the responsible course. They burned them instead, because selling them would have meant putting back into circulation the exact thing they had been delivered from, which would pass the evil on. Repentance that is careful to recoup its losses has not quite finished. Some obedience costs you nothing because you found a way to make the disposal profitable, and then there is the kind in this verse.

Counted as loss. Paul, who was in Ephesus in these years, later wrote what that arithmetic looks like from the inside: whatever gain he had, he counted as loss for the sake of Christ, because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord (Philippians 3:7–8). That is why the bonfire was not a tragedy. The magicians had found something worth more than their trade, and it was not a better technique but a person. Christ had given himself for them, and a library of spells was a small thing to give back. The smoke over the square was a confession that Jesus was worth more.

In the flow. Verse 20 is the last of Luke’s short progress reports on the word (6:7; 12:24) before the story turns toward Jerusalem and Rome. It closes the battle that began at verse 11: the power of Jesus cannot be borrowed, bought or mixed with magic, and the word won.

Is burning books not what fanatics do? Not this kind of burning. Nobody seized these scrolls or banned them; their own owners carried them to the fire, at their own loss, because they had been set free from what was written in them. The gospel had advanced in Ephesus by reasoning and persuasion (v. 8), and Luke never shows Christians destroying other people’s property or silencing their opponents. What burned in the square was a confession: we were wrong, and we will not pass this on. A church that tried to win by burning other people’s books would have forgotten this chapter.

Should Christians do the same today? Items that are themselves tools of the occult, divination or idolatry should be destroyed, not sold or passed on, since that would put them into other hands. The point is a clean break, at cost, with what once ruled us. The same principle reaches further: whatever feeds your particular sin, the subscription, the app, the bottle, the contact in your phone, should be cut off decisively rather than kept within reach. Jesus spoke of tearing out an eye rather than keeping it to sin with (Matthew 5:29–30). Not every possession is evil, and Christian freedom is real. But what has become a snare should go in the fire, not in the attic.

Increase and prevail. Prevail means grew strong, overpowered: the word of the Lord overpowered the magic of Ephesus, at the point where Christians destroyed their own property in public.

Why make the word itself the thing that grows? Why does Luke put it so oddly, rather than simply saying more people believed? On purpose; it is one of his favourite ways of speaking (6:7; 12:24; 13:49). Two reasons. First, he is deliberately picturing the gospel as a living seed: the very word for increase (auxanō, grow) is the language of living, fruitful things, the word of Jesus’ parables where the kingdom-seed sprouts and grows of its own God-given life (Mark 4:8, 26–29); the seed is the word (Luke 8:11). The gospel is planted in the world and grows like wheat, and believers are its fruit. Second, and more pointedly, by making the word the actor Luke takes the credit off the preachers and puts it on God: it is not Paul’s cleverness or the church’s strategy that conquers Ephesus, but the word itself, alive with God’s own power (Romans 1:16; Isaiah 55:11). So the strange phrasing is really a confession of faith: watch the word, not the men, and take heart, for that same living word is still growing and prevailing in the world today.

On a Tuesday. What do you need to burn? Christ gave himself for you and his Spirit now lives in you, so get rid of whatever ties you to sin, whatever it costs, and do it so that there is no way back. No break of ours is ever as clean as it should be, but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19); so each time you find a scroll you kept, bring it to him and burn that too.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was famous for magic spells. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, about a day’s wage: fifty thousand was a fortune.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome." And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Resolved in the Spirit. Many see this as the hinge of the book: the rest of Acts works out this one sentence. Paul was collecting money from the Gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26), and meant to deliver it himself. In the Spirit could mean his own spirit or the Holy Spirit; given how the Spirit steers Paul throughout, the Spirit-guided sense fits well.

I must also see Rome. Look at the route: Macedonia, Achaia, Jerusalem, Rome. He goes through Macedonia and Achaia (chapter 20), is arrested in the temple at Jerusalem (chapter 21), and reaches Rome years later, after governors, a king, an appeal to Caesar, a shipwreck and a snakebite, in chains at the empire’s expense (chapter 28). The plan was right, God kept it, and the keeping of it cost Paul his liberty.

Must. The little word must (dei) is Luke’s word for divine necessity, the same one that stood over the cross: not blind fate but God’s settled purpose, for he works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11). Paul had wanted to see Rome for years (Romans 1:11–13), but this is obligation, not preference, and the Lord confirms it after the riot in Jerusalem: as he has testified in Jerusalem, so he must testify also in Rome (23:11).

The Master’s road. Luke has told this story before. In his Gospel Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), under the same must: the Son of Man must suffer many things and be raised (Luke 9:22). Now the servant resolves to go to Jerusalem, and what waits for him there is the Master’s road walked again: a mob shouting Away with him, a Roman officer, trials before governors and a king. Paul is not copying Jesus to earn anything. He is following the one who went first and went further, to a cross where he bore what no servant ever could. Because he went up to Jerusalem and suffered and rose, his servants go up to their own Jerusalems unafraid.

Timothy and Erastus. He sends people ahead, as by now he always does. Erastus may be the city treasurer of Corinth (Romans 16:23), whose name may appear on a paving stone found there recording an Erastus who laid the pavement at his own expense. The identification is debated, but if it holds, a senior municipal official is being used as a messenger.

He stayed. Having decided to go, he stayed on and finished, and wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus during this time (1 Corinthians 16:8). The riot happens to a man who had made up his mind to leave and had not yet left, the moment at which most of us are most inclined to coast.

How may a believer know his decisions are Spirit-guided today? First, let the anxiety down. The apostles received extraordinary, direct steering because of their unique founding role; God’s ordinary way is quieter, and he has not promised you a voice in your head for every choice. So how does the Spirit lead? Chiefly through the Word. Spirit and Scripture always go together: he guides by lighting up the Bible he inspired, which is a lamp to our feet and equips us for every good work (Psalm 119:105; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). Most of God’s will is already plainly revealed: be holy, love, forgive, flee sin, serve. So the Spirit-led life is, nine times in ten, simply the obedient life.

A renewed mind. Then through a renewed mind and sanctified wisdom. For what Scripture does not directly settle, which job, where to live, the Spirit leads not by bypassing your thinking but by maturing it: be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God (Romans 12:2); and if you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously (James 1:5). Add prayer (Proverbs 3:5–6), godly counsel (Proverbs 15:22), and the providence of opened and closed doors. Inner promptings and a sense of peace may play a part (Philippians 2:13), but they are never to be trusted alone; they must be tested by Scripture and wisdom, for the heart can deceive (Jeremiah 17:9; 1 John 4:1).

The shape of a life. And most freeing of all: the clearest mark of being led by the Spirit is not a feeling about one decision but the shape of a life. All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Romans 8:14): led, in context, to put sin to death and live as God’s children; and the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience and the rest (Galatians 5:22–23). So a choice made in love, humility, holiness and faith, by a person walking closely with God, is a Spirit-led choice, even if no special feeling attends it; while one driven by pride, lust, greed or self-will is not, however peaceful it feels. Does it square with Scripture? Have I prayed for wisdom and sought counsel? Is my heart surrendered? Then decide, and trust him with the outcome: the heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (Proverbs 16:9). He is kind enough to redeem even our wrong turns (Romans 8:28). A Christian walking with God need not fear missing God’s will; the Guide is faithful.

What if I made a decision in good faith and it went badly? Then you are in Paul’s company. His plan to see Rome was right, and it took him through arrest, storm and shipwreck. A hard outcome does not prove a wrong decision; obedience often leads through suffering, as it led our Lord. If, looking back, you see that you acted in pride or haste, confess it, and receive his forgiveness. If you acted in faith and it still went hard, do not torment yourself with what might have been. The Lord who establishes our steps also works through the steps we wish we had not taken, and nothing in your path is outside his care.

On a Tuesday. If you have already decided to move on from something, a job, a ministry, a town, finish well where you are. Do not coast in Ephesus.
verseByVerse.note: Erastus may be the city official of Corinth whose name appears on an inscription there.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No little disturbance. Understatement: it means a riot that filled the city’s great theatre. And a line later Demetrius brought no little business to the craftsmen. The same phrase on both is probably no accident. The size of the disturbance and the size of the profits are being measured against each other, and Luke expects you to notice which caused which.

The Way. One of the earliest names of the Christian movement, and Luke uses it repeatedly (9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). Jesus said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6); the Old Testament pictures the life of faith as a road, the Way of Holiness (Isaiah 35:8); and Christianity is a road travelled after Jesus: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him (Colossians 2:6).

Demetrius the silversmith. Ephesus lived on its temple. The temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, said to be four times the size of the Parthenon. Pilgrims came from across the empire and bought something to take home, and miniature silver shrines of the goddess were the premium souvenir. Demetrius made them.

Artemis of the Ephesians. Artemis (the Romans’ Diana) was not quite the classical Greek huntress but a local mother goddess of fertility, shown with many breasts or eggs, protectress of the city. So the gospel collides with a formidable triple alliance: a famous false god, fierce civic pride (Ephesus called itself the goddess’s temple keeper, v. 35), and big money. The gospel had already burned the magic books (v. 19); now it threatens the idol trade.

Religion was big business. The man who starts the riot is not a priest or a philosopher but a manufacturer, and what has gone wrong is his order book. In the next verse Demetrius will say the quiet part aloud to his own guild, and only afterwards reach for the goddess. Luke could have written this as a clash of religions. He writes it as a trade dispute with a religious vocabulary, which is what it was.

In the flow. The riot is the last great scene of the Ephesian years. In verses 11 to 20 the word overcame demons and magic; in verses 23 to 41 it meets money and civic religion, and again it wins without a blow being struck, while an official of the empire finds no crime in it.

What if my own job is connected to something I now see is wrong? Then you face the choice the Ephesian craftsmen faced, and Scripture will not let you dodge it. Some work is plainly incompatible with following Christ: making idols, selling occult services, producing pornography, defrauding people. If your livelihood depends on such things, you must leave it, trusting God to provide, as the magicians did with their scrolls. Much work is a mixture: an honest job in a company that also does wrong things. There, seek wisdom, refuse to do wrong yourself, and pray about whether to stay. Talk it through with your pastor. Christ asks for costly obedience, and he has never let anyone who gave up something for his sake be a loser in the end (Mark 10:29–30).
verseByVerse.note: The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Artemis of Ephesus was a mother-goddess of fertility, not the huntress of Greek myth.

parallels.desc: a wide door, and many adversaries

verseByVerse.quote: These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, "Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A guild meeting. Not of priests or temple authorities, but of his own silversmiths plus the workmen in similar trades, perhaps the men who supplied the silver and the shops that sold the shrines. Demetrius has understood that his grievance is an industry’s grievance and has organised accordingly.

From this business. One of the most candid speeches about opposition to the gospel anywhere in Scripture. No theology: the first thing out of his mouth, to fellow tradesmen, is the money. He will produce Artemis in a moment, when he needs a crowd. As in Philippi (16:19), the gospel threatens those who profit from falsehood.

The engine and the paintwork. Watch the order, because it is the anatomy of much resistance to Christ. First, in private, the interest: our wealth. Then, in public, the principle: the honour of the goddess and the dignity of our city. The interest is the engine and the principle is the paintwork, and Luke has arranged the speech so that we hear the private version first. Demetrius is not lying about the facts; the falling sales and the threat to the temple’s standing are real. He is choosing which true thing to say to which audience.

Not only in Ephesus. It would be comfortable to leave that with first-century idol manufacturers. The mechanism is ordinary and works in people who are not conscious of it: when the gospel threatens something we are getting, an income, a position, a habit, the objection that forms in us almost never presents itself as this would cost me. It presents itself as a reasonable difficulty with the faith. So put a question to your own objections: what would I have to give up if this were true? It is not a way of dismissing anybody’s argument, which must be answered on its merits. But Demetrius is in Scripture to tell us that the stated reason and the real reason are often two different things, and that the man himself may not have noticed.

Lovers of money who ridiculed him. Luke’s Gospel has shown this scene in miniature: you cannot serve God and money, Jesus said, and the Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things and ridiculed him (Luke 16:13–14). Demetrius is the same pattern on a civic scale. And the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58); he is the one Master who gives to his servants rather than taking from them, and so those who belong to him can loosen their grip.

Is it wrong for a Christian to want to be wealthy? Wealth itself is not sin; Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly, and honest work that prospers is a gift of God. But the desire to be rich is dangerous: those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and many senseless and harmful desires, for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:9–10). The test is Demetrius’s: when money and truth collide, which gives way? A Christian holds wealth with an open hand, gives generously, refuses to gain it dishonestly, and is content with what God provides (Philippians 4:11–13; Hebrews 13:5). If truth is bending to protect your income, money has become your master.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hostile witness. This is among the best evidence in the chapter. Demetrius has every interest in exaggerating the threat, but he is speaking to men who can check him, about a market they all trade in, and he reports an effect measurable across the province. Luke’s own claim in verse 10, that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, could be read as an evangelist’s enthusiasm. Here is the same claim from the accounts department of the idol trade.

Not gods. That is Paul’s preaching summarised by an opponent, and it is accurate (17:29; 1 Corinthians 8:4). It is also the argument of the Hebrew prophets: Isaiah’s mockery of the man who cuts down a tree, burns half of it to roast his dinner and bows down to the other half (Isaiah 44:14–20), and Jeremiah’s idols like scarecrows in a cucumber field, which cannot speak and have to be carried (Jeremiah 10:5). And Demetrius is the one man in Ephesus who cannot honestly disagree, because he makes them.

The escalation. A masterpiece of its kind. The trade, which is what he actually cares about, occupies one clause. Then the temple, then the goddess, then her standing before Asia and the world, and by the end of the sentence a fall in souvenir sales has become a threat to the cosmic order, which nobody could be accused of self-interest for defending.

Counted as nothing. But he has accidentally said something about the gospel that is truer than he knows. That is precisely what the gospel does to an idol: not attack it, not vandalise it, but reduce it to what it always was. An idol has power over a person only while he believes it holds something up: his safety, his luck, his city’s greatness. Once he sees that an idol has no real existence and that there is one God (1 Corinthians 8:4), the silver shrine is still on the shelf, but it has lost its grip on him. Paul’s own letter to this city reminds the Ephesians that they had once been without hope and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:12).

Within a few centuries. The temple lay in ruins and the goddess was forgotten. Sacked by the Goths and later quarried for stone, its site had to be dug out of a marsh in the nineteenth century; today a single reconstructed column stands. The word of the Lord endures.

The temple not made with hands. Ephesus was proud of one building, and Paul later wrote to the Christians of this city about another: in Christ the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:20–22). That is the final answer to the silversmiths. The Artemision was a wonder of the world; the church in Ephesus was living stones in a temple the Lord himself was building.

What are the idols made with hands today? Most of ours are not carved, but they are still made by us: money, status, a career, a body shaped and photographed, a home, a political cause, a relationship, a reputation, even a ministry. Anything we look to for the security, meaning or approval that only God can give has become an idol, and it is made with hands because we built it. The test is simple: what would devastate you to lose, what do you daydream about, where does your money and time go when no one is watching? Idols are not removed only by smashing them, but by finding something better. Show your heart the beauty of Christ, and the shrines lose their shine.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's companions in travel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great is Artemis. A cry of civic and religious pride, used in Ephesian worship, and inscriptions confirm the title. A guild meeting about profits ends in religious chanting, and the transition takes no time at all. The men who came in worried about their order books go out shouting for their goddess, and the two things have fused completely.

Sincere passion for an interest. That fusion is one of the most dangerous things in the chapter. A man can defend an interest with real religious passion and be quite sincere in the passion. The feeling is not manufactured; these men were genuinely enraged. But it had been aroused by a threat to something else, and it is the sincerity that makes it so hard to see.

The theatre. The noise, the running, the rumour outrunning the fact. The theatre at Ephesus is still there, cut into the side of Mount Pion and looking down the marble street to the old harbour; it seated about twenty-five thousand people, and you can sit where the crowd sat. That is where a mob went when it wanted to be a public meeting.

Gaius and Aristarchus. They could not find Paul, so they took two of his colleagues. Aristarchus of Thessalonica turns up again and again: on the journey to Jerusalem (20:4), on the ship to Rome (27:2), and in prison with Paul at the end, his fellow prisoner (Colossians 4:10). Dragged into a theatre by a mob, he stayed with the apostle to the chains.

Seized because they were near. Nobody was shouting about Gaius and Aristarchus. They were seized because they were near Paul, the ordinary experience of everyone close to a person in the front line: the family, the colleagues, the host who lent the house, as Jason had found in Thessalonica.

Let these men go. There is one arrest in the Gospels that went the other way. When the soldiers came for Jesus in the garden, he stepped forward and said, If you seek me, let these men go (John 18:8), and his friends walked free while he was bound. Gaius and Aristarchus were dragged off for standing near Paul, and Paul could do nothing to stop it. Christ is the one leader whose nearness, in the end, buys his people’s safety. They may suffer for being near him, as Aristarchus did to the end; but the sentence that mattered fell on him alone, and they go free.

How do I tell whether my zeal is for God or for something of mine? Ask what makes you angry, and why. Righteous zeal is grieved most by what dishonours God and harms others; self-interested zeal flares when our comfort, status, group or pride is threatened, and then borrows God’s name. Ask whether your passion makes you more like Christ, patient, truthful, willing to suffer, or more like the theatre, loud, vague and ready to drag someone off. And invite a wise friend to tell you honestly. Zeal is good when it is according to knowledge (Romans 10:2), and when it would be just as fierce if nothing of yours were at stake.

On a Tuesday. Think of the Aristarchuses in your church, those who suffer because they stand near the front line: the pastor’s family, the missionary’s children. Bring them before God one by one.
verseByVerse.note: The theatre at Ephesus seated about 25,000 people. Gaius and Aristarchus were Paul’s travelling companions.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples would not let him. Of course he wished to go in: the largest audience he would ever have had, and his two friends on the floor of the theatre. And the Ephesian Christians stopped him.

Courage restrained. Paul is the apostle, and these are converts of two or three years. They overruled him, and Luke records it without a hint that they were wrong. A man who cannot be restrained by the people around him is not brave but unaccountable. Paul submitted.

The Asiarchs. The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province, associated with the provincial council, the imperial cult and the public games: part of the official religious establishment. And Luke says they were Paul’s friends. He does not say they were converted, but some of the most powerful men in Asia, whose duties included promoting a religion Paul preached against, sent urgent private messages when his life was in danger: another sign for Theophilus that respectable men did not see Paul as a criminal.

Both at once. Two years of daily teaching in an open hall had won Paul such friends. He had preached against idols in the city of Artemis, hard enough to dent an industry. And the officers of the rival religion liked him enough to try to save his life. Those two things are meant to be held together, and most of us manage only one of them.

Not before the hour. Paul’s Lord had walked this line first. At Nazareth a furious crowd drove Jesus to the brow of a hill, and passing through their midst he went away (Luke 4:29–30); no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30). When the hour came he gave himself up. Paul’s friends were asking him to keep his life for the hour God appointed, and not to spend it on a theatre.

Can I be friends with people whose beliefs I think are false? Yes, and you should be. Jesus was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Luke 7:34), and Paul’s friendship with the Asiarchs did not soften his message. Friendship is not endorsement. It is the ordinary love of neighbour, and it is often the road along which the gospel travels. Be honest about what you believe, never mock what they hold dear, and let them see that your convictions make you kinder, not harder. The danger is not in having unbelieving friends but in letting them shape your loves more than Christ does (1 Corinthians 15:33). Keep your heart anchored in him, and open your door.

On a Tuesday. Who in your life has permission to tell you no? If no one does, give it to someone this week.
verseByVerse.note: The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province associated with the provincial cult of the emperor.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mob called an assembly. Luke’s word for the gathering is ekklēsia, the ordinary Greek term for a citizens’ assembly (v. 39) and the New Testament’s word for the church. So this chapter has an ekklesia which is a mob, gathered by a grievance and unable to say why it is present. Christ’s ekklesia is called out by his voice and gathered around him (Matthew 18:20); it always knows why it has come.

What a senseless god makes. A whole city roaring itself hoarse for two hours (v. 34), and most of the rioters cannot say why they are there. You shall not fall in with the many to do evil (Exodus 23:2). Deeper still, this is what idolatry does to a mind: claiming to be wise, they become fools (Romans 1:21–22). Worshippers grow like what they worship, and the babble of the theatre is idolatry’s darkened mind made audible, while the Word gives a man back his right mind, as the delivered demoniac sat clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15).

Alexander. The Jewish community pushes a spokesman to the front, perhaps to show that they had nothing to do with Paul, since Jews also refused idols and were in real danger of suffering for somebody else’s preaching. The synagogue that had seen Paul leave two years earlier finds that the city cannot tell them apart.

How do I avoid being swept along by the crowd? Know what you believe and why, before the noise starts. Read Scripture daily, so that your mind is shaped by God’s word rather than by the latest outrage. Be slow to share, quick to check, and wary of anything that makes you feel certain without giving you reasons. Keep company with wise people, not only loud ones. Pray for a calm mind (Philippians 4:6–7). And remember that the majority has often been wrong: the crowd once chose Barabbas. A Christian is free to stand alone, because he does not stand alone; he stands with Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Alexander may have been put forward to show that the Jews had no part in the Christians’ activity.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Jew. To the crowd, Jews and Christians were the same, since both rejected Artemis. Alexander never said a word. They shouted him down before he could begin, and went on shouting.

Two hours. Thousands of people chanting five words in a stone bowl built to carry sound, like the prophets of Baal crying from morning until noon, with no voice and no one answering (1 Kings 18:26). Repetition is not truth. Their goddess could not hear them.

With one voice. The one thing in the day that was unanimous. Verse 32 said most of them did not know why they had come. They did not need to know. A slogan does not require you to have a reason; it requires you to have a side, and it will supply the feeling of certainty at no cost. Two hours of Great is Artemis settles nothing and answers nobody: Paul’s argument is not refuted and Alexander is not heard. But for two hours the theatre was full of people who felt entirely sure.

Another crowd, another cry. Scripture shows one other vast crowd crying out with one voice, and the difference is instructive. John saw myriads of myriads around the throne, saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:11–12). They too repeat and are unanimous, but their song gives its reason: for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9). Ephesus shouted that Artemis was theirs. Heaven sings that the Lamb has made them his. One chant needed two hours of noise to keep itself sure; the other will never run out of reasons.

Of the Ephesians. The slogan asserts not that Artemis is true, but that she is ours: civic pride wearing a goddess. And people seldom need two hours of chanting about something nobody doubts. The volume is the sound of a religion that has begun to feel the ground move.

Is repetition in Christian worship wrong too? Not in itself. The psalms repeat, his steadfast love endures for ever, twenty-six times in Psalm 136, and heaven repeats holy, holy, holy (Revelation 4:8). What Jesus forbade was heaping up empty phrases, as if God would hear us for our many words (Matthew 6:7). The difference is whether the words are true, understood and meant. A chorus sung with the mind engaged and the heart lifted to a God who hears is worship. Five words shouted for two hours to a goddess who cannot hear is noise. So sing gladly, and sing with understanding (1 Corinthians 14:15).

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, 'Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town clerk. One man walks out in front of thousands and quiets them. He was the city’s senior executive officer, who drafted the decrees, ran the assembly, and above all was answerable to Rome for order. He had the strongest personal reason in the theatre to end this.

Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis? He begins by agreeing with them, and this is the shrewdest thing in the speech. He does not tell an inflamed crowd that it is wrong. He tells them that they are so obviously right that the shouting is unnecessary. Temple keeper (neōkoros) was an official title of honour Ephesus held, confirmed by inscriptions and put on its coins, and he uses it deliberately: your status is not in question.

The sacred stone. The Greek word means fallen from Zeus, or from heaven: possibly a meteorite, worshipped as an image of Artemis, and the town clerk waves it as his clinching argument. They revered the falling rock while missing the God who made the heavens, worshipping the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25).

Do nothing rash. And there is the turn. Artemis is secure; why riot? If your position is unassailable, then this behaviour is beneath it. A city that is certain of its goddess does not need to roar for two hours in a theatre.

What cannot be denied. The clerk’s undeniable things were a title, a temple and a rock, and history has denied all three. Luke’s book has a different list. In Jerusalem the council that wanted the apostles silenced had to admit that a notable sign had been done through them and they could not deny it (4:16), and it had been done in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and whom God raised from the dead (4:10). The faith rests not on a stone that fell out of the sky but on a man who came out of a tomb, seen alive by hundreds of witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:6).

A competent bureaucrat. Luke reports this speech at length and with evident approval, although its argument is entirely pagan. He is not endorsing the theology. He is showing that the riot was ended by an ordinary official doing his job properly.

Why does Luke include a pagan speech in Scripture without correcting it? Because Scripture faithfully records what people said, without endorsing all of it. The Bible accurately reports the words of Satan, of Job’s comforters and of this town clerk; inspiration guarantees that the record is true, not that every speaker was right. Luke expects his readers to see the irony for themselves: a man defending what cannot be denied, in a city whose temple is long since gone. And he wants us to see God’s hand in ordinary order. The clerk was wrong about Artemis and right about the riot, and God used the second for his people’s good.
verseByVerse.note: The town clerk was the chief civic official, answerable to Rome for public order. The “sacred stone” was probably a meteorite venerated as an image of the goddess.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers. This is a formal finding, delivered in public by the senior officer of the city: Paul’s companions are innocent. Two charges are named and both are dismissed. Sacrilegious means temple robbers, a serious crime everywhere in the ancient world; blasphemers of our goddess means public abuse of Artemis.

Without vandalism and without mockery. After two years of Paul preaching against idols, nobody in the theatre could name a shrine he had touched. Paul had dented the magic trade, damaged the souvenir industry across the province, and persuaded a great many people to abandon the city’s religion, and he had done it without vandalism and without mockery. He argued that the idols were nothing. He did not throw anything at them.

A standard often failed. That is a standard the church has frequently failed since, and the failure is usually defended as boldness. Insulting a thing is much quicker than dismantling it. Ridicule also flatters the heart: it lets us feel superior and win the room without having to love the person in front of us. Paul’s two years produced a bonfire lit by the magicians themselves, and not one prosecutable act. The truth undermines idols without our ridicule.

Innocent, like his Master. Luke has recorded verdicts like this before. Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), and the centurion at the cross said, Certainly this man was innocent (Luke 23:47). Now a pagan official pronounces Paul’s companions blameless, and the servant’s innocence points back to the Master’s. But one difference matters more than any likeness. Paul’s companions were declared innocent and let go. Jesus was declared innocent and crucified anyway, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18).

The courts are open. Now the clerk turns it back on the man who started it: if Demetrius has a case, there is a court sitting and a governor to hear it. He had no case at law, which is why he had gone to the guild and the theatre instead. A grievance that will not go to the proper place for a hearing usually would not survive one.

But are Christians not supposed to call false religion false? Yes, and Paul did, plainly: gods made with hands are not gods. The question is how. You can say that something is untrue without sneering at the people who believe it or ridiculing what they hold sacred. Paul reasoned, explained, and pointed to the living God; he did not deface statues or mock worshippers. Speaking the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15) means being clear about what is false and gentle with those who are deceived, remembering that we were once deceived too (Titus 3:3). Mockery hardens people; patient truth, by God’s grace, sets them free.

On a Tuesday. Read back over the last thing you posted or said about another religion or worldview, and ask whether a thoughtful adherent would find it fair. If not, put it right.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The regular assembly. The word is ekklēsia again, this time in its precise civic meaning: the constitutional assembly that met on fixed days with an agenda and a procedure. The clerk is drawing the line between that and the crowd in front of him, and the difference is not the number of people or the strength of their feeling. It is whether there is a process by which anybody could be shown to be wrong.

In danger of being charged. Here is the real argument, kept until last. Rome could punish a city for rioting by removing its privileges as a free city. The clerk was worried about Rome, not Artemis: they had spent the afternoon handing the proconsul a reason to take their liberties away.
