No cause that we can give. He does not say the cause is weak. He says there is nothing they could put in writing. Somebody would have to draft the report, and that somebody is him. So the riot that was called to defend the greatness of Artemis ends with the city’s chief officer explaining that it cannot be explained.

The charge of rioting. Luke knows the irony. At Jesus’ trial his accusers said he stirred up the people (Luke 23:5), and Pilate released instead a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection (Luke 23:19, 25). The innocent was condemned as a troublemaker and the rioter went free. At Ephesus the roles fall the right way round. Yet every believer is a kind of Barabbas: the guilty one let go because the innocent took the sentence. The peace we enjoy, with God first and in the city after, was bought by his condemnation.

Why should Christians value law and order? Because God ordained governing authorities for our good, to restrain evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:1–4), and because the gospel spreads more freely where there is peace. Paul urged prayer for rulers precisely so that believers might lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way, and so that all may hear the truth (1 Timothy 2:1–4). That does not make the state our saviour, and it does not mean every law is just. But a Christian should be a good citizen, thankful for courts that are open and officials who do their jobs, and should pray for them, as God used this clerk.
verseByVerse.note: Rome could punish a city for unlawful rioting.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He dismissed the assembly. So the great riot of Ephesus ends: not with an earthquake or a sermon, but with a municipal officer sending everybody home.

Two assemblies. Luke may be drawing one last contrast. The assembly of Ephesus is dismissed by a clerk; the assembly of Christ answers to another Lord. Jesus said, I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18), and in this chapter he has done it in the city of Artemis. The clerk’s ekklesia went home. Christ’s ekklesia in Ephesus would receive an apostle’s letter, and later a word from the risen Lord himself (Revelation 2:1–7).

The restraint of the story. Luke had material for a very different ending, and he ends the whole Ephesian ministry with a man closing a meeting. That is how God most often works, and not how we most often tell the story. No apostle spoke, and nothing happened that anybody would call supernatural. The church was preserved that afternoon by the professional instincts of an official, the friendship of some provincial aristocrats, and a few disciples who would not let Paul go in.

Ordinary means. Every one of them was the hand of God, and not one of the people involved knew it. A habit of mind that only counts God present when something inexplicable happens leaves most of a life looking empty. The God who threw open the prison at Philippi with an earthquake protected his people at Ephesus with a competent civil servant, and Luke gives both episodes the same weight.

How can I see God’s hand in ordinary things? By remembering that providence is God’s most holy, wise and powerful preserving and governing of all his creatures and all their actions (Westminster Shorter Catechism, answer 11; compare the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.1 and the Westminster Confession 5.1), and that he works through means far more often than without them. The doctor’s skill, the friend’s warning, the delayed train, the job that fell through: these are not God’s absence but his usual way of working. Practise looking back at the end of a day and asking where he kept you, fed you, warned you or guided you. You will find him everywhere. And that will make you more thankful, and less anxious, for the God of the ordinary is the God of every hour.

The three years close. Twelve men who had never heard of the Holy Spirit; two years in a rented hall; a province evangelised by people whose names we do not know; the magic trade bankrupted by its own practitioners; a riot that ended in a finding of innocence. To this congregation will be written the letter that begins with God choosing his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Some of the earliest manuscripts lack the words in Ephesus at Ephesians 1:1, so the letter may have been written for several churches of the province, Ephesus among them. Luke’s own summary was given at verse 20: so the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.

19.theology: The word of God as the power of mission. Ephesus shows what the word of God, taught day after day, can do. Two years in a lecture hall, and all Asia hears: not by travel or strategy but by daily teaching, received by hearers who carry it home. The word creates the church. That is why Paul later charges Timothy to preach the word, in season and out of season (2 Timothy 4:2).
19.examples:
Then: All Asia hears the word from a lecture hall in Ephesus, a bonfire worth more than a century’s wages is lit in public, and the word of the Lord prevails, not by weapons or political power, but by the truth about the living God and the risen Christ.

Now: Churches are always tempted to replace patient teaching of the word with something more immediately impressive: spectacle, experience, technique, programmes. Ephesus was won by a man who reasoned from the Scriptures daily for two years. The word has lost none of its power; the question is whether we will give it the time and the central place it needs.

20.title: Farewell to Ephesus
20.text: <sup>1</sup>After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. <sup>2</sup>When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece. <sup>3</sup>There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia. <sup>4</sup>Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. <sup>5</sup>These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas, <sup>6</sup>but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days. <sup>7</sup>On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. <sup>8</sup>There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. <sup>9</sup>And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. <sup>10</sup>But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” <sup>11</sup>And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed. <sup>12</sup>And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted. <sup>13</sup>But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. <sup>14</sup>And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene. <sup>15</sup>And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. <sup>16</sup>For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost. <sup>17</sup>Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. <sup>18</sup>And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, <sup>19</sup>serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews; <sup>20</sup>how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, <sup>21</sup>testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>22</sup>And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, <sup>23</sup>except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. <sup>24</sup>But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. <sup>25</sup>And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. <sup>26</sup>Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, <sup>27</sup>for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. <sup>28</sup>Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. <sup>29</sup>I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; <sup>30</sup>and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. <sup>31</sup>Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears. <sup>32</sup>And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. <sup>33</sup>I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel. <sup>34</sup>You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. <sup>35</sup>In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ <sup>36</sup>And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. <sup>37</sup>And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him, <sup>38</sup>being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
20.overview:
After the riot Paul leaves Ephesus, strengthens the churches of Macedonia and spends three winter months in Greece, where he almost certainly wrote Romans. A plot sends him back overland, with men from the Gentile churches carrying the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and Luke rejoins him at Philippi (“we”). At Troas, on the first day of the week, the church gathers to break bread; during Paul’s long teaching Eutychus falls from a window, is picked up dead, and is given back alive.

Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul calls the Ephesian elders to Miletus. His farewell is the only speech in Acts addressed to Christian leaders. He reviews his ministry, faces the chains ahead, charges them to guard the flock God bought with his own blood, warns of wolves, and commends them to God and the word of his grace. Then they kneel, weep and see him to the ship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul leaves Ephesus for Macedonia and Greece until a plot sends him back overland. At Troas, on the first day of the week, Eutychus falls from a window and is picked up dead, and is taken home alive. The party sails down the coast, past Ephesus, because Paul is hurrying to Jerusalem for Pentecost.
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and Table on the Lord’s Day

The gathering at Troas on the first day of the week to break bread (v. 7) is the clearest picture in Acts of the church’s Sunday worship. The day of the resurrection became the day of gathering. Reformed churches see here the pattern of Christian worship: the word taught and the Supper shared, together, when the church meets on the Lord’s Day.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked the twenty miles from Troas to Assos alone while the others sailed, perhaps to pray as he moved toward Jerusalem and the suffering that awaited him. Now: Time alone with God still prepares Christ’s servants for costly obedience, and it usually has to be made on purpose, as Paul made his.

verseByVerse.quote: "After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 20 is a chapter of farewells. Paul revisits the churches of Macedonia and Greece, raises a young man who fell from a window during a long Sunday service, and at Miletus gives his only recorded speech to Christian leaders, his farewell to the elders of Ephesus: the New Testament’s great charge to pastors. At the centre stands one astonishing phrase: the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (v. 28). Every farewell, warning and tear in this chapter is measured by what the flock cost the Shepherd.

Not driven out. The riot did not drive Paul away. He had resolved to leave for Macedonia before Demetrius ever called his guild together (19:21), and he did not slip away. The Christians of Ephesus would still be living in that city after his ship sailed, so he gathered them and put heart into them, and then left. That word encouraging, used again in the next verse, often turns up in Paul on the way out of somewhere. Strengthening people you are leaving behind is a very different discipline from inspiring people you are about to lead, and it has almost no reward in it.

And departed for Macedonia. To Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea. Luke compresses some of the most turbulent months of Paul’s life into this sentence. Somewhere on this journey Paul went to Troas expecting Titus with news from Corinth, and Titus was not there: his spirit was not at rest, so he took leave of them and went on to Macedonia (2 Corinthians 2:12–13). He had an open door and could not use it, because he was too anxious. In Macedonia he was afflicted at every turn, with fighting without and fear within (2 Corinthians 7:5). Then Titus arrived with good news, and out of that relief Paul wrote 2 Corinthians, the most personal and least guarded of his letters. Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth. Luke is writing history and gives us the route; Paul’s letters give us what the route cost.

Comfort that comes through Christ. In the letter he wrote from Macedonia at this very time Paul names the source of that encouragement: as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too (2 Corinthians 1:5). It was not a gift of temperament. It was the comfort of a crucified and risen Lord, flowing through a man who had been afflicted himself and was passing on what he had received.

What if I feel anxious even while serving God? Then you are not alone, and you are not disqualified. The apostle who wrote do not be anxious about anything (Philippians 4:6) once could not use an open door because his spirit was not at rest. Anxiety is not the same as unbelief; it is a burden to be carried to God, and Paul carried his, and God comforted him by the coming of Titus (2 Corinthians 7:6). So tell God plainly what you fear, ask others to pray, and look for the Titus he sends. And do not judge other Christians by their outward record. The calmest-looking believer in your church may be fighting fears within.
verseByVerse.note: Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There he spent three months. Paul was very probably at Corinth, and the three months are probably the winter, when the sea lanes closed and few ships sailed.

The letter written in the wait. This is very probably when he wrote the letter to the Romans, around AD 57. Luke does not mention it, but the evidence inside the letter is clear. Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1), Corinth’s eastern port. He sends greetings from Gaius, who is host to him and to the whole church (Romans 16:23), one of the two men Paul baptised at Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). He mentions Erastus, the city treasurer, and a paving stone at Corinth still records an Erastus, possibly the same man. And he says he is on his way to Jerusalem with the collection from Macedonia and Achaia (Romans 15:25–26), exactly where Acts finds him as the three months end.

Enforced inactivity. So this letter, which had a part in Augustine’s conversion, set Luther free, and has shaped Christian thought for twenty centuries, was composed during a three-month wait by a man who could not travel. Luke gives it five words. The most productive quarter of Paul’s life, measured by what survived it, looked from outside like a delay. That is a hard word for anyone whose sense of worth hangs on being busy and useful: God is often doing the most in us when we can do the least.

Romans 8 under a death threat. Consider what was on Paul’s desk in those weeks: that God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8), and that nothing in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:31–39). Within weeks those sentences were tested by a plot against his life, and they held.

A plot. Luke gives no details. Perhaps they meant to kill him on a pilgrim ship bound for Passover, crowded with Jews going up to the feast; and Paul was probably carrying a large sum of money.

Back through Macedonia. A longer route by land, with weeks of delay. And the detour produced the week at Troas, the raising of Eutychus, and the farewell at Miletus that is the theological centre of this half of the book. None of it happens if the ship sails. He makes the wrath of man to praise him (Psalm 76:10), and no detour in the life of his people is wasted.

Is it lack of faith to take precautions against danger? No. Faith trusts God; it does not ignore what God lets us see. Jesus withdrew when his enemies sought to kill him before his hour (John 8:59; 10:39), and Paul escaped Damascus in a basket and changed his route here. To refuse sensible precautions in the name of faith is not trust but testing God, which Jesus refused to do (Matthew 4:7). So lock your door, take your medicine, avoid the dangerous road, and pray. Then, when danger cannot be avoided in the path of obedience, as it could not at Jerusalem, go forward without fear. Wisdom and courage are friends.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Romans during these three months in Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven men. Luke rarely gives a list like this, and when he does the list itself is the point. Seven men, named with their home towns, from three Roman provinces, Macedonia, Galatia and Asia, walking together in one party. And they are very probably there because of money.

The collection. For years Paul had been gathering a relief fund from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He gives instructions about it to Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:1–4), devotes two whole chapters to it (2 Corinthians 8–9), and tells the Romans he is on his way to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints (Romans 15:25–26). These men probably represented the giving churches (1 Corinthians 16:3–4; 2 Corinthians 8:19–21): Gentile believers carrying their own gift, a living picture of the Gentile church’s love for the Jewish church.

An audit committee of seven. Paul explains why they are coming: he aims at what is honourable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (2 Corinthians 8:21). He would not carry other people’s money alone, not because he might steal it, but because somebody might one day say he had, and the gospel would wear the accusation. An apostle who had seen the risen Christ travelled with what was in effect an audit committee of seven.

The grace these men carried. When Paul pleaded with Corinth to finish this collection, his final argument was not need or duty but Christ: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he was rich and made himself poor for your sake, so that his poverty might make you rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). Seven men walking to Jerusalem with a purse were acting out in miniature the journey of the Son of God from glory to the poor.

Two names to keep. Tychicus will carry the letters to Ephesus and Colossae for Paul from prison (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7). And Trophimus, an Ephesian, is the man some Jews will claim to have seen with Paul in the temple: the false accusation that sparks Paul’s arrest and eventually sends him to Rome in chains (21:29).

Is this Gaius the same as the others? Is this Gaius of Derbe the same as the Macedonian Gaius of 19:29, or the Gaius of Romans 16:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:14? Gaius was a very common name, and Luke gives these two different homelands. They were probably different men.

Why should a church care about financial accountability if its leaders are godly? Because godly leaders are still sinners, and because the reputation of Christ is at stake, not only theirs. Paul was as trustworthy as any man who ever lived, and he still insisted on witnesses. Good practice protects the innocent from suspicion as much as it guards against the guilty. In practice that means more than one person counting the offering, clear records, independent checking, open reporting to the members, and no leader having sole control of funds. If you serve as a treasurer or deacon, welcome scrutiny gladly. If you are a member, ask kindly how it is done. It honours the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: These men probably represented the churches sending money for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We again. The pronoun has changed: Luke is back. His we last appeared at Philippi in chapter 16 (16:17); then the narrative went back to they for four chapters and some years. Now, at Philippi, it becomes we again.

Luke in Philippi. Many conclude that Luke had stayed there the whole time, in the city where Lydia was converted and the jailer’s household baptised, while Paul was in Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth and Ephesus. Nobody wrote a chapter on what he did. And Philippi is the church Paul singles out as the only one that supported him when he left Macedonia (Philippians 4:15–16), and the one he writes to with more warmth than any other. Perhaps somebody had been there, quietly, for years.

After the days of Unleavened Bread. Passover week, spring of AD 57. They waited for the feast to finish before sailing, and Luke notes it without comment. A Jewish believer was free to keep such days as custom, provided no one made them a condition of acceptance with God.

The Lamb already slain. Paul spent that Passover week knowing what the feast had always pointed to. He had written to Corinth that Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). Every Jewish household that week was sweeping out leaven and remembering a lamb; the little church at Philippi could keep the same days with open eyes, for the Lamb had come, and the whole Christian life had become the feast that follows the sacrifice.

Five days. The crossing had taken two days the other way (16:11). Probably contrary winds; Luke does not say.

Seven days. That is a long stop for a man in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, and the Sunday gathering is the only thing Luke mentions that could account for it. Paul would refuse to enter Ephesus because he could not spare the days (v. 16), and he sat in Troas for seven of them, waiting for the day the believers already met. The apostle worked round the congregation’s diary rather than the other way about.

Is it so important to gather with the church every week? Yes. It is not the only place we meet God, but it is the place he has promised to meet his people together, in the word, the Supper and prayer, and we are told not to neglect meeting together, as is the habit of some (Hebrews 10:24–25). Paul, with every reason to hurry, waited a week rather than miss it. Illness, necessary work, caring for others or travel may sometimes keep us away, and there is no guilt in that. But a Christian who regularly lets lesser things crowd out the Lord’s Day gathering is starving himself and depriving others of his gifts. Plan your week around it.

For worship. Paul waited seven days at Troas to keep one appointment with the church, and the Lord of the church keeps every one of his. He has not missed a gathering of his people since the evening of the first Easter Day, when he stood among his frightened disciples and said, Peace be with you. When his church gathers, in a city hall or an upper room or a kitchen, the host is already in the room.
verseByVerse.note: “We” resumes: Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first day. This is the plainest narrative description we have of a Christian church meeting: the first day, the gathered church, the broken bread, the teaching. The first day of the week is Sunday, an ordinary working day in a world where the seventh day was the recognised Jewish holy day; Sunday was not a public holiday in the empire for another two and a half centuries. So they met very early or, as here, in the evening, after work. They met on the first day because that was the day the tomb was found empty (Luke 24:1), and it became the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10; 1 Corinthians 16:2). Nobody in the New Testament argues for this. It has simply already happened, in a church far from Jerusalem, within about twenty-five years of the resurrection.

Known in the breaking of the bread. Luke’s phrase covers both a shared meal and the Lord’s Supper, which the early church did not separate. He has used it before, on the evening of the very first Lord’s Day, when the two from Emmaus told the others how he had been known to them in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:30–35). At Troas they were not remembering an absent founder. They were keeping a meal whose host had risen.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath and Sunday. Seventh-day Adventists and others hold that Christians must keep Saturday as the Sabbath; some Christians see no special day at all. Between these, two views are held by many Reformed and evangelical Christians. One, the historic position of the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds that the fourth commandment is moral and abiding, and that from the resurrection the Sabbath was changed to the first day, the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy in worship and rest (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8). The other holds that the Sabbath, as a sign of the old covenant, is fulfilled in Christ, and that the Lord’s Day is the church’s day of gathering without Sabbath law. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17). The church from the beginning gathered on the first day, the day of resurrection. The Lord’s Day is not a burdensome law but a gift and a privilege: a day Christians gladly set apart to gather, worship, break bread, hear the word, rest and do good, out of joy and wisdom rather than under rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). The Westminster and 1689 view, that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment, is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.

Fulfilled in Christ. The Sabbath was God’s weekly picture of rest: work stopped, and Israel remembered that God had finished creation and had set them free from Egypt (Exodus 20:11; Deuteronomy 5:15). In Christ the thing pictured has come. He has finished the work of our salvation, and whoever trusts him rests from trying to earn God’s favour (Hebrews 4:10). The believer’s deepest rest is not a day but a person, and the first day is the day we gather gladly to celebrate him.

Does this mean Sunday is the Christian Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, hold that it is; this commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ and the first day is kept gladly, without binding anyone’s conscience, while both sides agree the gathering should not be neglected. (See John 20:1 for the fuller answer.)

Was this the Lord’s Supper? Most likely yes, eaten within a shared meal (2:42, 46; 1 Corinthians 11:20–26). The New Testament does not fix how often the Supper should be observed; this passage suggests it was a reason for the weekly gathering, and many churches celebrate it weekly for that reason, while others hold it monthly or less often. And if Luke counts the day from sunset, as Jews did, the gathering may have been on Saturday evening; if from midnight, as Romans did, Sunday evening. Paul planned to leave on the next day, which fits either.

Until midnight. The verb is dialegomai, to discuss, to reason back and forth, the word used of him in the synagogue and the hall of Tyrannus. There were questions. He was leaving in the morning and might not be back, so he kept going. Anyone who has sat up too late with somebody they will not see again understands that clause.

Many lamps. Very likely an eyewitness detail. Many oil lamps in a crowded upper room on a spring night throw out heat and fumes: the reason a young man was sitting in an open window at midnight, and the reason he could not keep his eyes open. Luke tells us the cause of the accident one verse before it happens.

So what does a faithful Lord’s Day look like? At its heart, what Troas shows: gathering with God’s people, hearing the word explained, sharing the Lord’s Supper, prayer and fellowship. Around that, rest from the ordinary grind of the week, time with family, works of mercy and necessity, visiting the sick and lonely, reading and conversation that feed the soul. Whatever your view of the Sabbath, avoid two errors: treating the day as just another day for shopping and chores, and turning it into a grim list of prohibitions. It is the day of resurrection. Let it feel like one.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday; this meeting was held in the evening, probably after the working day.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eutychus. The name means fortunate, often given to slaves, and given what is about to happen it is either painfully ironic or, in the end, exactly right. Perhaps a slave who had worked all day. Luke calls him the youth in verse 12, very possibly still a boy, and he is in the window because the room is hot and full of lamp smoke, and because at a crowded meeting a boy sits on the ledge. He went under gradually and then completely; anybody who has fought sleep in a warm room knows that the second stage is not a decision.

Told against nobody. This story is often told as a joke against the boy or against long sermons, and Luke tells it against nobody. Paul does not scold him, and Luke does not moralise. It is a comfort to preachers whose hearers doze, and a gentle warning to long-winded ones. Even Paul put someone to sleep.

Taken up dead. Not as though dead. Luke the doctor (Colossians 4:14), who was in that room, says he was picked up dead. He could have softened it, and the softening would have made the story less exposed to challenge; he says the young man was dead, in a house full of witnesses, in a document addressed to a named reader who could have asked them.

Death in a room gathered for the risen Lord. It happened in the middle of an ordinary church gathering, on the first day of the week, among people who had met because Jesus had been dead and was alive. The worst thing that can happen to a family happened in the room where the resurrection was being proclaimed. Either the Lord they had gathered to remember holds the keys of death, as he said he does (Revelation 1:18), or the evening was over.

What if I struggle to stay awake or concentrate in church? Most Christians do sometimes, and God knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). Tiredness after a hard week is not a sin. But there are practical helps: get enough sleep on Saturday, sit where you can see and hear, follow the passage in your Bible, take notes, and pray before the service that God will open your ears. If you are a preacher, love your hearers by being clear and not needlessly long. And if you see someone nodding, be gentle. The Lord did not scold Eutychus; he gave him back his life.

For worship. The Lord Jesus knows the weight of tired eyes. In Gethsemane he found his friends asleep and said the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak (Mark 14:38). He did not cast them off; he died for them before the next sunset. He sees the youth at the window as surely as the apostle in the centre of the room, and when the worst falls on his people, he is already on the stairs.
verseByVerse.note: Eutychus means “fortunate.” Oil lamps in a crowded upper room would have made the air close.

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, "Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him." And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Down the stairs. Paul goes down the stairs, gets on the ground, and picks the boy up and holds him. Any Jew in the courtyard would have recognised that posture. Elijah stretched himself upon the widow’s dead son three times and cried to the LORD (1 Kings 17:21–22); Elisha lay upon the Shunammite’s dead boy, and the child’s flesh grew warm (2 Kings 4:34). Paul is doing what the prophets did.

In the flow. Peter knelt beside Tabitha and she rose (9:40); now Paul bends over Eutychus and he lives. And before Paul tells the Ephesian elders that he does not count his life precious (v. 24), Luke lets us see that his Lord has power over death. A man who has seen a dead boy given back can walk toward prison without fear.

A greater than Elijah in the room. Yet Elijah cried out, asking; Paul announces that the boy’s life is in him. In Luke’s Gospel Jesus took a dead girl by the hand, called to her, and her spirit returned (Luke 8:52–55), and Peter told a paralysed man that Jesus Christ heals him (9:34). The apostle bends over Eutychus in the prophet’s posture, but the life that comes back into him is the risen Lord’s to give.

His life is in him. Paul speaks to the crowd standing round in the dark, and in the present tense: not that he was never dead, but that his life had returned.

Until daybreak. Very probably the Lord’s Supper, at last, after midnight. A young man has just been raised from the dead in the courtyard, and they go back upstairs, break bread, and talk until the sun comes up. Luke gives the raising one verse and the talking much the same. The extraordinary thing was not treated as the important thing: the church at Troas had one night with the apostle, and they spent it at the Lord’s Table, asking him questions until it was light.

Why does God raise some and not others? We do not know, and Scripture does not pretend to tell us. He raised Eutychus and Tabitha, and he let James be killed by the sword and Stephen be stoned. These raisings were signs, pointing to the resurrection of Jesus and to the final resurrection of all his people, not promises that every death will be reversed now. What Scripture does promise is better: that for those who are in Christ, death is not the end, and on the last day every believer will be raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:52). If you have buried someone you love who trusted Christ, their life is in them still, hidden with Christ in God.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alive. They took him away, presumably home, to whoever had been waiting up, and Luke does not tell us that scene. Somebody had to be told what had happened and then how it ended. Alive. Not a little comforted is an understatement that makes the reader supply the feeling, which is how the deepest relief is usually described by people who have been through it.

The same word. The verb is parakaleō, to comfort, to come alongside and hold a person up: the verb of verses 1 and 2, for what Paul had been doing in town after town. On this night God did it.

Not a rule about outcomes. One more thing, because the church has been carrying its own dead ever since. This is not a promise that the young man in your house will be given back; Luke has already recorded James executed in a single sentence (12:2), and he expects you to hold both. What this night shows is what the apostle did when the worst had happened: he went down the stairs and got on the floor and put his arms round the young man.

A small Easter at Troas. Eutychus was given back for a few more years, and he would die again. The comfort that outlasts him rests on another death and rising: since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:14). That is the hope for every family whose dead are not given back on the stairs.

How can I comfort someone whose loved one has died? Do what Paul did first: go down the stairs. Be there. You do not need the right words; your presence, your arms, your tears and your practical help say more than explanations. Do not offer quick answers or promise what God has not promised. Listen. Pray with them if they want it. Bring meals, remember the anniversaries, keep calling after the funeral when everyone else has stopped. And when the time is right, gently hold out the hope of the resurrection to those who are in Christ, for we do not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

verseByVerse.quote: But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s own arrangement. Luke tells us this was arranged in advance and was Paul’s own decision, and does not tell us the reason. The ship had to round Cape Lectum; the road across the neck of land was about twenty miles on foot. Paul had been awake all night. He sent his companions round by sea and walked it alone.

Why walk alone? We are not told, and the honest thing is to say so. It is often suggested that he wanted the day for solitude and prayer before the journey to Jerusalem, and that is entirely plausible for a man heading toward imprisonment who has just told a church he will not see them again. It is also possible he wanted to visit believers on the way, or simply could not face company after the night at Troas. Luke may well have known, and he did not write it down.

Hours alone, the harder way. What the verse does establish is that Paul deliberately arranged several hours by himself, at the cost of a twenty-mile walk on no sleep, when time was short. He was almost never alone, and this whole chapter is a crowd. When he wanted hours to himself he did not cancel anything; he took the harder route to the same place.

A ship’s log. Assos, Mitylene on Lesbos, then Chios, Samos, Miletus: Luke writes down the ports of call day by day, as a man keeping a log does, and many think he kept just such a record.

The road one man walked ahead. That road to Jerusalem had been walked before. When Jesus went up for the last time he was walking ahead of the Twelve, and those who followed were afraid (Mark 10:32). In the end he went alone: his friends slept, fled and denied him. That is why no servant of his walks that road as alone as he did. Paul could take the harder way without companions because the Lord who had gone ahead had promised to be with his people always (Matthew 28:20).

How do I find time alone with God in a busy life? Paul’s answer here was to take the harder road: he walked twenty miles rather than lose the hours. Most of us need something less dramatic but just as deliberate. Choose a regular time, often early before the house wakes, and guard it. Use the walk to the station, the drive, the lunch break, the evening walk round the block. Take a Bible and a simple plan: read a passage, think about it, pray it back to God. Our Lord himself rose very early and went out to a desolate place to pray (Mark 1:35). If he needed it, so do you.
verseByVerse.note: Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos and Miletus were ports down the coast of Asia Minor and its islands.

verseByVerse.quote: And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days. Three anchorages, each recorded: coastal ships often sailed by daylight and put in at night. Miletus lay about thirty miles south of Ephesus. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add a stop at Trogyllium; the earliest do not.

Past Ephesus. Ephesus had been nearly three years of his life, and his ship goes past and does not turn in. The reason Luke gives is not danger but time. If he set foot in that city the whole congregation would come, with meals and questions and people needing to be seen, and a day would become a fortnight. Love has a way of detaining people, and he had a deadline. So he sends for the elders and meets them in a port where nobody can keep him.

By Pentecost. Fifty days after Passover. He was carrying the collection, and Pentecost was a pilgrim feast, so the city would be full of Jews from every province: the largest possible gathering to see a gift from Gentile churches to Jewish believers. And Pentecost was the feast of firstfruits, and the day the Spirit fell.

The harvest of that first Pentecost. On that day the exalted Christ received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured him out (2:33). Paul is hastening back to the same feast with its fruit from far beyond Israel, calling his work a priestly service, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit (Romans 15:16). The Lord had promised his witnesses would reach the end of the earth (1:8), and here is a party of Gentile believers on its way to show that he kept his word.

If possible. Absolute clarity about the destination, and no pretence of certainty about the timetable.

Is this a proof that Paul still kept the Jewish festivals? In part, yes, but read it carefully. It does show that Paul, himself a Jewish believer, still moved within the rhythms of the Jewish calendar and valued the feast. Yet his haste was very likely as much missional as ceremonial: Pentecost packed Jerusalem with pilgrims from the dispersion, a prime moment to bear witness, as at the first Pentecost, and Paul was carrying the relief collection from the Gentile churches, which he wanted to deliver to the saints (24:17; Romans 15:25–26). So the verse shows him honouring the festival and the Jerusalem gathering, not keeping it as a binding law required for righteousness. Luke does not spell out his full motive, so we should not over-press it either way.

How does that square with dying to the law? How does it square with Romans 7, where Paul says we have died to the law (7:4–6)? It squares perfectly, once we see what died to the law means. Paul is not saying the believer is now lawless, or that God’s righteous will has been abolished; in the very same chapter he calls the law holy and righteous and good (7:12). He means we have died to the law as a condemning covenant and master, the regime that could only accuse and curse us, so that we now belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit by the Spirit, not by the old written code. A believing Jew keeping Pentecost, then, is no contradiction at all. He is not under the law as a way of being justified, for his justification is in Christ alone, so he is free to keep the feast, not to earn standing, but as heritage, devotion and a bridge to his people. Reformed teaching distinguishes the moral law (God’s lasting commands, summed up in the Ten), the ceremonial law (the sacrifices and rituals that pointed to Christ) and the civil law (Israel’s national statutes), and draws a careful line between keeping a custom freely and keeping it as a requirement. The test is this: a practice done to be saved or accepted, or imposed on others as necessary, denies grace and must go; the same practice done freely, in love, binding no one, is Christian liberty. Paul hurried to Pentecost as a free man in Christ, not as a slave under law, and that is the whole difference.

How do I say no to people I love without being unloving? By remembering that love has a direction, not only a warmth. Paul loved the Ephesians as much as any church, and he still sailed past, because the work God had given him lay in Jerusalem. Saying no to a good thing in order to do the thing God has given you is not coldness; it is faithfulness. Explain honestly, as Paul did by sending for the elders. Make what time you can, in a way that does not derail the calling. And trust God with the people you cannot stay with. They are his before they are yours.

For worship. The Lord Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem, and nothing could turn him aside, because he was going there to die for us. Paul hoped to arrive in time, if possible. Christ never needed those words: his hour arrived exactly when the Father had appointed it, and nothing in our salvation was ever left to chance.
verseByVerse.note: Miletus lay about 30 miles south of Ephesus. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–38 — The Miletus Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Miletus Paul calls the Ephesian elders. He reminds them how he lived and taught among them, humbly and with tears, holding nothing back. Bound by the Spirit, he goes to Jerusalem expecting prison, caring only to finish his course. He charges them to guard themselves and the flock God bought with his own blood against wolves from outside and twisted teachers from within, commends them to God and the word of his grace, and recalls Jesus’ words that giving is more blessed than receiving. Then they kneel, weep, and go with him to the ship.
verseByVerse.theology:
Elder, Overseer, Shepherd

Elder (v. 17), overseer and shepherd (v. 28) name one office: elder for maturity of character, overseer for the duty of watching over, shepherd for the work of feeding and care. Reformed churches have long seen here the clearest description of the pastoral office: men placed by the Holy Spirit to guard, feed and care for the people in their charge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul warned of wolves from outside and of men from within who would twist the truth. Both came: by the time of Revelation the Ephesian church had tested false apostles, yet had abandoned the love it had at first (Revelation 2:1–7). Now: Every congregation faces both dangers, and the safeguard is the same: the word of God’s grace, held by leaders whose lives match what they teach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the summons cost. Work out what that message cost, because Luke does not. A messenger travels a day or more; the elders have to drop what they are doing and travel back. So Paul probably waited several days at Miletus, a considerable sacrifice from a man who has just refused to enter Ephesus for lack of time. He would not spare a fortnight for the city; he spent days on the elders, because what he had to say was for the leaders alone: it is all about what happens after he is gone, and they would have to do it.

The elders of the church. Elders, plural: a group of leaders in one church (14:23). There were by now believers all over that city and probably several house congregations, and Luke calls them the church in the singular and their leaders elders in the plural.

The only speech to Christians. This is the only full speech in Acts that Paul makes to Christians. His other recorded addresses are to synagogues, philosophers, governors and mobs. This one is to the church, and it is the closest thing in Acts to Paul talking the way he talks in his letters, recorded by a man who was sitting there.

Three words for one group. He sent for the elders, and in verse 28 he tells the same men that the Holy Spirit had made them overseers, to shepherd the flock. Whatever distinctions later centuries drew between elder, bishop and pastor, Paul calls the same men by all three names inside eleven verses.

Titles borrowed from Christ. Before these words belonged to the men at Miletus, they belonged to Christ. Peter, a fellow elder, calls the Lord Jesus the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls (1 Peter 2:25), and promises elders the unfading crown of glory when the chief Shepherd appears (1 Peter 5:1–4). The flock has one Shepherd who owns it and many under-shepherds who keep it for him, doing on a small scale, under orders, what the risen Christ does for his whole church.

Does this settle how a church should be governed? It settles less than some think and more than others admit. Christians differ here: episcopal churches hold that bishops as a distinct order developed rightly from the apostles’ own oversight; Presbyterians see the elders of local churches joined in wider courts; Congregationalists and most Baptists see each local church, under its elders, as self-governing. What this passage plainly shows is that in Ephesus a plurality of elders shepherded one church, and that elder, overseer and shepherd named the same men. Whatever your church’s structure, these are the marks to look for: more than one leader, men qualified by character (1 Timothy 3:1–7), feeding and guarding the flock, and accountable to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they came to him, he said to them: 'You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves know. He opens by putting himself on trial and calling them as witnesses (again in v. 34). He is not telling them what his ministry was like; he is asking them to confirm it, and some had watched him at the bench, in the lecture hall and in their own houses. Ministry is first a life lived openly before people (1 Thessalonians 2:10), and a man can only speak like this if the record will bear it. It is the opposite of a testimonial, which is what you produce when the people who actually know you are not in the room.

In the flow. The speech looks back on his three years with them (vv. 18–21), looks ahead to Jerusalem and chains (vv. 22–27), charges the elders to guard the flock (vv. 28–31), and commends them to God and his word (vv. 32–35). Here the apostle hands his work over to ordinary local leaders, the pattern for the church after the apostles.

With all humility. Four things in a life’s work, and not one of them is what a man would choose for himself. Serving (douleuōn) is the word for a slave’s work, not a leader’s: Paul begins the summary of his apostolic career by describing himself as somebody else’s property. Then humility. In the Greek world lowliness was not generally a virtue; it was the disposition of the servile, and Greek moralists commonly counted it a fault. Christianity took a quality the world despised and made it the first thing an apostle says about his ministry.

Why humility changed sides. Paul gave the answer himself, writing to Philippi: Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). The word for servant there is the noun of Paul’s verb here. Humility changed sides in the ancient world because the Lord of glory took a slave’s form. When Paul calls himself the Lord’s slave, he is wearing his Master’s clothes.

And with tears. Paul wept (v. 31; 2 Corinthians 2:4; Philippians 3:18), repeatedly, over years, and thought it worth recording as a defining feature of his work. Weigh that against how we would summarise a successful ministry. Paul had planted churches across a continent, written letters that would outlast the empire, and raised the dead. Asked to characterise the three years, he says: I was a servant, I was lowly, and I wept a great deal.

And with trials. The only one of the four that came from outside, and he names it without heat: no complaint, just the fact that there had been plots and they had cost him. The man who could wish himself accursed for the sake of his own people (Romans 9:3) is describing what some of them had done to him, without a word of bitterness.

What does humility look like in a church leader, or in me? Not thinking little of yourself so much as thinking of yourself less. It looks like doing jobs no one sees, admitting mistakes quickly, listening more than speaking, being glad when others are praised, accepting correction, and refusing titles and privileges that set you above the flock. Jesus washed his disciples’ feet and said, I have given you an example (John 13:15). Humility is not a technique for leadership; it is what grows in someone who has seen the cross and knows what he has been forgiven. Ask God for it, and ask the people closest to you where you most lack it.

On a Tuesday. Ask the hard question of yourself: could the people who know you best stand up and confirm the way you have lived among them? If not, the remedy is not a better testimonial but a changed life, beginning today, and it begins at the cross, where Christ freely forgives what those people have seen.

verseByVerse.quote: how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I did not shrink. The verb means to hold back out of fear; it could also be used of drawing in a sail. It is what a man does when he sees where a conversation is going and decides not to go there. Paul chooses the negative deliberately, here and at verse 27. He does not say I told you everything easily. He says I did not shrink, which admits there was something to shrink from. He knew which subjects would cost him a hearing, a friendship or a household’s welcome, and he went ahead anyway.

The honest shape of it. Everyone who has had to say a hard thing to somebody they love knows the moment that verb describes. And the reason we shrink is nearly always the same: we want to be liked more than we want the other person to be well. The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25).

In public and from house to house. Both matter, and the second is the expensive one. Public teaching is efficient: one preparation, many hearers. House to house means the same truth delivered again and again to small groups in their own rooms, where they can interrupt, and where you have to know their names.

Repentance and faith. The content of three years, in two nouns that go together but are not interchangeable (Mark 1:15; Hebrews 6:1). Repentance toward God: a turning round, and toward God, not merely toward better behaviour; not primarily regret about actions but a change of allegiance. Faith in our Lord Jesus Christ: the trusting, aimed at a person rather than merely a doctrine.

Our Lord Jesus Christ. Imagine saying the full title in a synagogue. Jesus: the man from Nazareth crucified within living memory. Christ: the Messiah Israel had waited for. Lord: the word Greek-speaking Jews read aloud for the name of the God of Israel. To call for faith in our Lord Jesus Christ was to say that a crucified man is Israel’s King and shares the name of God. That claim cost Paul synagogue after synagogue, and it is the only thing that makes repentance safe: a sinner can turn to God without terror because the Lord he trusts has already borne his sin.

Neither survives alone. Repentance without faith is remorse, which has destroyed people. Faith without repentance is mere agreement, which has comforted many who never changed direction. Paul preached both to everybody, the religious and the pagan alike.

Which comes first, repentance or faith? They are two sides of one turning, and in real life they arrive together. You cannot truly turn from sin to God without trusting his mercy in Christ, and you cannot truly trust Christ as Saviour while clinging to the sin he came to save you from. Sometimes Scripture names one first (Mark 1:15), sometimes the other (Acts 11:21). Do not wait to feel sorry enough before you trust Christ, and do not imagine you can trust him while refusing to turn. Both are gifts of grace, and both go on for the whole Christian life: we keep repenting and keep believing until we see him.

For worship. The Lord Jesus taught in public and from house to house before his servant did. At one door in Jericho he said, Today salvation has come to this house (Luke 19:9), and a lifetime of grasping turned round in an afternoon. He grants the repentance he calls for (11:18) and gives the faith that rests on him (Ephesians 2:8), and there is joy over each sinner who turns before the angels of God.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Constrained by the Spirit. The word means bound: bound by the Spirit before being bound by chains (21:33). Some take it of Paul’s own spirit (KJV, bound in the spirit); most modern versions read it as the Holy Spirit, which fits 19:21. The binding was not a voice overriding his will, but a settled conviction, formed in prayer and confirmed over months, that God wanted him in Jerusalem.

Not knowing. What he is not told matters. He has the direction and the general shape of the outcome, and no details at all. That is almost always the arrangement in Scripture, though we tend to imagine that guidance means being shown the plan. Abraham was told to go to a land that God would show him, which is not the same as being shown it.

In every city. Through prophets (21:4, 11). The Spirit who constrains him to go has been telling him, city after city, what is waiting at the other end. He is being sent, and being told what it will cost, and both are the work of the same Person.

The Spirit who foretells sufferings. The Spirit of Christ in the prophets was predicting the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories (1 Peter 1:11). Jesus told his disciples three times that rejection and death waited for him in Jerusalem, and then went. Now the Spirit does for the servant what he did for the Master: he names the suffering beforehand and leads into it. For Christ, and for those who belong to him, the way to glory runs through the city where chains are waiting.

Was Paul disobeying the Spirit by going on? The question arrives shortly. In the next chapter, disciples at Tyre tell Paul through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem (21:4), and Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and prophesies his arrest, and everyone present begs him not to go (21:11–12). This verse points to the best answer, and may be one reason Luke recorded it. What the Spirit revealed, consistently and in every city, was the suffering. What the disciples added was the conclusion, therefore do not go, and that was love talking. They had the message right and drew from it the inference any of us would draw about somebody we loved. Agabus, notably, does not tell him not to go; he says what will happen, and it is the bystanders who beg. Luke’s wording at 21:4 is strong, and honest readers still find it hard; but this reading fits everything Luke tells us.

If God is leading me, should I expect things to go smoothly? No. Following the Spirit led Paul into chains, led the apostles into prison, and led our Lord to the cross. Hardship is not proof that you have missed God’s will, and ease is not proof that you are in it. Jesus told his disciples that in the world they would have tribulation, and to take heart, because he has overcome the world (John 16:33). So do not measure guidance by comfort. Measure it by Scripture, by wisdom, and by whether you are walking in faith and love. Sometimes the right road runs straight through the hard place, and the Lord walks it with you.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not precious to myself. This is the sentence the whole speech turns on, and it is not bravado. (The KJV’s finish my course with joy follows a fuller text; with joy is missing from the earliest manuscripts, and the sense is unchanged.) Paul is not saying his life is worthless; he has stopped treating his own survival as the thing to be protected (Philippians 1:21). It is a comparison, not a denial: if only I may finish. The whole force of the sentence is in the ranking.

My course. The word means a race, the distance a runner is set to cover, used of John the Baptist at 13:25. Paul will use the picture once more, from a Roman prison with his execution close: I have finished the race, I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). A course is a fixed distance. The question is never how far you have got compared with anybody else, but whether the ground assigned to you has been covered.

The ministry that I received. It was handed to him, not chosen (9:15; Galatians 1:1), on a road to Damascus, to a man travelling the opposite way. That is why he can hold his life so lightly. A man who chose his own work has to defend it, and himself with it. A man who was handed his work has only to finish it.

The gospel of the grace of God. The whole of it, in a single phrase: not to build a movement or win arguments, but to bear witness that God gives what nobody has earned. And grace in Paul’s mouth is never a vague kindness in the sky. The grace of God has appeared, he would write, in our Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us (Titus 2:11–14), and he knew it at first hand: though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent, the grace of our Lord overflowed for me (1 Timothy 1:13–14).

Your own version of the sentence. Ask what your own version of that sentence would be: what it is you would have to finish for the rest to be worth spending. Most of us have never written it down, which is why so much of our lives is spent protecting things we would not, on reflection, have chosen to protect.

Does this mean I should not care about my health or safety? No. Your life is a gift from God and your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and the sixth commandment requires us to preserve our own life as well as others’ (Westminster Larger Catechism 135). Paul took precautions, changing his route to escape a murder plot (20:3). What he refused was to make safety his highest value. The question is one of ranking: when staying safe and staying faithful collide, faithfulness wins. Most of us will never face that choice in its starkest form. But we face smaller versions daily, comfort against obedience, and this verse tells us which to choose.

What is my course, if I am not an apostle? Every believer has one: the life, callings and relationships God has assigned you, and the good works he prepared beforehand for you to walk in (Ephesians 2:10). For most of us that means faithfulness in ordinary things: loving a husband or wife, raising children in the Lord, working honestly, serving in a local church, bearing witness to neighbours, enduring illness or loss with faith. It is not measured against anyone else’s race. You finish your course by keeping the faith in the place God put you, until he calls you home.

For worship. The Son of God did not count his life precious to himself. He laid it down for us, and on the cross he cried, It is finished. His was the only race ever run without a stumble. Paul could spend his life like a runner spending the last of his strength because his Lord had already reached the line for him, and he who began a good work in us will bring it to completion.

parallels.desc: I have finished the race

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will not see my face again. That is the sentence the elders will still be weeping over at the end of the chapter (v. 38), and Luke tells us so explicitly: it was this word, more than anything else, that broke them.

Did it turn out to be true? It should be said honestly that we do not know. Paul expected to go from Jerusalem to Rome and then on to Spain (Romans 15:24, 28), and the letters written after his first Roman imprisonment appear to have him back in this part of the world: he tells Timothy he had urged him to remain at Ephesus while he went into Macedonia (1 Timothy 1:3), which is difficult to fit anywhere except a later journey. Paul may later have revisited the area after his first Roman imprisonment, but he did not expect to. If that is right, then Paul’s expectation here was not fulfilled in the way he thought, and there is no reason to be uncomfortable about saying so: he says I know, and what he knew was that imprisonment awaited him (v. 23), and he drew the natural conclusion. An apostle writing Scripture is protected from error in what he teaches. He is not thereby given a timetable of his own future, and Luke faithfully records what Paul expected. This passage is one of the places where the difference shows. It is also possible that Paul passed through the region later without seeing these particular men again, so that his words held exactly as he spoke them.

Innocent of the blood of all. Legal language, and Ezekiel’s (Ezekiel 33:1–9). The watchman who blows the trumpet has delivered his soul; the one who stays silent has the blood of the fallen required at his hand. Paul used the same formula at Corinth (18:6): the watchman answers for the trumpet, not for the walls. The sword is coming because sin is real and the Judge of all the earth is just, so silence about it is never kindness.

A handover. At Corinth he said it to people who had rejected him. Here he says it to men who have believed him, and it is his discharge, dated like a legal handover: from this day it is yours.

Proclaiming the kingdom. Paul sums up his three years in a Gentile city as proclaiming the kingdom. Acts is framed by it: the risen Jesus spoke about the kingdom for forty days (1:3); Philip preached it to Samaritans (8:12); Paul reasoned about it at Ephesus (19:8); and the book closes with him in Rome proclaiming the kingdom of God (28:31).

Where Christians differ on the kingdom. This touches a real difference among Bible-loving Christians. Many of our dispensational brothers (who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, with God’s purposes for Israel kept distinct from his purposes for the church) reserve the kingdom, especially the Davidic kingdom of the Old Testament promises, for a future, literal reign of Christ over restored national Israel in the thousand years of Revelation 20; on the classic scheme the kingdom was offered to Israel, rejected and postponed. Their concern is worthy: they want God’s promises to Israel taken seriously, not quietly absorbed into the church. And many of them now grant that the kingdom was genuinely inaugurated at Christ’s exaltation (Acts 2:30–36), while still holding a future fulfilment for Israel.

The kingdom now. From the Reformed side, the simplest point is that Scripture, nowhere more than in Acts, treats the kingdom as a present reality preached and entered. Believers have already been transferred to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13); the kingdom of God has come upon you, said Jesus (Matthew 12:28). The church is not simply identical with the kingdom, for God’s reign is wider, but it is the kingdom’s present people, awaiting the day it is consummated over all the earth. If you belong to Christ, you already live under the reign of the King, even as you pray your kingdom come.

Am I responsible for the blood of people I never warned? The watchman’s words are first for those with a public charge, like Paul and these elders, and they are solemn. But every Christian has neighbours who will one day face God, and love will not leave them unwarned. The point is not to load you with guilt for everyone you have not evangelised; Christ’s blood covers that failure too, for those who confess it. The point is to make you faithful from today. Pray for the people around you, live so that your faith is visible, and when the door opens, speak of Christ plainly and kindly. Blow the trumpet you have been given. The walls belong to God.

parallels.desc: the watchman

verseByVerse.quote: "'for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole counsel of God. The ground of the innocence he has just claimed rests on one word. The whole. Not the important parts, not the parts that went down well in Ephesus. All of it: sin and grace, judgment and mercy, election and evangelism, doctrine and duty.

The shrinking verb again. The second time he has used it (v. 20). Nobody omits doctrine by deciding to be unfaithful. It happens by small, reasonable decisions: this congregation is not ready; this is not the moment; I will come back to it.

What tends to go missing. In a comfortable generation it is judgment, hell and the wrath of God. In an anxious one it is assurance, election and the sheer freeness of grace. In a moralistic church it is justification; in a lax one it is holiness. Every era edits toward what its own people find congenial, so the omission is almost never visible from inside. The test is not only whether your preaching is true but whether it is whole. A ministry can say nothing false for thirty years and still leave a congregation with a God smaller than the one in Scripture.

The counsel has a centre. Paul would soon write to this church that God has made known the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in him (Ephesians 1:9–10). What Paul declared was not a syllabus of topics laid side by side but one plan with one centre, the Son, and every doctrine he taught in Ephesus was a road leading to him.

How can I make sure I am getting the whole counsel of God? Read the whole Bible, not just your favourite parts; a plan that takes you through every book over a year or two is a great help. Sit under preaching that works through books of the Bible, so that the text sets the agenda rather than the preacher’s preferences. Notice the subjects you instinctively avoid, the passages on judgment, or suffering, or giving, or sexual holiness, or election, and go and read them. Use a good confession or catechism, which summarises the whole of Scripture’s teaching. And let every part lead you back to the centre: Christ crucified and risen.

verseByVerse.quote: "Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yourselves first. That order is not politeness. Paul puts the elders’ own souls in front of the congregation’s, and everything that follows depends on it. A man who neglects his own walk with God (1 Timothy 4:16) does not stop working; he goes on preaching, visiting and organising, and the machinery runs for years on nothing. What he is then feeding people is his own emptiness, competently disguised.

In the flow. Here the speech turns from I to you. The whole counsel he declared, they must guard, and the watch he kept, they must keep (v. 31). The wolves (vv. 29–30) show why the charge is urgent; the commendation to God and his word (v. 32) shows why it is not hopeless.

All the flock. Not just favourites: not the promising members, not the ones who contribute, not the ones who are easy to be with.

Made by the Holy Spirit. Not Paul, though he had appointed elders elsewhere (14:23), and not the congregation alone: the Holy Spirit put them there. That is at once steadying and frightening. Steadying, because a man placed by the Spirit does not have to keep earning the position, and the Spirit will supply what the work demands. Frightening, because he cannot lay it down lightly, and the accounting will be with the one who appointed him.

Elders and overseers. Two names for one office (v. 17; Titus 1:5–7; 1 Peter 5:1–2); overseer gives us the word bishop. Elders for their maturity, overseers for their watching over, shepherds for their care.

With his own blood. Before he tells them what to do, he tells them what the flock is worth. Obtained is a purchase word: bought for oneself. The church belongs to God, bought with a price, and the price is named.

How can God bleed? God is spirit and has no blood, so how can God bleed? Only because the One who shed it, Jesus, is God. It is one of Scripture’s most powerful affirmations of Christ’s deity: the blood of the cross can be called God’s own blood because the man who hung there is the eternal Son in our flesh (so too they crucified the Lord of glory, 1 Corinthians 2:8). Theologians call this the communication of attributes: what is true of either nature may be said of the one person. Two things shine: the deity of your Saviour, for the cross measures how high the One who died for you truly is; and the worth of the church, a flock so precious that God bought it with his own blood. Some manuscripts read the church of the Lord, and some translate with the blood of his own, meaning his own Son; but the reading of God has strong early support and is followed by most modern Bibles, and it expresses what the church has always confessed: the one who died is God the Son. Pastors care for people Christ died for. That is why they matter so much.

Does this mean Christ died only for the church? The verse says Christ purchased the church, which fits the Reformed teaching that he died to secure the salvation of his people (John 10:11; Ephesians 5:25). It does not by itself say only, but it shows that Christ’s death had a definite object: his church. He did not die to make salvation merely possible for everyone and certain for no one. He died to buy a people, and he will have every one of them. This is often called definite or particular atonement. Many faithful Christians, Arminians among them (those who hold that Christ died equally for every person and that each one’s free response decides), read verses such as 1 John 2:2 as teaching that he died for all in the same way, and they love the cross no less; all agree that Christ is to be freely offered to everyone.

What overseers should oversee. To care for is to shepherd: to feed the flock with sound teaching, guard it from wolves and error (vv. 29–30), lead it, and care for souls (Hebrews 13:17). It is the care of souls by the Word, not the managing of people’s private lives.

Lording it and leaving it. There are two ways to fail the flock. Overreach: elders are not to domineer over those in their charge, but to be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3); it shall not be so among you, said Jesus (Matthew 20:25–26). An elder’s authority is ministerial: he applies God’s Word; he does not make new laws. God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster Confession 20.2), and an elder may not bind believers with man-made rules where Scripture is silent (do not handle, do not taste, do not touch, Colossians 2:20–23), or police what God has left to Christian liberty (Romans 14). Negligence is the opposite ditch and just as grave: Ezekiel’s woe falls on shepherds who fed themselves and did not strengthen the weak or seek the straying (Ezekiel 34). An elder who will not teach hard truth, watch for wolves, or address serious, unrepentant sin (1 Corinthians 5) has abandoned his post, and abdication dressed as tolerance is no virtue.

Where is the line? The Word of God. Elders are firm where God is firm: on the gospel, sound doctrine, clear moral commands, the church’s worship and order, grave unrepentant sin. They are free where God leaves free, protecting liberty in disputable matters rather than policing it (Romans 14:1–4). Two reminders keep the balance. The flock is not theirs but God’s: they are under-shepherds of the Chief Shepherd, accountable to him (1 Peter 5:2–4), not owners. And Paul’s first word is pay careful attention to yourselves: the elder who watches his own soul shepherds with the right blend of courage and gentleness. The aim throughout is the flock’s good, served gladly, never for power, money or ego (1 Peter 5:2–3). And abuse of that trust, spiritual, emotional or any other kind, is never to be tolerated or covered: it is the wolf in the shepherd’s coat, and the flock must be protected from it.

Fierce wolves. False teachers from outside, false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15). Paul expects the attack as soon as the apostle is gone.

What should I do if I think my church leaders are overstepping, or neglecting the flock? Pray first, and examine your own heart; it is easy to mistake a leader’s faithful firmness for overreach, or his patience for neglect. Then go to him privately and humbly, as Matthew 18:15 directs, with specifics rather than complaints.
