Leaders are to be respected and obeyed in the Lord (Hebrews 13:17), but they are not above Scripture, and an accusation against an elder, properly attested, is to be taken seriously (1 Timothy 5:19). If there is abuse of any kind, do not stay silent: protect the vulnerable first, go to other elders or outside authorities, and report crimes to the police. Christ owns his flock, and he hates the shepherd who harms it.

On a Tuesday. Think of the member of your church you find hardest to love, and remember the price paid for them.
verseByVerse.note: Paul calls the same men elders (v. 17) and overseers — two names for one office. “With his own blood” — the blood of God’s own Son. Some manuscripts read “church of the Lord”; “his own blood” may also be rendered “the blood of his Own” (ESV notes).

parallels.desc: shepherds who feed themselves

verseByVerse.quote: "and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From among your own selves. The wolves were coming from outside. This is worse: some of the men in that room, or men very like them, currently sound and currently trusted. That is a hard thing to say to friends on the last afternoon you will spend together. And it happened: Paul later wrote to Timothy in Ephesus about false teachers there (1 Timothy 1:3–7, 19–20), and Jesus commended Ephesus for testing false apostles (Revelation 2:2).

After them. Not after a doctrine, nor even primarily into error, but a personal following gathered round a man. The doctrinal deviation is the method; the following is the aim. A teacher whose adherents are identifiable by their attachment to him has already shown you what Paul is warning about, whatever the content turns out to be.

Twisted things. Bent out of shape. Heresy is rarely a flat denial; it is truth bent just enough to mislead (Colossians 2:4), and almost every distortion adds to Christ, subtracts from him, or perverts his grace. Back then: the legalism that added circumcision and the law of Moses to Christ for salvation (Galatians; Acts 15); the Colossian error of secret knowledge, angel-worship and asceticism (Colossians 2); the denials of Christ’s true humanity (1 John 4:2–3) or of the resurrection (2 Timothy 2:17–18); and grace perverted into sensuality (Jude 4). And much was teaching for shameful gain (Titus 1:11).

The same three twists today. Adding: the prosperity gospel, promising health and wealth to enough faith or giving, and the perennial legalism that makes rules the measure of acceptance (Colossians 2:16). Subtracting: the emptying of the faith that denies Christ’s deity, the bodily resurrection, the atonement or Scripture’s authority, leaving a tame God who exists to make you comfortable; and the universalism that twists God is love into all paths lead home. Perverting grace: a cheap grace that drops repentance and holiness. So the Berean test (17:11): does this teaching exalt Christ and humble me, or exalt the teacher and serve his crowd and his wallet? A heart full of the real Christ (Colossians 3:16) is not easily sold a counterfeit.

Therefore be alert. One imperative, and it is not be learned or be organised. It means stay awake, the word of a watchman on a night shift. The danger it assumes is not that the elders will lose the argument but that they will not notice in time.

Night or day, with tears. Three years, night and day, every one, with tears: a record and a standard. This is what it took to build what you are now responsible for, and what it will take to keep it. No elder meets that standard without fault, and Paul himself had not yet arrived (Philippians 3:12). The Chief Shepherd kept his watch without a lapse, and his faithfulness, not theirs, is their standing before God; that frees them to keep the watch gladly, and to begin again when they fail.

Three years? Chapter 19 gives three months and two years (19:8, 10), and a further while (19:22). Ancient reckoning often counted any part of a year as a year, and the total comes close to three.

What was Paul admonishing them about? The word (noutheteō) means to warn and earnestly counsel, and chiefly he was guarding them from exactly these twisted teachers (vv. 29–30), pleading with each to hold fast to Christ. But it was wider: he had not shrunk from declaring the whole counsel of God (v. 27): sin and judgment, repentance and holiness, the cross, the suffering on the road into the kingdom (14:22). Why the tears? Because souls and eternity were at stake, and Paul loved these people. Real pastoral love is never bland; it warns, and warns weeping, as he told the Philippians even with tears (Philippians 3:18). The tears answer both ditches of verse 28: no negligent shepherd, for he warned relentlessly; yet no domineering one, for he warned with tears, not contempt. It is the model for every parent, friend and elder who must one day say a hard word: warn, yes, but with a breaking heart for the one you love.

How can an ordinary Christian tell a true teacher from a false one? Look at three things. His message: does it agree with the plain teaching of Scripture, and does it put Christ crucified and risen at the centre, or does it add to him, take from him, or make grace an excuse for sin? His life: is he humble, honest with money, faithful in marriage, accountable to others (1 Timothy 3:1–7)? His fruit in his followers: do they become more like Christ and more attached to the whole church, or more attached to him and suspicious of everyone else (Matthew 7:15–20)? You do not need to be a scholar. Read your Bible, belong to a faithful church, and ask whether the teacher is pointing you to Jesus or to himself.

Who are we to call anyone’s teaching false? We would have no right, if the standard were our own opinion. But Paul is not measuring teachers by his taste. He measures them by the gospel God revealed, and he applies the same test to himself: if even he or an angel from heaven preached a different gospel, he would be under God’s curse (Galatians 1:8). Humility does not mean pretending every claim about Jesus is equally true. It means submitting your own views to Scripture first, and then loving people enough to warn them when a message will cost them their souls. A shepherd who sees the wolf and says nothing is not humble; he is negligent.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one's silver or gold or apparel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God and the word of his grace. Having sobered them thoroughly, he tells them what they actually have. Not a structure, not a strategy, not a successor, not himself: God, and the word of his grace, the gospel now preserved in Scripture. That is the protection against wolves.

What is missing. Paul does not appoint a replacement, set up a chain of command back to Jerusalem, or tell them whom to consult. He left the church he had worked hardest for with God and a message. That is either reckless or the most confident thing in the chapter, and the next clause tells you which.

Commend. To entrust, to hand over for safekeeping. Paul deposits the elders with two keepers who never leave: God himself, and the word of his grace. The under-shepherd departs, but the Chief Shepherd remains.

Able to build you up. Able carries the whole weight, whether it refers to God or, as most take it, to the word of his grace: not a hope that they will manage but a capacity that belongs to the word itself. Build up is the construction word (Ephesians 4:12). The gospel is not lifeless information but a living means by which God grows his people strong (1 Peter 2:2), as in this very city the word of the Lord kept growing and prevailing (19:20). So a church grows after even a great leader is gone by the word of grace, fed on and held fast.

The inheritance. The future hope of all God’s holy people (26:18; Ephesians 1:14, 18; 1 Peter 1:4). The same word that builds them up now secures their future, and it is an inheritance, not a wage: given to children by grace, not earned.

Heirs because of the Heir. God has appointed his Son the heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and those who belong to him are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). They share the inheritance because they share in him. The word of grace is the message about him, the holiness is his gift, and the inheritance is his estate, opened to his brothers.

Those who are sanctified. Those who have been sanctified: a settled standing, not an achievement. It means all true believers, everyone God has set apart for himself in Christ (1 Corinthians 6:11; Hebrews 10:10), not an elite who have made themselves holy enough.

Silver or gold or apparel. The turn from the inheritance of the saints to other people’s clothes is not odd in the ancient world. Wandering teachers living off admirers were a recognised trade and nuisance, and good clothing was portable wealth, the sort of gift a grateful household gave a visiting teacher. So Paul, having handed the church over, establishes that he is not leaving with anything (1 Thessalonians 2:5). There will be no suggestion, after the ship sails, that the apostle did well out of Ephesus.

If the word is enough, why do we need pastors and teachers? Because the word is God’s chosen instrument, and pastors are his chosen servants of the word. Paul did not commend them to God and the word instead of elders; he commended the elders themselves to God and the word. Teachers do not add to Scripture’s power; they open it, apply it, and guard it, as Paul did for three years. The danger is when people trust the teacher more than the text, or think a church cannot survive without a particular man. It can. Every faithful pastor’s goal is to point his people so firmly to God and his word that they would stand if he were gone.

parallels.desc: whose ox have I taken?

verseByVerse.quote: "'You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
These hands. He very likely held them up, and everyone there knew what was on them: the calluses of a man who had cut leather and cloth for a living, for years, in their city. And Paul’s trade had supported the team: the apostle was paying for others.

To help the weak. We would expect him to say he worked so as not to be a burden, and he says that elsewhere (1 Thessalonians 2:9). Here the reason is better: he worked so that there would be something to give away (Ephesians 4:28). The strength to help the weak came out of the bench. The work is not what prevents ministry, nor merely what permits it; it is the source of the surplus that makes generosity possible.

The words of the Lord Jesus. Jesus never says this sentence in Matthew, Mark, Luke or John; it was passed down by those who heard him, the only saying from Jesus’ earthly ministry that Paul quotes in Acts. The world itself could not contain the books that might have been written (John 21:25); this is one line of the enormous remainder, preserved by the providence of God. And Paul says remember, not as it is written: these men may never have read a Gospel, and he expects them to have it by heart.

The hands behind these hands. Paul held up his own calloused hands and then pointed past them to the Lord Jesus. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The tentmaker’s hands had given years of evenings to the weak of Ephesus; the hands of Jesus were nailed open for the weak of every nation. It is more blessed to give than to receive is not a proverb from a wise man. It is the self-portrait of the Giver.

Does this mean pastors should work and not be paid? No. Paul insists that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that elders who labour in preaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17–18). Paul gave up that right for the sake of the gospel in some places. Both are honourable: a paid minister, and one who works to support himself.

A testable claim. Nearly everyone alive believes, in practice, that receiving is the better arrangement. Jesus says it is the other way round, and the man quoting him had built a life on it and was standing there with the calluses to prove it.

Is it wrong to receive help when I need it? No. The saying does not make receiving shameful; it makes giving blessed. Paul himself gladly received the Philippians’ gifts and called them a fragrant offering (Philippians 4:18). There are seasons, illness, poverty, old age, grief, when God calls us to receive, and pride that refuses help can rob others of the blessing of giving. Receive with gratitude and without embarrassment. And when the season turns, give with the same joy. The whole church is a circle of grace, in which every member both gives and receives, and Christ is the first giver of all.

For worship. The blessedness of giving is God’s own blessedness before it is ever ours. The Father gave the Son, the Son gave himself, and the Spirit is given and distributes his gifts to every member of the church. From all eternity the life of God has been a life of glad giving, and the Lord Jesus, who knew that joy before the world began, put it into one sentence his friends could not forget. Every time one of his people gives in his name, a little of that eternal joy spills over into a tired world.
verseByVerse.note: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in the Gospels; it was remembered and passed on.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He knelt down. Very likely near the harbour, in front of a ship’s crew, a group of grown men got down on the ground. Standing was the ordinary Jewish posture for prayer; people knelt when something weighed too much for standing: Solomon at the temple, Daniel, Stephen as the stones came down, Jesus in Gethsemane. And with them all: not over them, but down among them. Paul’s ministry in Ephesus ended, as it had been carried on, in prayer.

Much weeping. Grown men, church leaders, weeping, and Luke does not tidy it up. There is a strain of Christian teaching in which composure is next to godliness. Here is the apostle who wrote that we do not grieve as those who have no hope, on the ground, in tears, in public, with his arms round men he did not expect to see again.

They embraced Paul. Literally, they fell on his neck: the phrase used of the father running to the prodigal (Luke 15:20) and of Joseph with Benjamin. Luke reaches for the language of family reunion to describe a parting, because that is what these men are and what they are losing.

A family made by Christ. A few years earlier most of these men had not heard of Jesus Christ, and several had probably bought silver shrines of Artemis. Now they are weeping by the water over a Jewish tentmaker. Only one thing turns strangers into family like that. The Son of God shared our flesh and blood and is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11, 14), and whoever is joined to him is joined to everyone else who is.

Is it unspiritual to cry? No. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, knowing he was about to raise him (John 11:35), and wept over Jerusalem. Paul wept, these elders wept, and the psalms are full of tears. Tears are not a failure of faith but often an expression of love, for those we lose, for sin, for the suffering of others. What Christian hope changes is not whether we weep but how: we grieve, but not as those who have no hope. So do not be ashamed of tears, your own or anyone else’s. God keeps count of them, and one day he will wipe every one away (Psalm 56:8; Revelation 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His face. Luke tells us which sentence did it, and it was not the one about chains, or wolves, or traitors. What these men could not bear was that they would not see his face. Not his letters, not his teaching. His face.

A human sorrow, uncorrected. Scripture does not correct that sorrow. Paul writes the same way: he longs to see the Romans (Romans 1:11), and endeavoured the more eagerly and with great desire to see the Thessalonians face to face (1 Thessalonians 2:17). The New Testament, largely a collection of letters, is oddly insistent that letters are not enough. These men were not being sentimental. They were being accurate about what a relationship is.

God did not send only a letter. That insistence goes back to God himself. Long ago God spoke to the fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). He did not save the world by correspondence. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), with a face that could be seen and a hand that touched lepers, and the light of the knowledge of the glory of God now shines in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

To the ship. They walk him down to the water, very likely as a formal escort, and stand there until he is aboard. The great Ephesian ministry ends at the water’s edge with a knot of men watching a ship pull out, and Luke’s next verse says they had to tear themselves away (21:1).

Enough. What Paul left them were the two things he named in verse 32: God, and the word of his grace. On the evidence of the following decades, the letter to the Ephesians, and the church still standing when Christ addresses it in Revelation, it was enough, though even then he had to call it back to the love it had at first (Revelation 2:4–5).

Will we really know one another in heaven? Yes. The hope of Scripture is not that we dissolve into a crowd but that we are raised as ourselves and gathered together with the Lord. Paul comforts the Thessalonians with the promise that they will be caught up together with those who have died, and that is meant to be a comfort precisely because it is a reunion (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). On the mountain of transfiguration Moses and Elijah were recognisable. And the face we will see above all others is his: they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads (Revelation 22:4). Every other face will be dearer for that.

For worship. The elders watched one ship go and could not follow it. The Lord Jesus has also gone from his people’s sight, but he has gone ahead to prepare the far shore, and he is coming back for every one of them. The parting at Miletus was real, and the reunion will be more real still, and at the centre of it will be the face that was marred more than any man’s for our sake, now shining like the sun.

20.theology: The Whole Counsel of God. Paul could tell the elders he was innocent of their blood because he had not shrunk from declaring the whole counsel of God (v. 27). That is the standard for every ministry of the word: not only true but whole, teaching the tenderness of the Father and the judgment of God, free justification and the holiness that follows it, the comfort of election and the call to repent.
20.examples:
Then: On the shore at Miletus, a man going to chains spent his last hours not arranging his escape but commending the elders to God. Their tears at parting were the fruit of three years of his tears among them.

Now: The questions for any ministry are Paul’s: did we hold anything back, or give people a comfortable Christ without his commands, grace without repentance, the promise without the warning? A church that has been taught the whole counsel is the one best able to recognise a twisted message when the wolves come.

21.title: Bound for Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. <sup>2</sup>And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail. <sup>3</sup>When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo. <sup>4</sup>And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed <sup>6</sup>and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home. <sup>7</sup>When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. <sup>8</sup>On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. <sup>9</sup>He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied. <sup>10</sup>While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. <sup>11</sup>And coming to us, he took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit, ‘This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’” <sup>12</sup>When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem. <sup>13</sup>Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” <sup>14</sup>And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” <sup>15</sup>After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. <sup>16</sup>And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge. <sup>17</sup>When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. <sup>18</sup>On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. <sup>19</sup>After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. <sup>20</sup>And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law, <sup>21</sup>And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. <sup>22</sup>What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come. <sup>23</sup>Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; <sup>24</sup>take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law. <sup>25</sup>But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.” <sup>26</sup>Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them. <sup>27</sup>When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, <sup>28</sup>crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.” <sup>29</sup>For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. <sup>30</sup>Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut. <sup>31</sup>And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. <sup>32</sup>He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. <sup>33</sup>Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done. <sup>34</sup>Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. <sup>35</sup>And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd, <sup>36</sup>for the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!” <sup>37</sup>As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” And he said, “Do you know Greek? <sup>38</sup>Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?” <sup>39</sup>Paul replied, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.” <sup>40</sup>And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:
21.overview:
Paul’s road to Jerusalem echoes Jesus’ own (Luke 9:51). At Tyre disciples, moved by the Spirit, urge him not to go; at Caesarea, in Philip’s house, the prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and foretells that the Jews will hand Paul over to the Gentiles. Paul answers that he is ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and the church says, “Let the will of the Lord be done.”

In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome him and praise God for the Gentile mission, but warn him of a rumour among thousands of Jewish believers that he teaches Jews to abandon Moses. To answer it he joins four men completing a vow. Near the end of the week Jews from Asia see him in the temple, accuse him of bringing a Gentile inside, and the city erupts. The Roman tribune rescues him, chains him and mistakes him for an Egyptian rebel, and Paul asks to address the crowd. The prophecy has come true: he is bound, and in Gentile hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Journey to Jerusalem and the Warnings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Tyre the disciples, prompted by the Spirit, urge Paul not to go up to Jerusalem; at Caesarea, in Philip’s house, Agabus binds himself with Paul’s belt and foretells Paul’s arrest. Paul is ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and they give way. In Jerusalem they lodge with Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guidance: a Revelation and an Inference

Nobody in this passage is a villain. The Spirit really did reveal what was waiting in Jerusalem, in every city (20:23); what he did not say was do not go. That was added by people who loved Paul. Agabus, a true prophet, announces the outcome and gives no instruction. The doctrine of providence makes the distinction bearable: because God ordains the end and the means together, a warning of suffering is often not a detour sign but the itinerary. Paul is told the cost in advance so that he can pay it with his eyes open.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A whole congregation at Tyre, children too, kneeling on the shore of a working harbour to pray for a man they had known for seven days, and then going home to supper while he sailed toward chains. Now: When someone we love walks toward a costly obedience we cannot talk them out of, we need what that church found on the beach: the grace to lose the argument and keep the love, and to pray with them that the Lord’s will be done.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 21 tells of Paul’s last journey to Jerusalem and his arrest there. All along the way believers warn him by the Spirit that chains await him, and beg him not to go; he goes anyway, ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. In Jerusalem a false rumour sets off a riot, and Roman soldiers rescue him from the mob. Like his Lord, he goes up to Jerusalem knowing what awaits him and is handed over to the Gentiles, and the chapter ends with the apostle on the barracks steps, in chains, holding the silence of a vast crowd, about to tell them about Jesus.

Parted. The word is too gentle. Luke’s verb means to pull away, and many translations render it tore ourselves away. It is the word for drawing a sword from its sheath (Matthew 26:51). Nobody walks away from an embrace like that. You have to be pulled out of it.

By a straight course. Then, without pause, the ship’s log: short daylight hops down the island chain off the south-west corner of Asia Minor, the shore always in view. By a straight course is the phrase used when the gospel first crossed into Europe (16:11). The winds are behind them; nothing in the voyage resists.

A ship crossing to Phoenicia. Patara was the great harbour of Lycia, where coastal traffic met the deep-sea freighters running east. A ship crossing over would strike out across the open sea: some four hundred miles to Tyre, perhaps five days with a following wind.

Why change ships? Because Paul is against a clock. He had already sailed past Ephesus rather than be detained there, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost (20:16). Coasting would never have made it. So a man who has been told in city after city that chains are waiting at the far end books himself a faster passage, in order to arrive sooner. That is not how we behave. We hurry toward what we want. Paul is hurrying toward what he has been warned about, and doing it with a traveller’s care: the right harbour, the right ship, the right sailing date. Obedience here is not a leap off a cliff. It is logistics.

A baptism he longed to have done. One other traveller in Luke’s writings hurried toward suffering. On his way to Jerusalem Jesus said, I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! (Luke 12:50). He did not drift toward the cross; he pressed toward it. Paul on a fast freighter is not repeating that finished work. He is showing the same kind of obedience, learned from the Lord who first set out for that city.

Does a smooth journey mean God approves of my plans? Not necessarily, and this voyage is the proof. Every circumstance here is quietly cooperating to deliver Paul to the city where he will be seized, beaten and chained. The road was smooth because God was getting him to prison. Easy circumstances are a mercy, and hard ones are not a sign of God’s displeasure; neither one tells you by itself whether you are walking in his will. That is learned from his word, from a good conscience and from wise counsel. So when doors open, give thanks without assuming they are a verdict on your choices, and when they slam shut, do not assume you have taken a wrong turning. Paul’s smoothest crossing took him to his chains, and his chains took him to Rome.
verseByVerse.note: Cos, Rhodes and Patara were ports along the south-west coast of Asia Minor; from Patara they crossed the open sea east toward Phoenicia.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leaving it on the left. A sailor’s sentence: running south-east, Cyprus slides past on the left, and Luke, on board, writes down which side it went by. Details like this are why many historians think these we passages come from an eyewitness.

Cyprus on the horizon. Cyprus is Barnabas’s home (4:36), where the first missionary journey began (13:4–6), and where Barnabas sailed with Mark when he and Paul parted (15:39). Now it passes and the ship does not stop. Luke simply names the landmark. But the longer you serve the Lord, the more of your life sits on the horizon like that: real, visible, unreachable, going by on the left while the wind takes you somewhere else.

Did Paul and Barnabas ever make it up? Scripture suggests they did, though Acts does not tell the story. Some years later Paul mentions Barnabas warmly to the Corinthians as a fellow worker who, like himself, earned his own living (1 Corinthians 9:6). And Mark, the young man they quarrelled over, ends up beside Paul: he is with him in his imprisonment (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24), and at the very end Paul asks for him because he is useful to him for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). The sharp disagreement was real, and so was the healing. Christians can disagree badly and still be reconciled, and God can use even their parting to send two missions out instead of one.

Tyre. The great port of Phoenicia, whose pride the prophets had denounced (Ezekiel 26–28). In that region a Gentile mother had begged Jesus for crumbs from the children’s table and gone home with her daughter healed (Mark 7:24–30). The crumbs have become a church.

To unload its cargo. Unloading a freighter by hand could take the better part of a week, and that is how long they stay (v. 4). The layover is a dockworker’s timetable, and God uses it to put Paul in front of a church he would otherwise have sailed past.

Where did the church at Tyre come from? Nobody in Acts was ever sent to plant it. Turn back to 11:19: those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen travelled as far as Phoenicia. There are very probably disciples in this port because Christians were once driven out of Jerusalem by a young Pharisee who was ravaging the church and dragging men and women off to prison (8:3). Paul is about to spend a week being fed and housed by the fruit of his own violence. He will kneel on their beach and pray with their children. The gospel does that: it does not merely forgive the persecutor, it seats him at the table of the people he scattered.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was a major port of Phoenicia, north of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: "And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having sought out the disciples. The verb means to find by searching. There was no building and no address. A stranger got off a ship in a pagan port and went looking, street by street, for people who belonged to Jesus. The church at Tyre was invisible from the street, and it was there.

Through the Spirit. Then the hard sentence. The tense suggests they said it again and again through the seven days, and Luke does not say they were mistaken about the source. So was Paul defying the Spirit? Paul had answered that a chapter earlier (20:22–23): the Spirit revealed the suffering, and the Spirit himself was leading Paul to Jerusalem (19:21). These disciples had a genuine revelation, and to it they added a conclusion of their own: therefore do not go. The conclusion was love talking, not prophecy. That is the most widely held explanation, and it fits Luke’s words; even so, this is one of the hard verses of Acts, and Christians who puzzle over it are not being faithless.

Where Christians differ: can prophecy be mistaken? Some cite this to argue that New Testament prophecy was fallible, mixing God’s revelation with human interpretation; they hold this out of care to take Luke’s words at face value, and the question is a fair one. This commentary’s view: what the Spirit revealed was true: chains awaited Paul. What the disciples drew from it, that he should avoid them, was their own conclusion. Revelation must be distinguished from our application of it. The Spirit’s word is never mistaken; our inferences can be.

Right about the revelation, wrong about the inference. The Gospels have a moment shaped exactly like this. Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, revealed by the Father in heaven; soon after, when Jesus says he must suffer in Jerusalem, Peter rebukes him: This shall never happen to you. And Jesus says, Get behind me, Satan! (Matthew 16:16–23). The same man, in the same conversation, right about the revelation and badly wrong about the inference, and the motive for the error was affection.

What do I do when a Christian friend says God has told them I should not do something? Separate the two halves of what they have said. Ask: what is actually being claimed as revealed, and what has been concluded from it? Then test both by Scripture. God has given his church a finished Bible, and no private impression can add a command to it or cancel one in it. A true word about coming trouble is not an instruction to avoid the trouble; very often it is God telling you the price in advance, so that you cannot say afterwards you were tricked into paying it. Receive your friend’s concern with gratitude, weigh it with your elders and with wise believers, and if it is love speaking rather than the word of God, thank them for the love and do what God has plainly called you to do.

With wives and children. This is a church that lost the argument and did not sulk. The whole congregation, small children included, walked a man they had known for seven days out through the gate and down to the water.

Kneeling on the beach. They knelt in the wet sand of a working harbour, in front of dockers and sailors. Luke reserves kneeling in Acts for moments that cost something: Stephen under the stones (7:60), Peter beside a dead woman (9:40), Paul with the Ephesian elders (20:36). They had known him seven days, and they loved him enough to bring the children. If a church cannot do in years what Tyre did in a week, the difference is not time.
verseByVerse.note: The Spirit revealed the danger ahead; the disciples concluded that he should not go.

verseByVerse.quote: "and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Farewell. Luke could have made a scene of this and refuses: farewells are exchanged and the gangplank is crossed. The moment does not need his help.

They returned home. Two parties leave the same beach. One boards a ship for Jerusalem, chains and a Roman barracks. The other shakes the sand off and goes home, to the nets and the warehouses and the children who now want their dinner. We are trained to think the ship is the real story. Luke wrote both halves of the verse down.

The ones who went home. This church took in strangers, fed them, prayed with them about a decision it could not change, and walked them to the water. No sermon of theirs survives, and none of them may ever have seen Paul again. And the Holy Spirit had it recorded in Scripture. Most of us are Tyre. The great work of God in our generation will pass through our town for about a week, and our part in it will be a spare bed, a meal, and a prayer on the way out. That is not the small version of the Christian life. That is the Christian life, and it is written down.

The hidden years in Nazareth. The Lord himself lived most of his life like Tyre. Luke records one episode from those years, and then that he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them (Luke 2:51). Before he had preached a sermon or worked a miracle, the Father said he was well pleased with his beloved Son (Luke 3:22). Those hidden years were part of the perfect obedience by which he saved us, and they make the kitchen, the workbench and the nursery holy ground, when the work is done for him (Colossians 3:23).

Is my ordinary life really service to God if I never do anything dramatic? Yes, and this verse says so in eleven words. The believers who returned home did not stop serving God when the ship left; they went back to the place he had put them. Hospitality, prayer, faithful work, raising children who have knelt beside a missionary: these are not the waiting room of the Christian life. The Lord Jesus said that whoever receives one of his servants receives him, and that even a cup of cold water given to one of his disciples will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:40–42). God sees the spare bed, and he wrote it in his book.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ptolemais. The old port of Acco, modern Acre, just north of Carmel. No mission to Ptolemais appears anywhere in Acts, and yet there are brothers to greet. It is the second church in this chapter that no one in Acts founded: refugees from Jerusalem had walked up this coast preaching as they went (11:19). The map of Christianity is not only drawn by strategy. A great deal of it was drawn by people running for their lives and talking as they went.

Philip the evangelist. Philip was one of the Seven appointed to wait on tables (6:5). He preached Christ in Samaria, baptised an Ethiopian official on the Gaza road, and was last seen preaching his way up the coast until he came to Caesarea (8:40). That was some twenty years ago, and he is still there, still serving. He is the only man in Scripture to wear the word evangelist as a title (compare Ephesians 4:11; 2 Timothy 4:5).

Why was Philip in Caesarea at all? Turn back to chapter 8. Saul approved of Stephen’s execution, a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and Saul was ravaging the church, entering house after house and dragging off men and women to prison. Those who were scattered went about preaching the word, and Philip went down to Samaria (8:1–5). Philip is in Caesarea because Saul of Tarsus drove him out of Jerusalem. He was a colleague of Stephen, one of the same seven, chosen on the same day, and Stephen had died at the hands of a mob whose coats were being minded by the man now standing on his doorstep asking for a bed.

The first wound was Christ’s. On the Damascus road the risen Lord did not ask Saul why he was persecuting Stephen or Philip. He said, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting (9:5). Every house Saul broke into, Christ counted as an attack on himself, and Christ was the first to forgive it. So when Philip opens his door, he is not deciding whether Saul’s past can be overlooked. The one most wronged has already settled it.

And he says come in. Not for an hour: stayed with him, and by verse 10 many days. Paul sleeps under the roof of the man he once drove out of Jerusalem. Reconciliation is not a warm feeling about someone at a distance. It is an address you are willing to sleep at and a table you are willing to eat at. Philip handed him a key, and Paul knocked, which for a proud man is the harder half. It is often suggested, too, that Luke gathered much of the early history of his book in these weeks, from the man who had lived it.

Does forgiving someone mean I have to have them in my home? Not always, and wisdom matters here. Forgiveness means giving up the right to repay, wishing the other person good and praying for them, and it is never optional for a Christian (Matthew 6:14–15; Ephesians 4:32). Full fellowship of the kind Philip offered rests on repentance: Saul had been changed by Christ, and everyone knew it. Where a person has not repented, or where there has been abuse, keeping a safe distance is not unforgiveness, and no one should be pressed to share a roof with someone who may harm them. But where Christ has truly changed both people, the gospel aims at more than a truce. It aims at a table.

On a Tuesday. If there is someone you have wronged, or who has wronged you, and Christ has been at work in you both, take one step toward that table this month: a letter, a call, a meal.
verseByVerse.note: Ptolemais is modern Acre. Philip was one of the seven chosen in Acts 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four unmarried daughters. Luke drops the words in as if noting the number of rooms in the house, and that casualness is the point. More than twenty years earlier Peter had read out Joel at Pentecost: your sons and your daughters shall prophesy (2:17). Here, on an ordinary day in Caesarea, the new age is four young women at the family table. Women received and exercised the gift of prophecy in the apostolic church (1 Corinthians 11:5), and nobody makes a fuss about it.

Whose daughters they are. Philip preached to Samaritans and to an African official when nobody else would, and he has four daughters who prophesy. Households take the shape of what the head of the house believes God is like.

Luke’s silence. Luke records that they prophesied and not one word they said, though the next paragraph gives Agabus’s prophecy in full. His interest here is the fact of the gift, and that should keep us from building either a doctrine or a grievance on the silence.

What the gift was for. Peter gave the reason the day it began: Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God, had received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and poured him out (2:33). The daughters of Caesarea prophesied because the crucified Nazarene was reigning, and the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy (Revelation 19:10). The Spirit never speaks to make his servants famous. He speaks to make the Son known.

Where Christians differ: prophesying women and church leadership. Some argue that because women prophesied, they may also hold the office of elder or pastor. This commentary’s view: prophecy and the office of elder are different things. Women prophesied, prayed and served in the apostolic church, and are honoured for it. The office of elder and authoritative teaching in the gathered church Scripture gives to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:6). The complementarian view (that men and women are equal in worth and gifting, with different callings in the home and the church) honours both truths: the full dignity and gifts of women, and the order God has given for the church.

Holding both together. The New Testament never sets these against each other. Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in the church (1 Corinthians 11:5) in the same letter in which he orders that gathering (1 Corinthians 14), and he restricts the standing authority to teach and govern a congregation to qualified men. Prophesying is a gift, not an office, and Luke is describing a household, not installing anyone in a pulpit. Many faithful Christians read these passages as opening every office to women, and argue it from the Scripture they love; hold your view with more charity toward them than the internet does. What is not in dispute is what Luke wrote: God pours out his Spirit on daughters.

Do women prophesy like this today? The church has never stopped needing the voices of its daughters, but the particular gift Luke describes belonged to the founding years. Most Reformed Christians believe the revelatory gift of prophecy belonged with the apostles to the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20) and ceased when Scripture was complete. Many brothers and sisters in Pentecostal and charismatic churches believe the gift continues today, and they too love the Spirit and the word; this commentary holds the other view, for the reason just given, without doubting their faith. What remains for every woman, as for every man, is the Spirit’s gift of speaking God’s finished word to others: teaching children and younger women (Titus 2:3–5), explaining the way of God more accurately as Priscilla did with Apollos (18:26), encouraging, comforting and warning one another (Hebrews 3:13). A woman who brings Scripture to bear on a friend’s grief is doing in her generation what these four did in theirs.

The church’s memory. The historian Eusebius records that Philip’s daughters later lived at Hierapolis in Asia and were remembered as living sources for the earliest days (though ancient writers sometimes confuse this Philip with the apostle). Not one syllable of theirs is in our Bible, and the church’s memory ran through them anyway.

For worship. The Lord keeps his promises down to the furniture. What he spoke through Joel he fulfilled in a house in Caesarea, in four young women whose names we do not know. He has never once forgotten a word he spoke, and he will remember every promise he has made to his church until the last is kept on the day his Son appears.

parallels.desc: your sons and your daughters shall prophesy

verseByVerse.quote: "While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. And coming to us, he took Paul's belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, 'Thus says the Holy Spirit, "This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agabus. We have met him. He foretold a great famine years before, and Luke adds drily that it took place in the days of Claudius (11:28). He has a verified track record.

Paul’s belt. He takes the long cloth belt from round Paul’s waist and ties his own feet and hands with it in front of the whole household. This is prophecy in the old manner. Isaiah walked barefoot for three years as a sign (Isaiah 20:2–4); Jeremiah wore a yoke through the streets (Jeremiah 27:2); Ezekiel laid siege to a brick on the floor (Ezekiel 4). A thing seen goes deeper than a thing heard. Everyone in that room would forget the sentence. Nobody would forget the belt.

Thus says the Holy Spirit. Thus says the LORD is the standing prophetic formula, the phrase that marks the difference between a man’s opinion and the speech of the covenant God. Agabus, a Jewish prophet in a Jewish house, takes it unaltered and puts the Holy Spirit’s name in it, as naturally as breathing. The doctrine of the Trinity was not invented by a later council; it lies in the floorboards of the church’s earliest speech, because these men saw no difference between the Spirit speaking and God speaking. There is none: the Spirit is God.

Into the hands of the Gentiles. Agabus does not say do not go. He says this is what will happen, and that is the difference between him and the disciples at Tyre, which is why Luke places them side by side. And the wording is the wording of the passion: Jesus said he would be delivered over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32). Paul has walked into his Master’s story, and the road to Jerusalem has only one ending for those who take it.

Did the prophecy come true, when it was the Romans who bound him? Yes, and the answer is ordinary biblical speech. When it happens, the Jews are trying to lynch Paul and it is the Romans who put on the chains (vv. 30–33). But Scripture routinely credits an act to the person who caused it rather than the hands that carried it out. Peter tells Jerusalem that they crucified and killed Jesus by the hands of lawless men (2:23); no Jew drove a nail, and Peter still says they did it. And there is a witness who settles it, because he was the man in the chains. Years later, in Rome, Paul sums up the whole affair to the Jewish leaders by saying that he was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans (28:17). That is Agabus’s prophecy, quoted back almost word for word, by the man best placed to complain if it had not come true. The fit is not wooden, and some readers press the difference, but this is how Scripture itself speaks.

Where Christians differ: do prophets like Agabus still speak today? Many Christians believe the gift continues, and they love the Lord and his word. They often point to 1 Corinthians 13:8–12 and 14:1, reading prophecy as lasting until Christ returns, and it is a serious argument. This commentary’s view: the more likely reading is that New Testament prophecy, as revelation from God, belonged with the apostles to the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and ceased with the completion of Scripture. Agabus’s words came true in substance: Paul was bound and handed over to the Gentiles. We hold this charitably toward brothers who see it differently, and we expect the Spirit to speak to his church today through the Scripture he has given, which is sufficient for everything we need for life and godliness.

For worship. The road the Spirit described for Paul was the road the Son of God had already walked: bound by his own people, handed over to the Gentiles, and led out to die. But Paul’s binding would carry the gospel to Rome; Christ’s binding carried our sins away. He let himself be tied so that we could go free.
verseByVerse.note: Agabus acts out his prophecy as the Old Testament prophets often did.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
We urged him. Read the pronoun. Luke is in the room, and on the wrong side. Writing years later, knowing Paul was right, he could have left himself out. Instead he puts himself among those who tried to talk the apostle out of obeying God. A writer polishing his own part would hardly do that. A man who knows he has been forgiven might.

The pressure of love. The pressure has become total: Tyre for seven days, now the whole household at Caesarea, Philip, the travelling companions, and the doctor who will be with him to the last (2 Timothy 4:11). Every Christian in the building is telling him not to go, like Peter trying to stop Jesus going to the cross (Matthew 16:22): natural, loving, and wrong. We prepare for opposition from enemies, but often the strongest force against your obedience will be the affection of people who cannot bear what it will cost you. They are not wicked. They are weeping. And their tears can do what threats never could.

Love received but not obeyed. Their love is not an argument: it is precious, it should be received warmly, and it settles nothing about what God has said. Nor is it an enemy: Paul does not rebuke them or accuse them of unbelief. And there is a quiet warning here. The approval of people we love is one of the sweetest things God gives, and for that very reason it can become the thing we most fear to lose, taking the place that belongs to God alone (Galatians 1:10).

How do I know when to listen to people who love me, and when to disappoint them? Ask what their counsel rests on. If they are pointing you to Scripture, to a clear duty you are neglecting, or to wisdom you have not weighed, listen hard; Proverbs says there is safety in many counsellors (Proverbs 11:14), and most of the time the people who love you are right. If they are asking you to step back from something God has plainly called you to, because the cost frightens them, thank them and stay the course. And if you are the one urging, as Luke was and as most of us mostly are, ask honestly whether you want someone to be careful because God has spoken, or because you cannot face losing them.

On a Tuesday. Be careful your love does not hold others back from God’s call: the missionary son, the friend taking a stand that will cost him his job. Tell them you will miss them, and then help them pack.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, "Let the will of the Lord be done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? He is not made of stone, and this verse exists to stop us thinking he was. The word translated breaking (synthryptō) means to break in pieces, and so to crush someone’s resolve; it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Their crying is not glancing off him. It is grinding him down, and he says so. Which means that Paul in this room is under two pressures at once, and only one of them is chains. The prospect of a Roman prison he can face. The thing that is actually crushing him is the sound of people who love him, sobbing. That is what he has to walk through to get to Jerusalem.

Ready to die. Ready is a settled word: not braced or resigned, but prepared, the way a soldier is. Not reckless but resolved, like his Lord, who set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Not only imprisoned, but even to die: he has priced the worst outcome in advance, which is why the weeping cannot move him. You cannot threaten a man with something he has already agreed to (Philippians 1:21). And he is ready to die not for a cause or the collection in his luggage, but for the name of the Lord Jesus. Persons are worth dying for in a way that projects never are.

Is it right to want to die for Christ? Paul is not seeking death, and Scripture never praises those who throw their lives away. He had escaped over the Damascus wall in a basket (9:25) and would shortly use his Roman citizenship to avoid a flogging (22:25). What he has done is settle in advance that his life is not his own, so that if obedience costs him his life, he will not hold it back. That is what every Christian is called to: not a death wish, but a heart that has already handed everything over. Most believers will never be asked to die for Christ. All of us are asked to live as people who would.

Is this not just religious fanaticism, the kind that makes people dangerous? Look at what Paul is ready for. He is ready to be bound and to die, not to bind anyone or to kill anyone. The Assassins who haunted Jerusalem in these very years carried daggers into festival crowds (21:38); Paul carries nothing but a message, and when the mob beats him he asks to speak to it. That is the difference between a fanatic and a follower of Christ. The fanatic will sacrifice others for his cause. The Christian has a Lord who gave himself for his enemies (Romans 5:8), and so he will lay down his own life for that Lord’s name, and never take another’s.

Let the will of the Lord be done. It may be the quietest great moment in Acts. They were not convinced; they ran out of arguments in front of a man who would not move, and they stopped. And the sentence they said is the one from the garden: not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). This is Gethsemane in a front room in Caesarea, prayed by ordinary Christians over a friend they expect to lose.

The real article. Anyone can say it about a matter still open. This room says it having lost the argument, about a man they will very likely never see again. That is not resignation, which gives up on the outcome; these people are handing it to a Person. There comes a moment in most Christian lives when the praying stops being about changing the verdict and starts being about trusting the Judge, and this is the sentence to have ready.

Is saying “Let the will of the Lord be done” giving up on prayer? No. These believers had prayed and pleaded, and they were right to; the Lord Jesus himself asked in Gethsemane that the cup might pass. Asking God boldly for what we long for and submitting to what he decides belong together in the same prayer. What changes at the end is not that we stop caring but that we stop insisting. We hand the outcome to a Father who is wiser than we are and who loves the person we are praying for more than we do. That is not defeat. It is the deepest kind of trust.

For worship. The prayer the Caesarean church managed through its tears had already been prayed perfectly, in the dark, by a man with nobody awake to hear him. The cup was not taken away, and he drank every drop. The will of the Lord was done, in his body, on a hill outside the walls, and that is the only reason there was a church in Caesarea to pray it at all.

parallels.desc: not my will, but yours

verseByVerse.quote: After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We got ready. The ordinary word for packing baggage and loading animals. After days of tears and prophecy, a group of men strap their bags on and set off on a walk of some sixty-five miles up to the ridge. Obedience, once the argument is over, mostly looks like luggage. Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet above the plain, and every Jew spoke of going up to it the way we speak of going home.

In the flow. The long journey reaches its goal, told as Luke told the last journey of Jesus (Luke 9:51): warnings, friends who would hold him back, and a final going up to the city. From here the missionary becomes a prisoner, and the rest of Acts shows the gospel reaching Rome through his chains.

What is in those bags? Luke does not tell you here, and that is one of the great restraints of Acts. For years Paul had been organising a relief fund among the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He gave Corinth detailed instructions about it (1 Corinthians 16:1–4). He devoted two chapters of a letter to persuading them to finish it (2 Corinthians 8–9). He told the Romans he was going to Jerusalem with aid for the saints, and asked them to pray that it would be acceptable (Romans 15:25–31). It was the great labour of his later ministry, a tangible proof that the Gentile churches and the mother church were one body. Luke gives it a single passing mention in the whole book, and not until Paul is on trial: he had come to bring alms to his nation (24:17). There is a lesson in the silence for anyone who handles money in the church, or quietly funds it. The thing Paul travelled for years to deliver gets no paragraph. The evangelist who had stayed in Caesarea for twenty years gets a verse and a title. Luke is not measuring by what a thing cost to arrange, and neither, in the end, is God.

Mnason of Cyprus. The lodging was arranged in advance, and look who was chosen. Mnason is a Cypriot with a Greek name, like Barnabas (4:36), and an early disciple, perhaps from Pentecost itself. Paul is arriving with uncircumcised Gentiles in a city where thousands of believers are zealous for the law (v. 20), and his host is a disciple of long standing, at home with Gentiles: a man who can put Trophimus the Ephesian in his spare room without the neighbours calling it a scandal.

Receiving the Lord at the door. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58), and he said that a welcome given to the least of his brothers is given to him: I was a stranger and you welcomed me (Matthew 25:35). When an old disciple from Cyprus made up beds for a Jewish apostle and his uncircumcised friends, he was opening his door to Christ, and Christ will remember it.

What does Christian hospitality look like when my home is small or my life is busy? It looks like Mnason: an open door to the person who needs one, at the moment they need it. It does not need a large house, a polished meal or a tidy kitchen. It needs a willingness to make room, and some thought about who would be uncomfortable elsewhere: the newcomer, the overseas student, the believer from a different background, the person whom others hesitate to have. Scripture makes hospitality a duty for every Christian, not a gift for a few (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), and older believers are often its best practitioners. A bed, a bowl of soup and a welcome can be the most strategic thing in the whole mission.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James and the elders welcome Paul, but warn him of a rumour that he teaches Jews to abandon Moses, and advise him to join four men completing a vow; the letter to the Gentile believers stands. Near the end of the week Jews from Asia seize him in the temple, claiming he has brought Greeks inside. The Roman tribune rescues him, binds him with two chains, takes him at first for an Egyptian rebel, and gives him leave to address the people.
verseByVerse.theology:
Liberty, Accommodation, and the Line That Does Not Move

Paul in the temple paying for offerings does not contradict Galatians; he applies it. The gospel had freed him from the law as a way of standing before God, and that freedom is what let him keep the customs without fear: only a justified man can pay for a lamb, relying on nothing in it before God, while meaning a great deal by it before his brothers. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

The line is drawn not at the act but at what the act is made to mean. When men demanded that Titus be circumcised, Paul did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved (Galatians 2:5). Here nothing is required of any Gentile, and James says so before anyone can misread the week. So bend as far as love can on matters of culture and conscience, and not at all on the ground of acceptance with God. And this wise and humble course failed: it put Paul in the temple to be seized. The outcome belonged to God, who made it the road to Rome (23:11).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: An apostle with Roman citizenship in his pocket, chained at the door of a fortress, spending his one request not on rescue but on permission to preach to the mob that had just beaten him. Now: God’s help does not always come from where we expect it: the church is nowhere in this scene, and a Roman cohort is everything. And the platform we are given is rarely the one we asked for: Paul wanted a cleared name and got a chain and a staircase. What has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Philippians 1:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Received us gladly. Relief as much as pleasure. Months earlier Paul had asked the Romans to pray that he might be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that his service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints (Romans 15:31). He was not sure the mother church would take what he was bringing. The first half of that prayer would be answered in an unexpected way. The second half is answered in this verse.

James and all the elders. The formal meeting happens the next day, with the full leadership assembled. James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church (15:13; Galatians 2:9). Luke mentions no apostles in the room; Peter had left Jerusalem years before (12:17). The church in the mother city is governed by James, presiding, with a body of elders. When the apostle to the Gentiles arrives, he does not summon them. He goes in to them, with his delegation, and reports.

A delegation with a bag. Went in with us: Luke is there, and presumably the delegates of 20:4. Men from several provinces, many of them uncircumcised Gentiles, walk into the leadership of the Jerusalem church carrying a large sum for Jewish believers they have never met (24:17). Paul had worked for years for the unity of the church to stop being only a doctrine and become a delegation standing in a room with a gift. Whatever happens in the next twenty verses, this happened first, and it happened gladly.

In the flow. Acts began in Jerusalem with the promise of witness to the end of the earth (1:8). Now the man who carried it furthest comes back with the fruit of the Gentile mission in his hands. This is the last time Acts shows the Jerusalem church at all, and Luke lets us watch the mother church and the Gentile mission embrace before he shows what the city will do with the man who joined them.

Two men the risen Christ appeared to. James, presiding, is the brother of Jesus, and during the Lord’s ministry not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). Paul, reporting, tried to destroy his church. Paul lists what changed both: then he appeared to James, and last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me (1 Corinthians 15:7–8). The sceptical brother and the persecuting Pharisee sit in one room as leaders of one church because Jesus came out of the tomb and showed himself to each.

Why does it matter how a church is governed? Because Christ is the head of his church and he has given it an order. In the New Testament, local churches are led by a plurality of elders, who are also called overseers and shepherds (20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7), with deacons serving alongside them (Philippians 1:1). Christians differ over the details, whether congregations are bound together under wider assemblies or govern themselves, and those views deserve a fair hearing. But every faithful view agrees on what this verse shows: leadership is shared, accountable and humble, and even an apostle submits his work to the brothers.

For worship. Gentiles who had once been far off came carrying gifts to Zion, as the prophets foresaw (Isaiah 60:5). But the true fulfilment is greater than any purse. The nations come to Christ himself and lay before him the only gift he wants: themselves, made one body by the blood that has brought near those who were far off (Ephesians 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: "After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, 'You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One by one. Item by item, and not brief. Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Lystra, Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus. The jailer at midnight. Lydia. The slave girl. Eutychus alive on the floor at Troas. Years of work, told out to men who had not seen any of it.

The grammar of a servant. Look how Paul tells it. God is the subject of every sentence; Paul is a preposition: through him. That is how he had learned to see, and it is why he could survive both the applause at Lystra and the stoning that followed it. He would write it to the Romans: I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me (Romans 15:18).

They glorified God. They did not congratulate Paul; they worshipped (compare 11:18). A church that can hear about work it did not do, in places it will never see, and respond by praising God rather than measuring itself, is a church in good health.

How many thousands. Then, in the same breath, the problem. The word is myriads, tens of thousands, though it can be used loosely of a vast number. The Jerusalem church has become enormous, and the elders say it with joy. And they call Paul brother. They are not interrogating an opponent; they are briefing a member of the family about a fire in the house.

Zealous for the law. The word is the one that gave the Zealot party its name. These are Jewish believers who keep the law of Moses as their way of life, not as their way of salvation: the Sabbath, the circumcision of their sons, the feasts, the food laws, and they love doing it. It is their culture and their identity. Tensions were rising in these years, with Jewish nationalism building toward the war with Rome that would come within a decade, and a zeal for the law could easily turn into suspicion of anyone who seemed to loosen it. Neither James nor Luke rebukes them. The Jerusalem Council had settled that Gentiles are not to be put under the law; it never said that Jews who believe must abandon it, and Paul never taught that either. What we have is one gospel producing two cultures, which is a triumph and a tinderbox in the same sentence.

Should Jewish believers keep the law today? Paul himself kept Jewish customs where they did not compromise the gospel (to the Jews I became as a Jew, 1 Corinthians 9:20), and a Jewish Christian is free to keep them as a matter of heritage and witness. What no one may do is make them necessary for salvation or impose them on Gentile believers (15:19–20; Galatians 2:14–16). The sacrifices and the temple are another matter: they were shadows fulfilled in Christ, and when the temple fell in AD 70 God himself brought that part of the old order to its end (Hebrews 8:13).

On a Tuesday. Give an account of your last year of Christian service, out loud, in Paul’s grammar: not what you managed or built, but the things God did, through you.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have been told. The verb is usually the word for instruction, the word from which we get catechism (Luke 1:4). The report had been passed on, perhaps even taught, to a great many people, and Luke’s passive quietly declines to say by whom.

An accusation nobody could check. The offence is said to have happened among the Jews who are among the Gentiles: out there, in synagogues hundreds of miles away that nobody in the room has attended. Nobody present can disprove it, and that is what gives it its grip.

Children and customs. The cradle and the calendar: what you do to your newborn son, and how your household lives its week. Say that a man is dissolving Jewish family life, in a city of law-zealous believers, and you have made him dangerous.

Was the rumour true? As stated, no; but it grew from a seed of truth, and it is worth seeing both halves. What was false: Paul never taught Jews to forsake Moses or to stop circumcising their children. He kept the customs himself, freely and gladly. He took a vow (18:18), circumcised Timothy (16:3), hurried to keep Pentecost (20:16), worshipped in the temple, and is about to join four men in their vow to show it. He told the Corinthians that a man called when circumcised should not try to undo it (1 Corinthians 7:18). The word in the charge is apostasia, rebellion, abandonment, and of that Paul was simply innocent; he called the law holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12).

The seed of truth. Here is what made the rumour believable. Paul really did teach something radical: that nothing, not circumcision, not law-keeping, makes anyone right with God; that justification, God’s verdict declaring a sinner righteous in his sight, is by faith in Christ alone (Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:28); that Gentile believers need not keep the law at all (15:19; he refused to circumcise Titus, Galatians 2:3–5); that the ceremonial law is a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17); and that the believer has died to the law as a way of standing before God (Romans 7:4–6). He taught that the customs are not required and count for nothing as the ground of salvation, and that Jew and Gentile are one in Christ. In the heat of controversy and hostile retelling, that got stretched into Paul tells everyone to forsake Moses. The rumour took you are free from the law and twisted it into you must abandon the law, and that gap is the whole point. Paul preached freedom, not apostasy: a Jewish believer is free to keep his customs as heritage and witness, free not to, and never to trust them for salvation.

What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come. A real pastoral problem. Certainly: no possibility of a quiet visit. Jerusalem is filling for Pentecost, the church numbers tens of thousands, and Paul has walked in with a band of Gentiles and a purse. The news is already moving through the city while the meeting is in progress.

Living your way back. What the elders do not propose is telling. They do not say, we will explain. They do not draft a statement or call an assembly so Paul can clear his name. These are experienced pastors and they know something we are slow to learn: a reputation is rarely repaired by explanation. Once a man is widely believed to be a certain kind of man, words about him, even true words, even his own, are heard as a defence and filed accordingly. So they look for something he can do instead. Not a claim but a fact; not a denial that can be disputed, but a week of conduct in public view. Whether the plan was wise is the question of the next verses. That the instinct was right is hardly in doubt.

What should I do if false things are being said about me? First, ask honestly whether any of it is true, as Paul’s case shows there is often a seed. Repent of what is yours and put it right. Then, where the charge is false, say so plainly once, to those who need to hear it, without bitterness. After that, let your life answer. Peter told believers slandered by their neighbours to keep their conduct honourable, so that those who speak against them would see their good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). You will not usually talk your way back; you can sometimes live your way back, slowly, in front of witnesses. And commit your name to God, who judges justly, as Christ did when he was reviled (1 Peter 2:23).

For worship. Paul was not the first to be falsely accused of destroying Moses. The Lord Jesus came not to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them (Matthew 5:17), and he was condemned as a lawbreaker. He kept the law perfectly and then bore its curse for those who had broken it (Galatians 3:13). That is why Paul could be free from the law and still honour it.
verseByVerse.note: The rumour was false; Paul opposed circumcision only when it was treated as necessary for salvation, especially for Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plan. Specific and public. Four men in the congregation are near the end of a vow. Paul is to join them, undergo purification with them, settle their bill at the temple, and be seen doing it, for a week, in the busiest place in the Jewish world at the busiest season of the year.

Four men under a vow. These men were ending a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), something entirely foreign to most of us, so it is worth explaining. A Nazirite vow was a voluntary dedication to the LORD for a set period, and it involved three abstentions: no wine or anything from the vine, not even grapes or raisins; no razor on the head, the uncut hair being the visible sign of consecration; and no contact with a dead body, even of a parent, as strict a purity rule as the high priest’s.
