At the end, the Nazirite came to the temple and brought the prescribed offerings for each man, a male lamb as a burnt offering, a ewe lamb as a sin offering and a ram as a peace offering, with grain and drink offerings (Numbers 6:13–21); his head was shaved and the hair burned in the fire under the peace offering. The whole process was costly in time, money and public visibility, and sponsoring it was a recognised form of piety: Josephus records that King Agrippa I paid for many Nazirites to be shaved when he came to Jerusalem.

Purify yourself along with them. A man back from the lands of the nations was probably reckoned unclean, and the remedy took seven days, with sprinkling on the third day and the seventh (Numbers 19:11–13): very likely the seven days of verse 27. Paul is inside the rite himself, with a completion date lodged with the priests.

Pay their expenses. Paul is settling that bill four times over: a wealthy patron’s gesture, from the man who had held up his calloused hands at Miletus (20:34) and now spends his own money on four other men’s lambs and rams.

Not an act. Is James asking Paul to put on an act? No. The vow is evidence designed to display a true impression, and it only works because it is true. Paul had taken a vow himself at Cenchreae (18:18). His respect for the law was real, but it had been lived out far away, where Jerusalem could not see it.

The line he will not cross. When men demanded that Titus be circumcised, Paul did not yield to them even for a moment (Galatians 2:3–5). The same knife, razor or offering can be either: the difference is what the act is made to mean. If a ceremony is required for salvation or imposed on Gentiles, Paul will fight it to the death. If it is a free man’s courtesy to his own people, he will pay for it out of his own pocket. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20): this is what it looked like in practice.

Where Christians differ: was this a compromise? Some think Paul compromised the gospel here, since temple offerings point to sacrifice already fulfilled in Christ. This commentary’s view: Paul taught that the law was not the means of salvation; he did not forbid Jewish believers from keeping customs as an expression of devotion. He became a Jew to the Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). The offerings that closed a vow did include a sin offering (Numbers 6:14), and that is the hard part. But Paul did not offer them as the ground of his acceptance with God, which rested on Christ alone (Hebrews 10:14). They were the ceremonial ending of a vow, Jewish custom kept while the temple still stood, as he had circumcised Timothy for the sake of Jews who knew his family (16:3). It was an act of love for weaker brothers, not a denial of grace. That it ended in his arrest doesn’t prove it was wrong; God used it to send him to Rome.

But how could a sin offering mean anything after the cross? The answer lies in what the old sacrifices ever did. Even in Moses’ day it was impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). They were shadows and signs, given by God to point forward to the one sacrifice that would. A godly Israelite who brought a sin offering was trusting the God who had promised that sacrifice, not the animal. So a shadow kept after the substance has come adds nothing to Christ’s work and takes nothing from it, as long as no one trusts it. Paul knew that his sins had been carried away once for all at the cross. While the temple still stood, he could take part in its customs for the sake of his brothers, as a man might keep an old family custom whose meaning has been fulfilled. What he could never do was rely on it, and he did not.
verseByVerse.note: These men were ending a Nazirite vow, which required costly offerings; paying for them was a recognised act of piety.

parallels.desc: the offerings when the days of separation are complete

verseByVerse.quote: "But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality." Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for the Gentiles. In the middle of asking a Jewish apostle to keep a Jewish vow, James interrupts himself to say, unprompted, that none of this touches the Gentiles. The agreement of chapter 15 stands.

A document still on file. This is the third statement of the Jerusalem decree. In the council debate James listed idols, sexual immorality, what has been strangled, and blood (15:20); the letter put them in a different order (15:29); and here, years later, James quotes the letter, in exactly that order. He is citing a document: settled business, still binding. The freedom granted to the nations at Jerusalem was not a temporary concession that quietly expired; it was a judgement that held.

Saying what an action does not mean. If Paul is seen paying for sacrifices, some observer will conclude that the Gentile churches must be next. James closes off that inference in the same breath. Wise leadership says out loud, in advance, what an action does not mean, while it can still be heard.

Does that decree still bind us? Its permanent parts, avoiding idolatry and sexual immorality, are moral commands repeated throughout the New Testament (1 Corinthians 6:18; 10:14). Its food rules, about blood and strangled meat, were for love’s sake in that setting, so that Jewish and Gentile believers could share a table, and Paul later treats food offered to idols as a matter of conscience and love rather than law (1 Corinthians 8; 10:25–33).

The next day. No argument is recorded, no conditions. The man who wrote that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you (Galatians 5:2) takes four men to the temple and submits to the purification. He can do it precisely because he believes what he wrote. A ceremony that cannot save him also cannot endanger him: his standing with God rested on Christ, so the custom could neither win God’s favour nor lose it (1 Corinthians 9:19). It is free, and because it is free, he can spend it on his brothers.

Ashes and blood. The rite was very probably the purification of Numbers 19, with the ashes of a red heifer. Hebrews names that very rite and sets it beside the cross: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:13–14). The shadow touched Paul’s skin. The substance had washed his heart.

Giving notice. The plan failed completely. The vow put Paul in the temple, in public, at the one moment when Jews from Asia who knew him by sight were in the city. The advice of the wisest men in the Jerusalem church, offered in love and accepted in humility, was the immediate cause of his arrest.

Was the plan a mistake, then? Some think so, since it led to his arrest. The more likely reading is that Paul acted in good conscience to remove a false charge and keep peace with Jewish believers, and that God used even the riot to bring him to Rome, as he would soon assure him (23:11). Most of us carry a private theology that says if we take the humble course, seek counsel and pay the cost ourselves, it ought to come out right. Here it does not. James was not foolish and Paul was not weak, and the plan blew up in their faces. Yet two nights later, in a Roman barracks, the Lord stood by Paul and told him to take courage, for as he had testified in Jerusalem, so he must testify in Rome (23:11). The failed plan was the road. Wisdom is not a guarantee of outcomes; it never was. It is faithfulness in the choosing, and God takes responsibility for the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, crying out, 'Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Almost completed. Five or six days through a seven-day rite; another day or two and Paul would have walked out with his name cleared. And it is not the Jerusalem believers who end it but Jews from Asia, pilgrims from Ephesus, where some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way (19:9). They know his face and his companions’ faces. A grievance some years old, from six hundred miles away, bought a festival passage, and it is standing in the temple court when he walks past.

Stirred up the whole crowd. They do not lodge a complaint with the temple authorities standing right there. They work the crowd.

Against the people and the law and this place. False witnesses said of Stephen that he never ceased to speak words against this holy place and the law (6:13–14), and behind both lies the charge against Jesus, that he would destroy the temple (Mark 14:58). The young man minding the coats at Stephen’s death was Saul of Tarsus (7:58), and before the next chapter is over he will tell this crowd so (22:20). The charge he once helped to prosecute is now the charge against him. God is not settling a score. It is something better: the persecutor has been so joined to the people he hunted that he now stands where they stood.

He even brought Greeks into the temple. This is the clause that turns a shouting match into a death sentence. The temple mount had an outer court that anyone could enter. Inside it, around the sacred courts, ran a low stone barrier, and at its openings stood notices warning foreigners away. Two of those stones have been found, in Greek: a complete one discovered in 1871, now in Istanbul, and a fragment found in 1935. The wording is preserved: no foreigner may enter within the barrier and enclosure around the sanctuary, and whoever is caught will have himself to blame for the death that follows. Josephus records that Rome, which jealously kept the power of execution to itself, allowed the Jews this one exception, even against a Roman citizen. So this is not an insult. It is a capital charge, shouted in a crowded court, and everyone who hears it knows that this trespass carries death. That is why the chapter goes from accusation to attempted murder inside two verses.

The wall that was already down. Out of the imprisonment that begins here comes a letter to Ephesus, the accusers’ city, which says that Christ has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility, and that Gentiles are no longer strangers and aliens but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:14, 19). The wall the mob was defending had already been demolished by the cross, and the letter announcing it was written from the chain their shouting produced. The mob was right that God is holy and the unclean cannot stroll into his presence. They were wrong about where the uncleanness lay. What keeps any of us out is sin, not birth, and it is taken away by the blood of Jesus, which alone gives us confidence to enter the holy places (Hebrews 10:19).

Why did God put up the wall in the first place? Strictly, the stone barrier of Herod’s temple was a later Jewish arrangement, but it expressed something God had built into the old covenant: a holy God dwelling among a sinful people, with courts and curtains marking how far each could come. Those boundaries taught that sinners cannot simply walk into the presence of God. They were never meant to be permanent. From the beginning God promised that all nations would be blessed through Abraham’s offspring (Genesis 12:3), and that his house would be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7). The wall kept the distance visible until the one came who could close it.

On a Tuesday. Ask whether you still keep any walls in your heart that Christ has torn down: a kind of Christian you would rather not sit beside. And if you feel like the outsider, hear Ephesians 2 as addressed to you. You are not a guest in God’s house. You are family.

For worship. Christ broke the wall down in his flesh: Paul’s phrase, and a violent one. It was taken into a body and killed there, so that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two. Every Gentile who has drawn near to God has come in through a torn body. And the stone with its warning sits in a museum under glass, out of work for nearly two thousand years.
verseByVerse.note: Inscriptions have been found from the temple’s barrier, warning Gentiles not to go beyond it on pain of death.

parallels.desc: the dividing wall of hostility

verseByVerse.quote: "For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They supposed. Luke shows, step by step, how the charge was manufactured, one of the most useful paragraphs in the New Testament for anybody on either end of an accusation. First, a true observation: they had seen Trophimus, an Ephesian delegate (20:4), with Paul in the city. Second, an inference: they supposed Paul had taken him inside. Nobody saw it, and no witness is ever produced. Third, certainty: by verse 28 the supposition is a shouted fact, and one man has become Greeks. Fourth, a crowd, and after that nothing can be undone, because a crowd cannot be shown evidence.

Sincerity is not a safeguard. These men need not be lying. They very likely believe it, defending the holiest place on earth from a defilement that never happened, and they will nearly kill an innocent man out of what they think is reverence. That is what religion becomes when it is a way of guarding ourselves rather than knowing God: zeal for his house without love for his ways. Jesus warned that whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God (John 16:2). The cure is not less reverence but the gospel, which humbles the temple zealot and the Gentile sinner at the same cross.

All the city was stirred up. Pentecost crowds, people running toward the noise with no idea what has happened, as the tribune will find them at verse 34.

The gates were shut. Partly crowd control, but very probably also this: a killing inside the sacred courts would defile them, so the man must be got outside before he is beaten to death. It is the reflex of the men who would not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, on the morning they arranged a crucifixion (John 18:28): meticulous about the floor, indifferent about the murder.

The last door. This is the last time Paul is recorded inside the temple. That building’s final act toward the apostle to the Gentiles is a door closing behind him. Within little more than a decade there would be no doors and no temple. The gospel had moved on.

How do I avoid becoming one of those who supposed? Practise saying the word. When you find yourself repeating something about somebody, stop and say out loud which part you saw and which part you supposed. It is astonishing how much of what we are certain about will not survive being spoken in that form. Then follow the rule Scripture gives the church: a charge is established by the evidence of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Timothy 5:19), and love believes the best until the facts say otherwise (1 Corinthians 13:7). Before you share, forward or post, ask whether you know it, or only assume it. Most mobs today begin with a screenshot.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were seeking to kill him. A lynching. Not threatening to kill him: seeking to. This is an execution in progress on the pavement of the outer court, carried out by hand, and the only reason it does not finish is a piece of Roman administration.

The tribune. He commanded the cohort in the Antonia Fortress, at the north-west corner of the temple platform, with stairs running down into the outer court; his title means commander of a thousand. Josephus records that at the great feasts soldiers were posted on the colonnade roofs, because festivals and riots came as a pair. The tribune is Claudius Lysias (23:26), who had bought his citizenship for a large sum (22:28). A man who had bought his way up, and God uses him to preserve the apostle to the nations.

Centurions. Plural: at least two centuries, so well over a hundred men, perhaps two hundred. And Luke says they ran: down the stairs, into the court, at speed, in armour.

They stopped beating Paul. Not when someone’s conscience woke up, or anyone remembered that no witness had been produced. They stopped when armed men appeared. That is often the way with human beings in a mass: restraint arrives from outside, or it does not arrive.

The doctrine comes down the steps. Only months before, Paul had written to Rome that the authority is God’s servant for your good, and he does not bear the sword in vain (Romans 13:4). The ink was barely dry, and now the doctrine came down the fortress steps in hobnailed boots and saved the man who wrote it.

The same sword, given from above. These soldiers served the same Roman power that had stood guard at another trial in this city some twenty-five years before. When Pilate told Jesus that he had authority to release him or to crucify him, Jesus answered that he would have no authority over him at all unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11). The Roman sword never belonged to Rome. On that Friday God allowed it to fall on his innocent Son, because the Son had come to bear the sentence his people deserved. On this afternoon the same God sent it running down the stairs to keep his servant alive. Both times, the sword moved only as far as heaven allowed.

In the flow. Again a Roman official stands between Paul and a hostile crowd, as Gallio did at Corinth (18:12–17) and the town clerk at Ephesus (19:35–41). Luke is building a case that runs to the end of the book: the authorities find in Paul nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29; 26:31).

Where was the church? Jerusalem contained tens of thousands of believers (v. 20), and not one of them appears in this paragraph. Perhaps they could have done nothing against a mob; Luke does not say, and we should not guess. But here the church is absent and the pagan garrison is everything. Sometimes the help God sends is not the help we would have chosen, does not come from the people we would have expected, and is still from God.

Should Christians thank God for the police and the courts? Yes. Paul tells us to pray for kings and all in authority, so that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Government is a gift of God’s common grace, his kindness to all people whether they believe or not, given to restrain evil in a fallen world, even when those who hold office do not know him. That does not mean every ruler is just or every act of government right: the same Rome that rescued Paul would one day execute him, and Christians must obey God rather than men when the two conflict (5:29). But where the law protects the weak and stops the mob, we should give thanks, pray for those who enforce it, and support them in doing it justly.
verseByVerse.note: The tribune commanded the cohort of Roman soldiers stationed in the Antonia Fortress, which overlooked the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two chains. Agabus’s prophecy is fulfilled (v. 11). Two chains probably means a wrist shackled to a soldier on either side. Luke has described that arrangement once before: Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains (12:6). That night an angel came, the chains fell off Peter’s hands, the iron gate opened by itself, and he walked out into the street. Nothing of the kind happens here. Paul’s chains stay on. From now to the end of Acts, Paul is a prisoner.

One loosed, one left. Two men, the same chains, the same God, opposite outcomes, and Luke reports both without a syllable of explanation. Scripture refuses to teach that faith always produces release, and equally refuses to teach that suffering is the mark of the truly spiritual. The Lord loosed one man’s chains and left the other man’s on, and both men were his.

Why does God rescue some believers and not others? Scripture does not give us his reasons in each case, but it does give us his character and his purpose. James was killed by the sword in the same chapter in which Peter was set free (12:2, 7). Hebrews 11 lists those who escaped the edge of the sword and, in the same breath, those who were sawn in two. Neither group had more faith; both are commended. God’s purpose in each life is his glory and our good, and sometimes that is served by rescue and sometimes by endurance. So if your chains have not fallen off, do not conclude that your faith is too small or that God has forgotten you. Paul’s stayed on, and through them the gospel reached Rome.

A bound man already. Follow one word backwards, because Luke has been laying a track. The verb for binding appears five times in two chapters. At Miletus Paul said he was going to Jerusalem bound in the Spirit (20:22). At Caesarea Agabus bound his own feet and hands and said the Jews would bind the owner of the belt (21:11). In the front room Paul said he was ready to be bound (21:13). Now the tribune orders him bound with two chains. The Spirit’s chain came first. By the time Rome puts iron on this man, he has been a bound man for months, and willingly. What the tribune does at the top of these steps does not make Paul a prisoner; it only confirms, in metal, a captivity Paul had already accepted from God. That is why there is no panic in him, and no sense anywhere in the rest of the book that something has gone wrong. It also explains the name he gives himself afterwards. Writing from custody he calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1, 9) and a prisoner for the Lord (Ephesians 4:1). Never once does he call himself Caesar’s prisoner. The chain changed owner the moment it was fastened. His imprisonment was an assignment from his Lord, and it would last exactly as long, and achieve exactly as much, as Christ intended (Philippians 1:12–13).

Who he was and what he had done. Arrest first, investigate second: poor justice, and here it saves a life. Those two questions open a process that runs through the Sanhedrin, two governors, a king, an appeal to Caesar and a shipwreck. A quarter of Acts is the answer to a soldier’s routine enquiry at the top of a staircase.

On a Tuesday. Name the chain you are wearing: the illness, the caring duty, the job you cannot leave, the limitation you did not choose. Then ask whose prisoner you are. If you belong to Christ, the answer is not the illness or the boss or the circumstance. It is him, and he does not waste his prisoners.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One thing, some another. Luke has written this sentence before, of the theatre at Ephesus (19:32). Two riots, two cities, one anatomy: a crowd entirely united in fury and unable to say what the charge is. Mobs have not gone out of fashion; they have moved indoors and online. The test is not how many are angry or how certain they sound, but whether any two of them, asked separately, would give the same account of what the accused actually did.

He could not learn the facts. The tribune asks for a charge, and thousands cannot produce a coherent answer. The first casualty of an outraged crowd is the truth it believes itself to be defending.

Carried by the soldiers. Into the barracks, up the steps from the temple court. Carried: lifted off his feet like a load. The press is so violent that the soldiers haul their beaten, chained prisoner above the crowd like baggage. The apostle to the Gentiles goes up the last flight with his feet off the ground, unable to help himself in any particular.

When you are carried. Some Christians will recognise that at once, because they are living in it: seasons in which you do not walk but are carried, by other people’s arms, where you did not choose, with no dignity left to protect. Luke does not treat that as a failure of faith. And the soldiers who thought they were suppressing a disturbance were carrying the word of God up a staircase; in a moment their prisoner will ask to preach.

Another beaten man on the road. Luke has written a scene like this once before. On the road out of this same city, after the scourging, the soldiers seized Simon of Cyrene and laid the cross on him, to carry it behind Jesus (Luke 23:26). The Son of God accepted the help of a stranger. He let soldiers handle him, strip him and nail him down, and he went to the bottom of human helplessness first, so that no believer would ever be carried anywhere he had not already been. The arms that held Paul on the stairs were Roman. The love that held him was Christ’s.

What if I feel helpless and humiliated, unable to do anything for myself? Then you are in good company, and you are not outside God’s care. Illness, old age, disability, a breakdown, a long hospital stay: all of them can leave a believer carried by others and stripped of dignity. Scripture never measures your worth by your independence. The Lord says to his people that even to their old age and grey hairs he will carry them; he has made, and he will bear (Isaiah 46:4). Let others help you without shame, and pray even from the stretcher. Paul’s most helpless moment was a minute from his greatest sermon in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.note: Steps led from the temple courts up into the fortress.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the mob of the people followed, crying out, 'Away with him!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Away with him. Two words in Greek. At the trial before Pilate they all cried out together, Away with this man (Luke 23:18; John 19:15). Luke has kept the cry until the last verse of the riot and set it down without comment. Paul shares his Lord’s rejection, in the same city, perhaps a few hundred yards from where Jesus was condemned.

The passion beneath the arrest. It is the fourth time in this chapter: deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles (v. 11; Luke 18:32); let the will of the Lord be done (v. 14; Luke 22:42); against the people, the law and this place (v. 28); and now the crowd’s cry.

What it does not mean. Paul is not a second saviour. Nothing he suffers atones for anybody; he is not carrying sin but a message. The likeness is family resemblance: if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). And the Lord had said it of this man on the day he called him: I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name (9:16). That promise is being kept on this staircase.

Being answered. Paul had asked for this: to know Christ and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death (Philippians 3:10). We are happy to pray the first half. We ask to be made like Jesus and are surprised at the shape the answer takes, but there is only one Jesus to be made like, and his road to glory went through a crowd exactly like this one. If we are given even a little of it, we are not being punished. We are being answered.

Does every hardship I face count as suffering for Christ? Not every hardship, but more than we think. Peter makes the distinction: suffering as a murderer or a thief or a meddler is no honour, but if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed but glorify God in that name (1 Peter 4:15–16). The mockery you receive because you will not join in, the promotion lost because you would not lie, the family coldness because you follow Christ: these are sharing in his rejection. Other troubles, sickness and loss and grief, are not persecution, but Christ is with you in them too, and he uses them to make you like himself (Romans 8:28–29). What matters is not to bring suffering on yourself by foolishness, and not to be ashamed of it when it comes for his name.

For worship. When that cry was raised against the Lord Jesus, twelve legions of angels were within call (Matthew 26:53), and he let the sentence stand. He went out of the city he had wept over, carrying the beam of his own execution, and did not open his mouth. Paul walked a road his Master had already walked to the end, with one difference: Paul was pulled out at the top of the stairs, and Christ was not, because there was nobody else who could go the whole way.

verseByVerse.quote: "As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, 'May I say something to you?' And he said, 'Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
May I say something to you? Consider where that sentence is spoken. Paul is at the top of the barracks stairs, seconds from being swallowed by a Roman fortress. He has been beaten by a mob, chained between two soldiers, and carried up the last flight because he could not walk. And he turns to the officer and asks, in courteous, educated Greek, for permission to speak. Remarkable composure.

Do you know Greek? The tribune is astonished, and his astonishment is the comedy of the scene. He had assumed he was dragging an illiterate agitator out of a temple brawl. One well-formed sentence and his whole assessment of the man collapses.

Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness? This is a real man and a recent manhunt. The historian Josephus tells the story twice: a false prophet from Egypt gathered a following in the wilderness, led them round to the Mount of Olives, and promised that at his command the walls of Jerusalem would fall so they could take the city. The governor Felix sent troops; the movement was cut to pieces; and the Egyptian himself escaped and was never caught. It had happened within the last few years, and the file was still open. So when an unidentified man is pulled out of a temple riot, the tribune reaches for the obvious hypothesis. That tells you what he thought he had in his hands, and explains the two chains. He believed he was holding a terrorist leader with followers somewhere in the hills.

Luke’s accuracy. This verse is a small window onto whether Luke can be trusted. Josephus gives two different figures for the Egyptian’s following: thirty thousand in one work, a number many think inflated, and in the other an affair in which four hundred were killed and two hundred captured. Luke reports the tribune as saying four thousand, a sober figure, and gives them a name current at the time: the Assassins, sikarioi, the dagger-men, who carried short curved blades under their cloaks and mingled with festival crowds to stab a man and disappear before he fell. Josephus describes them in these very years, though he treats them as a group distinct from the Egyptian’s followers; a Roman officer lumping rebels together is just what we might expect. That is the vocabulary of someone who knew Judea at the time. Luke’s history matches Josephus, and this is his habit everywhere: he gets the ranks right, a proconsul on Cyprus, politarchs at Thessalonica, Asiarchs at Ephesus, a town clerk, and here a tribune. Accuracy in small things does not by itself prove a resurrection, but it shows what kind of writer this is. The man who is this careful about the size of a rebel band is the same man who tells you that a tomb outside Jerusalem was empty on the third day, and he expects to be read the same way in both places.

Why should historical details like this matter to my faith? Because Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas that would be just as true if nothing had happened. It rests on events: a man who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, rose on the third day, and appeared to witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Luke tells us at the start of his Gospel that he investigated everything carefully so that his reader might have certainty (Luke 1:3–4). When he proves reliable in small things that we can check, it gives us good reason to trust him in the great things we cannot. Your faith rests finally on God’s word, which the Spirit confirms in your heart, but God has given his word in history, and where historians can check it, it stands up well.

For worship. The Lord rules over misunderstandings as surely as over storms: because the tribune had him wrong, he asked, and the conversation began that ended with permission to preach. And the true Messiah was mistaken for a rebel too. The crowd chose Barabbas, a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city (Luke 23:19), and sent the Prince of Peace to the cross in his place. The guilty rebel walked free while the innocent one died, and that exchange is the gospel Paul is about to preach.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus describes an Egyptian false prophet who led followers to the Mount of Olives a few years earlier and escaped when the Romans attacked. The “Assassins” were extremists who stabbed opponents with hidden daggers in crowds.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul replied, 'I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.' And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No obscure city. Understatement an educated Greek would hear as good manners, and true: Strabo said the people of Tarsus surpassed even Athens and Alexandria in devotion to learning. In one clause Paul tells the tribune: I am not your Egyptian, I am a Jew, and a man of standing.

What he does not say. He does not say he is a Roman citizen, the most powerful fact about him in that fortress. He will produce it in the next chapter, in one quiet question, when they stretch him out for a flogging (22:25–29). He is not asking to be rescued. He is asking for something else.

Permit me to speak to the people. Minutes ago they were beating him to death, and they are still howling at the foot of the stairs. A man with a legal trump card in his pocket, at the door of safety, uses his one request to go back out and talk to them. He had written of great sorrow and unceasing anguish in his heart for the sake of his brothers (Romans 9:1–3). He meant it, and this staircase is the proof.

What Paul could only wish. To be accursed for his brothers was a wish he could never fulfil, and he knew it; no man’s curse can save another. But there is one who did what Paul could only wish. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and he was cut off, outside the walls of this very city, for the sake of people who had rejected him. Paul’s longing on the steps is a reflection of that love. The love that made him ask to face the mob was first the love that sent his Lord to the cross for people like them, and for people like him.

Motioned with his hand. The speaker’s gesture (13:16; 26:1), except that this hand is bruised and chained to a soldier.

A great hush. Thousands who were screaming for a lynching fall silent because a beaten man lifted his hand. The Hebrew language is very probably Aramaic, the language of the street and the kitchen. He could have used Greek. He chooses their mother tongue, and they became even more quiet (22:2). The last thing he does before he tells them about Jesus is honour them.

Stand back and look. James’s plan has failed and everything Paul arranged has come apart. And he is standing above perhaps the largest Jewish crowd he has addressed in years, in total silence, with Roman permission, about to tell them how he met Jesus of Nazareth. He did not get the platform he might have asked for; he got the barracks steps. Years later he wrote the sentence that explains this chapter: what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Philippians 1:12).

How can I love people who have hurt me badly? Not by pretending the hurt did not happen, and not in your own strength. Paul’s love for this crowd came from somewhere: he had himself once been the one shouting, and Christ had loved him anyway. The more clearly you see how much you have been forgiven, the more room there is in you for those who wrong you (Luke 7:47; Ephesians 4:32). Begin by praying for them, honestly, even if the first prayers are short. Then look for one concrete good you can do or say to them, as the Lord commands (Luke 6:27–28). Love for enemies does not mean trusting the untrustworthy or staying where you are in danger. It means wanting their salvation more than your vindication.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person who has most recently hurt you, and ask what your instinct toward them is, a wall or a hearing. Then look for a chance to speak of Christ in a language they can hear.
verseByVerse.note: Tarsus was a proud and prosperous city, known for learning. The “Hebrew language” was probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea.

21.theology: The Will of God and the Path of Suffering. Acts 21 shows that knowing the will of God does not mean avoiding what it contains. Paul knows chains await him and goes anyway; his friends, who cannot change his mind, submit. Their words are not fatalism but the willing trust of people who know whose will it is. God works his purposes through suffering, not only around it: Paul’s chains will take the gospel to Rome.
21.examples:
Then: A man walking knowingly toward chains, with weeping friends who have said all they can and now can only pray.

Now: Every Christian has to learn to pray those words when the Lord’s will leads into what we would not choose: illness, loss, rejection, persecution. We pray them as followers of a Lord who first prayed, not my will, but yours, and went to the cross for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells his story in three scenes: the road to Damascus, where the risen Jesus of Nazareth stopped the persecutor; Damascus, where a devout law-keeping Jew restored his sight and called him to be baptised; and the temple, where the Lord sent him away from Jerusalem, far off to the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sovereign Grace, and a Commission Older Than the Convert

Ananias’s word for what God did to Saul is appointed (22:14), and Paul wrote later that God had set me apart before I was born (Galatians 1:15). Nothing in the account belongs to the convert: Christ sought him, struck him down, named him, and told him what he would do.

Two guards keep this from being abstract. On the timing of the new birth Scripture is reticent, and we should be too: regeneration is the Spirit’s secret work, known by its fruits (see the note at vv. 9–10). And on wash away your sins (v. 16), the sign is spoken of in the language of the thing signified; the blood of Christ does the washing, and baptism pictures and publishes it.

The chapter’s summit is what grace does with a specific, named, unforgettable sin. The man who guarded the garments at Stephen’s stoning is sent to the ends of the earth with Stephen’s message. The blood of the Righteous One proved stronger than the blood that was shed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A frightened disciple in Damascus was given the address of the man holding warrants for his arrest, and went. He knew his own name was probably on the list. He walked into that house and said two words before anything had been proved about the blind man sitting there: Brother Saul.

Now: Picture the person whose arrival in your church on Sunday would be hardest to absorb: someone with a history, and a history with you. Suppose the Lord has laid hold of them. How long before anyone says brother, and means it? The church does not decide who its family is; it recognises whom the Lord has already taken in.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.' And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 22 is Paul’s first defence, spoken to the Jerusalem crowd from the steps of the fortress. He tells his own story: a zealous Jew, trained by Gamaliel, a persecutor of the Way, until Jesus met him on the Damascus road. They listen until he says the word Gentiles, and the riot erupts again; about to be flogged, Paul claims his Roman citizenship. The chapter shows that the mission to the Gentiles came from Christ himself, the risen Lord of glory who calls himself by the name of a despised village and stops his fiercest enemy on a road to send him with mercy to the ends of the earth.

Brothers and fathers. Two words in, and he has done something the crowd will not have expected. Brothers and fathers is how Stephen began his defence before the council (7:2), and the young man holding the coats that day was Saul of Tarsus. He is opening his own trial with the dead man’s opening line, and before he finishes he will say Stephen’s name out loud (v. 20).

A defence that is a story. The word for defence is apologia, a formal answer to a charge, the word that gives us apologetics (1 Peter 3:15). And Paul’s apologia is not a rebuttal of the temple accusation, nor a legal argument, though he has a good one. He tells them what happened to him. Given one chance to speak to people who have just tried to kill him, one of the best trained minds in the early church gives his testimony.

Stephen’s first line and Stephen’s Lord. Why borrow Stephen’s opening? Because Paul now shares Stephen’s ending. Stephen saw the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (7:55–56); since then Saul has seen the same Jesus on a road at noon, and he stands on the steps to say what Stephen said: the one you crucified is alive and reigning.

Even more quiet. A Jew from Tarsus was easily suspected of having gone half Greek. Then out comes the language of the street and the kitchen (probably Aramaic, which Luke calls Hebrew), fluent and native. Their theory about the man dies in the first three syllables.

Speaking so they can hear. That courtesy cost Paul nothing and bought him twenty verses of silence from a crowd that had been beating him ten minutes earlier. The gospel does not need softening. But the man carrying it can decide whether he will make it as easy as possible to hear, or as hard.

Do I need a dramatic story to give my testimony? No. Paul’s story was dramatic, but what made it a testimony was not the drama; it was that it was true and that it pointed to Christ. A testimony is simply an honest account of what Jesus has done for you: what you were like, how he showed you your need, how you came to trust him, and what has changed. For many believers raised in Christian homes the honest story is quiet: I cannot remember a day when I did not know about Jesus, but I remember when he became mine, and I can tell you what he has been to me since. That is a real testimony, and God uses it. Keep it short, keep Christ at the centre, and keep yourself out of the spotlight.

For worship. The God who stilled this crowd stills the raging of the nations (Psalm 65:7), and he speaks to sinners where they are. He did it supremely in his Son: the eternal Word took flesh and spoke Aramaic in Galilee, so that we could hear God in a human voice. He comes near, speaks our language, and calls us by name.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s first defence, to the Jerusalem crowd.

parallels.desc: Stephen’s same opening

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am a Jew. Some twenty years after the Damascus road, before a crowd that has just accused him of apostasy, the first thing Paul says about himself is in the present tense. Then a standard rabbinic biography in three verbs: born, brought up, educated. The weight falls in the middle: raised in Jerusalem from youth (26:4), the city they are standing in. He is no outsider legislating for Jerusalem from a distance.

At the feet of Gamaliel. Literal: pupils sat on the floor before the rabbi’s seat, and Gamaliel the Elder was the most respected teacher of the age. When the council wanted the apostles dead, Gamaliel told them to leave these men alone, in case they were found opposing God (5:34–39). His own student went out with warrants. It is possible to sit at the feet of a wise man for years, honour his name, and miss the one sentence he said that mattered.

Every credential counted loss. Paul lists his qualifications to people who prize them, but he would tell the Philippians what the list was worth to him now: his strict training, his Pharisaism, his zeal, his blamelessness under the law (Philippians 3:5–6), all counted as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Philippians 3:8). Whatever went wrong in Saul of Tarsus, it was not slackness. He had every advantage religion can give, and none of it could find the Messiah. The Messiah found him.

Zealous for God. He credits them. He looks at a mob that has just tried to lynch him and says, in effect: your zeal is real, and it is for God, and I know because it was mine. He would write that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Romans 10:2), kind and devastating at once, because he had been the case study.

To the death. And he adds men and women, as Luke had said of him (8:3). A man making a real confession does not round the number down. His audience hears a list of qualifications; he means it as a charge sheet, and the gap between those readings is the whole speech.

Is sincerity enough before God? No, and Paul is the proof. He was utterly sincere, disciplined and devout, and he was fighting God. Sincerity tells us how earnestly a person holds a belief; it cannot tell us whether the belief is true. Jesus warned that the hour would come when whoever killed his disciples would think he was offering service to God (John 16:2). What saves is not the strength of our zeal but the object of our faith: Christ himself. That should humble every earnest Christian too. The safeguard is not less zeal but zeal kept open to Scripture, and a readiness to be corrected by it.

On a Tuesday. Before your next conversation with someone who opposes the faith, find one thing about them you can honestly credit, and say it.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day; students sat at their teacher’s feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "'as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole council of elders. Paul names witnesses who could contradict him. The high priest had since been replaced, but the council could confirm that such letters had been issued, by men with no reason to protect him.

Letters to the brothers. Paul still calls the Jews of Damascus brothers. And letters makes Saul something worse than a hothead. Damascus lay outside Judea, so Saul applied for warrants; somebody drafted and sealed them, and a journey of about a hundred and forty miles was funded and planned. This was not a riot. It was a filing system. Some of the worst things done to the church are done on paper, in office hours, by men who believe they are serving God.

In bonds. Saul travelled to Damascus to put chains on people, and he tells the story from inside a Roman chain: the man who set out to bind is bound.

About noon. Chapter 9 does not mention the hour; before Agrippa Paul adds that the light was brighter than the sun (26:13). At midday in Syria, whatever flashed around Saul was not dawn, heat-shimmer or a dream; naming the hour closes every ordinary explanation. Jesus had called himself the light of the world (John 8:12), and the man who believed he was defending the light of Israel met that Light on a public highway at the brightest hour of the day, and it struck him blind.

What if I cannot point to a moment like this in my own life? Then you are like most Christians. Paul’s conversion was unique because his calling was unique: he was made an apostle, a witness of the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:8). God does not promise lights from heaven to the rest of us, and the absence of one is no sign that he has not called you. Lydia’s heart was opened quietly while she listened by a river (16:14); Timothy learned the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15). The question is not how vividly you remember the beginning, but whether you trust Christ now. The same Lord who flashed around Saul shines in every believer’s heart to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And I answered, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said to me, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? As in 9:4. Take the doubled name first. When God says a name twice in Scripture it is never filler: Abraham, Abraham, with the knife raised (Genesis 22:11); Moses, Moses, at the bush (Exodus 3:4); Simon, Simon (Luke 22:31). It is the address of someone who knows the person and means to stop them where they stand. And it is the Hebrew form of the name, spoken, as Paul tells Agrippa, in the Hebrew language (26:14). The risen Lord of heaven, speaking out of a light brighter than the sun, addresses a man in his mother tongue, which is exactly what Paul is doing for this crowd as he tells the story. He learned it from the Lord.

Why are you persecuting me? The question carries a great weight of theology. Not why are you persecuting my people, or my church. Me. Jesus had been at the right hand of the Father since his ascension. Saul had never been one of his followers. And Jesus says: me. Every door Saul kicked in, every woman he dragged out, every prison sentence he arranged, was laid on the body of the Lord of glory as personally as the nails. This is the seed from which much of Paul’s theology grows. He would spend his life writing that the church is the body of Christ, that we are members of one another, that no one ever hated his own flesh but nourishes and cherishes it as Christ does the church (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 5:29–30). He did not construct that doctrine in a study. It was handed to him in one question on a road, and it cost him his sight.

Does Jesus really feel what happens to his people? Yes. He is in heaven, glorified, beyond suffering in his own body, but he is united to his people so closely that what is done to them is done to him. What does that union actually mean? Believers are joined to Christ by the Holy Spirit and by faith, as the body is joined to its head (Ephesians 1:22–23; 1 Corinthians 6:17): his life flows into them, and what touches them touches him. He said the same of the last day: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). Two things follow. If a believer in your church is being mistreated, overlooked, gossiped about or frozen out, Christ takes it personally, and he does not grade the offence by how important the person is. And if you are the one suffering, you are not suffering alone or unnoticed. Before Saul had finished his question, heaven had registered every name.

Who are you, Lord? The word can mean no more than sir, and on Saul’s lips at that instant it may have meant little more. But you cannot ask that question of that light and keep the word small. The answer will fill it up.

Jesus of Nazareth. In chapter 9 the answer is simply I am Jesus (9:5), and before Agrippa the same (26:15). Only here, to a Jerusalem crowd, does Paul add of Nazareth, the name with the sneer in it: can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46), and Nazarene was these people’s label for the sect (24:5). The despised man whom Jerusalem had crucified is the Lord of glory speaking from heaven, and he is not embarrassed by the village.

For worship. He had every right to announce himself by the titles now indisputably his. And out of that light he said: Jesus of Nazareth, the name that had been a joke. He carries the marks of the nails still, and he will answer to the name of the town they sneered at for ever. Heaven’s glory has a carpenter’s address, and the Lamb who was slain is not ashamed of a single scar.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, "What shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saw the light but did not understand. This is the verse people bring as a contradiction, and it deserves a straight answer. In chapter 9 the men heard the voice but saw no one (9:7). They saw the light, but not the Person in it, whom only Saul saw. And the Greek verb akouō can mean to hear a sound or to understand speech; Luke uses a slightly different construction in each place, and scholars weigh that differently, but the double sense of the verb is not in doubt. Stand next to someone on a phone call: you hear a voice, and not a word of what it says. Everyone on the road heard something. One man heard words.

Inside the light and hearing only weather. Several men stood in that light, close enough to lead Saul by the hand, and nothing happened to them; not one is heard of again. Nearness to revelation is not revelation. You can sit in the same pew, under the same preaching, close enough to touch someone whom God is at that moment laying hold of, and hear only a noise.

What shall I do, Lord? Then Saul speaks a sentence he had never spoken before. The question of a new disciple: total surrender. Lord: he has a new master. Here was a man who had known exactly what to do for years. He had a programme, a mandate, letters in his bag, a route, a list of names, and the backing of the highest religious court in Israel. In one question all of it is handed over. He does not ask what has happened, or whether the letters are still valid. He asks for orders.

All that is appointed. The answer is deliberately not enough: go into the city and wait. He is not given the plan: not the journeys, the letters, or Rome. God gives the next step and withholds the itinerary. Had Saul been handed his whole assignment on that road, shipwrecks and cells included, he would have received it as information. Instead he received it as obedience, one instruction at a time, from a Lord he was learning to trust.

Was Paul born again at this moment? We are not told, and we should not pretend to know what Scripture does not say. Luke tells Paul’s conversion as a connected whole: the encounter on the road, three days of blindness and prayer (9:9, 11), then Ananias, the filling with the Spirit, and baptism (9:17–18; 22:16). Regeneration is the Spirit’s secret work, known with certainty only to God; we see its fruits, not its moment. What we can see is that by verse 10 Paul calls Jesus Lord, surrenders his whole programme, asks for orders and obeys, and soon is found praying, all marks of a heart already being turned by grace. Since the new birth produces faith and repentance, it is reasonable to think the Spirit was already at work beneath that submission. What Scripture leaves unclear, the when, it more than makes up for in what it makes blazingly clear, the who. Christ sought the persecutor, struck him down, named him, and summoned him. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus seized Paul.

Could Paul’s experience have been a hallucination or a seizure? The details tell against it. A hallucination is private, but his companions saw the light and heard a sound. A seizure does not overturn a man’s deepest convictions and send him, for thirty years, through beatings and prisons to preach the faith he had tried to destroy. No argument compels a sceptic, but this one deserves an honest weighing. And Saul did not meet a vague presence. He met a particular person who named himself: Jesus of Nazareth, a man Saul had every reason to think cursed by God, since he had been hanged on a tree (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). Nothing in Saul’s mind was waiting to invent that. The best explanation of the changed man is the one he gave himself: the crucified Jesus was alive, and appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:8).
verseByVerse.note: His companions saw the light and heard a sound but could not make out the words.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brightness of that light. Led by the hand is the verb for guiding a small child or a blind beggar. He set out to bring believers back in bonds, and arrives helpless, unable to find a door. Three days without sight, food or drink, praying (9:9, 11): everything he had relied on, his learning, his warrants, his certainty, was taken off him in an afternoon, and what was left sat in the dark and prayed.

A guide to the blind, led by the hand. Paul later described the man he had been: sure that he was a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness (Romans 2:19). Jesus came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind (John 9:39), and on the Damascus road both happened to one man. Christ would send him to the nations to open their eyes (26:18), and he began that mission by closing Saul’s.

A devout man according to the law. Watch how Paul introduces Ananias to this audience. When Luke introduced the same man in chapter 9 he called him simply a disciple at Damascus (9:10). Paul, standing before a Jerusalem crowd that believes he abandoned Moses, stresses his Jewish piety rather than his discipleship, and his good name not with the church but with the synagogue, with neighbours who did not share his faith.

Same story, different rooms. Before a king in chapter 26 he leaves Ananias out altogether, because a provincial holy man means nothing to Agrippa; here he makes him the hinge, because to this crowd he means everything.

Is it dishonest to tell my story differently to different people? No, as long as everything you say is true. Paul never changed the facts. He chose, from among true things, the ones that would help a particular audience understand. We all do this: you explain your work one way to a child and another to a colleague. What would be dishonest is inventing details, hiding what you believe in order to be accepted, or telling one group what you would deny to another. Paul became all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22), but he never became a liar. Ask of every version of your testimony: is it true, and does it point to Christ?

A good name outside the church. The qualification Paul cites is not Ananias’s gifts or visions but his reputation among outsiders. An overseer must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7), Paul would write, and perhaps he learned it here: the first Christian to lay hands on him was a man whose unbelieving neighbours had nothing bad to say about him.

On a Tuesday. Ask what your unbelieving neighbours would say about you if someone asked. Ananias’s good name opened a door for the gospel; so can yours, in paying bills, keeping promises and treating people kindly.

verseByVerse.quote: "'came to me, and standing by me said to me, "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brother Saul. These (9:17) are the first words a Christian is recorded as speaking to Saul the believer. Ananias had protested that he knew how much evil this man had done to the saints (9:13–14). He knew about the letters, and his own name may well have been on them. To knock on that door was to walk into the one house in Damascus a Christian had most reason to fear.

Brother. He came anyway, and the first word was not a caution or a probation. Brother. Between Saul’s crimes and that word there is no negotiation. Ananias calls him brother because the risen Christ has claimed him. The church does not decide who its family is; it recognises whom the Lord has already taken in.

How quickly should a church trust a notorious sinner who professes faith? Welcome and trust are not the same, and Scripture gives us both. Ananias welcomed Saul at once as a brother, because the Lord had told him plainly that Saul was his chosen instrument (9:15). The Jerusalem church, without that word, was afraid of him until Barnabas vouched for him (9:26–27). Today we have no vision to tell us, so the church receives a professing believer warmly, as a brother, while positions of trust, leadership or access to the vulnerable wait for the fruit of a changed life (1 Timothy 3:6, 10). Where someone has abused others, wise safeguards are an act of love for everyone, including him. But the greeting should not wait. Say brother, and mean it.

At that very hour. The first thing Saul’s restored eyes rest on is the face of a man he had come to put in chains, calling him family. He had been blind for three days, and a good deal longer than that: a learned man who could not see the one at the centre of his own Scriptures. Both blindnesses ended in the same room, through an ordinary, obedient disciple.

For worship. Brother is the word Christ himself is not ashamed to say to us (Hebrews 2:11). He said it of people who had just deserted him, on the morning of his resurrection: go to my brothers (John 20:17). Every welcome the church gives a forgiven enemy echoes the welcome the Son of God gave us, when we were the ones with warrants against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he said, "The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of our fathers appointed you. Paul’s whole defence hangs on this phrase. Not a new God, but the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the phrase of Peter (3:13; 5:30) and Stephen (7:32). The charge is apostasy; his answer is that the God who commissioned him is the God his accusers were named after. Appointed means chosen for a task: God had set him apart before he was born (Galatians 1:15). The light at noon was God keeping an appointment made before Saul existed, which is worth knowing if your own conversion looked, from the inside, like an accident.

The Righteous One. A title for the Messiah. Peter used it in the temple (3:14), and Stephen in the sentence that got him killed: the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered (7:52). Saul was very likely there. That title may have gone into his ears from a dying man he was helping to execute, and the next time he heard it, it was given to the one who had just spoken to him from heaven. Grace is not tidy about how it gets a word into a man.

Seeing and hearing. These verbs are the foundation of Paul’s apostleship: Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? (1 Corinthians 9:1). His authority rests not on intellect or results but on having seen the risen Christ and heard him speak.

A witness to everyone. A witness in court is asked only what he saw and heard, which is why the least articulate Christian can do it. And to everyone: not a syllable about Gentiles yet. The scope is already total, said in the softest form available, and the crowd lets it go by. Soon Paul will say it in the one word they cannot bear.

Are there apostles like Paul today? Not in the sense Paul was one. An apostle in this full sense had to have seen the risen Lord and been sent by him personally (1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), and Paul calls himself the last to whom Christ appeared (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles laid the foundation of the church once, and we build on it through their writings in the New Testament (Ephesians 2:20). Missionaries and church planters are sometimes loosely called apostles, meaning sent ones, but no one today carries the authority of Peter or Paul. That is not a loss. It means the voice of the apostles still speaks, unchanged, every time we open the Bible. Ananias spoke the words of appointment, but it was the risen Lord who had chosen Paul and shown himself to him, and that is the mark no later leader can claim.
verseByVerse.note: “The Righteous One” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.' When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now why do you wait? Urgency. You have sat in this dark room for three days, Ananias is saying. That is long enough. Stop being a secret.

Wash away your sins. This sentence is often used to argue that the water itself does the saving, so it needs answering carefully. It does not say the water washes. It holds four things together, and the last clause is what the sentence hangs on: it is faith, calling on Christ, that receives forgiveness (Romans 10:13); baptism is its outward sign.

Calling on the name he came to bind. Saul had come with authority to bind all who call on the Lord’s name (9:14). Now he is told to call on that name himself, the name of Joel’s promise, that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved, which Peter applied to Jesus at Pentecost (2:21, 36). Saul goes down into the water trusting not the water but the Christ he calls on.

Where Christians differ: does baptism wash away sins? Some take this verse to teach that the water of baptism itself removes sin. Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read it this way, pointing also to Peter’s words at Pentecost (2:38) and to the statement that baptism now saves you (1 Peter 3:21). This commentary’s view: Saul had already met the risen Lord, called him Lord, and been addressed as brother before his baptism. Sins are washed away by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7; Revelation 1:5), received by faith; baptism is the God-given picture and sign of that washing (1 Peter 3:21: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the appeal to God for a good conscience). Baptism should not be delayed, but it is not the cause of forgiveness.

Let Paul interpret Paul. If anybody had reason to believe his sins went down a Damascus drain, it was Saul of Tarsus. What did he write afterwards? That Abraham received circumcision as a sign and seal of the righteousness he had by faith (Romans 4:11): the sign certifies a righteousness already given. That Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel (1 Corinthians 1:17), and that he could barely remember whom he had baptised in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14–16), which is not how anyone speaks about the thing that saves. In Cornelius’s house the Spirit fell before anyone brought water (10:44–48), and the dying thief was promised paradise that day (Luke 23:43).

The sign and the thing signified. Scripture often speaks of the sign in the language of the thing signified, because God does not mean the two to be pulled apart. A sign points beyond itself, as a wedding ring points to a marriage it did not create. Baptism pictures the washing that only the blood of Christ performs, assures the believer that it is real, and joins him publicly to the one who did the washing. Ananias is not telling Saul how to get clean. He is telling a man who has been made clean to go and say so, in water, before witnesses. And Saul believed, then was baptised: the pattern throughout Acts, and why this commentary holds to believer’s baptism. Many faithful Christians, christened as infants, see baptism as the sign given to believers and their children as circumcision was; we gladly honour them as brothers who love the same Saviour.

I believe in Christ but have never been baptised, so does it matter? Yes, it matters, though not because your salvation hangs on the water. Christ commanded his disciples to be baptised (Matthew 28:19), and every believer in Acts was baptised promptly after believing, often the same day. Baptism is the Lord’s appointed way for you to confess him publicly, to be marked as belonging to his people, and to receive the strengthening of faith he gives through it. Staying unbaptised is like keeping a wedding ring in the drawer: the marriage is real, but you are hiding it. Speak to your pastor or elders this week. For a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, baptism was the point of no return. It is meant to be that for us, too.

Praying in the temple. Then Paul moves the story somewhere his accusers will not expect. He is on trial for defiling the temple, and he tells them his commission was given to him inside that building, while he was praying. The God they think he has abandoned met him in their own house.

On a Tuesday. If you have been baptised, ask whether anything else in your following of Christ is still unannounced: a faith your colleagues have never had to notice, an obedience pending because going public would cost something. You need not wait until you can obey perfectly: the water points not to your record but to Christ, who obeyed perfectly in your place. Ananias’s question is the whole application.

For worship. Saul’s sins were not vague. He had faces in his memory, and Stephen’s blood, and he was told that the whole account could be washed: not managed, not offset by a life of service, but washed. The man who guarded the coats at a murder was made as clean as if he had never touched them, by the blood of the Righteous One. That blood has never met a stain it could not lift.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and saw him saying to me, "Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me." And I said, "Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Get out of Jerusalem quickly. A new detail: in Acts 9 the believers sent him away because of a plot (9:29–30). Luke gives the human side there; Paul gives the divine side here.

In the flow. The third scene of Paul’s story, the one he has been building toward: the mission to the Gentiles was commanded by the Lord, in Israel’s holiest place. It answers the charge that he taught everyone everywhere against this place (21:28). His mission to everyone everywhere began in this place, at prayer.

Testimony about me. The testimony is about Jesus, and its rejection is his. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). Paul is not being told he has failed as a preacher, but that the city which would not have the Lord will not have his witness either.

Lord, they themselves know. And Paul argues. He puts a case, and a good one: in Jerusalem, the man saying that Jesus rose is the man they commissioned to stop it. They have the paperwork. If that change will not persuade them, what could? The Lord says no.

A good plan refused. Paul’s reasoning is not selfish; Jerusalem is the most dangerous city on earth for him. He offers the Lord the most strategic use of his own conversion, and the answer is: get out, quickly. God’s refusal is not always a verdict on the quality of the plan. He has a larger map you are not being shown. And the refusal took Paul to Tarsus, Antioch, Galatia, Macedonia, Asia and, in the end, Rome. The whole Gentile mission flows from a no that Paul argued against, and on the barracks steps, twenty years later, he is making the same argument before the very audience the Lord said would not accept it.

Is it wrong to argue with God in prayer? Not if it is the honest pleading of a child who will still obey. Abraham pleaded for Sodom (Genesis 18:22–33), Moses argued for Israel (Exodus 32:11–14), and the psalms are full of complaint and reasoning. God invites us to bring him our reasons and our longings. What makes Paul’s prayer godly is what he does next: when the Lord answers, he goes. Arguing becomes sin when it turns into refusal, or into the sulking assumption that God owes us an explanation. Pour out your case; then say, as Paul effectively did, your will be done, and pack your bags.

The experiment, run at last. On the barracks steps Paul is making that same argument, some twenty years later, before the very audience the Lord said would not accept it, and the riot that ends the speech shows who was right.

On a Tuesday. Name before the Lord the good thing you were not permitted to do: the ministry you were suited for and not given. Then look at where his no has taken you instead, and thank him for the larger map you cannot yet see.

For worship. The Lord who said no to Paul in the temple was sending him to the nations, to us. And behind it stands the Father who once said no to his own Son’s prayer that the cup might pass, because a greater salvation was coming through the cross. He refuses us because he is bringing many sons to glory, and he knows the way.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.' And he said to me, "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen your witness. The evidence Paul offers is not his training or his zeal but the worst thing he ever did. Witness (martys) is the courtroom word used of Paul’s own calling (v. 15); the church came to use it of someone killed for his testimony because of days like this one.

Standing by and approving. Three verbs, none softened. Standing by: close enough to see it. Approving: agreeing. Watching over the garments: the smallest job at the scene, and the one he names. A man managing his guilt reaches for the version in which his part was marginal. Paul knows the man who holds the coats is in the stoning, making it easier, wanting the outcome. He never forgot it (1 Corinthians 15:9; 1 Timothy 1:13). The memory stays, but the debt has been cancelled at the cross (Colossians 2:13–14).

If God has forgiven me, why do I still remember what I did? Because forgiveness is not amnesia. God promises to remember our sins no more (Hebrews 8:12), meaning he will never hold them against us; he does not promise that we will forget. Paul remembered Stephen for the rest of his life, and the memory did not crush him. It humbled him and made him grateful: he called himself the least of the apostles, and in the same breath said, by the grace of God I am what I am (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). When the memory comes back, do not argue with it and do not wallow in it. Take it straight to the cross, and let it become a reason for praise rather than despair.

Far away to the Gentiles. At Pentecost Peter told a Jewish crowd the promise was for all who are far off (2:39), and nobody rioted, because a Jerusalem crowd hears far off and thinks of Jews in Babylon. Paul fills the same distance with the word they cannot hold. I will send you comes from the root that gives us apostle: the mission to the Gentiles was Christ’s command, given in the temple, to a man on his knees in the middle of an argument he was losing.

The mountain top. A man confesses that he held the coats at the first martyr’s death, and the answer from heaven is not a rebuke or a lesser assignment but a commission to the ends of the earth with the message he tried to strangle. Stephen died praying, Lord, do not hold this sin against them (7:60), as his Lord had prayed for the men driving the nails (Luke 23:34). The most famous answer to that dying prayer was standing at the edge of the crowd with his arms full of coats.

Is it fair that the man who helped kill Stephen was forgiven? Not if fairness means everyone getting what he deserves, because grace is by definition what nobody deserves. But it is not unjust, because Saul’s guilt was not ignored. It was laid on Christ and punished there in full (Isaiah 53:5–6), so that God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). And the objection cuts both ways. The religious person who resents mercy to the worst of sinners has usually forgotten that he needs exactly the same mercy. The person who thinks himself too far gone has just been answered: if Saul, then anyone.

On a Tuesday. If something in your past seems to disqualify you from serving Christ, bring it to him unsoftened, as Paul did, and hear what he says to forgiven sinners: go. And pray for the persecutors of the church in our own day by name, as Stephen did. You may be praying for the next Paul.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — The Roman Custody and Paul's Citizenship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the word Gentiles the crowd erupts. The tribune orders Paul to be examined by flogging, until Paul’s question about an uncondemned Roman citizen stops the whips. Next day the tribune brings him before the council to learn the real charge.
verseByVerse.theology:
Rights as Tools, Not Shields

Paul neither renounces his citizenship nor hides behind it. At Philippi he produced it only after the beating (16:37); on the barracks steps he withheld it to gain a pulpit (21:39); here he uses it seconds before a scourging that could have ended a man who must testify at Rome. The deciding question is not what will hurt least but what will serve most, and it has to be asked fresh each time.

God gave the sword to the state (Romans 13:4), and he uses it, often through officials with no interest in him: a centurion protecting his career and a tribune worried for his position do not know they are keeping the apostle alive. God’s providence does not need the cooperation of the people it employs.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Four officials in turn, Lysias, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, examined the case against Paul, and not one could name a crime (23:29; 25:18, 27).

Now: Where the church is opposed, it is worth being clear about which thing is happening.
