Sometimes Christians are rebuked for genuine wrongdoing, and the right response is repentance, not a persecution story. But when the file keeps coming back empty and the offence is the message itself, the answer is not outrage but to keep doing what the empty file says you were doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.' And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Up to this word they listened to him. They gave him a real hearing: the light, the voice, Ananias, the trance. Then one word, Gentiles, and the crowd went off like a match in a gas leak. They could accept a vision, even a converted persecutor, but not that God would send a Jew to save Gentiles without first making them Jews, as at Nazareth, when Jesus spoke of a widow of Sidon and a Syrian leper and the synagogue tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:25–29).

Grace as a possession. It is not simply racial hatred. It is a sincerely held conviction that God’s grace is a possession rather than a gift, and once you believe you hold something by right, everyone who receives it freely looks like a thief. Their own Scriptures had said it: I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6). In this very temple Simeon had called the infant Jesus a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32). This crowd is not defending the Bible against Paul. It is shouting down the book it holds.

Away with such a fellow from the earth! The cry is the one they raised at the bottom of these same steps minutes earlier (21:36), and the one Luke recorded when a Jerusalem crowd stood before Pilate and shouted, Away with this man (Luke 23:18). The servant is getting his master’s reception, in his master’s city, in his master’s words.

Cloaks and dust. Dust in the air is an old gesture of grief and rejection (Job 2:12; 2 Samuel 16:13); tearing off cloaks a gesture of horror, or a preparation for stoning (7:58). Paul has just told them he minded the garments at Stephen’s execution, and now a mob that wants him dead is throwing off its garments. Luke does not need to comment.

Could I be like this crowd? Yes, and it is a useful question to ask. It is easy to read them as monsters and move on. But every one of us has a sentence about God that we would find hard to say amen to: a truth about whom he saves, or what he has a right to do, or whom he loves, that we would rather were not so. It may be that God could save the person who wronged you, or that he loves people of a nation or party you despise, or that your own good record earns you nothing. Find yours. The sentence that makes something in you go quiet and resistant marks the place where you have decided that God belongs to you, rather than you to him. Bring it to him and ask him to change your heart.
verseByVerse.note: Throwing dust in the air and tearing off cloaks were gestures of outrage.

verseByVerse.quote: "the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, 'Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Examined by flogging. The tribune has understood nothing, so he reaches for the standard tool and seeks the truth by torture. This is not the synagogue’s thirty-nine lashes, which Paul had taken five times (2 Corinthians 11:24), but the Roman scourge: leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, the punishment that went before crucifixion, which could cripple or kill. And it is not even a sentence, only a way of getting information.

In the flow. Here the chapter turns from the crowd to the courts. From now to the end of Acts Paul speaks as a prisoner, with Roman law setting the pace, and the citizenship he is about to claim is the thread by which God will draw him to Rome (23:11; 25:11).

There is no malice in it. That is what makes it chilling. The tribune has just saved Paul’s life twice. Great cruelty is often committed this way, by ordinary people following procedure.

Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned? A calm question at the last moment, and a legal one. Two words carry it: Roman, and uncondemned (akatakritos), untried, with no verdict entered. Two crimes, then: flogging a citizen, and doing it without trial. Under the old Roman laws a citizen could not be scourged without trial, and the principle was so deeply felt that Cicero built a famous prosecution on it, declaring that to bind a Roman citizen is a crime and to flog him an outrage. Paul is not asking a favour. He is telling a Roman officer that he is about to break Roman law. Christians may use legal rights to protect themselves and the gospel (16:37).

The back that was not spared. One prisoner in this city had already felt the scourge. Pilate had Jesus flogged though he found no guilt in him (John 19:1–4), and Jesus said nothing to stop it: I gave my back to those who strike (Isaiah 50:6). Paul holds a right and uses it, lawfully. His Lord held every right in heaven and on earth and laid his back down for the whip, because he had come not to escape our punishment but to bear it.

Why did he not say this at Philippi? Because at Philippi he did not say it until afterwards. He and Silas were beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison, and only the next morning, when the magistrates wanted them quietly gone, did Paul mention that they had beaten uncondemned Roman citizens publicly (16:37). He took that beating with the card in his pocket, and out of it came a midnight hymn, an earthquake, and a jailer and his household saved. So the difference is not that Paul had learned his lesson. It is what the suffering would accomplish. At Philippi a beating served the gospel, so he took it. Here a scourging might well have killed him, and he was meant to testify in Rome. A chapter ago he held this same card on these same steps and did not play it, because what he wanted then was a pulpit, not a rescue (21:39).

So when should a Christian stand on his rights, and when should he suffer wrong? Paul’s rule seems to be: what will serve the gospel and the good of others? Jesus taught us to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:39), and Paul told the Corinthians it was better to be wronged than to drag a brother to court (1 Corinthians 6:7). Yet he also appealed to Caesar and claimed his citizenship. The difference is not between strong and weak faith. Personal insults and losses we are usually called to bear quietly. But where injustice threatens our life, our ability to serve Christ, or other people who depend on us, using lawful protection is not unspiritual. Victims of abuse, for example, should never be told that Christian meekness means staying silent; the law is God’s gift for their protection. Ask God for wisdom, and ask what will honour Christ most.
verseByVerse.note: Roman interrogation of non-citizens often used the scourge; flogging an uncondemned Roman citizen was illegal.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, 'What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.' So the tribune came and said to him, 'Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?' And he said, 'Yes.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen. The centurion knew the law. He does not argue with Paul or check his story. He goes straight to his commander. The junior officer at the whipping post knows something his commander has forgotten on a bad afternoon: that a career, and possibly a neck, is about ten seconds from ending. To flog a citizen could cost the tribune everything.

Tell me, are you a Roman citizen? And the tribune comes himself. He does not send a clerk. Falsely claiming citizenship was punishable by death, so the claim was usually believed. There were no papers to produce on a staircase; a citizen’s status was registered in the archives of his home city, and checking would take weeks or months. The empire’s law had teeth pointing both ways, and everybody knew it. A man in Paul’s position either was a citizen or was signing his own death warrant, and the tribune could see he was no fool.

And he said, Yes. One word stops a Roman cohort. Count what Paul had already absorbed while holding it in his mouth: the mob’s beating, chains, the stairs taken like freight, a post. Until now saying it would have bought him comfort and cost him a hearing.

Rights held as Christ held his. Self-denial is neither pretending you have no rights nor noisily renouncing them. It is holding them loosely enough that the question is never what may I claim but what will serve. Paul had learned that from Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6). Every lesser right in a Christian’s pocket is held in his shadow.

God’s quiet instruments. None of these men cares about the gospel; they are protecting themselves, and God uses a frightened officer’s self-preservation to keep his servant alive.

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune answered, 'I bought this citizenship for a large sum.' Paul said, 'But I am a citizen by birth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A large sum. There is a needle in that sentence, and some wounded pride: he had paid a fortune for his status, and he is looking at a battered provincial just untied from a post. Under Claudius citizenship could be bought through bribes; Dio Cassius says it became cheap as the market grew crowded. His name probably records the transaction: Claudius Lysias (23:26), Claudius taken from the emperor with his citizenship.

But I am a citizen by birth. Literally, but I was even born one: an older and more honourable claim than the tribune’s, prepared by God’s providence long before Paul was born. He does not gloat. The prisoner has the older claim, the commander bought his way in, and it is the commander who is now in legal danger.

How did people become Roman citizens? It was a prized and fairly rare status, carrying real protection: no flogging without trial, the right to a proper hearing, and the right of appeal to Caesar, which Paul will later use (25:11). It could come by birth from citizen parents, as with Paul; by purchase, often through bribery, as with the tribune; by being freed from slavery by a Roman master; or by grant of the emperor, for service to Rome, for long service in the auxiliary army, or to a family or a whole city. A man could hold it as a Jew and a citizen of Tarsus at the same time, as Paul did.

The freest man in the room. Paul in chains keeps turning out to be the freest man in every room he is dragged into: calmer than the tribune, more secure in law than the officer holding him. He learned it from his Lord, who stood bound before Pilate and told him he would have no authority over him at all unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11). If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:36).

For worship. Paul prized far more a citizenship neither bought nor inherited: our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ (Philippians 3:20). The tribune paid a large sum for his. Ours was bought not by us but for us, with Christ’s blood, by the one who became an outcast so that outcasts could be fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:19).
verseByVerse.note: Citizenship could be bought through bribes under Claudius. Paul was born a citizen, probably because his father or grandfather had been granted it.

verseByVerse.quote: "So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune also was afraid. Even chaining a citizen without trial was illegal. But the tribune still leaves Paul in custody overnight. Fear of consequences is not repentance, and it does not produce prompt justice; it produces a sleepless night and a decision in the morning.

The real reason. A thread Luke has pulled for two chapters. At the riot the tribune could not learn the facts (21:34); later he will write that Paul was charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29), and Festus will find no charge of the evils he expected (25:18). Official after official examines this case and finds no crime. That is Luke’s quiet defence of the faith: Christianity is not being convicted; it is being disliked.

All the council. The Sanhedrin, the council that condemned Jesus and Stephen. A pagan officer with no authority over their religious business orders them to convene, and they come, at the convenience of a Roman soldier trying to fill in a form correctly.

The whole way round the room. The chapter opened with Paul telling the crowd that the council could bear witness that he had walked out of their chamber with warrants (v. 5). It closes with him standing before that same body, in Roman custody, as one of the people those letters were written against, before the court that condemned his Lord, as the Lord said when he claimed him: I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name (9:16). The young man who left the council with warrants returns as the accused, and would not trade places with his younger self for anything.

What does Luke want me to learn from all these trials? That the faith you hold is innocent of the charges brought against it. Again and again in Acts, Roman officials find that Christians have broken no law; they are opposed because of the gospel itself. That should give you courage. When Christianity is mocked as harmful or hateful, you need not be ashamed; examine the charge, admit any real faults in Christians, and then stand calmly, as Paul did, knowing that the truth will bear examination. And it should give you patience. God often vindicates his people slowly, through ordinary courts and slow procedures, rather than by lightning.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

22.title: Paul's Defence Before the Crowd
22.text: <sup>1</sup>“Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.” <sup>2</sup>And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said: <sup>3</sup>“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. <sup>4</sup>I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women, <sup>5</sup>as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. <sup>6</sup>“As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me. <sup>7</sup>And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ <sup>8</sup>And I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’ <sup>9</sup>Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. <sup>10</sup>And I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do.’ <sup>11</sup>And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. <sup>12</sup>“And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there, <sup>13</sup>came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him. <sup>14</sup>And he said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; <sup>15</sup>for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. <sup>16</sup>And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’ <sup>17</sup>“When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance <sup>18</sup>and saw him saying to me, ‘Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’ <sup>19</sup>And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you. <sup>20</sup>And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ <sup>21</sup>And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’” <sup>22</sup>Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.” <sup>23</sup>And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air, <sup>24</sup>the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. <sup>25</sup>But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?” <sup>26</sup>When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.” <sup>27</sup>So the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” And he said, “Yes.” <sup>28</sup>The tribune answered, “I bought this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I am a citizen by birth.” <sup>29</sup>So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. <sup>30</sup>But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them.
22.overview:
From the steps of the Antonia Fortress Paul speaks to the crowd that has just tried to kill him. This is the second of three accounts of his conversion in Acts (9:1–19; 26:9–18), each shaped for its audience. Before a Jewish crowd, in their own language, he stresses how Jewish his story is: Gamaliel, zeal for the law, a devout Ananias, “the God of our fathers”, and a commission given in the temple itself.

The crowd listens until he says the Lord sent him to the Gentiles, and then explodes. About to be flogged, Paul claims his Roman citizenship, and the alarmed tribune summons the Sanhedrin to learn the real charge. Luke shows again that the real offence of Paul’s gospel is grace to the Gentiles, and that God uses Roman law to protect the messenger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Before the Sanhedrin and the Plot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the council Paul is struck, rebukes the high priest, and yields to a verse of the law. He names the resurrection as the issue, the assembly divides, and soldiers snatch him away. That night the Lord stands by him; next morning forty men swear to kill him, and his nephew carries the warning to the tribune.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Promise That Does Not Remove the Danger

Acts 23:11 is the hinge of the second half of the book. The Lord does not promise release or comfort; he gives an assignment and guarantees its completion: you must testify also in Rome. Luke uses that must for the sufferings of the Son of Man, so Paul’s arrival in Rome is now as certain as the cross.

God ordains the end, and he ordains the means, and the means are startlingly ordinary: a boy who overhears something, an officer protecting his career, a duty roster. Paul believes the promise and at once calls a centurion. Certainty about the outcome does not make action unnecessary; it makes action possible without panic. And the instruments need not be godly or even willing: the Lord uses Claudius Lysias unimproved.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A conspiracy of more than forty men, sworn under a self-curse and endorsed by the chief priests and elders, was defeated by an unnamed young man who heard something and had the nerve to walk across a city and say it.

Now: Few of us are given a Paul-sized life; many of us are at some point given the nephew’s. You know something, or you are near enough to act, and you have about a minute to decide whether it is your business. The act looks too small to matter, and you may never be told how it turned out. Do it anyway, and ask for the courage the Spirit gives (2 Timothy 1:7). The size of the outcome has never been the measure of the obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: "And looking intently at the council, Paul said, 'Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.' And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. The council that condemned Jesus now cannot reach a verdict on his apostle, and God keeps his promise through ordinary means: a boy’s ears, a soldier’s caution, a Roman letter. At the centre stands the Lord Jesus himself, beside a bruised prisoner in the dark, saying the words that hold the rest of the book together: take courage.

And looking intently at the council. Luke’s verb, to fix the eyes and not look away, is what the council did to Stephen when they saw his face like the face of an angel (6:15), and what Stephen did when he gazed into heaven and saw the Son of Man standing (7:55). Now the man who held the coats that day stands where Stephen stood, before the same body, and it is Paul who does the gazing. Paul can look the council in the eye because he has seen the same Jesus Stephen saw. He walked out of this chamber once with letters authorising him to arrest Christians in Damascus (9:1–2; 22:5). Some of the older men in front of him may remember signing.

In all good conscience. The verb means I have conducted myself as a citizen, lived as a member of God’s people. It is a public word, from the root Paul uses when he tells the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). He is not claiming a warm inner feeling but saying that his public conduct as a member of this people will stand inspection. And he addresses them as equals: brothers, not rulers.

Is Paul claiming to be sinless? No, and he said so himself. He wrote that he was not aware of anything against himself, but that this did not acquit him, for it is the Lord who judges (1 Corinthians 4:4). That is the whole doctrine of conscience in two sentences: a clear conscience is a witness, and a witness is not a verdict. Paul knew he had persecuted the church, and called himself the foremost of sinners for it (1 Timothy 1:15), while also saying he had acted ignorantly in unbelief (1 Timothy 1:13). Not sinless, then, but sincere then, and forgiven now. His claim is that he has not been playing a double game. Before his conversion he opposed Jesus because he thought it was obedience; after it he served Jesus for the same reason. There is no stretch of his life he is hiding.

To strike him on the mouth. No charge, no evidence, no witness, no verdict, and the presiding judge orders the defendant hit in the face. Striking an accused man before trial was illegal, as it was when Jesus was struck before the same office (John 18:22). Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest from about AD 47 to 58. Josephus, no friend of Christians, records that he sent his servants to the threshing floors to seize the tithes that belonged to the ordinary priests, so that some of the poorer priests starved. When the revolt against Rome began in AD 66, Jewish rebels found him hiding in an aqueduct and killed him.

How do I know whether my conscience is really clear? A clear conscience is easy to counterfeit. It is not the same as feeling fine about yourself; anyone can feel fine with a low enough standard or a short enough memory. A conscience is only as good as what has taught it, so it must be trained by Scripture, not by your feelings or your culture (Hebrews 5:14). The practical test is Paul’s: is there anything in your life you would need to edit before it could be read aloud to the people you live and work with? Where there is, confess it to God, put right what you can, and receive his cleansing (1 John 1:9). And where your conscience still accuses you of what Christ has forgiven, remember that his blood purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14).

On a Tuesday. No one but Christ has lived a single day of perfect obedience, and because his obedience is counted as yours, you can look at your own record without dread. So take five minutes tonight and ask the Lord to show you anything you would hide from the people in the next room, and bring it to him before you sleep.
verseByVerse.note: Ananias was high priest from about AD 47 to 58; Josephus describes him as greedy and violent.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Paul said to him, 'God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?' Those who stood by said, 'Would you revile God's high priest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! The image is Ezekiel’s. Ezekiel watched builders put up a flimsy partition and then coat it with whitewash so that it looked like masonry, and God’s word to them was that the rain would come, the wall would fall, and the whitewash would go down with it (Ezekiel 13:10–15). Jesus called the Pharisees whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside and full of dead men’s bones within (Matthew 23:27). Paul’s charge is precise rather than merely rude: you sit in the robes of the office that exists to administer God’s law, and you have broken it in your first act. The whitewash is the office. Behind it nothing bears weight.

Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck? The accusation is procedural, which gives it its edge. The law forbade punishing without trial and required judges to judge righteously (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 25:1–2). The judge was breaking the law he was meant to uphold. That is graver than it sounds. Israel’s judges sat in God’s name, for the judgment is God’s (Deuteronomy 1:17), so a judge who breaks the law from the bench does not only wrong a prisoner; he profanes the seat of the holy Judge of all the earth (Genesis 18:25). And the first half, God is going to strike you, is best read as a prediction rather than a curse. Paul does not ask God to do anything. He states what is coming. And God did strike him: he was murdered some eight or nine years later.

Would you revile God’s high priest? Insulting the high priest was serious, and a bystander says so.

Where Christians differ: was Paul wrong to speak this way? Some contrast Paul’s words with Jesus, who did not revile when reviled (1 Peter 2:23). This commentary’s view: Paul’s words were true and prophetic, and his protest against injustice was right. Yet he immediately acknowledged that speaking evil of a ruler was forbidden (v. 5), showing a humble, teachable spirit. Even apostles could speak in heat. What marks Paul is not perfection, but his quick submission to Scripture when reminded.

Set beside his Lord. When Jesus was struck by an officer before the high priest, he said: if what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me? (John 18:23). That challenges the injustice without a raised voice; Paul’s answer is hotter. Only one man has ever been reviled and answered with perfect meekness and perfect truth at once. The rest of us, even apostles, have something to learn when struck.

How long did the correction take? Here is where the profit is. Everyone has flares of temper. The measure of a man is almost never whether something rises in him when he is struck in the face. It is what governs him immediately afterwards: whether a word of Scripture can stop him mid-sentence, or whether he has to be right for another twenty minutes first. Paul was stopped by one line of Exodus quoted by a bystander he had every reason to ignore.

Is it ever right for a Christian to speak sharply against injustice? Yes. The prophets did, Jesus did in Matthew 23, and Paul’s protest here was just. Silence in the face of wrongdoing, especially when the weak are being harmed, is not meekness but cowardice (Proverbs 31:8–9). But sharp words must be true, aimed at the wrong rather than the person’s humiliation, and governed by love for God’s honour rather than our own. Ask before you speak: is this true, is it necessary, and am I angry for God’s sake or for mine? And when you get the tone wrong, as Paul acknowledged he had in addressing a ruler, say so quickly, without retracting the truth.
verseByVerse.note: A whitewashed wall looks solid but hides the crumbling beneath.

parallels.desc: you shall do no injustice in court

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, "You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest. On trial for his life, struck without a charge, Paul has just delivered a stinging and accurate rebuke, and a bystander says one sentence, and he stops. He does not flatter or retract the substance; he puts himself under a verse.

Did Paul really not know? We cannot be certain, and the text does not settle it. The plain reading is a genuine apology, and there are several possible reasons he did not recognise the man. Paul had been away from Jerusalem for years, and in this period high priests were appointed and deposed often, by the Herodian kings and the Roman governors. This was an informal session called by a Roman (22:30), so the high priest may not have been robed or seated in his usual place. And Paul may have had poor eyesight, which some infer from Galatians 4:15 and 6:11. A few read the sentence as irony: I did not recognise a man acting like that as God’s high priest. We need not choose unkindly. There is no reason to doubt Paul’s honesty. What is not in doubt is what matters most: the moment he learns it is the high priest, he yields to Scripture.

For it is written. The verse is Exodus 22:28, and its shape matters: you shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people. The two halves sit in one line. Israel was taught to treat contempt for the office as close to contempt for the God who allowed it to exist, even when the officeholder is a disgrace. Paul had written under Nero that the authorities that exist have been instituted by God (Romans 13:1). He was right about Ananias, and angry, and provoked, and still a text of Scripture brought him to a full stop.

The Ruler they reviled. The verse Paul bows to has an edge no one in the room would have wanted to hear. Micah had promised that from Bethlehem would come a ruler who would shepherd God’s people Israel (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:6), and this is the court that condemned him. Luke records that the men guarding Jesus that night mocked him, beat him, blindfolded him and heaped insults on him (Luke 22:63–65), and the council then took him to Pilate. Paul bows to it for one hot word against a corrupt priest; the same line had stood over the night when Israel’s rulers handed Israel’s true Ruler to the Gentiles, and they never heard it.

How can I respect leaders who do not deserve it? By separating the office from the person, as Paul does here. Rulers, employers, church officers and parents hold their position by God’s ordering, and Scripture tells us to honour the position even when the person is unworthy (1 Peter 2:17–18). Honour does not mean pretending they are good, flattering them, or obeying them when they command sin (5:29). It means speaking about them without contempt, praying for them, using proper channels to challenge wrongdoing, and refusing to mock them, even online. You can tell the truth about a leader’s failings and still guard your tongue. Paul did both in the same breath.

parallels.desc: nor curse a ruler of your people

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, 'Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.' And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One part were Sadducees. Paul knew the seam in the council because he had been trained on one side of it. The Pharisees, whose name probably means the separated ones, were a lay renewal movement, popular with ordinary people, devoted to the written Scriptures and to the tradition of the elders, the oral law Jesus rebuked them for exalting (Mark 7:8–13). They affirmed the resurrection, angels and spirits, and God’s providence. Their besetting danger, which Jesus exposed, was legalism and pride, yet Nicodemus, Gamaliel and Paul himself were Pharisees. The Sadducees were the wealthy priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple and cooperated with Rome. They rejected the oral tradition and denied the resurrection, angels and spirits. After Jerusalem fell in AD 70 the Sadducees faded; later rabbinic Judaism descends from the Pharisees.

I am a Pharisee. True, and in the present tense, as in 22:3. Paul wrote the same to the Philippians years after his conversion: as to the law, a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5; 26:5). He thought of the gospel not as the abandonment of Israel’s hope but as its fulfilment. The Pharisees were waiting for the resurrection of the dead. Paul’s news was that it had begun.

The hope and the resurrection of the dead. Was this a shabby trick, a man setting his enemies against each other to save his skin? Two things say no. First, it is true. He is on trial because he preaches that a crucified man is alive. Take the resurrection out of the case against Paul and there is no case: no riot, no council, no chains. He said the same to Felix (24:21), to Agrippa (26:6–8), and finally to the Jewish leaders in Rome: it is because of the hope of Israel that he wears this chain (28:20). A man does not repeat a courtroom trick four times before four audiences; he repeats a conviction.

The assembly was divided. Second, it exposes the court. A court that can be split in half by one true sentence about God was hardly functioning as a court. Paul did not create the division; he revealed that the body sitting in judgment on the resurrection of Jesus could not agree whether there is any resurrection at all. And the outcome is telling: the supreme court of Israel takes up the case of Jesus Christ for the last time in Acts, and it cannot reach a verdict.

Why does the resurrection matter so much? Because everything hangs on it. If Christ has not been raised, Paul wrote, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). The resurrection is God’s public declaration that Jesus is his Son (Romans 1:4), that his death paid for sin in full (Romans 4:25), and that death itself has been beaten. Paul says Jesus was raised for our justification, and justification means God declaring a sinner righteous in his sight, not for anything in the sinner, but because Christ’s righteousness is counted to him through faith (Romans 4:5). It is also the pattern and promise of our own future: the body that is buried will be raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42). So the hope of a believer is not merely that the soul goes to heaven at death, though it does, but that on the last day Christ will raise our bodies and make all things new. That is the hope of Israel, and Paul was willing to wear a chain for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees' party stood up and contended sharply, 'We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit. Luke stops the action to explain the parties to his Gentile reader. The Sadducees seem to have held the five books of Moses as binding and rejected doctrines they could not find clearly there. A man who believes there is no resurrection and no judgment has every reason to run the temple as a family business, which, by the accounts we have, is much what they did.

Jesus answered them from Moses. At the burning bush God says, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob: present tense, centuries after all three were buried. He is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him (Luke 20:27–38; Matthew 22:31–32). On all this the Pharisees were right.

A spirit or an angel. Party loyalty overcame their hostility. They allowed that his Damascus experience might be genuine, an echo of Gamaliel’s caution (5:39). They will allow a spirit, or an angel. What nobody in that chamber says is the one word Paul actually said, which is Jesus. An angel is a safe explanation: if an angel spoke to Paul, the Pharisees were still right about everything and nothing needs to change on Monday. But if it was Jesus of Nazareth, risen and speaking, then the men who arranged his execution have a problem that no amount of correct doctrine about resurrection in general can solve.

An inch away. The most dangerous position in the chapter is not the Sadducees’. The Pharisees are an inch away and perfectly comfortable: orthodox about the resurrection, defending the apostle, generous, reasonable, and completely unconverted. It is entirely possible to hold the resurrection as a doctrine, defend it in an argument, be annoyed by people who deny it, and never once have dealt with the risen Christ himself.

If I believe all the right things, how do I know I have actually dealt with Christ? Ask whether your beliefs have brought you to him or only to agreement about him. Saving faith is not just assent to true statements; it is trusting Jesus himself, coming to him as a sinner and resting on him for salvation (John 1:12; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 14.2; the Westminster Confession 14.2). The signs are personal: you pray to him and not only about him; you are sorry for sin because it grieves him; you find that his word has authority over your choices; you love his people. If you are unsure, do not settle the question by examining your doctrine again. Go to him now and ask him to receive you. Those who come to him he does not turn away; he has said so, and he has never once gone back on his word (John 6:37). A heart troubled by this question is usually a heart he is already drawing.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and probably held the five books of Moses above the rest of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Torn to pieces. Luke’s word means to tear in two, the word used of the man who wrenched apart the chains that bound him (Mark 5:4). The tribune is afraid the Sanhedrin will physically pull him to pieces between them. This is the supreme council of Israel, traditionally seventy-one men, convened to weigh a question of God’s law, and it has to be broken up by pagan soldiers before somebody is torn apart.

Take him away by force. The verb is for snatching out of danger (8:39; 1 Thessalonians 4:17). Count the rescues: in two days the tribune has saved Paul from the temple mob (21:32), from his own flogging order (22:29), and now from the court that was supposed to try him. Every institution in Jerusalem that exists to do justice has failed in turn, and the only working authority left in the holy city is a Roman garrison commanded by a nervous officer who does not worship the God of Israel.

What institutions become. A man is safer this week in the custody of the empire that, by early tradition, will one day behead him than in the hands of those who taught him the Scriptures. That is not an argument against the Scriptures. It is a warning about what religious institutions become when they stop believing the thing they exist to guard. Both parties kept the outward forms of faith after the heart had gone out of them, which Paul calls having the appearance of godliness but denying its power (2 Timothy 3:5).

Before councils, as he said. None of this took the Lord by surprise. In Luke’s Gospel Jesus warned his disciples that they would be delivered up to synagogues and prisons and brought before kings and governors for his name’s sake, that this would be their opportunity to bear witness, that some would be put to death, and yet that not a hair of their head would perish (Luke 21:12–18). Paul is living that sentence line by line. The court that condemned Jesus cannot silence his witness before the work is done, because the Lord who foretold the hearing also set its limits.

What should I do if my church or denomination seems to be losing its way? First, examine whether it really has: is the problem the gospel itself, or only preferences and style? If the gospel is truly at stake, speak up through proper channels, pray for your leaders, and stand with others who hold to Scripture. Churches can be reformed; the Reformation itself began as a call to return to the word. If, after patient effort, a church has abandoned the gospel or will not discipline serious error, it may be right to leave quietly and join a faithful church, without bitterness. But be slow to give up on God’s people. Christ is still the head of his church, and he purifies it in his own time.

verseByVerse.quote: "The following night the Lord stood by him and said, 'Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.' When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The following night. Paul had come to Jerusalem carrying a relief fund gathered over years from Gentile churches, a gift meant to prove that the two halves of the church were one. Instead: a rumour campaign among the believers, a vow that blew up in his hands, a lynching in the temple court, chains, a whipping post escaped by seconds, and a supreme court that dissolved into a brawl. He was probably discouraged.

The voice that was waiting. And there was worse, because another voice was available to him that night. At Tyre the disciples had told him not to go up to Jerusalem (21:4). At Caesarea Agabus bound himself with Paul’s belt, and the whole company wept and begged him not to go. Every one of those warnings could now be reread as a verdict: you were told; this is your own doing. That is the night the Lord came. Not an angel; when it is an angel later in the voyage Luke says so (27:23). Here it is Jesus himself (compare 2 Timothy 4:17), and the verb means he stood over him, the way someone stands at the bedside of a man who cannot get up.

Take courage. The word is what Jesus said to the terrified disciples on the water: take heart; it is I (Matthew 14:27), and to the eleven on the last night: take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33). It is never a general encouragement to be positive. It is what the Lord says to frightened people, at close range, about himself.

Testify also in Rome. The sentence opens by looking backwards. That week, the riot, the interrupted speech, the brawl, the Lord files as witness borne. And that quietly settles the question hanging since chapter 21: was Paul wrong to come? The risen Christ’s own summary of the week is that his servant bore witness in Jerusalem. Then the promise. Luke uses must for the fixed purposes of God: the Son of Man must suffer and be raised (Luke 9:22). Paul’s arrival in Rome, his long desire (19:21; Romans 1:10–11), has been placed in the same category as the cross and the empty tomb. This promise held him through two years in prison, a storm, a shipwreck and a snakebite.

What the Lord does not promise. He does not say I will get you out of this. Every hardship ahead, the cell, the storm, the wreck, is still coming. What Paul is given is not an exemption. It is an assignment that will hold.

Does God make promises like this to me? Not this exact one; you have not been told you will preach in Rome. But every believer has promises from the same Lord that are just as fixed: that he will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5), that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6), that nothing can separate you from his love (Romans 8:38–39), and that he will raise you on the last day (John 6:40). Those promises do not tell you how next month will go. They tell you how the story ends, and that the work God has given you will not be cancelled by anything this week can do. Many Christians in a hard season ask to be told how it ends. We have been told, and it holds.

When it was day. Luke sets the two sentences side by side with nothing between them. The promise comes at night; the conspiracy is sworn at dawn. Theirs is a hunger strike for murder, sworn the morning after the Lord has said that this man will preach in Rome. The oath is already broken before it is sworn.

For worship. Consider the Lord in that room. He did not send word. He came, into a garrison cell in an occupied city, and stood over one bruised man in chains, and spoke about the future as one who owns it. He came to Elijah under the broom tree with food and sleep before any word of correction. He was tried by this same council and struck in the face in this same city. He stands by his servants still, at the hour when every human support has gone, and says what only he has the right to say: take courage.

verseByVerse.quote: "There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. They went to the chief priests and elders and said, 'We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than forty. Forty is not a mob; it is an organisation. Somebody recruited them and worked out the ambush point, and it was all done between dawn and the time the nephew overheard it.

They bound themselves by an oath. They put themselves under an anathema, a self-curse, something like may God do so to me and more also if I eat before this man is dead. They are staking their standing before God on a murder.

Did forty men really starve to death? Almost certainly not, and the reason is instructive. The rabbis allowed vows to be released if they became impossible to keep; the Mishnah’s tractate on vows discusses exactly this, and a man could go to the teachers to be freed from an oath that circumstances had made impossible. Presumably they did not starve. That tells you something about religion of that kind, the kind that swears murder before God. It can produce the zeal to swear before God that you will commit a murder, and also the legal machinery to let you off the oath when the murder does not come off. Enormous seriousness about the form; nothing underneath it.

They went to the chief priests. The assassins lay it out to the men Paul stood before the previous afternoon, as men who expect a welcome. Luke records no objection. Not one priest says this is murder. These are the custodians of the law that says you shall not murder and you shall not bear false witness, and their recorded response is silence and then cooperation.

They had welcomed such an offer before. These chief priests had welcomed a conspirator once already. Luke tells how Judas went to the chief priests and officers to discuss how he might betray Jesus, and they were glad and agreed to give him money (Luke 22:4–5). That plot put the Son of God on a cross, and even that was God’s chosen way to save the world. The men who now agree to an ambush for the servant are the institution that bought the betrayal of his Master, and they are no more in control this time than they were then.

Not the blow but the memo. The council is asked to contribute not the weapon but a letter: a perfectly ordinary official request that Paul be brought down for further questioning, accurate in form, innocent on paper, and fatal. That is how respectable people take part in evil: not the blow, but the memo; not the lie, but the phrasing that lets the lie work.

How might I be complicit in wrong without realising it? By the small things that make someone else’s wrong possible. Signing off a report you know is misleading. Wording a reference to hide what you know. Staying silent in a meeting where someone is being treated unjustly. Forwarding a rumour. Looking away from abuse because raising it would be awkward for the organisation. Scripture holds us responsible not only for what we do but for the evil we enable or excuse (Proverbs 24:11–12; Ephesians 5:11). Ask the Lord to show you any piece of paper you have signed, sentence you have worded, or silence you have kept that made something possible you would never have done with your own hands. Then put it right if you can.

parallels.desc: Saul’s rash oath

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.' Now the son of Paul's sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As though you were going to determine his case. The forms of justice are the bait for murder, and the ambush is set in the narrow streets between the fortress and the council chamber.

The son of Paul’s sister. Out of nowhere, Paul has family. This is the only mention of Paul’s immediate family in the New Testament, and it lasts seven verses. After verse 22 the young man walks out of Scripture; we do not know whether he was a believer, or how he heard the plan. Paul told the Philippians that for Christ’s sake he had suffered the loss of all things (Philippians 3:8), and we are not told what that cost him at home. Here, at least, one member of his family was willing to cross the city for him.

He told Paul. It was brave and entirely ordinary: he heard something, walked to the barracks, and said it aloud to the right person. On one side: forty sworn men, the chief priests and elders, the machinery of the Sanhedrin. On the other: one unnamed young man who overheard a conversation. The young man wins completely. The difference is not the boy. It is the sentence spoken in the barracks the night before: you must testify also in Rome. His word needed nothing more than a young man’s ears and feet.

Is God really involved in small coincidences like this? Yes. Nothing happens by chance. Scripture teaches that God governs all his creatures and all their actions, down to the fall of a sparrow and the hairs on our heads (Matthew 10:29–30; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.1; the Westminster Confession 5.1). Usually he does it not by miracles but through ordinary means: someone in a particular room at a particular hour, and then having the nerve to speak. That is what providence looks like from the inside. So when you happen to hear something, or notice something, or find yourself near enough to help, do not dismiss it as coincidence. Ask whether this is the moment God has placed you for, and act.
verseByVerse.note: This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul called one of the centurions and said, 'Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.' So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, 'Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul called one of the centurions. He has in his pocket the most extraordinary assurance any man in that building could hold. Only hours earlier the risen Lord had stood beside him in the dark and told him he would testify in Rome. He could have done nothing and called it faith. Instead he calls a centurion with a short, calm request.

God ordains the means as well as the end. This is the man who, on a sinking ship, having been told by an angel that every soul aboard would survive, saw the sailors lowering the lifeboat and told the centurion that unless these men stayed in the ship, they could not be saved (27:31). He believed the promise absolutely, and he also spoke up. A man who truly believes he cannot fail is free to be thoroughly practical, because he is no longer trying to save himself by his competence.

If God is sovereign, why should I bother taking precautions or making plans? Because the God who decides the end also decides the means, and our actions are among his means. He promised Hezekiah fifteen more years and also told him to put a fig poultice on his boil (Isaiah 38:5, 21). He has appointed that the hungry are fed through work, that the sick are healed through doctors and medicine, that sinners are saved through preaching. Trusting God means doing the wise thing and then leaving the outcome to him, without either panic or presumption. Lock your door, see your doctor, plan your budget, and pray, and you will find that faith and prudence are not rivals but friends.

Paul the prisoner. The centurion’s phrase is unintended testimony. An officer of the Roman army has just run an errand for a man in chains, and does not seem to notice anything odd about it. Paul later called himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1): not Rome’s prisoner, but Christ’s.

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately, 'What is it that you have to tell me?' And he said, 'The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Took him by the hand. Claudius Lysias commands a thousand men and has spent two days dealing with riots. A frightened young man is brought to him, and he takes him by the hand and walks him aside: a kind, almost fatherly touch. Luke’s word for the nephew allows a wide range of ages; he may have been a boy. Privately is not sentiment; it is competence, and protection. If it became known who had informed, the boy’s life would be in danger. The tribune manages the whole disclosure so that no one in the barracks can see who told what.

The report. It is brief, specific and honest: he does not claim to have seen knives. He gives the shape of the request that is coming and why it is a lie, and lets the officer draw the conclusion.

God uses him as he is. Luke is quietly setting a pagan Roman’s conduct beside that of the chief priests, a few verses after they were told about a murder and said nothing. The tribune has no interest in the God of Israel. His motives are mixed at best: he is protecting a Roman citizen he has already wrongly chained, and he knows what happens to officers who lose prisoners to lynch mobs. God uses him anyway, without improving him first, keeping the promise of Rome through a nervous officer’s self-interest and a small kindness to a frightened boy.

Does God use unbelievers to help his people? Yes, constantly, and Scripture is full of it. He used Pharaoh’s daughter to save Moses, Cyrus the Persian to send Israel home (Isaiah 45:1–4), and Roman soldiers to rescue Paul three times in two days. The kindness of unbelieving doctors, teachers, neighbours and officials is part of God’s common grace, his goodness to all people and through all people. That should make us grateful rather than suspicious toward those outside the church who do us good, and it should make us pray for them, that the God who is using them would also save them.

On a Tuesday. When someone younger, weaker or frightened comes to you with something hard to say, do what the tribune did: take them aside, make it safe for them to speak, and protect them afterwards. Above all when a child or vulnerable person tells you about abuse: believe them enough to act, report it to the proper authorities, and never hush it up to protect a church or a family’s name.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.' So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, 'Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Waiting for your consent. Every part of the machine is assembled, and the whole thing waits on one signature from one Roman officer who is about to refuse. That is the story of the plot against Paul, and in a sense of every plot against the purposes of God: enormous preparation, total commitment, and one small permission that never comes.

Against the Lord and against his Anointed. The church in Jerusalem had already prayed over plots like this. When the council threatened Peter and John, the believers quoted the second psalm, in which the kings of the earth set themselves and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against his Anointed, and they named its fulfilment: Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against the holy servant Jesus (4:25–27). The rage that fell on the Anointed now falls on his witness. And the same psalm says what heaven does about it: he who sits in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:4).

Tell no one. It is the last thing anyone says to Paul’s nephew in the Bible, and that is the end of him in the record.

What if I never see what came of my faithfulness? Then you will be in the company of most of God’s servants. The nephew never knew, unless someone told him later, that his walk across Jerusalem helped carry the gospel to Rome. Hebrews says of the faithful that they died not having received the things promised, but having seen and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). God does not owe us a report on the results of our obedience, and much of what we do for him will only be shown to us at the last day. Then the Lord will bring to light the things now hidden, and each one will receive his commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:5). Do the one thing you can do, and leave the report with him.

The plotters outplayed. The plot is known completely to the one man with power to stop it. The plotters think they are hunting; they will wait hungry for a prisoner who left under armed guard at nine in the evening, in the opposite direction. Luke never tells us what became of them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tribune sends Paul by night to Caesarea under a large escort, with a letter to the governor Felix. Felix agrees to hear the case when the accusers arrive and keeps Paul under guard in Herod’s praetorium.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Wearing a Uniform

Nothing in this section is miraculous, and that is the point. The God who opened the Philippian jail with an earthquake here uses an officer’s fear, a troop deployment and a self-serving letter.

Two guards keep this from turning into fatalism. Providence does not excuse the wickedness it employs: the chief priests who agreed to supply the pretext for a murder are guilty of it, and Luke’s silence about Lysias’s letter is not approval. And providence does not promise comfort: this chapter’s happy ending is a two-year detention under a governor hoping for a bribe. The pattern is Joseph’s: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The tribune’s letter told the governor a true story arranged to flatter its author. He moved one clause and let his superior draw a generous conclusion.

Now: Take the story you tell most often about a hard episode: why the job ended, why the friendship cooled. Every detail probably happened. Lay it beside a transcript, as Luke lays this letter beside chapter 22, and ask whether the sequence is right and whether the motive you imply is the one you had. In Christ you already have the approval that counts, so you have nothing to win by editing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he called two of the centurions and said, 'Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two hundred soldiers. Do the arithmetic, because Luke expects it: 470 soldiers to protect one prisoner from forty assassins, moving out at night to escort him some sixty miles. That is nearly half the Jerusalem garrison, in a city that has rioted twice in three days. He does it for two reasons, and Luke lets both stand. The threat is real: forty men sworn to die trying. And his own neck is on the line, because he has already wrongly chained a Roman citizen, and a dead one in his custody would finish him.

The third hour of the night. About 9 p.m. And mounts were to be provided for Paul, more than one: perhaps for changes of horse so the pace never had to drop, or for his companions.

Bring him safely to Felix. The verb means to bring through danger to safety, and Luke will use it again of every soul reaching land from the wreck (27:44; 28:1). The tribune wants his prisoner delivered alive to a governor; the Lord wants his witness delivered alive to Caesar. For one night those two intentions run on the same road, and only one of them knows the destination.

Seventy horsemen and twelve legions. When the soldiers came for Jesus in Gethsemane, Matthew tells us he said that he could appeal to his Father and at once be sent more than twelve legions of angels, and he would not, because the Scriptures had to be fulfilled (Matthew 26:53–54). The Master refused an escort from heaven so that he could be handed over. The servant is given an escort from Rome so that he can be kept for his work. Both nights were ordered by the same Father, and the servant is guarded because the Master was not.

Why does God protect some Christians so dramatically and not others? We are not always told, and we should not pretend to know. This same Lord let James be killed by the sword (12:2) and let Stephen be stoned, and, as the early church remembered, would one day let Paul be executed in Rome. What we know is that no believer dies one moment before his work is done, and none is kept alive one moment after God calls him home. Paul himself wrote that to live is Christ and to die is gain (Philippians 1:21). God’s protection in this world is real and often wonderful, but it is not the whole of his care. His deepest protection is that nothing, not even death, can separate us from his love in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour of the night was about 9 p.m. Felix, a former slave, was governor of Judea from about AD 52 to 59.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he wrote a letter to this effect: 'Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Claudius Lysias. The commander finally gets a name, very likely the name he bought with his citizenship (22:28). His Excellency is the title Luke uses for Theophilus (Luke 1:3).

The man Paul is being sent to. Felix will hold Paul for two years, so it is worth knowing who he was. Antonius Felix was a freed slave. His brother Pallas was the powerful freedman secretary of the emperor Claudius, and that connection, not merit, raised Felix to the governorship of Judea, an almost unheard-of post for a former slave. The historian Tacitus said he exercised royal power with the mind of a slave. He was cruel and corrupt. He was married to Drusilla, a Jewish princess, daughter of the Herod Agrippa who killed James (12:1–2); he had persuaded her to leave her husband for him. She will sit beside him while Paul reasons about the judgment to come (24:24–25). He would keep an innocent man in custody for two years hoping for a bribe (24:26). And it is into that man’s jurisdiction that the Lord Jesus Christ is sending his apostle, on purpose, under armed guard.

Why would God send Paul to a man like Felix? For the same reason he sent Moses to Pharaoh and Jesus ate with tax collectors: because wicked rulers need the gospel too. Felix would hear Paul speak of faith in Christ Jesus, and he would tremble (24:25). He did not repent, as far as we know, but he was given the chance, and a corrupt governor heard the truth from the one man in his province who could not be bribed. God often puts his people in front of the hardest hearts, not by accident but by appointment. If you work for, live with, or answer to someone like Felix, you may be the only clear witness to Christ they will ever meet.
verseByVerse.note: Claudius Lysias probably took the emperor’s name when he bought his citizenship.

parallels.desc: “most excellent”

verseByVerse.quote: "'This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having learned that he was a Roman citizen. Every word so far is accurate, and this clause turns the whole sentence. Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen, and implies he rescued Paul because he was a citizen. Lay the letter beside the record: he intervened because a riot was in progress (21:31–32), chained Paul, and ordered him examined under the scourge. He learned of the citizenship at the last moment, from Paul himself, tied to the post (22:25–29). He invents nothing. He simply moves one clause and lets the reader assume a motive.

An honest historian. Luke includes it and says nothing. He trusts the reader of chapter 22 to notice the seam, which is a quiet reason to trust him: a man inventing a case for Paul would hardly leave discrepancies lying about in his own evidence.

The mirror. The tribune has arranged true facts so that they flatter him, and we are fluent in this too. It is the sentence about a colleague that is technically correct, the account of why a relationship ended, or why you left a job, in which nothing is invented and the shape is still wrong. Underneath it is usually a heart that wants the approval of people more than it fears God. The gospel loosens that grip, because in Christ we already have the one approval that finally counts, and there is nothing left to win by editing (Galatians 1:10).

Is it lying if everything I say is true? It can be. Truthfulness is not only avoiding false statements; it is not deceiving. The ninth commandment forbids not only outright lies but anything that prejudices the truth, including misleading arrangement of facts and leaving out what would change the picture (Westminster Larger Catechism 145). If you intend someone to believe something false, the accuracy of each sentence does not make you honest. Ask: what will my hearer conclude from what I have said, and is that conclusion true? Christ is the truth (John 14:6), and his people are called to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), not merely to avoid technical falsehood.
verseByVerse.note: Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Questions of their law. Religious disputes, as Gallio said (18:15): that is what the empire saw. A Roman officer heard a man say his whole case turned on the resurrection of the dead and filed it as a dispute about Jewish regulations. He was looking straight at the most important claim ever made and could not see it.

Charged with nothing. A Roman official declares Paul innocent, and Luke records such verdicts repeatedly: Festus will find no charge of the evils he expected (25:18, 25), and Agrippa will say this man could have been set free (26:31–32). Paul, like Jesus, was innocent under Roman law; Luke’s Gospel has Pilate say three times that he found no guilt in him (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). Luke is building a legal case in the pages of a history, and he never once tells the reader what to conclude.

Is Christianity just a private religious matter, as the tribune thought? No. The resurrection of Jesus is either the hinge on which everything turns or it is nothing, and the one thing it cannot be is a question of religious law. If a crucified man walked out of a tomb in Jerusalem, then death has been beaten on its own ground, every grave is provisional, and the risen one holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). That makes Christ Lord of public life as well as private devotion: of work, politics, money, family and the future of the world. The world has often treated the gospel as a harmless local matter. It is the news that the King has come.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I sent him to you at once. The tribune passes the problem upwards, and puts the plot on the official record. Ordering his accusers is the hinge: it moves the venue. With one administrative sentence the trial of Paul is lifted out of Jerusalem and out of the Sanhedrin’s reach, and placed in a Roman provincial court. There, before Festus, he will do what no man could do before the Sanhedrin: appeal to Caesar (25:11). A Roman citizen’s appeal compels the state to carry him, at its own expense and under guard, to Rome.

The plot that carried him to Rome. The whole apparatus of the forty men produced exactly one result: it frightened a Roman officer into moving Paul to a court from which he could appeal to the emperor. The plot to keep Paul from Rome is the means by which Paul reaches Rome. Luke has shown this before: the scattering meant to destroy the church spread it (8:1–4). Joseph said it first: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). And Luke’s Gospel had closed with the deepest case of all, the risen Jesus asking two bewildered disciples whether it was not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory (Luke 24:26). Paul is walking his Master’s road.

Does this mean the evil done to me does not hurt, or does not matter? No. Paul would spend two years in a cell as a direct result of this letter, and it hurt. God never calls evil good, and he will judge those who do it. The comfort is not that opposition will fail to wound. It is that opposition cannot get outside God’s use of it. There is no hostile act available to your enemies that God has not already given a purpose. That allows you to grieve honestly over what has been done to you, to seek justice where it is right, and still to trust that your Father is weaving even this into good for you and glory for himself (Romans 8:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Antipatris. The logistics are the point. From Jerusalem the road drops out of the hill country through narrow passes: perfect ambush country, where cavalry is nearly useless. It comes out on to the plain at Antipatris, a town Herod the Great built and named after his father, some 35 to 40 miles from Jerusalem, and beyond it ran open, mostly Gentile country.

Letting the horsemen go on. The foot soldiers went back to a city short of troops; the cavalry took him the last 25 miles to Caesarea at speed.

The fulfilment, unfelt. The sentence spoken in a cell is being carried out by 470 men on a road in the dark, most of them tired, few if any of them praying, all of them simply doing their job. The Lord who stood beside Paul the night before is not named in these verses, and he is doing everything in them. The night march is not the gap between the promise and its fulfilment; it is the fulfilment, in progress, unfelt.

Why does God feel absent when I most need him? Feelings are not a reliable gauge of his presence. Here he was keeping his promise through every mile of road, and nothing in the scene felt holy. The psalmists knew nights when God seemed far away (Psalm 13:1; 88:14), and they kept praying into the silence. God has promised to be with his people always (Matthew 28:20), and his presence does not depend on our sense of it. When you feel nothing, hold on to what he has said, keep to the ordinary means he gives, his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of his people, and expect that one day you will look back and see that he was carrying you the whole way.
verseByVerse.note: Antipatris was about 35 miles from Jerusalem; the road beyond was safer, running through mostly Gentile country.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caesarea. On the coast, Caesarea was the Roman capital of Judea. Paul would be held here for two years (24:27), and from here he would sail for Rome. It was here, in Philip’s house, that Agabus took his belt and bound his own hands and feet (21:8–11). His words have come true in substance, though it was Roman soldiers who actually put on the chains (21:33). On the way up to Jerusalem Jesus had told the Twelve that the Son of Man would be delivered over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32). It has happened to the servant as it happened to his Lord.

They presented Paul also. Paul is now, formally and finally, out of the council’s jurisdiction. The high priest who had him struck in the mouth will next appear as a plaintiff, coming down in person with a hired advocate (24:1), and he will lose.

A real loss and a door. About twelve days earlier (24:11) Paul had walked into Jerusalem hoping to be welcomed by the church and heard by his own people. He leaves under armed guard at night, rejected by his nation. It is a real loss, and Luke does not dress it up. But the door that shut behind him in the temple (21:30) turned out to be a door he was meant to be on the other side of.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea.

verseByVerse.quote: "On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, 'I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.' And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod's praetorium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What province. Felix’s first question is not about God, or the resurrection, or even the riot. It is a check on jurisdiction: is this case legally mine? Cilicia was then attached to Syria, whose governor would hardly want a minor case from Judea, so Felix kept it. That small procedural moment decided where Paul would spend the next two years of his life.

I will give you a hearing. Roman law required the accused to face his accusers (25:16). He will hold the hearing, find nothing, and then leave Paul in custody anyway, partly to please the Jewish leaders, partly in hope of a bribe (24:26–27).

Herod’s praetorium. It was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, by the sea, now the governor’s residence. Paul was probably not in a common cell, and later Felix would order that he have some liberty and that his friends be allowed to care for him (24:23).

The governor’s house, again. This was the residence from which Pontius Pilate had ruled Judea a generation earlier. Paul is lodged in the house of the office that sentenced his Lord. He would later remind Timothy of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession (1 Timothy 6:13). Now the servant is kept under a governor’s roof to make his own confession before governors and kings.

The chapter from end to end. It opened with a man struck on the mouth; it ends with him alive in a palace by the sea, recorded as charged with nothing. And yet nothing is resolved. He is still a prisoner, well over a thousand miles from Rome, and two years are about to disappear in this palace: two years of a mission-driven man’s life with no journeys, no new churches, no visible fruit.

What do I do with long seasons of waiting? Hold both halves together, because this is where most Christian lives are actually lived. The promise is certain and the waiting is long. Paul did not waste his two years: he spoke with Felix and Drusilla about faith in Christ, received his friends, and was being prepared for Rome. Use your waiting the same way. Keep the means of grace, serve whoever is in front of you, pray for the work you cannot yet do, and refuse to call the time wasted. Those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31). Waiting is not God’s absence from your life. It is often where he does his deepest work in you.

For worship. The Lord gave his servant a sentence, not an itinerary. He knew one sentence, spoken in the dark by someone who stood beside him: take courage. On some days that is the whole visible foundation of a Christian life, and it holds, because of who said it. The Lord Jesus is faithful, and the one who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.note: Herod’s praetorium was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, used as the governor’s residence.

23.title: The Plot and the Providence
23.text: <sup>1</sup>And looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” <sup>2</sup>And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. <sup>3</sup>Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?” <sup>4</sup>Those who stood by said, “Would you revile God’s high priest?” <sup>5</sup>And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’” <sup>6</sup>Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees.
