It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” <sup>7</sup>And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. <sup>8</sup>For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. <sup>9</sup>Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?” <sup>10</sup>And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks. <sup>11</sup>The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” <sup>12</sup>When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. <sup>13</sup>There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. <sup>14</sup>They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.” <sup>15</sup>Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” <sup>16</sup>Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. <sup>17</sup>Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” <sup>18</sup>So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.” <sup>19</sup>The tribune took him by the hand, and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” <sup>20</sup>And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him. <sup>21</sup>But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” <sup>22</sup>So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.” <sup>23</sup>Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. <sup>24</sup>Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.” <sup>25</sup>And he wrote a letter to this effect: <sup>26</sup>“Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings. <sup>27</sup>This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen. <sup>28</sup>And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. <sup>29</sup>I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. <sup>30</sup>And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.” <sup>31</sup>So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. <sup>32</sup>And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. <sup>33</sup>When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him. <sup>34</sup>On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, <sup>35</sup>he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.
23.overview:
Paul stands before the Sanhedrin, the council he once served. Struck on the high priest’s order, Paul flares up and then submits to Scripture. Naming the resurrection as the real issue, he splits the council between Pharisees and Sadducees, and the tribune has to rescue him again.

That night the Lord stands by Paul and promises that he must testify in Rome. Next morning more than forty men swear to kill him, but his nephew hears of it, and the tribune sends Paul by night under heavy guard to the governor Felix at Caesarea. God keeps his promise through a boy’s ears, a centurion’s errand and a Roman army.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Flattery and four charges; a point-by-point defence; a private sermon that makes a governor tremble; and two years in prison.
verseByVerse.theology:
Almost Persuaded: the Sin of the Postponed Decision

Felix is one of the most sobering figures in Acts because nothing about him is dramatic. He understands the gospel accurately (v. 22), sends for the preacher often (v. 26), and on the first hearing it frightens him. Yet, as far as Scripture records, nothing stands between him and the kingdom except a word: later.

Scripture never treats delay as neutral ground (Hebrews 3:15; 2 Corinthians 6:2). Felix seems to have felt more at the first conversation than at any that followed: repeated hearing without submission does not keep the heart tender.

So conviction is not conversion. A frightened conscience saves nobody; what God calls for is not to be moved but to come. Grace is sovereign and free: no one comes unless the Father draws him, and whoever comes will never be cast out (John 6:37, 44). The only sane response to a conviction you can feel is to come to Christ while you feel it.

Alongside Felix stands Paul, and the contrast is the chapter’s argument. One man is free and cannot decide; the other is in chains and cheerful (v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Asked by the man who could have freed him to speak about faith in Christ Jesus, Paul chose righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, to a governor known for a court that could be bought and a wife taken from another man. He did not trim one of the three.

Now: Most of us will have something true to say to someone who holds an advantage over us. The pressure is not usually to lie but to select: to say the two things that will land well, leave out the third, and call it tact. Ask what your version leaves out, and why it is always the same one. Love tells the truth about sin and judgment, and then tells of the Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: 'Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 24 is about two kinds of delay: a corrupt man putting off God, and God, who is never late, keeping his promise to bring his servant to Rome in his own time.

After five days. Caesarea is sixty miles away, a Gentile city with a temple to Augustus on the hill. The high priest goes anyway, with elders, and hires a professional. The man who a week ago ordered Paul struck (23:2) now stands in a Roman hall as a plaintiff, because here his office counts for nothing. Tertullus was hired to present the case in Roman legal style; he may have been a Greek-speaking Jew, or a Roman.

Much peace. Tertullus begins where every trained speaker began, with flattery designed to win the judge’s goodwill before a single fact is mentioned, and it is mostly false. Felix had governed Judea for about five years, and the province had rarely been less peaceful. He crucified rebels in numbers, and his rule provoked more unrest than it ended. Josephus records that he arranged the murder of the former high priest Jonathan, who had been urging him to govern better. So the high priest of Israel sits and listens while his paid advocate thanks a murderer for the peace.

The things that make for peace. Tertullus thanks a governor for peace, on behalf of a city that had turned away the one who brings it. Luke tells how Jesus, coming down toward Jerusalem, wept over it because it did not know the things that make for peace (Luke 19:41–42). He made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). Now the high priest of that city pays a man to praise Felix for a tranquillity that never existed, while the prisoner in the dock carries the only peace Jerusalem was ever offered.

Why is flattery so dangerous? Because it is not a compliment but a transaction. It is offered because the flatterer wants something and judges that you will pay for it in goodwill. Felix took the payment. He let a delegation from a nation he had bled thank him for their tranquillity, and did not correct them. Scripture warns that a flattering mouth works ruin (Proverbs 26:28) and that a man who flatters his neighbour spreads a net for his feet (Proverbs 29:5). The deeper danger is to the one who swallows it. Every time we accept praise we know is false, we lose a little of our ability to hear the truth from anybody, including God. So give honest encouragement freely, but be suspicious of praise that is useful to the giver, and be most suspicious of the praise you most enjoy.

For worship. God cannot be flattered (Jeremiah 17:10). That is terrifying to the flatterer and the best news in the world to the sinner, because the God who cannot be bought has given freely what no one could pay for. We come with nothing, and he receives us for the sake of his Son, whose mouth had no deceit in it and who never spoke a word he did not mean.
verseByVerse.note: Tertullus was a professional advocate hired to present the case. Opening with flattery of the judge was standard courtroom style; Roman historians remember Felix’s rule as harsh and corrupt.

verseByVerse.quote: "'in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To detain you no further. Then comes the standard promise of brevity. Kindness here means clemency, the quality of a judge who does not press the law to its harshest edge.

Respectable persecution. The forty men under an oath failed. This second attempt is entirely respectable: a lawful summons, a professional advocate, a formal hearing, correct procedure, courteous language. The assassins could not lay a finger on him; the lawyers very nearly did. Persecution rarely arrives dressed as persecution; it comes as a correctly worded complaint, with everyone behaving well. And Luke lets the other side’s best speaker go first, uninterrupted. A book nervous about its case seldom does that.

We and I. Tertullus says we throughout: we accept this, we beg you, we have found this man. He is a hired speaker, in the case a matter of days, and the we is a professional’s fiction. Paul, when his turn comes, will say I: I went up to worship, I take pains, this I confess. He has no delegation behind him and no advocate beside him. Faithfulness usually has to be done in the first person singular, by someone standing up alone.

What should I do when I have to stand alone for Christ? Remember that you are not as alone as it feels. Paul had no advocate in that hall, but he had the Lord’s word from the barracks (23:11), and later he would write that at his first defence no one came to stand by him, all deserted him, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17). When you are the only one at work, in your family or in your class who will speak for Christ or refuse to join in wrong, speak calmly, speak for yourself, and do not pretend to a crowd you do not have. Then find fellowship afterwards: tell your church, ask for prayer, and let others stand with you next time.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A plague. The indictment lands, four charges expertly built. First, the man himself: not this man is troublesome, but this man is a disease. It is the language you use of something to be stamped out rather than answered: before you can do something terrible to a man, you have to stop describing him as one. And Luke’s reader has heard this opening before. At the trial of Jesus the council told Pilate, We found this man misleading our nation (Luke 23:2). Tertullus begins the same way, we have found this man, and the servant is charged in the words once used against his Master.

Stirs up riots. Second, sedition, the most serious accusation before a Roman governor. The charge is hard to answer because it is built on a true fact with a false cause attached. Riots really did follow Paul, from Pisidian Antioch to the temple days ago. Tertullus takes that pattern and reverses the arrow: trouble happens where Paul goes, so Paul makes the trouble. Whether the preacher is the arsonist or the man who turned the lights on is exactly the question the charge is built to skip.

A ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. Third, the sect. The ringleader is the man in the front rank of the line. Sect means a party, like the Pharisees (15:5); here it suggests an unlicensed splinter group. Nazarenes, a Jewish name for Christians still used in Hebrew and Arabic, appears only here in the New Testament, and it is meant as a sneer (compare 22:8).

The name heaven answers to. The sneer tells the truth, and no one in that hall knew it. The risen Lord named himself by the village from the middle of a light that outshone the noon sun (22:8), and Pilate fixed it above his cross as a taunt (John 19:19). Men still use it as an insult. He wears it as a name.

He even tried to profane the temple. Fourth, the religious charge, and false (21:28–29). It is the one charge with teeth in both legal systems, since Rome allowed the Jews to execute even a citizen for going beyond the barrier. It has also quietly shrunk: in the temple it was a flat assertion (21:28); here it is that he tried. And we seized him is a polite description: they were trying to kill him.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verses 7–8 that they would have judged him by their own law, but Lysias took him away with violence. It is probably a later addition, shifting the blame onto Lysias. The earliest and best Greek manuscripts lack it, and it looks like a scribe’s attempt to explain how Paul came to be in Roman custody. There is irony in what it says: it has Tertullus complain that Lysias snatched Paul out of their hands with great violence, when those hands were at that moment beating him and seeking to kill him (21:31–32). A scribe’s tidying accidentally records the prosecution’s view of a rescue: how dare the Romans stop us.

What should I do when Christians are called a danger to society? First, check whether there is any truth in it, and repent of it where there is: Christians have sometimes deserved criticism. Then answer calmly, with facts, as Paul is about to do. Peter told believers to keep their conduct among unbelievers honourable, so that when they speak against them as evildoers, they may see their good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). It is true that the gospel does disturb things: a quiet town gets loud when the light is turned on, because sin does not like to be seen. That is not the same as causing a riot. Do not be ashamed of disturbing darkness; be ashamed only of disturbing it unlovingly.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verse 7 a complaint that Lysias had taken Paul away by force. “Nazarenes” was a name for Jesus’ followers.

verseByVerse.quote: "'By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A verse with no number. Open an ESV at this page and you will notice that the text runs from verse 6 to verse 8. The verse numbers in our Bibles are not part of Scripture; they were added in 1551 by the printer Robert Estienne, working from a Greek text based on late manuscripts. Far older copies found since lack the words of verse 7; translators follow them but keep the old numbering. The KJV and NKJV still print the words. You meet the same thing at 8:37 and 15:34, and will again at 28:29.

Does this mean the Bible is unreliable? No, it shows the opposite. We can see where a line entered the text precisely because we have so many manuscripts, thousands of them, from many centuries and countries, more than for any other ancient book. Scholars can lay them side by side and see exactly where a copyist’s explanation crept in. Nothing in the Christian faith depends on any of these few disputed lines. And look at what the translators do with them: they print them in a footnote in your own Bible, where you can read them. A book with something to hide does not publish its own variants for the ordinary reader to check. God has preserved his word, and he has also given his church the means to see where human hands added to it.

Words that will not pass away. Behind the patient work of copyists stands the Lord’s promise that his words will not pass away (Luke 21:33). They reach us through thousands of hands, some careless and a few meddling, and the word still comes through. The church’s care with the text is not what keeps it. The Lord keeps it, and the church’s care is one of the means he uses.

By examining him yourself. This is the genuine verse 8, and it is the shrewdest sentence in the speech. Tertullus has charges and no witnesses, and Roman law required evidence. So he does what an advocate does when the evidence is thin: he hands the work to the judge. It sounds like confidence and is the opposite. And his advice was taken. Felix did examine Paul, often, over two years (v. 26). What he found out was not sedition. He got a sermon on righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come, and it frightened him into ending the interview.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews also joined in the charge. Agreement is the whole of their contribution. Luke’s word means piling on: a crowd rather than a witness list.

Consensus is not evidence. A courtroom insists on the difference; ordinary life almost never does. As far as we know, none of the men affirming this was in the temple court when Paul was seized. The people who were there, the Jews from Asia who started the riot, are not in the room, and Paul is about to say so (v. 19). Agreement feels like confirmation, when very often it only means they all heard it from the same place.

Sincerity is not innocence. These men are probably not lying the way a criminal lies; most likely believe every word, inherited from a source they never checked. A man can be entirely honest and entirely wrong, and do great damage while behaving well throughout. Paul knew that better than anyone in the room.

A chorus he once faced. Luke’s readers had seen this before. Mark tells us that when Jesus stood before the council, many bore false witness against him, and their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:56); in the end the council condemned him on his own confession that he was the Christ. His servant now meets the same chorus, and the same Lord stands with him.

How do I avoid joining in when everyone around me agrees about someone? Ask the courtroom question: who actually saw it, and where are they? If the answer is nobody, or someone who is not here, then you do not know it, however many people are nodding. Refuse to add your voice to a charge you cannot verify. Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8), and it also refuses to multiply rumours. Where there is a real concern, the right course is to go to the person, or to those with proper responsibility, not to the crowd (Matthew 18:15–17). And if you discover you have joined in unfairly in the past, put it right with the person you wronged.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: 'Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For many years you have been a judge. Felix had been in office for about five or six years. Paul’s opening is respectful without flattery, one sentence of courtesy that is true and relevant: he is glad to answer to someone who knows Jewish affairs and can actually weigh a Jewish religious dispute. There is a way to address a powerful and corrupt man that neither grovels nor postures, and it consists mostly of refusing to say anything untrue.

Cheerfully. The word means in good spirits, with a settled heart. He has been beaten, chained, nearly flogged and targeted by a murder plot, and has just heard himself called a plague. That is not temperament. The Lord had stood by him in the dark and said take courage (23:11), and a man who knows the assignment holds can afford to be cheerful in a courtroom, because the courtroom is not what decides.

Not more than twelve days. Paul starts with arithmetic, because arithmetic can be verified. Set that number against the charge of worldwide sedition: he has been in the country a week and a half, and the governor’s own staff can confirm every day of it. And the last words matter: to worship. Not to organise or agitate, but to keep a feast and bring gifts to the poor.

In the flow. This is the first of three defences before Roman rulers (25:8; 26:1–29). It answers each charge in turn, sedition (vv. 11–13), the sect (vv. 14–16) and the temple (vv. 17–19), and then brings the whole case down to the resurrection (vv. 20–21).

How should I answer someone who attacks my faith? Like Paul: calmly, respectfully and factually, with gentleness and respect, as Peter says, keeping a good conscience (1 Peter 3:15–16). Do not flatter your opponent and do not sneer at him. Begin, where you can, with something true you can honestly acknowledge. Then answer the actual charge, not a different one, with facts that can be checked. Do not be rattled if you cannot answer everything; it is fine to say you will think about it. And remember that the outcome does not rest on your performance. Your Lord has his own purposes for the conversation, and you are free to be cheerful in it.
verseByVerse.note: Felix had been in office for several years.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disputing with anyone. Paul denies the sedition charge with a list of places. He names every place where an agitator would have had to be seen agitating, and invites them to produce one person who saw it.

In the temple and in the synagogues. The list has an echo. When the high priest questioned Jesus on the night of his arrest, Jesus answered that he had spoken openly to the world, had always taught in synagogues and in the temple, had said nothing in secret, and that his hearers could be asked what he had said (John 18:20–21). An officer struck him for it. Paul makes the same plain defence. The faith that follows Jesus has nothing to whisper in a corner, because its Lord never did.

Neither can they prove. Everything in the defence rests on this. Under Roman law, the burden of proof was on the accusers, and an accuser who brought a charge he could not sustain might himself be liable. Paul is not asking for mercy; he is pointing at an empty table and asking the court to notice that nothing has been put on it.

A faith that asks to be examined. Christianity has never asked to be exempted from the question of evidence. The faith is a set of claims about things that happened in public: a man executed under a named governor, a tomb found empty, witnesses who could be questioned and were. Paul’s own summary of the resurrection appearances says that most of the five hundred were still alive and could be asked (1 Corinthians 15:6), and he wrote that within about twenty-five years of the events, while those witnesses lived.

Can a Christian always demand proof when accused? Only if he is innocent. The honest edge of this verse cuts both ways. Paul can say prove it because there is nothing to find. A Christian accused of something he has actually done may not hide behind procedure, and a church may not hide wrongdoing, especially abuse, behind lawyers, silence or a concern for reputation. The church has sometimes done exactly that and brought the name of Christ into disgrace. The right to say prove it belongs only to the one who could survive the investigation. If you are guilty, the Christian path is confession, repentance and making things right (Proverbs 28:13), not a clever defence.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This I confess. Here the defence stops being legal and becomes testimony. Confess is the verb for openly acknowledging what you believe, the word the New Testament uses for confessing Christ before men. The Way is Luke’s name for the Christian faith (9:2; 19:9, 23): not a club or a theory but a road to walk, because Jesus himself is the way to the Father (John 14:6). It is not a new religion but the fulfilment of the old. Paul is telling a Roman court, in front of the high priest of Israel, that the man in chains is the one worshipping Israel’s God rightly.

Believing everything. This answers the rumour that started all the trouble in chapter 21, that he taught Jews to forsake Moses. He believes more of the book than his accusers, not less, and the difference is not that he has subtracted anything but that he has seen it arrive. He had learned to read it as the risen Jesus taught his disciples, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets and showing them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). The Law and the Prophets have not been discarded; they have been kept.

Which these men themselves accept. The Pharisees did, at least. He grants his accusers their orthodoxy on this point instead of scoring one.

Both the just and the unjust. Then he adds the phrase nobody asked for, the only place in Acts where Paul spells out that the resurrection is not only for the righteous. It is Daniel’s vision (Daniel 12:2) and the Lord’s own teaching: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29). Why say it here, to a governor who has asked nothing about the last things? Perhaps because Felix is listening. A few verses later, in private, Paul will reason with him about the coming judgment, and Felix will be afraid. The charge laid in open court goes off later, in the governor’s conscience.

Where Christians differ: the resurrection of the unjust. Some teach that the wicked will simply cease to exist (annihilationism), or never be raised. This commentary’s view: Paul says both the just and the unjust will rise. Jesus says some to eternal life, and some to eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; John 5:29). The wicked are raised to stand before God and face conscious, eternal judgment. This is the historic Christian teaching, sobering and true. Some sincere evangelicals hold annihilationism, reading Scripture’s language of destruction as a final ending; this commentary believes that eternal punishment, set beside eternal life in the same sentence, tells against it, but we differ from them as brothers.

What will the body of the resurrection Paul hoped for be like? For believers, Scripture says it will be our own body, raised and transformed: the same person, but imperishable, glorious, powerful, and fitted for the life of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Christ will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The risen Jesus could be touched, ate fish, and still bore his wounds, so our future is not a ghostly existence but real, bodily life in a renewed creation. Until then, believers who die are with the Lord, conscious and at rest (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). The unjust will also be raised bodily, to stand before God. That is why the question is never whether you will rise, but what you will rise to.

For worship. The God of the fathers had not changed his mind or grown tired of the promise in two thousand years. He spoke to Abraham about a family and to Daniel about the dust waking, and he kept every word, and the keeping of it was a grave outside Jerusalem that could not hold what was put in it. The God of the fathers is the God of the empty tomb. The hope of Israel and the risen Christ are not two things, and no court in the world has jurisdiction over either.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, and some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "'So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I always take pains. So: because of the coming resurrection and judgment. The hope of judgment shapes how we live, and Paul knew whose judgment it is: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). Take pains is the athlete’s word, to train by discipline and repetition. Paul is describing not a placid temperament but a practice: a clear conscience is something you build, daily, by keeping the accounts short. When something goes wrong with God he deals with it; when something goes wrong with a person he deals with that too. He says toward both God and man because people try to settle the first while leaving the second standing. It is the claim that got him struck on the mouth (23:1), and the quiet foundation of his whole defence: Paul can invite investigation because he has spent more than twenty years making sure there would be nothing to find. That does not mean Paul thought himself sinless; he called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). A clear conscience means nothing is left buried: every sin brought to God is washed in the blood of Christ, which purifies the conscience (Hebrews 9:14), and every wrong done to a person is put right as far as it can be.

How do I keep short accounts with God and others? Each day, at its end, ask the Lord to show you where you have sinned, and confess it specifically, not vaguely (1 John 1:9). Then ask whether anyone needs an apology or a repair from you, and do it soon, before it hardens. Jesus said that if you remember at the altar that your brother has something against you, you should go first and be reconciled, then come and offer your gift (Matthew 5:23–24). Pay what you owe. Return what you borrowed. Correct what you said that was untrue. None of this earns God’s forgiveness, which is free in Christ. It is how a forgiven person lives, and it keeps the conscience tender instead of calloused.

Alms to my nation. The alms were the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–28). He came with gifts, not trouble: money carried across the empire by Gentile Christians to show that the church was one body and not two. This is the only time Acts mentions it.

Half a line. For Paul the collection was years of letters and personal risk (2 Corinthians 8–9); for Luke it is a subordinate clause. Much of the work that costs a Christian most is recorded nowhere, summarised by someone else in half a line, and known in full only to God. And there is a bitter irony: the mention of alms in open court may well have been the moment a thought entered Felix’s head, because two verses from the end of the chapter we learn what the governor really hoped for: that money would be given him by Paul (v. 26).

For worship. Every hidden labour of love is seen by the Lord. He is not unjust so as to overlook our work and the love we have shown for his name in serving the saints (Hebrews 6:10). And he gave more than alms: he gave himself. The Lord Jesus, rich beyond all counting, made himself poor for our sake so that his poverty might make us rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), and Paul set that truth at the heart of his appeal for this very collection.
verseByVerse.note: The alms were the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "'While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Purified in the temple. They accused him of profaning the temple: he was purified, in the middle of the very rites that prove it. They accused him of stirring up riots: there was no crowd and no tumult until his accusers created one. Paul was standing in a holy place, having completed a purification and paid the expenses of four other men’s vows (21:23–24), when men from Asia pointed at him and started shouting.

Some Jews from Asia. The sentence breaks off into the sharpest legal point of the speech. The men who actually saw the alleged offence, the Jews from Asia who assumed he had brought Trophimus past the barrier and raised the shout (21:27–29), are not in the room. Roman law expected accusers to appear in person, and abandoning a charge you had raised was itself an offence. Paul does not call them liars; if they have a case, let them come and make it. That is the confidence of a man who would rather be examined than excused.

Let them come and make it. Paul had already put this challenge to a higher court, writing to Rome: who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, and more than that was raised, and is at the right hand of God interceding for us (Romans 8:33–34). A man who has heard every charge against his soul answered by the death and intercession of Christ can say calmly to a human court: if they have anything against me, let them come.

What if someone has a complaint about me but will not say it to my face? You cannot force them, and you are not bound to answer charges that no one will own. But you can make it easy to be honest with you. Let it be known that you welcome direct correction, and when you hear second-hand that someone is unhappy, go to them gently and ask whether you have wronged them (Matthew 5:23–24). If they will not speak, commit the matter to God and keep your conscience clear. And refuse to treat anonymous accusations against others as established, especially in church. Scripture requires charges to be brought openly, on the evidence of witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Timothy 5:19), and a church that acts on whispers will soon be ruled by them.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law expected accusers to appear in person.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: "It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What wrongdoing they found. Paul turns to the men who are present: you were at the council a week ago; tell the governor what crime you established. It is a safe dare: the council collapsed into a brawl and never reached a finding.

This one thing. Paul keeps bringing the resurrection back to the centre, and this settles a question about the council: was it a manoeuvre? A week later, before a governor who cannot be split, with nothing to gain by it, he repeats it as the one accurate summary of the whole case. A trick is used once and dropped; Paul says it again and again (26:6–8; 28:20).

The charge sheet reduced to one sentence. Paul has answered each charge and reduced the case to one question, a theological one, not a crime: are the dead raised? Paul is right, and Felix knows it, which is exactly why the next thing that happens is not a verdict.

Why is the resurrection, and not something else, the heart of the matter? Because it is God’s verdict on Jesus. The cross by itself might have been the death of one more good man. The resurrection declares that the man who died was the Son of God (Romans 1:4), that the sacrifice was accepted and our justification secured (Romans 4:25), and that he now reigns as Lord and Judge, for God has given assurance of this to all by raising him from the dead (17:31). Justification means God’s verdict that a guilty sinner is right with him, not because of anything in the sinner but because Christ’s righteousness is counted to everyone who trusts him. Every other Christian truth rests on it. That is why apologetics in Acts keeps coming back to the empty tomb, and why your faith can too. When you are unsure what to say, say this: Jesus rose from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, 'When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.' Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rather accurate knowledge of the Way. Felix understood the Christian movement better than the people arguing before him. Perhaps from his Jewish wife, or from Christians in Caesarea, he seems to have known that the Nazarenes were not insurrectionists and that Paul was innocent. And he did nothing.

Put them off. He does not convict Paul, because he cannot. He does not release him, because that would cost him with the Jewish leaders. So he finds a third option, one of the most recognisable moves in human affairs: he asks for more information. It sounds like diligence. Lysias never came, as far as we know, and there is no sign that anyone sent for him. The adjournment was not a step toward a verdict but a substitute for one.

The sin that does not look like sin. This is the sin of the chapter. Felix is scrupulously reasonable. He simply declines to act on what he already knows, and dresses the refusal in procedure, and because the procedure is real, nobody can accuse him of anything. We are more likely to fail this way than any other: not by deciding against the truth, but by finding a legitimate reason to postpone deciding for it. He just never got round to it, on purpose, for two years.

Another governor who knew. Luke’s reader has met this kind of judge before. Pilate examined Jesus, found no guilt in him and said so, and yet, when the crowd pressed him, he released the man they asked for and delivered Jesus over to their will (Luke 23:22–25). Felix knows the Way, knows the charges are empty, and leaves Paul in chains to please the same leaders. The servant is treated as his Lord was, by the same kind of man, for the same reason.

Some liberty. The word means a loosening of the conditions. Prisoners relied on friends for food and care, and Luke and others probably visited. The two years were not blank, and the God who gave a discouraged prisoner an open door and perhaps a doctor for company was doing something, even while the governor was doing nothing.

Is it wrong to want more information before making a big decision? No; wisdom often requires it, and Scripture commends the one who hears before he answers (Proverbs 18:13). The question is whether you are gathering information in order to decide, or in order not to. Felix already knew enough. When you notice that the facts are clear and you are still asking for more, that the right course is plain and you are still consulting, ask honestly what you are afraid it will cost you. Then name the cost before God, and decide. This applies above all to the call of Christ himself. You do not need one more argument to believe him. You need to stop postponing.

For worship. Our God has never once put off what he knows to be right. He spoke, and it came to be; he promised, and he performed. Felix put off the truth for a convenient season. The Lord of the Way is never early, never late, and never slow.

verseByVerse.quote: "After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drusilla. Luke names her, and the name carries a history that makes the next verses almost unbearable. Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, the king who killed James with the sword and was struck down in this very city for accepting the shout that he was a god (12:1–23). Her brother was Agrippa II and her sister Bernice, and both will walk into this same palace in the next chapter to hear this same prisoner. She was now about twenty. She had been married to Azizus, king of Emesa, and Josephus records that Felix, wanting her, used a Cypriot magician to persuade her to leave her husband and marry the governor instead.

Righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment. They sent for the prisoner perhaps out of curiosity, and few sermons in Acts are more precisely aimed. Righteousness is both the character God requires and the justice a judge is meant to give: preached to a corrupt, unjust governor who was at that moment hoping the defendant would offer him a bribe (v. 26). Self-control, mastery of one’s appetites: preached to a couple in an adulterous marriage, with the woman he had taken from another man sitting at his side. The coming judgment: preached to a man who judged others and had never seriously considered being judged. Paul preaches to Felix’s life, not just his mind.

Faith in Christ Jesus, preached as judgment. Felix asked about faith in Christ Jesus, and Paul answered with righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come. That is not a change of subject, for each of the three leads to Christ. The righteousness God requires is found in no governor and no prisoner, only in Christ, whose righteousness is given to those who believe (Philippians 3:9). Self-control is beyond a slave of appetite until the Son sets him free. And the judgment belongs to Christ: the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). The prisoner in front of Felix was telling him the name of his Judge, and offering him that Judge as his Saviour. And faith in Christ is more than knowing about him, which Felix already did (v. 22). It is trusting him, leaning your whole weight on him for pardon, the way a drowning man takes hold of the rope thrown to him.

Why did Paul begin with judgment, not with good news? He was asked to explain faith in Christ Jesus, and this is how he did it. It is not how most of us would begin with a governor. But it is how the New Testament habitually begins with the comfortable and the powerful: with God’s standard, our failure to meet it, and the day it will be assessed. There is no good news in a pardon until there is bad news in a verdict. A man who does not know he is condemned will not value a Saviour. That does not mean every conversation must start with hell; Paul began differently in Athens (17:22–31). It means that the gospel always includes the truth about sin and judgment, and that loving people means telling them, gently and plainly, before it is too late.

Is it not manipulative to frighten people with judgment? Only if the judgment were invented to control them. But Paul gains nothing by frightening Felix; he is the one in chains, and his honesty will cost him two more years of them. A watchman who blows the trumpet when he sees the sword coming is not manipulating the city; he would be guilty if he kept quiet (Ezekiel 33:6). Fear of a real danger is the right response to it, and Jesus himself warned his friends plainly whom to fear (Luke 12:4–5). What would be manipulative is to frighten people and then sell them something. Paul offered Felix nothing to buy. He pointed him to a Saviour who gives himself freely to anyone who comes.

Felix was alarmed. The word means filled with fear. This is not irritation or intellectual disagreement. The governor, in his own palace, became frightened. No sign was given. A prisoner talked, and the word of God found the conscience of a man who had buried it, and he could not sit still under it. This is the work Jesus said the Spirit would do in the world, convicting it concerning sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8), and Paul’s three subjects closely match the Lord’s three words. What frightened Felix was the holy God behind the prisoner’s words.

Go away for the present. A convenient time, as older translations put it: few words spoken to the gospel are more dangerous. He was genuinely under conviction, and he postponed, and as far as Scripture records, the convenient time never came. The Bible’s word is always now: today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Hebrews 3:15); now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

What should I do if I feel convicted but not ready? Do not wait to feel ready; you never will. Conviction is God’s mercy, the Spirit showing you your need of Christ, and it is meant to drive you to him now, not to be managed until it fades. You do not have to understand everything or fix your life first. Come to Christ as you are: confess your sin to him, ask him to forgive you for his death’s sake, and trust his own promise that he will never cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37). Then take the next step he shows you: talk to a pastor or a Christian friend, open the Bible, begin to obey. The only wrong response is Felix’s: later.
verseByVerse.note: Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I; she had left her first husband to marry Felix.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He hoped that money would be given him. Luke gives the real reason, and it is squalid. Taking bribes for releasing prisoners was illegal but common, and Felix had reason to think it possible: he had heard Paul mention in court that he had come bringing alms for his nation (v. 17), and perhaps thought Paul had wealthy friends. Paul never paid. A payment would have been easy, arguably even reasonable, with two years of his life on the other side of the scale. There are things a servant of Christ cannot buy his way out of without ceasing to be one.

He sent for him often. Many conversations, no conversion. Felix heard the gospel repeatedly, over two years, from one of its ablest explainers, and it did him no good, because he was never listening for the answer; he was listening for an opening. Hearing without heeding hardens. Felix did not reject the gospel once and walk away; he kept coming back, interested, curious, even entertained, and each conversation left him a little less able to feel the fear he had felt the first time. It is possible to attend church for forty years the way Felix attended these conversations.

Can I have heard the gospel too many times? You can have heard it many times without obeying it, and that is a dangerous place to be, because the heart grows used to what it resists (Hebrews 3:13). But as long as you still care about the question, the door is open. The cure for familiarity is not to stop listening but to start obeying: to stop treating sermons as interesting and to ask, each time, what God is telling you to do, and then do it. If you have grown up hearing the gospel and it has never moved you, pray honestly for a new heart, which God alone can give (Ezekiel 36:26). He delights to answer that prayer.

When two years had elapsed. Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in office about two years later. Felix was recalled to Rome after violent clashes in Caesarea between Jews and Gentiles, which he had put down brutally. Two years, and Luke gives it a clause: after the promise of Rome (23:11), no trial, no verdict, no release. One of the most fruitful missionaries in history, with churches round the Aegean needing him and a promise from the Lord in his pocket, sat in a provincial palace while a corrupt official waited for an envelope that never came.

Felix left Paul in prison. On his way out of office, with no case to answer, he chose one last time to keep an innocent man in custody as a parting gift to people he had spent years mistreating. It did not work. Josephus records that the Jewish leaders of Caesarea went to Rome to accuse him anyway, and that he escaped punishment only through his brother Pallas’s influence at court. He sold his integrity, and did not even get the price.

Why does God let his people wait so long? These two years are in the Bible for everyone who has been given a word from God and then handed a long stretch of nothing. The honest question is not whether God keeps his promises but what they feel like from inside the waiting. Paul did not know he had two years. He only knew he had today, and then another one. And the promise had not weakened by a syllable. Delay is not decay. God is not slower than his word (2 Peter 3:9), and a promise sitting apparently idle is not going stale. It is being carried by someone who does not need to hurry and never forgets. What looked from the cell like silence was the Lord of history arranging a governor’s recall, a successor’s ambition, an appeal to Caesar, and a ship. These years were not wasted: perhaps Luke wrote his Gospel; certainly Paul prayed; and God was keeping him safe for Rome.

For worship. Our God is never in a hurry and never late. He let Joseph sit in an Egyptian prison for years, forgotten by the cupbearer, until the day he was raised to save his family. He let his Son lie in the tomb until the third day, not a moment longer. Every hour of Paul’s two years was in his hand, and so is every hour of ours, and at the end of the waiting there is always a ship, and Rome, and the face of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in 62. Paul had been in custody at Caesarea for two years.

24.title: Paul Before Felix
24.text: <sup>1</sup>And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. <sup>2</sup>And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation, <sup>3</sup>in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. <sup>4</sup>But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. <sup>5</sup>For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. <sup>6</sup>He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. <sup>8</sup>By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.” <sup>9</sup>The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so. <sup>10</sup>And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. <sup>11</sup>You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem, <sup>12</sup>and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. <sup>13</sup>Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me. <sup>14</sup>But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, <sup>15</sup>having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust. <sup>16</sup>So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. <sup>17</sup>Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings. <sup>18</sup>While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia— <sup>19</sup>they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me. <sup>20</sup>Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, <sup>21</sup>other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.’” <sup>22</sup>But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.” <sup>23</sup>Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs. <sup>24</sup>After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. <sup>25</sup>And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.” <sup>26</sup>At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. <sup>27</sup>When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.
24.overview:
Five days after Paul reaches Caesarea, the high priest arrives with a hired advocate, Tertullus, who flatters the governor Felix and charges Paul with sedition, leading the Nazarene sect and attempting to profane the temple. Paul answers calmly, point by point, and brings the case down to the resurrection.

Felix, who knows a good deal about the Way, adjourns the case and keeps Paul for two years. When Paul speaks to him and Drusilla about the coming judgment, Felix is afraid and sends him away until a convenient time. The chapter is a portrait of a man who heard the gospel often and put it off, set beside a prisoner who was settled enough to be cheerful.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Festus and the Appeal to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The leaders’ second ambush plot is bypassed by Roman procedure. Before Festus, Paul answers in one sentence, refuses to be handed over as a favour, and appeals to Caesar. When Agrippa arrives, Festus tells him the case, and the king asks to hear Paul.
verseByVerse.theology:
Lawful Means and the God Who Uses Them

May a believer use the legal protections available to him, or is that a failure of faith? Acts answers plainly. Paul had the risen Christ’s promise that he would testify at Rome (23:11), and he used a lawful right to get there. Faith in the promise did not make the appeal unnecessary; it made it obvious. Providence employs means, even unspiritual ones: a citizenship register, a governor’s ambition, a form to fill in.

Two guards. The lawfulness of the means does not sanctify the motives of those who supply them: Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, is doing what Felix did. And God’s certain purpose does not cancel real injustice. Four officials find no crime, and Paul stays in chains. Both are true.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Festus described the Christian faith to a king with complete accuracy and total detachment: a dispute about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. It never crossed his mind that if it were true it might concern him.

Now: Anyone long in a pew can state the resurrection as accurately as Festus did. The question is whether it has ever been allowed to be about you. Say the sentence out loud, a certain Jesus, who was dead, and who is alive, and if nothing moves, go to the living Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. A new governor meets the same old plot, and Paul’s appeal to Caesar begins to keep the Lord’s promise of Rome. Through every powerful man in the chapter, the risen Christ is moving his servant exactly where he said he would.

The setting. Paul has now been in custody at Caesarea for two years (24:27). Felix has been recalled, and Porcius Festus has arrived, around AD 59. He would die in office about two years later, and within about seven years the province would be in open revolt against Rome.

Three days. The new governor lands, and within three days he is on the road to Jerusalem, which suggests what he had been told about a posting already smouldering. He introduces himself to the people who can make his term ungovernable, and they are ready for him.

Laid out their case against Paul. Two full years have passed since the riot in the temple and the forty men’s oath. Governments and high priests have changed. And Paul is still the first item on the agenda: not one of several matters raised with the incoming governor, but the thing they came to say.

Two years from two sides. For Paul, two years of nothing whatever happening. For his enemies, two years of unbroken attention. Hatred keeps long accounts; a grudge will run for years on nothing at all. The verb Luke uses for what they do to Festus means to press, to urge with insistence. They are lobbying, on day three, before the man has unpacked.

The establishment that pressed Pilate. This is the same priestly establishment that nearly thirty years before had stood in front of another Roman governor and pressed him about another prisoner, until their voices prevailed and Pilate granted their demand (Luke 23:23–24). The Lord had warned his disciples that if they persecuted him, they would persecute them too (John 15:20), and on the Damascus road he said that to strike his people was to strike him (9:4). So the lobbying of Festus is the old campaign against Jesus of Nazareth, still running against the man who preaches him alive. The first one ended at an empty tomb.

Is chief priest the same as high priest? Not quite. The high priest (singular) was the one supreme religious officer of Israel, the single man who alone entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement (such as Caiaphas, or Ananias at Paul’s hearing before Felix). The chief priests (plural) were the wider circle of leading priests, the priestly aristocracy who ran the temple: the serving high priest, former high priests (who kept the title and influence even after Rome deposed them, which is why Annas is still called high priest in Luke 3:2), the heads of the few wealthy high-priestly families from whom high priests were chosen, and senior temple officers like the captain of the temple and the treasurers. So the high priest sits at the very top, and the chief priests are the powerful establishment gathered around and beneath him (mostly Sadducees; see 5:17). It is this priestly ruling class that appears again and again in the Gospels and Acts as the ringleaders against Jesus and his apostles.

Why was Paul left in prison for two years if he was innocent? Because Felix wanted money from him and favour from the Jewish leaders (24:26–27), and an untried prisoner cost him nothing. It was a real injustice, and Luke does not pretend otherwise. But the two years were not empty. Paul’s friends were allowed to visit and care for him (24:23), and it may well be that Luke, who seems to have been nearby, used this time to gather the eyewitness accounts behind his Gospel (Luke 1:1–4). God’s delays are never wasted time, even when they are someone else’s sin.

On a Tuesday. Is there anyone you have been carrying a grievance against for years, simply keeping it current? Bring it by name to the God who has forgiven you far more, and begin to pray for the person’s good.

verseByVerse.quote: "asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem — because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asking as a favor. The word is charis, a favour, a kindness. It is the word for the grace of God, used here as the ordinary currency of Roman public life: you do this for me now, and I am in your debt. They are opening an account with the new governor, a favour to start his term well.

An ambush. Luke cuts in with the truth in a subordinate clause. Festus does not know it; on its face the request is reasonable. We watch him weigh a murder plot hidden from him and visible to us.

The same trap twice. Two years ago the forty men asked for exactly this: a transfer to Jerusalem, with an ambush on the road (23:12–16). The plan is unchanged: two years of failure has not produced a rethink, only a fresh attempt on a fresh governor.

Respectable men. The people who wanted Paul dead were not monsters. They were religious men, respected men, who over two years quietly kept a murder on the agenda and learned to think of it as the defence of God’s honour. Nobody arrives there in one step, but by a series of small permissions, each one granted to yourself on the grounds that the cause is good. The Lord warned his disciples of exactly this: the hour would come when whoever killed them would think he was offering service to God (John 16:2).

An hour not yet come. Mark tells us that the same leadership once sought how to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him (Mark 14:1), and for a long while they could not, because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30). When it did come, it came not because the plotters had finally won, but because the Son laid down his life of his own accord, and their plot became the means of the world’s redemption by the definite plan of God (2:23). The ambush cannot fall while Christ’s word about Rome is unkept, and when Paul’s own hour comes it will come as his Master’s did: at the appointed time, in the Lord’s hands, not the plotters’.

Does this mean the Jews as a people were against Paul? No. Luke is describing a particular group of leaders, the priestly establishment and those around them, not the Jewish people as a whole. Paul himself was a Jew, as were Jesus, all the apostles and thousands of believers in Jerusalem (21:20). Paul loved his people so much that he could wish himself cut off from Christ for their sake (Romans 9:1–3). Christians have sometimes read passages like this as permission for contempt toward Jews, and that is a grievous sin. The lesson of this verse is not about one nation’s wickedness but about what religious people of any nation can become when they decide that their cause justifies anything.

verseByVerse.quote: "Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. 'So,' said he, 'let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Kept at Caesarea. Festus says no, for entirely the wrong reason. He is not protecting Paul, whom he has never met, but his own jurisdiction: a new administrator does not begin his term by handing a prisoner over as a personal favour.

Let the men of authority go down with me. The offer is fair, and inconvenient: if they want this case heard, they must travel sixty miles to argue in a Roman hall on Roman terms. And with it the ambush is dead: not discovered, simply bypassed, because the road Paul was to be killed on is now a road he will not travel.

Providence through procedure. A tribune’s fear (22:29), a nephew’s ears (23:16), and now a Roman rule about where a case must be heard: three times Paul’s life has been saved by the most ordinary means. Providence is God’s ceaseless upholding and steering of all he has made, so that nothing happens by mere chance: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord (Proverbs 16:33).

A jurisdiction above the governor’s. Festus is defending his jurisdiction, and he has no idea whose jurisdiction he lives under. The risen Christ had told his disciples that all authority in heaven and on earth had been given to him (Matthew 28:18), and that includes a Roman governor’s authority over a docket in Caesarea. Pilate heard the same truth from the prisoner in front of him: he would have had no authority at all unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11). The governor’s rule about venues is a small thread in the hand of the King.

Does providence mean I will always be kept safe? No, and Scripture is honest about it. The providence protecting Paul here is the same providence that did not protect Stephen, or James, whom Herod killed with the sword while Peter walked out of prison past the guards (12:1–11). God’s care is real, and it is not a guarantee of safety. What it guarantees is that nothing will cut short the work he has assigned you, and that whatever does come will be made to work for your good (Romans 8:28). Paul had been told, in a barracks in Jerusalem, that his work included Rome, so the road to Jerusalem could not be the end of it. Your own times are in God’s hand (Psalm 31:15), whether they are long or short, and you are immortal until your work is done.

Should I pray for officials who are not Christians? Yes, and this passage shows why. Paul tells Timothy to pray for kings and all who are in high positions, so that believers may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and he wrote that when the emperor was Nero. God uses ordinary, unbelieving officials to restrain evil and protect his people, often without their knowing. Pray by name for your local councillors, your judges, your police and your national leaders: that they will be fair, honest and wise, and that they will come to know Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eight or ten days. Luke does not pretend to know exactly: the habit of a writer who sets down what he was told, vagueness included.

Stood around him. Luke’s verb means encircling, the way the mob did in the temple court. The setting has changed; the posture has not.

Many and serious charges. Many, serious, unproven, as before (24:13). They cannot establish a single count, so they bring many, and they make each one grave. The hope is that twenty unproven things will feel heavier than one.

No smoke without fire. The tactic often works, because we treat volume as evidence. No smoke without fire is precisely the error the courtroom exists to prevent. Many damaged reputations are built this way: rarely by one provable offence, almost always by an accumulation of unprovable ones, none ever tested. Roman law’s answer is the whole of Paul’s defence: they could not prove it.

Many bore false witness against him. The tactic was used first on the Master (Mark 14:56). The charges failed there too, until the high priest asked him directly whether he was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed, and he answered, I am (Mark 14:61–62). He was condemned in the end for no crime, only for the truth about himself. The servant faces many charges that cannot be proved; his Lord, against whom nothing could be proved, accepted the sentence that the true charges against his people deserved.

What should I do when someone tells me several bad things about another person? Ask the question Roman law asked: what can actually be shown? Do not let the number of stories stand in for evidence. Ask the speaker whether he has gone to the person himself (Matthew 18:15). Refuse to pass the stories on. And if you have a responsibility in the matter, insist on hearing the person accused, face to face, before you form a view; Scripture requires two or three witnesses before a charge is accepted (Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Timothy 5:19). Many charges cannot make a lie true.

What if I am the one being accused of many things I cannot disprove? Do what Paul did. Answer what can be answered, plainly and without bitterness, and leave the rest with God. You cannot chase down every rumour, and trying to will consume you. Keep doing what is right, so that those who speak against you are put to shame by your conduct (1 Peter 2:12; 3:16). Tell a trusted elder or friend what is happening so that you are not alone with it. And remember that the Lord Jesus was surrounded by false witnesses whose testimony did not even agree (Mark 14:56); when he was reviled, he did not revile in return, but entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul argued in his defense, 'Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither against the law nor against the temple nor against Caesar. It is the shortest defence Paul makes in the whole book, and the brevity is itself an argument: there is nothing new to answer. The three headings cover religion and politics alike. The law: the charge that he teaches Jews to forsake Moses, which started the riot in chapter 21 and was never true. The temple: the charge that he brought a Gentile past the barrier, which has been shrinking since it was first shouted. Caesar: nobody had formally raised this one today, and Paul names it deliberately. Tertullus had called him a plague who stirred up riots (24:5), and Paul knows that the charge which matters in a Roman court is the political one, so he denies it flatly.

His Master before him. The same three kinds of charges were brought against Jesus, who was said to be misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar and claiming to be a king (Luke 23:2), and against Stephen, who was accused of speaking against the holy place and the law (6:13). The servant is not greater than his master.

The shape of a clean answer. Paul does not argue that the charges are unkind, or that his accusers are hypocrites, or that he has been badly treated, all of which were true and none of which is relevant. He addresses the actual counts, in the actual categories the court recognises, and he stops. A man with a clear conscience can afford to be brief.

Did Paul still keep the law of Moses as a Christian? He kept it among Jews, freely, for the gospel’s sake, but not as the ground of his acceptance with God. He circumcised Timothy (16:3), took part in a temple vow (21:26), and kept the feasts, because he chose to become as a Jew to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). He never taught Jews to abandon their customs. What he denied was that keeping the law could justify anyone (Galatians 2:16), and that Gentile believers had to become Jews to be saved (15:1–11). To justify is to declare a person right with God, and God gives that verdict only on the ground of Christ’s obedience, received by faith. So his denial here is entirely honest: he had broken neither the law nor the temple’s rules, and he had never been disloyal to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, 'Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?' But Paul said, 'I am standing before Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wishing to do the Jews a favor. Luke has used that phrase before. The last governor left office desiring to do the Jews a favour, and left Paul in prison to do it (24:27). Pilate before him, wishing to satisfy the crowd, handed Jesus over to be crucified (Mark 15:15). Festus is a better official by any ordinary measure, and within two weeks Luke files him under the same sentence. The problem was never Felix’s laziness. A man whose position depends on the goodwill of people who want an innocent man dead will find a way to give them something, and he will not experience it as corruption. He will experience it as being reasonable.

Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me? The form of it is mild. Festus does not order Paul to Jerusalem; that would be indefensible. He asks. Before me, he says: it will still be my court, my authority, my verdict. What he is proposing is a change of venue that sounds like a courtesy and would in fact put Paul on a road where men are waiting to kill him, and into a city where the Sanhedrin would effectively decide the case. Festus does not know about the ambush. But he does know he is offering to move a prisoner into the reach of people who have been demanding him for two years, and he is doing it because it would be convenient. Paul knew what awaited.

Caesar’s tribunal. Paul’s answer is legally exact, and it closes the door. A provincial governor’s court was not an alternative to Caesar’s authority; it was Caesar’s authority, delegated. Paul is already in the correct court, and moving him to Jerusalem would abandon the very jurisdiction Festus is exercising.

As you yourself know very well. The phrase is stronger in Greek: you know better than that. Paul tells a Roman governor, in open court, that he knows the truth and is manoeuvring anyway: bold, respectful and plain.

Knowledge without consequence. Felix too had a rather accurate knowledge of the Way (24:22). Two governors knew, and neither did anything with the knowing. The danger is not ignorance but knowledge held without consequence: seeing clearly what is right and routing around it, politely, for reasons that sound sensible later.

Christ did not please himself. At Pilate’s judgment seat the favour-seeking of a governor fell on the one man in history who never once courted anyone’s favour at the cost of the truth. Christ did not please himself, Paul would write; the reproaches of those who reproached God fell on him (Romans 15:3). He bore the cost of Pilate’s wish to please, and of every such wish in us, so that people-pleasers could be forgiven and set free to please God. Paul’s calm refusal to be managed in this courtroom is the freedom of a man who has been bought by that Lord.

Is it wrong to want to please people? Not in itself. Paul tried to please everyone in everything for the sake of their salvation (1 Corinthians 10:33), and we are told to please our neighbour for his good (Romans 15:2). The sin is pleasing people at the cost of truth or justice, when their approval matters more to us than God’s. Paul’s own test was sharp: if I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). The question is never whether others are pleased, but whether, to please them, you are doing what you know to be wrong.

How do I speak truth to someone in authority over me? As Paul did here: respectfully, plainly and briefly. He did not insult Festus, raise his voice or accuse him of corruption. He simply stated the facts and named what Festus already knew. Address the person with the honour due to his office (1 Peter 2:17), speak to the specific issue, avoid exaggeration, and do not threaten. Then leave the outcome with God. Courage and courtesy are not opposites; in the mouth of a Christian they belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: "'If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.' Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, 'To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not seek to escape death. Before the appeal comes the offer: Paul begins not by claiming his rights but by conceding the court’s right to kill him if the charge stands. Then he points out that none stands. He is not trying to escape justice but to stop an injustice.

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians believe the death penalty is always wrong, often from a deep concern for mercy and for the risk of executing the innocent. This commentary’s view: Paul here accepts that some crimes deserve death and that the state may impose it, as he teaches in Romans 13:4 (the governing authority does not bear the sword in vain), grounded in Genesis 9:6. The state has the God-given right to punish grave crimes, including with death, though it must do so justly, with due process and certain guilt. Christians may disagree on when it is wise to use it.

No one can give me up to them. The verb is the verb for granting a favour: no one can make me a present to these men, not even the governor.

I appeal to Caesar. It was one of the oldest and most jealously guarded rights a Roman citizen had: the right to have his case lifted out of a provincial court and heard by the emperor himself. Once made, the appeal could not easily be refused, and the governor could no longer convict or, in practice, release. His remaining duty was to forward the prisoner to Rome with a written statement of the charges. This is why Agrippa will remark, at the end of the next chapter, that this man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar (26:32).

Did Paul make a mistake? No. And the reason is not legal but theological. It was settled two years earlier in a dark barracks in Jerusalem, when the Lord stood by him and said he must testify also in Rome (23:11). Paul is not gambling. He is holding a promise, and he has just been handed the only legal mechanism in the Roman world that guarantees delivery: to Rome, at the state’s expense, under guard. Paul used his rights wisely, and God used them to send him where Jesus promised.

Which Caesar. This is around AD 59, and the emperor is Nero, at that point still in the early years that Roman writers themselves regarded as good government, before the fire, before the persecution in which, as the early Christian writers report, Paul would die. He goes to Rome under the protection of the man under whose rule, by that same early testimony, he would be put to death.
