To Caesar you shall go. The formula is final, and Festus means nothing by it beyond a legal duty. But it is the promise of the risen Christ (23:11), coming back to Paul out of a Roman governor’s mouth with the full weight of the empire behind it.

How the Lord governs the world. Not usually by suspending it, but by running it. The kings of the earth take counsel together, and their counsel is his instrument (Psalm 2:2–4; Acts 4:27–28); decree after decree signed against his people has ended by moving the gospel further down the road.

Using lawful rights. It is right for a Christian to use his lawful legal rights, and Paul does so without a flicker of guilt; earlier he invoked his Roman citizenship to stop an illegal flogging (22:25–29) and refused a quiet, hushed-up release (16:37). Nor does this contradict the command to turn the other cheek, which forbids personal revenge (Matthew 5:39; Romans 12:19), not the lawful appeal to the authority God ordained to do justice (Romans 13:4). Paul forgave his persecutors personally and used the courts; the two sit together.

But does this fit with Paul’s warning against going to court? In 1 Corinthians 6:1–8 Paul forbids believers to sue one another before unbelievers. Here Paul is a believer accused by unbelievers, appealing to a Roman court for justice. Christians may use the courts and civil rights to defend themselves and others; they should not take a brother to court.

Free to use them, free to give them up. Use lawful protections without bitterness, for justice and not for getting even, and remember they are a freedom, not always a duty (1 Corinthians 6:7, “Why not rather suffer wrong?”).

How do I know when to use a right and when to give it up? Ask what will serve the gospel and the good of others, not merely what will protect me. Paul insisted on his rights when silence would have let injustice stand, harmed others, or hindered his mission (16:37; 22:25). He laid them down when insisting would have put an obstacle in the way of the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12). If you are being wronged, and using a lawful protection would stop the wrong without revenge, use it. If insisting would damage a brother or a witness for a small personal gain, let it go. When unsure, seek counsel from wise believers.

For worship. Paul appealed to Caesar and lived. His Lord made no appeal and died. On the night he was betrayed he could have asked his Father for more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53), and he asked for nothing, because the Scriptures had to be fulfilled and sinners had to be saved. Because he made no appeal, the guilty may now make theirs, not to Caesar but to the throne of grace, where their sentence has already been borne. Blessed be the Lord who would not save himself, so that he might save us.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman citizen could appeal to be tried by the emperor himself — at this time Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, saying, 'There is a man left prisoner by Felix,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agrippa the king and Bernice. They came, as client rulers did, to welcome the new governor, and the name alone would have carried a chill. Herod the Great tried to kill Jesus in the cradle and murdered the infants of Bethlehem to do it (Matthew 2:16). Herod Antipas, his son, beheaded John the Baptist to save face at a birthday party (Mark 6:26–27), and when Jesus was finally sent to him on the morning of the crucifixion he treated him with contempt, dressed him in splendid clothing as a joke, and sent him back (Luke 23:11). Herod Agrippa I killed James with the sword and was struck down for accepting the shout that his voice was a god’s (Acts 12:2, 23). Now his son Agrippa II, the last of the line in the New Testament.

Near the gospel and far from it. In four generations not one Herod has ever done anything with it but destroy it, mock it, exploit it, or find it interesting. Nearness to the gospel is not the same as receiving it, and it does not accumulate down a bloodline. Access is not the scarce commodity. Willingness is, and it is the gift of God: left to ourselves we do not want him, and it is God who makes the unwilling willing, drawing them to his Son (John 6:44) and working in them both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). Parents grieving a wandering child should hear the other half of that truth: because willingness is God’s gift, no son or daughter is beyond his reach, and prayer for them is never wasted.

The true King of the Jews. The family’s quarrel was always, at bottom, with one person. Herod the Great slaughtered children because Magi came asking for him who had been born king of the Jews (Matthew 2:2). Each Herod ruled by Rome’s permission, and each found himself confronted by a King whose throne no emperor gave: the Son to whom God would give the throne of his father David, whose kingdom would have no end (Luke 1:32–33). Agrippa II has come to Caesarea to honour a governor. Before he leaves he will hear about that King.

The right man to consult. He ruled territories to the north and east of Galilee, and Rome had given him a peculiar portfolio: oversight of the temple, the keeping of the high priest’s vestments, and the right to appoint and depose the high priest himself. He was an expert in Jewish customs and questions (26:3).

Bernice. Bernice is his sister. She had been married to her uncle, was widowed young, and for long periods afterwards lived in her brother’s household, an arrangement that produced a persistent rumour of incest, reported by Josephus and openly mocked in Rome by the satirist Juvenal. She would later become the mistress of Titus, who destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70. Luke names her without comment and lets the reader supply what he knows.

A man left prisoner by Felix. Two years of a Roman citizen held without a verdict, compressed into one dismissive clause. Left, the way you leave a coat behind in a house you have moved out of.

The forgotten file. It is not usually malice; nobody’s file is anybody’s priority. When your own situation feels like an oversight rather than a plan, remember that Paul was a line item in a handover briefing, and he was exactly where the Lord had told him he would be. At his conversion the Lord had said that Paul would carry his name before Gentiles and kings (9:15). The forgotten prisoner was about to stand before a king.

If my family has no Christian history, am I at a disadvantage? No. Grace does not run in bloodlines, either for blessing or for doom. The Herods show that a family can be near the gospel for generations and never receive it; the rest of Scripture shows that God delights to call people from families with no faith at all, as he called Abraham out of a home of idol worshippers (Joshua 24:2). And if you are the first believer in your family, you may be the beginning of a new line. Pray for your relatives by name; God saves whom he wills, and no family is too far from him.
verseByVerse.note: King Agrippa (Herod Agrippa II) was the son of Herod Agrippa I and ruled territories to the north-east. Bernice was his sister.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not the custom of the Romans. Festus tells Agrippa the story of his week, and every clause is true. But he does not mention that the priests had asked for a transfer to Jerusalem as a favour (v. 3), and when he mentions his own offer of a Jerusalem trial (v. 20) he recasts it as bewilderment, though it is the very thing that would have handed Paul over to his accusers and gutted the principle he is now quoting so proudly.

The flattering arrangement. Lysias did the same in his letter, rearranging one clause so that his rescue of Paul looked principled rather than accidental (23:27). Neither man invents a fact, and Luke sets the arrangement beside the events without comment, for a reader who has the transcript.

A magnificent principle. But what Festus cites is the reason Paul is still breathing. Roman practice held that a man could not be condemned unheard, and that accuser and accused must stand face to face. Scripture had said it long before: a single witness was not enough, false witnesses were to be punished (Deuteronomy 19:15–19), and even Nicodemus had to remind the Pharisees that the law does not judge a man without first hearing him (John 7:51). The right to face your accuser is still a foundation of a just court.

Rome’s custom and Israel’s law. The men entrusted with the law of God, who knew that a matter is established by two or three witnesses, asked for a sentence of condemnation on a man they had not allowed to speak, asked for it as a favour, and were planning an ambush on the road. The pagan governor said no, because it was not the custom. Rome’s custom was better kept than Israel’s law, not because Rome was righteous but because the men holding the law had stopped letting it govern them. They decided that this once the procedure could be set aside, and became the sort of people a pagan has to restrain.

By oppression and judgment. The principle Festus quotes saved Paul. It did not save Jesus, though he stood before a Roman governor bound by the same custom. Pilate heard him face to face, examined him, declared him innocent, and then delivered him over to their will (Luke 23:22–25). Isaiah had seen it long before: by oppression and judgment he was taken away (Isaiah 53:8). Every safeguard bent around the one truly innocent man, because the Father had purposed that he should bear the condemnation of the guilty. The servant is sheltered today by a rule his Master was denied.

Can unbelievers sometimes act more justly than believers? Yes, and Scripture is not embarrassed to say so. God has written the work of his law on every human heart (Romans 2:14–15), and by his common grace unbelievers often see and do what is fair. Abimelech rebuked Abraham for a lie (Genesis 20:9), and here Festus restrains the priests. That should humble the church, not unsettle it. It does not mean unbelievers are saved by their fairness, but it does mean Christians have no excuse for being less honest, less just or less fair than the world around them.

verseByVerse.quote: "'So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I made no delay. Festus wants the king to notice his efficiency, and he has earned it: Felix left the case for two years, and Festus had it on the tribunal within a fortnight. Competence in office is no small thing; a prompt hearing is a mercy to the man waiting for it.

Speed is not integrity. None of that stopped him doing the one thing that would have killed Paul. He was prompt, correct and as far as we know uncorrupt, and eight verses earlier he asked whether the prisoner would care to be tried in the city where men were waiting to kill him, because it would please the people he had to work with. You can be blameless in every procedure that can be audited and still make the one decision that matters on the basis of who you need to keep happy.

Never early and never late. Set beside Festus the one whose timing was always perfect and never self-serving. Jesus told his brothers that his time had not yet come (John 7:6), and he would not be hurried by anyone’s agenda. Then, when the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), toward the city where men were waiting to kill him, not to please anyone but to do his Father’s will. Festus was prompt in what gets inspected; Christ was prompt in obedience, and it took him to a cross for us.

How do I know whether my decisions are driven by fear of people? Ask three questions. Would I decide differently if no one important would ever find out? Am I avoiding the right course because of one person’s reaction rather than because it is wrong? Am I describing my choice to myself in words like sensible, realistic or not worth the trouble, when the honest word would be afraid? The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the Lord is safe (Proverbs 29:25). Bring the decision to God in prayer, ask what he requires, and do that, however competent the alternative looks.

verseByVerse.quote: "'When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No charge of such evils as I supposed. Festus had expected sedition, fraud, violence, the ordinary business of a troublesome province, and the prosecution had nothing.

Their own religion. The word can mean religion, and it can mean superstition, fear of the gods. To a Jewish king it sounds neutral; a Roman of his class would hear the contempt in it.

A certain Jesus. A Roman governor summarises the entire Christian faith in a subordinate clause and files it under local religious trivia. The phrase means some Jesus or other: a name you have no reason to remember, a few days’ journey from the hill where it happened. The name at which every knee will one day bow is, to Festus, a detail in a religious quarrel he is trying to get out of.

Who was dead. This is not in dispute. Nobody in the room, on either side, questions that Jesus of Nazareth was executed and buried. The death of Christ is common ground between the apostle and the men trying to kill him.

Whom Paul asserted to be alive. The tense matters: Paul kept on asserting it. It was a claim he would not stop making, from Damascus to Rome.

Festus has got it exactly right. Christianity is, at bottom, a dispute about whether a particular dead man is alive. Paul said as much himself, in writing, to people who were trying to spiritualise it: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Festus, who believed none of it, put his finger on the hinge of history.

Accurate and untouched. So the gospel can be stated accurately by someone completely untouched by it. It never occurred to Festus that if the claim were true, it would concern him personally. Those who have been in church longest might ask whether it has cost them anything or moved anything in them lately. If not, the answer is not to know less but to come to the living Christ himself, who welcomes the long-time churchgoer as freely as the stranger, and who can still make an old truth burn.

How can we be sure Jesus really rose? The evidence is strong, and it begins with the very fact this verse records: nobody disputed the death. Jesus was publicly executed by professionals and buried in a known tomb. Within weeks his followers were proclaiming in the same city that the tomb was empty, and his enemies never produced the body, though that would have ended the matter. More than five hundred people saw him alive, many of them still living when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). That list is not a late legend: Paul wrote it within about twenty-five years, passing on a summary he had himself received, probably within a few years of the events. Frightened disciples became fearless, and men like Paul, an enemy, and James, a sceptical brother, were transformed. Men do not die for what they know to be a lie. No argument compels belief, and honest people weigh this evidence differently. And alongside the evidence, the Spirit himself bears witness through the Word that it is true.

For worship. A certain Jesus, who was dead. He was dead: the centurion certified it and the tomb received him. And he is alive, in a body, at the right hand of the Majesty on high, holding the keys of Death and Hades. Festus is dust; Agrippa is dust; Nero is dust. And the certain Jesus whose name the governor could not be bothered to learn is on the throne of the universe tonight, and every one of those men will bow the knee at his name. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, and who lives for ever and ever.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At a loss. The word pictures finding no way through. Festus is not being falsely modest: his training does not equip him to open whether a crucified Galilean is alive.

I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem. He omits that it was to please the Jews. Being at a loss, he did not adjourn or take advice; he proposed the one course that would have ended Paul’s life.

Confusion is not neutral. When a man genuinely does not know what to do, he does not stop; he falls back on whatever pressure is strongest in the room. Festus’s bewilderment produced not caution but a proposal that pleased the people he needed (v. 9). So the test is not whether you know what to do; often you will not. The test is what you reach for when you do not know. Festus reached for the least friction, and it nearly killed the apostle to the Gentiles.

The question no tribunal could open. Festus was at a loss because the case had come down to a person, and the question about that person was one no Roman court could settle: is the crucified Jesus alive? God had already answered it. Paul had told the philosophers of Athens that God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and has given assurance of it to all by raising him from the dead (17:31). Festus, puzzling over how to investigate the risen man, is himself the one under investigation. The prisoner’s Lord is the governor’s appointed Judge, and the day is fixed.

The decision of the emperor. The title is the Greek for Augustus, the revered one, with a hint of worship in it, and it meant Nero. Festus reports the appeal as an inconvenience, not knowing he is describing the promise of 23:11 moving one more stage down the road.

What should I do when I genuinely do not know what to do? Stop and pray before you act, and ask God for wisdom; he gives it generously to those who ask (James 1:5). Search the Scriptures for any principle that bears on the decision. Seek counsel from wise and godly people, not merely from the people who will be pleased by one outcome (Proverbs 15:22). Do the right things you already know, even if the larger picture is unclear. And watch which way the pressure in the room is pushing you; if your uncertainty keeps landing on the option that pleases the powerful, be suspicious of it. It is often wiser to wait than to reach for the easiest course.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Agrippa said to Festus, 'I would like to hear the man myself.' 'Tomorrow,' said he, 'you will hear him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I would like to hear the man myself. The tense can mean I have been wanting to. Agrippa had probably heard of Paul for years. And a Herod has said this before.

The Herod who wanted to see Jesus. Of Herod Antipas, when reports of Jesus reached the palace, Luke wrote that he sought to see him (Luke 9:9). On the morning of the crucifixion he finally got his wish, hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but Jesus made no answer (Luke 23:8–9). Few silences in the Gospels are more terrible. Curiosity had had its years to become something else and had refused, and when the moment came there was nothing left to say to him.

Tomorrow you will hear him. Now the last Herod wants the same, and the outcome is different. Paul will preach to this king one of the fullest and most personal defences in the book (26:27), and it will bring him close enough, or stung enough, to ask whether Paul thinks he can make him a Christian in so short a time (26:28). That is mercy. Antipas mocked, and got silence; to the merely curious Agrippa God sends one of the finest preachers of the age with a message shaped for his exact history and knowledge.

Curiosity is not conversion. But Luke goes on to record what Agrippa did with it, and the answer is nothing. He heard the whole thing, agreed it was harmless, remarked to Festus that the man could have been released, and went home a king. Curiosity about Christ can be a door, but some enjoy the subject for years and have never once been to Christ for mercy. Agrippa wanted to hear the man. He got exactly what he asked for, and it was not what he needed, because he never asked for what he needed.

How do I talk to a friend who is curious about Christianity? Welcome the curiosity and take it seriously. Answer honest questions honestly, and admit when you do not know. But do what Paul will do with Agrippa: move gently from the interesting to the personal. Ask what they make of Jesus himself, not only of the arguments. Tell them what Christ has done for you. Invite them to read one of the Gospels with you. And pray for them, because curiosity becomes faith only when God opens the heart (16:14). Do not be content to keep a curious friend interested for years; lovingly ask where they stand.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a hall full of pomp, with the province’s officers and leading men present, Festus brings Paul in. He has found no crime, yet he must send the prisoner to the emperor, and he hopes Agrippa’s hearing will give him something to write.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Platform the World Cannot Help Providing

Jesus said that being brought before kings and governors for his name’s sake would be your opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). The hostility of the council, the ambition of two governors, the curiosity of a king and a problem with a covering letter together seat the ruling class of a province in front of a preacher. The opposition built the platform and handed the prisoner the floor.

This is neither triumphalism nor passivity. God often works through nobodies in obscurity. But when he uses the machinery of the age, he needs neither its permission nor its goodwill.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Everything visible in that hall belonged to the other side. Paul had a chain and the floor, and within a day he had spoken so directly to the king that Agrippa had to answer him.

Now: The principle shows up in smaller rooms: the meeting where you are the least senior person present, the family table where your faith is the odd position. Paul never got a better platform than the one his enemies built for him. He used the floor he was given, with the chain on.

verseByVerse.quote: "So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. And Festus said, 'King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
With great pomp. Luke’s word is the root of our fantasy: a display put on to be looked at, the whole power structure of the province in one hall.

Paul was brought in. He does not enter; he is brought. And he is in chains: he says so himself before the hearing ends, in one of the most gracious sentences in Acts, when he tells this room he wishes every one of them were as he is, except for these chains (26:29). Festus has just admitted he cannot say why the prisoner is there; the one man in the room who knows exactly what is going on is the one in irons.

The whole Jewish people. Festus is overstating; thousands of Jewish believers would have said otherwise. But he has just entered into the record, in front of the province’s assembled nobility: they were shouting that he ought not to live any longer. And the governor is about to say, in the next breath, that he found no ground for it whatever.

He ought not to live any longer. Paul is not the first prisoner over whom that was shouted. Before Pilate the crowd cried out together against Jesus, Away with this man, and then, Crucify, crucify him (Luke 23:18, 21). Paul heard the same cry on the barracks steps (22:22). But the shout over Christ did not have the last word. Men said he ought not to live; God raised him, and he lives for ever. That is exactly why they want Paul silenced: the man in chains keeps saying that the one they shouted down is alive.

In the flow. At Paul’s conversion the Lord said he would carry his name before Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel (9:15), and here all three are in one hall.

Is it wrong for Christians to enjoy ceremony, wealth or fine things? Not in itself. God made a world of beauty, and Scripture describes the splendour of Solomon’s temple and the glory of the new Jerusalem without embarrassment. The danger is in what Luke’s word exposes: display for its own sake, splendour used to make ourselves look great, trust placed in what will fade. Enjoy good things with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4; 6:17), use them generously, and never confuse them with true greatness. The question is whether the things you have are pointing others to God or to yourself.

parallels.desc: I will speak of your testimonies before kings

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing deserving death. A Roman governor is putting a prisoner on a ship to the imperial court, and he cannot say what the man is accused of. The file is empty.

The verdicts filed. Every authority that has examined Paul has found no crime: Gallio (18:14–15), Lysias (23:29), Festus twice, and soon Agrippa (26:31–32). Luke simply files the verdicts, and they echo another set in his first volume, when Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), and sent him to the cross anyway.

Nothing definite to write to my lord. Sending a prisoner to the emperor with no charge would make him look foolish, so he hopes that after the king has examined Paul, he may have something to write. Then there is the phrase a Christian reader should not walk past: my lord, kyrios. Festus uses it of Nero as the ordinary courtesy; within a generation Domitian would want to be addressed as lord and god.

Two lordships in one sentence. For the man in chains that word means somebody else entirely. Paul had written to Corinth that there is one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6), and he would write to Philippi that God has given Jesus the name that is above every name, so that every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:9–11). He is being shipped to Caesar’s court for the specific purpose of saying so. Two lordships are named in a single sentence, and the governor can see only one of them.

Is it wrong for a Christian to call anyone lord or to honour rulers? No. Scripture tells us to honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17) and to give respect and honour to whom they are owed (Romans 13:7). Paul himself addresses Festus as most excellent (26:25). Courtesy to those in authority is right. What a Christian cannot do is give any ruler the worship, absolute allegiance or final obedience that belongs to Christ alone. That is why believers in the early centuries would honour Caesar but would not say Caesar is lord in the sense of Caesar is god, and many died for it. When a ruler’s command contradicts God’s, we must obey God rather than men (5:29).

On a Tuesday. Let your life be so honest at work, so faithful at home, so clean in your dealings, that anyone who looked for something to accuse you of would come away with an empty file. You will not manage it perfectly, and before God you need not: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, his clean record is counted as yours (Philippians 3:9), and his Spirit is making yours cleaner year by year.

For worship. Nero was lord of the world for fourteen years and died by his own hand at thirty. Jesus Christ was lord of nothing anyone could see, and he is Lord tonight. The title Festus gives Nero in passing is a courtesy; the title Paul gives Jesus in chains is a fact, and every tongue will one day say so, to the glory of God the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It seems to me unreasonable. The chapter ends on a bureaucrat’s complaint about paperwork. But hear what it concedes: he knows the thing is unreasonable, says so out loud, and does it anyway.

A system that worked as designed. Everyone with the power to judge knows Paul is innocent, and none of them sets him free. The system worked exactly as designed, and still could not do the right thing, because at every stage there was somebody who needed a favour.

And yet. Here is what the promise of Rome (23:11) looks like from ground level: a governor who cannot fill in a form. Not an angel or an acquittal, but a procedural embarrassment that will put Paul on a ship at imperial expense and carry him to the one city he had been promised. It is a real injustice and also the exact mechanism of a promise. The Christian life is mostly lived in that overlap.

A charge written over the cross. Festus cannot find a charge to write against Paul. Over his Lord a charge was written and set up for all Jerusalem to read: “This is the King of the Jews” (Luke 23:38). Pilate meant it as the crime; God made it the truth. And Paul would later write that something else was nailed there with it: the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands, which God set aside, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The servant goes to Rome with a blank charge sheet, because there is nothing to write. The sinner goes free before God with a cancelled one, because everything that could be written against him was written over Christ, and paid.

Why does God allow innocent believers to remain in chains? Scripture does not give us every reason, but it gives us enough to trust him. Paul’s chains carried the gospel to places no free preacher could reach: the praetorian guard and Caesar’s household (Philippians 1:12–13; 4:22). Suffering for righteousness joins believers to Christ, who suffered unjustly first (1 Peter 2:19–23), and it bears witness to the world that he is worth more than freedom. God will one day judge every injustice openly (2 Thessalonians 1:6–8). Until then, he does not waste a single day of his people’s suffering. Many Christians today are imprisoned for no crime but their faith, and they need our prayers, our letters and our advocacy.

On a Tuesday. Find out about one believer, or one church, imprisoned or persecuted for faith in Christ today, through a ministry that serves the persecuted church, and pray for them this week, remembering them as though in prison with them (Hebrews 13:3).

For worship. Festus wanted something to write, and he will get chapter 26. God turns a governor’s embarrassment into a pulpit, an unjust chain into a passage to Rome, and a cross that every court agreed was unreasonable into the salvation of the world. Not one of his promises has ever failed. To him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus, throughout all generations, for ever and ever.

25.title: Paul Before Festus
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. <sup>2</sup>And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him, <sup>3</sup>asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem—because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way. <sup>4</sup>Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. <sup>5</sup>“So,” said he, “let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.” <sup>6</sup>After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. <sup>7</sup>When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove. <sup>8</sup>Paul argued in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.” <sup>9</sup>But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?” <sup>10</sup>But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well. <sup>11</sup>If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.” <sup>12</sup>Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.” <sup>13</sup>Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. <sup>14</sup>And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left prisoner by Felix, <sup>15</sup>and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. <sup>16</sup>I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him. <sup>17</sup>So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought. <sup>18</sup>When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. <sup>19</sup>Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. <sup>20</sup>Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. <sup>21</sup>But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.” <sup>22</sup>Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” said he, “you will hear him.” <sup>23</sup>So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. <sup>24</sup>And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer. <sup>25</sup>But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. <sup>26</sup>But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write. <sup>27</sup>For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.”
25.overview:
A new governor, Porcius Festus, arrives about AD 59, and the Jerusalem leaders at once ask for Paul to be brought to Jerusalem, intending to ambush him on the road. Festus hears the unproved charges in Caesarea instead. When he proposes a trial in Jerusalem to please the Jews, Paul uses his right as a citizen and appeals to Caesar.

Festus must now send a report to the emperor, and he can find no crime. When King Agrippa II and Bernice visit, he sums up the dispute as being about “a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive,” and the chapter ends with the prisoner brought in before the assembled power of the province.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells his story in order: the strict Pharisee on trial for Israel’s hope (vv. 2–8); the persecutor (vv. 9–11); the risen Jesus on the road and the commission (vv. 12–18); his obedience and his message (vv. 19–23). Festus interrupts, Agrippa turns it aside, and Paul prays that all may become as he is, apart from the chains (vv. 24–29). The officials agree he could have been freed (vv. 30–32).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel as Israel's Hope, Not Israel's Rival

The spine of this speech is that the Christian faith is not a new religion. Paul stakes everything on continuity: he is on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers (v. 6), he says nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass (v. 22), and he asks the king the question that would settle it: do you believe the prophets?

That claim rests on three things the Old Testament had promised and Paul insists are now fulfilled: a Messiah who must suffer (Isaiah 53; Luke 24:26), a resurrection that opens the age to come (Daniel 12:2), and light reaching the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). Take away the third and the first two become a private Jewish matter, which is what his opponents wanted and what he would not give them.

Underneath lies grace that is entirely from God's side. Paul was not seeking; he was in a raging fury, and he was stopped, named and commissioned. Every clause of the commission in vv. 17–18 is something done to people, not by them: eyes opened, a realm changed, a dominion broken, sins forgiven, a place given.

And the chapter guards that against cheapness: performing deeds in keeping with their repentance (v. 20). The works are never the root but the fruit (Ephesians 2:8–10). A sovereign work of grace produces a visibly different life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Agrippa heard the gospel from the apostle to the Gentiles, in his own theological vocabulary, from a man who prayed for him out loud in open court. He did not refute a single point; he made a wry remark and stood up.

Now: There was no considered rejection, and the standing up was the answer. Many decline Christ that way, with a subject changed, an evening that ran late, a genuine intention to come back to it. If you have been near this for years, the question is not whether you have objections; Agrippa stated none. It is whether the conversation has quietly been allowed to end the same way again and again. Christ still receives all who come to him (John 6:37), and Paul's one request at the start of the speech, that the king would hear him patiently, is still the only thing being asked.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Agrippa said to Paul, 'You have permission to speak for yourself.' Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: 'I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 26 is Paul’s greatest defence and the third account of his conversion: the strict Pharisee met by the risen Jesus and sent to turn the Gentiles from darkness to light. A prisoner holds up the risen Christ before the whole power of a province.

In the flow. The speech runs in a clear order: a courteous opening (vv. 2–3), his life as a Pharisee and persecutor (vv. 4–11), the risen Jesus on the road and the commission he gave (vv. 12–18), Paul’s obedience and his message (vv. 19–23), and the closing exchange with Festus and Agrippa (vv. 24–29).

Permission to speak. Paul has been waiting more than two years for this sentence. A mob, a brawling council, a governor hoping for a bribe, and a second out of his depth: four occasions, and not one of them a fair hearing. Now a king with a working knowledge of the Hebrew Scriptures says: speak.

Stretched out his hand. It is the orator’s gesture, and there is a chain on that hand. Paul will mention it himself before the afternoon is out: except for these chains (v. 29).

I consider myself fortunate. The word is makarios, the word of the Beatitudes: blessed, happy, well off. On trial for his life, Paul calls himself fortunate, not because Agrippa is powerful but because he can follow the argument and will not hear the word resurrection as provincial nonsense. Paul is not counting his chances of acquittal. He is counting his chances of being understood about Jesus Christ. And Jesus’ promise is being fulfilled: Paul would carry his name before kings (9:15).

A fortunate man in chains. Our arithmetic measures a day by what it cost us. Paul has been in custody for two years on a charge the governor cannot put into writing (25:26–27), and his verdict on the afternoon is that he is a fortunate man, because someone competent is finally going to hear about Christ. Measure your own least free places this week, the hospital bed, the difficult office, the family table where faith is mocked, by the same rule: someone there may hear about Jesus.

Your opportunity to bear witness. The Lord had said his followers would be brought before kings and governors for his name’s sake, and this would be their opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). Jesus added a promise: I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict (Luke 21:15). The speech before Agrippa is not Paul’s talent on display. It is the risen Christ, who once stood silent before Herod Antipas, now speaking through his servant to Antipas’s great-nephew.

Who were Agrippa and Bernice? Herod Agrippa II, great-grandson of Herod the Great, ruled territories north and east of Galilee and had the Roman right to appoint the high priest, so Festus wanted his advice on a Jewish matter. Bernice was his sister. Festus had recently replaced Felix as governor.

The accusations of the Jews. Luke’s shorthand throughout Acts means the Jerusalem leadership who brought the case, not the Jewish people as such, and certainly not Jews as a race. The man speaking is himself a Jew arguing from the Hebrew prophets. This book has been misread down the centuries to justify appalling things; it does not say them.

Why does Luke tell Paul’s conversion three times? Because it matters enormously to the story and to the gospel. Luke tells it first as narrator (9:1–19), then in Paul’s words to a Jewish crowd (22:3–21), and now to a king. Ancient writers repeated what they most wanted remembered. The conversion of the church’s fiercest enemy proves that the gospel is God’s work and not man’s, it explains why Paul went to the Gentiles, and it shows that Christ can save anyone. Each telling is shaped for its hearers, but the heart is the same: the risen Jesus met Saul and sent him.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "'especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Customs and controversies. Agrippa knows the practices and, more useful still, the arguments, such as the old quarrel over the resurrection. He is competent to hear this case.

Patiently. The word is makrothumōs, literally with a long temper rather than a short one, the family of words used of God’s own longsuffering. Paul asks the king for a small share of that quality: do not become irritated with me before I have finished.

Beginning with Moses. Paul’s long speech follows a pattern set by the risen Lord himself. On the road to Emmaus, Luke tells us, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). Christ did not hand those disciples a slogan; he gave them an afternoon and a whole Bible, because he fills it. Paul is about to do the same for a king (26:22–23).

An overlooked reason. What follows is not a legal defence, and Paul knows it: he will barely address the charges, and tell instead how the risen Jesus stopped him, arguing from Moses and the prophets. That takes time. Impatience, not hostility, is a common reason people never deal with Christ: the subject is given a few minutes, and the verdict is reached on a case that was never heard. Paul is not asking Agrippa to agree, only to stay in the room long enough for the argument to be made.

What if I am the impatient one? Then give Christ a fair hearing, deliberately. Many Christians as well as unbelievers grant the Bible a few distracted minutes and then decide what they think. Read one whole Gospel, Mark or Luke, in two or three sittings, as you would read any serious book, and ask what kind of person Jesus is. Sit through a sermon without checking your phone. When a hard passage troubles you, stay with it long enough to understand it before you set it aside. God promises that those who seek him with all their heart will find him (Jeremiah 29:13).

For worship. Paul asked a king for a little patience; God bore with the persecutor Saul until the day he stopped him, and bears with us still. The Lord’s patience means salvation (2 Peter 3:15).

verseByVerse.quote: "'My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Known by all the Jews. Paul opens with the public record. He was raised in Jerusalem, trained under Gamaliel, one of the most famous rabbis of the age (22:3), and made his reputation in front of witnesses who are still alive. They could testify, if they are willing: the prosecution has the evidence and will not produce it, because the evidence helps the defendant. They cannot say Paul left Judaism because he never understood it. He understood it better than they did.

The strictest party. The word is akribestatēn: the most exact, with no margin of error (compare 22:3). He is claiming to have belonged to the most exacting school available, and thoroughly.

He does not disown it. He said the same to the council (23:6) and wrote it years later (Philippians 3:5). Paul never regarded following Jesus as leaving Israel. He regarded it as Israel’s hope arriving. His conversion was not from irreligion to religion, but from the best religion without Christ to Christ.

Closing the exits. Every generation reaches for a comfortable explanation of conversion: he was badly taught, unhappy, young, searching. Paul closes the exits one by one. He had the best training in the nation, status and approval, and he was riding a career hard in the opposite direction, and winning. Whatever happened to him on that road, it was not the collapse of a man who had run out of alternatives. It was the interruption of a man who had none of the usual reasons to be interrupted.

The exactness he found in another. The strictest Pharisee in Jerusalem was chasing a righteousness measured to the last tithe of mint. What he found on the Damascus road was that someone had already kept the law with that exactness and more: not an iota, not a dot, had been left unfulfilled by Christ (Matthew 5:17–18). Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4). The Pharisee did not abandon his longing for an exact righteousness. He found it, complete, in the obedience of Jesus, and received it as a gift. What does that mean? When a person trusts Christ, God counts Christ’s perfect obedience as his, so that he stands before God clothed in a righteousness he did not earn (Philippians 3:9).

Does a strict religious upbringing count for anything with God? It can be a great mercy, because it fills the mind with Scripture and the habits of worship, as Paul’s did. But it cannot save. Paul later listed every one of his religious advantages and then said he counted them all as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus his Lord (Philippians 3:4–9). What God requires is not a good record but a righteousness that comes through faith in Christ. If you were raised in the church, thank God for it, and make sure you are trusting Christ himself and not your background.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On trial because of my hope. He is in chains, prosecuted by his own nation’s leaders, on a charge that comes down to this: he believes what Israel has been praying for, morning and evening, for centuries. Paul is on trial for being a faithful Jew who believes God’s promise has been kept.

Night and day. Twelve tribes: all Israel, as one people. Their worship was hope, waiting for God to act. He grants his accusers’ piety warmly: the prayers are real.

Accused by Jews. That is what makes the charge so strange, and so sad: Jews accuse a Jew for believing the Jewish hope. A thing can be prayed for so long that the praying becomes the settled shape of life, and the arrival of the answer feels less like fulfilment than like disruption. They wanted the right thing and got it, and did not recognise it, because it came in a form that cost them something.

The threads of the hope. The hope Paul is on trial for has three strands, and all three have come true in Jesus: the resurrection of the dead, the heart of it (23:6; 24:15, 21); the promised Messiah (13:23, 32–33); and the redemption of Israel, for which Paul wears his chain (28:20).

Rooted in the Old Testament. The resurrection was promised there: “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2; compare Job 19:25–27; Isaiah 26:19). It was woven into Jewish prayer, very probably by Paul’s day: the Amidah, the standing prayer said daily, still praises God as the One who revives the dead. The Messiah is the promise to the fathers: Abraham’s offspring (Genesis 22:18) and David’s everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16). And the redemption of Israel is the prophets’ great restoration hope (Isaiah 40–66; Ezekiel 36–37). Paul’s claim is simply that this whole age-old, daily-prayed hope has been answered in the risen Jesus.

Can I pray for something for years and miss it when it comes? Yes, and this verse is a warning. God often answers in a form we did not expect, and if we have fixed in our minds exactly how the answer must look, we may resist it when it arrives. Many in Israel expected a Messiah who would conquer Rome; God sent one who conquered sin and death by dying. Pray humbly, holding your requests open to God’s wisdom. And search the Scriptures to learn what he has actually promised, so that you recognise his answer, which is always, in the end, more of Christ.

For worship. The twelve tribes worshipped night and day, and God was not deaf to one of their prayers. Luke shows us where the waiting led: an old widow in the temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day, looked on an infant brought there by his parents and began to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:37–38). The centuries of prayer had a face. God gave more than Israel dared to ask, a King who has conquered death, so that the hope of the fathers is now the living hope of everyone who trusts him.

parallels.desc: because of the hope of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "'Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? Paul turns, mid-speech, and asks a question, and the Greek is plural. Any of you. He is no longer speaking only to the king. He has turned to the whole hall: the tribunes, the leading men of Caesarea, the governor, Jews and Gentiles alike. He puts one question to a room full of pagans and a Jewish monarch, and then goes straight back to his story without waiting for a reply. The question is not a debating trick. It is asking people to state their actual objection.

Not the hard part. If there is a God at all, the Creator who gives life and breath to all (17:25) and made the heavens and the earth out of nothing, then raising one dead man is not the hard part. A God who can start life from nothing can certainly restart it. So the question is not whether resurrection is possible, but whether God is God. Anyone who grants a Creator has already granted the harder thing.

What would follow if it were true. When someone says the resurrection is impossible, ask what would follow if it were true. If a dead man walked out of a tomb in Jerusalem, then he is who he said he is, and the universe has an owner, and everyone in it has an appointment. Honest people do have real questions about the evidence, and they deserve real answers; Paul gives his own list of witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8. But for some, the case against the resurrection is less an argument about evidence than a preference about consequences, wearing an argument’s clothes. Paul knew that from the inside, which is why the very next sentence is about himself.

I myself was convinced. Paul admits he once thought it incredible too, at least of Jesus. He was convinced that opposing Jesus was a duty. His conscience was fully engaged, and it was pointing the wrong way. A man can be sincere, devout and at peace with himself, and be at war with God. Sincerity is not a defence. Paul’s was total, and it made him more dangerous rather than less.

God’s verdict on the name. Saul opposed the name because he was sure God had disowned the man: a Messiah does not die on a Roman cross. The resurrection reversed that verdict in public. Jesus was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). If God raises the dead, and if he raised this man, then the name Saul fought is the name God has vindicated, and the persecutor was fighting God. The resurrection is God’s answer to everyone who has ever said no to Jesus.

How do I know my own convictions are not wrong, as Paul’s were? By testing them against Scripture, not against the strength of your feelings. The Bereans checked even Paul’s preaching against the Scriptures daily (17:11). Ask whether your conviction exalts Christ or opposes him, whether it agrees with the plain teaching of God’s Word, and whether it produces love, humility and holiness or pride and harshness. Be willing to hear correction from mature believers. And pray, as the psalmist did, that God would search you and see if there is any grievous way in you (Psalm 139:23–24). A conscience must be taught by God’s Word to be a safe guide.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many of the saints. Nothing compelled it; no prosecutor has raised his past. Paul volunteers the worst thing about himself to a king, in detail. Many of the saints: he calls his victims saints, God’s holy people. Back then he would have called them heretics.

I cast my vote. The Greek is a voting idiom, literally I cast down a pebble, the stone dropped into an urn to register a verdict, a dark pebble for condemnation. Whether he was formally a council member the text does not settle. It does give a plural: when they were put to death. That suggests Stephen was not the only one, though Luke tells us only of him.

Tried to make them blaspheme. The verb is imperfect: he kept trying, repeatedly, as a method. This is pain applied to force Christians to curse Christ, persecution attacking the soul. Some eighty years later the Roman governor Pliny wrote that he released anyone who would curse Christ, since none of the real Christians could be made to do it.

In raging fury. The phrase is perissōs emmainomenos, exceedingly mad, and the verb is from mainomai, to rave, to be out of one’s mind. In thirteen verses Festus will shout that Paul is out of his mind, from the same root (v. 24), and Paul has already answered him. The madness in this story was not the preaching of a risen Christ. It was a brilliant, devout, exactingly trained man in a raging fury, dragging women out of their houses in the name of God (8:3). He would call himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).

Why say it to a king? Because Paul is not building a character reference; he is building an argument, and his own biography is the evidence. Something turned that man into this one. No education did it, no disappointment did it, no gradual softening did it. In a moment he will name what did: the risen Jesus on the road.

The name they would not curse. Saul tried to force the saints to call Jesus accursed, and he very probably believed it himself. A man hanged on a tree was under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23), and to a Pharisee a crucified Messiah was a contradiction. What the risen Lord taught him was that the curse was real and that Jesus had borne it, not for any sin of his own: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The man who pressed Christians to curse Christ would later write that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says Jesus is accursed (1 Corinthians 12:3). He had learned whose curse it was, and whose blessing it bought.

The freedom of the forgiven. A man who has genuinely received mercy loses the need to manage his own reputation. Paul can say the worst about himself calmly, in public, to power, without flinching or excusing, not because the sin was small, but because the pardon is settled. People still uncertain of their forgiveness edit. The freedom to tell the truth about your own past is one of the quieter proofs that grace has actually landed. A person who knows God has forgiven him no longer needs other people’s good opinion to feel safe, because it is God who justifies, and no one else can condemn (Romans 8:33–34).

Can God forgive someone who has done something truly terrible? Yes. Paul had helped to kill Christians, and Christ forgave him completely and made him an apostle. He says that he received mercy precisely so that Christ might display his perfect patience in him as an example to those who would believe (1 Timothy 1:16). There is no sin so great that the blood of Christ cannot cleanse it, for those who repent and believe. Forgiveness does not erase earthly consequences, and where it is possible, the forgiven person should make things right. But the guilt before God is gone, and no past can cancel the welcome of Christ. And if that seems unfair to the people he hurt, remember that grace is always unfair in our favour: no one is forgiven because he deserved it, the respectable no more than the violent (Romans 3:22–24).

Should I tell other people about my past sins? Not everything to everyone. Paul told his story where it served the gospel and glorified Christ, not to dwell on the sin or to shock. Confess your sins fully to God; confess to those you have wronged, and seek their forgiveness. Share your past more widely only when it will help others see the grace of Christ, and with wisdom about who is listening and what details are fitting. The aim is always to make much of the Saviour, never of the sin.

For worship. Saul dropped his dark pebble into the urn against the saints, and the Judge of all the earth dropped none against Saul. The verdict he deserved fell instead on the Christ he hated, who bore the condemnation of the persecutor and then met him on the road with a pardon. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20). Blessed be the Lord whose love is stronger than our fury, and whose pardon is so complete that his people can tell the truth about themselves without fear.
verseByVerse.note: “Cast my vote” may mean he voted as a member of a council, or simply that he approved of the executions.

verseByVerse.quote: "'In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Authority and commission. The word for commission is epitropē, a delegated authority, a warrant. It was no private vendetta: the prosecution’s own institution issued the warrants. Then he met a higher authority.

At midday. Two details, chosen for the man in the chair; the first he had given the crowd too (22:6), the second is new. At midday: not dusk or a lonely vigil, but the hour when nothing looks mysterious. Brighter than the sun: under the fiercest natural light his world knew, something outshone it, and it was not of this order of things at all. It was the glory of the risen Christ, the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Those who journeyed with me. He argues like a witness rather than a mystic: something objective happened on that road at noon in front of company.

The third telling. The three tellings (9:1–19; 22:3–21; and here) differ in emphasis, not in substance. To a Jewish crowd Paul made Ananias the hinge, because a devout man of good reputation in Damascus was everything to that audience. To a king, Ananias disappears entirely, and the commission comes straight from the mouth of the risen Christ on the road. Paul does what every honest preacher does: he tells the same true story with the part the hearer most needs. A king needs to know who gave the orders.

Does Jesus still appear to people like this today? Not in the way he appeared to Paul. Paul’s vision of the risen Christ was part of his unique calling as an apostle, and he calls himself the last to whom Christ appeared in that way (1 Corinthians 15:8). God now speaks to us through his completed Word, and he brings people to faith through the preaching of Christ (Romans 10:14–17). We hear stories, sometimes from places with little access to the Bible, of people dreaming of Jesus, and Christians assess such claims charitably and differently. But any experience must be tested by Scripture and must lead a person to the Scriptures and to the church. You do not need a light from heaven: in the gospel you have the same Christ who met Paul.

For worship. At noon, under a burning sky, the Lord of glory let a sliver of his brightness through, and it outshone the sun. John saw the same face on Patmos, like the sun shining in full strength (Revelation 1:16), and fell at his feet as though dead, as Saul fell in the dust. One day the city of God will have no need of sun or moon, because the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23). The light that blinded the persecutor will be the everlasting day of the redeemed.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We had all fallen. Three things appear only in this telling. At 9:7 the companions stood speechless; a party knocked flat does not stay flat. The falling is itself the point: this is what happens when sinners meet the holy God. Ezekiel fell on his face before the glory (Ezekiel 1:28), Isaiah cried out that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5), and here a whole travelling party lies in the dust at noon because the risen Jesus has shown a little of his glory.

In the Hebrew language. This is the detail Paul saved for a Jewish king. The Hebrew language here most likely means Aramaic, the everyday tongue of the Jews of Palestine. The risen and glorified Christ, enthroned at the right hand of God, blazing brighter than the Syrian noon, speaks the language of Galilean villages and Jerusalem streets. He did not shed his humanity at the resurrection. The man who is Lord of all still speaks like a man from Nazareth.

Kick against the goads. A goad was a long pole tipped with iron, used to drive oxen. If the animal resented it and lashed backwards, its own kick drove the point deeper. The proverb was well known in the Greek world for resisting the gods, so both halves of the room could follow. Readers of the KJV or NKJV will also find this saying at 9:5; it is there only in later manuscripts, and the earliest have it only here, which is why modern Bibles print it only in this chapter.

A goad you have felt. Its first meaning is that resisting God hurts only the one who resists. Many hear more, fairly: you cannot kick against a goad you have never felt. The persecution had been hurting the persecutor.

What the goads were. Scripture does not say what the goads were, and it would be wrong to pretend otherwise. But in the chapters before Saul’s conversion Luke has laid things in front of us, and it is hard not to notice them: a face like an angel’s in a courtroom (6:15); a dying man praying for his killers, out loud, while Saul held the coats (7:58–60); people who would not curse the name however hard they were pressed; and behind it all the uncomfortable possibility, for a man trained to read Moses and the prophets exactly, that these people might be right. He would have called it noise. It was a goad.

The kicking does the damage. There are people who have been arguing with something for years: a verse that will not leave, a memory of a Christian who was inexplicably kind, a suspicion at three in the morning that the case for meaninglessness is weaker than they say in daylight. It is easy to kick at it harder. The Lord’s word to Saul is that the kicking is what is doing the damage. The goad was never the injury. It was the mercy. Paul kicked, and Christ conquered him. Grace does not drag us in against our will. It is effectual, which means it always achieves what God intends: it changes the will itself, so that we come willingly (Philippians 2:13).

If grace is effectual, why does God plead with people at all? Because God’s pleading is one of the means by which his grace works. He does not save people like stones, but as persons, through his Word: he speaks, warns, invites and goads, and by his Spirit he makes the heart willing to hear (John 6:44–45; 2 Timothy 2:25). The invitations of the gospel are sincere, and everyone who comes will be received (John 6:37). And when someone does come, it is because God first drew him. That is why we pray for unbelievers and keep speaking to them: the goads are God’s, and he uses them.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything God has been pressing on you for a long time, a sin to give up, a person to forgive, a step of obedience, a truth you keep arguing with? Stop kicking. The hand on the goad belongs to the Saviour who bore your curse, and his Spirit makes the yielding possible: name it before him today.
verseByVerse.note: A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; kicking against it only hurt the ox. It was a Greek proverb for resisting fate — or here, God.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said, "I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who are you, Lord? I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. Saul asks the shortest and most important question a human being can ask, and he gets a name in reply, as before (9:5). Not a title. Not a description of divine glory. A name belonging to a man from a village in Galilee whom Saul knew perfectly well to be dead, and whose followers he was at that moment travelling to arrest.

Whom you are persecuting. Present tense, and not whose people: the Lord of glory says that to lay hands on a believer in Damascus is to lay hands on him. It is the seed of everything Paul would later write about the church as the body of Christ: the Head feels every blow struck at his members. The point for Agrippa is simpler and harder: the man you all agree was executed is speaking, and he is taking the arrests personally.

Rise and stand upon your feet. The words are Ezekiel’s. Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you (Ezekiel 2:1), spoken to a man flat on his face before the glory of God, who is then sent to a rebellious people. Paul is being commissioned in the language of the prophets, and a king who knows his Scriptures would hear it.

Servant and witness. The two words that define the rest of his life. The first is hypēretēs, an assistant, a man under orders. The second is martys, a witness, one who testifies. A witness has no freedom to improve the account. It is the plainest possible description of a preacher, and it is the reason Paul could say later that he decided to know nothing among the Corinthians except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). In this account, Paul compresses Ananias’s words into Jesus’ own, since they came from Jesus.

Those in which I will appear to you. The Damascus road was not the last of it. There would be more revelations to come: the night vision at Corinth (18:9), the Lord in the temple (22:17), the Lord standing by him in the barracks (23:11), and whatever it was he could not put into words (2 Corinthians 12:1–4). Christ was not commissioning him from a distance and leaving him to it.

When was Paul born again? Readers have long asked whether Paul was already regenerate as he answered Who are you, Lord? Scripture does not pin the moment. The marks of a heart already being turned are plainly present, and the certain thing is not the when but the who: sovereign grace seized the persecutor. To be born again means to be given new spiritual life by the Holy Spirit, a new heart that loves God instead of resisting him (John 3:3–8; Ezekiel 36:26). Whenever it happened in Saul, it was God’s work from first to last (John 1:13).

Am I a servant and witness too, if I am not an apostle? Yes, in your own measure. Paul’s commission was unique: he was an eyewitness of the risen Christ, sent with apostolic authority. But every Christian is called to serve Christ under orders and to bear witness to what he has done (1 Peter 2:9; 3:15). You are not asked to be original or impressive. You are asked to tell the truth about Jesus as Scripture reveals him and as you have known him: what he has done, who he is, and what he has done for you. A witness only reports. That frees you from the pressure to persuade by your own cleverness.

For worship. The Lord who said to Saul, Rise and stand upon your feet, had himself lain in a tomb and risen from it. He lifts his fallen enemy from the dust and gives him work to do. He was himself the Servant of the LORD and the faithful witness (Revelation 1:5), and he makes servants and witnesses out of rebels. He answers persecution with a commission.

verseByVerse.quote: "'delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Delivering you. It is not the promise we would have written. The word exairoumenos here means rescuing out of, which presupposes being in. It is protection of the kind Jeremiah was promised (Jeremiah 1:8). And that is exactly how it went. He was stoned, flogged, shipwrecked, imprisoned and, as the early church remembered, executed in Rome. Every rescue happened, and not one of them was an exemption. Paul was delivered out of things, never spared them.

To open their eyes. The fullest statement of the commission in Acts, in five clauses. To open their eyes: not to inform people, but to make blind people see. The assumption underneath is that the human problem is not primarily a shortage of information. Paul had all the information and was blind, and Paul, struck blind, was sent to open eyes.

From darkness to light. A change of realm, not of opinion. In a life it looks like this: before, a person does not know God and does not want to; afterwards he knows him, loves him and begins to walk in his ways, not perfectly but truly. God has called his people out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9).

From the power of Satan to God. Modern readers skip this clause. The New Testament says people are not neutral: they are held. Mostly in the ordinary machinery of self-interest, appetite, fear of what people think, and the settled conviction that one’s life is one’s own. It is a real dominion with a real ruler, and getting out of it is not a matter of trying harder. Conversion is a change of kingdom: God has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13).

Receive forgiveness. Receive: the posture of someone with open hands, not someone settling an account. This is the first gift.

A place among those sanctified. A place: the word is klēros, a lot, an inheritance, a share, a seat at the table with the holy ones. Sanctified: set apart as God’s holy people. And the ground of it, stated last so nobody can mistake it, is not works or law, but faith in me. It is a summary of the gospel from the lips of Jesus himself.

The Servant’s commission. A light for the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon: that is Isaiah, describing the task of the Servant of the LORD (Isaiah 42:6–7, 16). Christ takes the Servant’s own commission and hands it to Saul of Tarsus. What the Messiah was sent to do, he now sends this man to do in his name.

Does being under Satan’s power excuse unbelievers? No. Scripture holds together two truths: people are held captive by the devil (2 Timothy 2:26), and they love the darkness and choose it (John 3:19). Satan’s rule is not something done to unwilling victims; it is a rule people prefer, because it lets them keep their lives as their own. That is why no one is excused, and also why no one can free himself. Only Christ, the stronger man, can bind the strong man and set his captives free (Luke 11:21–22). This should make us humble about our own conversion and full of hope for others.

What does sanctified by faith mean here? It means set apart as God’s own, made holy in status, at the moment of faith. In the New Testament sanctification has two sides. There is the once-for-all setting apart of the believer, so that every Christian is a saint (1 Corinthians 6:11). And there is the lifelong work of the Spirit making us actually more holy (1 Thessalonians 4:3; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Here Jesus speaks of the first: by faith in him, a person is given a place among God’s holy people. The second follows, and the first is its foundation.

For worship. The risen Christ fetches people out of the dark, not by improving them but by moving them. He forgives the sort of man who had been dragging his followers out of their homes, and gives him a share in the inheritance of the saints. The whole chain, from the opened eye to the place at the table, is the work of the Lord Jesus Christ upon people who were doing nothing but resisting him, and there is no other explanation for a single Christian who has ever lived.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ commission echoes the calling of Isaiah’s Servant.

parallels.desc: to open the eyes that are blind

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not disobedient to the heavenly vision. It is a remarkable understatement, and the understatement is the point. Roughly twenty-five years, three missionary journeys, churches in a dozen cities, floggings, a stoning, three shipwrecks and daily anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:23–28): I was not disobedient. There is no sense of achievement in it, and no self-pity either. Just a man reporting that he did as he was told.

First to those in Damascus. Trace the geography and you are looking at the outline of the book: Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and the end of the earth (1:8). One honest question: Paul tells the Galatians that in his early years the churches of Judea did not know him by sight (Galatians 1:22). The likeliest answer is that here he is summing up his whole ministry, including later visits and the believers who heard him in Jerusalem (9:28–29; 15:3), not describing the first weeks after his conversion.

Obedience to a person. The heavenly vision was the risen Jesus, and what Paul preached is the very commission the risen Lord gave his disciples: that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47). Repentance in Paul’s mouth is never a self-improvement scheme. It is turning to God through Christ, in his name, toward a forgiveness he has already purchased. The call to repent is good news because of who stands behind it.

Deeds in keeping with their repentance. Repent: change your mind. Turn to God: change your direction. And then do things that match, as John the Baptist preached (Luke 3:8). Deeds do not save; they show that repentance is real. Paul is not saying the deeds earn the turning; he spent whole letters demolishing that. Justification, God’s verdict that a sinner stands righteous before him, rests on Christ’s righteousness counted to the one who trusts him, never on the sinner’s own record (Romans 4:5). He is saying the deeds demonstrate it. By grace you have been saved through faith, not a result of works, and then, in the very next breath, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:8–10). The works are not the root. They are the fruit, and a tree with no fruit on it after several seasons invites an honest question about the root.

Where Christians differ: faith and works. Some think Paul and James contradict each other on faith and works. This commentary’s view: Paul teaches that we are justified by faith alone (Romans 3:28), and here, that true repentance produces fitting deeds. Works are not the root but the fruit (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:18). Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone.
