Name one. Repentance in the New Testament is specific: name one thing. A conversation you have been avoiding because you were in the wrong. Money that is not yours. A habit conducted privately. A person you have written off. What is the deed that would be in keeping with the repentance you would say you have? If nothing comes to mind, ask God quietly to show you; and if a great deal comes to mind and you feel crushed by it, remember that wanting to turn is already his work in you.

What if I have repented but keep falling into the same sin? Then keep repenting, and do not despair. Repentance is not a single act at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life. A believer may struggle with the same sin for years, as Paul himself describes (Romans 7:15–25). The question is not whether you ever fall, but whether you hate the sin, confess it, and fight it, using the means God gives: prayer, Scripture, accountability and removing what feeds it (1 John 1:8–9). Fitting deeds include getting up again. And remember that your standing with God rests on Christ’s obedience, not on your record of victory.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass:'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason. Paul puts the cause plainly: this, the Gentile mission, the opened eyes, the place among the sanctified given to outsiders by faith, is why they tried to kill him. Not the resurrection in the abstract, but with the door left open: a risen Messiah who welcomes Gentiles on the same terms as Jews, by faith, without first making them Jews (15:9–11).

The help that comes from God. The word epikouria, only here in the New Testament, carried a military flavour: reinforcements arriving for a position under pressure. Paul does not say he has been resilient; he says help arrived from outside.

To this day. That phrase gathers up a list: the basket over the Damascus wall, the stoning at Lystra, the prison at Philippi, the mob in the temple, the forty men and their oath. Every one of those should have ended the story, and Paul’s account of why it did not is one word: help came. Perseverance does not feel like strength of character from the inside. It feels like being kept, like arriving at the end of another week still believing, and being unable to identify a single heroic decision that accounts for it.

The ally who stood by him. The help had a name. A few sentences earlier Paul quoted the risen Christ’s promise on the road: delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles (26:17). Every rescue was that promise kept (18:10; 23:11). The reinforcements that kept arriving were not luck or stamina. They were the risen Jesus keeping his word to the man he had sent.

Both to small and great. He is standing in front of a king, a governor, the tribunes and the aristocracy of a Roman capital, and he mentions the small first. Slaves and kings alike; today, the great. He had said the same things to a jailer at midnight and to women at a riverside. The gospel Paul preached to Agrippa is the gospel he preached to the man who guarded him.

Nothing but what the prophets and Moses said. And here is the heart of his whole defence. Paul claims not to have added a syllable. Everything he preaches, he insists, was already in the books read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath (15:21), books Agrippa himself knew well. The charge against him is innovation; his answer is that he is the conservative in the room, and his accusers are the ones who have stopped believing their own Scriptures.

How do I experience God’s help today? Usually not in dramatic rescues, though God can give them, but in being kept: given strength for the day, grace to endure, wisdom at the moment you need it, the encouragement of a friend, a promise from Scripture that comes alive, a door that opens or closes. God has promised never to leave or forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5–6), and his grace is sufficient in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Ask for his help specifically in prayer, and then look back regularly and notice where it came. Most believers, when they look back honestly, can say what Paul said: to this day, I have had help from God.

For worship. They were all speaking of him. Moses at the burning bush and the passover lamb; the seed of Abraham in whom the nations would be blessed; David’s son on a throne that would not end; the child born in Bethlehem, too small a town to matter; the Servant with no beauty that we should desire him, despised and rejected, wounded for transgressions not his own, silent before his shearers, numbered with the transgressors, and afterwards seeing the light of life and being satisfied. Some thousand years of writing, all of it converging on one week in Jerusalem and one man walking out of a tomb. The whole library was about him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.' And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, 'Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
That the Christ must suffer. This is the summit of the speech. That the Christ must suffer: the must is doing enormous work. For most first-century Jewish expectation, a suffering Messiah was not merely unexpected; it came close to being a contradiction in terms. The Messiah was the one who ended suffering, not the one who absorbed it. The suffering was the appointment, and the Scriptures foretold a suffering Messiah (Isaiah 53; Psalm 22). The Lord himself made the same point on the Emmaus road: “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26; see 24:46).

The first to rise from the dead. Others had been raised before: the widow’s son, Jairus’s daughter, Lazarus. But every one of them died again. Christ is the first to rise and stay risen, out the far side of death permanently, in a body that cannot die. That is why Paul elsewhere calls him the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20, 23) and the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18): not the only sheaf, but the first of a harvest, and the guarantee that the rest is coming.

What did Paul mean by proclaim light? Not a vague glow of enlightenment, but something concrete: God’s saving rescue dawning on a world sunk in darkness. Paul is not coining an image; he is quoting Isaiah. The very phrase, light to our people and to the Gentiles, is the language of the Servant Songs, the passages in Isaiah about the Lord’s chosen Servant: “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6); a light for the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners (Isaiah 42:6–7). In Isaiah, light stands with three things: salvation, the opening of blind eyes, the freeing of prisoners. That is what the light is: God’s saving deliverance, sight for the blind, rescue for those in the dark.

The sunrise. Paul had already applied Isaiah 49:6 to his mission (13:47), and his commission was to turn people from darkness to light (26:18). The engine of the verse is that Christ proclaims light by being the first to rise from the dead: the resurrection itself is the sunrise, new-creation life breaking over the grave (Isaiah 9:2; 60:1–3).

Where did Moses and the prophets say this? Paul does not list the texts, but the apostles preached from them: the suffering servant of Isaiah 52:13–53:12 and the sufferer of Psalm 22 for the death; Psalm 16:8–11 (compare 2:25–31; 13:35) and Isaiah 53:10–12 for the resurrection; and the promise to bless the nations through Abraham and to make the servant a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6; compare 13:47).

Simeon’s song. Luke opened his Gospel with old Simeon lifting the infant Jesus and calling him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel” (Luke 2:32), again Isaiah 49, again light for Gentiles and Israel. What Simeon sang at the cradle, Paul declares at the climax of the mission: the same Isaianic light, for the same two peoples. So the reader can hold this: Christ crucified and risen is God’s promised light, salvation, sight and life, now streaming to Jew and Gentile alike. For everyone who has ever sat in a long inward darkness, this is the gospel: the Light has come, and his name is Jesus.

Why must the Christ suffer? Because there was no other way to save sinners: God’s justice required that sin be punished, his love purposed to save, and at the cross Christ bore in our place the penalty our sins deserved (Isaiah 53:5–6). (See Luke 9:22 for the fuller answer.)

Is it not unjust for God to punish the innocent in place of the guilty? That would be unjust if Christ were an unwilling third party dragged in from outside. But he is God the Son, who came willingly and laid down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). The Judge did not punish a stranger. God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins, the sacrifice that takes the full weight of his just anger and so removes it (1 John 4:10). And those who trust Christ are joined to him, so that his death really counts as theirs (Romans 6:5–8). The cross is not injustice. It is the holy God satisfying his own justice at his own cost.

You are out of your mind. The governor loses his composure and interrupts a prisoner mid-sentence. Luke does not say which phrase provoked him, but the likeliest is the resurrection, not the light for the Gentiles, which no Roman would mind. Most educated Greeks and Romans found bodily resurrection absurd (17:32). His diagnosis is almost affectionate: your great learning, literally your many letters, is driving you mad. Festus has decided that Paul is a scholar who has read himself into a delusion. It is the oldest way of not answering an argument: locate a cause for the belief and you need not examine the reasons for it. He is saying not that Paul is wrong but that he is unwell, which is easier. Jesus too was called mad (Mark 3:21; John 10:20).
verseByVerse.note: Most educated Greeks and Romans found bodily resurrection absurd.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said, 'I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Most excellent Festus. Told in public that he is insane, Paul neither loses his temper nor grovels. He addresses Festus by his correct title, most excellent, the formal style of address for a governor, and then flatly denies the charge. He gives the office its honour and gives the accusation nothing at all.

True and rational words. True (alētheias): factually true, words of truth. Rational (sōphrosynēs): soundness of mind, sober judgment. It is the exact opposite of mania, the word Festus has just thrown at him. He claims the opposite virtue, in the vocabulary the room respects, and he has already answered the charge: the only madness in this story was the persecutor’s raging fury (v. 11), and it ended on the Damascus road.

The king knows about these things. Agrippa knew the facts. He is not being asked to accept a private experience he has no way of assessing. He is being asked about recent, public, checkable history in his own territory.

Not done in a corner. It has been a mainstay of Christian apologetics ever since. The mystery religions of the ancient world did their business in corners: secret rites, private initiations, truths for insiders that could never be checked. Paul says his message is the opposite kind of thing. The life, death and resurrection of Jesus happened in public, under a Roman governor whose name is on record, in front of hostile witnesses who were still alive. Christianity stakes everything on a claim about a particular execution and a particular tomb, in a particular week, in a city you can still walk around. Paul was asking for that to be investigated.

Is faith opposed to reason? No. Biblical faith is not believing without evidence or against it; it is trusting God on the basis of what he has shown and said. Paul reasons here from history and from Scripture, and the New Testament everywhere appeals to witnesses and facts (Luke 1:1–4; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8; 1 John 1:1–3). Faith goes beyond what reason alone can reach, because it is personal trust in Christ worked by the Spirit, but it is never unreasonable. Christians are to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in them, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

For worship. The Lord Jesus told the high priest that he had spoken openly to the world and said nothing in secret (John 18:20), and he saved the world the same way: on a hill outside the city, under a notice written, John tells us, in three languages for every passer-by to read (John 19:20). The last act will not be done in a corner either: he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7).

verseByVerse.quote: "'King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.' And Agrippa said to Paul, 'In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe. Paul turns from the governor, who has just called him mad, and puts a direct question to the king, and then does not wait for the answer. He supplies it himself. It is the boldest moment in the speech, and it is also a beautifully laid trap, though not a cruel one. Consider Agrippa’s position. If he says yes, I believe the prophets, he has conceded the entire argument, because Paul has just spent twenty verses demonstrating that the prophets promised a suffering and rising Messiah who would bring light to the Gentiles. If he says no, he has publicly renounced the Scriptures in front of the Jewish subjects whose high priest he appoints, with Roman officers listening. He can neither affirm nor deny. So he does the third thing.

In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian? The Greek here, en oligō, is genuinely ambiguous, and honesty requires saying so. It can mean in a little time, and it can mean with little effort, by a little argument. The ESV notes that the question can also be read: in a short time would you persuade me to act like a Christian? The King James took it as degree and gave us the famous rendering, almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian; most modern translations take it as time. The tone is not recoverable from the page. Read one way it is a courtroom deflection with a smile in it, probably ironic or evasive: do you think you can make me a Christian so quickly? Read another, it is the nearest a Herod ever came. The old rendering became a famous hymn and sermon, but probably misreads him.

Christian. What is not ambiguous is the word he reaches for. It appears only three times in the New Testament: coined as a nickname at Antioch (11:26), used by Peter of those who suffer under it (1 Peter 4:16), and here, on the lips of a king, almost certainly with an edge on it. Agrippa will not name the man; he names the party. Either way, he changed the subject, and a few sentences later he stood up and left.

Moses, the prophets and one risen from the dead. To believe the prophets is to be pointed at Jesus, who said that if they believed Moses, they would believe him, for Moses wrote of him (John 5:46). This scene almost acts out the story of the rich man and Lazarus, where Abraham says: If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). Here is a king who knows Moses and the Prophets, hearing a witness of the one who did rise, and he deflects. The prophets and the risen Christ speak with one voice, and the heart that will not hear the one will not hear the other.

Almost persuaded. Whatever Agrippa’s tone, the old rendering has fixed on a tragic spiritual place. To be almost persuaded, interested, impressed, moved, near the kingdom, is still to be on the wrong side of the line; almost saved is wholly lost. Many perish not as scoffers but as the almost: those who came close, admired the gospel, felt its pull, hesitated, and never crossed over. Paul longs that they would become not almost, but altogether, such as he is (v. 29). And do not mistake weak faith for almost. A trembling believer who clings to Christ, doubts and all, has crossed the line; the almost are those who admire Christ and will not come to him, and anyone who wants to come is welcome today (John 6:37).

How should I respond when someone deflects the gospel with a joke? Gently, and without letting it close the door, as Paul does in the next verse. Smile, take the humour in good part, and then return kindly to the real question: but what do you actually think of Jesus? Humour is often a shield people raise when a subject gets too close. Do not attack the shield or force your way past it. Show that you care more about the person than about winning the exchange, and leave the door open for another time. Then pray, because only God can turn a deflection into a question.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the question can also be read “In a short time would you persuade me to act like a Christian?” “Christian” was still a nickname used by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains.' Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whether short or long. A king makes a joke, and the awkward moment should pass. Paul does not let it. Whether short or long: he picks up the king’s phrase and refuses the exit. Little or much, quickly or slowly, it does not matter to me; what I want is the thing itself.

He prays out loud. In a Roman audience hall, on trial, Paul prays out loud. I would to God is not a figure of speech; it is a wish addressed to God in the hearing of everyone present. He stops arguing and starts interceding, in public, for the man judging him.

Such as I am. He owns nothing, everyone in that room outranks him, and he is bound for Nero. He looks around at the king in his state and Bernice in her jewels, and what he feels is not envy. It is pity. He wishes every one of them had what he has. He was richer than all of them: forgiven, free in soul, a child of God. By the grace of God he was what he was (1 Corinthians 15:10), and grace was the one thing in that room he could give away.

Except for these chains. A kind clause, with a touch of grace and wit; he may well have lifted his chained hands. It tells you what he was asking for: not sympathy or release, but Christ, and he was careful to specify that he was not wishing his suffering on them, only his Lord. And it tells you the chains were on his mind. He knows exactly what he is wearing and mentions it lightly, without complaint, as the one part of his life he would not pass on.

Then the king rose. Nobody answers. A direct appeal, and the response is not a refutation but an adjournment. That is how many people decline Christ, then and now. Not with an objection, which at least takes the thing seriously, but by finding that the hour is late and there are other matters and the conversation has reached a natural close. Agrippa did not say no; the standing was the answer. He heard the gospel from the apostle to the Gentiles, and walked away.

Is it proud to wish that others would become like me? It would be proud if Paul meant his personality, achievements or opinions. He means his faith in Christ, his forgiveness, his standing as a child of God: things he received as a gift and did not earn. Paul could say, be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), because what he wanted others to copy was his Saviour. A Christian should long for others to have what he has in Christ, and this is not pride but love. The test is whether you would gladly see them surpass you, as long as they have Christ.

For worship. Paul wished them everything he had except his chains. Christ wished us everything he had and took the chains himself. He was bound in the garden and led bound to the high priest (John 18:12, 24), and he bore the sentence our sin had earned, so that his people might have all of him and none of what they deserved. Every throne in that hall was poorer than Paul’s cell, because Christ was in the cell. The Lord gives himself to his people, and with himself, everything.

parallels.desc: an ambassador in chains

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, 'This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.' And Agrippa said to Festus, 'This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Doing nothing to deserve death. The verdict is delivered in the corridor, after the doors have closed, where it costs nothing and changes nothing. That is at least the fifth time (18:14–15; 23:29; 25:18, 25–27). Now a Jewish king, a Roman governor and the senior officers of the garrison agree among themselves that the prisoner has done nothing at all. It is just as it was with Jesus before Pilate and Herod (Luke 23:14–15). Christianity was investigated repeatedly by the authorities best placed to convict it, and the file kept coming back empty.

Could have been set free. Legally, Agrippa is very probably right. Once a citizen’s appeal to the emperor had been formally registered, releasing the prisoner would have been at the least an affront to Caesar. The case belonged to Rome. So the natural reading is that Paul made a mistake: that he was a few weeks too quick, and talked himself out of an acquittal.

The appeal was the road. Except that the reader knows something Agrippa does not. Two years earlier the Lord had stood beside him in a barracks cell in the dark and said he must testify also in Rome (23:11). The appeal was not a miscalculation. Released in Caesarea, Paul walks out into a province where a standing conspiracy has already sworn to kill him and where the leadership has twice tried to have him moved somewhere they could reach. What looked like the closing of a door was, in fact, the only route to the city he had been promised, and he would travel it at imperial expense, under armed guard, as a protected prisoner of the state. Paul’s chains would carry the gospel to the capital of the world and into the emperor’s own guard (Philippians 1:12–13, if, as most think, that letter was written from Rome).

Another prisoner who could have gone free. Luke’s readers had heard this before. Pilate, too, wanted to release a prisoner he knew to be innocent, and said so to the crowd (Luke 23:20). Jesus could have gone free, by Pilate’s wish or by a single word in his own defence. He did not, and Barabbas walked out instead (Luke 23:25). The difference is that Paul’s chains were laid on him, while Christ took his of his own will. No one takes my life from me, he had said; I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). The one who could have been set free stayed bound, so that the guilty could be released.

Right verdict, wrong question. Agrippa has just delivered the correct verdict on Paul, and walked out of the room without dealing with a word Paul said. He got the legal question right and the only question that mattered wrong. He pronounced the prisoner free, and left as the one still bound. Luke does not tell us why, but a king had much to lose: a Herod who bowed to a crucified Jew would forfeit the favour of Rome and the respect of the priests he appointed in a single afternoon. Position, approval and comfort are strong chains, and they are invisible to the man who wears them.

In the flow. These verses close the trial narrative of chapters 21 to 26 with a Jewish king’s verdict, and the appeal points forward to Rome (28:31). The chains do not stop the word; they carry it.

What if a decision I made seems to have closed a good door? Bring it to God honestly, and remember Paul. A choice that looks like a mistake may be the very road God intends. If you acted in good faith and with prayer, trust that the Lord, who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11), has not been taken by surprise. If you acted wrongly, confess it, and know that God weaves even our failures into his purposes for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Either way, do not live in endless second-guessing. Ask what faithfulness looks like now, on the road you are actually on.
verseByVerse.note: Luke repeatedly shows Roman officials finding Paul innocent.

26.title: Paul Before Agrippa
26.text: <sup>1</sup>So Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: <sup>2</sup>“I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews, <sup>3</sup>especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently. <sup>4</sup>My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. <sup>5</sup>They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee. <sup>6</sup>And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, <sup>7</sup>to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king! <sup>8</sup>Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? <sup>9</sup>I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth. <sup>10</sup>And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. <sup>11</sup>And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities. <sup>12</sup>In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. <sup>13</sup>At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me. <sup>14</sup>And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ <sup>15</sup>And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. <sup>16</sup>But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you, <sup>17</sup>delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles—to whom I am sending you <sup>18</sup>to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, <sup>20</sup>but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance. <sup>21</sup>For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. <sup>22</sup>To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass: <sup>23</sup>that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.” <sup>24</sup>And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.” <sup>25</sup>But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. <sup>26</sup>For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner. <sup>27</sup>King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” <sup>28</sup>And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” <sup>29</sup>And Paul said, “Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am—except for these chains.” <sup>30</sup>Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them. <sup>31</sup>And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, “This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.” <sup>32</sup>And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
26.overview: This is Paul’s fullest defence, given before King Agrippa II, Bernice, the governor Festus and the leading men of Caesarea, and the third account of his conversion in Acts. Paul presents his whole life as one story of Israel’s hope: the strict Pharisee and persecutor, the risen Jesus on the Damascus road, the commission to open the eyes of Jews and Gentiles, and a message that says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets foretold. Festus calls him mad, Agrippa deflects, and the officials agree he has done nothing wrong.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Setting Sail and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The voyage runs from Caesarea along the coast to Myra, where Paul’s party boards an Alexandrian grain ship (vv. 1–6); slowly, against the wind, to Fair Havens on Crete, where Paul’s warning is outvoted (vv. 7–12); then into the northeaster, which drives the ship for many days until all hope is lost (vv. 13–20). The section ends with Paul standing up among them with an angel’s promise: the ship will be lost, but not one life (vv. 21–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
What God Actually Promised

The theology of this section turns on the difference between what God promises and what we assume he promises.

The angel's word had two halves: there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship (v. 22), and we must run aground on some island (v. 26). God guaranteed every person. He did not guarantee the vessel, the cargo, the owner's fortune or a safe arrival at a chosen port, and he said so in advance. Every one of those was lost, and the promise was kept in full. That is the shape of the promises Scripture makes to God's people: his love, his presence, their good and their homecoming, not the preservation of their circumstances (Romans 8:28, 38–39).

Alongside that runs the chapter's second theme: providence works through means, never around them. God decreed that all 276 would live, and he decreed the whole chain that delivered it, from the cables round the hull to the swimmers going first.

And note the instruments God employs. Not one of them is a believer. A centurion's kindness, a crew's seamanship, an officer's fear for his own career: the Lord uses them all, and they go off duty with no idea what they have been part of.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The disaster began with a harbour that was safe and boring. Fair Havens would have kept 276 people alive all winter, but staying meant four idle months beside a small village with a valuable cargo earning nothing. So the professionals took a vote and ran for somewhere better, forty miles down the coast, and a gentle south wind that morning seemed to confirm it.

Now: A following wind on the morning of a decision feels like a green light and is often just the weather. Before you leave something safe and unglamorous that is working, a steady job, an ordinary church, a routine that keeps you upright, ask whether the only real argument against it is that it is dull. And if you have already sailed and the storm has come, the God who kept every soul on that ship has not stopped keeping his own.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 27 is an eyewitness account of a voyage and a shipwreck. Paul, a prisoner, sails for Rome. He warns against sailing so late in the season and is ignored; a hurricane drives the ship for two weeks, and all hope is lost. Then Paul stands up: an angel of the God he belongs to has promised that not one life will be lost. He encourages them, gives thanks for bread, and all 276 reach land. The prisoner becomes the leader, and God keeps his promise through storm, sailors and planks. It is a chapter about God’s sovereignty over wind, water and the decisions of men, and about a God who never mislays a single soul entrusted to him.

We should sail for Italy. The we is back. Luke last used it as the company arrived in Jerusalem (21:18), and everything since, the riot, the barracks, the council, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, has been told from outside. Now the narrator is aboard again. What follows is one of the most detailed accounts of a sea voyage to survive from the ancient world, because a man who was there wrote it down: the ports, the winds, the depths in fathoms, the sailors’ slang for a gale, the exact sequence of emergency measures. Luke writes as a man remembering, not reconstructing, and sailors who have studied his account have found his seamanship remarkably accurate.

The Augustan Cohort. An imperial regiment, and a name worth remembering. Julius treats Paul well throughout, and before the chapter is over he will save Paul’s life.

A ship of Adramyttium. Adramyttium was a port in north-west Asia Minor. The ship was a coastal trader heading home, and it would hug the coast, calling at ports where they could find a ship for Italy.

A prisoner for Christ Jesus. On paper Paul now belongs to Rome, but this voyage began with another word. In the Jerusalem barracks the risen Lord stood by Paul and told him that as he had testified about him in Jerusalem, so he must testify also in Rome (23:11). Every soldier, ship and harbour in this chapter is serving that sentence. That is why, writing from prison, probably in Rome, Paul never calls himself Caesar’s prisoner. He is a prisoner for Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1). The chain belongs to the emperor; the man belongs to Christ. And the Lord who sends him into Gentile hands walked that road first, delivered over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32) for the salvation of Jew and Gentile alike.

In the flow. These last two chapters are the end of a road Luke has been building since his first page. The risen Lord promised that his witnesses would reach the end of the earth (1:8). In Ephesus Paul resolved that he must also see Rome (19:21); in the barracks the Lord confirmed it (23:11); before Festus the appeal to Caesar fixed the route (25:11). Acts 27 is the last and hardest stage of that journey, and Luke gives it more space than almost any other episode in the book, because it shows what his whole history has been proving: nothing, not councils, courts or the sea itself, can stop the word of the Lord from reaching the place he has said it will go.

Aristarchus. Aristarchus first appears when a mob in Ephesus seized him and dragged him into the theatre because he was known to travel with Paul (19:29). He was one of the companions who carried the collection to Jerusalem (20:4), and years later, writing from prison in Rome, Paul calls him my fellow prisoner (Colossians 4:10). Prisoners do not travel with friends; a Roman transport is not a passenger service. The most likely explanation, and the one most commentators reach, is that Luke and Aristarchus were permitted aboard as Paul’s personal attendants, as prisoners of status sometimes were: they accepted the standing of a prisoner’s servants in order to go.

Who would get on the boat with you? Two men, at the end of Paul’s usefulness to anyone, arranged their lives so as to be on that ship. Neither of them had to. Aristarchus had already been mobbed once for the association, and Luke had a profession he could have practised anywhere. That is worth turning on yourself before the storm starts, because it is a plainer question than it looks. Paul spent twenty-five years pouring himself into people, and at the end of it there were two who would get on the boat. Not two hundred. Two, and that was riches. Who would get on the boat with you? And whose boat are you on?

Who was Luke, and how do we know he was there? Luke was a doctor (Colossians 4:14), a Gentile companion of Paul, and the author of both the Gospel of Luke and Acts (Luke 1:1–4; Acts 1:1). In several passages of Acts he slips from they to we (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), quietly telling us that he was present. He was with Paul on this voyage and later in Rome, and he stayed with him to the end (2 Timothy 4:11). That is why this chapter reads like a log: it is the testimony of a careful eyewitness.

On a Tuesday. Friends who stay with you in hard times are a gift from God; the Friend who never leaves you makes you one. Think of a believer you know who is going through a long trial, illness, imprisonment, a hard marriage, a slow grief, and who has fewer friends now than when life was easy. Get on the boat: visit, write, sit with them, stay.
verseByVerse.note: “We” returns: Luke sails with Paul. Adramyttium was a port in north-west Asia Minor. Aristarchus later shared Paul’s imprisonment.

parallels.desc: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner

verseByVerse.quote: "The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. And putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sidon. Sidon was a Phoenician port north of Tyre, about seventy miles up the coast from Caesarea. It was the first day of the voyage.

Julius treated Paul kindly. The phrase for being cared for means to receive attention, to be looked after; it is ordinary Greek, though it could be used of nursing the sick. Paul has spent two years in custody and a season of hearings; the man is worn out, and the centurion lets him go ashore to be tended by the believers there, probably under guard. Julius did not have to. A prisoner appealing to Caesar was a serious charge to be responsible for, and letting him out of sight in a friendly port was a professional risk. He took it on the first day.

Keep an eye on this centurion. He will side against Paul at Fair Havens and be wrong; he will act on Paul’s word at the anchors and be right; and at the end, when the soldiers propose killing every prisoner aboard, he will overrule them because he wants Paul alive (v. 43). Luke is not sentimental about him, but he is one of a long line of decent pagans in this book whose ordinary kindnesses God uses without their knowledge.

Letting himself be cared for. Look too at what Paul receives. He has spent his life being the one who gives, and here he is simply a tired man being looked after by friends, and he lets them do it. Some Christians cannot accept help and mistake that for strength. Paul, on the first afternoon of the last voyage of his life, let the church at Sidon take care of him.

I was in prison and you came to me. Jesus said that on the last day the King will tell his people that he was in prison and they came to him, and that whatever they did for one of the least of his brothers, they did for him (Matthew 25:36, 40). The church at Sidon was caring for Christ in the person of his worn-out servant. And the Lord who will say that made himself the needy one first: born where there was no room, provided for by the women who followed him (Luke 8:3), bound and led away. He counts every kindness to his chained servants as done to himself.

Under the lee of Cyprus. Under the lee means on the sheltered side, out of the wind. They hug the eastern and northern coast of Cyprus for protection, because the prevailing north-westerly winds of late summer are already dead against them. Four verses in, and the wind is contrary; it will stay contrary for the whole chapter. This is not a voyage that goes well and then goes wrong. It is hard from the first hour.

How can I care for Christians who are in prison or hardship? Do what the believers at Sidon did: when the opportunity comes, receive them, feed them, rest them and encourage them. Scripture says to remember those in prison as though in prison with them (Hebrews 13:3). In practice that may mean writing to persecuted believers through organisations that serve them, supporting the families of those imprisoned for their faith, visiting Christians in local prisons through a chaplaincy, or simply caring practically for a worn-out pastor or missionary home on leave. Small kindnesses, offered at the right moment, can strengthen someone for the storm ahead.

On a Tuesday. If you have any authority over others, at work or at home, use it as Julius did: notice who is exhausted, and give them leave to rest.
verseByVerse.note: Sidon was a Phoenician port north of Tyre. “Under the lee” means sheltered from the wind by the island.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia. A geographical note that Luke leaves entirely alone. Cilicia is Paul’s home province. Somewhere over the northern horizon is Tarsus: the city he was born in, the city he named to the tribune with a flash of pride, a citizen of no obscure city (21:39), the city he was sent back to for years of obscurity after Jerusalem became too dangerous (9:30). He sails past it in chains, and there is no record that he ever sets foot there again. Luke does not remark on it, but it is one of the quiet costs of a life spent going where you are sent: the places that formed you slide past on the horizon, and you do not get to stop.

He set his face. Luke has told a journey like this before. In his Gospel, Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), and from that verse on everything moves toward the cross, and he does not turn aside. The Son of Man who had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58) had left far more than a home province; he had left the glory he shared with the Father. Paul at the rail, watching Cilicia slide past, is following a Master who never stopped to go home on the way to the place he was sent, and whatever Paul loses on this coast, he loses for a Lord who lost far more for him.

Myra in Lycia. Myra, on the south coast of Asia Minor, was one of the great transhipment ports of the eastern Mediterranean, a major stop for the grain ships from Egypt. It was later the home of Bishop Nicholas, the original Saint Nicholas. The Alexandrian grain fleet, sailing from Egypt to Rome, could rarely make the direct westward run against the prevailing winds. The standard route was north to the Asian coast, then west along it. Myra is where you changed from a coastal vessel to an ocean-going one.

How ordinary the mechanism is. The Lord had said Paul must testify also in Rome (23:11). The way that promise advances, on this particular afternoon, is that a centurion goes down to the harbour at Myra looking for a westbound ship, and finds one. And it is a threshold nobody notices. Up to now the voyage has kept near the coast, hopping from port to port. From Myra, Paul is on an ocean-going freighter crossing open water. The safe part of the journey is over, and it ends without a warning, as it usually does.

What about the costs of going where God sends? They are real, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise. Following Christ may mean leaving home, family, familiar places and plans, and sometimes never returning (Luke 9:57–62). Jesus promised that no one who leaves such things for his sake will fail to receive many times more in this age, and in the age to come eternal life (Luke 18:29–30). It is not unspiritual to feel the loss; Paul surely did. But it is never wasted. The places that slide past on your horizon are in God’s keeping, and the city he is taking you to is better.

On a Tuesday. Every port on the way was in God’s plan, and so is every stage of your journey. If you are in an ordinary in-between place this week, a waiting room, a commute, a temporary job, a season of transition, thank God that he is moving his purposes forward through it, even when nothing seems to be happening.
verseByVerse.note: Myra, on the south coast of Asia Minor, was a major stop for the grain ships from Egypt to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A ship of Alexandria. An Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy means a grain freighter, and it is worth knowing what that was, because it explains most of what goes wrong in this chapter. Rome could not feed itself. The city’s bread depended on Egyptian wheat, shipped every year in enormous merchantmen, vessels far larger than most others afloat, the largest perhaps 180 feet long and carrying a thousand tons or more. The emperors treated the grain supply as a matter of state security, offered the shippers guarantees and inducements under imperial contract, and expected the fleet to keep running. That is why there are 276 people aboard this one, and it is also why she is at sea this late in the year with a cargo she cannot afford to hold over till spring. The commercial pressure behind the whole voyage is standing in the background of every decision that follows.

Bread for Rome. Rome sent this ship to Egypt for bread, and the empire’s whole machinery stood behind the cargo. Nobody in Rome had sent for the prisoner. Yet the wheat in that hold will end on the sea floor off Malta (27:38), and the prisoner will reach Rome and spend two years teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ (28:31). It is the contrast Jesus drew between food that perishes and the bread of God, who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:27, 33). Emperors could keep Rome’s granaries full for a season. Only Christ could feed her for ever, and he was sending his word there in chains.

Slowly and with difficulty. The verbs tell the story. Cnidus is on the south-west tip of Asia Minor, and the intended route was west past it and across to Greece and Italy.

Under the lee of Crete. They turn south-west, round the eastern cape of Crete at Salmone, and creep along the island’s sheltered southern shore: a substantial detour that puts them where they must not be at the time of year they must not be there.

How disasters are assembled. Nothing dramatic has happened yet: no storm, no crisis, no decision anyone would call a mistake. Just weeks of a wind that will not cooperate, a schedule quietly falling apart, and a ship pushed by ordinary weather toward a place nobody chose. Many disasters are assembled like that, from small pressures none of which seemed worth stopping for. The moment to stop is usually long before it feels necessary, and stopping then rarely looks heroic.

Do contrary winds mean God is against my plan? Not necessarily. Paul was exactly where God wanted him, on the way to the city God had named, and the wind was against him from the first day. Difficulty is not proof of disobedience, and ease is not proof of blessing. Sometimes God closes a road to redirect us (16:6–7); sometimes he lets us struggle on the right road to teach patience. The question is not how hard the journey is but whether you are going where his Word and wise counsel point. If you are, keep going, slowly if need be. And watch for the small pressures that push you toward decisions you would never have chosen at the start.
verseByVerse.note: Ships from Alexandria carried Egypt’s grain to feed Rome. Cnidus lay at the south-western tip of Asia Minor; they turned south to shelter behind Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fair Havens. With difficulty again. And then the name, which Luke surely enjoyed writing: Kaloi Limenes, Fair Havens. It is a small bay on the southern coast of Crete, and it still bears the name today. The one genuinely safe place in the chapter is called Fair Havens, and they will leave it.

Lasea. Ruins have been found nearby. There is nothing wrong with the harbour except that it is small, not well protected for winter, and dull: a roadstead beside a minor town, with nothing to do for four months. It would have kept them alive. It simply was not where anyone wanted to spend the winter.

A safe place that was inconvenient. The whole disaster turns on that. The ship is not lost through recklessness or wickedness. It is lost because a safe place was inconvenient. The obviously ruinous choices are easy to see; it is harder to notice the moment when something safe and unglamorous was available, a job that was not exciting, a church that was ordinary, a routine that was working, and the whole reason for leaving it was that it was dull. The northeaster is six verses away, and every soul aboard would give everything they own to be back in the boring harbour.

What safety looked like from inside. Be fair to them, though. Wintering there meant four months with a valuable cargo idle, an owner losing money daily, and 276 people confined beside a village that could barely feed them. On the morning of the decision the safe option did not look safe at all, merely irritating. Hindsight makes Fair Havens shine. The right decision rarely announces itself as the right decision. Usually it just looks like the dull one.

How do I know whether to stay or move? Begin with Scripture and prayer, and ask whether either option would require you to disobey God. Then ask honest questions. Why do I want to leave: because something is wrong, or because it is dull? Is the new thing necessary, or only better? What would I lose if it went badly, and could I bear it? Seek the counsel of mature believers who know you (Proverbs 15:22). Weigh your responsibilities to family and church. If staying is faithful and safe, boredom alone is a poor reason to go. And if you do move, go humbly, knowing that God can redirect you.
verseByVerse.note: Fair Havens was a small bay on the south coast of Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, saying, 'Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voyage was now dangerous. Sailing in the Mediterranean was considered dangerous from mid-September, and stopped altogether from mid-November to March. They are somewhere in the dangerous window, with the door closing.

The Fast was already over. The Fast is the Day of Atonement, which falls in late September or October; in AD 59, the likeliest year of this voyage, it probably fell on 5 October. Luke, very probably a Gentile, dates the voyage by the Jewish calendar, a small sign of the world he and Paul shared.

Once for all. Once a year on the Fast the high priest went behind the veil with blood for the sins of the people, and the next year he went again; Hebrews says that very repetition showed those sacrifices could never take sins away (Hebrews 10:1–4). On board this ship sailed the apostle of the High Priest who entered the holy places once for all, not by the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, securing an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12). That is, his one death paid for his people’s sins completely, so that no further sacrifice will ever be needed (Hebrews 10:14). The Fast was over for that year. In Christ it is over for good, and Paul is carrying that news to the heart of the world.

Paul advised them. A prisoner giving advice. Paul was an experienced traveller: writing to Corinth some years before this voyage, he had already listed three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea (2 Corinthians 11:25). The man warning them had perhaps been in the water more often than most of the crew.

I perceive. This needs saying carefully, because it is easy to get wrong in the direction of piety. Paul is not prophesying. His verb is I perceive, I observe: the language of assessment, not revelation. He does not say thus says the Lord, and Luke does not present it as a word from God. This is common sense from experience: the season is gone, the ship has fought a headwind for weeks, and the passage ahead is open water.

Right about the storm, wrong about the deaths. Paul read the danger rightly, but not its outcome. He said there would be loss of life, and there was not: not one person died, as the angel would tell him later (v. 22) and as the last verse of the chapter records. Luke leaves the discrepancy standing without explanation, and that is a mercy to the reader. Scripture is not claiming that a godly man’s seasoned judgment is the same thing as divine revelation. Paul, giving his best assessment, was right about the storm and wrong about the deaths. Paul, delivering a message from an angel thirteen verses later, was exactly right about everything.

How do I tell a godly person’s opinion from a word from God? Ask where it comes from. A word from God for us today is what Scripture says, rightly understood, and it binds the conscience. Anything else, however wise or sincerely felt, is counsel: to be weighed, tested against Scripture and received with gratitude or set aside. Be wary when anyone, including yourself, says God told me about a decision that Scripture does not address. Better to say what Paul said here: I perceive, I think, this is my judgment. That is honest, humble, and often very helpful. Christians differ here. Many brothers and sisters believe God still gives prophetic impressions today, and they agree that every such word must be tested and may never bind another’s conscience (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21). This commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that now the canon of Scripture is complete, Scripture is the one word that binds us; but both sides can agree to call a judgment a judgment.
verseByVerse.note: “The Fast” is the Day of Atonement, in late September or October. Sailing became dangerous from mid-September and stopped altogether in winter.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pilot and the owner. And who would not have listened to them? There is a lazy reading of this verse in which the worldly men ignore the man of God and get what they deserve, and it teaches something false. Consider the room. On one side, the kybernētēs, the sailing master who handles this ship for a living, and the nauklēros, the owner or charterer whose money is aboard. On the other, a prisoner in chains with a religious reputation, no nautical qualification and no standing to be speaking at all.

Not suitable to spend the winter in. Fair Havens is a poor harbour, exposed and next to a village. Phoenix, some forty miles farther west along the same coast, is a proper wintering port, a harbour of Crete facing both south-west and north-west. The distance is a single day’s easy sail.

The majority decided. It was not the centurion’s decision alone. Luke records something like a vote, and the professionals, the owner, the officers and most of the company all landed the same way. Every part of that is reasonable. On any ordinary reckoning, they were right and Paul was wrong. But the majority was wrong. Truth is not decided by vote. There is a reason the heart likes a majority, though. Going with the crowd feels safe, and if things go wrong the blame is shared. That is the fear of man, and Scripture says it lays a snare, while whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25). We all bend to the crowd at times; Christ never let it overrule his Father’s word, even when Peter urged him to spare himself (Matthew 16:21–23), and his perfect obedience is counted as ours when we trust him.

Their voices prevailed. Luke has recorded a vote like this before. At the trial of Jesus the chief priests and rulers, the religious experts of the nation, and a crowd with them, shouted against the one man in the room who was right, and Luke writes, with terrible brevity, that their voices prevailed (Luke 23:23). The majority was never more wrong than on the day it condemned the Son of God. Yet even that vote could not overturn the counsel of God. The rejected stone became the cornerstone, and the sentence passed by the many became the salvation of many: the crowd’s verdict sent him to the cross, and on the cross he gave his life as a ransom for sinners (Mark 10:45). The vote at Fair Havens will serve him too.

The competent men got it wrong. So resist the moral that expertise is not to be trusted; the crew’s expertise is about to keep everyone alive for two weeks. The point is narrower and stranger. Competent men, with good information and sound reasons, deciding a matter squarely inside their field, got it wrong; expertise and profit can blind. And the one man with no business having an opinion got it right, by ordinary observation, not by revelation.

How do you know in advance? That leaves a genuinely uncomfortable question rather than a tidy lesson: how do you know, in advance, which kind of situation you are in? Most days the pilot and the owner are right. Luke does not offer a method for telling. He simply records that on this occasion the majority of qualified people, voting sensibly, sailed a ship into the worst storm of their lives. The one protection Luke does show is small and available to anyone: the harbour was safe, and the alternative was better rather than necessary. Nobody on that ship had to move. They moved because forty miles of improvement seemed worth a day’s risk at the wrong time of year.

Should Christians defer to experts? Generally, yes, in their fields. God gives real skill to doctors, engineers, pilots and lawyers, and it is wise and humble to listen to them. But experts are fallible, they can be influenced by money or pressure (the owner had a cargo to sell), and they cannot speak with authority on moral questions or on what God has said. So listen carefully, ask questions, seek a second opinion when much is at stake, and notice when someone with less standing but real experience is raising a concern. And never let a majority, however expert, persuade you to do what Scripture forbids.

On a Tuesday. In the next decision you face with others, ask the quiet person in the room what they think. And before you choose the better option over the safe one, ask whether you actually need to move at all.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenix was a better harbour farther west along Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The south wind blew gently. This may be the most dangerous sentence in the chapter, and it describes perfect weather. A gentle southerly is exactly the wind you want to run west along the southern coast of Crete, and it arrives as if on cue, confirming everything the majority concluded. Luke’s word for their state of mind is precise: supposing. They supposed the thing was settled and the plan was working.

Weather is not confirmation. A favourable circumstance following a decision feels overwhelmingly like confirmation, and it is nothing of the kind. Every soul on that ship read the soft south wind as a green light. It was simply the weather. Christians are especially prone to this: a door opens easily, a house sells, the money arrives just in time, and it is taken as proof that God has blessed the decision. Sometimes he has. But the gentle south wind blew for the ship that was about to be destroyed, at precisely the moment that made the destruction possible. A headwind that morning would have kept them alive.

The northeaster. Luke gives the sailors’ own name for it, Eurakylōn, a rough dockside hybrid of the Greek word for the east wind and the Latin for the north, found nowhere else in Greek literature: a landsman writing down the term he heard shouted on deck. (The KJV, following later manuscripts, calls it Euroclydon; the earliest read Euraquilo, the northeaster, which is why modern Bibles differ.) The word for tempestuous is typhōnikos, typhoon-like, a hurricane-force wind. Struck down from the land is exact too. Crete’s mountains rise to some eight thousand feet, and the killing winds there fall off the high ground without warning, hitting a ship from the very shore she was hugging for safety.

The house the stream could not shake. Jesus ended his great sermon in Luke’s Gospel with weather of exactly this kind. The one who comes to him, hears his words and does them is like a man who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock, and when the flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it (Luke 6:47–49). The sailors’ foundation was a gentle south wind and a majority vote, and it lasted an afternoon. Christ does not promise his people that they will miss the northeaster. He promises himself as the rock beneath them when it falls, and his word as the one forecast that never deceives.

How do I tell whether an open door is God’s guidance? An open door alone tells you very little; it may be God’s provision, or simply the weather. Guidance comes first from Scripture: is the choice in line with what God has commanded and with his priorities for your life? Then pray, seek the counsel of wise believers, and consider your gifts, responsibilities and motives honestly. Circumstances can confirm a decision made on those grounds, but they cannot replace them. Be especially cautious when the circumstance happens to give you exactly what you already wanted. And whatever you decide, hold it humbly, ready for God to redirect you.

For worship. The winds belong to the Lord. He makes the clouds his chariot and rides on the wings of the wind; the gentle south wind and the howling northeaster both run at his command. And the Lord who sends the storm is the Lord who stands in it with his people. When the winds of Galilee fell on the disciples’ boat, he was there, and with a word he rebuked them. The storm that struck down from the mountains of Crete did not catch him by surprise; it was already folded into his promise to bring his servant to Rome. Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
verseByVerse.note: The northeaster (Euraquilo) was a violent wind sweeping down from the mountains of Crete.

parallels.desc: he raised the stormy wind

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Could not face the wind. Three phrases, each a stage of surrender. The ship was caught: Luke’s word is the one used of a person seized or arrested. She is not struggling any more; she has been taken. Could not face the wind: antophthalmein, literally to look in the eye. Ancient ships often had eyes painted on the bow, and this one could not look the wind in the eye. A ship survives heavy weather by keeping her head into it. Turned broadside, she rolls; turned tail, she runs wherever the wind sends her.

Driven along. They stop trying. Luke puts it in the passive: we were driven along. They are no longer sailing; they are cargo, and the storm carries them.

There is a time to stop fighting. There are situations in which the competent, faithful thing to do is to stop trying to make headway and keep the hull together while you go where you are being taken. Anyone who has sat with a serious diagnosis, a bereavement or a stretch of depression knows the difference between the phase where effort still moves you and the phase where it does not, and the instinct is to treat the second as a lapse of faith. Luke does not. He records it as what the professionals did, and it was right: keep the hull together, with the simple means of grace, rest, prayer however feeble, the company of believers, and leave the direction to him. They gave way for fourteen days, the promise held, and every person walked out of the surf alive. Being carried is not the same as being lost. The question in a storm is not whether you are making progress, but whose hands the wind is in.

Even winds and water obey him. That question has an answer with a name. In Luke’s Gospel, when a windstorm came down on the lake and the disciples cried out that they were perishing, Jesus rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they asked who this could be, who commands even winds and water, and they obey him (Luke 8:23–25). The same Lord now reigned at the right hand of God, and the wind driving that helpless ship across the sea was a wind that answered to him. To be carried by a storm that obeys Christ is a very different thing from being lost in one. And look at how the disciples felt when the storm stopped: they were afraid, and they marvelled (Luke 8:25). They had been frightened of the storm; now they were afraid of him, because they had just seen the Creator at work in their boat. That holy fear is the right response to Christ, and it is the one fear that drives out all the others.

Why does God not calm every storm, as Jesus did on Galilee? Because he has more than one way of saving his people. Sometimes he stills the storm (Mark 4:39); sometimes he brings us through it, as he did here; and sometimes he takes us home through it. In every case he is equally sovereign and equally present. A calmed storm shows his power over creation; a storm endured shows his power to keep his people and to fulfil his word in the worst conditions. If he has not calmed yours, it is not because he cannot, or does not care. It is because he is doing something through it that a calm would not do (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

verseByVerse.quote: "Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship's boat. After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cauda. Cauda is a scrap of land about twenty-three miles south of Crete, and running past it buys them a few minutes of slightly calmer water. Luke gives us what the crew did with those minutes, in order, and every item is exactly what a competent crew would do.

The ship’s boat. The dinghy had been towing astern, normal practice in fair weather. By now it was swamped and battering the hull, and if it broke loose they would lose their only means of getting ashore. Hauling a waterlogged boat aboard in a gale is brutal work, and Luke’s we suggests that the passengers, the doctor among them, were hauling on the ropes too.

Undergird the ship. Cables were probably passed under the hull and winched tight over the deck, like a belt around a barrel, to stop the timbers working apart, as the strain could split the ship open. It was a last resort.

The Syrtis. Here is the fear that shaped the next fortnight. The Syrtis were vast shifting sandbanks off the coast of Libya, south-west of them and directly downwind: shallow, unmarked and constantly moving, a place where a ship went aground miles from anywhere and was slowly broken up while the crew watched. Roman writers used the name as a byword for hopeless destruction. The crew were being blown toward the one place they most feared, and they knew it.

They lowered the gear. The phrase is vague in Greek and probably means they set a drag, a sea anchor, or lowered the mainsail, to slow the drift and keep the bow steady. That is the whole strategy: not escape, not progress, but time, in the hope that the wind changes before the sandbanks arrive. They drifted for two weeks and never reached the Syrtis. Nobody aboard could have told you why.

Is it faithless to take precautions when God has promised to keep us? No. The crew did everything a competent crew should, and Paul never rebuked them for it; later he would insist that they stay and use their skills (v. 31). Faith does not mean neglecting means. Nehemiah prayed and set a guard (Nehemiah 4:9). Take your medicine, buckle your seat belt, save for the future, lock your door, and trust God. Precautions become faithless only when we trust them instead of him, or when fear drives us to grasp for control he has not given us.

You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. The deepest answer to that question was given in the wilderness. When the devil set Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple and quoted Psalm 91 at him, the promise that angels would guard him, he was inviting the Son of God to prove his trust by throwing away every ordinary safeguard. Jesus answered that it is said, You shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Luke 4:9–12). Faith of that kind does not leap to force God’s hand; it hauls in the boat, passes the cables and leaves the outcome with him.

For worship. The Lord sets the bounds of the sea and says, Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed. The Syrtis lay downwind for fourteen days, and the ship never reached it, because the God who marks out the sands with his finger had marked out a different shore. He holds the drift of every ship and the course of every life. We do not see his hand on the tiller, but it is there, and it is steady.
verseByVerse.note: The ship’s boat was a dinghy towed behind. Cables were passed under the hull to hold it together. The Syrtis were dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. And on the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jettison the cargo. Two days, two decisions, and together they measure how bad it had become. Day two: the cargo. This is an Egyptian grain freighter, and the wheat in her hold is the entire purpose of the voyage: the owner’s investment, the crew’s wages, the reason they were at sea in October at all. They begin heaving cargo over the side and the last of the wheat will follow on the final night (v. 38).

With their own hands. Day three: the tackle. Spare spars, rigging, gear, perhaps the main yard: the equipment you need to sail the ship even if you survive. Throwing it away is an admission that there may be no sailing left to do. And Luke means with their own hands literally: the sailors are hauling their own livelihood to the rail and pitching it into the sea, one armful at a time. Everything that could go, went.

Something greater than Jonah. Jonah’s sailors threw their wares into the sea too (Jonah 1:5), and their storm came because of one man running from God; it ended only when that man was thrown overboard and went down into the deep. On Paul’s ship the one man is going where God sent him, and his presence will save everyone aboard without anyone being thrown in. Jesus said that something greater than Jonah had come (Luke 11:30–32). Unlike Jonah, he had done nothing to deserve the storm, and he went down into the deep of death of his own will, so that the storm of God’s judgment falls silent for everyone who belongs to him.

Profit, tools, hope. Watch the sequence, because it is the sequence of many serious troubles: first the profit goes, then the tools, and then hope itself (v. 20). And every item that went overboard was valuable and correctly thrown away. In a storm the question stops being what is this worth? and becomes will this keep me afloat? People discover in a hospital corridor, in a matter of hours, what took the crew three days: that almost everything they had been carrying was cargo, genuinely valuable and, at the critical moment, weight. The ship that reached Malta arrived with nothing in the hold and every soul aboard alive.

How do I let go of things I have valued? Begin by naming them before God honestly: possessions, plans, reputation, comfort, a dream. Thank him for them, because they were gifts. Then ask which of them you are holding so tightly that they are weighing you down, keeping you from obedience or peace. Jesus said a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15), and Paul counted everything loss compared with knowing Christ (Philippians 3:8). Letting go is often painful, and grief over what is lost is not unbelief. But what you lose for Christ, or in the storms he sends, is never the thing that keeps you afloat. He is.

parallels.desc: the mariners hurled the cargo into the sea

verseByVerse.quote: "When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, 'Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither sun nor stars. To a first-century sailor that sentence is not scene-setting. There was no compass. Position and heading were worked out from the sun by day and the stars by night, corrected by known landmarks. Take away sun and stars for many days and a ship does not merely feel gloomy. It is genuinely, absolutely lost. Nobody aboard knows where they are, how far they have run, or which way they are pointing. They are somewhere in the middle of the sea, in the dark, going fast, in an unknown direction.

All hope was at last abandoned. Luke’s no small tempest is deliberate understatement, and the phrase after it is not. Three things about it. First, the verb suggests something gradual: hope was stripped away day after day, and the ESV catches it exactly: at last. Second, the word for saved, sōzesthai, is the word for salvation; here it means rescue from the sea, and Luke will sound it again until the last verse. Third, Luke includes himself. All hope of our being saved. The man writing this is a Christian, a companion of Paul, and he says plainly that he stopped believing they would live.

Despair is not the same as unbelief. Scripture does not tidy that up. It does not report that the believers aboard kept a serene confidence while the pagans panicked. An apostle and two of his friends were on that ship, and Luke says plainly that hope ran out. The man who wrote a Gospel gave up hope in a storm, God did not hold it against him, and the promise did not depend on his morale. Paul himself once despaired of life itself, so that he would rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). What is the difference? Unbelief refuses to trust what God has said. Despair is what a believer feels when he can see no way out and has not yet heard God speak into it. Luke had no word yet about the ship; when it came (vv. 22–25), they all took heart (v. 36).

While the sun’s light failed. Luke records that as Jesus hung on the cross there was darkness over the whole land while the sun’s light failed, and that in that darkness he committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:44–46); Matthew and Mark add that he cried the forsaken words of Psalm 22. The Son of God went into a darkness deeper than any storm, to bear the judgment our sin had earned, and he came out of it on the third day. So a believer in the dark is never as alone as he feels. His Lord has been further into the night than he will ever go, and he is a high priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

Without food. Fourteen days of this. No cooking fires in a pitching hull, stores soaked with seawater, and men too frightened and too sick to eat what there was. They are starving as well as terrified.

Paul stood up among them. His opening line is not what a modern reader expects. Paul is about to tell a shipload of exhausted, hopeless people that an angel spoke to him and nobody will die, and there is no earthly reason for any of them to believe him. So he establishes the one credential he has: I told you before, and I was right; now listen. He is not scoring a point. He is buying a hearing, and he needs one badly.

What should I do when I have lost all hope? Tell God, honestly; the psalms are full of people doing exactly that (Psalm 88). Do not make big decisions alone in the dark. Eat, sleep and let others help you, as Paul is about to insist. Hold on to God’s promises even when you cannot feel them; your feelings do not change his faithfulness (Lamentations 3:21–24). Speak to your pastor or a trusted believer, and if despair has become persistent or you are thinking of harming yourself, seek medical help at once; that is not a lack of faith but a good use of God’s gifts. And remember: the promise did not depend on Luke’s morale. It does not depend on yours.

On a Tuesday. If you know someone who has lost hope, do not lecture them. Sit with them, make sure they have eaten, and when the time is right, tell them gently what God has promised.
verseByVerse.note: Without sun or stars, ancient sailors had no way to navigate.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take heart. Yet now: two words turning the whole chapter. Everything before them has been loss: the cargo, the tackle, the sun and stars, and finally hope itself. Everything after them is promise. The word Paul uses for take heart is euthymein: be of good cheer, keep your spirits up. It is a different word from the one the Lord spoke over Paul in the Jerusalem barracks, tharsei, take courage (23:11). The Lord’s word to Paul in the dark was courage; Paul’s word to a shipful of starving pagans is cheer. He is telling them, on a sinking ship, that things are actually going to be all right.

Only of the ship. A promise of God, now revealed, and astonishingly precise.
