Both halves matter, and both will come true to the letter: not one person will die, and the vessel will be smashed to pieces. Paul does not soften the second half to make the first more welcome. He tells them the ship is gone in the same sentence in which he tells them they are safe. A lesser comfort would have promised everything and delivered part; this promises exactly what will happen.

The God to whom I belong. He names his God before he passes on the message, and the two phrases are as short and complete a description of a Christian as any in Acts. To whom I belong: a possession, not a client. Paul is owned. And whom I worship: the word is used of religious service. Belonging and serving, in that order, because the second follows from the first. He says it to a deck full of men who most likely honoured Isis and Serapis, the gods of Alexandria, or the emperor, without apology, at the one moment they are all guaranteed to be listening.

Should believers expect an angel like this today? Angelic appearances were never everyday even in the Bible; they cluster at the great hinge-moments, and Acts is exactly such a moment, God steering his apostle on a once-for-all mission. Today God ordinarily guides and comforts by surer, settled means: his completed Word, indwelling Spirit, prayer and unseen providence; “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). Angels are not idle. They are still ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), often unseen, so God remains free to use them; what we must not do is expect or chase visible appearances (Colossians 2:18).

Everything the angel gave Paul, you already have. This is the comfort that should settle your heart, and it comes by a surer voice. Paul got one whispered do not be afraid; you hold a whole Bible of God’s fear not, and the promise “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). Paul was told the storm would not wreck God’s purpose; you have the pledge that nothing will be able to separate us from the love of God, and that he works all things for your good (Romans 8:28, 38–39). Paul had an angel beside him for a night; you have the Spirit of Christ within you for life, and the Son himself, greater than all angels (Hebrews 1:4). An angel is only a servant; you have the Master. So in your storm, do not pine for a vision. The same God who would not let the sea swallow Paul reigns over every wave of yours.

What does it mean to belong to God? It means you are his by creation, and if you are a Christian, his by redemption: bought with a price, the precious blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 6:19–20; 1 Peter 1:18–19). You are not your own. That is a claim on your whole life, your body, money, time and choices; and it is also the deepest security there is, because God does not lose what belongs to him (John 10:28–29). The Heidelberg Catechism begins here: my only comfort in life and in death is that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. You belong to God; that is your security in every storm. Say Paul’s phrase to yourself this week whenever fear rises: the God to whom I belong and whom I worship. And look for a moment, as Paul did, when the people around you are listening, to name your God plainly and without embarrassment.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and he said, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you." So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid, Paul. Paul was very probably afraid too. The angel does not begin with information but with comfort for the apostle himself. The man who would stand up and encourage 275 people had first to be encouraged.

You must stand before Caesar. The word for must is dei, Luke’s word for the fixed purposes of God, the same one used of the Son of Man who must suffer, and the one the Lord used in the Jerusalem barracks: you must testify also in Rome (23:11). The storm has changed the route and not the destination. Look at how the reassurance is framed. The angel does not say you will survive. He says you must stand before Caesar, so the guarantee of Paul’s life is a promise about God’s purpose, and Paul’s survival is simply what that purpose requires between here and Rome.

God has granted you all. The verb is kecharistai, from charis, grace: to give freely, as a favour, with no obligation on the giver. God has graciously given Paul the 275 other people on the ship; perhaps Paul had been praying for them. A cargo of pagan sailors, Roman soldiers and prisoners, several of whom would cheerfully have killed Paul, and one group of whom will propose exactly that in eighteen verses, are spared, as a gift, because of one man’s presence among them.

The pattern of the righteous one. Scripture does this repeatedly. Potiphar’s household was blessed for Joseph’s sake (Genesis 39:5). Abraham pleaded with God down to ten righteous men who would have saved a city (Genesis 18:32). Here the gift is credited to one man among nearly three hundred. The ordinary Christian has no idea what his presence is worth to the people around him, and will not find out in this life; Paul did not know until an angel told him. The office where you are the only believer, the family that finds you difficult, the ship you happen to be on: you cannot see the accounts, and it is a mercy that you cannot.

Those whom you gave me. Behind this gift stands a greater one. On the night before the cross Jesus prayed to his Father about the people you gave me out of the world, and said that he had guarded them (John 17:6, 12). Paul was granted 275 lives for one voyage, and the gift reached no further than the beach; it saved none of them from their sins. The Father’s gift to the Son is a people from every nation, chosen before the foundation of the world, and the Son secured them at the cost of his own life. Scripture’s word for this is election: God’s free choice, made before any of them was born or had done anything good or bad, of those he would save, flowing from his love alone (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 9:11). Christ died for those given to him, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28). Reformed Christians call this definite or particular redemption: Christ’s death was aimed at, and actually secures, the salvation of a particular people, the sheep for whom the good shepherd lays down his life (John 10:11, 15). Many faithful Christians believe instead that Christ died for everyone in the same way; all agree that the offer is free to all, and that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (John 6:37).

Exactly as I have been told. The whole of Christian confidence is in that last clause. Paul’s assurance is not about the weather, the ship, the crew or his own resilience, and he does not say I have a good feeling. He is standing on a disintegrating ship in a fortnight-old gale, unable to see the sky, with nothing he can see to support it, and the sole ground of his composure is that God is not a liar. That is faith: not wishful thinking, but trust in a promise.

Were the 275 saved eternally because of Paul? No. They were spared from drowning because of Paul; that is the gift God gave him. Eternal salvation is never inherited from someone else’s faith or presence. Each person must personally repent and believe in Christ (16:31; Romans 10:9–13). A believer’s presence can bring real blessing to unbelievers around him, protection, kindness, the restraint of evil, and above all the hearing of the gospel. But only Christ’s righteousness saves, and it is received by each one through faith. Pray that those around you, blessed by God’s kindness for your sake, will come to know him for themselves.

On a Tuesday. Faith is trusting that God will do exactly what he said. Choose one promise of God this week, such as John 10:28, and when the storm rises, say Paul’s words over it: I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. And pray by name for the unbelievers around you; you may be on their ship for a reason.

For worship. How generous is the God who said it. He owed that ship nothing: a crew that would shortly try to desert, soldiers who would shortly propose murder, prisoners shipped to Rome to face judgment. The promise concerned one prisoner only, and into it he swept every soul on the vessel, freely, as a gift, because it pleased him to give them to his servant. That is the God of heaven. He gives more than was asked, to people who did not ask, and so quietly that 275 men walked up a beach on Malta without the faintest idea that they had been handed to somebody as a present.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we must run aground on some island.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must run aground. In the same breath as the news that nobody dies, from the same angel, comes the rest: the ship will be destroyed. Must again: God’s plan included the shipwreck. Not rescue from the storm, but rescue through it.

The wreck is inside the promise. The shipwreck is not a failure of the promise, nor an exception to it. God told them in advance that the disaster was part of the plan. Almost every instinct we have treats catastrophe as evidence that a promise has failed, and the ship breaking up on the rocks would look, to anyone in the water, exactly like God not keeping his word. It was the word. And the promise did not include calm seas, a change of wind, the salvage of the wheat, or the ship. It included one thing: every person would live. The owner lost everything he had, and the promise was kept in full.

Necessary that the Christ should suffer. Luke’s must here is the same small word he used of Jesus. The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected and be killed, and on the third day be raised (Luke 9:22). On the Emmaus road the risen Lord asked whether it was not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory (Luke 24:26). His disciples had treated the cross as the end of every promise; it was the promise. The wreck of Christ’s body on the cross looked to everyone watching exactly like God failing, and it was God keeping his word to the letter. Every lesser wreck in a believer’s life sits inside that one.

What exactly did God promise? Here is a question to ask slowly, because many Christians need it more than they need another verse about victory. Think of the thing in your life you have been treating as proof that God did not come through. The illness that was not healed. The marriage that ended anyway. The job that went. The prayer that got the answer you were not asking for. Now ask a harder question than why did this happen? Ask: what exactly did God promise? He has never promised the ship. He has promised, to those who are his, that nothing will separate them from his love (Romans 8:38–39), that he works all things together for their good (Romans 8:28), that he will never leave them (Hebrews 13:5), and that he will bring them home. Read the list again and notice what is not on it. Comfort is not on it. Property is not on it. The preservation of your circumstances is not on it. The wreck may well be inside the promise.

Told in advance. God does not spare them the shipwreck, and he does not hide it from them either. For the rest of the storm those men live with the knowledge that the ship is doomed, and also that they are not. That is often how God deals with his people: not by removing the wreck, but by telling the truth about it early enough that when the timbers finally go, it is not the end of the world. Jesus did the same for his disciples: in the world you will have tribulation, he told them, but take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

How do we know Paul was not simply deluded? It is a fair question, and Scripture itself tells us to test such claims: a prophet whose word does not come true has not spoken from the Lord (Deuteronomy 18:22). So test this one. Paul did not offer a vague comfort. He named things no one aboard could arrange: the ship would be lost, every life would be kept, and they would run aground on an island. Any one of those could have failed in front of 275 witnesses, and Luke, who was standing there, records that every one came true. A deluded man hopes. This man made a forecast that could be checked, and the sea checked it. A sceptic may answer that the record comes from Paul’s own friend, written after the event. That is true, and in the end the question is whether Luke is a trustworthy witness; but he wrote while soldiers, sailors and prisoners from that ship could still have contradicted him, and his account of the voyage has held up well wherever it can be checked.

Does God promise that Christians will be spared suffering? No. He promises to be with his people in it, to use it for their good, and to bring them safely home. Jesus warned that his followers would suffer (John 15:20), the apostles taught that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (14:22), and Paul himself would die in Rome. Teaching that faithful Christians will always be healthy, prosperous and safe is not the gospel. But neither is despair. What God promises, he keeps entirely, and the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed (Romans 8:18).

For worship. God keeps every word, the hard ones and the glad ones alike. He said the ship would be lost and every life kept, and both halves came true. And he has gone ahead of his people onto the shore. The risen Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first to come up out of the surf of death alive and never go back into it, and where the firstfruits stand, the harvest will follow. Every believer who goes down in the last wreck will be brought up on that beach after him. He who promised is faithful.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the fourteenth night the ship nears land in the dark (vv. 27–29). Paul stops the sailors abandoning ship (vv. 30–32), urges everyone to eat, and gives thanks for bread in front of them all (vv. 33–38). At dawn they run for a beach, strike a reef, and the stern breaks up; the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops the soldiers killing the prisoners, and everyone reaches land, some swimming and some on planks (vv. 39–44).
verseByVerse.theology:
Certainty and Effort Are the Same Faith

Verse 31 is the hinge. Nine verses after an unconditional promise that not one life would be lost, Paul says that unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved. Both are true, because God decrees the means as well as the end. The same logic governs the meal at dawn: eat, because God has guaranteed you will live and you will need the strength.

The section also shows how God's promises are usually fulfilled: not by suspending the ordinary world but by working through the wreckage of it. There is no calmed sea and no angel carrying anyone ashore, only exhausted people swimming, and others clinging to planks off the ship that has just broken up beneath them.

And quietly at the centre: the prisoners live because the centurion wanted Paul. Condemned men, under a sentence they had earned, are spared on account of the worth of another. Luke does not press the point. He does not have to.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An hour before the ship broke apart, Paul took a piece of bread and thanked God for it out loud where everyone could hear. He was in chains, the vessel was doomed, and he was about to swim for his life. A shipful of frightened people watched a man be visibly grateful to God, and Luke says they were encouraged, and they ate.

Now: Paul's argument had been outvoted at Fair Havens. What reached them now was one man's confidence in God holding steady when there was no visible reason for it. The people around you may forget what you said about God when things were going well; they will remember what you did on the worst morning of your life. That steadiness is not a performance you must produce; it is what the God who keeps his word gives his people in the storm.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourteenth night. Two full weeks of being carried through a gale with no sight of sun or stars, little food to speak of, and no idea where they are.

The Adriatic Sea. The Adriatic in ancient usage was not the narrow sea between Italy and the Balkans that bears the name today. Sailors used it for the whole central Mediterranean, the open water between Greece, Italy, Sicily and North Africa. Luke is not saying they were blown up past Italy; he is saying they were somewhere in the middle of a very large sea.

The sailors suspected. Suspected: not saw. It is the middle of the night in a storm, and there is nothing to see. So how did they know? Very probably they heard it. Surf breaking on a shore carries a long way across water, and it makes a sound no experienced sailor mistakes for anything else. After a fortnight of hearing nothing but wind and open sea, somebody on that deck caught a different note in the darkness and knew what it meant.

The sound of danger. The sound of land is, for now, the sound of danger. Out in deep water a ship can be driven for weeks and survive. Land is where ships die: a lee shore in a gale, in the dark, with no chart and no way of knowing what lies under the surface. The thing they have been longing for is the thing that may destroy them.

Twenty fathoms, then fifteen. A weighted line dropped over the side, the standard method. A fathom was about six feet: a hundred and twenty feet, then ninety. The bottom is coming up fast. Two soundings, and now they have a rate as well as a depth, and the arithmetic is terrifying. At that rate of shoaling they will soon be on the rocks.

Details that fit a witness. A small note that has interested historians: the depths Luke records, taken in that order and at that spacing, correspond closely to the approach to St Paul’s Bay on Malta as it has been surveyed. And modern sailors who have calculated the drift of a large ship from Cauda in such a wind reckon that it would reach Malta in about fourteen days. Luke’s account fits remarkably closely. Detail like this does not by itself prove the story, but it is just what we would expect from a writer who was aboard, as his we claims.

The same pen at the tomb. The man who wrote down two soundings in the dark, in order, wrote the last chapter of his Gospel with the same care. He recorded the stone rolled away, the empty tomb, and the risen Lord showing his hands and feet and eating a piece of broiled fish in front of his disciples, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as they could see that he had (Luke 24:2–3, 39–43). The faith of Christians does not rest on a mood or a vision. It rests on a risen Christ, attested by witnesses who counted what they saw.

Do these accurate details really matter for faith? Yes, in their place. Faith does not rest on nautical measurements, but on Christ and his Word. Yet the accuracy of Luke’s details, the winds, the ports, the depths, the titles of officials, has been confirmed again and again where it can be checked, and it shows that he was a careful historian who wrote what happened (Luke 1:1–4). If he is trustworthy about the soundings off Malta, there is good reason to take him seriously about the empty tomb in Jerusalem. Accuracy in small things does not prove a miracle, but it shows a witness who cared to get things right. The Bible’s history is not a decorative frame around spiritual truths; it is the place where God has acted.

On a Tuesday. When you have no idea where you are in life, keep doing the simple, faithful things: the soundings. Read, pray, worship, work, listen. God is bringing you somewhere, even in the dark.
verseByVerse.note: In ancient usage the Adriatic Sea included the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy and Sicily. The ESV notes that twenty fathoms is about 120 feet and fifteen about 90 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the ship's boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four anchors from the stern. Four anchors off the stern is unusual, since a ship normally anchors by the bow, and it is precisely right here. Anchoring by the stern holds the vessel with her bow pointed at the shore, so that at first light they can cut the cables, hoist a sail and run her straight up the beach without having to turn in the surf. It is a considered manoeuvre by men who know exactly what they intend to do at dawn. Admiral Nelson was said to have read this chapter before the Battle of Copenhagen, where his ships anchored by the stern.

Prayed for day to come. The verb can mean to wish or to pray, and the most natural reading is that these are the sailors praying: not Paul, not Luke, but pagan seamen hanging on four cables in the dark with rocks somewhere ahead, praying for morning. Luke reports it without scorn. He does not call it superstition and he does not pretend it was conversion. It is what men do when there is nothing left to do, and the God who was actually holding that ship gave them the morning anyway.

Seeking to escape. Then, in the same breath, the ugliest thing in the chapter. The crew decide to save themselves and abandon the passengers, and they swing out the dinghy they nearly killed themselves recovering days earlier.

Under pretense. A lie, and a good one: bow anchors would be a sensible addition, and running them out by boat is how it is done. What they are actually doing is abandoning more than two hundred and fifty people on a ship they believe is about to break up, taking the only boat and all the seamanship aboard. And they had heard Paul’s promise that not one life would be lost. Their considered response was to leave in the dark while everyone else was praying.

Assenting and resting. Do not merely condemn them; the instinct is not exotic. Under real pressure, people who have genuinely heard a promise of God still make private arrangements. The promise is believed in the way one believes a weather forecast: taken seriously, hedged against. There is a difference between assenting to a promise and actually resting your weight on it, and the difference does not show up until it is dark and the boat is in the water.

The hired hand flees. Jesus described exactly what the crew were doing: the hired hand sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, because he cares nothing for them. Against that he set himself: I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11–13). On the night of his arrest Christ did not lower a boat. He stepped forward to the men with swords and told them, if you seek me, let these men go (John 18:8), and then went alone to the cross. Every Christian rests on a Saviour who stayed when staying cost him everything.

Does God hear the prayers of unbelievers? God hears everything, and in his kindness he often gives good things to people who do not know him: sun and rain, food and gladness, and a morning after a terrible night (14:17; Matthew 5:45). But the promise that God will hear and answer as a Father is for those who come to him through Christ, the one mediator (John 14:6, 13–14; 1 Timothy 2:5). An unbeliever’s cry for help can be the first stirring of seeking God, and he invites all to call on him in truth. If you pray for morning, pray to the God who made it, through the Saviour he has sent.

On a Tuesday. Where are you quietly making private arrangements against God’s promises, the secret savings you trust more than God, the escape route you keep open in case obedience costs too much? The Saviour who stayed for you when staying cost him everything is worth resting your weight on: close one this week.
verseByVerse.note: Anchors from the stern kept the bow pointing toward land, ready for beaching.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, 'Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.' Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship's boat and let it go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless these men stay. Here is a key sentence in the Bible on the relationship between God’s promises and human action, and it is spoken by a man in chains in the middle of the night. Set it against what Paul said nine verses earlier. There, on the authority of an angel: there will be no loss of life among you, an absolute, unconditional promise, no exceptions, no fine print. Here, on his own authority: unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved. Read flatly, those two statements contradict each other. Either everyone is certainly saved, or their salvation depends on whether some sailors stay aboard. Both are true, and here is why.

The decree includes the means. God does not merely decree ends; he decrees the means by which the ends arrive. A decree, in this sense, is God’s settled purpose: what he has determined will happen, which nothing can overturn (Isaiah 46:10; Ephesians 1:11). When he determined that every soul on that ship would live, he determined the whole chain that would bring it about, including a boat cut loose at midnight, the seamanship needed to beach a ship at dawn, and a prisoner noticing what the crew were doing and saying something. The sailors were needed to beach the ship. The promise did not float free above the events. It was fulfilled through them. So Paul’s absolute confidence in the promise and his urgent intervention to secure it are not in tension at all. They are the same faith. He believed the outcome was certain, which is exactly why he was not paralysed. A man who thinks everything depends on his own vigilance is too frightened to act well, and a man who thinks nothing depends on him does not act at all. Paul is neither.

Divine sovereignty and human means. Some say that if God has determined something, our actions do not matter. This commentary’s view: this verse refutes it. God had decreed the end (all saved) and the means (sailors staying, eating, swimming, planks). God’s sovereignty does not make human action pointless; it makes it meaningful. As with salvation: God has chosen his people, and calls them through preaching (Romans 10:14; 2 Timothy 2:10). The decree includes the means.

The definite plan and lawless hands. The clearest case of all is the cross. Peter told the crowd at Pentecost that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and that they had crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (2:23). Nothing was ever more certainly decreed than the death of Christ, and nothing was ever carried out through more human choices: a traitor’s bargain, a governor’s weakness, soldiers with nails. Jesus held both together himself on the night he was betrayed: the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed (Luke 22:22). God had fixed the end, the death of his Son for sinners, and he brought it about through real human choices for which real people were answerable. Decree and means meet in him.

If God has already decided, why bother? This is the answer to the oldest bad question about providence. Because the bothering is part of what God decided. The sailors staying aboard was not an alternative to the promise; it was the promise arriving. And it lands on ordinary life immediately. If God has promised to keep you, then read your Bible, go to church, confess your sin, and stay away from what will ruin you, not although he has promised, but because the keeping happens through exactly those things. Paul writes it out plainly elsewhere: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). The for in that sentence is the whole doctrine.

The soldiers cut away the ropes. The soldiers act instantly, and perhaps too enthusiastically: cutting the boat adrift removes it as an escape route and as a piece of equipment, so now everybody swims. But look who is giving orders. A chained prisoner speaks, and a centurion’s men reach for their swords at once. At Fair Havens nobody listened to Paul. Thirteen days of storm later, he is the only voice on the ship that carries. Authority in a crisis has a way of migrating to whoever turns out to know what is actually happening.

Does this mean salvation is conditional and can be lost? No. Saved here means rescued from the sea, as in v. 20 and v. 44. But there is a parallel: God had promised that all would be saved (v. 24), and the promise was kept through means, including the sailors staying aboard. In the same way, God keeps his people to the end, and the warnings and commands of Scripture are among the means he uses.

Should I still evangelise if God has chosen his people? Yes, all the more. God’s choice is the reason evangelism will not be in vain. Paul endured everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation (2 Timothy 2:10), and in Corinth the Lord told him to keep speaking because he had many people in that city (18:9–10). We do not know who the elect are; we are told to preach to everyone. God brings his chosen ones to faith through ordinary means: the gospel spoken, a book given, a friend’s invitation, a prayer. You may be the means he has decreed.

verseByVerse.quote: "As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, 'Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, For not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul urged them all to take some food. As day was about to dawn, the most spiritual man aboard spends the last hour before the wreck telling everyone to have breakfast. He has an angelic promise, an audience that is finally listening, and one hour left. He could preach. Instead he does triage, and the triage is physical: they will need strength for the swim.

In suspense and without food. In suspense means watching, waiting, keyed up: fourteen days of vigilance with no relief. And without food does not mean a total fast. On a pitching ship with no galley fire and stores fouled by seawater, nobody has eaten a proper meal in a fortnight. They are about to attempt perhaps the most demanding thing any of them will ever do, beach a disintegrating ship and swim through surf to an unknown shore, in a state of near-collapse.

It will give you strength. The word is sōtēria, literally salvation, safety, deliverance: eating is part of their rescue. The logic is the same as with the boat and the sailors, applied to a man’s body. The reason to eat is that God has promised nobody will die. Not despite the promise, but because of it: God has guaranteed the outcome, so get some bread inside you, because you will need the strength for the swim. There is a kind of piety that would have prayed instead of eating. Paul does both, and he is not confused about which one supplies calories.

Ordinary pastoral care. Fourteen days of terror have left a whole ship’s company exhausted and unfed, and the apostle’s response is to make them eat. When Elijah under the broom tree wanted to die, God’s first provision was a meal and a sleep, twice, before a single word of correction (1 Kings 19:5–8). A great deal of what looks like spiritual crisis is a body that has not eaten or slept, and Scripture is more willing to say so than we usually are.

Not a hair is to perish. The phrase is an old Hebrew proverb of complete safety: it is how the people swore that Jonathan would not be touched (1 Samuel 14:45), and how David reassured a widow about her son (2 Samuel 14:11). It is also almost exactly what the Lord Jesus promised his disciples about the persecutions coming on them, not a hair of your head will perish (Luke 21:18), said, remarkably, in the same breath as some of you they will put to death (Luke 21:16). So the promise guarantees not that nothing will touch you, but that nothing will be lost. Men may take your life, but they cannot take you from Christ, and the body they kill he will raise (Luke 12:4–7; John 6:40). Paul, an hour from the rocks, is handing on his Lord’s own words, and they are as safe as the One who spoke them, who keeps every one of his people for the resurrection, down to the last hair.

Is it unspiritual to care about food, sleep and medicine when I am struggling? No. God made us bodies as well as souls, and he cares for both. Jesus fed the hungry crowds, and told his tired disciples to come away and rest (Mark 6:31). Eating properly, sleeping, exercising, and seeing a doctor when you need one are ways of receiving God’s good gifts, not signs of weak faith. Low mood and spiritual dryness are often made worse by exhaustion and hunger. Look after your body, and then bring your soul to God as well. Paul did both, and so should we.

On a Tuesday. If someone you know is in crisis, take them a meal before you take them advice.

parallels.desc: not one hair of his head shall fall

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took bread. Four verbs: took, gave thanks, broke, began to eat. Luke has written most of that sequence before. He wrote it in an upper room: he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them (Luke 22:19). He wrote it at a table in Emmaus, where two disciples recognised the risen Christ in exactly that gesture (Luke 24:30). And he is writing it again now, on the deck of a doomed grain ship, in front of soldiers and sailors and prisoners.

Is this the Lord’s Supper? Almost certainly not, and it is worth being careful rather than romantic about it. There is no cup, no words of institution and no gathered church; this is a shipload of pagans, and the Lord’s Supper is not given to unbelievers. What Paul is doing is what any devout Jew did as head of a household before a meal: taking bread, blessing God for it and breaking it. But Luke chose those verbs, and Luke does not use that sequence carelessly. He wants his reader to hear the echo, and the echo says something true: the same Lord who broke bread with his disciples on the night he was betrayed is present with his servant on this ship, and the ordinary act of thanking God for food is the sign of it.

In the presence of all. He does not mutter it or wait until he is alone. In front of a shipful of frightened pagans, a chained prisoner audibly thanks the God of Israel for a piece of bread, an hour before the ship breaks apart. He has nothing, he has eaten little in two weeks and is about to swim for his life, and his posture toward God is gratitude, out loud. It is the habit of a man who gave thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

On the night he was betrayed. The deepest thing the echo carries is not a rite but a posture. When Jesus took bread and gave thanks in the upper room, he did it with the cross hours away, knowing exactly what the next day held (Luke 22:15–19). Paul, an hour from the wreck, does what his Lord did: he receives the ordinary gift of food with thanks while the danger is still in front of him. That is not a sacrament on a ship. It is a disciple who has learned from his Master that the Father can be thanked before the rescue arrives, because the Master’s own thanksgiving was answered by an empty tomb.

They all were encouraged. A shipful of people who had abandoned hope watch one man give thanks, and something changes in them. Luke’s word is the same one Paul used at v. 22: they became of good cheer. Not because the danger had lessened; the rocks were still there. Because one man’s confidence in God was visible, and courage is contagious in a way that argument is not.

Should I give thanks for meals in public, in a restaurant or at work? It is a good and natural habit, and it can be a quiet witness, as Paul’s was. There is no rule about how long or how loud it must be; a brief, sincere thanks is enough. Avoid display, which Jesus warned against (Matthew 6:5), but do not hide your gratitude out of embarrassment either. If you are with unbelievers, you might simply say, I am just going to thank God for this, and do it. Thanksgiving for daily bread is one of the simplest ways to show that you live before God.

For worship. How worthy of that confidence was the Lord he thanked. He had not calmed this sea. For fourteen days he had sent no light and no let-up, and he was as fully in command of every one of those days as on the evening he stood up in a fishing boat on Galilee and told a storm to be still. The One who gathers the wind in his fists is not less sovereign when he does not use them, and he is not absent when the sky is shut. He kept every soul on that vessel and brought them all out of the surf, exactly as he said. That is who is worth thanking for a crust of bread on a sinking ship.
verseByVerse.note: Paul gives thanks as the head of a Jewish household did before a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: "(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
276 persons. Luke drops the number in the middle of the action, like a man checking a ledger. He has recorded a promise, there will be no loss of life among you, and he is establishing the figure that promise has to be measured against. Everything now depends on how many walk out of the water, so he tells you exactly how many went in.

Some manuscripts read seventy-six. The ESV notes the variant. The number 276 is far better attested, and the shorter reading probably arose from a copyist’s confusion of Greek numerals. A large grain ship could easily carry that many; Josephus tells of sailing in one with six hundred aboard.

Every one counted. God did not promise to save a shipload. He promised not to lose a person, and Luke gives us the arithmetic because the arithmetic is the point. Two hundred and seventy-six individuals, soldiers, sailors, prisoners, the owner, a doctor, a Macedonian, an apostle, and every one of them is counted, and every one arrives. That is the arithmetic of the Good Shepherd. Jesus said it was the will of the Father who sent him that he should lose nothing of all that had been given him, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39). Luke’s 276 is a small picture, on one voyage, of the count Christ will make at the end of all things, and it will come out exactly.

Throwing out the wheat. They need the hull riding high so she will run as far up the beach as possible before grounding. So the wheat goes, and with it the entire purpose of the voyage (see v. 6). Every ounce of it is now at the bottom of a bay off Malta.

Failed and succeeded. The voyage failed completely, by every measure it was undertaken for. And it succeeded entirely, because the one cargo God cared about on that ship was a prisoner he had promised to get to Rome, and 275 people he had thrown in as a gift.

Does God care about me as an individual, or only about his people as a whole? Both, and the one does not swallow the other. God loves his church as a whole, the bride of Christ, and he also knows each of his people by name (John 10:3). Jesus told of a shepherd who left ninety-nine to find the one, and said there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:4–7). He counts the hairs of your head. Luke counted 276, and God counted each one. You are never lost in the crowd to him.

On a Tuesday. Look around your church this Sunday and notice someone you have never spoken to. God has counted them. Learn their name.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy-six. A large grain ship could carry several hundred people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not recognize the land. Daylight at last, after fourteen nights, and they still do not know where they are. Not one man aboard, crew included, recognises the coastline in front of them. It is Malta, at the place traditionally called St Paul’s Bay, off the main shipping route, and they will not learn its name until they are ashore (28:1).

A bay with a beach. Luke is cautious: if possible. Nobody is confident. They can see one feature that offers any hope at all, a bay with a beach rather than cliffs, and the plan is to drive the ship straight at it and hope.

They cast off the anchors. Three actions, and any sailor reading this will recognise every one. They cast off the anchors: not weighed but cut. Four anchors and their cables abandoned on the bottom, because hauling them up would take time they do not have and weight they cannot carry. This is a one-way manoeuvre. The instant those cables part, there is no stopping and no second attempt.

The rudders. Ancient ships were steered by two great oars, or rudders, one each side of the stern. They had been lashed up out of the way for a fortnight so the storm would not smash them. Now they are freed, because for the first time in two weeks the ship is going to be steered somewhere on purpose.

The foresail. A small headsail, enough to give steerage way and drive her forward. It is a good plan, executed correctly by professionals who have been awake for two weeks, and Luke records each step. Everything they can control, they control. Then it goes wrong, through something no seamanship on earth could have prevented.

All things were created through him. Every rope, timber and gust they worked with had been made through the Son: all things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17). And when the Son came into his own world, he came as a craftsman; the people of Nazareth knew him as the carpenter (Mark 6:3). The skill on that deck was a gift from the One the sailors did not know, exercised in a world he upholds. Common grace means God’s goodness to all people, believers or not: sun and rain, food, skill and sense (Matthew 5:45). It is never faceless. It is the kindness of Christ to people who have not yet heard his name.

Is it right to admire unbelievers’ skill? Yes. Every good skill comes from God, the giver of every good and perfect gift (James 1:17), and he gives them to believers and unbelievers alike by his common grace. Bezalel’s craftsmanship was the gift of God’s Spirit (Exodus 31:1–5); the pagan sailors’ seamanship here was his gift too. Thank God for the surgeon, the pilot, the engineer and the electrician, whether or not they know him. Honour their work, and pray that they will come to know the Giver.

For worship. The Lord is the Lord of the morning. For fourteen nights the sailors had prayed for day, and he gave it, on a coast they did not know, with a bay and a beach he had shaped there long before any ship was built. He goes ahead of his people into places they cannot recognise; the land is strange to them, and it is not strange to him. And the One who gave that crew their dawn will bring his people at last to the morning that has no night after it, where they will need no lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light.
verseByVerse.note: Ancient ships were steered by two large oars (rudders) at the stern.

verseByVerse.quote: "But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Striking a reef. Luke’s phrase is literally that they fell into a place between two seas, as the ESV notes: a shoal or spit with open water on both sides, the sort of hidden bar that produces a cross-current. A likely spot has been identified in St Paul’s Bay, between the mainland and a small island. The point is that it was invisible. From a ship’s deck at dawn, in surf, off an unrecognised coast, there was no way to see it. Nothing in the crew’s handling was wrong. They hit something they could not have known was there.

Not how we prefer disasters to work. The wreck is not caused by the bad decision at Fair Havens; that produced the storm, and they survived the storm. It is caused by an underwater ridge nobody could see, a short distance from safety, at the end of a manoeuvre performed correctly.

The bow stuck. The two halves of the sentence are the two halves of their situation. Forward, the ship is jammed solid in the bar. Aft, she is being demolished by the sea, plank by plank, with 276 people standing on her. This is the worst moment of the voyage. The storm was survivable because the hull held. Now the hull is coming apart underneath them, off an unknown shore, and there is no boat, because they cut it away in the dark.

Half the promise kept. At this moment the angel’s promise is exactly half fulfilled. There will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship (v. 22). The ship is being destroyed in front of them, precisely as God said. The destruction of the vessel is not the promise failing; it is the promise coming true, and the half they are watching is the half they were told to expect. That is very often the position of faith: the painful part of the promise arriving on schedule, and nothing yet to show for the good part but the character of the one who said it.

Remember how he told you. The disciples once stood exactly there. On the Friday the painful half of what Jesus had told them came true as he had said: he was delivered into the hands of sinful men and crucified. For two nights and a day they had nothing to show for the other half, that he would rise on the third day, except the word of the one who said it. Then the women found the stone rolled away and heard the angels say, Remember how he told you (Luke 24:6–7). Every believer standing on a breaking wreck stands where they stood on the Saturday, and the Saviour who kept the second half of his word for them will keep it for us.

Why do bad things happen when I have done everything right? Because we live in a fallen world where hidden reefs exist, and not every hardship is a punishment or the result of a mistake. Jesus said the man born blind was not suffering because of his sin or his parents’ (John 9:1–3), and that those killed when a tower fell were no worse than anyone else (Luke 13:4–5). God is sovereign over such things, and he has purposes in them, often hidden from us. Do not torment yourself searching for what you did wrong when Scripture gives you no reason to. Bring the pain to God, and hold on to what he has promised.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the reef is literally “a place between two seas” — perhaps a sandbar where currents met.

verseByVerse.quote: "The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers’ plan. A brutal verse, and it needs its context. Under Roman military discipline, a guard who let a prisoner escape could be made to suffer the penalty the prisoner would have suffered. Luke has shown us this twice: Herod executed the sentries when Peter got out (12:19), and the Philippian jailer drew his sword on himself rather than face what was coming (16:27). These soldiers are doing brutal arithmetic about their own necks, at the one moment when prisoners are about to be in open water in the confusion of a wreck. The prisoners have just survived fourteen days of storm on the promise of a God they do not know, and their reward at the water’s edge is nearly a drawn sword.

Wishing to save Paul. Julius intervenes, and Luke tells us exactly why: he wanted Paul alive. Not the prisoners: Paul. And because he wanted this one man to live, he vetoed the killing of every man in the group, so a shipload of anonymous convicts, whose names nobody recorded and whose crimes we will never know, walked out of the surf alive because of the man they happened to be travelling with. God’s promise was kept, through a centurion’s will.

The third time. That is the third time in this chapter that Paul’s presence has saved people who had no idea it was doing so. The angel gave him the lives of all 275 others (v. 24). His warning about the sailors kept the crew aboard (v. 31). And now his value to a Roman officer turns aside the swords.

The shape of the gospel. It is hard to read that pattern and not see the shape of the gospel in it, not because Luke says so, but because the shape is unmistakable once you have seen it elsewhere: people with nothing to commend them, under a sentence they had earned, spared entirely on account of the worth of another. And at the centre of everything stands One who did not merely happen to be standing nearby, but who deliberately took the place of the condemned and let the sentence fall on himself. The prisoners on that beach owed their lives to a man they had probably never spoken to. Every Christian owes rather more than that, to a Man who sought him out.

Those who could swim. Having saved their lives, the centurion organises the evacuation, swimmers first, so that the strongest are ashore and able to help the rest. Sensible, decent leadership from a pagan officer, and it is the last thing he does in the book.

Should I stay in a workplace or family where I am the only believer? Usually, yes, unless you are being drawn into sin or are in danger. Paul taught that each believer should remain in the situation in which God called him, as far as it is right to do so (1 Corinthians 7:17–24), and that a believing husband or wife can be a blessing to an unbelieving household (1 Corinthians 7:12–16). Your presence may be doing more good than you know: restraining evil, showing kindness, earning trust, and keeping the gospel within reach. If you are in danger, abused, or being pressured to deny Christ, seek help and safety; God does not ask you to stay in harm’s way.
verseByVerse.note: Guards who let prisoners escape could face their punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: "and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On planks or on pieces of the ship. Look at how the promise of God is kept. Not by a calmed sea, not by an angel carrying them ashore, not by anything anyone would call a miracle. Nearly three hundred starving, exhausted people go over the side into cold surf at dawn and thrash their way to a beach, and the ones who cannot swim cling to broken bits of the ship that has just been destroyed under them. The wreckage is the lifeboat. It is easy to wait for God to keep his promises in a manner we would find impressive. He is far more likely to keep them by way of a plank: something splintered off the thing that fell apart, floating within reach at the moment you go into the water.

All were brought safely to land. Luke’s last word on the voyage is the arithmetic, and it is perfect: two hundred and seventy-six went aboard, and two hundred and seventy-six came ashore. The ship is matchwood in the bay behind them and not one human being is missing. Paul’s own earlier assessment had feared the loss of lives; the word of God went further.

Brought safely. Luke chooses his verb with care at the very end. Brought safely, diasōthēnai: saved through, rescued completely. It is built on the ordinary Greek root for save, and he has been sounding that note through the whole chapter: all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned (v. 20); unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved (v. 31); and now, at last, all were saved through to land. A reader who knows what that word carries in the rest of Acts is meant to feel the resonance, and Luke does not press it.

Is the shipwreck a picture of salvation? Luke does not present it as an allegory, and we should not turn every plank into a symbol. The story is history, about real people rescued from a real sea. But some have rightly seen in it a picture of how God saves: the ship of this world breaks apart, but all whom the Father has given to Christ are brought safely home, some swimming, some clinging to planks, but all safe (John 6:39). The parallel is in the faithfulness of God. He promised, and he lost no one. That is exactly what Jesus says of those the Father has given him.

In the flow. The voyage ends on the word Luke has been saving for it: all were brought safely through. Every line of the chapter has moved toward this sentence, from Paul’s warning (v. 10) through the angel’s promise (vv. 22–26) to the count of 276 (v. 37), so that the reader can check the promise against the result. The next chapter opens with the same word (28:1), and on Malta the islanders will decide that the sea has let a guilty man go. Luke has already answered them. The God who kept every soul in the storm was keeping his word to bring his witness to Rome, and nothing in the book will be allowed to stop it.

For worship. He said not one of them would perish, and not one of them perished. That is simply what his word is like. It does not arrive tidily, or on the schedule anyone would have chosen, or in a form that would look well in a painting, but it arrives, in full, down to the last person on the roll, because the One who gave it does not deal in approximations and has never yet mislaid a single thing entrusted to him. Most of those dripping on that foreign shore had no idea whose word had carried them in. Glory to the God who keeps his promises to the last soul.

parallels.desc: three times I was shipwrecked

27.title: Storm, Shipwreck, and Sovereignty
27.text: <sup>1</sup>And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. <sup>2</sup>And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica. <sup>3</sup>The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. <sup>4</sup>And putting out to sea from there we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. <sup>5</sup>And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia. <sup>6</sup>There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. <sup>7</sup>We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. <sup>8</sup>Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea. <sup>9</sup>Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, <sup>10</sup>saying, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.” <sup>11</sup>But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. <sup>12</sup>And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there. <sup>13</sup>Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. <sup>14</sup>But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land. <sup>15</sup>And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. <sup>16</sup>Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. <sup>17</sup>After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along. <sup>18</sup>Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. <sup>19</sup>And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. <sup>20</sup>When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. <sup>21</sup>Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss. <sup>22</sup>Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. <sup>23</sup>For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, <sup>24</sup>and he said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ <sup>25</sup>So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. <sup>26</sup>But we must run aground on some island.” <sup>27</sup>When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. <sup>28</sup>So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms. <sup>29</sup>And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. <sup>30</sup>And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship, and had lowered the ship’s boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow, <sup>31</sup>Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” <sup>32</sup>Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go. <sup>33</sup>As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. <sup>34</sup>Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, for not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.” <sup>35</sup>And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. <sup>36</sup>Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves. <sup>37</sup>(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) <sup>38</sup>And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. <sup>39</sup>Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. <sup>40</sup>So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach. <sup>41</sup>But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf. <sup>42</sup>The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. <sup>43</sup>But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land, <sup>44</sup>and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land.
27.overview: Luke’s account of the voyage to Rome is one of the most detailed descriptions of ancient seafaring that survives. In 1848 James Smith, a Scottish yachtsman who sailed these waters, showed that its winds, depths, distances and manoeuvres fit the conditions closely: this is the log of an eyewitness. Paul, a prisoner, sails late in the season against his own warning, and a gale drives the ship for two weeks until all hope is gone. Then the prisoner takes charge, with an angel’s promise that the ship will be lost but not one life, and all 276 reach the shore of Malta. The chapter is a lesson in providence: God’s promise is certain, and he keeps it through ordinary means, sailors, anchors, food, a centurion’s decision, and planks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Malta and the Journey to Rome
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On Malta the islanders welcome the survivors with a fire (vv. 1–2). A viper fastens on Paul’s hand, and the islanders judge him first a murderer, then a god (vv. 3–6). Publius takes them in, and Paul heals his father and many others (vv. 7–10). After three months they sail on to Puteoli, where they find believers, and so to Rome, where brothers walk out along the Appian Way to meet Paul, and he thanks God and takes courage (vv. 11–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Through People Who Never Know

Everything Paul needs in this section is supplied, and hardly any of it comes from a believer: a fire lit by islanders who worship other gods, three days' hospitality from a Roman official, a winter's provisions, a ship dedicated to Castor and Pollux, a favourable wind. God furnishes the last stage of his apostle's journey almost entirely out of pagan hands, and none of them knows what it is doing. The Reformed conviction that God governs all things through secondary causes, the ordinary people and events of the world, is not an abstraction in Acts: it is a bonfire on a wet beach.

The viper episode adds the other half. The Maltese read Paul's circumstances and drew a confident conclusion about his standing with God, and they were wrong twice, in opposite directions, within one evening. You cannot read a person's standing before God off the surface of their life.

And the section's tenderest theology is in v. 15. Paul took courage, which means he needed to. God's provision for a discouraged apostle was not an angel this time but a handful of ordinary Christians who walked out along a road to be standing there when he passed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Believers in Rome heard that a prisoner they had never met was on the road. They walked, thirty-three miles to Three Taverns, forty-three to the Forum of Appius, and waited at the side of the Appian Way. They did not free him or improve his legal position by a single clause. They turned up, and the apostle to the Gentiles thanked God and found he could go on.

Now: The strong Christian you know may need this more than he will say; Paul had faced down a mob, survived a shipwreck and shaken off a snake, and still arrived on that road with his courage low. Showing up rarely feels worth the trip, and you may never learn whether it mattered. Luke thought it mattered enough to record in the sentence before Paul walks into Rome, and it is the love Christ has first shown you that you carry down the road.

verseByVerse.quote: "After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Acts 28 brings Paul to Rome at last. On Malta he survives a viper’s bite and heals the sick. In spring he sails for Italy, is met by believers on the road, and enters Rome as a prisoner. He explains the hope of Israel to the Jewish leaders from Moses and the Prophets, and when many reject it, quotes Isaiah and declares that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles. The book ends with Paul under house arrest for two years, teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance. The story of Acts ends there; the story of the word goes on, because the risen Christ is still building his church.

Malta. They did not know where they were until somebody told them. A whole ship’s company stands dripping on a beach at dawn, and the first piece of information anyone acquires is the name of the place. Malta is a small island about sixty miles south of Sicily, well off the route to Italy. They have been blown something like five hundred miles in a fortnight.

The native people. Luke’s word is barbaroi, which came into English as barbarians and has picked up a sneer it does not carry here. To a Greek speaker it simply meant people who did not speak Greek; the word imitates the sound of unintelligible speech, bar-bar. The Maltese spoke a Punic dialect descended from Phoenician. Luke is not insulting them, or calling them savage; he is telling you that nobody on that beach could understand the locals and the locals could not understand them.

Unusual kindness. The word is philanthrōpia, literally love of human beings, the root of our philanthropy. Luke marks it as unusual, more than anyone had a right to expect. Nearly three hundred strangers come out of the sea at dawn: soldiers, prisoners and sailors with nothing left, speaking a language nobody understands, on a small island at the start of winter. They are a burden of the first order, and every one of them will need feeding.

They kindled a fire. What the islanders do is build a fire for wet, exhausted survivors in late autumn. No sermon, no miracle: wet wood, rain coming on, and people who did not have to bother getting a blaze going for a crowd of foreigners who could not thank them in any language they knew.

The kindness of God our Saviour. Luke’s word for the islanders’ kindness appears only once more in the New Testament, and Paul is the one who uses it. When the goodness and loving kindness of God our Saviour appeared, he writes, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy (Titus 3:4–5). The Maltese lit a fire for strangers who had nothing to offer. That is a small, true picture of what God has done in Christ on an infinitely greater scale: he came to a world of wrecked people, strangers and enemies to him, and welcomed us when we had nothing to bring.

How God provisions the journey. Look at how God has been provisioning this journey: a centurion’s courtesy at Sidon, a crew’s seamanship in the gale, and now a bonfire on a beach, lit by people who had never heard the name of the God who sent them their guests. He does not seem to need religious instruments. He uses what is there, and the people he uses generally never find out.

Should Christians accept help from people who do not share their faith? Yes, gratefully. Paul accepted the islanders’ fire, Publius’s hospitality and the provisions they loaded on board. All good things come from God, and he often gives them to his people through unbelievers. Receive such kindness with thanks, honour the givers, and let your gratitude be a witness. And remember the obligation that runs the other way: Christians are to do good to everyone, not only to fellow believers (Galatians 6:10). The islanders’ kindness is a standard the church should never fall below.

On a Tuesday. God welcomed you in Christ when you had nothing to bring. Think of the newcomers in your street or church this month, a refugee family, an international student, a lonely new neighbour, and light a fire for one of them: an invitation, a meal, a lift. You do not need to share their language to share your kindness.

For worship. The God who brought every soul out of the sea had already prepared a fire for them on the shore. He is the Lord who goes before his people, who sets a table in the presence of their enemies and lights fires on strange beaches. And once, on another shore, after a long night on the water, the risen Christ himself stood by a charcoal fire with fish laid on it and bread, and said to his weary disciples, Come and have breakfast. How kind is the God who meets the shipwrecked with warmth.
verseByVerse.note: Malta lies south of Sicily. The islanders spoke a Phoenician dialect, not Greek — hence “native people.”

verseByVerse.quote: "When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, 'No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A bundle of sticks. Paul is the senior figure in this company by any spiritual measure: an apostle of Jesus Christ, the one person aboard whose word turned out to be worth anything. He is also an ageing man who has been beaten more times than he can count and has just struggled ashore from a wreck. And he is collecting firewood: not directing the collection, not resting by the blaze while others fetch it. This is the man who wrote that Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). He had learned it from someone.

A viper came out. Exactly what happens when you throw a bundle of sticks on a fire: something cold-blooded that was sleeping in it, sluggish from the cold, wakes up in the heat.

No snakes on Malta today? A word on an old objection, since a thoughtful reader may meet it. There are no venomous snakes on Malta today, and sceptics have made something of that. It is not much of an argument. Two thousand years of dense settlement on a small island, which was more wooded then, can easily wipe out snake populations, and the more telling detail is in the text itself: the islanders recognised the creature on sight and knew precisely what to expect from it. They were not guessing. They stood there waiting for a specific and familiar death. Luke himself does not call it a miracle; he reports what the islanders expected and that Paul came to no harm, and leaves the reader to weigh it.

No doubt this man is a murderer. Perhaps they saw his chains; certainly they have a theology, a good deal more common than its pagan dress suggests. Justice is Dikē, a Greek goddess, retribution personified, the power believed to pursue the guilty. Their reasoning is tight: this man survived a shipwreck, which looked like a reprieve; now a viper has him; so the reprieve was an illusion and the debt has been collected.

Half right. Half of that is right, and it is the half we are least comfortable with. There is a moral order. Guilt is real, and it is not finally evaded. What is wrong is the arithmetic: the assumption that you can read a person’s standing with God off the surface of his circumstances. It is the mistake Job’s friends made through most of the book of Job, and what the disciples assumed about the man born blind (John 9:2–3). It is alive in every sickroom where somebody wonders aloud what they did to deserve this. The islanders’ logic is coherent, and their conclusion is the opposite of the truth: the man with the snake on his hand is the one person on that beach whom God had promised to bring safely to Rome.

Justice had already been satisfied. The islanders were right that justice is not evaded, and wrong about where it had fallen. The man with the viper on his hand had once been a persecutor of the church, guilty of far more than they imagined (1 Timothy 1:13–15). But his sentence had already been carried out, on another man. Christ bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), and for Paul, as for everyone in Christ, Justice has nothing left to collect. That is what it means that Christ died in our place: the penalty has been paid once, and God does not demand it twice (Romans 8:33–34). The viper was not a debt collector. It was a cold creature in a bundle of sticks, under the hand of the God who had promised Paul Rome.

Does my suffering mean God is punishing me? Not necessarily, and for a Christian, never in the sense of paying for your sins. Christ has borne the punishment for all the sins of his people (Isaiah 53:5; Romans 8:1). God does discipline his children, out of love, to train them (Hebrews 12:5–11), and sometimes suffering is the natural consequence of a particular sin, which should be confessed and forsaken. But much suffering has no direct link to any sin of ours; it comes from living in a fallen world, and God uses it for our good and his glory (John 9:3; Romans 8:28). If you are unsure, ask God to show you anything you need to repent of, and then rest in his love.

On a Tuesday. Since your Lord stooped to wash feet, look for the firewood job this week: the small, unglamorous task in your home, church or workplace that nobody wants, and do it.
verseByVerse.note: “Justice” was a goddess who was believed to pursue the guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: "He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He shook off the creature. The understatement is Luke’s, not Paul’s. No drama, no speech, no gesture toward heaven. He shakes his hand over the flames and goes on with the evening. Paul must stand before Caesar (27:24), and no snake could stop that.

Authority to tread on serpents. Luke had recorded the promise behind this moment. Sending out the seventy-two, Jesus gave them authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and said nothing would hurt them; and at once he turned their eyes away from the wonder: do not rejoice in this, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:19–20). Paul behaves on the beach like a man who has taken that lesson to heart. He makes no sermon of the snake and no show of his safety. What mattered was not power over a viper but the Lord who gave it, and a name written in heaven that no viper could touch.

Waiting for him to swell up. Luke, who was a doctor, gives the two things the islanders were watching for, in words that medical writers also used: local swelling and inflammation, or sudden collapse. They knew the symptoms. Everyone on that beach is now staring at one man’s hand.

They said that he was a god. Within one evening, on exactly the same evidence, Paul goes from murderer to deity. Nothing about him has altered; he has not spoken or argued his case. The crowd ran their theology forward, found the result unacceptable, and reversed it, and their second verdict is as wrong as their first, and more dangerous.

Lystra in reverse. He had been through this before, at Lystra, but in the opposite order: there a healing brought out the priest of Zeus with oxen and garlands, and Paul tore his clothes and ran into the crowd shouting that he was a man like them (14:11–15), and soon afterwards the same crowd stoned him. Luke does not record a protest here, but there is no shrine on Malta and no cult of Paul in the record; only a sick man being visited and prayed for. He answered the compliment by behaving like a servant.

Judged by the crowd. It is easy to be governed by verdicts of this quality. The people who decide you are wonderful and the people who decide you are worthless are frequently the same people, working from the same evidence, a fortnight apart. A man who needs the first verdict will be destroyed by the second. Paul appears to have taken no notice of either.

Where Christians differ: snake-handling. Some groups handle venomous snakes in worship, citing this and Mark 16:18. This commentary’s view: Paul did not pick up the snake on purpose; it bit him by accident, and God protected him. Mark 16:9–20 is absent from the earliest manuscripts, and is not a command. Deliberately testing God this way is forbidden (Matthew 4:7). God protects his servants in their work; he does not ask us to court danger.

How should I respond to praise and to blame? With the same steadiness, because neither is the final verdict. Paul wrote that it was a very small thing to him to be judged by any human court; it is the Lord who judges him (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Receive praise graciously and pass the glory to God; receive criticism humbly, asking whether there is truth in it, and change if there is. But do not build your sense of worth on either. Your standing rests on God’s verdict in Christ, and that does not swing with the crowd.

For worship. The Lord is the shield of his servants. The serpent struck, and the hand that held it was the hand God was keeping for Rome. And far greater than the shaking off of a viper is the victory foretold in Eden, when the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head, though his own heel would be bruised. On the cross the old serpent struck the Son of God, and the Son of God crushed him. All glory to the Christ who has disarmed the powers and triumphed over them, and in whom his people need fear no serpent at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Publius. Luke’s title for him is prōtos, literally the first man, and it quietly vouches for him. Inscriptions found on Malta, in Greek and in Latin, show that first man of the island was the actual formal title of the leading official there. Luke used the local title correctly, long before anyone could have checked him from a reference book.

Three days. This is not a dinner party. Publius takes on the feeding and sheltering of the shipwreck company for three days, and even if it is only the officers and their charges rather than all 276, it is serious generosity at the beginning of winter.

Fever and dysentery. Here Luke the physician is precise. The Greek reads, literally, fevers and dysentery, a plural that medical writers of the period used for fever that comes in recurring bouts. Many have suggested this was Malta fever, a bacterial infection often carried in goat’s milk, so common on the island that nineteenth-century physicians named it after the place. That cannot be proved, but the description fits.

Visited him and prayed. Three verbs, and the order is the whole of it. He visited: the apostle goes to the sickroom. He prayed, before he touched him, because the power was God’s; Paul does not treat the gift as something he carries in his pocket. He laid his hands on him and healed him. Luke, who elsewhere is careful to say that it is the name of Jesus that heals (3:16; 4:10), writes it plainly and briefly.

As at Capernaum. In his Gospel, Jesus entered Simon’s house, where Simon’s mother-in-law was ill with a high fever; he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. Then, as the sun was setting, all who had any who were sick brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them (Luke 4:38–40).
