A house, a fever, hands laid on, then the whole district at the door: the pattern on Malta is the pattern of Capernaum. Luke is not saying Paul is a second Jesus; the islanders had just made that mistake. He is saying the risen Lord is still at work on Malta, through his servant, as he was in Galilee in person.

Does this mean healing ministries continue today? These healings confirmed Paul as an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12), as the gospel came to a new people. Yet Paul himself left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and advised Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). Believers still pray for the sick, as James teaches (James 5:14–15), and God heals as he wills; but no one today holds the apostle’s gift. This commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that such sign gifts marked out the apostles and their message and ceased with them. Many faithful Christians believe God still gives gifts of healing today; we gladly agree with them that God heals in answer to prayer, and that every claim must be tested by Scripture.

Healing as correction. Paul has just been declared a god by the people of the island, and the next thing he does is go and sit with one sick man and pray for him. The healing does not follow the acclaim as a demonstration. It follows the acclaim as a correction of it.

How should I pray for someone who is sick? Pray boldly and humbly together. Ask God plainly to heal, because he is able and he invites us to ask (James 5:14–16; Philippians 4:6). Ask also for what he has certainly promised: his presence, strength to endure, wisdom for the doctors, and the person’s spiritual good. Use medical help gratefully, as one of God’s means. Visit, as Paul did; sometimes the visit is the greatest comfort. And leave the outcome to God without guilt. If healing does not come, it is not because your faith was too small; God’s will is wiser than ours, and for his people the final healing is certain at the resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: “Chief man” (literally “first man”) was the title of the Roman official on Malta, found in inscriptions there. Luke, a doctor, names the illness precisely.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of the people. The word spreads, and Malta comes to the door. Luke’s verb, etherapeuonto, gives us therapy; it is the ordinary word for being treated and made well, and Luke uses it throughout his Gospel for what Jesus did. Its tense suggests a stream of people over the weeks, not one occasion. Some suggest that Luke the doctor also treated them medically.

No sermon in the text. Luke records no preaching on Malta: three months on the island, and not one sermon in the text. Two things should be said. First, Luke is plainly not telling us everything. He compresses three months into a few verses, and it is very hard to imagine that Paul spent a winter among people who had watched God heal their sick and said nothing about him; the silence is Luke’s, not Paul’s, and a church has existed on Malta from early times. Second, what Luke does record is a season in which the gospel travelled almost entirely by kindness received and returned: a fire lit by strangers, a house opened, a sick man prayed for, a queue of islanders healed, provisions loaded aboard at the end.

Mercy and the message. Now, mercy shown to a body is not a substitute for telling people about Christ, and it must never be offered as one; a man can be cured of dysentery and still be lost for ever. Paul knew that better than anyone and spent his life saying so. But mercy is not less than a sermon either, and it is very often the thing that gets a sermon listened to.

Tell John what you have seen. When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus pointed to what was happening around him: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news preached to them (Luke 7:22). The healings were never the whole message. They were the King’s signature on it, the signs Isaiah had promised of the kingdom’s arrival. The cures on Malta bore the same signature. Every islander who walked away well had been touched by the risen Christ through his servant, and the mercy pointed past itself to the Healer who will one day make all things new.

The Maltese test. Most Christians will not preach a sermon this year. Every Christian will have a winter’s worth of small chances of exactly the Maltese kind: the practical thing done for someone who cannot repay it, the visit made, the meal taken round. Paul gathered sticks and sat with a man with a fever, and there is no record that he thought either was beneath his calling.

How do I hold together good deeds and gospel words? Do both, and do not let either crowd out the other. Jesus healed and preached; the early church fed widows and proclaimed Christ. Good deeds show the love of God and give credibility to the message (Matthew 5:16; 1 Peter 2:12). Words explain whose love it is and how a person can be saved, because faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:17). In practice: serve people generously, and when the door opens, as it often will, gently tell them why you do it and about the Saviour who has done so much more for you.

verseByVerse.quote: "They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever we needed. The company arrived on Malta having thrown everything they owned into the sea, and they leave three months later with a fully provisioned ship. The honours may have included gifts, though Luke does not say; what he says is that the islanders supplied their needs. Every scrap of it came from people who worshipped other gods and had no notion that they were outfitting the apostle to the Gentiles for the last leg of his journey to Caesar.

After three months we set sail. Early in the spring, around February, when sailing resumed. They set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island: another Alexandrian grain freighter, the same class of vessel that was wrecked in the bay three months earlier. They get on board anyway, which is its own quiet comment on how the promise of God is meant to be held: not by avoiding the kind of thing that went wrong last time.

The twin gods. Luke names the figurehead, which he did not have to do. As the ESV notes, the twin gods are the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus in the old stories and patron deities of sailors, who prayed to them for safe passage. Ships were often known by their figureheads, so this vessel was, in effect, called the Heavenly Twins. So the apostle of the living God completes his journey to Rome under their painted faces, having been fed all winter by islanders who had thought he was a god himself. Luke notes it, perhaps with a smile.

The sons of Zeus and the Son of God. The irony runs deeper than the paint. Sailors believed Castor and Pollux came to rescue ships in storms. In the worst storm of all, on the voyage just ended, no twin god came. The One who kept that ship was the God and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, whose Son really did come down, not in sailors’ legend but in flesh, and who rescues not by a light at the masthead but by a cross and an empty tomb. Paul could sail under the painted twins without a flicker of anxiety because he knew the only Son of God, and the twins were wood: an idol has no real existence (1 Corinthians 8:4).

Should Christians avoid everything linked with other religions? Not everything. Paul taught that an idol is nothing, and that the earth is the Lord’s, so a Christian may eat food bought in the market, travel on a ship with a pagan figurehead, use the days of the week named after Norse gods, or live in a city full of temples (1 Corinthians 10:25–26). What we must never do is take part in the worship of other gods, or act in a way that leads a weaker believer to violate his conscience (1 Corinthians 8:9–13; 10:20–21). Ask: am I worshipping, or merely living in a world where others worship? Am I harming anyone’s faith? Then act with freedom and love.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the figurehead was the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, twin sons of Zeus and protectors of sailors.

verseByVerse.quote: "Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Syracuse. Syracuse was the chief city of Sicily.

Rhegium. Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy, at the Straits of Messina, and Luke’s phrase we made a circuit probably describes tacking, working the ship up the coast against an unhelpful wind.

A south wind sprang up. After everything, a following breeze. Rhegium to Puteoli is around two hundred miles, and they cover it in two days, a fast passage by any standard. The contrast with the previous voyage is total, and Luke does not point it out. Weeks of fighting a headwind, a fortnight driven blind through a gale, a wreck; and now, on the last stretch, the wind simply gets behind them and they fly.

Puteoli. Puteoli, on the Bay of Naples, was the main port for the Alexandrian grain ships, some 140 miles from Rome by road. Ships of this class were famous there; the philosopher Seneca describes the crowds of Puteoli turning out to watch the Alexandrian grain ships come over the horizon, because the whole city knew what they carried. So the voyage ends the way it should have ended months ago: an Alexandrian grain ship making a fast run into Puteoli with a south wind behind her. Whatever is in her hold, what she is actually delivering is one prisoner, and neither the master nor the centurion nor the port has any idea that this is the only cargo the voyage was ever really for.

He brought them to their desired haven. Psalm 107 sings of those who go down to the sea in ships: the Lord raises the storm, they reel and are at their wits’ end, they cry to him, he makes the storm be still, and he brings them to their desired haven (Psalm 107:23–30). On Galilee the disciples watched Jesus do what that psalm says only the LORD does (Luke 8:24–25). Paul’s voyage reads like that psalm told at length, and this verse is its last line: a south wind, a fast run, a harbour at last. The Lord who commands winds and water brought his servant into Puteoli, and he will bring all his people, after every storm, into the harbour he has prepared.

Should I be suspicious of easy times, after what happened with the south wind in chapter 27? No; be thankful, and humble. The lesson of the gentle south wind at Crete was not that good weather is dangerous, but that good weather is not proof that every decision was right. Here the south wind is simply God’s kindness after the storm, and Luke records it without suspicion. Receive easy seasons as gifts, enjoy them, give thanks for them, and keep walking carefully. God is as much in the fair wind as in the gale, and both serve his purpose.
verseByVerse.note: Syracuse was the chief city of Sicily; Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy; Puteoli, near Naples, was the main port for the grain ships.

verseByVerse.quote: "There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There we found brothers. Nobody sent them. There is no record in Acts of a mission to Puteoli, no apostle assigned to the Bay of Naples. Paul arrives in Italy, so far as we know for the first time, and discovers that Christians are already there. The gospel had been moving all along, underneath the narrative Luke has been telling: along the trade routes, in the luggage of merchants and sailors and slaves whose names nobody wrote down. Someone carried the message to this port, and Luke does not know who, and neither do we.

Seven days. They take the company in for a week, which means the centurion Julius must have agreed to it, one last courtesy from a man who has been quietly decent to Paul since Sidon, and a sign of his respect for him. A week would have included a Lord’s Day together, worshipping with brothers they had never met.

I will build my church. The brothers at Puteoli are the plainest evidence in the chapter of who has really been running the mission. The risen Christ, who told his disciples they would be his witnesses to the end of the earth (1:8), had been sending his word ahead along the shipping lanes through people whose names are lost, and when his apostle finally comes ashore in Italy, Christ’s church is waiting on the quay to take him in. Jesus said he would build his church (Matthew 16:18). At Puteoli he shows that he does not need his great apostle in order to do it, and still delights to use him.

And so we came to Rome. A few words, dropped in without ceremony, and the entire book has been travelling toward them. There is no flourish: just a plain sentence of arrival between a week’s hospitality at Puteoli and the final road, the Appian Way. That restraint is not coldness. The promise never needed decorating. God said Rome, and here is Rome, and the right way to record it is flatly, because that is what happens to the things God has said.

What stands behind the words. Paul’s great desire to see Rome (19:21; Romans 1:10–15). A promise made in the dark of a Jerusalem barracks by the Lord himself: you must testify also in Rome (23:11). A conspiracy of forty men sworn to prevent it. Two years in a cell at Caesarea under a governor angling for a bribe. Festus, an appeal to Caesar, Agrippa. A fortnight in a storm with the sun and stars blotted out. A shipwreck. A viper. A winter on Malta. And Luke’s whole account of the fulfilment is: and so we came to Rome. Not as Paul had planned, but as God had promised.

Who founded the church in Rome? Not Paul, who wrote to it before he had visited (Romans 1:13; 15:22–24), and nothing in Scripture says Peter did. It most likely began with Jews and converts from Rome who were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (2:10), and with believers who moved there. Here the Roman Christians come out to meet Paul.

Does a church need a famous founder to be real? No. The churches at Puteoli and Rome were real churches long before an apostle arrived, planted by ordinary believers whose names are lost. What makes a church is not a famous founder or an unbroken line of bishops, but the presence of Christ among believers gathered under his Word, with the preaching of the gospel and the ordinances he gave (Matthew 18:20; 28:19–20). The foundation of every true church is the teaching of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). An ordinary congregation of faithful believers is as truly the church as the church at Rome.

For worship. And so we came to Rome. Every word of God arrives like that: plainly, at last, exactly as he said. Not one of his good promises has ever failed. The Lord who said Rome brought his servant to Rome through plots and prisons, storms and serpents, and he will bring all his people to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God. One day the whole redeemed church will say it together, standing in the new Jerusalem: and so we came home. Faithful is he who calls you; he will surely do it.
verseByVerse.note: From Puteoli the journey to Rome continued by road, the Appian Way.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns. Roman Christians who have heard that Paul’s party is on the road walk out to meet him, like citizens going out to meet a dignitary. The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stops on the Appian Way, about forty-three and thirty-three miles from Rome: on foot, a long day or two out and as long again back. Ordinary believers with jobs and households took days to go and stand at the roadside on the chance of meeting a prisoner.

They had never met him. Paul had written to this church perhaps three years earlier: the letter we call Romans, perhaps the most closely argued document in the New Testament, sent to a congregation he had wanted to visit for years (Romans 1:11–13; 15:23–24). Its last chapter greets some twenty-six people by name, and some of them, in all likelihood, were standing on that road.

Paul thanked God and took courage. This is one of the tenderest sentences in Acts. Look first at what it admits: took courage means he needed some. Paul, who faced down a mob from the barracks steps and told a shipful of despairing men that not one of them would die, is, on the road into Rome, a man whose courage is running low. He is going to the capital as a prisoner to be tried before Nero; he is ageing, he has been at sea for months, he has lost everything he owned, and the outcome is a matter of life and death.

Not an angel, but brothers. What God sends him is not an angel. He had an angel earlier in the story, and it was exactly what was needed then. Here, on the Appian Way, the provision is a small crowd of Christians standing by the road because they wanted to see him. And Paul thanked God: he looks straight past the people to the One who sent them, and then his courage comes back.

Not ashamed to call them brothers. Paul had never met these people, and he greets them as family on sight, because they share one elder Brother. Hebrews says that the Son is not ashamed to call his people brothers, and that he was made like them in every respect so that he could help those who are being tested (Hebrews 2:11, 17–18). The Christ who sympathises with a weary servant does not always send an angel. He sends his body, which is what the New Testament calls the church (1 Corinthians 12:27). The men on the Appian Way were Christ’s own kindness walking down the road, and when Paul thanked God for them, he was thanking him for the love of Christ made visible.

The strong need it too. This cuts two ways. If Paul needed this, the strong Christians around you need it, and they will not tell you so. And the walk to the Forum of Appius accomplished nothing practical: those men did not free him or improve his legal position by a single clause. They simply showed up, and the apostle to the Gentiles thanked God and found he could go on. Few of us think turning up is worth the trip. Luke thought it was worth a verse.

Allowed to stay by himself. House arrest, chained to a soldier, probably in a rented apartment. A mild form of custody, perhaps on the strength of Festus’s letter and Julius’s report. Readers of the KJV or NKJV will find an extra clause here, that the centurion handed the prisoners over to the captain of the guard; it is in later manuscripts but not the earliest, so most modern Bibles leave it out.

Was Paul in prison? He was in military custody, chained to a single soldier, but allowed to live in his own rented quarters and to receive visitors freely (vv. 23, 30). He was a prisoner awaiting trial before Caesar, and the gospel still went out unhindered.

How can I encourage a mature Christian, such as my pastor? Simply, and specifically. Turn up: be there, at the hospital, the hard meeting, the anniversary of a loss. Tell them, in a sentence or a short note, one particular way God has used them in your life. Pray for them and let them know you do. Offer practical help without waiting to be asked. Do not assume they have plenty of encouragement; often the people who give the most receive the least. Paul’s courage was renewed by people who did nothing but walk out to meet him.
verseByVerse.note: The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stops on the Appian Way, roughly 40 and 30 miles from Rome. Paul was kept under house arrest, chained to a soldier.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days after arriving, Paul calls the Jewish leaders of Rome, tells them he is innocent and has no charge against his nation, and says he is bound for the hope of Israel (vv. 17–22). On an appointed day he expounds the kingdom of God and Jesus from the Law and the Prophets; some are persuaded and others disbelieve, and Paul closes with Isaiah 6 and the sending of salvation to the Gentiles (vv. 23–28). Acts ends with two years of open, unhindered preaching in his rented house (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Book Has No Ending

The abrupt close of Acts is a decision, not an accident. Luke had written the death of Stephen and the death of James; he could have written the death of Paul. Instead he stops with his hero alive, chained, and preaching, because his subject was announced in his first chapter and it was never Paul: you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). The word has travelled from Jerusalem to Rome and is being preached in the capital without restriction.

Two guards keep the final word, unhindered, from becoming triumphalism. First, unhindered does not mean unopposed; every hindrance in the book was real and several were lethal, and Paul himself would very probably die under Nero within a few years. Second, the man is still in chains as the book closes. Luke's claim is not that the church wins its comfort, but that the word of God cannot be stopped, which is a sturdier promise and the only one he offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The last thing Luke shows us is a prisoner in a rented room, chained by the wrist to a soldier, unable to leave the building or visit a single church he had planted. And out of that room, on the traditional reckoning, came Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon, while the changing guard carried the gospel through the imperial barracks until there were believers in Caesar's own household.

Now: The circumstance that looks like the end of a person's usefulness is often the beginning of the part that outlasts them: illness that stops a working life, a redundancy, years of caring for children or a parent that shrink the world to a few rooms. Each of those puts you in a room with a few people who cannot easily get away from you. Paul's chain did not end his ministry; it relocated it. He simply welcomed whoever came through the door, every day, for two years, kept by the same Lord who had kept him through the sea.

verseByVerse.quote: "After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, 'Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The local leaders of the Jews. He has just arrived in the capital after a journey of months that nearly killed him, he is chained to a soldier, and he waits only three days before convening a meeting. And look at whom he sends for first: not the Roman church, though some of them had walked thirty or forty miles to meet him, but the synagogue. Paul could not go to the synagogue, so he invited the synagogue to come to him. Jews had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion (18:2), and there were many synagogues in the city.

To the Jew first. This is the pattern of his whole ministry, held to the last scene of the book: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16), the principle he had written to these very people. In Pisidian Antioch, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus he went to the synagogue first and was driven out or forced to withdraw, city after city. It never altered the order in which he knocked on doors, because he loved them; he had written to this city that his heart’s desire and prayer to God for them was that they might be saved (Romans 10:1).

In the flow. With verse 17 the last scene of Acts begins, and Luke has shown it to us many times: Paul in a new city, the Jews first, the Scriptures opened, some persuaded and others refusing, and the gospel then carried to the Gentiles (13:44–48; 18:5–6; 19:8–10). Here it happens for the last time, in the capital. Verses 17–22 clear the ground: Paul is innocent, and he has come to accuse no one. Verses 23–28 give the message and the divided response. The pattern that began at Pentecost reaches Rome intact, and the book ends where its programme pointed (1:8).

Brothers. Every word of that opening is chosen with care, and the care is pastoral rather than legal. He calls them brothers, still. He speaks of our people and the customs of our fathers. Before he defends himself at all, he plants himself inside the family. Whatever these men have heard about the sect, the person in front of them is not an outsider making a case against them.

I was delivered. The summary, which is scrupulous. He does not say the Jews of Jerusalem tried to murder him, though some did. He does not mention the forty men and their oath. He uses a passive, I was delivered, and moves on.

They wished to set me at liberty. The book has recorded one official finding of no crime after another, from Gallio at Corinth to Agrippa (18:14–15; 23:29; 25:25; 26:31–32), and now Paul states the cumulative verdict to the Jewish leadership of Rome as simple fact, because by this point it is.

Desiring to release him. The parallel with Luke’s Gospel is close and deliberate. Jesus too was handed over by the leaders of his own nation into the hands of the Romans; Pilate examined him, said three times that he found no guilt in him, and, Luke records, desired to release him (Luke 23:4, 14–16, 20–22). Paul’s summary of his own case is almost a summary of his Lord’s. The difference is the ending. Pilate could have released Jesus and did not, because the innocent One had come to be numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37): counted among criminals, as Isaiah 53:12 foretold, so that he could bear their sin and die in the place of the guilty. Paul walks his Master’s road because his Master walked it first, all the way to the cross.

Should Christians share the gospel with Jewish people today? Yes, with love, respect and humility. The gospel is for the Jew first and also for the Greek (Romans 1:16), and Jesus is the only way to the Father for all people (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). Paul’s example shows how: as a brother, honouring the Scriptures and customs Jewish people cherish, showing that Jesus is the fulfilment of Israel’s own hope, and never with contempt. The history of Christian mistreatment of Jews means that many Jewish people hear the name of Jesus with pain, so earn trust, listen well, and let your life show the love of the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar — though I had no charge to bring against my nation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Compelled to appeal to Caesar. Two things are being said, and the second is the one that matters. First, the appeal was forced. Compelled is the word: he was left with no other route. Festus had proposed sending him back to Jerusalem for trial, which would very likely have been a death sentence, and the appeal was the only door left open.

No charge to bring against my nation. The second thing is a remarkably gracious sentence. An appeal to Caesar put a case before the emperor’s court, and it might have been open to Paul to raise counter-charges: attempted murder, false witness, conspiracy, malicious prosecution by the leadership of his own people. He had ample evidence and he had suffered enormously. He declines. He tells the Jewish leaders of Rome, on his first day of business with them, that he has come with no accusation against his nation.

What he declined to prosecute. A mob in the temple court that beat him. A high priest who ordered him struck on the mouth. Forty men under an oath to assassinate him. Two years of his life in a cell at Caesarea. A campaign of hostility spanning a quarter of a century and half the empire. And when he finally reaches the court with power to do something about all of it, he says: no charge.

He had written the reason. The man had written the reason to this city already. He had told them of his great sorrow and unceasing anguish of heart, so that he could wish that he himself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers, his kinsmen according to the flesh (Romans 9:1–3). That is not diplomacy. A man who could wish himself cut off for their sake is not going to sue them.

Entrusting himself to him who judges justly. Paul learned this from Christ. Peter describes the Lord at his trial: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Jesus had every charge to bring against those who arrested, mocked and crucified him, and at his trial he brought none. Like a lamb led to the slaughter he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7), and he left his case with his Father. Paul’s no charge before Caesar is a small echo of that silence. A man who has been forgiven an infinite debt can let a lesser one go.

The wronged who let it go. Paul had a genuine case, and nobody would have blamed him for pressing it. He let it go: not by pretending it had not happened or minimising it, but by declining to use the leverage he actually had, because the people who had wronged him were the people he most wanted saved. Paul was right, everyone knew it, and he came into Rome with nothing to file.

How do I forgive without pretending that nothing happened? Forgiveness is not saying the wrong was small or did not matter; Paul named exactly what had been done to him. It is releasing the debt: giving up the right to make the other person pay, and leaving judgment to God, who will judge justly (Romans 12:19). It does not always mean restoring full trust at once, especially where there has been abuse; trust is rebuilt over time, if repentance is real, and safety matters. But it does mean refusing revenge, praying for the person’s good, and, where you can, doing them good. Ask God for help; this is the work of grace, not willpower.

On a Tuesday. Is there a case you are still keeping ready to file, in your heart if not in court? Christ dropped every charge against you: name it before God today, and ask his Spirit for the grace to come into the room with nothing to file. When the grievance creeps back, as it will, your standing does not hang on how well you forgive; Christ forgave his enemies perfectly, in your place.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.' And they said to him, 'We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hope of Israel. He says it with the chain on his wrist and a soldier at the other end of it. The hope of Israel: he has used the idea at every stage of this long legal ordeal, to the council (23:6), to Felix (24:15), to Agrippa (26:6–8), and it has meant the same thing every time: the resurrection of the dead, and the coming of the Messiah in whom the promise to the fathers is kept. Paul’s whole defence has been that he is on trial not for abandoning Israel’s hope but for believing it has arrived. Christianity is the fulfilment of Israel’s hope, not its rejection. That means three things: the God Christians worship is the God of Abraham, the Bible Jesus preached from is Israel’s Bible, and the Messiah Christians trust is the one Israel’s prophets promised (Luke 24:44; Romans 15:8).

Because of it. He does not say despite the hope of Israel I am in chains, as though the two were in tension. He says because of it. The chain is not the price of a mistake or the interruption of his ministry. It is what holding Israel’s own hope has cost him.

A horn of salvation in the house of David. Luke’s two volumes begin and end with this hope. Before Jesus was born, the priest Zechariah blessed the God of Israel for visiting and redeeming his people, raising up a horn of salvation in the house of David, and remembering the oath he swore to Abraham (Luke 1:68–73). Now, some thirty years after the cross, its apostle sits in Rome with a soldier at his side and says this is the hope he is chained for: not an idea or a mood, but the promise to the fathers kept in Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen. To be chained for the hope of Israel is to be chained for him.

No letters from Judea. Their answer is a little surprising. Nothing has arrived from Jerusalem: no formal notification, no warning. Luke does not say why, and honest commentators do not pretend to know. The likeliest explanation is the sailing season: Paul left Caesarea in the autumn and the sea closed behind him, so no ship could have carried a dispatch ahead of him through the winter. It is also possible that the Jerusalem leadership, having twice failed to get a conviction and more than once failed to get him killed, had concluded the case was not worth pursuing to Rome.

None of the brothers. For the first time in years Paul is speaking to a Jewish audience that has not been prepared against him. Nobody here has been told what to think of him. It is a small mercy and a real one, the kind that never looks like providence at the time: a winter storm closing the shipping lanes, and a prisoner in Rome getting a fair hearing because of it.

Should a Christian be ashamed of suffering for the faith? No. Peter writes that if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name (1 Peter 4:16). There is a difference between suffering for doing wrong, which brings no credit, and suffering for Christ, which is an honour (Acts 5:41; 1 Peter 2:19–20). Paul wore his chain without embarrassment because it was the badge of the hope he held. If you are mocked, passed over or opposed because you follow Jesus, you are in the company of the apostles and of Christ himself.
verseByVerse.note: “The hope of Israel” is the promised Messiah and the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We desire to hear from you. An honest and rather appealing reply. They know nothing about Paul; they know something about the movement, and what they know is that it has a bad reputation in every city.

Everywhere it is spoken against. That was true. Luke’s own book is the evidence: uproar or persecution at Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Corinth, Ephesus and Jerusalem. These men are reporting the public reputation of the Way accurately, and it was what Simeon foretold over the infant Jesus: this child is appointed for a sign that is opposed (Luke 2:34). Within about four years Nero would blame the Christians for the great fire of Rome, and the Roman historian Tacitus would call the faith a deadly superstition.

A party within Judaism. The word they use is hairesis, a party or school of thought. It is the word from which we get heresy, but without that weight yet; it is the same word used of the Pharisees and Sadducees as parties within Judaism (5:17; 15:5). At this stage the Christians are, to a Roman synagogue, one more faction inside the Jewish world, and a disreputable one.

History in the room. Around AD 49 the emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome, and the Roman historian Suetonius, writing decades later, says the expulsion followed disturbances stirred up over one Chrestus, probably a garbled reference to disputes about Christ. Luke has told us the consequence in passing: Aquila and Priscilla turning up in Corinth because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome (18:2). Some of these leaders may remember being put out of their homes over this sect. Their caution is earned.

Only fairness. And yet they ask him to explain himself, and they set a date. That is more than Paul got in most cities: people with a bad impression and real grievances who nevertheless decide to hear the man out. It is not faith. It is only fairness. But Christianity has rarely asked for more than that as a starting point, and it does not often get it. And a bad name is not a refutation. What matters about any message is not how it is spoken of but whether it is true, and these men, to their credit, wanted to hear it for themselves.

On account of the Son of Man. The sect was spoken against because its Lord was spoken against first. Jesus told his disciples that a servant is not greater than his master, and that if they persecuted him they would persecute them too (John 15:20). And he pronounced a blessing on exactly this: blessed are you when people hate you and exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man; rejoice in that day and leap for joy, for your reward is great in heaven (Luke 6:22–23). The bad name that reached Rome ahead of Paul was a share in Christ’s own reproach, the scorn and shame the world heaped on him (Hebrews 13:13), and Christ’s reproach has always ended in glory.

Should we try to make Christianity more acceptable, so that it is not spoken against? We should remove every unnecessary offence: harshness, hypocrisy, foolishness, unkindness, a bad reputation that we have earned (1 Peter 2:12; 3:15–16). But we must never remove the offence of the gospel itself. A crucified Messiah was a stumbling block and folly from the start (1 Corinthians 1:23), and Jesus warned his followers that they would be hated for his name (Matthew 10:22). The aim is not to be spoken well of by everyone (Luke 6:26), but to be spoken against, if at all, only for Christ.

On a Tuesday. When you meet someone with a bad impression of Christianity, do what these men did for Paul: ask honestly what they have heard, and listen before you answer.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In greater numbers. They set a date, and when the day comes there are more of them than before. Word has gone round the synagogues of Rome, and the room is full.

From morning till evening. Sunrise to sunset, perhaps ten or twelve hours, of one man teaching the Scriptures to a room of people who had come to make up their minds about him. Luke stacks up three verbs for what Paul did, and each says something different. He expounded: exetitheto, to set out, to lay open, the patient work of taking a text apart and showing what is inside it. This is exposition, not oratory.

Testifying and trying to convince. Testifying: bearing witness, the courtroom word. He is not offering an opinion; he is reporting what he has seen. Trying to convince them: the verb means to persuade, and it is in a tense that means he kept at it. He is not content to state the case and leave the outcome to atmosphere. He argues, all day, because he wants these particular men to believe. And the two subjects are the two great themes of Acts together: the kingdom of God, and Jesus (v. 31; 1:3).

Kingdom-proclamation from first to last. The book ends with Paul testifying to the kingdom of God, and the last verse says the same (v. 31). Acts opens with the risen Jesus speaking about the kingdom of God (1:3) and closes with Paul preaching it in Rome: the whole mission of the church framed, start to finish, as kingdom-proclamation. The kingdom of God means God’s rule exercised through his King: Jesus reigning now at the Father’s right hand, bringing people under his gracious rule through the gospel, and one day returning to put every enemy under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:24–25). Readers differ graciously on what that means now: the Reformed reading holds that the kingdom has already come in the risen King and spreads wherever the gospel is believed, while many dispensational brothers (who see God’s plan unfolding in distinct eras, with a separate future for national Israel) reserve its fullness for that future. The point here is simply that the kingdom was Paul’s message to Jew and Roman alike, in this age, now.

The Law of Moses and the Prophets. As Jesus did on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27, 44), Paul argues from the whole Old Testament, because all of it points to Jesus. Does the Law of Moses and the Prophets leave out the Psalms, the wisdom books and the histories? No. It was the everyday twofold name for the entire Bible (Matthew 5:17; 22:40; Romans 3:21). The Jews also divided their Scriptures in three, the Law (Torah), the Prophets (Nevi’im) and the Writings (Ketuvim), together the Tanakh; and the Prophets included the great narrative books, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, so even on that reckoning much of the story falls under that word.

The whole Old Testament testifies to Jesus. The threefold shape was known in Paul’s day too: the prologue to Sirach (about 130 BC) speaks of the Law and the Prophets and the other books, and Luke gives the fuller form on Jesus’ own lips: “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44). In practice Paul ranged across all of it; his sermon in Acts 13 reasons from Psalms 2 and 16 as freely as from Isaiah and Habakkuk. What the reader should hold is Luke’s constant point: all of it testifies to Jesus. Paul spent a whole day doing just that: showing the kingdom and the King hidden in plain sight on every page Israel already revered.

Some were convinced. After all of that, the full day, the whole Old Testament, one of the finest minds in the early church working on an audience genuinely willing to listen, the outcome is split. That is the last word Acts has on how people respond to the gospel, and it declines to be tidy. Paul did everything right. The hearers came in good faith. Some believed and some did not, as Luke has reported since Pentecost, without embarrassment. And the explanation he gives in the next verses lies not in the preaching but in the heart: this people’s heart has grown dull (v. 27). Unbelief is often, at bottom, more than a shortage of evidence. The same day, the same Scriptures and the same preacher left one man persuaded and the man beside him unmoved, and Isaiah’s words locate the difference in the heart: what we do not want to be true, we find reasons not to see.

What if I share the gospel faithfully and people still reject it? Then you are in the company of Paul, of the prophets, and of Jesus himself. Your responsibility is to be faithful, clear and loving; the results belong to God, who alone gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Do not conclude that you did it wrong, or that the message needs changing. Keep praying for those who said no; some who reject the gospel today will receive it later. And remember that in this very room some were convinced. God always has his people, and his word does not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

On a Tuesday. Open the Scriptures and show people Jesus. Some will believe. Choose one Old Testament passage this week, Genesis 22, Psalm 22 or Isaiah 53, and read it slowly, asking where it points to Christ. Then share what you see with one person.

verseByVerse.quote: "And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: 'The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: "Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disagreeing among themselves. The day ends without resolution. Divided, they are still arguing as they go out of the door, and Paul lets them go with a single parting statement: a quotation.

The Holy Spirit was right. Look at how Paul introduces the quotation, because that clause is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament about what Scripture is. The Holy Spirit was right in saying: the speaker is God. Not Isaiah wrote, not it says in the prophets: the Holy Spirit said this. Through Isaiah the prophet: and yet it came through a man, in his own idiom, in the eighth century BC, out of his own vision in the temple. That is the doctrine of inspiration in the form Scripture usually gives it: God speaking, and a real human being genuinely writing. Peter puts it the same way: men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21).

To your fathers. There is a third thing in the clause, easily passed over. The Spirit said it to Isaiah’s generation eight hundred years earlier, and Paul applies it, without apology, to the men walking out of his lodging that evening. Your fathers: Paul identifies them with their unbelieving ancestors. Scripture is not a record of what God once said to other people. It is God’s address to whoever is in the room.

Hear but never understand. The quotation is Isaiah 6:9–10: the words given to Isaiah at his commissioning, when he saw the Lord high and lifted up in the temple. This is the hardening passage, the Old Testament text the New Testament quotes most often on the subject of unbelief. Jesus quoted it to explain why he taught in parables (Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10). John quoted it to explain why the miracles had not produced faith (John 12:40). The New Testament’s explanation of Israel’s unbelief is that it was foretold, and that it is God’s judgment on hardened hearts. Paul does not soften it, but he does not use it to vent his own anger either: it is God’s verdict, not Paul’s grudge. He states it and leaves. The text does the work.

He saw his glory. John adds one thing about this passage that changes how the whole scene reads. Right after quoting these words of Isaiah 6, he says that Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him (John 12:41), and the him is Jesus. The Lord high and lifted up, whose train filled the temple, was the Son. So the men walking out of Paul’s lodging were not turning away from a theory about the Messiah. They were turning from the King of Isaiah’s vision, whom the seraphim hailed as holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3), who had come in flesh, died and risen, and was being offered to them that very day. And remember what that holiness did to Isaiah. His first words were, Woe is me! For I am lost, for I am a man of unclean lips (Isaiah 6:5), until a burning coal from the altar touched his mouth and his guilt was taken away. The message of hardening came from that same holy throne. To walk away from Christ is not to decline a point of view; it is to turn one’s back on the Holy One who alone can take guilt away.

If God hardens hearts, is that unfair? No, though it is deeply sobering. God never hardens an innocent heart; he gives over to hardness those who have already closed their eyes to the light they have (Romans 1:21–24). Pharaoh repeatedly hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32), and God, as he had said he would, confirmed it in judgment (Exodus 4:21; 9:12). Hardening is judgment, and judgment is just. At the same time, no one who longs to see and hear and turn will ever be turned away; the desire itself is a sign of grace (John 6:37). If you are worried that you are hardened, the worry is good evidence that you are not. Come to Christ now.

On a Tuesday. Before you open your Bible this week, pray the psalmist’s prayer: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law. And treat each passage as God’s address to you, today, in the room where you are.

parallels.desc: keep on hearing, but do not understand

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grown dull. The word is epachynthē: grown fat, thickened, insensitive. And Isaiah built the verse deliberately. Going in, the sequence runs heart, ears, eyes: the heart dulls first, then the hearing goes, then the eyes shut. Coming out, in the healing clause, it runs the other way: see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn. The way out is the way in, run backwards. It is a description of how a person comes to faith, written in reverse as a description of how they avoid it.

Their eyes they have closed. They closed them: that is active. In the Greek Paul is quoting, the shutting of the eyes is something the people do to themselves, the deliberate refusal to look at something they suspect they will have to act on. And yet in Isaiah 6 the prophet is commissioned to produce this effect: make the heart of this people dull, lest they see with their eyes. God sends the message knowing, and in some sense intending, that it will harden. Hardening is both their choice and God’s judgment (Romans 1:24; 11:7–8).

Both sides held together. Scripture never flattens these into one. Paul wrestled with it for three chapters in the letter he had already sent to this city (Romans 9–11), and his conclusion was not a formula but worship: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). What he refuses to do, and what we must refuse, is to let either side cancel the other. The hardened are genuinely responsible, and God is genuinely sovereign over the outcome. A reader who has to flatten one to keep the other has stopped reading the Bible and started tidying it.

Never a weapon. What must not happen is that this verse becomes a weapon. Paul quotes it in sorrow, about his own people, having just spent a full day trying to persuade them.

And I would heal them. The last clause changes the colour of everything before it. The sentence does not end with judgment. It ends with a physician. The whole terrible mechanism of dulled hearts, stopped ears and shut eyes exists in the text to explain what is being kept out, and what is being kept out is healing. God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11).

With his wounds we are healed. The healing this sentence holds out has a name and a price. Jesus called himself a physician who had come not for the well but for the sick, to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:31–32). And the prophet who received this hardening commission went on to describe how the healing would be paid for: the Servant was pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). That is the medicine at the door in this verse. Shut eyes do not merely miss a doctrine. They miss a wounded Saviour offering healing through the wounds he bore for sinners.

How would I know if my own heart is growing dull? Watch for the signs Isaiah describes, in their order. Does God’s Word still move you, or do you hear it without being affected? Do you avoid passages or sermons that might require you to change? Has a known sin stopped troubling you? Do you find yourself more interested in arguing than in obeying? A dull heart rarely notices its own dullness, so ask a trusted friend too. The remedy is the healing clause run forward: look honestly, listen to God’s Word, ask him to give you understanding, and turn. He still says, I would heal them. And if the very question troubles you, take that as a good sign: a hardened heart does not worry about its hardness. Grief, depression and dry seasons are not the same thing as a dull heart, and the Spirit is at work in anyone who wants to see and hear.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sent to the Gentiles. Paul’s last recorded words to a Jewish audience in Acts, and they need careful handling, because they have been badly misused. This salvation of God: the same salvation, not a substitute or a second-best. It has been sent: a passive; God sent it, and this is not Paul’s decision or Paul’s reprisal. This is the third and final turning to the Gentiles in Acts (13:46; 18:6): in Asia, in Greece, and now in Rome. And the promise that they will listen is a plain, confident future, fulfilled through the centuries as Gentiles in their millions have listened and believed. Most Christians reading this are Gentiles who listened.

All flesh shall see the salvation of God. Luke chose an unusual word for salvation here, and he has used it only twice before, both at the very beginning of his Gospel. Old Simeon, holding the infant Jesus in the temple, said that his eyes had seen God’s salvation, a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:30–32). And John the Baptist’s ministry was introduced with Isaiah’s promise that all flesh shall see the salvation of God (Luke 3:6). So the last word Paul speaks to Israel in Acts closes a circle that Luke opened over a baby’s head. It is the child Simeon held, now crucified, risen and preached, and it is being carried to the nations exactly as Simeon said.

What it does not say. It does not say God has finished with Israel. It cannot, because the man speaking had already written, to this very city, the definitive answer to that question: “I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite” (Romans 11:1). Paul is himself the counter-example, and he says so. On any reading, a Jew is saved exactly as a Gentile is, by faith in Jesus the Messiah. He goes on in that letter to speak of a remnant now, a hardening that is partial and temporary, and a future in which mercy comes round to Israel again (Romans 11:5, 25–26). And note what happened in the room that very day: some were convinced (v. 24). Even in this final scene the response is divided, not uniform. Some Jews in Rome believed Paul that afternoon.

Where readers differ on Israel. This is also the point in Acts where readers in our own congregations will differ, and the difference should be handled with respect rather than scored. Many dear brothers and sisters hold that God’s promises to national Israel await a literal future fulfilment, and they hold it because they take the promises seriously and refuse to spiritualise them away, and that instinct deserves respect. Many Reformed teachers, too, expect a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, while others read all Israel (Romans 11:26) as the full number of God’s people, Jew and Gentile. The Reformed reading emphasises rather that all God’s promises find their Yes in Christ and that Jew and Gentile are made one new man in him (2 Corinthians 1:20; Ephesians 2:14–16), and that is the more likely reading, because the New Testament itself declares the promises fulfilled in Christ and his one people. What both readings hold, and this is far more than what separates them, is that God has not finished with the Jewish people, that his covenant faithfulness does not fail, and that Romans 11 forbids any Gentile Christian from the smallest trace of superiority: do not be arrogant toward the branches (Romans 11:18).

A note on the missing verse 29. Readers following in an older Bible will find a verse 29 here: that when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves. They will not find it in the ESV, which prints it only as a footnote, noting that some manuscripts add it. This is not something being removed from Scripture. It is the opposite: the earliest and best Greek manuscripts do not have the sentence, and it appears to have been added later by a copyist, most likely drawn from v. 25 to smooth the transition into v. 30. Modern translations set it in a footnote so the reader can see exactly what the evidence is. Nothing whatever hangs on it; the substance is already in v. 25, where they departed disagreeing among themselves. It is worth knowing that this openness is a strength rather than a weakness: the manuscript record of the New Testament is so rich that we can see precisely where a later hand has smoothed a seam, and say so out loud in a footnote.

Does this mean Gentile Christians have replaced the Jews? No, not in the sense of Gentiles taking Israel’s place while Jews are shut out. Paul’s picture is of one olive tree: unbelieving branches broken off, Gentile branches grafted in by faith, and natural branches able to be grafted back in if they do not continue in unbelief (Romans 11:17–24). There is one people of God, made up of believing Jews and believing Gentiles, saved the same way, by grace through faith in the same Messiah. Gentile believers stand only by faith, and must never boast. If anything, this verse should make every Gentile Christian humble and grateful, and eager to see Jewish people come to their Messiah.

On a Tuesday. If you are a Gentile believer, you are the fulfilment of this verse: you listened. Pray this week for Jewish friends, neighbours or people you know of, that God would graft them back into their own olive tree. And examine your heart for any trace of pride toward them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 29: “And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves.”

parallels.desc: your saving power among all nations

verseByVerse.quote: "He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two whole years. Two years, around AD 60 to 62. Luke gives no verdict, no trial, no execution, no release: just two years, and then he stops writing. Paul is under military custody, chained by the wrist to a rotating guard, in rented lodgings he is paying for himself, perhaps with gifts from the churches (Philippians 4:10–18). He cannot go out, so everyone comes in.

Welcomed all. Jews and Gentiles, the curious and the convinced, householders and slaves like Onesimus (Philemon 10), and, since the guard changed shift by shift, a steady procession of soldiers who had no choice but to stand there and listen. Paul mentions the result in a letter very likely written from this house: the gospel had become known throughout the whole imperial guard, and there were saints in Caesar’s household (Philippians 1:13; 4:22).

The prison letters. On the traditional view this is where Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon were written: in these two years, in this room, by a man chained to a soldier. The chain that stopped him travelling produced the letters that reached further than his travelling ever did.

The kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus Christ. Luke’s last sentence, and every word of it is chosen. The book opened with the risen Christ spending forty days speaking about the kingdom of God (1:3); it closes with his prisoner doing the same in Rome. And Luke gives Paul’s subject its fullest name. At Pentecost Peter ended the church’s first sermon by declaring that God had made this Jesus, whom they crucified, both Lord and Christ (2:36). The last sentence of the book has the same claim taught, openly, in the city of the emperor whom Festus called my lord (25:26). Caesar had the title. Jesus has the throne.

With all boldness and without hindrance. With all boldness: parrēsia, the frank, unguarded speech of a free man. It is the word the church prayed for when the authorities first told them to be quiet (4:29), and God gave it then and has not withdrawn it now. Without hindrance: akōlytōs. This is the very last word of the Greek text of Acts. Luke ends his two-volume history on an adverb, and the adverb is unhindered. Paul was in chains; the word of God was not (2 Timothy 2:9).

Why does it stop there? The question every reader asks is what happened to Paul. The honest answer is that Luke does not tell us, and the reasons offered are worth weighing. Some think he wrote before the case was decided, which would explain the abruptness. Others suggest a third volume may have been intended. But the strongest reason is simply that Luke has finished the story he set out to tell. His subject was never Paul’s biography; it was announced in the first chapter: you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). The gospel has reached the capital of the world and is being preached there without restriction. That is the end of the story.

What happened to Paul. As for the man: early tradition, outside Scripture and therefore held loosely, says he was released, travelled again, possibly to Spain as he had hoped (Romans 15:24), was re-arrested, and was beheaded at Rome under Nero, probably about AD 64–67; Scripture itself ends with him in prison expecting death (2 Timothy 4:6). The Pastoral Letters read as though they come from that later period, and 2 Timothy sounds very much like a man writing his last letter. But Luke will not end there, and that is a decision, not an accident. He had written the death of Stephen and the death of James. He ends instead on an adverb about the word of God, which runs on, unhindered, from Jerusalem to Rome and to the ends of the earth. The book is unfinished because the story is unfinished. We are in it.

What the word came through. Consider what that word has come through to earn the adverb. It was ordered silenced by the Sanhedrin, and it spread. Its first martyr was stoned outside the city, and it spread. Herod put James to the sword and Peter in prison, and the angel opened the door, and the word spread. It was flogged out of Philippi, shouted down in Thessalonica, laughed at in Athens, rioted against in Ephesus, and dragged through four courts. Forty men swore an oath to stop it and failed. The sea rose against it for fourteen days and put it on a beach, alive. A snake fastened on it, and it shook the snake into the fire. And here at the end, the emperor of the world has the preacher chained by the wrist in a rented room in his own capital, and the word of God walks in and out of that room, all day, every day, for two years, and no one on earth can lay a finger on it. Unhindered.

If the story of Acts continues, are there still apostles and apostolic miracles today? The mission continues; the apostolic office does not. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, sent by him personally, and they laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Corinthians 15:8). Their teaching, now written in the New Testament, is complete and sufficient. What continues is the work they began: the word preached, the gospel spreading, the Spirit giving new birth, Christ building his church through ordinary believers and faithful pastors. You are not an apostle, but you are part of the story they started, and the same Lord is with you to the end of the age. Christians differ on whether gifts such as healing and prophecy continue in other forms. This commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that the sign gifts which marked out the apostles ended with them; but all agree that God still answers prayer, and that no one today speaks with an apostle’s authority.

On a Tuesday. The story of Acts continues, and you are in it. Wherever your own limits are this year, illness, age, a small life, a hard place, ask how the word can go out through you without hindrance: to the people who come to your door, the letters you write, the friend you pray for, the child you teach. Proclaim the kingdom and speak of the Lord Jesus Christ, boldly, by the Spirit who gave the first believers their boldness (4:31). The word is not bound.

For worship. The last thing to say about the book of Acts is not about Luke, and not about Paul. Thirty years before that rented room, a handful of frightened people stood on a hillside outside Jerusalem watching a man go up out of their sight. They had nothing: no standing, no money, no protection, no plan anyone would have funded. What they had was his word that they would be his witnesses to the end of the earth, and the promise of his Spirit, and the memory of an empty tomb. And he did it. Not they; he. He poured out the Spirit at Pentecost, and three thousand came in. He struck down his own worst enemy on the Damascus road and made him the apostle to the nations. He stood beside his servant in a barracks cell in the dark and told him he would see Rome, and then he held a ship’s company together for fourteen days to keep the appointment. Every mile of it was his doing, and every soul brought in was his. The Lord Jesus Christ is building his church, exactly as he said he would, and the gates of hell have not prevailed and will not. He is doing it still, in places no apostle ever heard of, in languages Luke could not have pronounced, through people whose names will never be written down, and he will not stop until the last of them is home. The chain was on the apostle’s wrist. It was never anywhere near the word of God.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon during this imprisonment. Luke ends with the gospel preached “without hindrance” at the heart of the empire.

parallels.desc: the word of God is not bound

28.title: Rome at Last
28.text: <sup>1</sup>After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. <sup>2</sup>The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold. <sup>3</sup>When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. <sup>4</sup>When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.” <sup>5</sup>He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. <sup>6</sup>They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god. <sup>7</sup>Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. <sup>8</sup>It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him. <sup>9</sup>And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured. <sup>10</sup>They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. <sup>11</sup>After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead. <sup>12</sup>Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. <sup>13</sup>And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli. <sup>14</sup>There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome. <sup>15</sup>And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. <sup>16</sup>And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him. <sup>17</sup>After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. <sup>18</sup>When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case. <sup>19</sup>But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—though I had no charge to bring against my nation. <sup>20</sup>For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.” <sup>21</sup>And they said to him, “We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you. <sup>22</sup>But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.” <sup>23</sup>When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. <sup>24</sup>And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved. <sup>25</sup>And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: “The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: <sup>26</sup>‘Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. <sup>27</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>28</sup>Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.” <sup>30</sup>He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, <sup>31</sup>proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
28.overview: The book ends where Jesus’ commission pointed: the word has reached the capital of the world (1:8). On Malta the shipwrecked party is welcomed by the islanders, Paul survives a viper’s bite, and he heals the father of Publius and many others. In spring they sail for Italy and walk the Appian Way to Rome, where believers come out to meet them. Under house arrest, Paul explains the hope of Israel to the Jewish leaders of Rome from Moses and the Prophets; some are persuaded and others refuse, and Paul quotes Isaiah 6 and announces that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles. Luke closes with two years of preaching in a rented house, with all boldness and without hindrance. The prisoner is chained; the word is not (2 Timothy 2:9).
